# Portable code and fast first demos on TI LaunchPad development kits

Source code, build scripts and measured results for 21 development boards: 16 TI LaunchPad and EVM kits, and 5 boards from other makers on the same tests. Application code stays apart from board code, so a demo moves to another board by changing a board folder, and every number is a CSV row with its source.

Errors seen on more than one board: [TRAPS.md](TRAPS.md). 1 kB = 1,024 bytes.

## Quick start: a changed blink in about ten minutes

The worked example below uses the [LP-MSPM0L1306](https://www.ti.com/tool/LP-MSPM0L1306) and a Mac (tested on macOS 15.7, Intel) with 6 GB free, `make` and Python 3.9 or later (`xcode-select --install`). Install four free tools, about 0.9 GB; CCStudio is not needed, and the SDK download needs a free myTI account. The same command drives the other kits listed under **Other boards** below, each with its own tools:

| Tool | Version tested | Where |
|---|---|---|
| MSPM0 SDK | 2.11.00.07 | [ti.com/tool/MSPM0-SDK](https://www.ti.com/tool/MSPM0-SDK) |
| SysConfig | 1.26.3 | [ti.com/tool/SYSCONFIG](https://www.ti.com/tool/SYSCONFIG) |
| TI Arm Clang | 5.1.1.LTS | [ti.com/tool/ARM-CGT](https://www.ti.com/tool/ARM-CGT) |
| xPack OpenOCD | 0.12.0-7 | [GitHub releases](https://github.com/xpack-dev-tools/openocd-xpack/releases), unpacked to `~/xpack-openocd-0.12.0-7` |

**Your computer.** Python 3.9 or later on each; per-OS folders and serial ports are in [docs/install-routes.md](docs/install-routes.md#your-computer).

| | First command | Python | Once only |
|---|---|---|---|
| macOS | `./start.sh mspm0l1306 blink` | `xcode-select --install` | nothing |
| Linux | `./start.sh mspm0l1306 blink` | `sudo apt install python3 make git` | the udev rule below |
| Windows (PowerShell) | `py start.py mspm0l1306 blink` | python.org installer | UniFlash or CCStudio, for the probe driver |

Linux udev rule, so your user can open the probe: `sudo cp ~/xpack-openocd-0.12.0-7/openocd/contrib/60-openocd.rules /etc/udev/rules.d/ && sudo udevadm control --reload && sudo udevadm trigger`. Tested: the whole route on macOS; on Linux the dry run, checks and tests in a fresh Ubuntu 24.04; Windows only in CI, no board.

Coming from STM32 HAL, Arduino, Zephyr or ESPHome: [PORTING.md](PORTING.md) has the route. Otherwise fetch the top of the repository (a few MB) and run the board's blink job:

```bash
git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git
```

```bash
cd fox-red-labs
```

```bash
./start.sh mspm0l1306 blink
```

`start.sh` adds the folders it needs (about 25 MB), names any missing tool, backs up the board's flash, builds TI's blink example, flashes it and times the LED pin through the debugger. Success is a blinking LED and a line starting `OK:`. With two boards plugged in, add `--probe <serial>` (`python3 tools/frl/frl.py detect` lists them); `--dry-run` checks the arguments without touching the board. Then change the pattern (on, off, on, off, in ms):

```bash
./start.sh mspm0l1306 blink --pattern 100,100,100,100,100,700
```

The second job prints your own text over the USB cable: `./start.sh mspm0l1306 print-a-message --message "hello"`. If no `OK:` line appears, the last line carries a code (`FRL-E...`) explained in [docs/frl-errors.md](docs/frl-errors.md).

The commands below need more than the sparse clone has, and Python 3.12 or newer (`.python-version` names the tested 3.14; `python3 -m pip install -r requirements.txt`). Add it with `git sparse-checkout add tools data mac-setup`, or clone without `--sparse` (about 500 MB).

<!-- routes:other-boards (written by tools/start/route_summary.py; do not edit by hand) -->
**Other boards:** `./start.sh <board id> <job>` drives 13 kits. With a recorded hardware run: LP-AM13E230 (`am13e230`: `blink`); LP-CC1354P10-1 (`cc1354p10`: `blink`); LP-EM-CC2340R5 (`cc2340r5`: `blink`, `print-a-message`); LP-EM-CC2755P10 (`cc2755p10`: `blink`); LP-EM-CC35X1 (`cc35x1`: `print-a-message`); LAUNCHXL-F2800137 (`f2800137`: `blink`, `print-a-message`); LP-MSPM0C1104 (`mspm0c1104`: `blink`); LP-MSPM0G3507 (`mspm0g3507`: `blink`); LP-MSPM0G3519 (`mspm0g3519`: `blink`); LP-MSPM0G5187 (`mspm0g5187`: `blink`); LP-MSPM0L1306 (`mspm0l1306`: `blink`, `print-a-message`); LP-MSPM0L2228 (`mspm0l2228`: `blink`); LP-MSPM33C321A (`mspm33c321a`: `blink`, `print-a-message`).

13 other boards with a folder have a manual path: `bash mac-setup/bootstrap.sh --check` lists the missing tools and their disk space, then follow the ten-minute path in the board folder's `README.md`. Each board's tools, probe, check, backup and recovery, and what is not yet tested: [docs/setup-coverage.md](docs/setup-coverage.md). For a kit not in the folder map, `python3 tools/frl/frl.py identify "<name printed on the board>"` returns TI's page for it. Board cores, memory and prices are in `data/boards.csv`; `site/hardware.html` compares them.
<!-- /routes:other-boards -->

Other boards on Linux and Windows: expected, not run ([docs/portability-of-the-recipes.md](docs/portability-of-the-recipes.md)).

An AI coding assistant reads `AGENTS.md` here and in the board folder; [START.md](START.md) is a prompt that runs the same steps.

## How the code moves between boards

Shared code lives once at the top level; a board folder holds only what that board changes. A board folder never holds a file a second board would copy unchanged.

- **`third-party/<project>/`**: upstream projects copied unmodified and pinned (LVGL, CoreMark, ArduinoCore-API and others), each with a `SOURCE.md` naming the commit, license and checksums. A change is a patch file beside the code, never an edit.
- **`portability/<layer>/`**: this repository's board-independent layers. `core/` is the same for every chip; `boards/<board>/` holds the pin map, SysConfig file and generated files. `BOARD=mspm0g3507 ./build.sh` in `portability/arduino/` builds unmodified Arduino libraries and sketches for that board.
- **`ports/<project>/`**: code from another ecosystem running on TI boards. `common/` is vendor-free with a host test; one folder per TI family holds the glue.
- **`<board>/`**: the board's SysConfig, linker and startup files, build script, README, `AGENTS.md` and `FAQ.md`.

Keep the application in a file with no device header. Put the board in a thin glue file (`board_init`, `uart_write`, `led_toggle`, `sleep_ms`). [PORTING.md](PORTING.md) has the route from another TI chip, STM32 HAL, Zephyr, ESPHome and Arduino.

## Run a demo on your board

Each build is one file in `docs/builds/` (start with [docs/builds/blink.md](docs/builds/blink.md); the list is [docs/builds/README.md](docs/builds/README.md)): parts, pin table and steps, one section per board, each opening with the `git sparse-checkout add` line its steps need. A board is marked tested with this setup, expected to work, needs adaptation or not assessed. The web pages are `site/projects.html`; which build ran where is `site/portability.html#builds`.

## Measured numbers, and how to read them

Every measured number is a row in `data/results/<board>.csv`: test, conditions, run count, date, the `source` file and how it was `checked`. A test that could not run is a row too, with a status (`not_run`, `does_not_fit`, `not_supported`, `waiting`, `failed`) and the reason. Timings are medians of three runs. Columns: [data/README.md](data/README.md). The suite of 385 tests: `data/benchmark-suite.json`.

```bash
python3 tools/results/check.py
```

The check validates every row. [docs/comparisons.md](docs/comparisons.md) puts the boards side by side, and `site/benchmarks.html` shows them.

## A TI board that is not listed

The guided tools refuse a board they have no notes for (`frl identify` returns `FRL-E010`), so nothing is flashed by guesswork. The manual path:

1. Find the closest listed board in `data/boards.csv`: same `line`, then same `core`. Its folder's `AGENTS.md` and `FAQ.md` are the best starting notes.
2. Read [TRAPS.md](TRAPS.md), then back up the new board's flash before the first write.
3. Build and flash TI's own blink example for the new part, unchanged, from its SDK. A port only counts once that works ([PORTING.md](PORTING.md) rule 1).
4. Move code with the matching route in [PORTING.md](PORTING.md). Most code needs only the board layer under `portability/<layer>/boards/` or the board's `.syscfg` to change.
5. Record what ran as rows in `data/results/<board>.csv`, including the tests that could not run, and give the board its folder as in the next section.

## Add a board or a demo

**A board:** a folder named by its id in `data/boards.csv`, with a `README.md` shaped like an existing board's (outcome first, then the ten-minute path, the build, the results and the problems), an `AGENTS.md` where every line cites a run, a `FAQ.md` with exact error text, and rows in `data/results/<id>.csv`. A file a second board would copy unchanged goes in `portability/` or `third-party/`.

**A demo or port:** upstream code into `third-party/<project>/` with its `SOURCE.md`, your code into `ports/<project>/`, numbers as result rows, and an entry in `site/data/ports.json` or `site/data/projects.json`. The maintainers regenerate the pages from those files. Reports from your own board go through the issue forms in [docs/how-to-contribute.md](docs/how-to-contribute.md).

## Traps

Read [TRAPS.md](TRAPS.md) before the first flash. Its six rules keep a board recoverable: name the probe by serial number, never write the boot configuration area (NONMAIN, CCFG, SCFG), back up flash first, never mass-erase, recheck pins after changing the device in SysConfig, and read RAM use from the linker map. When a command fails, search its exact error text in the board's `FAQ.md`, then the table in [TRAPS.md](TRAPS.md#if-you-see-this); `FRL-E...` codes are in [docs/frl-errors.md](docs/frl-errors.md). The backup:

```bash
python3 tools/frl/frl.py backup --board <board> --probe <serial>
```

# Start with your code: what ran on a TI development kit

Coming from STM32, Arduino, ESPHome, MicroPython, Zephyr or another vendor's SDK? Pick yours below.

57 ports run on 16 TI kits and 2 other boards. Plus 66 chip-to-chip tests inside TI's families (53 run on the board): [portability/matrix.csv](../portability/matrix.csv). Site page: [site/ports.html](../site/ports.html).

17 of these ports change another project's code: 0 merged there, 0 with a pull request open, 17 in this repository only. 13 more came from code that takes no outside changes.

Terms: [vocab](vocab.md). 1 kB = 1,024 bytes.

Contents: [An ESPHome, Arduino, MicroPython or Zephyr project](#an-esphome-arduino-micropython-or-zephyr-project) · [Code written for another chip or tool](#code-written-for-another-chip-or-tool) · [One TI chip to another](#one-ti-chip-to-another) · [How a port is made](#how-a-port-is-made) · [Questions people ask](#questions-people-ask) · [Hand the folder and its AGENTS.md to your coding assistant](#hand-the-folder-and-its-agentsmd-to-your-coding-assistant)

## An ESPHome, Arduino, MicroPython or Zephyr project

Copy a card's files, run its command and compare with what you see.

### ESPHome

**ESPHome Zigbee device on the LP-EM-CC2755P10** · Works · LP-EM-CC2755P10

You get: An ESPHome YAML with cc27xx: builds and flashes a Zigbee device that joins Home Assistant on the LP-EM-CC2755P10.

Copy these files: [ports/esphome-ti](../ports/esphome-ti)

Run this command:

```bash
cd ports/esphome-ti
python3.12 -m venv venv && ./venv/bin/pip install "cbor2<6" esphome==2026.9.1
./venv/bin/esphome compile frl-cc27xx.yaml
./venv/bin/esphome upload frl-cc27xx.yaml
```

You see: The device appears in ZHA, Home Assistant's built-in Zigbee support, with an LED switch and a chip temperature sensor.

Upstream: in this repository only; not sent to ESPHome

Measured: A repeat compile takes 27 s and the image is 262.7 kB of flash with 124.4 kB of RAM free. The LED switches at a median of 85 to 92.5 ms.

Limits: Zigbee only, no Wi-Fi. After a second flash, remove the old device from Home Assistant first, or it does not rejoin.

[See the run](../site/project-esphome.html#e192)

**ESPHome Zigbee device on the LP-EM-CC2340R5** · Works · LP-EM-CC2340R5

You get: The same YAML with cc23xx: runs a Zigbee end device on the LP-EM-CC2340R5.

Copy these files: [ports/esphome-ti](../ports/esphome-ti)

Run this command:

```bash
cd ports/esphome-ti
python3.12 -m venv venv && ./venv/bin/pip install "cbor2<6" esphome==2026.9.1
./venv/bin/esphome compile frl-cc23xx.yaml
./venv/bin/esphome upload frl-cc23xx.yaml
```

You see: The end device joins Home Assistant's Zigbee integration (ZHA) with an LED switch and a chip temperature sensor.

Upstream: in this repository only; not sent to ESPHome

Measured: The image is 219.9 kB of flash, with 4.0 kB of the chip's 36 kB of RAM free. Over five runs 93 of 100 commands passed.

Limits: Zigbee only, no Wi-Fi. As a router it needs the heap cut by 2 kB, and the chip temperature reads about 10 C low.

[See the run](../site/project-esphome.html#e191)

**ESPHome Wi-Fi device on the LP-EM-CC35X1** · Works · LP-EM-CC35X1

You get: A Wi-Fi ESPHome device runs on the LP-EM-CC35X1 with ESPHome's native API: a client on the board got 20 of 20 switch commands confirmed.

Copy these files: [ports/esphome-ti](../ports/esphome-ti)

Run this command:

```bash
cd ports/esphome-ti
python3.12 -m venv venv && ./venv/bin/pip install "cbor2<6" esphome==2026.9.1
read -p "Wi-Fi name: " SSID && read -s -p "Wi-Fi password: " WIFIPW
printf 'wifi_ssid: "%s"\nwifi_password: "%s"\n' "$SSID" "$WIFIPW" > secrets.yaml
./venv/bin/esphome compile frl-cc35xx.yaml
./venv/bin/esphome upload frl-cc35xx.yaml
```

You see: The board joins Wi-Fi after a reset and logs "[I][wifi]: Connected" on its serial port at 115200 baud.

Upstream: in this repository only; not sent to ESPHome

Measured: A repeat compile takes 23 s. A 24-hour soak confirmed 5,616 of 5,620 commands and rode out 22 access-point drops.

Limits: Home Assistant has not adopted the board.

[See the run](../site/project-esphome.html#e193)

### Arduino

**Arduino sketches on the LP-EM-CC2340R5 and LP-MSPM0G3519 through the Zephyr-based core: Blink and AnalogReadSerial** · Works · LP-EM-CC2340R5, LP-MSPM0G3519

You get: Arduino's stock Blink and AnalogReadSerial run unchanged on the LP-EM-CC2340R5 and LP-MSPM0G3519 through the Zephyr-based core.

Copy these files: [portability/arduino/zephyr/README.md#take-it-with-you](../portability/arduino/zephyr/README.md#take-it-with-you)

Run this command:

```bash
export AM=$HOME/zr-arduino ZP=$HOME/zephyrproject TC=$HOME/zephyr-toolchain
git init "$AM" && git -C "$AM" remote add origin https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/ArduinoCore-zephyr.git
git -C "$AM" fetch --depth 1 origin af5b8610f9be6d7b962e2ba6dd8e6859697c44ff && git -C "$AM" checkout FETCH_HEAD
mkdir -p "$AM/zephyr/blobs" && cp -R third-party/arduino/ArduinoCore-API/api "$AM/zephyr/blobs/ArduinoCore-API"
git -C "$AM" apply "$PWD/portability/arduino/zephyr/serial-blocking-write.patch"
portability/arduino/zephyr/build-cc2340r5.sh Blink
```

You see: Blink toggles the board's LED pin; AnalogReadSerial prints 10-bit readings at 9600 baud on the probe's serial port.

Upstream: in this repository only; not sent to ArduinoCore-zephyr

Measured: Images are 22.8 to 38.3 kB of flash and 4.8 to 6.1 kB of RAM. On the LP-MSPM0G3519, Wire reads the touch controller 100 of 100 times and SPI loopback returns 256 of 256 bytes.

[See the run](../site/project-arduino.html)

### MicroPython

**MicroPython 1.29.0 on the LP-EM-CC2340R5 through upstream's Zephyr port** · Works · LP-EM-CC2340R5

You get: MicroPython's own Zephyr port runs on the 36 kB LP-EM-CC2340R5: a >>> prompt, with Pin, ADC, PWM, SPI and I2C from Python.

Copy these files: [ports/micropython/zephyr-cc2340r5/README.md#take-it-with-you](../ports/micropython/zephyr-cc2340r5/README.md#take-it-with-you)

Run this command:

```bash
export MP=$HOME/micropython ZP=$HOME/zephyrproject TC=$HOME/zephyr-toolchain OUT=$PWD/out/build-mp-cc2340r5
git clone --depth 1 --branch v1.29.0 https://github.com/micropython/micropython.git "$MP"
ports/micropython/zephyr-cc2340r5/build.sh
```

You see: The probe's serial port at 115200 baud shows the banner "MicroPython v1.29.0 ... zephyr-lp_em_cc2340r5 with cc2340r5" and a >>> prompt; print(1+1) prints 2.

Upstream: in this repository only; not sent to MicroPython and Zephyr

Measured: The image is 174.8 kB of flash and 29.9 kB of RAM with a 20 kB heap; the stock settings overflow the RAM by 46.8 kB. Pin.irq saw 10 of 10 edges.

Limits: PWM duty_u16 needs a one-line patch, which is in the folder. SPI data is unchecked without a loopback wire, and no I2C device was on the bus.

[See the run](../site/project-micropython.html)

Measured: The image is 292.3 kB of flash and 83.6 kB of RAM with a 48 kB heap.

[See the run](../site/project-micropython.html)

### Zephyr

**Zephyr on the AM62L's Cortex-A53: from on-chip SRAM, and on one core beside Linux** · Works · TMDS62LEVM (AM62L)

```bash

cd "$HOME/cube"
git sparse-checkout set --no-cone '/.gitmodules' '/Projects/NUCLEO-G071RB/Examples/GPIO/GPIO_IOToggle/' '/Projects/NUCLEO-G071RB/Examples/GPIO/GPIO_EXTI/' '/Projects/NUCLEO-G071RB/Examples_LL/USART/USART_Communication_Tx_VCP_Init/' '/Projects/NUCLEO-G071RB/Examples/ADC/ADC_MultiChannelSingleConversion/' '/Projects/NUCLEO-G071RB/Examples/TIM/TIM_PWMOutput/'
git checkout 446ebe396489ca75679caa80887d7257efe92e3d
git submodule update --init --depth 1 Drivers/BSP/STM32G0xx_Nucleo
WS=$HOME/ccs-workspace
mkdir -p "$WS/.claude/skills"
cp -R "/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/Code Composer Studio.app/Contents/Resources/ai/skills.alpha/ti-ccstudio-migrate-to-ti" "$WS/.claude/skills/"

```

You see: The skill ships in CCStudio 21.0.1's skills.alpha folder, for evaluation. Open CCStudio on that workspace, run /ti-ccstudio-migrate-to-ti ~/cube/Projects/NUCLEO-G071RB/Examples/GPIO/GPIO_IOToggle MSPM0G3507. The first example blinks LED1 on the LP-MSPM0G3507.

Measured: GPIO toggle, serial port and PWM channel 4 ran as written. The button interrupt needed one fix and the ADC with DMA three: the button polarity, the DMA source address and the DMA sample count.

## How a port is made

Every port followed the same five steps.

1. Find the calls. Build the other project for the TI chip as it is. List every missing function, header and type the compiler names. That list is the whole job.
2. Write a thin layer, not a fork. Answer those calls in one shim file on the TI side (388 lines for ESPHome's Zigbee code, 30 lines for MSPM0 apps on the CC2340R5, 13 lines for MSPM0 on the AM13E230). Leave the other project's files as they shipped, so its updates still apply.
3. Build with the vendor's own tools. Use TI's compiler, SDK and SysConfig, from one command or the other project's own command (esphome compile). For a plain-C library with no peripheral, start from ports/minmea/build.sh: the SDK's startup file and linker file, no SysConfig. Record flash and RAM from the map file.
4. Run it and check one thing a person would notice. The LED switched from Home Assistant, the digit read right, the packet received. For a library with no LED or serial output, read its result variables with a debugger or add a UART print. Built is not ran, and ran is not checked. Each card says which one happened.
5. Write down where it stopped. Failures stay on the page with the exact error and the cause, whether a tool or the chip.

## Questions people ask

### Is there an Arduino IDE board package for MSPM0?

No. There is a layer for your own build, and Arduino sketches run through Zephyr on the LP-EM-CC2340R5 and the LP-MSPM0G3519. You cannot pick a TI board in the Arduino IDE.

### Which kit should I buy first?

The LP-MSPM0G3519 runs the most cards on this page: 16 of 57. Next come the LP-MSPM33C321A with 15 and the LP-MSPM0G3507 with 11. For ESPHome, take an LP-EM-CC35X1 for Wi-Fi, or an LP-EM-CC2340R5 or LP-EM-CC2755P10 for Zigbee only. The Board menu above lists the cards for any kit.

### Which kit runs ESPHome on Wi-Fi?

The LP-EM-CC35X1, with the cc35xx platform. The LP-EM-CC2340R5 and LP-EM-CC2755P10 cards are Zigbee only.

### How many of the Cmsemicon examples show output?

21 of the 34 have a result checked on a pin or serial line: serial text, a toggling pin or a CRC match. The other 13 ran without crashing and show nothing a probe can see.

### Do all the Renesas FSP examples run on the LP-MSPM0G3519?

Four of five. The timer-triggered ADC example runs up to its DMA chain, and its two-group DMA transfer does not complete. The unchanged I2C example reports a missing ADXL345 and prints 65535 for every axis, so it needs five constants changed for the touch controller.

### Does MicroPython I2C work on the LP-MSPM33C321A?

I2C opens and writes, and every read hangs until a hardware reset. Pin, float math and SPI work, and Zephyr has no ADC or PWM driver for this chip.

### Can I move an STM32 HAL project to MSPM0?

Yes, with TI's migration skill. On the LP-MSPM0G3507 it moved STM32CubeG0 examples for GPIO, UART, ADC with DMA and PWM: 3 of 5 ran as written and 2 after corrections. I2C, SPI and timers were not run.

### Can ESPHome run on a TI chip?

Yes, through the external platforms in ports/esphome-ti. cc27xx for the LP-EM-CC2755P10 and cc23xx for the LP-EM-CC2340R5 run ESPHome Zigbee devices that join Home Assistant. cc35xx gives the LP-EM-CC35X1 a Wi-Fi ESPHome device with the native API. You run esphome compile and esphome upload as usual, and TI's compiler and SDK do the build underneath. The cc27xx and cc23xx platforms are Zigbee only.

### Does MicroPython run on a TI chip?

Yes. MicroPython's own Zephyr port runs on the LP-EM-CC2340R5 and the LP-MSPM33C321A with a >>> prompt. A new MicroPython port boots on the LP-MSPM0G3519 and drives a touch screen from Python.

### Does Zephyr run on TI chips that have no upstream board?

On the LP-MSPM0L1306, yes: with the board file and a fixed GPIO driver it runs CoreMark in 4 kB of RAM. On the LP-AM13E230 it boots and toggles an LED, and Zephyr's own blinky does not build because Zephyr has no GPIO or serial driver for that chip.

### Does Rust run on MSPM0?

Yes. A Rust blinky and a serial hello run on the LP-MSPM0L1306 with the community embassy-mspm0 crate.

### Can I run another vendor's example code on a TI microcontroller?

Often, with a thin layer. 34 Cmsemicon CMS32 examples ran on an LP-MSPM0L1306 with most of their main.c files untouched, and ST's STM32G4 HAL GPIO and UART examples run on the LP-AM13E230 through TI's HAL layer. Timers, clocks and ADCs are where layers stop.

### How much MSPM0 code moves to TI's wireless chips or to other MSPM0 parts unchanged?

Inside MSPM0, most examples move with a SysConfig device change (all 133 ported images that built ran on the L1306). To the CC2340R5, 0 of 10 driver examples build unchanged and 10 of 10 with a 47-line shim. The Move across TI chips page lists every test.

### Can I use an AI coding assistant for a port like this?

Yes. Give it the folder and the board's AGENTS.md. The prompt at the bottom of the page does that.

### Does TI's CC1407P radio host driver work on a C2000 chip like the TMS320F2800137?

Not as shipped. It fails to compile with 524 errors (no uint8_t, and a packed attribute the C2000 compiler rejects). With both worked around it compiles, but 11 of its 12 message structs come out a different size from the bytes on the SPI wire, because the C28x has no 8-bit byte. A field-by-field packer gives the right transmit bytes (17 of 17 cases equal to an Arm host, no radio attached), and the driver does not call it. On MSPM0 hosts it runs: 21,658 of 21,658 packets on an LP-MSPM0G5187.

## Hand the folder and its AGENTS.md to your coding assistant

Open a clone of the repository in your coding assistant and paste this, with the two blanks in angle brackets filled in.

```text
Port <project or library> to the <TI board, for example LP-MSPM0G3507>. Read AGENTS.md first: it lists the board folders (the LP-MSPM0G3507's is mspm0g3507/) and how the repository is laid out. Then read docs/ports.md and that board folder's AGENTS.md and FAQ.md. Check that TI's compiler and the board's SDK are installed in the folders the board README names; if not, run bash mac-setup/bootstrap.sh --check and tell me what it reports. Follow the method in docs/ports.md: build the project unchanged for the TI chip and list every missing call, answer them in one shim file without editing the project's own files, build with TI's tools from one command (for a plain-C library, start from ports/minmea/build.sh) and report flash and RAM, then tell me how to check it on the board and the one thing I should see. If it stops, give me the exact error and where it stopped.
```

## Status words

- **Works**: ran on the development kit and did what it should.

# Four ways to blink an MSPM0 LaunchPad: CCStudio, VS Code, terminal or Zephyr

You do not need Code Composer Studio (CCStudio) to blink an MSPM0 LaunchPad, but one path needs it for an AI assistant to drive the board. Pick the path that matches the tools you already use. Facts checked against public TI docs, the VS Code marketplace and the Zephyr project on 2026-10-04. Terms: [vocab](vocab.md).

## The one fact that decides most of it

TI's four MCP servers (project build, debug, SysConfig, serial) are started by CCStudio and only run while CCStudio is open with an AI-enabled workspace. There is no standalone download of them. So:

- Want the agent to build, flash, set breakpoints and read variables through TI's own servers? CCStudio has to be installed and running.
- Want to type in VS Code or a terminal instead of CCStudio's editor? Fine. TI documents the MCP JSON for any client, and Claude Code in a terminal attaches to the same servers while CCStudio sits in the background.
- Want no CCStudio at all? Then the agent gets a compiler and a flasher, and debugging comes from OpenOCD and GDB, which is a different, rougher experience.

## Path A: TI's front door (CCStudio + Claude Code inside it)

Install: CCStudio 21.0.1, MSPM0 SDK, turn on the AI Assistant Configurator.
What you get: the full agent loop. It edits the SysConfig file, rebuilds, flashes, runs, reads the UART, sets breakpoints.
Easy: one installer, one checkbox, the agent sees the hardware.
Hard: CCStudio is a 1 GB Theia IDE. First launch, workspace concepts and the auto-generated CLAUDE.md block take some getting used to.
Board: any MSPM0 LaunchPad, including the LP-MSPM0C1104.
Timed on the LP-MSPM0G3507: [mspm0g3507/README.md](../mspm0g3507/README.md).

## Path B: VS Code or terminal, CCStudio hidden in the background

Install: everything in Path A, plus Claude Code CLI and the MCP JSON from TI's AI chapter with Mac paths.
What you get: Path A's agent loop from the editor you already use. CCStudio stays open but you never look at it.
Easy: same capability as A; your own editor.
Hard: two apps running, one of them only as a daemon; the MCP servers die when CCStudio closes; path strings in the JSON are platform-specific.
Board: same as A.
Fits anyone who already works in VS Code.

## Path C: no CCStudio. Compiler, SysConfig CLI, make, OpenOCD

Install: TI Arm Clang (free standalone download), SysConfig standalone, MSPM0 SDK (the examples ship makefiles), TI Embedded Debug for VS Code (TI's own extension: OpenOCD build with XDS110 support, GDB, Cortex-Debug).
What you get: `make` builds the example, OpenOCD flashes it, VS Code debugs it. The agent gets a shell, not TI's MCP servers. Third-party OpenOCD MCP servers exist and are chip-agnostic.
Easy: no IDE; everything is a command; feels like ESP-IDF or Pico SDK.
Hard: four separate installs with paths to wire together; TI's own forum shows the VS Code debug extension failing for users where CCStudio worked; MSPM0 has a NONMAIN flash region that can brick the chip permanently if a flash operation is interrupted, and the safety rails for that live in CCStudio's flash loader.
Board: any MSPM0 LaunchPad.
This path exists and works, with the most setup of the four.

## Path D: Zephyr

Install: Zephyr SDK and west, a custom OpenOCD build (the Zephyr SDK's OpenOCD does not support the XDS110 probe; TI's own Zephyr guide says so).
What you get: `west build -b lp_mspm0g3507 samples/basic/blinky` and `west flash`. The Arduino and ESP32 crowd's mental model.
Easy: one build system across vendors; the agent already knows Zephyr well.
Hard: board support is upstream for LP-MSPM0G3507 (status Maintained) and in TI's downstream for G3519 and L2228, not for the C1104; the custom OpenOCD step; a documented case in Dec 2025 of two LaunchPad kits left unreachable after `west flash`. The cause was a clock driver bug that stopped the CPU, not a NONMAIN write; the fix is Zephyr PR 102668, merged 2026-02-03.
Board: LP-MSPM0G3519 (already in the TI cart) or LP-MSPM0G3507. Not the C1104.

## Not a path today

Arduino and PlatformIO: no official MSPM0 core. See [ports.md](ports.md) for the Arduino layer this repo ships.

## Which path to start with

1. New to TI tools: Path A on any MSPM0 LaunchPad, such as the LP-MSPM0C1104.
2. Already in VS Code: Path B, which keeps Path A's agent tools.
3. Want no IDE: Path C. Keep a spare board, because an interrupted flash can lock a chip.
4. Already use Zephyr: Path D on the LP-MSPM0G3507 or LP-MSPM0G3519, not the LP-MSPM0C1104.

## Sources

- CCStudio AI chapter, MCP servers only while CCStudio runs, JSON for other clients: <https://software-dl.ti.com/ccs/esd/documents/users_guide/ccs_ai.html>
- TI Embedded Debug for VS Code: <https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=ti-development-tools.ti-embedded-debug>
- TI E2E, VS Code debug extension failing where Theia works (MSPM0G3507): <https://e2e.ti.com/support/microcontrollers/arm-based-microcontrollers-group/arm-based-microcontrollers/f/arm-based-microcontrollers-forum/1549606/mspm0g3507-ti-embedded-debug-vscode-extension-not-working>
- Zephyr board page, lp_mspm0g3507: <https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/boards/ti/lp_mspm0g3507/doc/index.html>
- TI downstream Zephyr support (G3507, G3519, L2228; XDS110 not in stock OpenOCD): <https://github.com/TexasInstruments/msp-zephyr>
- Zephyr issue, LaunchPad bricked by west flash, fixed Jan 2026: <https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/issues/100734>

# How do you bring up a new motor, driver or power supply on the LP-AM13E230 and measure it?

Run this checklist each time the motor bench changes: a new supply, a new motor, a new driver board or a new controller. It comes from bringing the AM13 SDK's Hall FOC firmware up on a DRV8376EVM and a BLY171S motor, then running it with no Hall sensors (2026-10-15 to 2026-10-17). Each step names what it caught on that bench.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). FOC is field-oriented control; a Hall sensor reports the rotor position.

## 1. Write down what you expect before anything moves

For every run, write the prediction first: current, speed, time to close the loop, what would count as a miss. Afterwards, sort every miss into one of three kinds:

- **Model error:** the simulation leaves something out. The speed loop model predicted an 11 ms rise; the board took 50 ms, because the model had no Hall timing and no speed ramp.
- **Parameter error:** the motor or board is not what its label or its preset says. The ESMO observer read the rotor angle 31 degrees off because its gains came from another motor.
- **Hardware or calibration deviation:** a part behaves differently from its documentation. The firmware's automatic Hall calibration left the Hall angle 49 degrees off the rotor, so Hall FOC drew about 1.5 times the current it needed.

## 2. Put the limits in the firmware, not the host

A page or a script cannot keep a motor safe; the board must. The guard (`am13e230/foc-drv8376/frl_guard.h`) stops every run on its own:

- a run time cap, and a stop 1 s after the host goes quiet;
- a phase-current trip checked every control interrupt (start at 1.0 A on a new motor, whatever its rating);
- a speed clamp;
- a bus voltage window that refuses a start and stops a run outside it;
- a stop if the background loop hangs.

Time the guard from the CPU's cycle counter: the solution's background tick is not a millisecond.

## 3. Change the supply on purpose

Set the guard's bus window for the supply before connecting it, and prove it refuses the wrong one:

| Supply | Window | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 12 V 0.5 A adapter | 10 to 14.5 V | the bench default |
| 20 V tool battery pack (five cells) | 15.5 to 21.5 V | 15.5 V keeps each cell above about 3.1 V; a pack fresh off the charger read 21.2 V on the board (2026-10-22) |

`python3 tools/motorlink/campaign.py supply pack20` sets it; with the window set for the pack and the adapter still connected, a start must be refused ("refused: bus out of range"). Check the driver board's rating (the DRV8376EVM takes 4.5 to 65 V, the BOOSTXL-DRV8323RS 6 to 54 V), and that the board's bus reading spans the new voltage (the DRV8376EVM reads up to 81 V). A battery needs a fuse in its lead every time: it can deliver far more current than the board.

Size the supply wire to the fuse, and the fuse to the board, before a battery goes on: a 5 A blade fuse and 20 AWG or heavier wire between the pack and the driver board. Small jumper wires carry about 1 A; on 2026-10-19 two of them between a 20 V tool pack and the DRV8376EVM melted behind a 30 A fuse, which lets the wire fail long before the fuse does.

Power the motor supply before the controller boots, or reset the controller after the supply is on. The AM13 FOC firmware measures the current-sense offsets once, at boot; if the driver's amplifiers were unpowered then, every phase reads a fixed false current. On the 20 V pack (2026-10-18) the board had booted with the pack off: all three phases read -1.53 A at standstill, and every start tripped within 1 ms at a "1.54 A peak" that was never there. Before the first run on a new supply, read the three phase currents at standstill; each must be within about 0.05 A of zero (`tools/motorlink/pack_campaign.py` checks this before every run).

## 4. Check the driver's own limit and fault pins before enabling it

If the DRV8376 reports a fault before the motor is enabled, its current-limit pin is floating: set it before enable. Read the driver's fault output and route it to the PWM trip. On a driver with SPI (DRV8323RS), read its fault registers too.

## 5. Find out what the motor really is

A new motor's label is a hypothesis. Measure:

- pole pairs, from Hall edges per mechanical turn;
- Hall order and type, by turning the shaft slowly by hand with the Hall lines logged;
- winding resistance, inductance and back-EMF, with the SDK's motor identification or a bounded test.

Feed the measured values to the model before predicting anything.

## 6. Check the angle, not just the spin

A motor can turn smoothly on a wrong angle and simply draw more current. Shift the FOC angle in steps at a steady speed and read the phase current: it is lowest at the true rotor angle (`campaign.py sweep`). Run a sensorless observer beside the Halls and compare (`frlGuard.obsMode`): two independent readings that agree are worth more than one calibration flag.

## 7. Measure with the vendor's own live link

The firmware streams variables over the LaunchPad kit's USB serial port (MotorVision). Use it before building any instrumentation of your own, and read the indices from the firmware's table, not the JSON beside it: in SDK 26.01.00.03 the two disagree.

## 8. Record it the same way every time

Write the expectation first. Keep the raw readings. Add a result row per number in `data/results/`, and a write-up with what it shows and its limits. Sort the misses into the three kinds above. Read the board's state through the debugger before any reset: a reset erases it.

## What changes from board to board

| Board change | What to redo |
|---|---|
| New supply | Steps 3 and 4 |
| New motor | Steps 1, 5 and 6; guard trip back to 1.0 A |
| New driver | Steps 2 to 4, the current-sense gain and offset, then 5 and 6 |
| New controller | Everything; the guard and the observer code are the parts that move with it |

Worked example with the numbers: [LP-AM13E230 FOC README](../../am13e230/foc-drv8376/README.md).

# Which TI LaunchPad kit can run a given port? What eight MSPM0, MSPM33, AM13 and CC35X1 boards did (checked 2026-10-21)

Terms: [docs/vocab.md](../vocab.md). Lessons by kind of change: [porting-lessons.md](porting-lessons.md). 1 kB = 1,024 bytes.

RAM decided most outcomes. Doom needed the LP-MSPM33C321A or the LP-EM-CC35X1 for RAM and the 128 kB and 32 kB parts could not hold it. llama2.c needed more flash than the LP-MSPM0G3519's 512 kB. The Game Boy links on the G3519 but only ran on the M33C321A. The first table lists which project ran on which chip and the resource that decided it. Below it, one table per chip lists the peripherals and features the ports used, with the number each produced.

| Chip | Clock | Flash | RAM |
|---|---|---|---|
| LP-MSPM0C1104 | 24 MHz | 16 kB | 1 kB |
| LP-MSPM0L1306 | 32 MHz | 64 kB | 4 kB |
| LP-MSPM0G3507 | 80 MHz | 128 kB | 32 kB |
| LP-MSPM0G3519 | 80 MHz | 512 kB | 128 kB |
| LP-MSPM0G5187 (with NPU) | 80 MHz | 128 kB | 32 kB |
| LP-MSPM33C321A | 160 MHz Cortex-M33 | 1 MB | 256 kB |
| LP-AM13E230 | 200 MHz Cortex-M33 | 512 kB | 128 kB |
| LP-EM-CC35X1 | 160 MHz Cortex-M33 | 8 MB external | 1,126 kB (data/boards.csv) |

Short names in the table: G3519 is LP-MSPM0G3519, M33C321A is LP-MSPM33C321A, AM13E230 is LP-AM13E230, CC35X1 is LP-EM-CC35X1. Tested with MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07, MSPM33 SDK 1.04.00.00 and TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS. TCM is fast tightly coupled RAM, XIP is execute in place, NPU is the neural processing unit, TMU is the trigonometric math unit, HSADC is the high-speed ADC, DWT is the Cortex-M cycle counter, p95 is the value 95 percent of queries stay under, STANDBY0 and STANDBY1 are the chip's low-power states (see vocab), DSLite is TI's command-line flash tool. Sizes are from [data/boards.csv](../../data/boards.csv).

## Project against chip

Works: it ran and did what it should; a note names any part that did not run. Should work: it builds, and only the named run is missing. Could work: porting effort stays, named beside it. Not for this chip: the named resource rules it out. A dash means no run is recorded.

</details>

## Questions

**Which chip ran the most projects?** Counting Works in the first table, the LP-MSPM0G3519 ran MicroPython, wasm3, 2048 and Minesweeper, CHIP-8, a ZX Spectrum, a UART bootloader and MP3 decode. The LP-MSPM33C321A ran Doom, a Game Boy, llama2.c and MP3 decoding, which need its RAM, FPU and 160 MHz.

**Will Doom run on an LP-MSPM0G3519?** No. Doom's static data alone does not fit in its 128 kB of RAM (the MicroPython full build leaves a 122 kB heap there). It ran on the LP-MSPM33C321A and the LP-EM-CC35X1; see [the Doom write-up](../../ports/doom/WRITEUP.md).

**Why does the EDUMKII screen not work on the LP-MSPM0L1306?** Header pins 13 and 17 are the debug pins SWCLK and SWDIO, so the screen, S1 and S2 cannot be reached. The analog parts of the pack ran.

**Why did the LP-AM13E230 never wake from STANDBY0?** Unknown. A watchdog interval was the only wake source and every connect after it failed with DSLite -613, -6310 or -6311. The SDK names a GPIO as the STANDBY wake source and the watchdog for STOP; no image with a GPIO wake was run, so whether the wake source was the cause is not confirmed.

**Does the LP-MSPM0G3519 have a floating-point unit?** No. MP3 decode there takes 25 times the M33C321A's cycles a frame.

**Why is my LP-EM-CC35X1 console silent after I change the flash layout?** It stays silent until `full_flash_erase`. Check the baud too: 921,600 for Doom, 115200 for SDK examples.

**Which chip do I buy for an NPU demo?** The LP-MSPM0G5187: its NPU ran a 64-tap FIR 29.7 times faster than the CPU build.

**Does the LP-EM-CC35X1 take BoosterPacks?** Not the EDUMKII, SHARP128 or BASSENSORSMKII: eight pins (three for SHARP128) cannot be freed with a jumper, a board layout limit.

**Which chip should a first port use?** The LP-MSPM0G3519 ran the widest range; take the LP-MSPM33C321A (1 MB, 256 kB, FPU) for decoders, language models and emulators. For a first port, open the [MicroPython README](../../ports/micropython/README.md).

# Which radio and which software should I pick for an MSPM0 or CC23xx board?

Terms: [docs/vocab.md](../vocab.md). Errors and fixes: [cc2340r5/FAQ.md](../../cc2340r5/FAQ.md). Site version: `site/choose.html`. Generated from `site/data/choose.json` by `tools/render_choose.py`; edit the JSON, not this file. Checked 2026-10-06. 1 kB = 1,024 bytes.

For a battery sensor that talks to a phone, pick Bluetooth LE. For a smart home you already run with a hub, pick Zigbee or Thread. For Apple Home, Google Home or Alexa, pick Matter, which runs over Thread or Wi-Fi. Pick Wi-Fi when the device is plugged in, and Sub-1 GHz when it is far from the house. For software, TI's SDK has the radio stacks and TI's compiler. On CoreMark at -O3 that compiler was 26 percent faster than GCC: 2.30 against 1.82 per MHz on the LP-MSPM0G3507. Zephyr lets the same code move between chips and vendors. With the same GCC compiler it cost us 4 to 8 percent on one LP-MSPM0G3507. The C library also differs.

Contents: the radios side by side; where Matter fits; Zigbee or Thread; each radio; more than one radio; Zephyr or TI's SDK; what next.

## The radios side by side

Matter is not on this table because it is not a radio. It runs over Thread or Wi-Fi, covered in the next section. Power figures come from data sheets at different voltages and power levels, so compare sizes and ignore exact ratios. Range depends on your walls more than the radio. 1 kB = 1,024 bytes.

| | Bluetooth LE | Zigbee | Thread | Wi-Fi | Sub-1 GHz |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| What else you need | A phone, or a Bluetooth adapter or proxy for Home Assistant | A Zigbee hub, such as a USB coordinator radio on Home Assistant | A Thread border router | Your Wi-Fi router | A second Sub-1 GHz radio to receive it |
| On a battery | Yes: a CC2340R5 sleeps at 0.71 µA | Yes, as an end device | Yes, as a sleepy end device | Hard: about 0.4 to 1 mA just to stay connected. CC3235SF 710 µA; CC3551E 430 to 975 µA, target values | Yes, for small readings |
| Sending, current | 5.1 to 10.7 mA (CC2340R5) | Same 2.4 GHz chips as Bluetooth | Same 2.4 GHz chips as Bluetooth | 217 to 286 mA (CC3235SF) | Not compared |
| Devices relay for each other | Not by default | Yes: mains-powered devices route | Yes: routers stay on, so they are mains powered | No: everything goes through your router | Depends on the protocol |
| Gets an IP address | No | No: the hub translates | Yes, IPv6 | Yes: IPv4, and IPv6 if your network has it | Depends on the protocol |
| Apple Home, Google Home, Alexa | Not checked for a home-made board; Matter is the standard path | Through a hub | Through Matter | Through Matter or the maker's app | No |
| Home Assistant | Bluetooth integration, BTHome | ZHA or Zigbee2MQTT | Thread integration, usually with Matter | MQTT, ESPHome and others | Through your own bridge |
| What was measured | 45 ms round trip on LP-EM-CC2340R5 | 95 ms per command from Home Assistant at first pairing; about 5 s after a re-pairing on LP-EM-CC2340R5 | Thread device builds did not fit 36 kB of RAM; they build completely for 64 kB and were not run | LP-EM-CC35X1 joined Wi-Fi and its ESPHome API answered 20 of 20 commands; Home Assistant adoption not run | Not measured |

## Where Matter fits

Matter is not a radio. It is a common language for smart-home devices, from the Connectivity Standards Alliance, that runs on IP networks: Wi-Fi, Thread or Ethernet. Bluetooth LE only sets a new device up. So you choose between Matter over Thread, which is low power and needs a border router, and Matter over Wi-Fi, which needs no extra box and uses more power. One Matter device can sit in Apple Home, Google Home, Alexa and Home Assistant at once. Matter needs a big part. TI marks Matter over Thread on the CC2755P10 as evaluation, and Matter over Wi-Fi on the CC3551E as production. The CC3551E board is the LP-EM-CC35X1. TI offers no Matter build for the CC2340R5.

## Zigbee or Thread: choosing between them

Both are low-power meshes on 2.4 GHz, good for battery sensors, and both work with Home Assistant. Pick Zigbee if you have a Zigbee hub or USB radio already. Pick Thread if you have a Thread border router, or want Matter on battery devices. Many Apple and Google home hubs are border routers, and Matter's low-power path is over Thread. Thread devices get IPv6 addresses; Zigbee devices need the hub to translate. On TI chips, Thread needs more memory in TI's builds: on the 36 kB CC2340R52 Thread device builds did not fit and Zigbee did.

## Bluetooth LE: when to pick it

Talks straight to a phone or computer, no hub. A CC2340R5 sleeps at 0.71 µA between radio events (data sheet).

Pick it when:

- A phone app should talk to it directly
- It runs for a long time on a coin cell
- You want readings in Home Assistant through a Bluetooth adapter or an ESPHome Bluetooth proxy (BTHome is an open format it reads)

Skip it when:

- Messages need to hop across the house through other devices: Zigbee and Thread do that by default
- It should appear in Apple Home or Google Home on its own: use Matter

- **Power:** 5.1 to 10.7 mA sending, 0.71 µA asleep (CC2340R5 data sheet, 3.0 V)
- **Address:** No IP address; a phone or hub talks to it
- **What was measured:** LP-EM-CC2340R5: on air 1.40 s after flashing, connects to a Mac in 0.55 s, 45 ms round trip for 20 bytes.

## Zigbee: when to pick it

A low-power mesh for lights, plugs and sensors, run by a hub. Mains-powered devices relay messages for the others.

Pick it when:

- You already have a Zigbee hub, such as Home Assistant with a USB Zigbee radio
- Battery sensors spread across a house
- You want it in Home Assistant through ZHA or Zigbee2MQTT

Skip it when:

- You have no hub and do not want one
- It should appear in Apple Home or Google Home without a bridge: use Matter

- **Channels:** Home Assistant suggests Zigbee channel 15, 20 or 25 "to avoid interoperability problems with Zigbee devices". Zigbee shares 2.4 GHz with Wi-Fi. Wi-Fi channels 1, 6 and 11 overlap Zigbee channels 11 to 14, 16 to 19 and 21 to 24 (from the channel frequencies), and 15, 20 and 25 sit in the gaps. That is the US Wi-Fi plan; in Europe, Wi-Fi channel 13 overlaps Zigbee 22 to 26
- **Address:** No IP address; the hub translates
- **Words:** A coordinator is the hub's radio. Mains powered means plugged into the wall. Zigbee2MQTT and ZHA are the two ways Home Assistant runs a Zigbee network
- **What was measured:** LP-EM-CC2340R5 as a Zigbee light in Home Assistant: 20 of 20 commands, 95 ms median at first pairing (2026-10-05); about 5 s per command after a re-pairing two hours later; the 2026-10-16 repeat did not join. **Tag: Unknown.** Suspected: the radio environment. TI's example listened on channel 11 only until all channels were set. **Tag: TI example default.** That default suits a bench, not a home.

## Thread: when to pick it

A low-power mesh like Zigbee, but every device gets an IPv6 address. It reaches your network through a border router.

Pick it when:

- You have a border router already: Apple TV 4K (2nd generation, or 3rd generation Wi-Fi + Ethernet; not the Wi-Fi-only model), HomePod mini, HomePod (2nd generation), Nest Hub (2nd gen), Nest Hub Max, Nest Wifi Pro, Google TV Streamer (4K), or Home Assistant with a Connect ZBT-1 (formerly SkyConnect) or ZBT-2 running the OpenThread Border Router app
- You plan to use Matter on battery devices
- Battery sensors that sleep: sleepy end devices keep the radio off most of the time

Skip it when:

- There is no border router in the house and you do not want one
- Your chip is the 36 kB CC2340R52: TI's Thread device builds did not fit it, while its Bluetooth and Zigbee examples did

- **Routers:** Keep the radio on all the time, so in practice they are mains powered (plugged in). A sleepy end device keeps its radio off most of the time
- **Address:** IPv6, inside and outside the mesh
- **On TI chips:** TI lists Thread device roles on the CC2340R53 (evaluation) and the CC27xx chips (production). On the CC2340R5 TI lists only the radio co-processor role, marked evaluation
- **What was measured:** Thread device builds for the LP-EM-CC2340R5 (36 kB of RAM) needed 7.5 to 23.8 kB more RAM. **Tag: Unknown.** Suspected: a chip limit. Only TI's configurations were built; a trimmed build might fit. They link for the 64 kB CC2340R53 and were not run.

## Matter: when to pick it

Not a radio. A common language over Thread, Wi-Fi or Ethernet, so one device works with Apple Home, Google Home, Alexa, SmartThings and Home Assistant at once.

Pick it when:

- It should work in any smart-home app, or several at once
- Other people, who may not run Home Assistant, will use it

Skip it when:

- Only you will use it, with Home Assistant: Zigbee or Bluetooth is simpler
- The chip is small. TI offers Matter only on bigger wireless parts, such as the CC2755P10 (Thread, evaluation) and the CC3551E on the LP-EM-CC35X1 board (Wi-Fi, production)

- **Runs over:** Thread or Wi-Fi (or Ethernet); Bluetooth LE only to set it up
- **What else you need:** A Matter controller (Apple Home, Google Home, Alexa or Home Assistant), and a border router for Thread devices
- **What was measured:** Not measured. TI offers no Matter build for the CC2340R5.

## Wi-Fi: when to pick it

Joins your home network directly. No hub and plenty of speed, at much more power.

Pick it when:

- It is plugged into the wall
- It sends a lot of data, or talks to a web service
- You want it on the network today with no hub, for example over MQTT into Home Assistant

Skip it when:

- It runs on a small battery: staying connected alone costs about 0.4 to 1 mA

- **Power:** 217 to 286 mA sending, 53 to 74 mA receiving, 710 µA staying connected (CC3235SF data sheet, 3.6 V). The newer CC3551E lists 430 to 975 µA connected, as target values
- **Band:** 2.4 GHz and often 5 GHz
- **TI boards:** LAUNCHXL-CC3235SF (Wi-Fi 4), LP-EM-CC35X1 (Wi-Fi 6 with Bluetooth)
- **What was measured:** Ran on the LP-EM-CC35X1: it joins Wi-Fi and its ESPHome API answered 20 of 20 commands from a client on the board. Home Assistant adoption is not run because the test network keeps clients apart. Evidence: docs/experiments/2026-10-13-esphome-cc35xx-platform.md.

## Sub-1 GHz long range: when to pick it

A lower frequency that reaches farther and passes walls better, for sensors at the far end of a garden or a farm.

Pick it when:

- The sensor sits past where 2.4 GHz reaches. In TI's example, the same radio performance gives 292 m at 868 MHz against 233 m at 2.4 GHz, and about twice the range through an 8-inch concrete wall
- It sends small readings, not much data

Skip it when:

- A phone or a standard smart-home app should hear it directly: phones have no Sub-1 GHz radio
- You read about 100 km records. Those need a slow long-range mode, high antennas and a clear line of sight

- **What else you need:** A second Sub-1 GHz radio at home to receive it, such as another TI board or a BeaglePlay
- **TI boards:** LP-CC1354P10-1, LP-CC1352P7-1
- **What was measured:** Not measured. An LP-CC1354P10-1 is on this bench.

## Running more than one radio

Yes, with limits. A bigger chip can run two radio stacks at once: TI lists Bluetooth together with TI 15.4 as shipping on the CC2755P10. TI's release notes say the CC23xx chips do not support two stacks at once. TI's two-radio example for the CC2755P10, Bluetooth with TI 15.4, was moved to the 36 kB CC2340R52. It did not link: 2.1 kB of RAM short even before its heap. **Tag: Unknown.** Suspected: a chip limit. Only TI's example was moved. A board can also carry two radio chips: the BeaglePlay has Wi-Fi plus a CC1352P7 for Bluetooth, Zigbee and Sub-1 GHz. Or let a hub join them: Home Assistant takes Zigbee, Thread, Bluetooth and Wi-Fi devices into one place. A CC2340R5 can also run Bluetooth or Zigbee, one at a time, by flashing different firmware.

## Zephyr or TI's SDK on a TI chip (MSPM0, CC2340R5)

You can write code for a TI board with TI's own SDK or with Zephyr. On 2026-10-06, PlatformIO's board list and MicroPython's download page did not list the MSPM0 or CC23xx boards. The checks ran on an Intel Mac running macOS 15.7.9, with Zephyr 4.4.2 and GCC 12.2, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1, SimpleLink Low Power F3 SDK 9.21.00.36 and MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07. The speed gap is mostly the compiler. With the same GCC compiler, Zephyr cost 4 to 8 percent on CoreMark, on one LP-MSPM0G3507. The C library also differs. The time-to-blink numbers below are not like for like.

| | TI's SDK | Zephyr |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | TI's drivers, examples and radio stacks, set up with SysConfig, TI's point-and-click tool | An open-source operating system, a Linux Foundation project, with one build tool (west) and one driver model across more than 1,000 boards |
| Boards on the Hardware page | All have a TI SDK | 8 of the 24 are in upstream Zephyr, the main Zephyr project (2026-10-06) |
| Radios | Bluetooth LE, Zigbee and proprietary 2.4 GHz, which is TI's own packet format, in the Low Power F3 SDK; Thread and Matter as separate downloads | Upstream Zephyr has no Bluetooth for the CC2340R5. **Tag: Third-party behavior.** TI's fork, its own copy of Zephyr, adds it, but on the test board its samples flashed and printed nothing. **Tag: Unknown.** The cause is not known. Suspected cause: tool or docs. One boot setting differs from upstream, and the fork is an older Zephyr (3.7), so it is one difference among several, not proven. |
| Speed, CoreMark per MHz, LP-MSPM0G3507 | 2.30 with TI Arm Clang, no operating system | 1.82 with GCC, the compiler Zephyr uses, no operating system, -O3 with loop unrolling |
| Same compiler, GCC 12.2 -O2, LP-MSPM0G3507 | 1.76, no operating system | 1.63 under Zephyr: 7.9 percent slower. The C library also differs. |
| Interrupt response, the time to react to a signal, LP-MSPM0G3507 | 29 to 36 CPU cycles, about 0.4 µs at 80 MHz, no operating system, TI Arm Clang | About 55 to 65 cycles net, roughly twice bare metal. 163 to 181 cycles under Zephyr with GCC, 99 to 126 of them Zephyr's slower timer read. |
| Moving to another vendor's chip | Start again with that vendor's tools | In the good case, change the board file, which describes the board's pins |
| Learning first | SysConfig is point and click | Devicetree, Kconfig and west; one training firm budgets two to four weeks for an experienced developer |
| On an Intel Mac | Works | Zephyr's guide says x86-64 macOS is not supported. **Tag: Third-party behavior.** The runs worked with workarounds, written up in mspm0g3507/zephyr/README.md |

### TI's SDK

TI's drivers, examples and radio stacks, set up with SysConfig.

Pick it when:

- You need a radio stack: Bluetooth, Zigbee, Thread and Matter come from TI
- You want TI's examples and its graphical setup
- Speed or a quick interrupt response matters: the fastest results came from TI's compiler with no operating system

Skip it when:

- You plan to move the same code to another vendor's chips
- You want one way of working across many vendors' boards

What was measured: LP-EM-CC2340R5: builds in 22 s with make and flashes in 7 s. Not like for like with the Zephyr times.

### Zephyr

An open-source operating system that runs the same way on many vendors' chips.

Pick it when:

- You may switch chips or vendors later
- You want one tool and one way of working across boards
- You want open source with a large community

Skip it when:

- You need Bluetooth on the CC2340R5 today
- Your board is not in upstream Zephyr: see each board's page
- You need the fastest code: TI's compiler, which Zephyr does not use, was 26 percent faster than GCC at -O3 on CoreMark (LP-MSPM0G3507) and was the bigger part of the speed gap

What was measured: LP-MSPM0G3507: 3 minutes from clean to blinking with this repo's script; 9.5 minutes the first time, while the workarounds were found. LP-EM-CC2340R5: blinking 82 s after the first command, with Zephyr installed. Not like for like with the TI SDK times.

## Three common questions, answered from the rows

Three common questions. Each answer gives the requirement, a configuration that ran, what limits it, and what no row establishes. Every number in the tables is read from the results store when the page is built. A constraint that is not measured names the experiment that would decide it, and until then the answer is a candidate. Terms: ZHA is Home Assistant's Zigbee integration. LQI and RSSI are the link quality and signal strength a radio reports. NNC is TI's neural network compiler. EnergyTrace is the current meter in TI's debug probe. FOC is field-oriented control, the usual motor-control math. The TMU is the C2000's hardware for sine, cosine and division.

### A Zigbee light or switch in Home Assistant: which TI board, and whether it responds fast enough

Requirement: A device that joins an existing Zigbee network run by Home Assistant (ZHA) and acts on a command within about a second.

**LP-EM-CC2340R5 with TI's onoff_light example from the SimpleLink Low Power F3 SDK, built as a router, plus the LP-XDS110ET debugger to program it.** (candidate, not a recommendation). It joined ZHA (Home Assistant's own Zigbee integration) 37 s after the flash finished, and 20 of 20 on/off commands from Home Assistant landed, median 95 ms, read from Home Assistant's own state. That meets the requirement on the first pairing. After a re-pairing two hours later the median was about 5 s, which does not, so the one-second part is met once and missed once. A repeat on 2026-10-16 did not join Home Assistant in four tries; until a new run passes, this is a record of one run, not a tested route.

Limiting factor: RAM, and the link. The router image leaves 799 B of the chip's 36 kB free, so there is almost no room for your own code in that build; the end-device image leaves 6.4 kB. The 5 s medians came with a weaker link (LQI, the link quality the radio reports, 36 to 48 against 60 at first). Cause unknown (suspected: radio environment).

| What | Value | Runs | Checked by | Date | Row's source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Join time, flash finished to listed in ZHA | 37 s | 1 | ha-state | 2026-10-05 | cc2340r5/zigbee/README.md |
| Command latency from Home Assistant, first pairing | 95 to 292 ms (median of 20 commands; the slowest was 292 ms) | 1 | ha-state | 2026-10-05 | cc2340r5/zigbee/README.md |
| Commands that landed, first pairing | 100 % | 1 | ha-state | 2026-10-05 | cc2340r5/zigbee/README.md |
| Command latency after a re-pairing two hours later | 5000 to 7000 ms (median of 30 commands with a weaker link; the slowest was 7 s) | 1 | ha-state | 2026-10-05 | cc2340r5/matrix/benchmarks.md |
| RAM left in the router image | 799 B (linker map, logging on) |  | linker | 2026-10-05 | cc2340r5/matrix/memory.md |
| Flash used by the router image | 275.7 kB |  | linker | 2026-10-05 | cc2340r5/zigbee/onoff_light/freertos/ticlang/onoff_light.map |

- Joins Home Assistant and takes commands: measured: yes, 20 of 20 at 95 ms median on the first pairing
- Stays joined and responsive for days: unmeasured. leave it paired for 72 hours with a command every minute and log the misses and the latency; the re-pairing figure (about 5 s) says the link can degrade, and no long run exists
- Battery life as a sleepy device: unmeasured. build the end-device image, measure sleep current and energy per command with the EnergyTrace probe at a stated voltage, then compute days from a named cell; nothing here was measured on a battery
- Room for your own code: measured: 799 B of RAM free in the router build and 6.4 kB in the end-device build (linker map); a real product needs the end-device build or a 64 kB part

Conditions:

- SimpleLink Low Power F3 SDK 9.21.00.36, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1, FreeRTOS, the SDK makefile's default flags
- LP-EM-CC2340R5, board revision not recorded, probe firmware 3.0.0.43; a previous owner's board
- Home Assistant with ZHA and a ZBT-2 coordinator on a Mac mini; LQI 60, RSSI -85 dBm at the first pairing
- measured 2026-10-05 from an Intel Mac, macOS 15.7.9

Not established:

- long-term reliability (one evening, two pairings)
- any battery figure
- behavior on the LP-EM-CC2340R53 TI sells now (64 kB RAM; the board tested is no longer listed)
- Apple Home, Google Home or Alexa: Zigbee reaches Home Assistant only; Matter is the route to those

Next: Before buying for this, decide the unmeasured constraint: Stays joined and responsive for days: leave it paired for 72 hours with a command every minute and log the misses and the latency; the re-pairing figure (about 5 s) says the link can degrade, and no long run exists; Battery life as a sleepy device: build the end-device image, measure sleep current and energy per command with the EnergyTrace probe at a stated voltage, then compute days from a named cell; nothing here was measured on a battery Reproduce: project-zigbee-light.html Errors and fixes: faq-cc2340r5.html#how-much-ram-is-left-for-your-code-after-the-radio-stack

### A small on-chip classifier under 5 ms per answer on a coin-cell budget: whether the MSPM0G5187's NPU reaches it

Requirement: A 4-class classifier on 4 sensor channels by 32 samples, answered in under 5 ms, in a few kB of flash and RAM, with the model's accuracy known.

**LP-MSPM0G5187 with the 8.5k-parameter occupancy model compiled by TI's NNC for the NPU, at 80 MHz.** (candidate, not a recommendation). The answer takes 2.12 ms on the NPU (the chip's neural processing unit) at 80 MHz, so the 5 ms budget is met twice over. The model objects take 14.0 kB of flash and 1.4 kB of RAM. The 20 stored test vectors give the same class on the board as on the Mac, so the port is right. For scale: TI's own CPU build of the same model (NNC, TI's neural network compiler) takes 45.64 ms, 21.6 times longer, and the fastest plain C build 35.27 ms; that last pair is not like for like because the plain C time also includes input quantization.

Limiting factor: What the model knows, not the chip. Balanced accuracy is the average of how often each class is caught. On a day the model never trained on it is 87.7 percent accurate overall but calls 159 of 170 three-person windows empty, a balanced accuracy of 40.2 percent; the 90.9 percent figure comes from a same-day split. And the time is the model call only: no sensor read, no sleep or wake, so it is not a pipeline latency.

| What | Value | Runs | Checked by | Date | Row's source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Model call on the NPU, 80 MHz | 2.116 to 2.155 ms (fastest of 20 vectors, best of 5 calls (best case); value_hi is the slowest vector; model call only) | 3 | vectors | 2026-10-09 | mspm0g5187/bench/ai/repeat.sh |
| The same model, TI's CPU build (NNC), 80 MHz | 45.644 to 45.675 ms (the like-for-like baseline) | 3 | vectors | 2026-10-09 | mspm0g5187/bench/ai/repeat.sh |

| Model RAM, NPU build | 1.4 kB | 1 | linker | 2026-10-09 | data/ai-model-sizes.csv |
| Energy above idle per inference, NPU | 4.23 to 4.92 uJ (steady loop, current above the board's idle reading times the best-case time; spreads 7 to 32 percent between runs) | 3 | by-us | 2026-10-09 | mspm0g5187/bench/power/energy_occ.py |

- Under 5 ms per answer: measured: 2.12 ms best case, 2.16 ms slowest vector, model call only
- Accuracy on data it did not train on: measured: 90.9% on a same-day block split; 87.7% overall and 40.2% balanced with whole days held out (tools/dataset/eval_occupancy.py); one room only
- Coin-cell life: unmeasured. measure the sleep current with the board's isolation shunts changed and the chip in STANDBY, then energy per wake-infer-sleep cycle with EnergyTrace at a stated voltage; today only a steady loop above a 16.4 mA board floor was measured, which says nothing about a sleeping product
- Works on your own sensor data: unmeasured. record your own sessions with tools/dataset/capture.py, train with the same recipe, and run the day-held-out evaluation; the model here learned one room

Estimates beside the result (added up, not tested together):

- The model's 14.4 kB of flash and 1.4 kB of RAM are the model objects only; TI's NPU example image around them, clock setup and startup included, is a separate measured image. Adding your sensor driver and a sleep loop is an estimate until it is one built image.

Conditions:

- MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS at -O2, TI NNC 2.1.2 for the NPU and CPU builds, int8
- LP-MSPM0G5187 Rev. A, 80 MHz from the SysConfig of TI's motor_bearing_fault_detection_ai_npu example
- three runs, each a full erase and flash, agreeing to the cycle; 2026-10-09; Intel Mac, macOS 15.7.9

Not established:

- any pipeline time (sensor to decision)
- any sleep or wake figure, so any battery life
- accuracy in another room

Next: Before buying for this, decide the unmeasured constraint: Coin-cell life: measure the sleep current with the board's isolation shunts changed and the chip in STANDBY, then energy per wake-infer-sleep cycle with EnergyTrace at a stated voltage; today only a steady loop above a 16.4 mA board floor was measured, which says nothing about a sleeping product; Works on your own sensor data: record your own sessions with tools/dataset/capture.py, train with the same recipe, and run the day-held-out evaluation; the model here learned one room Reproduce: project-small-ai-model.html Errors and fixes: ../mspm0g5187/FAQ.md#the-occupancy-model-scores-909-percent-on-its-test-set-but-much-less-on-a-new-day-why

### A 50 kHz motor-control loop: which board keeps up, and how much of the period is left

Requirement: A PWM-triggered loop (ADC sample, one field-oriented control step, new PWM value) that completes well inside a 20 us period, with the CPU time it takes known.

**LAUNCHXL-F2800137 (TMS320F2800137 at 120 MHz) with the TMU build of a control-loop harness, code in RAM.** (candidate, not a recommendation). Trigger to new PWM value takes 2.4 us mean (2.33 to 2.42 us over 1,000 interrupts) with the TMU, the chip's hardware for sine, cosine and division, in one field-oriented control (FOC) step. At 50 kHz the period is 20 us, so the loop uses about 12 percent of it. The loop still updates every period up to 336 kHz, and at 100 kHz it takes 26.4 percent of the CPU.

Limiting factor: This is one FOC step on a fixed input, not a motor: no current sensing chain, no observer, no fault handling, no communications. The 336 kHz figure is where the harness stops updating in time; your loop has more in it.

| What | Value | Runs | Checked by | Date | Row's source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Trigger to new PWM value, TMU, code in RAM | 2.4 us (mean of 1,000 interrupts; 279 to 290 cycles) | 1000 | by-us | 2026-10-06 | c2000-launchpad/bench/control-loop.md |
| Worst case as a share of a 10 us period (the 100 kHz benchmark period; halve it for 50 kHz) | 24.2 % | 1000 | by-us | 2026-10-06 | c2000-launchpad/bench/control-loop.md |
| Jitter, worst minus best | 0.092 us | 1000 | by-us | 2026-10-06 | c2000-launchpad/bench/control-loop.md |
| Highest rate that never misses a period | 336.13 to 336.13 kHz (measured on the board, 3 trials) | 3 | readback | 2026-10-08 | c2000-launchpad/bench/ctrl/build-tmu/run-fom.txt |
| CPU load at 100 kHz | 26.4 to 33.3 % (value_hi keeps the timing checks in) | 3 | readback | 2026-10-08 | c2000-launchpad/bench/ctrl/build-tmu/run-fom.txt |
| The same loop without the TMU (C library math) | 3.7 us (two compiler flags differ, not isolated) | 1000 | by-us | 2026-10-06 | c2000-launchpad/bench/control-loop.md |

- Completes inside a 20 us period: measured: 2.4 us mean, about 12 percent of the 20 us period; the benchmark row says 24.2 percent of its 10 us period
- Behaves with a real motor, current sensors and an observer: unmeasured. run TI's motor-control kit example with a motor and current sensing on this board and time the same trigger-to-PWM path inside it; the harness here is one FOC step on a fixed input
- Code in flash instead of RAM: measured: 2.58 us mean with the end-of-conversion interrupt from flash, 2.32 us with the loop copied to RAM at startup

Conditions:

- TI C2000 compiler 25.11.1.LTS at -O2, C2000Ware 26.02.00.00 LTS, --tmu_support=tmu0 and --fp_mode=relaxed for the TMU build
- LAUNCHXL-F2800137, board MCU109A, chip TMS320F2800137 silicon revision B, probe firmware 3.0.0.43; a used board
- ePWM1 50 kHz trigger, 9-cycle sample window, 1,000 interrupts; the rate sweep and CPU load on 2026-10-08; the loop times 2026-10-06; Intel Mac, macOS 15.7.9

Not established:

- anything with a motor attached
- the F28P65x or other C2000 parts (the LAUNCHXL-F28P65X has its own rows)
- the loop with communications or a second interrupt running

Next: Before buying for this, decide the unmeasured constraint: Behaves with a real motor, current sensors and an observer: run TI's motor-control kit example with a motor and current sensing on this board and time the same trigger-to-PWM path inside it; the harness here is one FOC step on a fixed input Reproduce: benchmarks.html#control Errors and fixes: faq-f2800137.html#how-fast-can-a-control-loop-run-on-the-f2800137

## Where to go next

Pick a board: open the [Hardware options page](hardware.html?need=zigbee) and press the need you chose. Hit an error: the LP-EM-CC2340R5 FAQ lists each one with its cause. Not measured: Wi-Fi, Sub-1 GHz, Matter, indoor range and battery life.
