# How do I collect my own sensor data to train a tiny AI model for a TI MSPM0 LaunchPad development kit (LP-MSPM0G3507, LP-MSPM0G5187)?

Have the board send one sensor reading at a time to your Mac over its USB serial port, at a fixed rate, and press a key on the Mac to say what you are doing while it records; the result is a CSV file with a label on every line. Then check the file, train a small neural network on it, shrink it to 8-bit numbers with TI's tools, and test it on the board with recordings it never saw before you trust it live. This repo has each piece: `portability/dataset-stream/` (board side), `tools/dataset/capture.py` (record and label), `tools/dataset/check.py` (rate, gaps, balance, plot, TI's dataset layout) and `tools/dataset/train.py` (train, quantize, test vectors).

**What has and has not run (2026-10-08).** The Mac tools pass their host tests on a saved log, and the training script ran end to end on made-up data. **The board-side capture has not run**: the BP-BASSENSORSMKII sensor BoosterPack plug-in module has not arrived, so no number on this page comes from a real sensor. Compiling a model from this dataset with TI's Neural Network Compiler has not run either (the same compiler route has run for the four room-occupancy models of this repo), and TI Edge AI Studio was not run. **There is no board program you can flash**: the board file that connects this code to a LaunchPad is written when the sensor arrives.

Terms: [docs/vocab.md](../vocab.md) (CNN, NNC, inference, golden vectors). Also used here: **quantize**, store the model's numbers as 8-bit integers so it fits and runs fast on a small chip; **ONNX**, a standard file format for trained models, which TI's compiler reads; **logits**, the raw score the model gives each class (the highest wins); **test vectors**, saved inputs with known right answers; **BoosterPack plug-in module**, TI's name for a board that plugs on top of a LaunchPad development kit; **TI Edge AI Studio**, TI's point-and-click tool for training models; **CSV**, a text file with one row per line and commas between values; **I2C**, the two-wire bus the sensor talks on; **UART** and **baud**, the serial link to the Mac and its speed in bits a second; **virtual environment**, a private folder of Python packages for one project; **NPU**, the G5187's neural-network accelerator; **QAT** (quantization-aware training), retraining a model while simulating 8-bit numbers so it loses little accuracy when stored that way; **confusion matrix**, a table of which class the model said against the true class; **ring buffer**, a fixed-size buffer that overwrites its oldest entry. Problems carry a cause tag: **Tool or docs** (a tool or a page is missing or wrong), **TI example default** (a TI example's setting causes it), **Setup or handling** (how the board or the Mac is set up), **Chip limit** (the silicon cannot do it), **Unknown** (not found; "suspected" names the lead). Board errors and fixes: [mspm0g3507/FAQ.md](../../mspm0g3507/FAQ.md). 1 kB = 1,024 bytes; 1 GB = 1,024 MB. Machine: Intel MacBook (Core i7-8750H), macOS 15.7.9. TI pages read 2026-10-08.

Contents: [what a dataset is](#what-is-a-dataset-in-plain-words) · [what you need](#what-do-i-need) · [stream](#step-1-how-does-the-board-stream-samples) · [record and label](#step-2-how-do-i-record-and-label-on-the-mac) · [how much](#how-many-samples-per-class-and-how-do-i-know-i-have-enough) · [clean and check](#step-3-how-do-i-clean-and-check-the-data) · [train](#step-4-how-do-i-train-a-small-1-d-cnn) · [compile](#step-5-how-do-i-quantize-and-compile-it-with-tis-nnc) · [test on the board](#step-6-how-do-i-check-it-on-the-board-before-trusting-it-live) · [washer, sounds and TI's datasets](#what-about-washer-vibration-sound-clips-or-datasets-ti-already-ships) · [questions](#questions) · [next](#what-is-next)

## What is a dataset, in plain words?

| Word | Meaning here |
|---|---|
| Sample | One reading of every channel at one moment: one line of the CSV file |
| Channel | One measured quantity, such as `ax` (acceleration along x) |
| Class | One thing the model should recognize, such as `idle`, `shake` or `circle` |
| Label | The class written next to each sample, set by the key you pressed |
| Window | A fixed run of samples the model sees at once. 128 samples at 100 samples a second is 1.28 s |
| Stride | How far the next window starts after the last one. Stride 32 with window 128 means windows overlap by three quarters |
| Segment | One unbroken stretch of one label in one recording |
| Train, validation and test split | Data to learn from, data to tune on, and data kept back to grade the model. Split by whole segment, never by window: neighboring windows share most of their samples, so a test window would be a near copy of a training window and the score would look better than the model is |

Balance matters because a model learns to guess the biggest class. In the public room-occupancy dataset earlier models of this repo used, 8,228 of 10.1k rows are "empty room", so a model that always says "empty" scores 81% and is useless. Aim for about the same number of windows in each class; `check.py` warns above 1.5 to 1.

## What do I need?

| Item | Version or part | Note |
|---|---|---|
| LaunchPad development kit | LP-MSPM0G3507 or LP-MSPM0G5187 | The G5187 also has an NPU and a microphone |
| Motion sensor | BP-BASSENSORSMKII (sold at TI.com): Bosch BMI160 accelerometer and gyroscope at I2C address 0x69 | Or the BOOSTXL-EDUMKII's analog accelerometer (Kionix KXTC9-2050) |
| Recording | Python 3 (3.14.7 here), pyserial 3.5, matplotlib 3.11.2 for the optional plot | In a virtual environment, about 126 MB with both |
| Training | Python 3.12.13, torch 2.2.2, numpy 1.26.4, onnx 1.22.0, onnxruntime 1.23.2, TI `tinyml_torchmodelopt` 1.5.0 | About 1.0 GB. torch 2.2.2 is the last PyTorch build for Intel Macs |
| Compiling | TI NNC 2.1.2 and TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS | On GitHub's Linux machines, an Apple Silicon Mac, Linux or Windows; not on an Intel Mac |

Set up the recording environment (any folder works; this one is in your home folder):

```bash
python3 -m venv ~/ds-venv
```

```text
~/ds-venv/bin/pip install pyserial==3.5 matplotlib==3.11.2
```

**Run every command from the top folder of this repository.** Commands that need no extra packages work with any `python3`; the ones that plot or record use `~/ds-venv/bin/python`.

## Step 1: how does the board stream samples?

The board takes one reading at a fixed rate and prints it as one line: time in milliseconds, then each channel in raw sensor counts.

```text
# dataset-stream v1 rate_hz=100 sensor=bmi160
t_ms,ax,ay,az,gx,gy,gz
0,12,-40,16390,3,-2,1
10,15,-38,16401,2,-1,0
```

The code is `portability/dataset-stream/core/` (`ds_stream.c` for timing and formatting, `bmi160.c` for the sensor), with the loop and the per-board pins in [`portability/dataset-stream/README.md`](../../portability/dataset-stream/README.md) and [`boards/README.md`](../../portability/dataset-stream/boards/README.md). Three choices in it matter for the data:

- **Fixed rate from a timer, not a delay.** `t_ms` is the time the sample was due, so if the loop runs late the skipped samples show as a gap of whole periods, and the board also prints `# overrun <n>`.
- **Raw counts.** At the BMI160's +-2 g range, 16,384 counts is 1 g. Flat on the desk, `az` reads about 16,384.
- **Room on the serial link.** At 115200 baud the link carries 11.5 kB a second. A six-channel line is at most 52 bytes, so 221 lines a second is the worst-case limit; typical lines are 23 to 40 bytes, and 100 Hz leaves room either way.

The core is set to 100 Hz and six channels (accelerometer and gyroscope); another rate, range or channel set means changing `ds_init`'s rate and the register values in `bmi160.c`. The Bosch data sheet (BST-BMI160-DS000-09, register 0x7E) says the BMI160 starts in suspend mode after power-up and measures nothing until two commands wake it. `bmi160_init` sends them. The host test checks that sequence against a fake sensor:

```bash
portability/dataset-stream/test/run.sh
```

It prints 29 `ok` lines and `OK`. Not run on a board.

## Step 2: how do I record and label on the Mac?

Plug the LaunchPad in and find its serial port. The debug probe shows two; use the one whose name ends in 1.

```bash
ls /dev/cu.usbmodem*
```

For the LP-MSPM0G3507 used here the two are `/dev/cu.usbmodemMG3500011` and `/dev/cu.usbmodemMG3500014` (recorded in [mspm0g3507/FAQ.md](../../mspm0g3507/FAQ.md)). The middle part, `MG350001`, is the probe's serial number. If nothing is listed, try another cable: some USB cables carry power only.

Record, with your probe's serial in place of `MG350001`. Each `--keys` item is one letter, `=`, and a class name.

```text
~/ds-venv/bin/python tools/dataset/capture.py --serial MG350001 --keys i=idle,s=shake,c=circle --out gestures-1.csv
```

While it records, press `i` and hold the board still, press `s` and shake it, press `c` and draw circles in the air. Space marks rows "none" (kept in the file, ignored later); `q` stops. A status line shows the label, the row count and the measured rate every second. When it stops it prints the rate from the board's clock, any gaps, and the rows per class.

This is the summary from the host test (made-up sine waves, not a sensor):

```text
wrote 3200 rows to fx.csv
board clock: 100.00 Hz (median step 10 ms), 32.02 s, largest step off the median 0 ms
gaps: 1 (3 samples missing); board reported 3 skipped; time resets: 0; unreadable lines: 2
  circle           900 rows      9.0 s
  idle             900 rows      9.0 s
  none             500 rows      5.0 s
  shake            900 rows      9.0 s
```

Record each class in at least three recordings, on different days or with the board held differently. A recording is one file. The last recording of each class becomes the test set, so the model is graded on a recording it never saw.

## How many samples per class, and how do I know I have enough?

Start with three sessions of two minutes per class. At 100 Hz with 128-sample windows and stride 32, a two-minute segment gives about 367 windows after trimming, so about 1,100 per class. The windows overlap, so the number that really counts is sessions, not windows.

Two checks tell you if you have enough:

1. `check.py` warns below 100 windows or below 3 segments per class (both can be changed with `--min-windows` and `--min-segments`).
2. Train once with two recordings per class and once with three. If the score on the held-out recording still rises when you add a recording, record more recordings. If validation is high but the held-out recording is much lower, your recordings are too alike: vary the grip, the speed and the place.

## Step 3: how do I clean and check the data?

```text
~/ds-venv/bin/python tools/dataset/check.py gestures-1.csv gestures-2.csv gestures-3.csv --plot gestures.png
```

What it does and why:

- **Drops the first second and the last half second of every segment** (`--trim-start 1.0`, `--trim-end 0.5`). Those are the moments you were pressing the key or starting to move.
- **Checks the sample rate** from the board's clock in each file, and warns if files differ by more than 2% or more than 1% of samples are missing.
- **Counts windows per class** and how they fall into train, validation and test.
- **Warns on imbalance** above 1.5 to 1, on a board reset mid-recording (time going backwards), and on values stuck at the sensor's limit (-32768 or 32767), which means the range is too small for the motion.
- **Prints a per-class summary** (mean, spread, min, max per channel). If two classes look the same here, the model will struggle too.
- **Plots** the first segment of each class with `--plot` (needs matplotlib). Look at it: shaking should look like a fast wave, circles like two slow waves a quarter turn apart, idle like flat lines.

It exits with 0 when every check passes and 1 with a `WARN` line for each problem. On the test log with the default 128-sample windows it warns that 3 windows per class is too few, which is right for 9 seconds per class.

| Warning | What to do |
|---|---|
| `fewer than 100: record more` | Record more of that class |
| `segment(s), fewer than 3` | Record that class in more separate sessions |
| `classes unbalanced` | Record more of the smallest class |
| `samples missing (more than 1%)` | Lower the rate, send fewer channels, or close other programs using the port |
| `clock went backwards` | The board reset; split the file at the reset or record again |
| `values at the sensor's limit` | Raise the range: in `bmi160_init` (`core/bmi160.c`), change the write to register 0x41 (the sensor's `ACC_RANGE` register) from 0x03 to 0x05 (+-4 g, 8,192 counts per g), record again, and pass `--scale 8192` to `train.py` |

Run the tool tests (no board):

```bash
python3 tools/dataset/test_dataset.py
```

It prints 22 `ok` lines and `OK`.

## Step 4: how do I train a small 1-D CNN?

Training needs a second Python environment, about 1.0 GB, built once by the steps in [`mspm0g3507/mcu-bench/edgeai/README.md`](../../mspm0g3507/mcu-bench/edgeai/README.md) (Python 3.12, because torch 2.2.2, the last PyTorch build for Intel Macs, does not install on 3.14). The command below runs it from there, `~/tinyml-bench/venv`. Recording uses `~/ds-venv`; training uses this one.

The recipe is the one the room-occupancy models of this repo used ([`mspm0g3507/mcu-bench/edgeai/README.md`](../../mspm0g3507/mcu-bench/edgeai/README.md)): train in PyTorch, then retrain with TI's NPU-style 8-bit quantization (`TINPUTinyMLQATFxModule` from TI's `tinyml_torchmodelopt`), export to ONNX, fold constants. That page has the environment setup, including why `tinyml_torchmodelopt` goes in with `--no-deps` on an Intel Mac and the two small fixes `train.py` carries for torch 2.2.2.

```text
~/tinyml-bench/venv/bin/python tools/dataset/train.py gestures-model gestures-1.csv gestures-2.csv gestures-3.csv --channels ax,ay,az --gen-c
```

The model (`--model tiny`, the default) is batch norm on the input (it rescales each channel to a steady range), a 1-D convolution of 8 filters 5 samples wide, a max pool, a convolution of 16 filters 3 wide, global average pooling and one fully connected layer. Input shape `(1, 3, 128, 1)`, TI's layout of channels, time, width 1. Raw counts are divided by `--scale` (16,384, so inputs are in g). It follows TI's NPU rules: channel counts multiples of 4, kernels 3 or 5, at least 16 inputs to the last layer.

What it writes to the output folder:

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `model_tinpu_int8.onnx` | The quantized model, the file TI's NNC and Edge AI Studio take |
| `result.json` | Float and 8-bit accuracy on the held-out segments, confusion matrix, which segments went where |
| `test_vectors.h` | Held-out windows (5 per class), their true class, and the class and logits onnxruntime gives |
| `labels.h` | Class names in output order and the input scale |
| `ds_model.c`, `.h` (with `--gen-c`) | A plain integer C version of the same model, checked against onnxruntime on every test window |

Measured on the made-up data (three sessions of 30 seconds per class, 258 test windows): the whole script took 10.9 s, the plain C gave the same logits as onnxruntime on 258 of 258 windows, and the model is 39,984 multiply-adds (one multiplication and one addition each) per inference with 795 bytes of weights. Built for a Cortex-M0+ with TI Arm Clang 4.0.4.LTS at `-Os` (the copy installed on this Mac; the compile job in step 5 uses 5.1.1.LTS) the plain C is 1.7 kB of code and 4.4 kB of RAM. Its accuracy was 100%, which says only that sine waves are easy; your real number comes from your real recordings.

## Step 5: how do I quantize and compile it with TI's NNC?

The model is already quantized by step 4. NNC turns the ONNX file into `tvmgen_default.h` and `mod.a` for the chip. TI publishes NNC 2.1.2 for Linux x86-64, Windows and Apple Silicon Macs, all on Python 3.10 (wheel index read 2026-10-08). There is no Intel Mac build. **Tool or docs.** On an Intel Mac, use one of these routes.

**Route 1: GitHub's Linux machines.** [`mspm0g3507/.github/workflows/nnc-compile.yml`](../../mspm0g3507/.github/workflows/nnc-compile.yml) installs NNC 2.1.2 and TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS, checks both downloads against checksums, and compiles for the LP-MSPM0G3507 CPU and the LP-MSPM0G5187 NPU (and a C2000 target); its first run, for the four occupancy models, took 2 minutes 9 seconds. GitHub runs a workflow only from `.github/workflows/` at the top of a repository, so copy the file there in a private repository of your own. Put `train.py`'s output folder (say `gestures-model/`, which holds `model_tinpu_int8.onnx`) in the repository, set `MODELS_DIR` to the folder above it, and replace the four occupancy names in the workflow's loops with `gestures-model`. Push, then start it and download the result (`<you>/<repo>` is your repository):

```text
gh workflow run nnc-compile.yml -R <you>/<repo>
```

```text
gh run download -R <you>/<repo> --name nnc-occupancy
```

The compile line it runs for the G3507 CPU is below; for the G5187 NPU the target is `"c, ti-npu"`. `$OPTS` is the TI Arm Clang options line set in the workflow, from TI's NNC user's guide (MSPM0 section).

```text
tvmc compile --target="c, ti-npu type=soft" --target-c-mcpu=cortex-m0plus model_tinpu_int8.onnx -o mod.a --cross-compiler="tiarmclang" --cross-compiler-options="$OPTS"
```

**Route 2: an Apple Silicon Mac, Linux or Windows with Python 3.10.** Install NNC from TI's package index, then run the same `tvmc` line with TI Arm Clang on the `PATH`:

```bash
pip3 install --extra-index-url https://software-dl.ti.com/mctools/esd/tvm/mcu ti_mcu_nnc
```

**Route 3: TI Edge AI Studio, point and click.** Edge AI Studio for Microcontrollers is version 1.7.0 (released 2026-07-11); the desktop app is for Windows and Linux only, so on a Mac use the cloud version at <https://dev.ti.com/edgeaistudio/> with a myTI account. TI's MSPM0 guide ("Deploying Machine Learning Models on TI MSPM0 Microcontrollers Using CCStudio Edge AI Studio GUI Tools", SDK docs, read 2026-10-08) gives these steps: create a project with the "Generic Time Series" task, import your data on the Capture tab, pick the device (MSPM0G5187 for the NPU, or MSPM0G3507) on the Model Selection tab, train on the Train tab, compile, and download the compiled model from the Deploy tab. The download holds an `artifacts` folder and a `golden_vectors` folder with `test_vector.c` and `user_input_config.h`.

Edge AI Studio and TI's command-line flow (tinyml-tensorlab) read a fixed folder layout: `classes/<class>/*.csv` plus optional `annotations/instances_train_list.txt`, `instances_val_list.txt` and `instances_test_list.txt` (Tiny ML Tensorlab user guide 1.4.0, "Classification Dataset Format"). `check.py` writes it, split by segment like `train.py`:

```bash
python3 tools/dataset/check.py gestures-1.csv gestures-2.csv gestures-3.csv --export-ti gestures-ti
```

TI's guide says a zip must have `classes/` at its top level, with no extra folder above it:

```bash
cd gestures-ti && zip -r ../gestures-ti.zip classes annotations && cd ..
```

Each exported file starts with a `time_ms` column; TI's loader drops any column whose name contains "time".

Two things on TI's pages to know. **Tool or docs.** TI's MSPM0 guide tells you to import `examples/nortos/LP_MSPM0G5187/edgeAI/time_series_data_capture/`; in MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07 the folder is `timeseries_data_capture`, and it has no `artifacts` folder or `test_vector.c` to overwrite, so you add those files rather than replace them. **Unknown.** The Tiny ML Tensorlab guide's comparison table lists the GUI's task types as "Arc Fault, Motor Fault", while the MSPM0 guide shows a generic time-series project; which applies to a new classifier in version 1.7.0 was not checked.

## Step 6: how do I check it on the board before trusting it live?

This board program is not written; the steps below are the plan, and nothing in this step has run. Run the held-out test vectors first. Build a small program that feeds each window in `test_vectors.h` to the model and compares the answer with `ds_test_expected_class`. With the plain C model, the logits must match `ds_test_expected_logits` exactly. With NNC, its float outputs should equal those integers: on the occupancy models all 80 values matched on the LP-MSPM0G3507. The harness for those models is the pattern: [`mspm0g3507/mcu-bench/edgeai-sdk/occupancy-nnc/main.c`](../../mspm0g3507/mcu-bench/edgeai-sdk/occupancy-nnc/main.c).

Only when every vector matches, go live:

1. Keep the last 128 samples of `ax`, `ay`, `az` in a ring buffer.
2. Every 32 new samples, copy them out oldest first as `[channel][sample]`, divide by 16,384, and run the model.
3. Print the class name from `labels.h` over the same serial port.
4. Do each motion 20 times and count the right answers. That count, not the training score, is the number to report.

If the vectors match but live answers are wrong, compare a live window with a recorded one: the usual suspects are axes in a different order, a different scale, or the board mounted differently from when you recorded.

## What about washer vibration, sound clips, or datasets TI already ships?

They have their own page: [docs/guides/dataset-variants.md](dataset-variants.md) covers recording a washer's phases with the same tools, collecting sound clips on the LP-MSPM0G5187, the stored test data in TI's AI examples, and two public datasets with their licenses.

## Questions

### Why might my BMI160 read all zeros for motion?

Send the two wake-up commands first (register 0x7E: 0x11, then 0x15), as `bmi160_init` does. **Tag: Unknown (suspected: TI example default).** The data sheet says both sensors start in suspend mode, and TI's `data_sensor_aggregator` example reads the data registers without ever writing 0x7E. This has not been seen: the BoosterPack has not arrived.

### What do I flash on the board before recording?

A program built from `portability/dataset-stream/` plus a board file for your LaunchPad. Not written: the board file does not exist for any board in this repo; `portability/dataset-stream/boards/README.md` lists the pins each one needs.

### Why do I need three sessions when one long recording gives thousands of windows?

Because the test must be a recording the model never saw. The tools split by segment (one unbroken stretch of one label), so a class needs at least three segments, and separate sessions make them differ the way real use will. With one segment per class, `check.py` puts every window in training and `train.py` stops with "every class needs windows in train and test". With two, one is training and one is test, with nothing to tune on.

### What happens to rows labeled "none"?

They stay in the CSV file and every tool skips them. Use space to mark the moments between classes (picking the board up, resting) so they do not teach the model anything.

### Does this work on Windows or Linux?

`check.py` and `train.py` do. `capture.py` reads key presses the macOS and Linux way (`termios`), so it is not written for Windows; pass the port with `--port` (on Linux usually `/dev/ttyACM0`). Tested only on macOS 15.7.9.

### Can I run TI's NNC on an Intel Mac?

No: TI's index has NNC 2.1.2 wheels for Linux x86-64, Windows and Apple Silicon Macs only (checked 2026-10-08). **Tag: Tool or docs.** Compile on GitHub's Linux machines with `nnc-compile.yml`, or use Edge AI Studio's cloud version.

### Will the model run on the LP-MSPM0L1306?

Not this one: the 3-channel, 128-sample plain-C model needs 4.4 kB of RAM and the chip has 4 kB. **Tag: Chip limit.** Stream data from the L1306 if you like, and run the model on a G3507 or G5187, or train a smaller window.

### Why is TI's "time_series_data_capture" folder missing?

In MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07 it is spelled `timeseries_data_capture`. **Tag: Tool or docs.** TI's Edge AI Studio guide for MSPM0 uses the other spelling.

### What does "unreadable lines: 2" in the capture summary mean?

Usually nothing to fix. **Tag: Setup or handling.** Expected, not seen on a board: a port opened in the middle of a line cuts that line in half. In the host test the 2 unreadable lines are a boot line and a cut-off line. `capture.py` counts any line that is not a comment, the header or a full row of whole numbers as unreadable and leaves it out of the CSV file. If the count keeps rising during a recording, check the baud rate (115200) and the cable.

### What do the "# overrun" lines mean?

The board was late and skipped that many samples. `capture.py` adds them up ("board reported 3 skipped") and leaves them out of the CSV file; `check.py` finds the same gap from the `t_ms` values and warns above 1% missing.

### capture.py says "stdin is not a terminal: no key presses, every row is labeled none; stop with --seconds". Why?

Run it in a Terminal window. **Tag: Setup or handling.** It was started with its input redirected or from a script, so it cannot read key presses. Use `--seconds` to stop it when you only want to test the link.

### I pressed the wrong key mid-recording. What now?

Press the right key at once. **Tag: Setup or handling.** The wrong label lasts until your next key press. Note the time; afterwards delete those rows from the CSV file or change their label column to `none`. The 1 s trim at the start of each segment hides a short slip.

### Why one Python for recording and another for training?

Recording needs only pyserial (and matplotlib for the plot), which install on any Python 3. Training needs torch 2.2.2, the last PyTorch for Intel Macs, which installs only up to Python 3.12. On an Apple Silicon Mac one Python 3.12 environment can hold both; not run.

## Limits

No LaunchPad board file exists for `portability/dataset-stream`, so no real recording, held-out score or on-board test-vector run is on this page. Edge AI Studio's cloud route and the LP-MSPM0G5187 microphone path have not been tried.

# How do I collect washer vibration (BMI160 on BP-BASSENSORSMKII) or sound clips (LP-MSPM0G5187) for a TI MSPM0 model, and which datasets does TI already ship?

Washer phases use the same tools as gestures: tape the board to the lid and press a key when the machine changes phase. Sound clips on the LP-MSPM0G5187 are labeled by folder instead of by key. And most of TI's AI examples already carry stored test data that shows the window shape each model expects. The main guide, with the tools and every step: [docs/guides/collect-a-dataset.md](collect-a-dataset.md).

**Status (2026-10-08).** None of this has been recorded on a board: the BP-BASSENSORSMKII sensor BoosterPack plug-in module and the LP-MSPM0G5187 have not arrived. The tables of TI's datasets are read from the SDKs installed on this Mac.

Terms: [docs/vocab.md](../vocab.md) and the terms in [the main guide](collect-a-dataset.md). Cause tags: **Unknown** (not found or not run; "suspected" names the lead), **Setup or handling** (how the board is set up or mounted). **Harmonic**: a vibration at a whole multiple of the main one. **Regression**: a model that outputs a number instead of a class. 1 kB = 1,024 bytes.

## Can I record "is the washer running" the same way?

Yes, with the same tools. Tape the LaunchPad and BoosterPack to the washer lid, power it from a USB battery or a long cable, and use keys such as `o=off,w=wash,p=spin`. A key press sets the label until the next one, so you only press when the machine changes phase. One wash cycle is one recording; record three different cycles. At 100 samples a second a recording can show shaking up to 50 Hz. A drum at 1,200 rpm shakes at 20 Hz, and its second harmonic (40 Hz) is close to that limit, so try 200 Hz, which shows up to 100 Hz. No washer has been recorded, so 200 Hz is a starting guess, not a tested setting. To change it, in `bmi160_init` (`core/bmi160.c`) change the write to register 0x40 (the sensor's `ACC_CONF` register) from 0x28 to 0x29, change the write to register 0x42 (`GYR_CONF`) from 0x28 to 0x29 so the gyroscope keeps up, and set the rate in `ds_init` to 200. Six channels at 200 Hz still fit the serial link: at most 52 bytes a line is 10.2 kB a second, against 11.3 kB at 115200 baud. TI's G3519 `washer_load_ai` example estimates the load from motor data instead; it needs no sensor but cannot tell you the phase of your own machine.

## How do I collect sound clips on the LP-MSPM0G5187?

For sounds, label by file instead of by key: one folder per class, one short clip per file (for example `clips/knock/knock_001.wav`). Two ways to get audio from the G5187:

- **The onboard microphone through TI's USB microphone example.** `examples/nortos/LP_MSPM0G5187/tinyusb/device_uac_microphone_i2s` makes the board a USB microphone: its `tusb_config.h` sets 48k samples a second, one channel, 2 bytes per sample, and its product string is `MicNode`. Plug a second cable into the chip's own USB-C port (bottom right), pick it as the input in Audacity or macOS's QuickTime Player, and record. Not run: the board has not arrived.
- **TI's wake-word input.** `edgeAI/wakeword_detection_ai_npu` samples an analog microphone on header pin 6 at 8 kHz and turns each 20 ms frame into 70 features. Record at 8 kHz from the same microphone if you want your clips to match what that model hears.

Keep every clip the same length and rate (1 s at 16 kHz mono 16-bit matches Google Speech Commands, below). This prints rate, channels and length for every clip, using only Python's standard library:

```bash
python3 -c "import wave,glob;[print(f, w.getframerate(), w.getnchannels(), round(w.getnframes()/w.getframerate(),2)) for f in sorted(glob.glob('clips/*/*.wav')) for w in [wave.open(f)]]"
```

Balance and recording rules are the same: similar clip counts per class, and test clips from a recording recording the model never trained on.

## Datasets TI already ships

TI's AI examples run on stored test data, so most need no sensor. That data is a good template for your own: it shows the window shape and the channel layout each model expects. From MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07 (`examples/nortos/LP_<board>/edgeAI/`):

| Example | Boards | Stored input | Classes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `hello_world_ai` | G3507, G3519, G5187 | 128 samples, one channel (`hello_world_testvector.h`) | sawtooth, sine, square |
| `gearbox_fault_diagnosis_ai` | G3507, G3519, G5187 | 4 vibration channels by 256 samples, from the public Kaggle "Gearbox Fault Diagnosis" data (SpectraQuest simulator) | healthy, broken tooth |
| `electrical_fault_ai_npu` | G5187 | 6 channels (currents and voltages) by 128 | no fault and five fault types |
| `linear_actuator_fault_ai` | G3519, G5187 | 3 channels by 1,600 | normal, spalling, lack of lubrication, backlash |
| `glass_break_detection_ai_npu` | G5187 | one clip of 24,000 16-bit samples | glass break, normal, similar sound |
| `machine_readable_code_classification_ai_npu` | G5187 | 28 by 28 image | QR code, barcode, other |
| `motor_temperature_ai`, `washer_load_ai` | G3519 (G5187 for the first) | motor signals | numbers, not classes (regression) |

C2000Ware 26.02 (`libraries/ai/examples/`), the MSPM33 SDK 1.04 and the AM13E230x SDK 26.01 ship `test_vector.c` files with golden outputs made by TI's ModelMaker, for arc fault, motor bearing fault (six classes), blower imbalance, fan blade anomaly and others. The `*_data_capture` examples (such as `timeseries_data_capture`, which samples the ADC at 5 kHz and sends it at 115200 baud) and `*_live_preview` examples stream to Edge AI Studio instead of to a CSV file; they are TI's own route to the same goal.

## Public datasets and their licenses

| Dataset | What it is | License (read 2026-10-08) |
|---|---|---|
| UCI Room Occupancy Estimation, id 864, <https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/864/room+occupancy+estimation> | 10.1k rows, one every 30 s: light, sound, CO2, PIR and temperature; 0 to 3 people. The four occupancy models were trained on it | CC BY 4.0: credit Singh and Chaudhari and the UCI repository |
| Google Speech Commands v0.02, <https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.03209> | 105,829 one-second clips of 35 words; download 2.26 GB from `storage.googleapis.com/download.tensorflow.org/data/speech_commands_v0.02.tar.gz` | CC BY 4.0, stated in the paper |

## Three questions an accuracy number can answer, and which one you are reading

A model page here can carry three different numbers, and they must not be read as one (adopted 2026-10-09):

1. **Did the port reproduce the model?** The 20 stored test vectors (occupancy) or the 10 shipped digits (BitNetMCU) give the same class on the board as on the Mac. That is a functional check of the port and the compiler. It says nothing about how often the model is right. Class agreement is also not identical numbers: an int8 NPU build can differ from the CPU build by a count in a logit and still agree on the class, and the pages say so where it happened.
2. **How accurate is the model on data it did not train on?** A held-out metric with the split named. The occupancy models' published 90.9 percent (8k model, int8) is on 1,001 windows cut in 48-minute blocks from the same room and the same days as the training data; neighboring blocks share conditions, so it is an optimistic figure. The stricter protocol holds out whole days: `tools/dataset/eval_occupancy.py --split day` freezes the split (test days 2018/01/10 and 2018/01/11) before any training, writes the windows for `train.py`, scores a model trained on them, and refuses to score when train and test share a block or day, when the windows do not match the model's input, or when a label is missing. The record it writes carries the dataset and model hashes, the window counts, the class distribution and the metric definitions. The dataset is one room: no split here measures a new room.
3. **Does it work in a real room?** Only a recorded trial with live sensors answers this, and none has been run for the occupancy models. The digit demo read finger-drawn digits on the touch screen, but nobody counted hits and misses, so it has no real-world accuracy either.

## Questions

### Is 200 Hz the right rate for a washer?

Start there and check the plot. **Tag: Unknown.** It is a starting guess from the drum speed, not a tested setting: no washer has been recorded. If the plot of the spin phase looks smooth with no fast wave, the rate is high enough; if it looks jagged at every sample, try higher.

### My washer phases all look the same in the plot. What now?

Mount the board more firmly and record again. **Tag: Unknown (suspected: Setup or handling).** Not seen here; a loose board or soft tape damps the shaking. Tape it flat to a hard panel, not the lid's soft edge, and keep the same spot for every recording.

### The LP-MSPM0G5187 gives no audio as a USB microphone. Why?

**Tag: Unknown.** Check that the second USB cable is in the chip's own USB-C port (bottom right), not the probe's, and that `MicNode` is picked as the input.

FILE: docs/guides/demos-only.md | How do I flash a TI demo onto an LP-EM-CC2340R5 or LP-CC1354P10-1 without building it?

# How do I flash a TI demo onto an LP-EM-CC2340R5 or LP-CC1354P10-1 without building it?

Run one script in Terminal: `python3 tools/demo_flash.py flash LP_EM_CC2340R5 basic_ble_app --yes`. It backs the board up, then flashes TI's ready-made Bluetooth example from the SDK, with no compiler and no CCStudio. `--yes` means go ahead; without it nothing changes.

**Limits.** The list and the dry run below ran on 2026-10-07. The real flash with `--yes` and the restore have not been run, so the backup folder this page describes has not been made on the test Mac. Time: about 10 minutes hands-on once the software is installed (estimate, not measured).

Terms: [docs/vocab.md](../vocab.md). The [SDK](../vocab.md) is TI's kit of examples for one chip family; [UniFlash](../vocab.md) is TI's flashing tool; the [probe](../vocab.md) ([XDS110](../vocab.md)) is the small debugger between the Mac's USB port and the chip; a [hex file](../vocab.md) is a built program ready to flash. Errors and fixes: the FAQ at the end of this page, [cc2340r5/FAQ.md](../../cc2340r5/FAQ.md) and [cc1354p10/FAQ.md](../../cc1354p10/FAQ.md). Checked on an Intel Mac, macOS 15.7.9, Python 3.14.7, UniFlash 9.6.0, SimpleLink Low Power F3 SDK 9.21.00.36 LTS, SimpleLink CC13xx CC26xx SDK 8.33.00.16. 1 kB = 1,024 bytes.

Contents: what you need; step 0, open Terminal; step 1, list the demos; step 2, dry run; step 3, back up and flash; what can go wrong; FAQ; next.

## What do I need first?

- **UniFlash 9.6.0 and the SDK for your board, under `/Applications/ti`.** The LP-EM-CC2340R5 needs the SimpleLink Low Power F3 SDK; the LP-CC1354P10-1 needs the SimpleLink CC13xx CC26xx SDK. Each is a macOS installer from ti.com (`ti.com/tool/download/UNIFLASH`, `ti.com/tool/download/SIMPLELINK-LOWPOWER-F3-SDK`, `ti.com/tool/SIMPLELINK-CC13XX-CC26XX-SDK`); install each to `/Applications/ti`, where the script looks. Room needed while installing: about 2.2 GB for UniFlash and 4.8 GB for the F3 SDK ([mac-setup/README.md](../../mac-setup/README.md) has the disk table). Or run this repo's installer, which adds UniFlash and the F3 SDK along with CCStudio and the rest of the kit (about 20 GB in all; not the CC13xx CC26xx SDK): `./mac-setup/bootstrap.sh --all` from the repo folder, explained in [mac-setup/README.md](../../mac-setup/README.md).
- **The board plugged in by USB.** The LP-EM-CC2340R5 has no USB port of its own; it needs its separate probe. The connection file (`.ccxml`) for each board is in its folder,; its probe serial number is the one `python3 tools/frl/frl.py detect` prints.
- **Python 3.** Open Terminal and run `python3 --version`. If macOS offers to install the Command Line Tools, accept; it takes several minutes.

## Step 0: Open Terminal and go to the repo (Terminal and Finder)

Every command on this page runs from the repo folder. A copy of the repository must be on your Mac ([START.md](../../START.md) shows how to clone it). If you are reading this page from a folder on your Mac, that folder is it.

1. Press Command-Space, type Terminal, press Return. A window opens with a line waiting for you to type.
2. Type `cd` (the letters c and d, then a space) and do not press Return. In Finder, find the repo folder and drag it onto the Terminal window: its path appears after `cd`. Now press Return. The folder can be anywhere.
3. Check you are in the right folder. This prints the folder's path:

```text
pwd
```

This prints `tools/demo_flash.py`:

```bash
ls tools/demo_flash.py
```

If it prints `ls: tools/demo_flash.py: No such file or directory`, you are in another folder; do step 2 again.

4. Check Python 3 is there. This prints a version such as `Python 3.14.7`:

```bash
python3 --version
```

If it prints a line ending in `command not found: python3`, install Python 3 from python.org (its macOS installer), then close Terminal and open it again. If macOS instead offers to install the Command Line Tools, accept; that also gives you Python 3 and takes several minutes.

## Step 1: What demos can I flash? (Terminal)

```bash
python3 tools/demo_flash.py list LP_EM_CC2340R5
```

The script names the boards `LP_EM_CC2340R5` and `LP_EM_CC1354P10_1`, with underscores; type them exactly, and `python3 tools/demo_flash.py list` with no board name shows them all.

The list shows every prebuilt hex file TI ships for that board. Hex size is the size of the hex file on disk. A hex file stores each byte as two text characters plus addresses, so it is about twice the bytes it puts in flash. On 2026-10-07 the LP-EM-CC2340R5 menu was:

| Name | Hex size (kB) | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `basic_ble_app` | 533 | Bluetooth LE example |
| `data_stream_app` | 528 | Bluetooth LE data stream example |
| `host_test_app` | 680 | Bluetooth test image for a host computer |
| four `mcuboot_*` images | 33 to 42 | Boot and update images, refused unless you add `--allow-boot` |

The LP-CC1354P10-1 menu on 2026-10-07 had `project_zero_app` (508), `simple_peripheral_app` (480), `simple_central_app` (480) and `host_test_app` (580), plus boot and update images. The LP-MSPM0G3507 has none: it flashes through [OpenOCD](../vocab.md), which this tool does not drive.

## Step 2: What will it do to my board? (Terminal)

```bash
python3 tools/demo_flash.py flash LP_EM_CC2340R5 basic_ble_app
```

With no `--yes`, this prints the exact UniFlash command and what it would back up, and changes nothing. Read it. On 2026-10-07 it printed this (paths shortened):

```text
board   LP_EM_CC2340R5 (probe LS470GTU)
demo    basic_ble_app  533 kB hex from simplelink_lowpower_f3_sdk_9_21_00_36_LTS
backup  would read: 0x0 for 524288 bytes, 0x4e020000 for 2048 bytes
command /Applications/ti/uniflash_9.6.0/dslite.sh --mode flash -c .../cc2340r5/CC2340R5.ccxml -e -f -u .../prebuilt_hexfiles/basic_ble_app.hex

DRY RUN: nothing was read or written. Add --yes to back up, flash and print the restore command.
```

In that command, `-e` is `--verbose` (it prints progress; it does not erase), `-f` loads the file into flash, and `-u` runs it afterward. UniFlash's default settings for the CC23xx chips are believed to erase the whole chip during every load, so what is on the board now is gone unless it is backed up; that is not checked (the CC2340R5 FAQ entry "How do I make a TI Zigbee example forget my network?" says the same). The setting on the CC1354P10 is not checked either, so treat it the same way. That is why the following step backs it up.

## Step 3: Back up and flash (Terminal)

```bash
python3 tools/demo_flash.py flash LP_EM_CC2340R5 basic_ble_app --yes
```

The script reads the chip's flash and its configuration area to a new folder under `<scratch>/runs/demo-flash/`, outside the repo because the backup can hold network keys. It stops without flashing if a read fails, if a file is the wrong size, or if the backup looks blank. Then it flashes.

What the output should look like (from the script's code; not run): the same four lines as the dry run, then `backup ok in <folder>`, then the end of UniFlash's own log, then `flash ok in <seconds> s`, then `to put the board back:` and one long command. Success is `flash ok`. Copy the restore command somewhere safe: select it in Terminal with the mouse, press Command-C, and paste it into a text file with Command-V. Leave the board's backup folder where it is; the restore command points to it.

To check the demo runs, scan with a phone Bluetooth app such as nRF Connect or LightBlue. TI's source for `basic_ble_app` names it `Basic BLE project` (in `basic_ble.syscfg`), and it advertises the 16-bit service `0xFFF0`; not checked: that the prebuilt file uses the same name. On the LP-CC1354P10-1, `project_zero_app` advertises as `Project Zero`. Bluetooth examples advertise; they do not blink.

The backup reads use UniFlash's `memory --range`, whose length counts 32-bit words, not bytes. The script divides by four and checks the file size, so a unit slip is caught.

## What can go wrong?

- **The connection fails.** **Setup or handling.** Check the probe's serial number in the `.ccxml`, press the board into its probe fully, and try another USB port. The CC2340R5 [FAQ](../../cc2340r5/FAQ.md) lists each UniFlash error.
- **Error -242, `A router subpath could not be accessed`, on the LP-CC1354P10-1.** **Unknown (suspected: Chip limit).** UniFlash allowed one connection per power-up while a Bluetooth program was running on this board. Unplug and replug the board before the backup, and again before the flash if it fails. Not run through this script.
- **A demo you flash replaces what was running.** **Setup or handling.** On a board that runs something you care about, such as a Zigbee light, keep the restore command and run it when you are done. The restore has not been run.
- **The demo does nothing you can see.** **TI example default.** Bluetooth examples advertise; they do not blink. Use a phone Bluetooth scanner, and read the example's own README in the SDK.

## FAQ

### The script says "REFUSED: ... is a boot manager or update image"

Leave the `mcuboot_*` images alone unless you are setting up over-the-air updates; if you are, add `--allow-boot`. **Tag: Setup or handling.** The script refuses them on purpose with `REFUSED: <name> is a boot manager or update image. It can replace the part of flash that decides what boots. Add --allow-boot if you mean it.` (seen 2026-10-07 in a dry run).

### The script stops with "REFUSED: backup looks blank. Nothing was flashed."

The chip read back as empty, so there was nothing to back up. **Tag: Unknown.** Not seen. A new or erased board reads this way, and so could a read that failed without an error. If the board really is empty, run the UniFlash command the dry run printed yourself; there is nothing to lose.

### The script stops with "REFUSED: memory read at 0x0 failed"

The full line ends `(wanted 524288 bytes, got ...)`. Fix the connection and run it again; nothing was flashed. **Tag: Unknown (suspected: Setup or handling).** The backup file came out the wrong size, which usually means the probe lost the board during the read. Not seen with this script.

### Flashing the LP-CC1354P10-1 fails with error -242, "A router subpath could not be accessed"

Unplug the board's USB cable, plug it back in, and run the command again. **Tag: Unknown (suspected: Chip limit).** While a Bluetooth program runs, the debugger reached this chip once per power-up in the tests; a pin reset through the probe did not help, and a different probe was not run. More in [cc1354p10/FAQ.md](../../cc1354p10/FAQ.md) and [tools/gatt_gen/README.md](../../tools/gatt_gen/README.md).

### How do I open Terminal and get to the repo folder?

Press Command-Space, type Terminal, press Return, type `cd` with a space, drag the repo folder from Finder onto the window, and press Return. **Tag: Setup or handling.** Every command on this page assumes you are in that folder; from anywhere else the script is not found. `ls tools/demo_flash.py` checks it. Step 0 above has the details.

### Will flashing a demo erase what is on my board now?

Assume yes, and let the script back the board up first. **Tag: Unknown.** UniFlash's default settings for the CC23xx chips are believed to erase the whole chip during every load, but that is not checked. The setting on the CC1354P10 was not checked either. The backup and the restore command are there so nothing is lost.

### How do I put the original firmware back?

Run the `to put the board back:` command the script printed after the flash; it writes the backup to the board. **Tag: Unknown.** The restore has not been run. To put TI's own demo back instead, flash `basic_ble_app` with this script; the CC2340R5 FAQ entry "How do I put TI's own Bluetooth demo back on the board?" has the details.

### How long does flashing a prebuilt demo take?

Not measured. **Tag: Unknown.** The estimate is about 10 minutes hands-on once UniFlash and the SDK are installed, most of it reading the output; the installs themselves take longer (see [mac-setup/README.md](../../mac-setup/README.md)).

### Can I use Web Bluetooth on my phone to see the demo?

On Android, Chrome has Web Bluetooth; on an iPhone, no browser does. **Tag: Third-party behavior.** MDN's compatibility data lists Safari, including Safari on iPhone, and Firefox as not supporting it (checked 2026-10-07). To see a demo on an iPhone, use a scanner app such as nRF Connect or LightBlue. The test page is [ports/ecosystem/webble/README.md](../../ports/ecosystem/webble/README.md).

### I flashed a demo and nothing blinks

That is expected for the Bluetooth demos: they advertise, they do not blink. **Tag: TI example default.** To see one, scan with a phone app such as nRF Connect or LightBlue. `basic_ble_app` advertises the name "Basic BLE project" and the 16-bit service UUID 0xFFF0, both set in TI's `basic_ble.syscfg` (F3 SDK 9.21.00.36 LTS). Not run on this board with this script.

### My Mac shows the old services after I flash a new demo

Restart Bluetooth on the Mac, or forget the device on a phone. **Tag: Third-party behavior.** macOS keeps a board's list of services per Bluetooth address and does not reread it after a reflash.

## Where do I go next?

Step 3 is the next move: run it on a board and time it. To change a demo you have to build it: [how to blink an LED on an LP-EM-CC2340R5 from a Mac](../../cc2340r5/README.md).

FILE: docs/guides/evaluate-a-presence-radar.md | How do I tell whether a TI 60 GHz presence radar (IWRL6432) would work in my conference room, how many people it would see, and at what range?

# How do I tell whether a TI 60 GHz presence radar (IWRL6432) would work in my conference room, how many people it would see, and at what range?

**Measured for 2x2 and 2x3, one pass each; 1x1 is refused by the demo.** With 2 transmit by 2 receive and with all antennas (2 by 3), an empty room for 60 s gave 0 flags in 240 frames, and a person sitting still at 2 m and at 4 m was held in 100 percent of frames. The radar flagged the person 3.9 to 6.7 s after the cue and cleared 10.7 to 14.1 s after they left, which is the demo's own hold time. A walk-in from behind the door was first flagged at about 6.5 m on 2x3. The 1x1 setting is refused with the shipped lines (error -40107). Single passes give no spread, so a difference of a second or two between 2x2 and 2x3 is inside the person's own timing. Nothing past 4 m seated or 7 m walking was tested. The demo also gives no head count: it reports four floor zones as occupied or not. The method: run the same short test with one, two and all three receive antennas on, record what the radar reports, and read five numbers: how far away a walking person is first seen (up to the 7 m edge of the zone boxes), how far away a person sitting still is still seen, how long it takes to notice an arrival and a departure, and how often it alarms in an empty room. Those say whether the radar would work in a room that size. A head count needs TI's people-tracking configuration, which has not been run here. Every cell below says whether it is measured, arithmetic, or not measured.

Terms: [docs/vocab.md](../vocab.md). Also used here: **FMCW radar**, a radar that sends a rising-frequency chirp and reads range from the frequency difference of the echo; **TX and RX**, transmit and receive antennas; **virtual antenna**, one transmit and receive pair treated as one antenna element (2 TX by 3 RX gives 6); **SNR**, signal-to-noise ratio, how far an echo stands above the noise; **TLV**, a typed block inside the radar's data frame; **zone**, one of the floor boxes the demo reports on or off; **range profile and bin**, the echo strength at each distance step (a bin is one step, 0.121 m here); **azimuth and elevation**, the angle across the room and the angle up and down; **FoV**, field of view; **FFT**, the calculation that turns samples into distance, speed or angle; **WCSP and AOP**, two package types of the same chip family (antenna in the package for AOP); **NRST**, the board's reset button; **E2E**, TI's support forum; **`channelCfg`, `sigProcChainCfg`, `aoaFovCfg`**, lines of the radar's configuration file (antenna masks, processing chain, angle limits); **clutter removal**, discarding echoes that do not move, such as walls and furniture; **minor motion**, small movement such as breathing or typing. Run on the IWRL6432BOOST with TI's Motion and Presence 2D demo from Radar Toolbox 4.00.00.05, macOS 15.7, results files dated 2026-10-10. TI documents read 2026-10-10 unless a date is given. Related: [the experiment page](../experiments/2026-10-10-radar-antenna-eval.md), [the results page](../../site/radar-eval.html), [the board's folder](../../iwrl6432boost/README.md).

Contents: [the answer](#what-does-the-evaluation-tell-me-and-what-can-it-not) · [the experiment](#what-is-the-experiment) · [the data](#what-data-is-recorded-and-what-is-worked-out-from-it) · [what to look for](#what-should-i-look-for-in-the-data) · [the conference room](#would-it-work-in-a-6-m-by-4-m-conference-room) · [questions to ask first](#what-should-i-ask-before-choosing-a-radar) · [run it yourself](#how-do-i-run-it-myself) · [limits](#limits-what-is-not-measured)

## What does the evaluation tell me, and what can it not?

It tells you, for one room layout and one radar chip with 1, 2 or 3 receive antennas:

- the farthest distance at which a person walking toward the radar is first flagged, up to 7 m: presence comes from the zone boxes, which end at 7 m, so a walk that starts at 8 m cannot show anything farther,
- the farthest distance at which a person sitting still is held as present, which is the harder case,
- the delay to flag an arrival and to clear after a departure,
- how many false alarms an empty room gives in an hour,
- which of the four floor zones fire, which is a rough "where".

It cannot tell you:

- **How many people are in the room.** The demo reports four zones on or off. Two people in one zone read as one. **Tag: TI example default.**
- **Power.** The demo does not report it on this board and the board's USB path hides the chip's rails. TI's data sheet figure is below; there is no measurement.
- **Your room.** Glass, metal shelving, a ceiling-mounted air vent or a fan all change the result. One room, one afternoon, one pass per setting: there is no spread.
- **The accuracy of position.** The demo gives zones and a range profile, not a distance for each person.

## What is the experiment?

One radar chip, three antenna settings, the same people doing the same passes for each setting, so the only change between runs is how many antennas are on.

**The radar.** The IWRL6432BOOST evaluation module. The chip has 2 transmit and 3 receive channels, works at 57 to 64 GHz with up to 7 GHz of sweep, and has a hardware accelerator for the FFT and detection steps (data sheet SWRS298B, board guide SWRU596, December 2022). Every other part in the family has the same 2 by 3 count: IWRL6432 WCSP (SWRS311), IWRL6432AOP (SWRS323B, one transmitter at a time), and IWRL1432 (SWRS313A, 76 to 81 GHz). **No TI part in this family has one transmitter and one receiver, so 1x1 here is a cost proxy: this chip with most of its antennas switched off, not a cheaper part.**

**The settings.** One line of the radar's configuration, `channelCfg <receive mask> <transmit mask> 0`.

| Setting | Line | Antennas on | Virtual antennas |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1x1 | `channelCfg 1 1 0` | 1 transmit, 1 receive | 1 |
| 2x2 | `channelCfg 3 3 0` | 2 transmit, 2 receive | 4 |
| 2x3 | `channelCfg 7 3 0` | 2 transmit, 3 receive (the shipped setting) | 6 |

**The placement.** Board on a stand at about 1.5 m, antenna side toward the room, nothing moving behind it, a tape line straight out from the board marked every metre to 8 m, and two chairs at 2 m and 4 m, as in the picture. The room has four zone boxes in the shipped configuration: left and right of the board's line (the split is at x = 0), near (0 to 3.5 m out) and far (3.51 to 7 m out), each up to 3 m high (`mpdBoundaryBox` lines in `PresenceDetect.cfg`). The boxes are 3.5 m wide each side, wider than the 4 m room, so a room that narrow splits as described below. The configured angle limits (`aoaFovCfg -70 70`) are wider than TI's 120 degree figure; the reason was not checked.

![Top-down layout: radar at the left, antenna side facing right, a line marked in metres to 8 m, chair 1 at 2 m, chair 2 at 4 m, start of the walk at 8 m](../../iwrl6432boost/eval/img/iwrl6432boost-eval-layout.png)

**The passes.** Each setting gets the same four, with a voice cue so every setting is timed from the same signal.

| Pass | What the person does | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| Walk in | Starts at 8 m, walks toward the radar at an even pace, one metre every 4 s, stops at 1 m, then leaves | The farthest distance a moving person is first seen; the clear delay after leaving |
| Seated at 2 m | Out of view, then on the cue sits still on the chair at 2 m for 45 s, phone down, then leaves | Whether a person who barely moves is held as present, and how fast they are noticed |
| Seated at 4 m | Same, chair at 4 m | The same at a longer range, where the echo is weaker |
| Empty room | Nobody in the room for a fixed window (300 s by default) | The false alarm rate |

The pace is 0.25 m a second, slow on purpose, so the distance at first detection is easy to read from the cue. A normal walking pace would give a coarser reading. The chairs are at 2 m and 4 m only; the tool accepts any other distance (see [run it yourself](#how-do-i-run-it-myself)).

## What data is recorded, and what is worked out from it?

Every frame the radar sends is one row in a CSV file per setting (`<date>-<setting>.csv`, written by the tool). Cue events are extra rows between frames.

| Field | What it is |
|---|---|
| `config`, `pass`, `round` | Which setting, which pass, which repeat |
| `t` | Time the Mac received the frame, in seconds |
| `frame` | The radar's own frame counter; a jump means lost frames |
| `pres` | 1 if any zone is on, from the presence block (TLV 315) |
| `z1` to `z4` | Each zone's state, from TLV 315. Zones 1 and 3 are the near boxes, 2 and 4 the far boxes |
| `peak_bin`, `peak_val` | The strongest bin of the range profile (TLV 303) and its value, searched between 0.25 and 7.5 m. A bin is 0.121 m: 256 samples at 12.5 Msps with a 60.5 MHz per microsecond slope is a sweep of 1,239 MHz, and c divided by twice that is 12.1 cm. Derived from the settings, not checked against a measured distance |
| `event` | `cue_enter`, `cue_leave`, `cue_go`, `mark_<metres>m` for the cue moments |

The frame rate is also recorded: the 2x3 evaluation setting (the shipped lines with `lowPowerCfg 0`) streamed 3.85 frames a second (231 frames in 59.7 s, no gaps, saved), against a configured period of 250 ms. The shipped image as found streamed 4.00 a second (384 bytes a frame, two TLVs). The 4 percent gap is unexplained. About 608 bytes a frame and TLVs 303, 306 and 315 were seen in the same run and not saved. That sets how finely times can be read: one frame is about 0.26 s.

**The numbers worked out from the rows** (`analyse_*` in `radar_eval.py`):

| Number | Definition |
|---|---|
| Detect latency | Seconds from the "enter" cue to the first two frames in a row with presence on |
| Clear latency | Seconds from the "leave" cue to the first frame with presence off that stays off for the next 3 s |
| Hold while seated | Share of frames with presence on, from 15 s after the enter cue to the leave cue. "Held at a distance" means at least 4 frames in 5 |
| Farthest distance held | The largest tested seated distance that was held |
| Walking detection range | The person's distance, interpolated between the called marks, at the first two frames in a row with presence on |
| Far-zone share | Share of seated frames where a far zone fired. A person at 2 m should mostly light the near zones |
| Median peak distance | Median `peak_bin` while seated, times 0.121 m. It should land near the chair's mark |
| False alarms per hour | Runs of presence-on frames in an empty room (runs less than 2 s apart merge), divided by the window, times 3,600. If there are none, the 95 percent upper bound is 3 divided by the window: 36 an hour for 300 s, 6 an hour for 30 min |

**Detect and clear latency include the person.** They are measured from this repo's voice cue, so they include the person's reaction and walking time. The same cue is used for every setting, so compare settings with each other; do not quote them as a sensor's delay. The two-frames-in-a-row rule ignores a one-frame blip, and times are read to one frame, about 0.26 s.

## What should I look for in the data?

Read each finding below against the rows, not against the summary alone.

### Why would more receivers give more range?

Each receiver hears the same echo plus its own noise. Adding the receivers up in phase makes the echo grow faster than the noise, which is about 10 times the base-10 log of the receiver count in decibels: 3 receivers against 1 is up to 4.8 dB, 2 against 1 is 3 dB. TI's range equation has an antenna gain term, `G_Rx` and `G_Tx`, and the range it gives grows as the fourth root of everything in the numerator (SWRA553A, February 2020, equation 2). So 4.8 dB, a factor of 3 in power, stretches the maximum range by 3 to the power of one quarter, about 1.32 times, 3 receivers over 1. If the demo also combines the transmit slots (6 virtual antennas), the factor is 6 to the power of one quarter, about 1.57. Which it does is not checked. Counting receivers only, 2 against 3 is about 10 percent shorter and 1 against 3 about 24 percent shorter; counting virtual antennas, 1x1 would be about 36 percent shorter than 2x3. This is arithmetic, not a measurement. TI's equation takes one antenna gain; a TI answer on the E2E forum ("AWR1843BOOST: Calculating Max range", date not captured) says the receiver count in the range formula is the number of virtual antennas. Combining that is not in any document that was read. If the demo adds the receivers without matching their phases, the gain is smaller. **Two transmitters add transmit power only if they transmit together:** in time-shared mode only one transmits at a time, and TI quotes an SNR gain of 10 times the log of the transmitter count only when they transmit together (SWRA554A, July 2018, section 4.2). Which mode the demo uses is not checked. The two transmitters add virtual antennas, so they sharpen angle; whether they also add range in the demo is not checked.

**Look for:** the farthest seated distance and the walking range falling as receivers come off, by about the arithmetic above. A much bigger drop means the demo's detector depends on the angle step; a smaller drop means the radar's range is limited by something else (the 7 m edge of the zone boxes, or the room).

### Why do more antennas separate more people?

The radar finds the direction of an echo from the small phase difference between antennas. More antennas in a row make the direction estimate sharper: for N antennas half a wavelength apart, the angle resolution is about 2 divided by N radians (SWRA554A, July 2018, equation 4), which is 114.6 degrees divided by N. Two people at the same distance from the radar and closer together sideways than that angle merge into one echo.

TI quotes the full 2 by 3 array on this board as 6 virtual antennas with 29 degrees of resolution across the room (azimuth) and 58 degrees up and down (elevation), 120 degrees by 80 degrees of view (the board's tool page, SWRU596 section 6 and the demo guide for SDK 05.05.00.02, read 2026-10-09). By the formula, 29 degrees is what 4 elements across the room give (2 divided by 4 radians) and 58 degrees is what 2 elements up and down give. How the 6 virtual antennas split into 4 and 2 follows the transmitter offsets on the board; the geometry file was not read.

| Setting | Azimuth resolution | Two people side by side at 2 m must be apart by | at 4 m | at 6 m |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2x3 | 29 degrees (TI) | 1.0 m | 2.0 m | 3.0 m |
| 2x2 | coarser than 29 degrees; about 57 degrees if two elements span the room (arithmetic, geometry not checked) | about 2 m | about 4 m | about 6 m |
| 1x1 | none: one antenna has no angle | not separable by angle | not separable by angle | not separable by angle |

The separation is range times the angle in radians, at the middle of the field of view; it is worse toward the edge (TI's own figure 12 in SPYY005A, July 2020, shows angle estimates getting less accurate away from straight ahead). **People at different distances are separated by range, not angle:** the range bin is 0.12 m, so two people in a line from the radar, a body-width apart or more, are different echoes. The trouble case is people side by side at the same distance, such as a row of seats facing a screen.

**Why 1x1 means presence only.** With one antenna there is no phase difference to read, so there is no direction. The radar can say something is there and roughly how far, not left or right. In this demo the left and right zones then cannot be told apart by angle.

**What was seen for 1x1 on 2026-10-10:** the demo answered the setting line and then refused to start. `sensorStart 0 0 0 0` returned `Error in setting up range profile:-40107`, and no frames came out. **Tag: Unknown (suspected: TI example default).** Suspected: the shipped processing lines (`sigProcChainCfg`, `aoaFovCfg`) assume more than one receiver; they were not changed to find out. The same demo may accept 1x1 with those lines changed, so "the demo refuses 1x1" is a statement about the shipped configuration, not about the chip.

### Why does a seated person disappear?

The configuration turns on `clutterRemoval 1`, which throws away echoes that do not move: walls, chairs, a monitor. A person sitting still is then seen only by small movement, such as breathing, a hand on a keyboard or a shifted foot. TI's file for this case says so in its header: it is "optimized to detect any kind of motion, including fine movements (even small movements that are present while sitting still, such as, movement caused by typing, breathing, etc.)" and reports no velocity (`PresenceDetect.cfg`, Radar Toolbox 4.00.00.05). The separate `minorStateCfg` line sets the thresholds for that small-motion state. A person who sits very still for long enough can fade out, and a person at a longer range has a weaker breathing echo, so a seated person is lost at a shorter range than a walking one. That gap is the number to read.

**Look for:** the hold share dropping with distance and with fewer receivers, and the far-zone share and median peak distance matching the chair. A person held in the wrong zone, or a peak far from the chair, points to a reflection off a wall.

### What does it cost in frame rate and power?

TI's data sheet gives about 1.2 mW average for presence detection at one update a second with 1 transmit and 1 receive channel, in the power-optimized supply layout for major-motion presence, which is not the seated case this guide tests; 7.8 mW in the lower-cost layout (SWRS298B; table numbers from notes of the Rev. A text, Rev. B not re-checked). That is the 1x1 setting, so the full 2x3 at the shipped 4 updates a second draws more, by an amount that was not measured. Slower frames should save power and lengthen every delay, since a frame is the smallest step of time; a slower period was not run. The shipped period is 250 ms. **Not measured:** the power of any setting. The board's 5 V USB path adds the probe and LEDs, so a USB meter reads hundreds of milliwatts and is not comparable to the data sheet.

## Would it work in a 6 m by 4 m conference room?

Take a room 6 m deep and 4 m wide, the radar on the middle of a short wall at 1.5 m, antennas facing the length of the room. Geometry first: TI's 120 degree view means the corners next to the radar's own wall are outside the view for the first 1.2 m out (at 1.2 m deep the view is 4 m wide, 2 m each side). The far corner is 6.3 m away on the diagonal. The shipped zones are left and right of the center line (x = 0) and near (0 to 3.5 m) and far (3.51 to 7 m), so the room splits into four areas: about 2 m by 3.5 m near and 2 m by 2.5 m far.

| | 1x1 | 2x2 | 2x3 (all antennas) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Demo accepts the setting | **No** with the shipped lines: `Error in setting up range profile:-40107` (measured 2026-10-10) | Yes: 25 of 25 lines Done, 4.0 frames a second, 768 bytes a frame (measured 2026-10-10). Started second in a boot it gave no frames | Yes when it is the first start in a boot: 3.85 frames a second with `lowPowerCfg 0` (measured). Started second in a boot it gave no frames |
| Walking person first seen at | Not measured | Not separable: the person stood in view at 8 m, so at least 8 m | About 6.5 m (first flagged 6.7 s after the cue, from behind the door, by the 4 s a metre pace; one pass). This test cannot read past 7 m. TI's anchors, which these passes cannot test: chip "typically up to 25 m" (SWRS298B); the IWRL6432WMOD module "human presence detection range typically 15 m at 0 degrees, 8 m at edge of FoV" (SWRS350B, a different antenna) |
| Seated person held to | Not measured | Held in 100 percent of frames at 2 m and at 4 m; flagged in 5.6 s and 3.9 s, cleared 10.7 s and 11.5 s after leaving (one pass each) | Held in 100 percent of frames at 2 m and at 4 m; flagged in 6.2 s and 4.3 s, cleared 12.3 s and 14.1 s after leaving (one pass each). Nothing beyond 4 m was tested. The guess before testing, not a TI figure, was 2 to 5 m. **The 6 m back row is outside what the passes test (2 m and 4 m)** |
| Expected range against 2x3, from SNR arithmetic | 24 to 36 percent shorter | about 10 percent shorter, or more | reference |
| Sees left against right | No (no angle) | Probably coarsely, not checked | Yes, to about 29 degrees |
| What it reports | Presence, no position | Presence and zones, probably coarse | Presence and four zones |
| People side by side that it could separate at 4 m | None by angle | About 4 m apart, if two elements span the room | About 2 m apart |

**How many people can the demo report?** Four zone flags, not a count. In the four areas above it can say which of the left-near, right-near, left-far and right-far areas have someone in them. Two people in one area read as one. Eight people around a table all fall in one or two zones. **Tag: TI example default.** A count needs one of TI's tracking configurations, which output moving points and follow them.

**What does TI ship for the IWRL6432?** From the Radar Toolbox 4.00.00.05 listing (published 2026-03-01, unpacked and read 2026-10-10, nothing run):

- The Motion and Presence Detection demo, prebuilt as a 2D image (the one in this repo's results) and a 3D image that clusters in height as well, for sit against stand or pet against human. Configuration folders for it: `motion_and_presence` (this repo's file), `doors_and_gates`, `height_based_detection`, `overhead_lighting` (ceiling mount) and `classification`.
- **A `people_tracking` folder with `wall_mount` and `ceiling_mount` configuration files for the IWRL6432BOOST.** The wall-mount file is `IWRL6432BOOST_Tracking_3Persons_7m_wall_mount.cfg`: `sensorPosition 0 0 2.5 0 15` (2.5 m up, a 15 degree tilt by the usual field order, not checked), with tracking lines (`trackingCfg`, `gatingParam`, `allocationParam`, `boundaryBox -7 7 0 7.5 -0.5 3`). The names say 3 people to 7 m. It has not been run, and the tracker's documentation was not read, so the 3-person limit is the file name's claim. Which of the two prebuilt images it needs is not checked.
- An Out of Box demo image (`out_of_box_L6432`) and an mmWave Demo image for the same chip. The Out of Box user guide in the toolbox lists the EVMs it supports and does not name the xWRL6432 in that list, though the image and source are in the package.

TI's older people-counting demos are for the IWR6843 class, which has more antennas (4 receive by 3 transmit). That is not this part.

## What should I ask before choosing a radar?

- **Ceiling or wall?** A wall unit at 1.5 m (this repo's test) sees people from the side. TI ships separate ceiling configurations for the IWRL6432 (`overhead_lighting`, `people_tracking/ceiling_mount`); a ceiling unit looks down and the zone map changes. Evaluate in the mount you will use; the passes in this repo do not transfer.
- **Glass and walls.** Radar reflects off metal, and some of it passes through many wall materials. Whether it sees people in the next room through your wall is a test, not an assumption: a person next door that shows up is a false alarm. Test with the door open and closed.
- **HVAC and fans.** A moving blade or a hanging curtain is motion. The empty-room pass is the check: run it with the air handler on, for at least 30 min per setting.
- **How fast must it react?** The delay numbers here include the person. Add the frame period (about 0.26 s here) to what you measure.
- **Seated or standing?** A room that is mostly people sitting still at a table is the hard case. Ask for the seated number at the farthest seat, not the walking range.
- **Power budget.** TI's 1.2 mW is for 1 transmit, 1 receive, 1 update a second. Decide your update rate and antenna count, then measure on your board's chip rails.
- **Do you need a count or only occupied-or-not?** Occupied-or-not is the demo that was measured. A count means the tracking configuration, a different test.

## How do I run it myself?

You need the IWRL6432BOOST, the stock Motion and Presence 2D demo running, a Mac with Python 3 and `pyserial`, and a person to walk (the tool talks to the board over its serial port and speaks cues out loud). From the repository root:

```bash
python3 iwrl6432boost/eval/radar_eval.py accept
```

Applies each setting, prints the board's answer to every line, and checks the stream.

```bash
python3 iwrl6432boost/eval/radar_eval.py empty --seconds 1800
```

The empty-room window for each setting. Leave the room.

```bash
python3 iwrl6432boost/eval/radar_eval.py run --passes walk,sit2,sit4
```

Each pass waits until the person says they are in place. The tool as written takes Enter in the terminal as the confirmation; it speaks cues with macOS `say`; and `radar_link.py` has the serial port name and configuration path written in (`PORT` and `CFG`), so edit those two lines for your machine. Add `--rounds 3` to repeat; the setting order rotates each round, so a slow drift in the room does not favour one setting.

```bash
python3 iwrl6432boost/eval/radar_eval.py restore
```

Puts the shipped configuration back.

```bash
python3 iwrl6432boost/eval/render_eval.py
```

Rebuilds the results page [`site/radar-eval.html`](../../site/radar-eval.html) from the summary files the tool writes.

**One reset first.** The shipped demo runs with `lowPowerCfg 1` and then ignores its command line, so the first change after power-up needs one press of the board's reset button (NRST, S2). The tool's configurations use `lowPowerCfg 0` so the demo stops and restarts between settings, and `restore` puts the shipped line back. **Tag: TI example default.** Source: `motion_detect.c`, "Sensor Stop command is honoured only when Low Power Cfg is disabled". Keep 20 cm between the board and a person while it transmits (SWRU596).

## Limits: what is not measured

- Every cell of the room table marked "not measured", and a second pass of every measured cell (all are single passes).
- A longer empty-room run for false alarms per hour.
- A seated pass at 6 m, the back row of the room. Put a chair at 6 m, and run `--passes sit6` (the tool accepts `sit` followed by any distance in metres).
- Repeats. One pass per cell gives no spread. Run `--rounds 3` or more and report the median and the range.
- A reference target (a corner reflector at a fixed range), to check the 0.121 m bin against a measured distance.
- Power per setting, with a meter on the chip's supply rail.
- A point-cloud or tracking run, to get a distance and a count for each person. This needs a flash of TI's other demo image, which moves one switch on this board.
- Whether the 1x1 setting starts once its processing lines are changed. A working 1 transmit, 1 receive presence configuration for an IWRL6432 or IWRL1432 would answer it; report the lines you changed.

To add a result: run the passes above, then `python3 iwrl6432boost/eval/radar_eval.py summarize` and `python3 iwrl6432boost/eval/render_eval.py`. The page and the room table here then take their numbers from the new files.

FILE: docs/guides/porting-lessons.md | What do you change when you port a project to a TI LaunchPad kit such as the LP-MSPM0G3519 or LP-MSPM33C321A? Lessons from 16 ports and 4 BoosterPack drivers (2026-10-21)
