# Can a C2000 LaunchPad (LAUNCHXL-F2800137, 16-bit char) host the BP-CC1407P radio driver?

**Short answer.** Not with TI's driver as it is. It does not compile for the C28x as shipped: 524 errors in 7 files, because the C2000 compiler has no `uint8_t` and rejects the GCC `packed` attribute the driver puts on 12 structs. Given C2000Ware's own `uint8_t` (16 bits) and with the attribute defined away by a compiler flag, all 7 files compile, but 11 of the 12 structs the driver lays over SPI bytes come out a different size than on Arm, and 29 shifts of event flags overflow a 16-bit `int`. So a C2000 host needs new code that packs and unpacks each message byte by byte; a recompile is not enough. Nothing was run: this is a compile check on a Mac, with no board or radio attached.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md) (C2000 and C28x, SPI, CRC, packed struct, bit field, byte order). Errors and fixes: [LAUNCHXL-F2800137 FAQ](../../c2000-launchpad/FAQ.md#libraries-written-for-8-bit-bytes). 1 kB = 1,024 bytes. Checked 2026-10-08 on macOS 15.7 (Intel) with TI's C2000 compiler 25.11.1.LTS.

**Question.** The BP-CC1407P is a radio that does not run your application: a host microcontroller drives it over SPI. Can a C2000 chip, whose smallest memory unit is a 16-bit word, be that host using TI's driver?

**Vendor position.** TI's product page for the BoosterPack, read 2026-10-07, says the plug-in ships a host driver "that can be ported to other MCUs". The supported hosts are five CC13xx and CC26xx LaunchPad development kits under the SimpleLink TRX plug-in 1.00.00.52. The LP-EM-CC2745R10-Q1 is also supported, under TI's Zephyr fork. No C2000 host is listed. The driver's own header defines its packed-struct macro for three compilers, IAR, "TI compiler" and GCC (`utility/utils.h`, lines 73 to 81), and says: "User must provide a definition for this macro if using a compiler other than the ones below."

The C2000 compiler's `stdint.h` defines `uint8_t` only for byte-addressed targets (MSP430, C55x byte mode, C6000, Arm, PRU, C7000, C29), not for the C28x. C2000Ware's driverlib adds its own: `typedef uint16_t uint8_t;` in `driverlib/f280013x/driverlib/inc/hw_types.h`, under the comment "Definition of 8 bit types for USB Driver code to maintain portability between byte and word addressable cores of C2000 Devices."

**What was tried.**

- **Driver source.** The SimpleLink TRX plug-in is not on this Mac. TI's Zephyr fork is: `simplelink-zephyr` tag `v3.7.0-ti-1.00.01_ga`, folder `drivers/misc/ti_cc140xp/host`, 10,958 lines. The plug-in is at `https://github.com/TexasInstruments/simplelink-trx-plugin` (or software-dl.ti.com, release 1.00.00.52). Whether its host folder is the same code was not checked.
- **Files compiled.** The 7 portable files: `trx_host.c`, `handlers/trx_host_handlers.c`, `private/trx_host_private.c`, `transport/spi_transport.c`, and the three in `utility/`. The two HAL files (`hal/platform_spi.c`, `hal/platform_util.c`) were left out. HAL means hardware abstraction layer: the small part of a driver that talks to one chip's peripherals, here Zephyr's SPI, GPIO and CRC calls, which every host writes for itself.
- **No change to TI's files.** This repo's stand-in for Zephyr's logging header compiles the log calls out (`c2000-launchpad/compile-checks/trx-host/stubs/`).
- **Compiler.** `cl2000 -v28 -ml -mt --float_support=fpu32 --abi=eabi --opt_level=2 --c99`, the flags of this repo's F2800137 bench builds. Three modes: the compiler's own types; C2000Ware's `uint8_t`; and C2000Ware's `uint8_t` plus `-D__packed__=`, which turns the packed attribute into an empty one.
- **Control.** The same 7 files and stubs for the Cortex-M33 with TI Arm Clang 5.1.1 and `-Wall`.
- **Sizes.** A small file of `sizeof` values for 12 message structs, compiled for both cores; the values are read from each compiler's assembly output.

Run it again:

```bash
c2000-launchpad/compile-checks/trx-host/check.sh plain
```

```bash
c2000-launchpad/compile-checks/trx-host/check.sh c2000ware-nopack
```

```bash
c2000-launchpad/compile-checks/trx-host/sizes.sh
```

The scripts read the driver from `~/zephyr-ti/ws/zephyr/drivers/misc/ti_cc140xp/host`; set `HOST=<folder>` to point elsewhere.

**How far it got.** Compile. Nothing was linked, flashed or run.

| Build | Files compiled | Errors | Warnings |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| Cortex-M33, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1 (control) | 7 of 7 | 0 | 0 |
| C28x, compiler's own types | 0 of 7 | 524 | 80 |
| C28x, C2000Ware's `uint8_t` | 2 of 7 | 60 | 51 |
| C28x, C2000Ware's `uint8_t`, packed attribute defined away | 7 of 7 | 0 | 51 |

The 51 warnings in the last build: 29 `#64-D` shift count too large (item 3), 15 `#548-D` transfer of control bypasses initialization, 3 `#190-D` enumerated type mixed with another type, 2 `#69-D` integer conversion changed the sign, 1 `#303-D` typedef name already declared, 1 `#1-D` no newline at the end of a file. Only the shift warnings were followed up.

**1. No 8-bit type.** 479 of the 524 errors read `"TRX.h", line 73: error #20: identifier "uint8_t" is undefined` (445 times) or the same for `int8_t` (34). **Chip limit.** The C28x cannot address a single byte, so its compiler has no exact 8-bit type. C2000Ware's typedef clears these errors.

**2. The packed attribute.** The other 45 errors, and all 60 in the second mode, read `error #1167: invalid attribute for "struct TRX_Phy_s"` and the same for 11 more structs in `TRX.h`. **Tool or docs.** The driver writes `__attribute__((__packed__))` directly in `TRX.h` instead of the per-compiler macro in its own `utils.h`, and the C2000 compiler rejects it. On the C28x every member is already at least one 16-bit word, so packing has no meaning there; `-D__packed__=` removes it without editing TI's files.

**3. Event flags past bit 15.** With both fixes, 29 warnings read `warning #64-D: shift count is too large` (28 in `trx_host_handlers.c`, 1 in `trx_host.c`). **Tool or docs.** `trx_host.h` defines 15 event flags as `(1 << 16)` to `(1 << 30)`. `1` is an `int`, which is 16 bits on the C28x, so those shifts are undefined in C. The driver's last four flags already use `1ULL`; the others need the same. What this build does with them at run time was not checked.

**4. Message sizes.** Size of each struct in the compiler's own unit: 8-bit bytes on Arm, 16-bit words on the C28x. On the C28x an SPI driver normally puts each received byte in its own 16-bit word, so a struct laid over that buffer must have one word per wire byte; the Arm column is the wire size, and the two columns must match for the driver's cast to work. That one-byte-per-word layout is this repo's assumption: no C28x HAL was written and no buffer was tested.

| Struct | Arm (bytes on the wire) | C28x (16-bit words) |
|---|--:|--:|
| `TRX_TransactionHeader` | 4 | 4 |
| `TRX_TransactionFooter` (the CRC) | 2 | 1 |
| `TRX_Request_Header` | 2 | 1 |
| `TRX_Request_LastStatus` | 4 | 2 |
| `TRX_Phy` | 3 | 2 |
| `TRX_Request_CommandStore` | 48 | 32 |
| `TRX_Request_CommandSubmit` | 3 | 2 |
| `TRX_Request_CommandStop` | 4 | 3 |
| `TRX_Request_ConfigStore` | 8 | 6 |
| `TRX_PowerMode` | 3 | 2 |
| `TRX_DeviceConfigData` | 12 | 11 |
| `TRX_Request_CommandStore_Transmit_Params` | 16 | 12 |

Only the transaction header matches, and only in count: it is a union of a 32-bit view (two words on the C28x) and `uint8_t u8[4]` (four words), so its two views no longer cover the same bits. The driver builds each message by casting an SPI buffer to one of these structs and uses `sizeof` for lengths (`SPI_TRANSPORT_HEADER_LEN` is `sizeof(TRX_TransactionHeader)`). On the C28x a `uint16_t` field fills one word where the wire has two bytes, and bit fields pack into 16-bit units, so the layout in memory is not the layout on the wire.

**Byte order** is not the problem: the C28x and the Cortex-M cores are both little-endian. **The CRC** (CRC-16 CCITT-FALSE over the SPI block) is computed in the HAL, which was not compiled; a C28x HAL would have to feed it one byte per 16-bit word.

**The line.** The driver compiles for the C28x only with outside help, and then it is still wrong where it matters: 11 of 12 message structs differ in size from the bytes on the wire. **Tool or docs.** TI's host driver assumes a host with 8-bit bytes, and it says it can be ported, but a port to a C2000 would need a rewrite of how every message is packed and unpacked (estimate, not built), beyond a new HAL. Verdict for builders: to put a BP-CC1407P next to a C2000 today, use a small Arm host (a CC13xx LaunchPad development kit or an MSPM0) between the two, or write the byte packing yourself.

- Serialize each message into a byte buffer with explicit shifts and masks, one field at a time, and keep the C28x structs only as in-memory copies. The 12 structs above are the list to cover.
- Change the 15 event flags to `1UL << n` or `1ULL << n`; the driver already uses `1ULL` for its last four.
- Use the C28x's `__byte()` intrinsic, which reads and writes one byte inside a 16-bit word, for the SPI buffers.
- Put an MSPM0 between the C2000 and the radio, talking to the C2000 over SCI or SPI with a simple 16-bit protocol. MSPM0 is byte-addressed, so the driver's own code would apply there.
- Compile the TRX plug-in's own copy of the host driver, once downloaded, to see whether it differs from the Zephyr fork's.

**Ask.** Has anyone run a TI CC13xx or CC14xx transceiver host driver on a C2000? Is there a TI-supported way to pack messages on word-addressed cores?

# Does the u8g2 display library compile for a TI C2000 LaunchPad (LAUNCHXL-F2800137), where a byte is 16 bits?

**Short answer.** Yes, with one line of your own: u8g2 2.37.1, the common library for small monochrome displays, compiles and links for the C28x with no change to its files once `uint8_t` is defined as `unsigned char`. A test program with u8x8 text and one u8g2 font for a 128x64 SSD1306 display takes 19 kB of flash and 8.3 kB of RAM. Two catches: the C2000 compiler has no `uint8_t` of its own, and if you take C2000Ware's (`uint16_t`), both fonts tried fail with `error #145`. Fonts and the frame buffer take twice the memory. Compile and link check only, on a Mac; not run on a display.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md) (C2000 and C28x, u8g2 and u8x8, SSD1306, link). Errors and fixes: [LAUNCHXL-F2800137 FAQ](../../c2000-launchpad/FAQ.md#libraries-written-for-8-bit-bytes). 1 kB = 1,024 bytes. Checked 2026-10-08 on macOS 15.7 (Intel) with TI's C2000 compiler 25.11.1.LTS.

**Question.** u8g2 is a widely used C library for small monochrome OLED and LCD screens, in Arduino sketches and plain C. Its code and fonts are written in terms of 8-bit bytes. Does it build for a chip that has no 8-bit type?

**Vendor position.** The C2000 compiler's `stdint.h` defines `uint8_t` only for byte-addressed targets (MSP430, C55x byte mode, C6000, Arm, PRU, C7000, C29), not for the C28x. C2000Ware's driverlib defines one for its own use: `typedef uint16_t uint8_t;` in `driverlib/f280013x/driverlib/inc/hw_types.h`, under the comment "Definition of 8 bit types for USB Driver code to maintain portability between byte and word addressable cores of C2000 Devices." On the C28x, `char` is 16 bits (`docs/vocab.md`, C2000). u8g2's own documentation was not checked for 16-bit `char`.

**What was tried.**

- **u8g2 2.37.1** (commit `414efcd`, BSD 2-clause), fetched by `third-party/u8g2/fetch.sh`: the core u8x8 and u8g2 files, the SSD1306 128x64 driver, and two fonts copied out of upstream's font files unchanged (`u8x8_font_chroma48medium8_r` for u8x8 text, `u8g2_font_6x10_tr` for u8g2). No u8g2 file was edited.
- **This repo's test program**, `c2000-launchpad/compile-checks/u8g2/u8g2_check.c`: u8x8 draws "Hello C28x" in the 8x8 font; u8g2 clears a full frame buffer, draws the same text in the 6x10 font and sends the frame. The byte callback stores each byte it would send in an array, so no I2C or SPI peripheral is involved.
- **Compiler and link.** `cl2000 -v28 -ml -mt --float_support=fpu32 --abi=eabi --opt_level=2 --c99`, linked with this repo's F2800137 flash layout and a 1,024-word stack. Three ways to get `uint8_t`: none (the compiler's own `stdint.h`); C2000Ware's `uint16_t`; and `unsigned char`, which is also 16 bits on the C28x.
- **Host emulation.** The same program built twice with the Mac's clang, with `uint8_t` 8 bits and then widened to 16 bits, and the bytes each sends compared; both builds take the two fonts as brace lists of numbers, because a string cannot fill a 16-bit array. This tests only whether u8g2 relies on 8-bit wraparound. It is not the C28x: `int` stays 32 bits on the Mac.

Run it again:

```bash
third-party/u8g2/fetch.sh
```

```bash
c2000-launchpad/compile-checks/u8g2/check.sh uchar
```

```bash
c2000-launchpad/compile-checks/u8g2/host_emulate.sh
```

`check.sh` also takes `plain` and `c2000ware`.

**How far it got.** Link. Nothing was flashed or run on a display.

| `uint8_t` from | Steps passed (27 files, then the link) | Errors |
|---|--:|--:|
| nothing (compiler's own `stdint.h`) | 0 of 28 | 2,702 |
| C2000Ware's `typedef uint16_t uint8_t` | 26 of 28 | 4 |
| `typedef unsigned char uint8_t` | 28 of 28 | 0 |

The link leaves out two compiled files, `u8g2_d_setup` and `u8g2_d_memory`, because they reference every display and buffer u8g2 supports; the test program's own setup covers the one SSD1306 128x64 display, so the sizes below are for that display only. The six warnings in the last build are five upstream files without a final newline and the linker's note that the entry point is `code_start`, not `_c_int00`.

**1. No `uint8_t`.** `"csrc/u8x8.h", line 215: error #20: identifier "uint8_t" is undefined`, then 2,701 more that follow from it (1,350 of them `error #91: function returning function is not allowed`); all of them go away once `uint8_t` is defined. **Chip limit.** The C28x cannot address a single byte, so its compiler has no exact 8-bit type. Define one before u8g2's headers.

**2. C2000Ware's `uint8_t` breaks the fonts.** `"extract/fonts_extract.c", line 11: error #145: a value of type "char [772]" cannot be used to initialize an entity of type "const uint8_t [772]"`, the same for the 979-byte font, then `error #10234-D: unresolved symbols remain` for both fonts at link. **Third-party behavior.** u8g2 stores both fonts compiled here as string literals, and C lets a string fill only an array of a character type; `uint16_t` is `unsigned int`. So does every other font in u8g2 2.37.1: all 2,043 in `u8g2_fonts.c` and all 131 in `u8x8_fonts.c` are string literals (counted in the upstream files), so the same error is expected from any of them; only these two were compiled. With `unsigned char`, which is 16 bits wide here, the fonts compile. **Tool or docs.** The `uint16_t` version comes from C2000Ware, whose comment says it is for its USB driver code, and nothing warns that it breaks string data. A C2000Ware project that includes `driverlib.h` gets the `uint16_t` version, so keep u8g2's files out of driverlib's reach (a separate file for the display code) or convert the fonts to brace lists.

**3. Memory, from the map** (the linker map). Flash 9.7k words (19 kB): 9,674 in `FLASH_MAIN`, 28 in `FLASH_BOOT`, 2 at `BEGIN`. RAM 4.3k words (8.3 kB), of which this repo's byte capture array is 2k words, the frame buffer 1,024 and the stack 1,024. Each font byte takes a word: `u8g2_font_6x10_tr` is 979 words (1.9 kB) where a byte-addressed chip stores 979 bytes, and the 128x64 frame buffer is 2 kB instead of 1 kB.

**4. Wraparound, host emulation.** Both builds sent the same 1.3 kB (each build prints `uint8_t is 8 bits` or `uint8_t is 16 bits` to confirm which it was). For this program's calls, u8g2 does not depend on a byte rolling over at 256. Other drawing calls, other fonts and 16-bit `int` were not covered.

**The line.** No line reached. It compiles and links; the screen does not draw. The one rule for builders: give u8g2 `unsigned char` as its `uint8_t`, not C2000Ware's `uint16_t`, and budget twice the bytes for fonts and the frame buffer.

- Run it: an SSD1306 on the F2800137's I2C pins with u8x8's hardware I2C callback, then compare the bytes on the bus with the host emulation's 1,356.
- Use the page buffer (`_1` setup, 128 bytes) instead of the full frame to save 896 words of RAM.
- Pack two font bytes per word with the `__byte()` intrinsic to halve font flash; that needs a change to u8g2's font reader.
- Check 16-bit `int` paths: large coordinates, `u8g2_uint_t` set to 16 bits, and the circle and line code.

**Ask.** Has anyone run u8g2 on a C2000? Did any drawing call misbehave where a byte would wrap at 256?

**Short answer.** Yes, the smallest one. # How much of CoreMark runs on a TI LP-MSPM0C1104 with 1 kB of RAM?

**Short answer.** None of it could be made to run. The standard 2 kB data set does not link (a 2.5 kB stack in 1 kB of RAM, and 20.2 kB of code in 16 kB of flash at -O3). Reduced 400 and 200 byte sets link at -Os, flash, then take a hard fault inside `core_bench_list`. They would not be valid CoreMark scores anyway.

**Question.** Does the reduced-data CoreMark give a per-MHz figure that can be compared with the LP-MSPM0L1306?

**How far it got.** Compile, link and flash passed. The run stops in a hard fault (`pc 0x0000154a`, `msp 0x1FFFFF30`) at the first instruction of `core_bench_list` that moves the stack pointer. The painted RAM shows the whole reserved stack used. A smaller data set did not change it.

# Can any room-occupancy model fit in the 1 kB of RAM on a TI LP-MSPM0C1104?

**Short answer.** Not as built. The smallest of this repo's four models (636 parameters) needs 1.2 kB of RAM for its two activation buffers and an input copy, 176 B more than the chip has even with no stack. The 1.7k-parameter model needs the same 1.2 kB; the two larger ones need 2.2 kB and 4.2 kB.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md) (stack, linker). Errors and fixes: [LP-MSPM0C1104 FAQ](../../mspm0c1104/FAQ.md). 1 kB = 1,024 bytes.

**Question.** Does a model that decides whether a room is occupied fit in 1 kB of RAM?

**Vendor position.** TI's Edge AI examples for MSPM0 target boards with 16 kB or more of RAM; the LP-MSPM0C1104 SDK folder has none.

**What was tried.** Four models in plain C at -Os and -O3, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1, 24 MHz, 512 B stack, link only (no run), `mspm0c1104/prebuild.sh`, 2026-10-08.

**How far it got.** Configure and compile passed. Link failed for all eight builds: 636 and 1.7k parameters needed 1.2 kB of `.bss` (688 B over with a 512 B stack); 8.5k parameters 2.2 kB and 18.8 kB to 19.2 kB of read-only data; 33k parameters 4.2 kB of RAM and 33.6 kB of weights, more than the 16 kB of flash.

**The line.** 1.2 kB of buffers against 1 kB of RAM.

**Ask.** If you have a model under 500 B of working memory for room occupancy, say so.

# Can a program on the ST NUCLEO-U083RC (STM32U083) use all 40 kB of RAM, or only the 32 kB ST's examples give it?

**Short answer.** All 40 kB. The RAM is one block from address 0x20000000 to 0x2000A000. ST's own example linker scripts give programs 32 kB, and so does Zephyr by default, but a program linked with the RAM length set to 40K filled and read back a 38 kB buffer with no error.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). Board page: [NUCLEO-U083RC README](../../nucleo-u083rc/README.md). 1 kB = 1,024 bytes. A linker script tells the compiler where memory is and how big it is.

**Question.** The data sheet says 40 kB of RAM. Do the tools let a program use it?

**Vendor position.** ST data sheet DS14463 Rev 2: "40-Kbyte SRAM with parity" for the STM32U083 (read 2026-10-07). STM32CubeU0 v1.3.0: 206 of the 209 linker scripts under `Projects/NUCLEO-U083RC` say `RAM (xrw) : ORIGIN = 0x20000000, LENGTH = 32K`, with the header "32KBytes RAM"; the three secure-boot projects (`OEMiROT_Loader`, `OEMiROT_Appli`, `Templates_ROT`) say 40K. Zephyr 4.4.2's `stm32u083Xc.dtsi` lists two regions, `sram1` at 0x20000000 (32 kB, the one programs use) and `sram2` at 0x20008000 (8 kB). STM32duino 3.0.0 lists 40 kB for the board.

**What was tried.** NUCLEO-U083RC (STM32U083 Rev A), GCC 12.2. First, over the debugger with the chip halted: fill 0x20000000 to 0x2000A000 with 0x5A5A5A5A, read it all back, then the same with 0xA5A5A5A5, then read 0x2000A000. Second, a program: ST's `GPIO_IOToggle` startup and HAL files, ST's linker script with `LENGTH = 32K` changed to `40K`, and a 38 kB static buffer filled with an address-based pattern and read back twice by the CPU.

**How far it got.** Verified. Both debugger patterns read back with 0 bad bytes of 40 kB; the read at 0x2000A000 failed, as it should. The program linked with 39.6 kB of RAM in use, ran, and reported 9.7k words from 0x20000040 to 0x20009840 with 0 mismatches.

**The line.** No limit reached: the last 8 kB is ordinary RAM directly after the first 32 kB. Nothing on the chip stops a program using it; the 32K in ST's linker scripts and Zephyr's choice of region are the limit. Not tested: whether that last 8 kB behaves differently in low-power modes (retention in Standby), which may be why ST keeps it separate.

**Ask.** Does anyone know why ST's U0 example linker scripts stop at 32 kB?

<!-- experiment

# How much does the flash wait state cost the ST NUCLEO-U083RC (STM32U083) at 48 MHz?

**Short answer.** Almost nothing. CoreMark gives 2.03 per MHz at 48 MHz with one flash wait state and 2.05 per MHz at the 4 MHz reset clock with none, a 1.3 percent difference. The likely reason is the chip's 1 kB instruction cache; it was not turned off to check. Same compiler, same files, same flags.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). 1 kB = 1,024 bytes. A wait state is a clock cycle the core waits for flash; CoreMark per MHz is iterations per second divided by the clock.

**Question.** Does running from flash at full speed cost this chip as much as it costs other M0+ parts?

**Vendor position.** ST data sheet DS14463 Rev 2: "1-Kbyte instruction cache" with "0-wait-state execution from flash" (read 2026-10-07). ST's `GPIO_IOToggle` example sets `FLASH_LATENCY_1` at 48 MHz.

**What was tried.** CoreMark (unmodified EEMBC files), GCC 12.2 `-O3 -funroll-loops`, bare metal, code in flash. Once at 48 MHz with ST's clock setup copied from `GPIO_IOToggle` (MSI range 11, one wait state), 3k iterations; once at the reset clock (MSI 4 MHz, no wait state), 1k iterations. SysTick counts CPU cycles; three runs each.

**How far it got.** Verified: every run passed CoreMark's own check, and the three runs at each clock gave identical tick counts.

| Clock | Wait states | Iterations per second | Per MHz |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 48 MHz | 1 | 97.35 | 2.028 |
| 4 MHz | 0 | 8.216 | 2.054 |

**The line.** No limit reached. For comparison on this bench, the same GCC 12.2 files on the LP-MSPM0G3507 gave 1.82 per MHz at 80 MHz with two wait states.

**Ask.** Has anyone measured the U0's cache hit rate on a larger program than CoreMark?

FILE: docs/experiments/2026-10-08-nucleo-u083rc-st-aes-example.md | Does ST's AES example run as shipped on the ST NUCLEO-U083RC (STM32U083), and how much faster is the hardware AES than software?
==============================================================================

<!-- experiment
id: E127
board: NUCLEO-U083RC
date: 2026-10-08
status: works
reached: verified
line: ST's CRYP_AESModes example ran as shipped on the NUCLEO-U083RC and passed its own checks (LD4 steady on); its README promises 192-bit keys that the code and the chip do not have. This repo's own timing put the AES block at 65 to 74 times tiny-AES-c by register writes and 20 to 37 times through ST's HAL.
stop: none
-->
# Does ST's AES example run as shipped on the ST NUCLEO-U083RC (STM32U083), and how much faster is the hardware AES than software?

**Short answer.** Yes. ST's `CRYP_AESModes` example, built from the command line with ST's GCC and flashed with ST's programmer, passed every encrypt and decrypt check it makes. On 1 kB of data, this repo's own test put the AES block at 65 to 74 times faster than the tiny-AES-c software library when the code writes the AES registers directly, and 20 to 37 times faster through ST's HAL calls (GCC 12.2 at -O3, 48 MHz). One mismatch: the example's README lists 192-bit keys; the code uses only 128 and 256, which is what the chip supports.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). Board page and fixes: [NUCLEO-U083RC README](../../nucleo-u083rc/README.md) and [FAQ](../../nucleo-u083rc/FAQ.md). 1 kB = 1,024 bytes. HAL is ST's driver library.

**Question.** Does ST's own AES example work out of the package, and how much of the hardware's speed survives ST's driver calls?

**Vendor position.** ST's data sheet DS14463 Rev 2 lists "AES: 128/256-bit key" for the STM32U083 (read 2026-10-07). The example's README says: "In this example, the following key sizes are used: 128, 192 or 256", and "When all ciphering and deciphering operations are successful, LED4 is turned on. In case of ciphering or deciphering issue, LED4 is blinking slowly" (STM32CubeU0 v1.3.0, `Projects/NUCLEO-U083RC/Examples/CRYP/CRYP_AESModes/README.md`).

**What was tried.** NUCLEO-U083RC (STM32U083 Rev A), STM32CubeU0 v1.3.0 at commit c87491e, ST's GCC 14.3.1 and STM32_Programmer_CLI 2.23.0 from STM32CubeCLT 1.22.0, on an Intel Mac. The example was built unchanged from its STM32CubeIDE file list by `nucleo-u083rc/prebuild.sh` and flashed with `STM32_Programmer_CLI -c port=SWD -w app.elf -v -rst`; LD4 (PA5) was read 20 times over 3.4 s through the debugger. For the speed comparison, this repo's own timing image times tiny-AES-c (commit 2385675, unmodified) against the AES block by direct register writes and by HAL `HAL_CRYP_Encrypt`/`Decrypt` in polling mode, on the same 1 kB of data as the LP-MSPM0G3507 run, with FIPS-197 and SP 800-38A vectors checked first. Three runs each; every run gave identical cycle counts.

**How far it got.** Verified. LD4 stayed on through all 20 reads (the failure path toggles it once a second). This repo's timing image passed every vector and matched software output byte for byte over 1 kB.

| AES-128, 1 kB, GCC 12.2 -O3, 48 MHz | Software (tiny-AES-c) | HAL | Registers | Speed-up, HAL | Speed-up, registers |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| ECB encrypt (cycles) | 397k | 20k | 6.1k | 19.6 | 65.1 |
| ECB decrypt | 724k | 20k | 10k | 35.6 | 71.5 |
| CBC encrypt | 405k | 20k | 6.1k | 20.0 | 66.3 |
| CBC decrypt | 755k | 20k | 10k | 37.1 | 74.4 |
| AES-256 ECB encrypt | 555k | 22k | 8k | 25.4 | 69.7 |

At -O2 the software is slower (527k cycles for ECB encrypt), so the ratios rise to 84 to 91 times by registers. The register path costs about 95 cycles per 16-byte block for AES-128 and 124 for AES-256, which fits the extra rounds AES-256 does. The HAL path costs about 20k cycles per kilobyte either way. The random-number generator filled 1 kB in 26k cycles (0.55 ms), with 50.2 percent ones, no repeated 32-bit word and no error flag.

**The line.** No limit reached. Two things to know: the HAL costs about three times the register path to encrypt 1 kB and about twice to decrypt, and the 192-bit key size in the README does not exist on this chip. The example prints its results only with `USE_VCP_CONNECTION` set to 1 in `main.h` (default 0) or through semihosting in STM32CubeIDE, so the output was not compared byte for byte with the example's `Expected_Results.md`; LD4 is its pass signal.

**Ask.** Has anyone timed ST's HAL CRYP calls against direct register access on another STM32U0 or STM32G0 part?

# Does Zephyr's upstream board for the TI LP-MSPM0G3519 build, flash and run from a Mac?

**Short answer.** It builds and flashes with TI's chip table missing from OpenOCD, but TI's blinky sample does not run: the core stops in the NMI handler with an SRAM double-error event. The larger benchmark app was seen transmitting on its serial port, so the board is not dead; the blinky failure is unexplained.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md) (NMI, ECC, OpenOCD). Errors and fixes: [LP-MSPM0G3519 FAQ](../../mspm0g3519/FAQ.md). 1 kB = 1,024 bytes.

**Question.** Can a builder follow Zephyr's own getting-started path to a blinking LED on the LP-MSPM0G3519 from a Mac?

**Vendor position.** Zephyr 4.4.2 lists `lp_mspm0g3519` as a supported board (UART, GPIO and CAN) and its runner is OpenOCD. The xPack OpenOCD 0.12.0-7 in use has no MSPM0G3519 in its part table.

**What was tried.** A Zephyr 4.4.2 checkout, GCC 12.2 cross toolchain, xPack OpenOCD 0.12.0-7, probe <probe serial> on firmware 3.0.0.43, 2026-10-08. `west build -p always -b lp_mspm0g3519 samples/basic/blinky`, then `west flash` with `--openocd` pointing at the xPack build. Three runs. Then reading the chip with OpenOCD: program counter, the NMI index and the stack pointer.

**How far it got.** Configure, compile and flash passed on all three runs: build 52.8, 51.5 and 47.7 s, flash 4.5, 4.5 and 4.8 s. OpenOCD prints "Unidentified PART" for the chip and flashes anyway. The image is 11.8 kB of flash and 4 kB of RAM. It did not run: the program counter reads 0x4a0 (`z_SysNmiOnReset`, a `wfi` loop) on every sample, the active exception is 2 (NMI), and `SYSCTL.NMIIIDX` reads 6, which TI's header names SRAMDED (SRAM double-error detect). The benchmark app (`mspm0g3507/mcu-bench`) built for the same board was seen running: its program counter was inside the UART transmit function and varied between samples.

**The line.** The blinky stops in the NMI handler with SRAMDED set. Cause not established. Two facts that may matter: Zephyr's board file puts `sram0` at 64 kB (bank 0, the bank with ECC, per the comment in Zephyr's devicetree), and the build summary reports only 256 kB of flash and 64 kB of RAM although the chip has 512 kB and 128 kB.

**Ask.** If you have a blinking Zephyr build on an LP-MSPM0G3519, say which commit and which flags.

FILE: docs/experiments/2026-10-09-am13e230-microstep-tmu.md | Does microstepping the kit stepper through the LP-AM13E230's PWM units cost the chip anything?
==============================================================================

<!-- experiment
id: E146
board: LP-AM13E230
date: 2026-10-09
status: parked
reached: run
line: The same six wires that stepped the kit 28BYJ-48 on and off now microstep it. The chip's PWM units give sinusoidal duties, updated 20,000 times a second. The update handler costs 138 cycles with the trig unit (1.4 percent of the CPU) and 246 with the C library sine (2.5 percent). Whether the shaft turns under this drive was not watched: the run was hands-free.

-->
# Does microstepping the kit stepper through the LP-AM13E230's PWM units cost the chip anything?

**Short answer.** Almost nothing. Four sinusoidal duties from the PWM units, recomputed 20,000 times a second, cost the chip 138 cycles an update with the trig unit (TMU) doing the sine, 246 with the C library sine on the FPU. That is 1.4 and 2.5 percent of a 200 MHz core. The other 97 percent is free for a current loop, a knob, a display, or a neural network. Nobody watched the shaft during this run, so "it turned" is not claimed here.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). Board page: [LP-AM13E230 README](../../am13e230/README.md), [FAQ](../../am13e230/FAQ.md). On-off version of the same wiring: [stepper on and off](2026-10-09-am13e230-stepper-uln2003.md). Program: `am13e230/stepper-uln2003/microstep/`. MCPWM is the chip's motor PWM unit. The TMU is its trig math unit, reached through compiler intrinsics. DWT is the core's cycle counter.

**Question.** After the on-off version, the question was whether a motor-control chip earns its keep on a hobby stepper, since four on-off pins and a delay loop run on any microcontroller. Microstepping is the first step up: each coil gets a sine-shaped duty instead of on or off, so the shaft moves in hundreds of positions per step instead of one. What does the update loop cost, and does the trig unit matter?

**Vendor position.** TI's motor examples for this board (`solutions/motor_control/`) are three-phase field-oriented control on a DRV8323RH or DRV8329A BoosterPack; none covers a stepper. The data sheet (SPRSPC3A) gives the TMU as single-cycle-throughput sine and cosine instructions. This repo's FOC step measured the C library pair at 513 cycles against the TMU's handful.

**What was tried.** Same six wires as the on-off version. IN1, IN2 and IN3 are on MCPWM4 outputs 1A, 2A and 3A. IN4 is on MCPWM1 output 2A, because PB7 has no free MCPWM4 output. Both modules run at 20 kHz. MCPWM4's counter-zero event interrupts at 20 kHz. The handler advances the electrical angle and takes two sines, since the other two coils are the negatives. It clamps each to its positive half, because the ULN2003 is unipolar, scales to a 95 percent peak duty and writes four shadow compare values. One shaft turn is 512 electrical cycles over 100,000 updates (5 s), then a 1 s pause with all coils at the 1-count minimum, then a turn back. Three images: `tmu`, where fastrts_tmu.h remaps sinf to the TMU; `sw`, with the C library sinf; and `noisr`, where the interrupt is never enabled. Each ran hands-free with the cycle counter read at handler entry and exit. Results were read from RAM over the probe after the run.

**How far it got.** Run. The handler count, phase and turn counters advanced as designed, with 6 turn cycles in the 75 s the first image ran. Not verified: that the shaft turned, since the run was hands-free. The on-off version on the same wiring turned in the on-off version.

| Image | Handler, mean | Best | Worst | Share of the CPU at 20 kHz |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| TMU sine | 138.2 cycles (0.69 µs) | 61 | 219 | 1.4 percent |
| C library sine | 245.6 cycles (1.23 µs) | 61 | 354 | 2.5 percent |

Best is a pause-phase call, the sine of zero. The figures cover the handler body only. Hardware interrupt entry and exit take about 12 cycles each way on a Cortex-M33 and are not included. The `noisr` image was meant to show the main loop's lost share directly. Its run time differed from the others by the flash tail, so that comparison is not reported.

**The line.** None reached. At 20 kHz the update takes 1.4 percent of the core with the TMU.

**Where it stopped.** Nowhere in the chip. The limit is in the driver. The ULN2003 is a bank of Darlington switches with about a 1 V drop and no current sensing, so the coil current follows the duty only roughly and nothing closes the loop.

**Ask.** Does the shaft move smoothly under the sine duties through a ULN2003, or does the Darlington drop flatten the waveform enough to cog? One look at the shaft answers it.

**What a reader should take.** Microstepping is cheap on this chip: the trig unit halves an already small handler. The remaining cost is not in the core but in the driver board, which cannot tell the chip what current flows. That is the next part to change.

FILE: docs/experiments/2026-10-09-am13e230-mspm0-driverlib.md | Does MSPM0 driverlib code run on the LP-AM13E230 with only a shim header?
==============================================================================

<!-- experiment
id: E148
board: LP-AM13E230
date: 2026-10-09
status: works
reached: verified
line: Three MSPM0 driverlib programs run on the LP-AM13E230: a GPIO toggle, a UART print and a timer PWM. All 53 lines of app code are unchanged, with a 13-line shim header. The PWM program needed the MSPM0 generated init copied with 1 line removed, because the AM13 SysConfig has no module for a timer in PWM mode.

# Does MSPM0 driverlib code run on the LP-AM13E230 with only a shim header?

**Short answer.** Yes, for these three programs. A GPIO toggle, a UART print and a timer PWM written for the LP-MSPM0G3507 build and run on the LP-AM13E230 with every line of their app code unchanged (53 lines of code in all). The shim is a 13-line `ti_msp_dl_config.h`. The reason is that the AM13 driverlib already carries about 530 macros that redirect MSPM0 names to its own (`DL_UART_Main_*`, `DL_TimerG_*` and the I2C names). What did not carry over is the part SysConfig writes: pin and peripheral setup, and for the PWM program the whole timer setup.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md) (DriverLib, SysConfig, shim). A shim header is a small file that makes one chip's names resolve on another. Board page: [LP-AM13E230 README](../../am13e230/README.md), [FAQ](../../am13e230/FAQ.md). Files: `portability/shim/mspm0_on_am13e230/`. Run 2026-10-09 on macOS 15.7 (Intel) with the AM13E2x SDK 26.01.00.03, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS, SysConfig 1.28.0 and MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07.

**Question.** A builder with MSPM0 code in hand wants to know how much of it moves to the AM13E230, which has the same driverlib style. An earlier check of this board compared function names only: 51 of the 70 MSPM0 GPIO functions exist on the AM13 under the same name. Does code that uses them build and run?

**Vendor position.** The AM13 driverlib headers say it in comments. `dl_unicommuart.h`, for example, carries `/*! Redirects to @ref DL_UART_Config */ #define DL_UART_Main_Config DL_UART_Config`, 182 such lines for the UART, 113 in `dl_timerg.h`, 124 and 111 for the two I2C roles. No page in the SDK user guide describes them. The 26.01.00.03 release notes list "GP Timer in PWM mode" under "Drivers and Sysconfig support" in "What Is Not Supported". Checked 2026-10-09.

**What was tried.** Three MSPM0 programs, built from the terminal by `build.sh` with the SDK's prebuilt libraries (same flags as the other AM13 builds here):

1. **GPIO toggle.** `mspm0g3507/src-g3507/gpio_toggle_output.c`, the LaunchPad blink that rotates three LEDs.
2. **UART print.** The MSPM0 SDK's `uart_rw_multibyte_fifo_poll.c`, which sends `MSP!`. The folder `mspm0g3507/` holds only the GPIO program as plain driverlib code, so two MSPM0 SDK programs stand in for UART and PWM.
3. **Timer PWM.** The MSPM0 SDK's `timx_timer_mode_pwm_edge_sleep.c`: two outputs from one timer, duty 75 and 50 percent.

For each, the AM13 side is a SysConfig file that names things the way the MSPM0 one did (`GPIO_LEDS`, `USER_LED_1`, `UART_0`), so the macros the app uses come out with the same names. The three LED pins sit on one port, because the MSPM0 generator names one port per group and the AM13 generator names one per pin.

**How far it got.** Run, all three.

| Program | Proof |
|---|---|
| GPIO toggle | The LED output register (PA5, PA6, PA7) read 13 times over the probe: only one of the three bits set at a time, cycling 0x20, 0x40, 0x80. The program blinks LED4 (PA5) first, as the MSPM0 one does its first LED |
| UART print | `MSP!` arrived on the backchannel serial port at 9600 baud. The program then waits for four received bytes with nothing connected, as its source does without a loopback wire |
| Timer PWM | A sampler in the same image read the two pins 400k times: PA3 high 74.9 percent, PA4 high 49.9 percent, against 75 and 50 in the MSPM0 SysConfig. 780 cycles in 400k samples at 100 kHz gives 195 Hz, which is 100 MHz / (256 x 2000) |

**Counts.** Lines of code, comments and blank lines left out.

| Program | App code lines | Unchanged | Edited | Shim header | AM13 SysConfig |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| GPIO toggle | 21 | 21 | 0 | 13 | 19 |
| UART print | 23 | 23 | 0 | 13 (same file) | 32 |
| Timer PWM | 9 | 9 | 0 | 13 (same file) | 7 |

The shim header's 13 lines hold 6 that matter: the include of the AM13 header, `CPUCLK_FREQ`, `delay_cycles`, and a 3-line `GPIO_LEDS_PORT` alias. The PWM program also has `pwm_init.c`: 36 lines copied from the MSPM0 generated config, of which 35 are unchanged and 1 is removed, plus 14 lines the AM13 generator would have written (power, pin mux, `SYSCFG_DL_init`), and a 10-line `board_pins.h` naming the timer and its pins. The sampler (`probe.c`, 18 lines) is test equipment, not part of the port.

**The line.** None reached in the app code. Four places where the MSPM0 side and the AM13 side differ, each handled once:

1. **No SysConfig for a timer PWM.** The AM13 generator offers GPIO, UART, ADC, MCPWM and timer capture and compare modules, but none for a general-purpose timer as PWM. The driverlib calls work (the PWM ran), so the MSPM0 generated init was copied. **Tool or docs.**
2. **One struct field is missing.** The field `.isTimerWithFourCC = false` in the MSPM0 PWM config does not exist in the AM13 `DL_Timer_PWMConfig` (the AM13 timers have two channels). It is the one removed line, and a shim header cannot add a struct field. **Chip limit.**
3. **Pin names differ.** MSPM0 `IOMUX_PINCM34` is AM13 `IOMUX_PINCM_PA3`; the pin function names differ too (`IOMUX_PA3_TIMG4_0_CCP0`). These come from the generator for GPIO and UART, and by hand for the PWM pins. **Tool or docs.** Look the AM13 names up in the generated `ti_msp_dl_config.h` or the device header.
4. **Port naming.** One `GPIO_LEDS_PORT` per group on MSPM0, one per pin on AM13. **Tool or docs.**

**Where it stopped.** It did not stop. Not covered: I2C, SPI, ADC, DMA and interrupt code. The ADC is the likely break: the AM13 has 12-bit converters with a different sequencer API (the release notes rename `DL_ADC_TRIGGER_ADC0_SEQ1` in this very release).

- All 270 LP-MSPM0G3507 SDK driverlib examples against the shim, as an earlier sweep did for the CC2340R5, to get a rate instead of three programs.
- The reverse: AM13 driverlib programs on an MSPM0.
- Running the copied PWM init with a four-channel timer to see whether the removed field matters on MSPM0.
- The I2C redirects (235 macros) with a sensor attached.

**Ask.** Would a team move an MSPM0 product to the AM13 this way, with SysConfig redone and the app code kept? The useful answer is which driverlib families their code uses beyond GPIO, UART and timers.

**What to do next.** On this evidence the app-level driverlib calls move; the configuration does not. Plan the work as redoing the SysConfig file and the pin list, then recompiling the app. The one place that needed hand work, a timer in PWM mode, is the one place the AM13 SysConfig has no module.

## Questions

### Does an MSPM0 `DL_UART_Main_Config` or `DL_TimerG_*` call compile on the AM13E230?

Yes in these programs. **Tool or docs.** The AM13 driverlib headers redirect about 530 MSPM0 names with `#define` lines, for example `#define DL_UART_Main_Config DL_UART_Config`. No SDK user guide page lists them.

### Why is there no SysConfig module for a timer in PWM mode?

The AM13 generator has none. **Tool or docs.** The release notes list "GP Timer in PWM mode" as not supported. The driverlib calls work: copy the MSPM0 generated init and remove `.isTimerWithFourCC = false`.

### Why does `.isTimerWithFourCC` fail to compile?

The AM13 `DL_Timer_PWMConfig` has no such field, because its timers have two channels. **Chip limit.** A shim header cannot add a struct field, so delete the line.

### Why does `GPIO_LEDS_PORT` not exist?

The AM13 generator names one port per pin, MSPM0 one per group. **Tool or docs.** This repo's 3-line alias in the shim header maps it.

FILE: docs/experiments/2026-10-09-am13e230-npu-nnc.md | Does TI's compiler put this repo's room-occupancy models on the LP-AM13E230's NPU, and how much faster is it?

<!-- experiment

reached: verified
line: TI's NNC ran all four room-occupancy models on the AM13E230's TinyEngine NPU with 20 of 20 test vectors right, 4.7x, 6.7x, 8.8x and 2.4x faster than NNC's own CPU build (8k model: 5.544 ms to 0.630 ms at 200 MHz). # Does TI's compiler put this repo's room-occupancy models on the LP-AM13E230's NPU, and how much faster is it?

**Short answer.** Yes. The NPU build matched the expected class on 20 of 20 test vectors in every run and took 0.107, 0.205, 0.630 and 9.535 ms on the 636, 1,748, 8,484 and 32.8k-weight models at 200 MHz. TI's own CPU build of the same model on the same core, clock and compiler took 0.499, 1.376, 5.544 and 22.91 ms, so the NPU is 4.7, 6.7, 8.8 and 2.4 times faster. The software-only build is verified the same way. The CDE build (custom instructions on the Cortex-M33) does not work: it compiles only after a compiler error is turned into a warning, and then the board halts before the first result.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). 1 kB = 1,024 bytes. NNC is TI's Neural Network Compiler. NPU is the chip's TinyEngine neural processing unit. CDE is the Arm Custom Datapath Extension.

**Question.** Does a model compiled by TI's NNC 2.1.2 run on the AM13E230's NPU and give the right answers, and does the CDE build do the same?

**Vendor position.** NNC 2.1.2 supports "AM13x and Arm Cortex-M33 core based devices" with three targets (NNC user's guide 2.2.4, <https://software-dl.ti.com/mctools/nnc/mcu/users_guide/compiling.html>, read 2026-10-09): the NPU (`--target="c, ti-npu"`), plain CPU (`type=soft`) and CDE (`type=m33cde`, compiled with `-march=thumbv8.1-m.main+cdecp0`). The guide says nothing about which compiler versions the CDE path was tested with, and its setup example names `ti-cgt-armllvm_4.0.3.LTS`; this repo used 5.1.1.LTS, the version the AM13E2x SDK asks for.

**What was tried.** The four models (the `occ_cnn_*` int8 ONNX models, 636 to 33k weights) compiled three ways with the guide's Cortex-M33 options. NNC 2.1.2 has no build for an Intel Mac, so the compile ran on a Linux machine through a GitHub Actions workflow: one run built the NPU and software targets for all four models, a second built the CDE target. Each result was linked on this Mac with TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS and the AM13E2x SDK and run from flash at 200 MHz: 20 vectors checked, then one `tvmgen_default_run` call timed with the DWT cycle counter, best of 5 per vector, fastest vector quoted. Three runs per image, each a full erase, flash and run. Rows: `data/results/am13e230.csv` (`ai_occ_latency`, variants `-npu`, `-nnc-cpu`, `-nnc-cde`).

**How far it got.** Verified for the NPU and software builds: 24 of 24 runs matched 20 of 20 vectors, and the fastest-vector cycle count was identical across the three runs on 7 of 8 builds (the 500-model NPU build differed by 11 cycles on one run, 21,333 against 21,344). The CDE build reached link and flash, and failed at run.

| Model | Multiply-adds | NNC CPU build | NNC NPU build | Speed-up | Runs |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| occ_cnn_500 | 11,328 | 0.499 ms | 0.107 ms | 4.7x | 3 |
| occ_cnn_2k | 33,856 | 1.376 ms | 0.205 ms | 6.7x | 3 |
| occ_cnn_8k | 157,824 | 5.544 ms | 0.630 ms | 8.8x | 3 |
| occ_cnn_30k | 610,560 | 22.91 ms | 9.535 ms | 2.4x | 3 |

Expectation, written before the run: 3 to 10 times on the 1,748- and 8.5k-weight models, with the 32.8k-weight model possibly losing a layer to the CPU. Both held (6.7 and 8.8 times; the 32.8k-weight model gains 2.4 times). The sibling experiment on the MSPM0G5187 is [mspm0g5187-npu-vs-cpu](2026-10-09-mspm0g5187-npu-vs-cpu.md); the full AM13E230 write-up, including the plain C comparison, is in [RESULTS-am13e230](../../am13e230/RESULTS-am13e230.md).

**The line.** Two limits, one of them hard.

- The CDE target. With the guide's options (`type=m33cde`, `-march=thumbv8.1-m.main+cdecp0`) the last compile step fails on all four models with `error: incompatible pointer types passing 'const uint32_t[16]' to parameter of type 'const int8_t *'` in NNC's generated `lib2.c` (`TINIE_fullyConnectedCDE`, and the bias argument of `TINIE_convolveCDE`), and `mod.a` is never written. With `-Wno-error=incompatible-pointer-types` a library comes out. Flashed, the image takes an instruction bus error before the first result: CFSR 0x00000100, HFSR 0x40000000 (FORCED), result block empty after 8 s, 0 of 20 vectors, on all four models, with the coprocessor-access bit for CDE set in CPACR or not. Cause unknown (the bus error is an instruction fetch; the faulting address was not read).
- The 32.8k-weight model gains least. NNC's compile log says `GCONV layer NOT offloaded to TI-NPU` (the weights could overflow the NPU's 18-bit accumulator), so one convolution stays on the CPU, as on the G5187.

**Ask.** Has anyone run NNC's `type=m33cde` output on an AM13E2x, and with which compiler version? If the bus error comes from pairing NNC 2.1.2 with Arm Clang 5.1.1, please say so.

FILE: docs/experiments/2026-10-09-am13e230-radar-host-parser.md | Can the LP-AM13E230 run the IWRL6432BOOST radar frame parser, with no wire to the radar?
==============================================================================

<!-- experiment
id: E149
board: LP-AM13E230
date: 2026-10-09
status: works
reached: verified
line: The radar stream parser used on the Mac runs on the LP-AM13E230 as 882 bytes of code and 152 bytes of state, fed from the USB serial port: 62 of 62 frame lines match the Mac parser on a real capture and 40 of 40 on a synthetic one, with no byte lost. The wire to a live radar was not made, and the real capture holds no point cloud, so range was checked on synthetic frames only.
stop: none
-->
# Can the LP-AM13E230 run the IWRL6432BOOST radar frame parser, with no wire to the radar?

**Short answer.** Yes. The parser that reads the IWRL6432BOOST's UART stream on the Mac was rewritten as a small streaming C parser and run on the LP-AM13E230, fed from the board's USB serial port by a replay from the Mac. On a real capture of 62 frames the board's output matched the Mac parser line for line, including the detected-object count in every frame. On a synthetic frame set of 40 frames it matched the Mac parser and the generator's own record, including the nearest range. The real radar was not wired to the board.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). A TLV is a type, length, value record inside a radar frame. The backchannel UART is the board's USB serial port. 1 kB = 1,024 bytes on this page. Board page: [LP-AM13E230 README](../../am13e230/README.md), [FAQ](../../am13e230/FAQ.md). Radar: [IWRL6432BOOST](../../iwrl6432boost/README.md). Files: `am13e230/radar-parser/`. Run 2026-10-09 on macOS 15.7 (Intel) with the AM13E2x SDK 26.01.00.03, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS and SysConfig 1.28.0.

**Question.** A radar that reports presence and points over a UART needs a host that reads the stream. If the host is a motor-control MCU rather than a Mac, does the parsing fit and keep up?

**Vendor position.** TI's Radar Toolbox 4.00.00.05 motion and presence demo writes a magic word `02 01 04 03 06 05 08 07`, a 40-byte header (version, total length, platform, frame number, CPU cycles, detected objects, number of TLVs, sub-frame number, all 32-bit little endian) and then TLVs of type, length and payload. The type numbers come from `motion_detect.h` in the toolbox. The shipped demo sends only the presence TLVs (315 and 319), and the object count is in the header. Checked 2026-10-09.

**What was tried.**

1. Took the Mac parser, `iwrl6432boost/tools/tlv_parse.py`, and wrote `tlv_parser.c`: the same rules (sync on the magic word, a header whose length is under 40 or over 65,536 is skipped and the scan resumes after the magic word, TLVs read while 8 header bytes fit inside the frame), one byte at a time, nothing buffered. It reads TLV 315 (presence flag and first zone byte) and TLV 1 (float points, 16 bytes each, nearest range computed as the square root of x squared plus y squared plus z squared).
2. Wrote a board program that moves bytes from the backchannel UART (UC4, 115200) into the parser and prints one line per completed frame. Nothing blocks: the main loop alternates between the receive FIFO and the transmit FIFO through a 4 kB output ring, so a long print cannot overrun the receiver.
3. Replayed the real capture, a 15 s capture of the shipped demo's UART stream (23.5 kB, 62 frames, recorded the same day), through the board's serial port at line rate. `replay.py` waits for the board's banner, sends the bytes and compares the board's lines with the Mac parser run on the same file.
4. The capture has no point cloud, so range could not be tested on it. A synthetic frame set was built from the documented format (`make_synthetic.py`): 40 frames, 0 to 12 points each, TLV 1 and 7 and 315, one unknown TLV type, one frame with no TLVs, short bursts of noise between frames and a false header with length 10 that the parser must skip. **This set is synthetic. It is not radar data.**

**How far it got.** Verified, on both sets.

| Set | Size | Frames | Board lines that match the Mac parser | Other check |
|---|--:|--:|--|---|
| Real capture | 23.5 kB | 62 | 62 of 62 | Object counts: 59 frames with 0, one with 5, one with 7, plus a malformed first frame (count 838860801) that both parsers read the same way |
| Synthetic | 7.5 kB | 40 | 40 of 40 | 40 of 40 against the generator's own record of objects, points and nearest range |

The board's counters after the synthetic run: 7.5 kB received (every byte of the file), 40 frames, 0 receiver overruns, 0 dropped output bytes. A line looks like `F2 L306 O12 T3 P1,2 N12 R2121`: frame 2, 306 bytes, 12 objects, 3 TLVs, presence byte 1 and zone byte 2, 12 points, nearest 2,121 mm (synthetic). The replay of the real capture took 2.1 s at 115,200 baud against the 15 s the recording ran, so the board kept up with a stream seven times faster than the radar sends it.

**The line.** None reached in the parser. It is 882 bytes of code and a 152-byte state struct, plus the 4 kB output ring and the 4 kB stack the project's linker file gives; the whole image uses 7.7 kB of flash and 12.2 kB of RAM. A first estimate put a streaming presence parser at under 100 bytes of state; this repo's is 152 with a result record and a point buffer in it.

**Where it stopped.** At the wire. Real radar to board was not connected, so three things are open: whether the board's UART keeps up with the radar's own timing and any gaps, the 1,250,000 baud setting the demo can use, and a stream that carries the point cloud (the shipped demo configuration does not). **Setup or handling** for the missing wire. **Unknown** for the three open items: nothing in the replay suggests a problem, but the replay is faster than the radar and has no gaps.

- Wire the radar's UART to a second AM13 UART (a different unicomm and pins) and parse the live stream, with the radar powered from its own USB port.
- Replay at 1,250,000 baud by running the board's UART faster, to see where the parser loses bytes.
- Use the trig unit or the NPU for the range and a presence rule, rather than a square root in the C library.
- Run the same C file on an MSPM0 and compare flash, RAM and cycles per byte.
- Capture a live stream with a point-cloud configuration, so range is checked on real data.

**Ask.** Would a motor-control team put the radar parsing on the same MCU as the motor loop? The useful answer is how many bytes of RAM and what share of the CPU they would give it.

**What to do next.** The host side of this radar is small. A byte-at-a-time parser in 882 bytes of code handled a real capture and a synthetic set with no lost byte, on a part that has a motor loop to run beside it. Wire the radar to a second UART and capture a point-cloud stream.

## Questions

### Can a motor-control MCU parse the IWRL6432BOOST UART stream?

Yes on a replay. The parser is 882 bytes of code and 152 bytes of state, and all 62 real frames and 40 synthetic frames matched the Mac parser. **Setup or handling.** The live radar was not wired.

### Why is the nearest range only checked on synthetic frames?

The shipped demo sends no point cloud. **TI example default.** The real capture has TLV 315 and a header object count, so range was tested on 40 synthetic frames only.

### Will it keep up at the radar's 1,250,000 baud?

Not tested. **Unknown.** The replay ran at 115,200 baud with no gaps.

### What is the first frame's object count of 838860801?

A malformed first frame in the capture. **Setup or handling.** Both parsers read it the same way.

# Can the TI LP-AM13E230 spin a hobby-kit motor with no soldering?

**Short answer.** Yes. The kit's 28BYJ-48 stepper turned one full turn each way, repeating, from four plain output pins on J4 and the board's 5 V on J3, through the kit's ULN2003 driver board. Six jumper wires, no breadboard, no soldering. The program is `am13e230/stepper-uln2003/`.

![The kit stepper on the desk, wired to the LP-AM13E230](../../am13e230/stepper-uln2003/am13e230-stepper-proof.jpg)

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md), [LP-AM13E230 FAQ](../../am13e230/FAQ.md). MCPWM is the chip's motor PWM (pulse width modulation) block. ULN2003 is a chip of seven switches that carries the motor current so the board's pins do not. A half-step is one move in an 8-state coil sequence; 4,096 of them turn the output shaft once. eQEP is the chip's quadrature encoder input, which reads a rotary knob. XDS110 is the programmer built into the LaunchPad. Tools: TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS, SysConfig 1.28.0, macOS, checked 2026-10-09. 1 kB = 1,024 bytes. Board page: [LP-AM13E230 README](../../am13e230/README.md). Wiring picture: [am13e230-stepper-uln2003.png](../../am13e230/stepper-uln2003/am13e230-stepper-uln2003.png).

**Question.** Which hobby-kit motor can this board spin with the parts in the box, and what does the board need to do it?

**Vendor position.** TI's motor examples for this board, in `solutions/motor_control/ufoc_lp_bxl/`, all need a BOOSTXL-DRV8323RH or DRV8329A BoosterPack and a three-phase motor. The SDK has no example for a stepper or a brushed DC motor. The user guide (SLVUDH9, read 2026-10-09) gives 5 V on J3 pin 21 and the MCPWM4 outputs on J4 pins 35 to 40.

**What was on the desk.** Three ways to spin something, none needing a motor BoosterPack:

| Motor | Driver | Soldering | Board pins |
|---|---|---|---|
| 28BYJ-48 stepper (kit) | ULN2003 board (kit, headers fitted) | none | 4 outputs, 5 V, GND |
| DC motor (kit) | L293D chip (kit, in the breadboard) | none | 2 PWM outputs, 5 V, GND |
| DC motor (kit) | DRV8833 carrier (TI chip) | headers first | 2 PWM outputs, 5 V, GND |

**What was tried.** The stepper through the ULN2003 board: four outputs on port B (PB3, PB1, PB2, PB7 on J4 pins 40, 38, 36, 34), the 8-state half-step sequence, 1.2 ms a step, 4,096 half-steps a turn, one turn each way with a 1 s pause, LED4 on while stepping, all coils off between turns. A first program drove a DC motor through the L293D on MCPWM4 outputs 1A and 2A (PB3 and PB1, J4 pins 40 and 38) at 20 kHz; it built and flashed in 8 s, and the DC-motor program is in `am13e230/motor-l293d/`.

**How far it got.** Verified: the shaft turned both ways on the first flash, seen on a video of the bench. The frame above is the saved record. The wiring takes about five minutes from the picture. The driver board's four LEDs chase with the coils.

| What | Value |
|---|---|
| Build, flash | 3.1 s, 4.2 s |
| Flash used | 8.0 kB |
| Step time, steps a turn | 1.2 ms, 4,096 half-steps (about 5 s a turn) |

**The line.** None found: this is four output pins and a 5 V rail, well inside what the board offers. Not measured: the real turn time against the 4,096-step assumption (the gearbox ratio on these motors is close to, not exactly, 64), the coil current, and the fastest step the motor holds from 5 V.

**Ask.** What gearbox ratio do these 28BYJ-48 motors really have (63.68:1 or 64:1), so the turn count can be checked against a mark on the shaft?

**What to take from it.** A motor-control chip does not need its motor BoosterPack to move something. The kit's stepper board is the no-solder, no-breadboard way in: four outputs and a sequence table.

**To try it.** Wire it yourself with [the program's README](../../am13e230/stepper-uln2003/README.md): build and flash take about 7 s. If it does not turn, see its "If you see" list, which carries the same fixes as the FAQ.

FILE: docs/experiments/2026-10-09-am13e230-stm32g4-hal-layer.md | Does STM32G4 HAL code run on the LP-AM13E230 through TI's compatibility layer?
==============================================================================

<!-- experiment
id: E34
board: LP-AM13E230
date: 2026-10-09
status: line found
reached: run
line: TI's STM32G4 HAL layer runs ST's GPIO and UART examples on the LP-AM13E230 with 3 and 7 lines added to ST's main.c, plus a 13-line and a 50-line TI-side shim; it has no clock tree, no timer and no ADC, so ST's timer examples stop at the first compile (90 and 87 errors), and its delay and timeout arguments count CPU cycles, not milliseconds.

-->
# Does STM32G4 HAL code run on the LP-AM13E230 through TI's compatibility layer?

**Short answer.** Yes for GPIO, UART and DMA, with two catches. All five of TI's layer examples build and run on the board (SPI only as far as it can without a second board). ST's own GPIO toggle and UART printf examples, written for a different chip family, run on it with 3 and 7 lines inserted into ST's `main.c` and no line of ST's changed. But the layer has no timer, no ADC, no clock tree and no I2C, and every delay and timeout you pass it is counted in CPU cycles, not milliseconds. ST's timer examples fail at the first compile.

Contents: the question, TI's position, what was tried, how far it got, edits to ST's examples, the line, where it stopped, ideas, the ask, what to do next, then four questions with answers.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md) (HAL, DriverLib, SysConfig, shim). Board page: [LP-AM13E230 README](../../am13e230/README.md), [FAQ](../../am13e230/FAQ.md). HAL is ST's driver library. "The layer" here is TI's `source/compatibility/stm32g4_hal`, a re-implementation of ST's STM32G4 HAL function names on top of TI's driverlib. Code and scripts: `am13e230/stm32g4-hal/`. DSLite is UniFlash's command-line flasher. A unicomm is one of the board's serial-capable peripheral blocks; the layer's `USART2` and the USB serial port of the LaunchPad development kit sit on different ones. 1 kB = 1,024 bytes on this page. Run 2026-10-09 on macOS 15.7 (Intel) with the AM13E2x SDK 26.01.00.03, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS, SysConfig 1.28.0 and DSLite from UniFlash 9.6.0.

**Question.** TI aims the pin-compatible AM13E230 at teams with working STM32G4 code. How much of that code compiles and runs on the AM13E230 as it is, and where does the layer stop?

**Vendor position.** The SDK release notes (26.01.00.03) list "STM G4 Compatible drivers for following peripherals: DMA GPIO SPI UART" as supported, and "STM G4 Compatible drivers support for I2C MCAN" and "Limited examples for STM G4 Compatible drivers" under "What Is Not Supported". Each of the five examples says it shows "that existing STM32G4 HAL [GPIO, DMA, SPI, UART] code can run with minimal modifications". TI's STM32G4 migration guide (SDAA226, March 2026) compares pins, peripherals and clocks; the word HAL does not appear in it, so the layer is documented only in the SDK's example pages and the release notes. Checked 2026-10-09.

**What was tried.**

1. Built TI's five LaunchPad examples with this repo's own script (`build.sh`, same compiler flags and prebuilt libraries as the SDK's other examples, no CMake), flashed each with DSLite and checked it.
2. Counted the layer's coverage: every function the layer's headers declare against every symbol in its prebuilt library (`libstm32g4_hal_ti_sdk_cfg_default_m33_ti_arm_clang.a`, read with `tiarmnm`).
3. Took ST's own examples for the NUCLEO-U083RC from STM32CubeU0 v1.3.0 (the same ones run on that ST board): the HAL GPIO toggle, the HAL UART printf, and for timers the HAL `TIM_DMA` (PWM through `HAL_TIM_PWM_Start_DMA`) and the LL `TIM_PWMOutput_Init`. Built each against the layer's headers with a stand-in `main.h`. Where it compiled, fixed only what the compiler named, and kept ST's `main.c` otherwise as shipped.

**How far it got.** Run for TI's three single-board examples and for ST's GPIO and UART examples. Built but not run end to end for the two SPI examples. Compile stopped for both ST timer examples.

| Example | Flash | RAM | What ran | How it was checked |
|---|--:|--:|---|---|
| TI `GPIO_IOToggle` (PB0) | 8.4 kB | 9.0 kB | Toggles | PB0 output register read 8 times over the probe: 0 1 0 1 0 0 1 1 |
| TI `UART_Printf` | 17.5 kB | 9.3 kB | Prints | Two lines at 115200 on the backchannel serial port: `UART Printf Example: retarget the C library printf function to the UART` and `** Test finished successfully. **` |
| TI `DMA_FLASHToRAM` | 17.8 kB | 9.3 kB | Passes | Transfer-complete flag 1, error flag 0, the 32-word destination buffer equals the source word for word, LED2 (PA5) output high on two reads |
| TI `SPI_Poll_Master` | 12.3 kB | 9.6 kB | Waits for the user button | LED2 toggles in the button wait loop (10 reads), button pin PB13 reads 1 (released). The transfer needs a button press and an STM32 slave on PA20, PB5 and PB10 |
| TI `SPI_Poll_Slave` | 11.3 kB | 9.3 kB | Times out | With no master on the wires it reached the error blink after its 5 s wait (8 reads, toggling). Not run against a master |
| ST `GPIO_IOToggle`, through the layer | 8.4 kB | 9.0 kB | Toggles | PA5 (LED4) output register read 10 times: 1 1 0 0 1 0 1 1 0 0 |
| ST `UART_Printf`, through the layer | 10.7 kB | 9.1 kB | Prints, with odd parity | Both of ST's lines on the backchannel read as 8 data bits and odd parity; read as no parity they come out garbled |
| ST `TIM_DMA` (HAL timer PWM) | n/a | n/a | Does not compile | 90 errors, 49 distinct missing names, the first `unknown type name 'TIM_HandleTypeDef'` |
| ST `TIM_PWMOutput_Init` (LL timer PWM) | n/a | n/a | Does not compile | 87 errors, 46 distinct missing names, the first `use of undeclared identifier 'LL_APB1_GRP1_PERIPH_PWR'` |

Flash and RAM come from the linker maps (RAM is `RAM_S` plus `RAM_C`). The SDK's own prebuilt copies of the five TI examples also ran clean in the earlier sweep of this board.

**Edits to ST's examples.** Lines of ST's `main.c` unchanged, inserted and changed, then the TI-side files each example needs.

| Example | ST `main.c` lines | Unchanged | Inserted | Changed or deleted | Lines of ST code switched off | TI-side shim |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|---|
| GPIO toggle | 204 | 204 | 3 | 0 | 32 | `main.h` 13 lines |
| UART printf | 310 | 310 | 7 | 0 | 48 | `main.h` 20 lines, MSP file 17, retarget file 13 |

What the inserted lines do. Both examples set the clock in a 32-line `SystemClock_Config` built on ST's RCC and PWR calls, which the layer does not have. `SYSCFG_DL_init();` was added (TI's clock setup from the `.syscfg` file) and the ST body was wrapped in `#if 0`. The UART example also needs `#if 0` around the prescaler and advanced-feature fields and the three `HAL_UARTEx_*` FIFO calls. The shim `main.h` stands in for ST's: it includes the layer's headers, maps `LED4` to PA5 (the same pin on both boards), turns ST's clock-enable macros into nothing, and redefines `HAL_Delay(ms)` to multiply by 200k cycles per millisecond. Its other jobs: `USART2` becomes `UART5` (the layer maps `USART2` to unicomm 1, but the USB serial port of the LaunchPad development kit is unicomm 4), and a small `BSP_LED_*` stand-in replaces ST's board support file. The UART MSP file replaces ST's 158-line `stm32u0xx_hal_msp.c` (RCC clock select, gate, alternate function 7) with TI's own pin setup on PA0 and PA1. The retarget file adds a `write()` that feeds each character to ST's `__io_putchar`, and turns off `stdout` buffering, because TI's C library only flushes on exit and the example never exits. TI's own `example.syscfg` for each example is used unchanged. ST's other files (`system_*.c`, `stm32u0xx_it.c`, `hal_conf`, `nucleo_conf`) are not used.

**The line.** The layer covers 65 of the 93 functions its headers declare.

| Part | Declared | In the library | Missing |
|---|--:|--:|---|
| Core (`HAL_Init`, tick, ids) | 19 | 3 | `HAL_DeInit`, `HAL_IncTick`, `HAL_InitTick`, `HAL_SetTickFreq`, `HAL_MspInit` and eleven more |
| GPIO | 8 | 8 | none |
| DMA | 11 | 11 | none |
| UART | 27 | 23 | `Transmit_DMA`, `Receive_DMA`, `RegisterCallback`, `UnRegisterCallback` |
| SPI | 28 | 20 | `Transmit_DMA`, `Receive_DMA`, `TransmitReceive_DMA`, `DMAPause`, `DMAResume`, `DMAStop`, the callback registers |

Beyond the function counts, four limits decide whether a given STM32G4 project moves:

1. **No clock, power or timer.** There is no RCC, PWR, TIM, ADC, I2C or CAN in the layer. Any project that sets its clock through ST's `HAL_RCC_*` or runs a timer, a PWM or a conversion needs those parts rewritten with TI's driverlib. **Tool or docs.** The release notes list I2C and CAN as not supported; the timer, ADC and clock gaps are not stated anywhere found.
2. **Time is in CPU cycles.** `HAL_Delay(x)` waits x cycles and `HAL_GetTick()` returns a 32-bit cycle counter at 200 MHz, which wraps every 21.5 s. ST's `HAL_Delay(100)` becomes 0.5 microseconds. Every timeout argument is in cycles too: ST's UART example passes `0xFFFF` as a transmit timeout, which is 0.33 ms, and a whole 70-byte string sent in one call with that timeout printed almost nothing until one character per call was sent, as ST's code does. **Tool or docs.** The unit is written once, as a comment in the SPI example's `main.c`, and nowhere on the example pages or in the headers.
3. **Peripheral instance numbers are TI's, not ST's.** `USART2` drives unicomm 1, not the pins ST's example sets up. The pin setup is not in the layer: each example brings its own MSP file with TI's `IOMUX_*` names. **Tool or docs.**
4. **Settings are partly ignored.** The UART code has a `TODO` for oversampling and one-bit sampling, so those fields are accepted and do nothing. **Tool or docs.** Parity, word length, stop bits and flow control are mapped and worked: ST's odd parity came out on the wire.

**Where it stopped.** For ST's two timer examples at the compile: the layer's headers define no timer type, no timer register names and no `stm32g4xx_ll_*` headers, so `main.c` fails on its first timer line. **Tool or docs.** That is a missing part of the layer, not a chip limit. The AM13E230 has timers and motor PWM units; TI's driverlib drives them, and the layer does not.

- An unmodified STM32CubeG4 example, as the question first asked, instead of the NUCLEO-U083RC ones. Only the STM32CubeU0 package is on this Mac. The U0 examples already differ from G4 ones in the clock calls, which is the part the layer drops either way.
- The two SPI examples against each other: a second board with an STM32G4 SPI slave, or one TI board per role with three jumpers (PA20, PB5, PB10) and a button press.
- Compiling the layer's source into the project instead of linking TI's prebuilt library, and adding `HAL_TIM_PWM_*` on top of driverlib's timer calls. The layer's source is 5 files, about 3,200 lines.
- ST's HAL interrupt-driven UART and DMA examples, which hit the missing `RegisterCallback`.

**Ask.** Would a team with real STM32G4 code put this layer into a product build? The question to someone with an STM32G4 project is which of its HAL calls beyond GPIO, UART, SPI and DMA it uses, since the timer, ADC and clock calls are the likely stop.

**What to do next.** The layer lets you keep ST's GPIO, UART, SPI and DMA code and its call names while you redo the clock, pins, timers and analog parts in TI's tools. In this repo's two ports ST's `main.c` kept every line it had, and the work was in the files around it. Check the delay and timeout units first: they compile without a warning and run wrong.

## Questions

### Why does `HAL_Delay(100)` return almost at once on the LP-AM13E230?

The layer counts cycles, not milliseconds. **Tool or docs.** `HAL_Delay(x)` waits x CPU cycles at 200 MHz, so 100 is 0.5 microseconds. Multiply your milliseconds by 200k, as this repo's shim `main.h` does. Source: `am13e230/stm32g4-hal/`.

### Why does a long `HAL_UART_Transmit` string print almost nothing?

The timeout is in cycles too. **Tool or docs.** ST's `0xFFFF` is 0.33 ms here, too short for a 70-byte string sent in one call. One character was sent per call, as ST's code does.

### Why does an STM32G4 timer, PWM, ADC or clock code fail to compile with `unknown type name 'TIM_HandleTypeDef'`?

The layer has no timer, ADC, RCC, PWR or I2C parts. **Tool or docs.** ST's `HAL_TIM_PWM_Start_DMA` example gave 90 errors and the LL timer example 87. Rewrite those parts with TI's driverlib.

### Why is the ST UART example's output garbled on the backchannel port?

The port needs 8 data bits and odd parity to read ST's setup. **Setup or handling.** Read as no parity, both lines come out garbled.

# Does upstream Zephyr run on the TI LP-AM13E230 from a Mac, flashed by OpenOCD built from source?

**Short answer.** Yes, with limits. Zephyr's `main` branch has a board for the LP-AM13E230, and from an Intel Mac it was built, flashed with OpenOCD built from source, and watched running. This repo's `led-proof` app (it writes the GPIO registers by hand) blinked LED4 and its counter rose by 4 per second. `hello_world` booted the kernel, reached `main` and went idle, but prints nothing, because the chip has no serial driver in Zephyr. Zephyr's own `blinky` does not build: the board file has no LED and no GPIO driver. OpenOCD built in 3.5 minutes; programming 12.6 kB took 0.1 s.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md) (OpenOCD, devicetree, XDS110). Recipe and commands: [am13e230/zephyr/README.md](../../am13e230/zephyr/README.md). Errors and fixes: [LP-AM13E230 FAQ](../../am13e230/FAQ.md). 1 kB = 1,024 bytes.

**Question.** Can a builder follow Zephyr's own board page for the LP-AM13E230, from a Mac, to a built image and a flash command?

**Vendor position.** Zephyr's board page for `lp_am13e230` (`boards/ti/lp_am13e230/doc/index.rst`, `main` on 2026-10-10) calls it "a development board based on the AM13E230x SoC, a 200MHz ARM Cortex M33 real-time motor control MCU with edge AI, TMU and 512KB on-chip flash". On flashing it says: "Support for AM13E230x has been merged in upstream OpenOCD but not picked up by Zephyr's **sdk-ng**. Until the Zephyr SDK is updated to use a commit of OpenOCD that includes support for this SoC, the user has to clone and build upstream OpenOCD separately and point `west flash` to that directory." Its steps: clone `openocd-org/openocd`, `git submodule update --init`, `./bootstrap && ./configure --enable-internal-jimtcl --enable-xds110`, `make`, then `west flash --openocd <path>/src/openocd --openocd-search <path>/tcl`. The page does not name a toolchain, a Zephyr SDK version or any known limit. Its supported-features table is generated from the board's YAML, which lists none.

**What was tried.** 2026-10-10, Intel Mac with macOS 15.7.9, 4 GB of free disk. The Zephyr 4.4.2 checkout used for the other boards has no such board, and updating it would change the build their pages document, so a separate workspace was made: a shallow clone of Zephyr `main` (commit `11808e9ea`, VERSION 4.5.0) plus the three modules the board needs (`hal_ti`, `cmsis`, `cmsis_6`, fetched with `west update --narrow`), 830 MB in all, in a scratch folder outside this repo. Same toolchain route that worked on the NUCLEO-U083RC: Zephyr SDK 0.17.4's GCC 12.2.0 with `ZEPHYR_TOOLCHAIN_VARIANT=cross-compile`. Builds of `samples/basic/blinky`, `samples/hello_world` and this repo's `am13e230/zephyr/led-proof`. Then upstream OpenOCD (`0f08cd377`) built from git with `--enable-xds110`. No board, probe or serial port was opened.

**How far it got.** Configure and compile pass for all three apps. Link passes for `hello_world` and `led-proof`; `blinky` fails to compile. Both linked images flashed with `west flash` through the new OpenOCD and ran (details in "Flash and run", below).

| App | Result | Flash | RAM |
|---|---|--:|--:|
| `samples/hello_world` | links, 32 s | 12.2 kB (2.33 percent of 512 kB) | 4.0 kB (4.07 percent of 96 kB) |
| `samples/basic/blinky` | compile error | | |
| `led-proof` (this repo's, direct register writes to PA5) | links, 25 s | 12.6 kB | 4.0 kB |

From the map: `hello_world` is 9.9 kB of code, 1.6 kB of read-only data, 256 bytes of vector table, 384 of interrupt table; RAM is 3.4 kB of stacks, 575 bytes of zeroed data and 32 of initialised data. OpenOCD: autoconf and automake installed with `brew` (23 s), `./bootstrap` 13 s, `./configure` 27 s, `make -j4` 79 s; the result prints "Open On-Chip Debugger 0.12.0+dev-g0f08cd3" and contains the `am13` flash driver and `target/ti/am13e230x.cfg`. The xPack OpenOCD 0.12.0-7 used for other boards (built 2025-10-04) has neither.

**Flash and run.** 2026-10-10, one probe, no wiring or board change.

- `SERIAL=AL130001 ./build.sh flash` (rebuild of all three apps, 37 s, then flash): OpenOCD found the XDS110 (firmware 3.0.0.43), the Cortex-M33 and the flash ("AM13: MAIN flash: 512 KB (256 sectors), 2 bank(s)"), auto-erased and wrote 12.6 kB in 0.106 s. The whole command took 2 min 12 s, nearly all of it the rebuild. No error. `west flash` printed no separate verify line.
- Run, `led-proof`: after `reset run`, `proof_count` (0x20000200) read 5, then 9 one second later, then 19 two seconds after that (about 4 per second, as a 250 ms toggle gives). Bit 5 of GPIO0 DOUT (0x400F1280) read 0, 0x20, 0x20, 0, 0 in five quick reads, so the pin moves. DSLite pin reads showed 0x20 and 0 alternating. A plain `west flash` with no reset leaves the program running: the counter was 14, then 18 one second later.
- Run, `hello_world` (12.2 kB written): it prints nowhere, so the core was read. With a hardware breakpoint on `main` (0x3d0) the core stopped there after a reset, so `main` is reached. Without the breakpoint, 1.5 s after reset the core was at 0x2592, inside `arch_cpu_idle`, with the link register in `idle`: the kernel booted, `main` ran and returned, and the chip sleeps in the idle thread.
- Restore: `./am13e230/blink.sh 250` (build 3.1 s, flash 3.6 s); pin reads afterwards alternated 0 and 0x20. The restore ran twice, the second after one extra flash of `led-proof`. The stepper wired to J4 lost its coil drive while the Zephyr images ran, as expected.
- Which tool proved it: OpenOCD flashed and read; DSLite read the pin independently.
- OpenOCD note: `mdw` returns its text instead of printing it, so `-c "init; ...; mdw ..."` prints nothing. Use one `-c` per command with `echo [mdw ...]`.

**The line.** Where it stops, in order:

1. `blinky`: `error: '__device_dts_ord_DT_N_ALIAS_led0_P_gpios_IDX_0_PH_ORD' undeclared here`. The board file `lp_am13e230.dts` defines memory and the pin-control node only: no `led0` alias, no GPIO node, no serial node, and no `zephyr,console` choice. Zephyr has no AM13 GPIO or UART driver at this commit (the pin-control node reuses the MSPM0 compatible string `ti,mspm0-pinctrl` and nothing enables a driver for it).
2. `hello_world` builds and would run, but its output has nowhere to go; the backchannel port `/dev/cu.usbmodemAL1300011` stays silent. A run can only be proven with the debugger.
3. The declared CPU clock is 32 MHz and there is no clock driver, so the chip stays on its reset clock; the board file's 32 MHz is what Zephyr's timing would assume, against the 200 MHz TI's examples run at. The clock the chip really starts on was not checked.
4. 77 warnings, all `implicit declaration of function '__rbit'`: Zephyr `main`'s `bit_rev.h` calls a function the CMSIS header for GCC does not define (it defines `__RBIT`). Nothing calls it, so the link is clean. `main` wants Zephyr SDK 1.0.1 (`SDK_VERSION`); 0.17.4 was used.

The cause of 1 is missing software, not this repo's toolchain: the board is a bring-up stub.

**Ask.** If you have run Zephyr on the LP-AM13E230, say which commit, which toolchain and how you saw it run (LED, debugger or serial).

<!-- experiment
