# Can the TI LP-AM263P decode H.264 video, with no video hardware and no operating system?

**Short answer.** Yes, in software. h264bsd, an open-source baseline-profile decoder in plain C, runs on one Cortex-R5F at 400 MHz with no operating system and decodes a 640x360 stream at 26 frames per second (15.2M cycles per frame, built with -Os). The CRC of the first frame, the last frame and all 30 frames together match the same decoder on the Mac (`3f93a620`). There is no video hardware on the chip, and the LaunchPad has no display, so the check is the checksum.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). 1 kB = 1,024 bytes. Board notes: [LP-AM263P README](../../am263p/README.md) and [FAQ](../../am263p/FAQ.md).

**Question.** Could the AM263P4 on the LaunchPad show or process H.264 video with what is on the chip, the SDK and open-source code?

**Vendor position.** The data sheet SPRSP81D (Rev. D, read 2026-10-09) lists the processing resources: "Single, dual, and quad-core Arm Cortex-R5F MCU with each core running up to 400MHz", "16KB I-cache ... 16KB D-cache", "256KB Tightly-Coupled Memory (TCM) with 32bit ECC per CPU core cluster", "3MB of On-Chip RAM (OCSRAM) 6 Banks x 512KB", and an octal SPI flash interface with execute-in-place. The feature list has no video encoder, video decoder, camera interface or display controller. The Cortex-R5F in this part has the VFPv3-D16 floating-point unit and no NEON (the SDK builds with `-mfpu=vfpv3-d16`). TI's E2E forum and the MCU+ SDK pages returned nothing for H.264 on AM263x, AM263Px or AM243x (searches 2026-10-09). The LaunchPad has no display or camera, so output can only be a checksum, or a frame read from RAM.

**What was tried.**

- Software: h264bsd (commit `42bcb5d`, 2022), `https://github.com/oneam/h264bsd`. Its files come from the Android Open Source Project, Apache-2.0, and its wrappers are MIT. It decodes baseline profile only (I and P pictures), written in plain C with no operating-system calls except `malloc` and `free`.
- Stream: the first 30 pictures (94.3 kB) of the repository's own `test_640x360.h264`: baseline profile, level 3.0, 640x368 coded and 640x360 cropped, one IDR and 29 P pictures, from a "Big Buck Bunny" clip. No ffmpeg on this Mac, so no stream of this repo's own was made.
- Program: `am263p/bench/h264/` (`h264_run.c` decodes the array and prints a CRC-32 of every frame; `r5_main.c` is the R5F platform; `host_main.c` is the Mac platform). The R5F build uses the SDK makefile pattern of the other bench programs (`am263p/tools/build_bench.sh`): `r5fss0-0_nortos`, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1, SDK 26.01.00.08, loaded into RAM with DSLite. `link_patch.py` rewrites the SDK's generated linker file: a 1.7 MB heap for the C library and an OCSRAM region of 2 MB, starting at the bottom of the RAM, with the two unused shared-memory regions moved out of the way. (The first attempt used 2.6 MB; see the line.)
- Mac reference (the expectation): the same sources and the same CRC code, compiled with `cc -O3` on macOS 15.7.9, Intel.
- Expectation for speed, before any run: this repo's estimate, with no source, is 100 to 200 cycles per pixel for a core with no vector unit, which gives 23M to 47M cycles per frame at 640x368 and 8 to 17 frames per second at 400 MHz.
- Commands to rebuild: `am263p/bench/h264/build.sh os` builds both, with the 2 MB layout (`H264_OCRAM_ORIGIN=0x70000000 H264_OCRAM_LEN=0x1F0000 H264_HEAP=1753088`). Run, with the serial port opened before the load:

```bash
python3 am263p/tools/run_imgs.py 1 "H264 END" 180 h264=<build folder>/h264os2.out
```

**How far it got.** Configure, compile, link, load into RAM, run, verified by CRC. No flash was written.

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Mac reference, 30 frames, two passes | 30 frames both times, frame 1 CRC `8af3c2f8`, frame 30 `83a9d8bb`, all frames together `3f93a620` |
| Heap the decoder needs at 640x368 | 1.58 MB at its peak (exact byte count in `am263p/data/logs/h264-mac-reference.txt`), 13 allocations (about four 345 kB frame buffers plus the rest) |
| R5F image, -O3 | 285 kB of code and constants, of which the decoder is 144 kB of code and 4.9 kB of tables and the stream is 94.3 kB; heap reservation 1.8 MB |
| R5F image, -Os | 182 kB; decoder 43 kB of code |
| R5F, -Os, 3 passes, 30 frames | 457.4M to 457.5M cycles per pass, 15.2M per frame, 26.2 frames per second; the IDR picture 35.4M cycles, each P picture 10.9M on average (316.2M for 29) |
| Checksums on the board | frame 1 `8af3c2f8`, frame 30 `83a9d8bb`, all `3f93a620`: identical to the Mac in all three passes |
| Heap peak on the board | 1.54 MB on 32-bit pointers (the Mac's 64-bit pointers use 1.58 MB) |
| Speed against this repo's estimate | estimate 8 to 17 frames per second; measured 26 |

The one-IDR-plus-29-P-pictures test is a small clip: a 640x360 frame is 337.5 kB of picture data, so only a few frames can sit in RAM at once.

**The line.** No limit reached at 640x360. Two things to know. First, the memory: the layout built first (heap and code spread over 2.6 MB of OCSRAM, from the data sheet's 3 MB) loaded fine but printed nothing, not even the first line, so the program stopped before `main`. The same program with a 256 kB heap and a 1.75 MB region ran, so the board's RAM looks like 2 MB, not 3 MB (the part's RAM-size fuse nibble reads 0 and no table for it was found; unconfirmed). The run that worked uses all of 0x70000000 to 0x701EFFFF, which includes the 256 kB the SDK keeps for its bootloader (free here because nothing boots), with a 1.7 MB heap: about 4 frame buffers of 345 kB at 640x368. Second, the -O3 build is 285 kB against 182 kB for -Os and does not fit that layout with the heap; speed at -O3 is not measured.

Licenses (checked against each vendor's license text): h264bsd is Apache-2.0 plus MIT with no chip restriction and no click-through; no SDK license was accepted and no vendor code with restrictive clauses was used. The clip is a "Big Buck Bunny" excerpt (Blender Foundation, CC BY 3.0 per the film's page; not re-checked). H.264 itself is covered by patents held by a licensing pool; software that decodes it may need a patent license. That is a business question this page does not answer and is not legal advice.

- A 320x240 or 176x144 test stream (no ffmpeg here: `brew install ffmpeg` then `ffmpeg -f lavfi -i testsrc=size=320x240:rate=15 -frames:v 30 -c:v libx264 -profile:v baseline -pix_fmt yuv420p out.h264`), which cuts the frame buffers to 115 kB each and fits TCM-plus-OCSRAM with room to spare.
- Measure -O3 and -O2 (the code is 3 times larger at -O3) with the heap shrunk by decoding a smaller frame.
- Put the hot inner loops (`h264bsd_reconstruct`, the deblocking filter) in TCM instead of OCSRAM through the cache.
- Use the other three cores: decode slices on different cores (the stream would need several slices per picture) or run deblocking on a second core.
- Ethernet streaming from a Mac into the board's two gigabit ports (`enet` examples), decoding in RAM.
- The other decoders on the survey list: Cisco OpenH264 (BSD, larger, used in a Renesas FreeRTOS package), tinyh264 (a WebAssembly fork of h264bsd), minih264 (encoder).
- Writing a frame out as a PGM over the UART to look at it on the Mac.

**Ask.** Anyone who has run an H.264 decoder on an AM263x, AM243x or other Cortex-R5F without NEON: how many cycles per macroblock did you measure, and which decoder?

# Does Wi-Fi provisioning over Bluetooth work on the TI LP-EM-CC35X1, and how long from power-up to joined?

**Short answer.** Yes. With TI's `ble_wifi_provisioning` example the board advertises as `TI CC3xxx`, accepts a network name, password and security type over Bluetooth LE, and joins the network. From reset to an IP address took 16.5 s and 17.8 s (two runs). About 9 s of that is the board starting and advertising; the join itself took 7.13 s after the connect request, both runs. It was driven from a Mac, so TI's phone app was not needed.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md) (provisioning, GATT, BLE). Errors and fixes: [LP-EM-CC35X1 FAQ](../../cc35x1/FAQ.md). 1 kB = 1,024 bytes.

**Question.** A Wi-Fi product with no screen needs a way to get the password in. Does TI's example do that, and how long does it take?

**Vendor position.** The example's README: install the "SimpleLink Connect" app on a phone, find "TI CC3xxx", open the "Wi-Fi Provisioning Over BLE" service, enter the network name, security type and password, press Connect (Wi-Fi SDK 10.20.00.39, read 2026-10-09).

**What was tried.** The example built unchanged (38 s) and was programmed through the Toolbox. A Python script on the Mac (`bleak`) found the board, wrote the network name to characteristic `0xCC01`, the password to `0xCC02` and the security type `2` (WPA2) to `0xCC04` of service `0xCC00`, then read `0xCC03`, which starts the connection and notifies the result. The network name and password stayed out of the repo.

**How far it got.** Verified. The board's serial log shows each field received, `WLAN CONNECT Requested`, the association, DHCP and an IPv4 address. The notifications were `01` at once and `02` after 6.26 s.

**The line.** No limit reached. The Bluetooth write of all three fields took 0.09 s, so nearly all of the 7.13 s is the Wi-Fi join.

**Ask.** Whether TI's phone app shows the same 6 s between pressing Connect and the green status.

FILE: docs/experiments/2026-10-09-cc35x1-wifi-csi-presence.md | Does TI's Wi-Fi CSI presence model on the LP-EM-CC35X1 detect a person in a room through the house Wi-Fi, and how well?

<!-- experiment

# Does TI's Wi-Fi CSI presence model on the LP-EM-CC35X1 detect a person in a room through the house Wi-Fi, and how well?

**Short answer.** It runs, and in this room it does not detect anyone. Over a 21-minute run on 2026-10-09 the board called "presence" in 533 of the 543 scored windows (98%; 571 of all 589 saved), whether the room was empty or not. In the one phase with a known label, the room empty with the door closed, 1 of 136 scored windows was right (mean probability of presence 0.92). The other three phases are not scored: the second cue (a spoken instruction) did not carry through the closed door and the cues after it were not followed, so who was in the room is unknown. The board's output looked the same in all four (mean probability 0.80 to 0.87). Fifteen seconds before the run, with a person sitting at the desk (no scored label), the same board read "empty" seven times in a row (probability 0.13 to 0.44). So the shipped model separates nothing here.

What works as TI describes: the image builds and signs from a Mac, the Wi-Fi login is typed to the board at run time, the first result arrives 7.4 s after the host asks for the stream, and one result comes every 2.0 s. The most likely reason for the failure (suspected, not tested) is the one TI's white paper gives: placement and the room change what the radio sees, and this model was trained in TI's rooms. A room-specific model needs TI's data-capture image and training.

Contents: Question, Vendor position, Expectation, What was tried, Test protocol, Test steps, How far it got (the results table), The line, Ideas, Ask. Related FAQ: [CC35X1 FAQ](../../cc35x1/FAQ.md).

Terms: CSI is channel state information (defined in the Question). The access point is the Wi-Fi router. DAP is the plugin's data-exchange protocol between board and host (a short binary frame). A window is one 2 s slice of CSI that gets one yes/no answer. NPU-CDE is the chip's neural-network accelerator. More terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). 1 kB = 1,024 bytes. Related: [Wi-Fi provisioning over Bluetooth](2026-10-09-cc35x1-ble-provisioning.md) (how the board got its Wi-Fi login without compiling it in).

**Question.** Wi-Fi channel state information (CSI) is how the radio sees the room: each packet from the access point arrives with a measured gain and phase for every subcarrier, and a person moving through the path changes them. TI shipped a pre-trained model for this on 2026-10-07. In a room that is not TI's, with a home access point, how often does it say "presence" when someone is there, and "empty" when nobody is?

**Vendor position.** Quoted from TI, all read 2026-10-09.

- TI.com use-case page "Wi-Fi sensing for presence detection": "occupancy sensing capabilities at no extra BOM cost, eliminating the need for extra components such as a PIR" and "works with existing Wi-Fi infrastructure". Its dataset table lists estimated accuracy for training, validation and testing: `wifi_presence_detection_dsi` (800 samples, the default) 99.16%, 99.16%, 98.75%; `dsd_2000` 97.67%, 97.67%, 99.00%; `dsd_4400` 97.27%, 97.35%, 99.55%. Model test accuracy 99.03% "based on TI's sample dataset"; latency 24.57 ms on the M33 core, 13.88 ms with the NPU-CDE; flash about 10.57 kB and 23.26 kB; SRAM about 4.11 kB and 5.38 kB.
- Example README (`edgeai_wifi_csi_occupancy_detection_live_preview/README.html`, plugin 1.20.00.00): needs an LP-EM-CC35X1 on an LP-XDS110, an access point's name, password, security type and MAC address, and Edge AI Studio. Each 2 s window of CSI is turned into a 64 by 26 input (FFT over time and over subcarriers), the model runs on the board, a 3-window soft average with a 0.5 threshold gives the decision. "WiFiPresDet_4.7k_CDE ... the only one validated end to end on the LaunchPad." Samples per window: 256, "no other Samples value is supported". CSI runs at 128 Hz, which needs `csi_config -s 1 -p 7`.
- White paper STDA051 "Sensing Without Sensors: Why Wi-Fi is the Smart Choice" (October 2026, 8 pages): Wi-Fi sensing "does not require a direct line-of-sight", trades "localization accuracy for the ability to work through obstacles", "consum[es] significantly more power than ultra-low-power sensing alternatives such as passive infrared", is "generally not optimized for battery-powered designs", and placement of sender and receiver "directly impacts sensing accuracy".
- TI gives no figure for a still person, for an unseen room, or for false alarms per hour.

**Expectation (this repo's, a guess).** The 99% figures are on TI's own recordings, in TI's rooms. An unseen room is expected to cost accuracy. Guess: empty room 90% or better of windows right; a person walking 90% or better; a person sitting still 60% to 90%, the weakest case, because the model was trained on motion. A result under 70% overall would mean the shipped model needs this repo's own data (the data-capture example and Edge AI Studio exist for that). Basis for the guess: the white paper's warning that placement changes accuracy, and the use-case page's description of its larger datasets as covering "a variety of human motions".

**What was tried.** Prepared without the board.

- Pages read, with versions, sizes and dates, in the table below.
- Downloaded the plugin (63 MB zip, SHA-256 `a4ba1aea...0856`, no sign-in needed) and the default dataset (45 MB zip, 803 CSV files of 256 windows by 52 subcarriers). The larger datasets (112 MB and 246 MB zips) were fetched, then deleted for space.
- Built both examples with TI Arm Clang 5.1.1 (TI tested 4.0.4.LTS) and SysConfig 1.28.0: `cc35x1/csi/build.sh`. TI's zip ships old generated files; they must be deleted and the `.syscfg` touched or the Toolbox signing step stops on a missing `action_request_extra.txt`. Live preview: 1,490 kB code and constants, 573 kB zero-initialised data; data capture: 1,375 kB and 487 kB. Both signed with the SDK example key (the board is activated with it).
- TI's example does not compile Wi-Fi credentials in. It takes them as console commands over the serial port at 921600 baud: `wlan_start`, `wlan_sta_role_up`, `wlan_connect -s "<name>" -t WPA2 -p "<password>"`, then `csi_enable`, `csi_config -s 1 -p 7`, `csi_set_mac -a 1 -m <access point MAC>`, `csi_get_results`. TI's helper `serial_automation.py` reads those from a JSON file with the password in plain text. Use `cc35x1/csi/csi_run.py` instead: it reads the name, password and MAC from environment variables or a hidden prompt, scrubs them from its saved log, and writes no file that contains them. Bluetooth provisioning (linked in the terms line) is the fallback and was not needed.
- Reading the result without Edge AI Studio: Studio 1.8.0 has desktop installers for Windows and Linux only. On a Mac only the cloud version (browser) exists, and the release notes do not say whether it can open a local serial port. The board reports each result as a DAP frame (class, probability of presence) once a host sends "start streaming". `csi_run.py` sends that frame and decodes the replies. The frame layout comes from the plugin's DAP source (`source/ti/ai/edge_ai/dap`); the parser passes a synthetic self-test (`python3 -I cc35x1/csi/csi_run.py --selftest`). The live exchange was untested at the time of writing, and the run below is its first test. It worked.

- Other presence routes in this repo, compared on facts only (none of them has been measured against another). This board is a Wi-Fi 6 chip on a LaunchPad plus a debugger. It uses the access point already in the house and needs no line of sight (TI). It gives one yes or no per 2 s window and no position. It needs continuous packets, so TI says it draws far more than a PIR and is not made for batteries. The IWRL6432 radar: its own 60 GHz transmitter, "typically up to 25 m" (data sheet), range and motion data rather than a single flag, about 1.2 mW at one update a second in the data sheet's power-optimized mode. It needs a clear view in front of the board and 20 cm between the board and a person. Board stock was "Out of stock" on ti.com when read. PIR: senses motion of a warm body, lowest power of the four (white paper). TI's PIR model runs on this same chip in 29.45 ms with 176 kB flash and 57 kB SRAM (TI.com PIR use case). Time-of-flight (VL53L1X): one narrow beam, about 3 cm to 4 m, sees only what crosses that beam. The same-room, same-hour comparison is in the ideas list below.

- First live run (2026-10-09): the login was typed into a shell at run time. Four script fixes were needed before the join went through, all in this repo's script or TI's console, none in the model. The board joined on the first full attempt and printed its access point MAC in the join message, which the script now reads instead of asking. The console then flooded with `ERROR rxData_DataPacketDisptcher(): Received VLAN packet - drop it` (33 lines in 60 s; the house network carries VLAN-tagged frames, a harmless message, see the FAQ) and printed `[CSI] DAP inferencing ready`, not the `DAP streaming ready` the README promises. The stream started anyway once the host sent the start frame. The script sent the start-streaming frame; the board acknowledged it and sent one inference every 2.0 s. The protocol then ran its four phases. The second cue was not audible from outside the closed door and the cues after the first were not followed, so only the first phase (empty, door closed) has a trusted label. The still and walking cases are not measured.

**Test protocol.**

- Setup: LP-EM-CC35X1 on the LP-XDS110ET (TGT VDD on EXT, probe <probe serial>), board USB-C and probe USB-C both into the Mac. Board on the desk in the test room, antenna end clear of the Mac and metal. The Mac is on the same Wi-Fi network as the board (TI: the keepalive needs the access point, board and host on one network). Record before starting: access point model and room, band and channel the board joins, straight-line distance from board to access point, walls between them, board height, where the chair is.
- Program the live preview image with the Toolbox (`programmer -i XDS110 -param1 E10000FQ programming --tool_settings <path to toolbox/tool_settings.json>`, absolute paths), reset, then run `csi_run.py`. It joins, enables CSI, starts the stream and walks through four phases of 5 minutes: empty, one person still, one person moving, empty again. About 21 minutes with the join.
- The first 20 s after each cue is not scored (the person is moving into place and the 3-window average needs 6 s to settle). That leaves about 140 scored windows per phase.
- Score each scored window: right if the board's class equals the phase label (empty 0, person 1). Report per phase: windows scored, correct, accuracy, mean probability. Report overall accuracy, the false-alarm rate (empty windows called presence) and the miss rate (person windows called empty). Also the join time and the time to the first result.
- Repeat once on another day or with the board moved, because one room and one hour is one sample. If the shipped model scores under 70%, run the data-capture image, record labelled data with Edge AI Studio cloud (or this repo's own CSV in TI's file format: `time` plus 52 subcarrier columns, 256 rows), and train.
- Visualisation: TI's CSI view (time and frequency domain) is in Edge AI Studio, which has no Mac desktop build. If the cloud version cannot reach the serial port, plot the CSI from the data-capture stream and from TI's `dsi` dataset (same 52-column format). Not built.

**Test steps** (the plan as run; about 25 minutes).

1. Plug the LP-XDS110ET into the Mac (USB-C), and the board's own USB-C.
2. In a terminal, type the line below with the real values (the script scrubs them from its log and saves them nowhere):
   `export FRL_WIFI_SSID='...'  FRL_WIFI_PSK='...'  FRL_AP_BSSID='aa:bb:cc:xx:xx:xx'`
   The access point's MAC is in its admin page, or Mac option-click on the Wi-Fi icon (BSSID).
3. Start the run. A voice cues each phase: "Leave the room now and close the door", "Come in, sit in the chair and stay still", "Stand up and walk around", "Leave the room again". Door closed means no one else in the room; anyone else in the house stays out of it.
4. Phone face down while sitting. Do not touch the board or the Mac during a phase.
5. Note the access point model and where it is.

Needs: (a) the USB connections, (b) programming this image over the board's current one (the board then runs the CSI example until it is reprogrammed; TI's blink and the Network Terminal images are rebuilt in a minute), (c) `pyserial` in a venv for the run, and (d) the Wi-Fi login typed into a shell as above.

**How far it got.** Link, sign, flash (52 s), boot, join, CSI stream, model output, the full 21-minute protocol. Right means the board's class equals the phase label; the first 20 s of each phase is not scored. Only the first phase has a trustworthy label: that cue was heard and the room was left. The second cue did not carry through the closed door and the cues after it were not followed, so phases two to four are kept for the board's output and not scored.

| Phase (what actually happened) | Windows scored | Called "presence" | Right | Mean P(presence) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Empty, door closed | 136 | 135 | 1 (0.7%) | 0.919 |
| Occupancy unknown (cued "sit still"; not heard outside the door) | 135 | 131 | not scored | 0.795 |
| Occupancy unknown (cued "walk around") | 136 | 131 | not scored | 0.842 |
| Occupancy unknown (cued "leave again") | 136 | 136 | not scored | 0.869 |
| **All four phases** | **543** | **533 (98.2%)** | only the first phase is scored | 0.856 |

Time from the host's start-streaming frame to the first result: 7.4 s. Result period: 2.0 s. Join time: not measured in this run (the join happened in an earlier attempt that stopped before the stream; TI's Network Terminal joined the same network in 5.74 s on 2026-10-08). Conditions: the test room, the house access point (model not recorded), band and channel not recorded, other people in the house not recorded. The Mac that ran the script stayed in the room.

**The line.** Most likely the model's weights in this room, not the pipeline (suspected: another spot and the lab's own data were not run). The pipeline produced steady, timed output; the output just did not follow the room. With the room empty and the door closed (the one phase with a known label) the board said "presence" 135 of 136 times, and 533 of 543 across the whole run. A detector that is always on is not a detector. The guess of 90% for an empty room was wrong by the whole range. Two things could still rescue the shipped weights and were not run: a different spot for the board (TI's white paper says placement "directly impacts sensing accuracy"), and a quieter network (the VLAN flood is dropped packets, but it shows traffic the model never saw). A room-specific model needs TI's data-capture image: record this room empty and occupied, train in Edge AI Studio, and run the same protocol again.

**Ask.** The DAP start-streaming frame `ED 08 00 9E` works (the board acknowledges with the same command byte and streams). Not established: whether Edge AI Studio's cloud version opens a local serial port on a Mac, and the board placement, distance to the access point and traffic when the shipped `wifi_presence_detection_dsi` set was recorded (TI's pages read do not give them).

## Side by side with the radar, 2026-10-10

**Overnight baseline (2026-10-10 to 2026-10-11).** The test room was empty and the rest of the house occupied but quiet (the house itself was not empty). The comparison above is one person in one evening; the overnight run is a free run in the empty room. The board's results and the radar's frames were logged on the same Mac clock. From 23:49 to 01:00:21 (the window ends where the logger's restart loop stopped; cause not found in its log), the Wi-Fi model classed **0 of 2,065 results as present** (median probability 0.013) over 1.19 h; the radar at a 12-frame hold gave 0 flags over the same window and on to 05:54 (6.08 h). So the model's evening behavior (present in 135 of 136 empty-room windows) was not noise: it followed activity elsewhere in the house, and in a quiet house it reads empty. It still cannot tell this room from the next one. Rows: `cc35x1 ai_presence_accuracy wifi-csi-empty-overnight`, `iwrl6432boost radar_false_alarm presence-2x3-hold12-overnight`.

**The line.** In the same room, on the same clock, the Wi-Fi model said "present" in every window of every pass, including the empty-room passes. It cannot be wrong about a person who is there and it is always wrong about an empty room. The IWRL6432BOOST radar followed the walks. Putting the two together with a rule can only help by lowering the Wi-Fi false alarms, and the radar has to do all of that work.

**What ran.** The board ran the live-preview image (programmed 2026-10-10 in 52 s with the Toolbox), logged by `csi_run.py --freerun` (login and start-streaming as before, then one host-timestamped row per result, about 2.1k rows from 20:35 to 21:51, all class "presence"). The radar test ran its in-and-out passes (empty, walk, seated at 2 m, seated at 4 m) in two rounds, 2 transmit by 2 receive and 2 by 3. `cc35x1/csi/compare_presence.py` joins the two on the Mac's clock. The label of each moment comes from the radar tool's own cue times: empty for the empty pass and before the enter cue and after the leave cue, person present between them. The 6 s after each cue are not scored (the board averages 3 windows). Only moments where both logs have a fresh value are scored. One sitting, one room, one access point, one person; not a general result.

| Round | Rule | Misses (person there, said empty) | False alarms (room empty, said present) |
|---|---|--:|--:|
| 2x2 | Radar alone | 0% (0 of 177) | 24% (81 of 337) |
| 2x2 | Wi-Fi alone | 0% (0 of 177) | 100% (337 of 337) |
| 2x2 | OR (either says present) | 0% (0 of 177) | 100% (337 of 337) |
| 2x2 | AND (both say present) | 0% (0 of 177) | 24% (81 of 337) |
| 2x2 | Radar confirms Wi-Fi (Wi-Fi flag and radar present within 5 s) | 0% (0 of 177) | 34% (113 of 337) |
| 2x3 | Radar alone | 2% (3 of 179) | 22% (74 of 338) |
| 2x3 | Wi-Fi alone | 0% (0 of 179) | 100% (338 of 338) |
| 2x3 | OR | 0% (0 of 179) | 100% (338 of 338) |
| 2x3 | AND | 2% (3 of 179) | 22% (74 of 338) |
| 2x3 | Radar confirms Wi-Fi | 0% (0 of 179) | 33% (112 of 338) |

Per pass, the empty-room pass alone (door closed, nobody in the room): Wi-Fi present in 100% of its windows in both rounds (28 and 29 windows); radar present in 0% of its frames in the 2x2 round and 24% in the 2x3 round (240 frames each; the 24% is not explained, nobody was seen entering). The radar's other "false alarms" are the minutes after the person left: the radar took 10.6 to 14.6 s to clear after the leave cue (Wi-Fi never cleared), and the label calls those moments empty after the 6 s settle band. Detect after the enter cue: radar 0 to 6.7 s, Wi-Fi 0.2 to 1.2 s, which means nothing because Wi-Fi was already "present". The full per-pass tables are in `data/results/cc35x1.csv` (variants `wifi-presence-*`) and come from `python3 cc35x1/csi/compare_presence.py --config 2x2-both` and `--config 2x3`.

**What each rule does with a sensor that is always on.**

- OR: identical to Wi-Fi alone, so it never helps. It would only add something if Wi-Fi ever missed a person, and it never did.
- AND: identical to the radar alone, because Wi-Fi is always true. Fusion here equals the radar, with the radar's own clear delay and its misses (3 moments in the 2x3 round).
- Radar confirms Wi-Fi: no misses in either round, but about a third false alarms, because the radar's 5 s agreement window keeps a flag alive after the radar's own clear. It trades the radar's 2% misses for about 10 more points of false alarms than the radar alone.

**Where fusion helps and where it cannot.** It helps in the case you would hope for: an empty room where Wi-Fi false-alarms and the radar is quiet. Here AND and radar-confirms turn Wi-Fi's 100% false alarms into the radar's 0% (2x2) or 24% (2x3) on the empty pass. It could also help a seated still person if the radar dropped while Wi-Fi held; that was not seen, because the radar held its seated person (misses 0 to 1% on the seated passes) and Wi-Fi never dropped. It cannot help when both sensors see the same person the same way, and it cannot rescue a model that says "present" regardless of the room: a rule that needs Wi-Fi to agree adds no information when Wi-Fi's answer never changes. The finding is about this model in this room (consistent with the 2026-10-09 run, 98% present); TI's training rooms and a retrained model are untested.

### Who was first, and where they agreed

**The line.** The radar was first by default and the only one that ever said "empty". The Wi-Fi class stayed at "present" in every row after the first minutes (none of about 1.1k rows after 21:15 were class 0), so it agreed with the radar whenever the person was in the room and disagreed in every empty moment and during every clear. Its probability p1 did move (62 rows below 0.9, down to 0.44), but no cut-off on it separates empty from occupied.

**Agreement per pass.** Moments are on the 0.5 s grid where both logs have a fresh value; "both off" is 0% everywhere because the Wi-Fi never said empty. Detect and clear times are in the table above: after the enter cue the radar flagged in 0 to 6.7 s and cleared 10.6 to 14.6 s after the leave cue; the Wi-Fi was already "present" before the cue and never cleared.

**2 transmit, 2 receive round, agreement.**

| pass | moments | both on | Wi-Fi on, radar off | radar on, Wi-Fi off | both off |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| empty 1 | 120 | 0% | 100% | 0% | 0% |
| walk 1 | 157 | 82% | 18% | 0% | 0% |
| sit2 1 | 191 | 53% | 47% | 0% | 0% |
| sit4 1 | 190 | 68% | 32% | 0% | 0% |

| shipped class | 100% (120 of 120) | 0% (0 of 134) | 49% (325 of 661) |

**Threshold result.** No threshold beats the shipped class. Up to 0.95 the Wi-Fi still calls the empty room present (97 to 100% of the empty pass) with few or no seated misses in the 2x2 round and growing misses in the 2x3 round; at 0.99 the false alarms fall (48% in the 2x2 round, 68% in the 2x3 round) only by missing the seated person about as often (47% and 66%). Agreement with the radar tops out at 57% (2x3 round, 0.99), which is no better than a coin that always says present. The model's probability carries a small amount of information (it dips a little more in the empty pass at 0.99), not enough to use.

**Timeline per pass.** One character per 2 s bin, 2 transmit by 2 receive round first. R is the radar (# present in at least half the bin's frames), W the Wi-Fi class, P the Wi-Fi probability (9 means 0.9 or more, 8 means 0.8 to 0.9 and so on), C the cues (E enter or go, L leave). A blank in W and P is a bin with no Wi-Fi result (the logger's result stream skips a window now and then). Read down a pass: the radar's # starts after E and ends 10 to 15 s after L; W is # throughout.

**Limits.** One room, one person, one placement of the CC35X1 (on the bench next to the Mac), one access point, a model TI trained elsewhere, two passes of each kind, and a label taken from cue times that the person may have followed a second or two late. The radar is the reference for "agrees with radar" but it is not ground truth: in the 2 by 3 round it flagged 24% of the empty pass, all in its first 14 s (the person may still have been leaving; unexplained). A retrained model, another placement or a different room could change the Wi-Fi result; this run says nothing about those.

## Empty room on the guest network, 2026-10-26

False presence in an empty room is 0.5 %: 5 of 947 windows over 33 minutes (23:01 to 23:34), median P(presence) 0.050, 95th percentile 0.438. TI's shipped presence model on the live-preview image, `csi_run.py --freerun`, the board joined to the guest network, the lab door closed, the rest of the house occupied. The five hits sit in two 5-minute blocks (3 % and 1 %); nobody was seen entering, and the lab camera, which sees only the bench, showed it empty at the start. Row `ai_presence_accuracy / wifi-csi-empty-guest-33min` in `data/results/cc35x1.csv`.

This agrees with the overnight run of 2026-10-11 (0 of 2,065 windows) and not with the first phase of 2026-10-09 (135 of 136 called present). The 2026-10-09 phase is now the odd one out, and its label is the weak part: the person had just left and the house was active. Read together, the shipped model's empty-room false-alarm rate is low in this room; what is still unmeasured is detection of a still person and the rate with people moving elsewhere in the house. The per-room training question from the 2026-10-09 page stays open for those cases, not for the empty room.

<!-- experiment

reached: verified
line: The TinyEngine NPU ran all four room-occupancy models with 20 of 20 test vectors matching: 3.0x faster than the best CPU build on the 636-weight model, 6.2x on the 1.7k-weight model, 16.7x on the 8.5k-weight model (35.27 ms to 2.12 ms) and 1.9x on 30k (129.40 ms to 69.40 ms), where one layer stays on the CPU.

# How much faster is the TinyEngine NPU on a TI LP-MSPM0G5187 than its own CPU?

**Short answer.** On the 8.5k-weight room-occupancy model the NPU takes 2.12 ms at 80 MHz. Against TI's own CPU build of the same model (NNC, 45.64 ms) that is 21.6 times faster, the like-for-like pair: same compiler, same clock, both timing the model call only. Against the fastest plain C build (35.27 ms at -O3) it is 16.7 times; that pair is not like for like, because the plain C figure also includes the input quantization (the plain C model call alone is 34.33 ms, so 16.2 times). All 20 test vectors gave the same class in every build. The gain shrinks at both ends: 3.8 and 3.0 times on the 636-weight model, 2.3 and 1.9 times on the 32.8k-weight model, by the two baselines. Every time on this page is the fastest of the 20 vectors, best of 5 calls each: a best case, not a typical or worst-case latency; the slowest vector ran at most 3.3 percent longer. Measured on 2026-10-08 and 2026-10-09 on a LaunchPad development kit with MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). Board page and fixes: [LP-MSPM0G5187 README](../../mspm0g5187/README.md) and [FAQ](../../mspm0g5187/FAQ.md). 1 kB = 1,024 bytes. NPU is the chip's neural processing unit. NNC is TI's neural network compiler.

**Question.** Does the NPU make a small neural network fast enough to matter, and where does the gain stop?

**Vendor position.** TI rates the NPU at 2.56 billion operations a second at 80 MHz (data sheet SLVSJB5B, rev. B, March 2026). The SDK READMEs for the edge-AI examples give CPU and NPU pairs on this chip: waveform classifier 54.06 ms and 5.84 ms, PIR 61.56 and 5.25, gesture 99.7 and 9.07, fall 8.56 and 0.67, character recognition 89.81 and 6.05 (read 2026-10-07).

**What was tried.** Four room-occupancy models (500, 2k, 8k and 30k parameters, int8, 20 test vectors each), compiled four ways: plain C at `-Os` and `-O3`, TI's NNC for the CPU, and TI's NNC for the NPU. One image per model and build, run bare metal on the MSPM0G5187 with TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS. Each vector is run once to check the class and then five times; the table shows the fastest run of the fastest vector, timed with SysTick on the CPU clock. TI's own CPU and NPU example pairs were also timed with a wrapper that times `tvmgen_default_run` and changes none of TI's source.

**How far it got.** Verified. Every image matched the expected class on all 20 vectors.

**What each number is (read this before the tables).** The harness runs each of the 20 vectors once to check its class, then five more times and keeps the fastest; the table shows the fastest vector of those twenty. That is a best case. The slowest vector is in the saved captures and in the results store (`value_hi`): on the NNC and NPU builds it ran 0.1 to 3.3 percent longer than the fastest (8k on the NPU: 2.116 to 2.155 ms), and both figures were identical on all three runs, so the three runs show repeatability of that statistic, not the application's worst case. No per-call samples were kept, so there is no distribution, no median and no 95th percentile here; the count of operations is fixed per model, which is why the spread is small. The clock covers the model call only (`tvmgen_default_run` to `tvmgen_default_finished`) on the NNC CPU and NPU builds, and input quantization plus the model call on the plain C builds (the model call alone is also in those captures as `runq`). None of this is a pipeline time: no sensor read, no feature extraction, no sleep or wake.

Two baselines, both from the rows in `data/results/mspm0g5187.csv`: the first table below sets the NPU against the fastest plain C build (not like for like, as above); the second sets it against TI's own CPU build of the same model, the pair TI's examples use.

| Model | Plain C `-O3` (CPU, with input quantization) | TI NNC CPU | NPU at 80 MHz | NPU against plain C `-O3` (not like for like) | NPU at 32 MHz |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 500 parameters | 3.92 ms | 4.94 ms | 1.29 ms | 3.0x | 2.88 ms |
| 2k | 9.05 ms | 11.98 ms | 1.45 ms | 6.2x | 3.23 ms |
| 8k | 35.27 ms | 45.64 ms | 2.12 ms | 16.7x | 4.77 ms |
| 30k | 129.40 ms | 159.22 ms | 69.40 ms | 1.9x | 161.01 ms |

TI's own example pairs, same method (first calls, model call only):

| Example | CPU | NPU | Clock | Gain |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| waveform classifier | 54.25 ms | 5.88 ms | 80 MHz | 9.2x (TI publishes 54.06 and 5.84) |
| hello world (sine, square, sawtooth) | 126.31 ms | 12.99 ms | 32 MHz | 9.7x |
| gearbox fault | 37.11 ms | 9.65 ms | 32 MHz | 3.8x |
| motor bearing fault | 106.80 ms | 1.28 ms | 80 MHz | 83x (TI publishes 229.01 and 1,087.98 ms for the whole pipeline) |

## NPU against CPU, same model, same clock (rerun 2026-10-09, three runs)

**Expectation, written before the rerun.** The first table compares the NPU with plain C at `-O3`. The fair pair for "what the NPU adds" is TI's own compiler on both sides, same clock, so the NPU gain should read larger than 3.0, 6.2, 16.7 and 1.9 times (NNC's CPU code is slower than plain C `-O3`), the 32.8k-weight model should stay the weakest because one layer stays on the CPU, and the gain should not depend on the clock (the NPU runs from the CPU clock). For energy: the NPU build spins the CPU while it waits, so the chip should draw about the same current in both builds and energy per inference should fall about as fast as time does.

**Method.** Four models, each as TI NNC CPU code (`ti-npu type=soft`) and as TI NNC NPU code, at 80 MHz and at 32 MHz (the 32 MHz CPU build is new). Each image was erased, flashed and run three times, 20 of 20 test vectors right on all 48 runs. The fastest-vector cycle count was identical on every run, so the three runs agree to the cycle.

| Model | Multiply-adds | Clock | CPU | NPU | Speed-up | CPU cycles per multiply-add | NPU cycles per multiply-add | Runs |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| occ_cnn_500 | 11,328 | 80 MHz | 4.938 ms | 1.292 ms | 3.8x | 34.9 | 9.1 | 3 |
| occ_cnn_500 | 11,328 | 32 MHz | 10.853 ms | 2.880 ms | 3.8x | 30.7 | 8.1 | 3 |
| occ_cnn_2k | 33,856 | 80 MHz | 11.978 ms | 1.451 ms | 8.3x | 28.3 | 3.4 | 3 |
| occ_cnn_2k | 33,856 | 32 MHz | 26.593 ms | 3.229 ms | 8.2x | 25.1 | 3.0 | 3 |
| occ_cnn_8k | 157,824 | 80 MHz | 45.644 ms | 2.116 ms | 21.6x | 23.1 | 1.1 | 3 |
| occ_cnn_8k | 157,824 | 32 MHz | 101.015 ms | 4.771 ms | 21.2x | 20.5 | 1.0 | 3 |
| occ_cnn_30k | 610,560 | 80 MHz | 159.219 ms | 69.396 ms | 2.3x | 20.9 | 9.1 | 3 |
| occ_cnn_30k | 610,560 | 32 MHz | 357.439 ms | 161.009 ms | 2.2x | 18.7 | 8.4 | 3 |

**Result.** The expectation held on all three counts. Against TI's own CPU code the NPU is 3.8, 8.3, 21.6 and 2.3 times faster at 80 MHz, and the numbers barely move at 32 MHz (3.8, 8.2, 21.2, 2.2). The 8k model is the sweet spot at about 1 cycle per multiply-add; the 636-weight model pays for NPU set-up per layer, and the 32.8k-weight model runs one convolution on the CPU (9.1 cycles per multiply-add). Cycles per multiply-add are a little lower at 32 MHz than at 80 MHz on both sides, probably flash wait states at the higher clock (not checked); time still scales with the clock.

**Energy per inference (EnergyTrace), two quantities.** EnergyTrace works on this board through `tools/energytrace/etcap.py` on this Mac (probe <probe serial>, 3.3 V from the probe, 2 kHz sampling). The probe reads everything on the target side of the isolation block: chip, LEDs, the audio circuits behind J6 and the probe's own floor, about 16.4 mA with the chip asleep in WFI at 80 MHz (not split; the split needs shunt changes on the board). Running a model in a loop adds 0.4 to 0.7 mA on top, about the same in the CPU and NPU builds, so energy follows time. Both figures below are current x 3.3 V x the model's best-case latency from the timing rows: a steady loop that never sleeps, not an integrated single inference, so a lower bound per inference and no guide to a product that sleeps. "Above idle" is the loop reading minus the same model's idle reading (its ordinary image asleep in WFI after its check), paired run by run; the subtraction of two readings that differ by 3 percent spreads 7 to 32 percent between runs, so the range is shown. The rows are in `data/results/mspm0g5187.csv`.

| Model | Above idle, CPU (median, min to max of 3) | Above idle, NPU | NPU saves (medians) | Whole board, CPU | Whole board, NPU | Loop current CPU / NPU | Idle |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|---|--:|
| occ_cnn_500 | 8.73 uJ (8.39 to 8.96) | 2.31 uJ (1.92 to 2.33) | 3.8x | 276 uJ | 72 uJ | 16.90 to 16.96 / 16.90 to 16.95 mA | 16.37 to 16.45 mA |
| occ_cnn_2k | 21.34 uJ (19.13 to 22.65) | 2.36 uJ (2.04 to 2.60) | 9.0x | 673 uJ | 81 uJ | 16.95 to 17.05 / 16.94 to 17.00 mA | 16.46 to 16.51 mA |
| occ_cnn_8k | 85.71 uJ (75.76 to 94.29) | 4.23 uJ (4.02 to 4.92) | 20.3x | 2,553 uJ | 119 uJ | 16.95 to 17.04 / 17.02 to 17.08 mA | 16.38 to 16.45 mA |
| occ_cnn_30k | 303.17 uJ (291.08 to 353.61) | 92.29 uJ (91.60 to 120.92) | 3.3x | 8,928 uJ | 3,857 uJ | 16.98 to 17.02 / 16.84 mA | 16.31 to 16.44 mA |

The whole-board ratios are 3.8, 8.3, 21.5 and 2.3 times, the same as the time ratios because the current is the same; the above-idle ratios land near them but carry the spread of the subtraction (the 500 and 32.8k-weight models' above-idle ranges overlap less than a factor of two from run to run, so read those two ratios as rough). No pair came out negative or inconclusive. The expectation held: about the same current, energy follows time. For a battery product, a loop that never sleeps hides the real gain. A product that wakes once a second spends almost all its energy asleep, and there the NPU's shorter run is what counts; the sleep current was not measured here, and no battery life can be given from these rows.

**Also repeated three times (TI's own example pairs, model call only).** Hello world 126.311 ms to 12.990 ms (9.7x, 32 MHz), gearbox fault 37.113 to 9.653 (3.8x, 32 MHz), motor bearing 106.798 to 1.283 (83x, 80 MHz), waveform classifier 54.307 to 5.858 (9.3x, 80 MHz, median of the fastest call kept per run). The waveform NPU run kept 10 calls per run and the spread across them was 5.85 to 6.02 ms.

Every row is in `data/results/mspm0g5187.csv`. The board was put back to TI's factory image afterwards; main flash and data flash read back identical to the backup.

**The line.** No limit reached; the gain depends on the model. The 636-weight model does little work per layer, so the NPU's setup per layer takes a large share of its 1.29 ms. In the 32.8k-weight model, NNC's compile log says `GCONV layer NOT offloaded to TI-NPU`, so that layer runs on the CPU and the NPU gain drops to 1.9 times. The NPU runs from the CPU clock: at 32 MHz the 8k model takes 4.77 ms, 2.25 times longer than at 80 MHz. The motor bearing pair is the odd one: TI's README lists the NPU version as slower than the CPU one, while the model-call-only timing here gives 83 times faster. TI's figure covers the whole example including the feature extraction, the timing here covers the model call, so they do not compare.

If a debugger reset lands while an earlier NPU run is still in progress, the next run hangs waiting for `tvmgen_default_finished`: the first vector passes and the second never ends, and NVIC shows the NPU interrupt pending. If you see that, start the image by flashing with DSLite and read the results after a wait, with no debugger reset. Five of this repo's first six NPU runs hung this way before resetting was stopped; the cause is this repo's, not the chip's.

**Ask.** Has anyone seen the NPU interrupt stay pending after a debugger reset on a G5187, and does a power cycle clear it?

## TI's other examples (ECG, fall, fan blade, character)

These four examples wait for a sensor (ECG front end, motion sensor, accelerometer) or for TI's drawing GUI, so on a bare board they never call the model. The build keeps everything of TI's (model library, SysConfig, clock) and swaps only `main()` for a small benchmark `main()`, which does the same start-up (including the NPU power-up on the NPU builds) and then calls the model 12 times on one fixed input. Timing is the same wrapper as the other examples: model call only, to the NPU done interrupt on the NPU builds, first 10 calls kept, 80 MHz, three runs each with a full erase, flash and run. Layer cost does not depend on the input values, so a fixed input times the same as a sensor frame.

Expectation, written before the runs: CPU and NPU times near TI's README figures, a 10 to 13 times speed-up on fall, fan blade and character, and for ECG (no TI latency) 60 to 150 ms on the CPU and 5 to 15 ms on the NPU.

| Model | Parameters (TI README) | CPU | NPU | Speed-up | Flash CPU / NPU | RAM CPU / NPU |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| fan blade fault (MLP, 3x128 input) | 5,228 | 1.762 ms | 0.182 ms | 9.7x | 1.43 / 2.13 kB | 1.00 / 0.85 kB |
| fall detection (CNN, 3x64) | 6K | 8.566 ms | 1.435 ms | 6.0x | 12.6 / 13.8 kB | 0.94 / 0.71 kB |
| ECG anomaly (CNN, 2.5k samples) | 55k | 496.5 ms | 96.6 ms | 5.1x | 63.5 / 86.9 kB | 18.0 / 12.9 kB |
| character recognition (CNN, 28x28 float) | 60,000 | 91.94 ms | 10.13 ms | 9.1x | 66.4 / 71.4 kB | 8.0 / 10.7 kB |

Flash and RAM are the model's own objects from the linker map (weights, model code, NNC runtime, model buffers); the image around them is excluded. They agree with the figures in TI's READMEs (ECG CPU 65.0 kB (decimal) against TI's 64.8 kB and 18.4 kB of RAM against 18.4 kB; fan blade NPU 2.18 kB against 2.178 kB). Every run of a build gave the same cycle count to the cycle (the models have no data-dependent branches), so the spread is zero.

What did not match the expectation:

- ECG is slow on both: 496.5 ms on the CPU (about 3 times the high guess) and the NPU gain is only 5.1 times, so one 2.5k-sample window takes 97 ms even on the NPU. TI publishes no latency for it.
- Fall detection on the NPU took 1.435 ms where TI's README says 0.67 ms (this repo's time ends at the NPU done interrupt; how TI timed it is not stated). The CPU matched TI's 8.56 ms (8.566). Gain 6.0 times, not 12.8.
- Character recognition: the CPU matched TI (91.94 against 89.81 ms); the NPU took 10.13 ms against TI's 6.05 ms. The model takes and returns float32, so the NPU build converts at the edges.
- Fan blade ships at the 32 MHz default clock (4.112 ms CPU, 0.406 ms NPU there). The table is at 80 MHz, set with the same clock-tree lines TI's own waveform example uses; nothing else in its SysConfig changed.

Output check. No example ships input data, so TI's expected output cannot be compared. What was checked: the CPU and NPU build of each model, given the same fixed input, return the same answer. ECG (-75, 26, -127, 52), fan blade and character recognition match exactly; fall detection differs by one count in one output (CPU 11, -76; NPU 11, -77), the same class. The character output is saturated at -2.0 for the first three classes on this synthetic input, so that one is a weak check.

Parameters come from each example's README ("Number of Parameters"). MACs: TI does not publish them for these examples (README tables list parameters, accuracy, flash, RAM and latency only) and the model library carries no layer shapes, so MACs are not given.

The board's flash was backed up on this Mac before the runs (TI's factory image) and restored with OpenOCD `program ... 0x0 verify`; main flash (128 kB) and data flash (8 kB) read back identical.

# Can NVIDIA's Holoscan body-pose demo run on the SK-TDA4VM, and what does the same graph cost on TI's parts?

Terms used here are in [docs/vocab.md](../vocab.md). Board page: [tda4/README.md](../../tda4/README.md).

**Question.** Note (2026-10-10): this page answers a narrower reading of the question. The actual target is the Holoscan Sensor Bridge role (camera into the TI chip, Hololink frames out over Ethernet), which this page does not cover. The numbers here stand as TDA4VM vision measurements.

Can the NVIDIA Holoscan body-pose estimation app, or its benchmark, run on the SK-TDA4VM, on the Arm cores or the R5F cores? If not, what does the same graph cost in compute and memory when it is built from TI's own parts?

**Vendor position.** NVIDIA, Holoscan SDK install guide (read 2026-10-09): the SDK packages need the CUDA runtime "even for CPU only pipelines"; the CMake build enables the CUDA language unconditionally; operators sit on NPP, TensorRT, Vulkan and NVIDIA's GXF runtime. License Apache-2.0.

TI, Edge AI SDK getting started and the model zoo (11.00.00.08): the SK-TDA4VM runs deep-learning models on the C7x DSP with its matrix accelerator (MMA) through TIDL, called from ONNX Runtime, TFLite or GStreamer's `tidlinferer`. TI's human-pose model `ONR-KD-7060-human-pose-yolox-s-640x640` is precompiled on the image. TI publishes no figure for this model on this board; its data-sheet page gives 2.03 ms for MobileNetV1 (224), 3.04 ms for regNetx-200mf, 5.03 ms for yolox-nano-lite (416) and 5.9 ms for ssdLite mobDet (320).

**What was tried.** Board: SK-TDA4VM (J721EXSKG01EVM, PROC112A1), TI Edge AI SDK 11.00.00.08 (Linux 6.12.17-ti, Arago 2025.01, Python 3.12, onnxruntime 1.15.0 with the TIDL execution provider, GStreamer with the `tiovx` and `tidl` plugins). No display, no Ethernet; everything over the serial console.

1. **Is Holoscan there, or installable?** Looked for `/usr/local/cuda`, `libcudart`, `nvcc` and `import holoscan` on the board. Not read: the Holoscan wheel's dependency metadata (would need a download; not done).
2. **The same graph with TI parts.** Holoscan's body-pose app is source, format convert, inference, post-process, visualize. TI's `edgeai-gst-apps` runs that chain as a GStreamer pipeline: `filesrc` to hardware H.264 decode, `tiovxmultiscaler` and `tiovxdlpreproc` (hardware scaler and OpenVX kernels), `tidlinferer` on the C7x/MMA, Python post-process on the A72, hardware H.264 encode to an MKV file (no display attached). Config: `tda4/tools/pose_file.yaml`; TI's sample clip `left-1280x768.h264`.
3. **Inference alone, both ways.** `tda4/tools/ort_bench.py` and `zoo_bench.py`: the same ONNX model through ONNX Runtime with the TIDL provider (C7x/MMA, int8 artifacts from the zoo) and with the CPU provider (two A72 threads, fp32 graph as shipped). Random input, one warm-up, median of 30 or 50 runs (3 on the CPU). Then every other model in `/opt/model_zoo` the same way.
4. **R5F.** Checked what the six Cortex-R5F cores run: `/sys/class/remoteproc` shows the main-domain pairs attached to TI's RTOS firmware (IPC, vision-apps services); they have no Linux, no Python, and no TIDL runtime. Nothing was run on them.

**How far it got.** Measured. Every step ran; no step was blocked.

| Item | Result |
|---|---|
| CUDA on the board | none: no `/usr/local/cuda`, no `libcudart`, no `nvcc`; `import holoscan` fails. Holoscan cannot be built or installed here |
| Pose model, C7x/MMA (TIDL) | 13.8 ms per inference (median of 30; 13.9 over 50), all 274 graph nodes on the accelerator, 176 MB process RSS, 2.5 s to load |
| Pose model, two A72 cores (ONNX Runtime CPU, fp32) | 1,767 ms per inference (median of 3; 1,786 over 5), 154 MB RSS |
| Ratio | 128x. The CPU run is fp32 and the accelerator run is int8, so this is the cost of falling back to the CPU, not a like-for-like core comparison |
| Whole graph, file in to encoded file out | 17.8 to 18.1 fps, 55 to 56 ms per frame by the app's own metric, two runs. Hardware decode and encode, accelerator inference, Python post-process |
| Memory the board gives Linux | 2,170 MB of the 4 GB; the rest is carved out (639 MB vision-apps heap for the DSPs and R5Fs, 512 MB CMA, 32 MB R5F network buffers; `dmesg`) |
| R5F | not a target: RTOS firmware, no Linux, no TIDL. The accelerator for this work is the C7x; the A72 pair can run the fp32 graph at 0.6 fps |

The rest of TI's zoo, inference only, same method (`data/results/tda4.csv`, test `dl_inference_ms`):

| Model | Input | C7x/MMA ms | A72 ms | Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MobileNetV1 mlperf (TFLite) | 224 | 2.17 | not run | |
| regNetx-200mf | 224 | 2.89 | 37.4 | 13x |
| yolox-nano-lite | 416 | 4.66 | 193 | 41x |
| ssd-lite mobv2 | 512 | 6.10 | 439 | 72x |
| ssdLite mobDet (TFLite) | 320 | 6.40 | not run | |
| deeplabv3lite mobv2 ade20k | 512 | 7.30 | 714 | 98x |
| yolox-s-lite widerface | 640 | 11.16 | 1,504 | 135x |
| yolox-s-lite coco | 640 | 11.68 | 1,523 | 130x |
| deeplabv3lite mobv2 robokit | 768x432 | 11.75 | 901 | 77x |
| deeplabv3 mobv2 ade20k mlperf (TFLite) | 512 | 12.11 | not run | |
| yolox-s pose | 640 | 13.76 | 1,767 | 128x |

TI's four published figures are within 7 to 10 percent of the values measured here for the same models (MobileNetV1 2.03 against 2.17, regNetx 3.04 against 2.89, yolox-nano 5.03 against 4.66, ssdLite 5.9 against 6.40); the values measured here include Python call overhead and a random input.

**The line.** Holoscan: no CUDA, so none of it runs here; that is a hard dependency, not a port effort. The graph it describes runs on the TDA4VM at 17.8 fps from decode to encoded output on TI's short left-1280x768 clip (a later run on a longer clip held 30 fps, paced by the clip), limited by the serial Python post-process and frame pull (56 ms per frame) rather than by inference (13.8 ms). On the A72 cores alone the same model gives 0.57 fps.

- The C++ `app_edgeai` or an all-GStreamer pipeline with `tidlpostproc`, which should lift the graph from 18 fps toward the 30 fps clip rate.

- A quantized (int8) ONNX graph for the CPU run, for a fairer core-to-core number.
- The two TFLite models and the three TVM models on the CPU (TVM needs the DLR runtime; not scripted).
- The small graph shim (`opgraph`) so the app code reads like a Holoscan app; and the second graph, tool tracking, after its licenses are read.
- Camera input and a display, once a webcam and a monitor are on the bench.

**Ask.** A reader who has run Holoscan's body-pose benchmark on an NVIDIA developer kit: what frame rate and memory did you see, with which model and input size, so the two graphs can be set side by side with the chips named.

FILE: docs/experiments/2026-10-10-am263p-xip-ladder.md | How much does it cost to run code from flash on the LP-AM263P, and do TI's AI models care?

<!-- experiment
id: E141
board: LP-AM263P
date: 2026-10-10
status: works
reached: verified
line: Running code straight from the LP-AM263P's flash works with only the USB cable. TI's own memcpy benchmark takes 8.7 times as long as from RAM with no extra cache and 2.4 times with TI's 64 kB cache; with smart placement it takes 9% less time than all-RAM. With the 64 kB cache, ten of TI's AI examples run within 2% of their RAM speed with their outputs checked (an eleventh is timed but fails TI's own check), and CoreMark matches RAM; one model, whose 167 kB of code and constants stream through the cache every inference, stays 6.9 times slower. # How much does it cost to run code from flash on the LP-AM263P, and do TI's AI models care?

**Short answer.** On the LP-AM263P (AM263P4 chip), code runs straight from the external flash with only the USB cable, and with TI's 64 kB flash cache most programs lose little or no speed. TI's AI examples and CoreMark run at RAM speed from flash with the cache, except one model too big for it.

| Code runs from | TI's memcpy benchmark | CoreMark | TI's AI examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| On-chip RAM | 14.6 ms | 1,464.5 per second | baseline |
| Flash, no extra cache | 8.7 times as long | 1,394.5 (4.8% lower) | same to 7.8 times as long |
| Flash + TI's 64 kB L2 cache | 2.4 times as long | 1,464.5 (equal) | ten within 2% of RAM, an eleventh within 2% with its output unconfirmed; one 6.9 times as long |
| Flash + TI's smart placement | 9% less time than RAM | not run | not run |

Three things to know before you rely on these numbers:

- **This repo's flash ran slow:** at 16.7 MHz, because the driver's high-speed read tuning (PHY tuning) failed on this repo's board. TI's pages, with tuning on, show plain flash at 3.7 times RAM where 8.7 was seen; the slower clock may not be the whole gap. Why tuning fails is unknown.
- **Opening the flash can write to it:** when that tuning fails, TI's flash driver erases and rewrites one 4 kB sector at offset `0x80000`. Back up the flash first (below).
- **One of TI's twelve AI examples fails its own check** on this board, with or without this repo's changes, and still prints "All tests have passed!!". Its timing is in the table; its output is not confirmed.

The first inference after a load is slower than the later (warm) ones, by 0.1 to 1.2 ms with no extra cache, while the caches fill.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md) (XIP, cache, OptiFlash, smart placement, PHY tuning, controlCARD, DSLite, development boot, golden values). 1 kB = 1,024 bytes. TI's benchmark is `examples/benchmarks/optiflash_benchmark` in the MCU+ SDK.

Problems and fixes: [LP-AM263P FAQ](../../am263p/FAQ.md). Rows: `data/results/am263p.csv`, tests `xip_memcpy_tasks`, `ai_vendor_example` (variants ending `-xip` and `-xip-l2-64k`) and `coremark`.

**Question.** If a program is bigger than the AM263P's 2 MB of usable RAM, or RAM must stay free for data, how much speed do I lose by running code from the flash, and do TI's caches get it back?

**Vendor position.** TI's MCU+ SDK 26.01 (read 2026-10-10):

- XIP page: "the flash memory is typically slower (~300MB/s bandwidth) vs RAM memory ( > 1600 MB/s)... execution speed, esp when code is not cached in the CPU cache, will be slower". It also says "The secondary bootloader needs to enable flash at highest throughput mode in this DAC mode, before booting the application."
- OptiFlash benchmark pages, with the sample output from TI's controlCARD (not the LaunchPad): 0 B memcpy test 12.45 ms from RAM, 46.57 ms plain XIP, 42.43 / 39.19 / 31.88 / 20.45 ms with an 8 / 16 / 32 / 64 kB L2 cache, 11.01 ms with smart placement.
- The OptiFlash examples ship for the controlCARD only; the flashing steps assume UART boot mode and the board's boot switches.

**What was tried.** LP-AM263P Rev A, MCU+ SDK 26.01.00.08, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1, SysConfig 1.28, Intel Mac. Programs were loaded into RAM with DSLite, the command-line loader that comes with CCStudio, while the chip waited (development boot). No switch was moved. TI's numbers come from its controlCARD, a plug-in card version of the board.

1. A RAM flash writer (TI's LaunchPad flash settings: octal DDR, 133 MHz input clock) erases and writes the code, reads it back through the driver and through the memory-mapped window, and refuses any address below 1 MB except the one block it writes back when restoring `0x80000`. Everything was written at 1 MB or 3 MB, space that read blank in this repo's backup of the board's flash.
2. `am263p/tools/xip_split.py` splits each build into the flash part and a RAM part that cannot write to flash.
3. TI's seven OptiFlash benchmarks, copied with the package changed to the one for the LaunchPad development kit.
4. TI's twelve AI examples that have test vectors and need no sensor, and TI's CoreMark example, in three layouts: TI's (all in RAM), code and constants in flash, and the same with the 64 kB L2 cache. A timer was added: one cold inference, then 101 timed inferences, median reported. Each layout was loaded three times.

**How far it got.** Every step ran, including putting the flash back: both test ranges erased and the `0x80000` block rewritten from this repo's backup, after which the lower 16 MB matched the backup byte for byte (2026-10-11). All 32 flash writes read back with zero mismatched bytes, through the driver and through the memory-mapped window (the writer prints `XIPFLASH OK ... mismatched_driver 0 mismatched_mmap 0`). Every run passed its own check: TI's "All tests have passed", CoreMark's checksums, and the AI examples' golden outputs, except one example that fails on its own (below).

**TI's OptiFlash benchmark** (16 tasks, 0 B copy, median of 3 loads; this repo's flash at 16.7 MHz, TI's with tuning on):

| Code runs from | LP-AM263P, ms | Against RAM | TI's page, ms | TI against RAM |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| On-chip RAM | 14.60 | 1.00x | 12.45 | 1.00x |
| Flash, no L2 cache | 126.55 | 8.67x | 46.57 | 3.74x |
| Flash, 8 kB L2 | 110.40 | 7.56x | 42.43 | 3.41x |
| Flash, 16 kB L2 | 91.82 | 6.29x | 39.19 | 3.15x |
| Flash, 32 kB L2 | 65.46 | 4.49x | 31.88 | 2.56x |
| Flash, 64 kB L2 | 34.57 | 2.37x | 20.45 | 1.64x |
| Flash, smart placement | 13.26 | 0.91x | 11.01 | 0.88x |

This repo's RAM time is 17% above TI's. Both are the AM263P at 400 MHz; TI's figure is from the controlCARD booted from flash through TI's bootloader, this repo's from the LaunchPad development kit loaded over the debugger. The cause is unknown. Smart placement beats all-RAM on both boards; the reason was not examined.

**TI's AI examples** (one inference, median of 101 after a cold first call, median of 3 loads, R5F at 400 MHz):

| Model | RAM, ms | Flash, no L2, ms | Flash, 64 kB L2, ms | First call from flash with no L2, ms |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| arc_fault | 2.928 | 3.114 | 2.929 | 3.679 |
| blower_imbalance | 1.717 | 1.786 | 1.717 | 2.369 |
| fan_blade_anomalydetection (output not confirmed, see below) | 2.955 | 4.957 | 3.012 | 5.296 |
| forecasting_pmsm_rotor_temp | 0.062 | 0.072 | 0.062 | 1.122 |
| generic_timeseries_anomalydetection | 4.719 | 6.521 | 4.738 | 6.677 |
| generic_timeseries_classification | 3.386 | 3.492 | 3.388 | 4.009 |
| generic_timeseries_forecasting | 0.915 | 7.165 | 6.293 | 7.262 |
| generic_timeseries_regression | 0.704 | 1.497 | 0.712 | 2.097 |
| hvac_indoor_temp_forecast | 0.117 | 0.147 | 0.117 | 1.249 |
| motor_fault | 0.960 | 0.960 | 0.960 | 1.528 |
| torque_measurement | 1.197 | 1.637 | 1.200 | 2.836 |
| washing_machine_load_weighing | 15.244 | 16.340 | 15.250 | 16.813 |

**CoreMark** (TI's example, -O3, 3 loads each): 1,464.5 per second from RAM, 1,394.5 from flash with no L2 (4.8% slower), 1,464.5 with the 64 kB L2.

**The line.** Nothing stopped. The cost of flash depends on how much code and constant data one pass touches.

- With no extra cache, the cost runs from nothing to 7.8 times (generic_timeseries_forecasting; the rest are under 2.2 times). motor_fault is 0.960 ms all three ways (suspected: its inner loop fits the core's own L1 cache). The two smallest models are not free: forecasting_pmsm_rotor_temp takes 16% longer and hvac_indoor_temp_forecast 26% longer. Each model's code size was not measured, so where the line falls is not known.
- With the 64 kB L2 cache, nine models land within 1% of RAM, two within 2% (one of them the model whose output is unconfirmed), and CoreMark matches RAM.
- A model larger than the cache streams from flash every time. generic_timeseries_forecasting links 100 kB of code and 66.8 kB of model constants into flash (from its map file) and stays 6.9 times slower with the cache. Keep a model like that in RAM, or let smart placement choose.

The first call after a load, with no extra cache, costs 0.1 to 1.2 ms more than a warm call on every model. It adds up when a model runs once after waking from sleep.

Three cautions from the run:

- **The flash ran slow.** **Tag: Unknown.** On every open, TI's driver printed `Flash_norOspiPhyTune : PHY enabling failed!!! Continuing without PHY...`, so the flash clock was 133.33 MHz / 8 = 16.7 MHz. TI's flash debug guide (SPRADS5, section 5.3.3) says this message means the tuning pattern is in flash but does not read back correctly. The pattern is there: a JTAG read of 0x80000 shows its 128 bytes. Cause unknown: this repo's loading method has not been separated from the board. If you see that message, your XIP numbers are slow numbers.
- **Opening the flash can write to it.** **Tag: TI example default.** When the tuning pattern does not read back, TI's flash driver (`Flash_norOspiPhyTune`, MCU+ SDK 26.01) erases the 4 kB sector at the tuning offset and writes the pattern there. On the LaunchPad that offset is `0x80000`, below the 1 MB guard of this repo's writer. Back up the flash first with `am263p/tools/flash_backup.sh`; The [LP-AM263P FAQ](../../am263p/FAQ.md) has the restore steps, and the block was written back, with the lower 16 MB then matching the backup exactly. On a board that has not run this repo's flasher, the script reads only the lower 16 MB of the 32 MB part (the flash wraps at 16 MB in its power-on mode); after a flasher run it reads all 32 MB, and this repo's upper half read blank.
- **fan_blade_anomalydetection fails its own check on this board,** with or without this repo's changes: TI's unmodified example matches 0 of 192 golden values, then prints "All tests have passed!!". Read the "Golden vectors matched" line, not the last line. Its timing above is real, but its output is not confirmed. The AM13E230 version of the same example checks the count and passes there.

- Get the high-speed read tuning to pass (TI's PHY grapher has no LaunchPad build), or boot from flash through TI's bootloader, then rerun the table. TI's own ratio suggests plain XIP would land near 3.7x.
- Smart placement for the AI models: TI's flow profiles a run, then a script picks the hot functions. Done here only for TI's memcpy benchmark, whose annotation file ships with the SDK.
- Keep the model constants in RAM and only the code in flash. That would probably fix the one model the cache cannot save; not run.
- Two or four cores running from flash at once. TI's XIP page says they split the flash bandwidth.

**Ask.** If you have run XIP on an LP-AM263P with PHY tuning passing, post your numbers for the same benchmark.

# Can one Matter thermostat on the LP-EM-CC35X1 work in Apple Home, Google Home, Alexa and Home Assistant?

**Short answer.** Yes for Apple Home. The image (a Matter Thermostat with heating and cooling setpoints and local temperature, plus an Occupancy Sensing sensor; 1,742.4 kB of application, 579 kB of RAM) runs on the CC3551E, Apple Home adds it as a thermostat, and the heating setpoint changes from the phone. TI ships no thermostat for this chip, so it is TI's lighting example with the data model and application swapped. After TI's Wi-Fi CSI presence image, every image programmed stayed silent, TI's own light included, until a full flash erase. Google Home, Alexa and Home Assistant are not run.

![Apple Home controlling the thermostat on the CC3551E: current 69 F (the 20.8 C fallback, no sensor wired), heat to 67 F, mode Heat](../../cc35x1/matter/img/thermostat-apple-home.png)

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). Build and sizes: [cc35x1/matter/README.md](../../cc35x1/matter/README.md), section "Thermostat image". Test plan: [COMPATIBILITY.md](../../cc35x1/matter/COMPATIBILITY.md). Wire format: [PROTOCOL.md](../../thermostat-system/PROTOCOL.md).

**Question.** Can one Matter-over-Wi-Fi device on the CC3551E be a thermostat that Apple Home, Google Home, Alexa and Home Assistant all take, with the radar's presence line as an occupancy sensor?

**Vendor position.** TI's release `matter-v1.5-ti-1.2-ea.2` lists Matter over Wi-Fi on the CC3551E as "Production Ready" and ships one example for it, the lighting app. Apple (Support 102135, 2026-05-07) lists thermostats and motion sensors among Home app Matter types. Google lists Thermostat and Occupancy Sensor as supported device types (developers.home.google.com/matter/supported-devices, read 2026-10-10) and needs a developer project for a test vendor ID. Amazon lists thermostats and sensors (developer.amazon.com Alexa Matter categories, read 2026-10-10). Home Assistant's controller is the Matter Server app (home-assistant.io/integrations/matter, read 2026-10-10).

**What was tried.**

- Looked for a TI thermostat target: `examples/thermostat/` in TI's fork has ten vendor folders and no TI one.
- Copied the lighting example, replaced its `.zap` endpoint with a thermostat (features heating and cooling, no presets or schedules) and added an Occupancy Sensing endpoint; replaced the light code with a task that reads `T,...` lines on a second UART and writes the clusters; added the second UART to a copy of TI's SysConfig file. Fallback with no line: 20.8 C and SW1 or SW2 step the setpoint by 0.5 C.
- Built in a throwaway linux/amd64 container. `generate.py -m` wants its output file to exist before it runs.

**How far it got.**

| Step | Result |
|---|---|
| Configure, compile, link, sign | Yes. 1,742.4 kB application, 1,747.9 kB signed, 1,741.6 kB flash, 579.3 kB RAM from `arm-none-eabi-size`; the light on the same tag is 1,752.1 kB and 578.9 kB |
| Flash | Yes, twice (2026-10-10): v1, then v2 with a boot line and a heartbeat every 5 s on the log UART. The programmer reported success each time |
| Boot, 2026-10-10 | Not seen, twice. The board had run TI's Wi-Fi CSI image the day before |
| Boot, 2026-10-11, programmed over the CSI image | Not seen: 0 bytes on both console ports through a probe reset and a J12 replug |
| Control: TI's own light image, programmed over it | Not seen either: 0 bytes after programming, after a replug of both cables, and after a second programming. So the fault was not this repo's image |
| Full flash erase, then the thermostat | Booted by itself as programming ended: this repo's boot line, Wi-Fi start, Matter server, "THERMO ready: UART2_1 115200, endpoint 1 thermostat, endpoint 2 occupancy", Bluetooth advertising 2.7 s after the boot line. Heap free at idle 149.7 kB, lowest 146.8 kB |
| Setup in Apple Home | Works (2026-10-11, an iPhone): added as "Matter Accessory", a thermostat, right after a fresh erase and program. One earlier scan hung on "Connecting" because the 300-second commissioning window had closed |
| Setpoint from Apple Home | Works: heat to 67 F set from the phone. Latency not timed |
| Google Home, Alexa, Home Assistant | Not run. Plan with vendor steps and hub hardware in COMPATIBILITY.md |
| Presence latency, offline control, four controllers at once, setup after a reflash | Not run: rows waiting in `data/results/cc35x1.csv`. The occupancy endpoint has no radar line wired |
| Log UART after Bluetooth starts | Turns to a stream of 0x00 and 0x80 bytes, the same at every host rate tried (1,200 to 115,200); fragments of the heartbeat come through. Cause not found |

**The line.** Not reached for Apple Home: it adds the thermostat and sets it. **Tool or docs**: the silence that blocked it for a day was the flash left behind by TI's CSI image, cleared by the Toolbox's `full_flash_erase`; the Toolbox guide does not say an erase is needed between images with different flash maps. The Thermostat cluster started with no delegate (no presets or schedules in the data model) and the second UART opened, both confirmed by the boot log. Writing the Occupancy attribute from the radar line is still untested.

**No TI example for this chip.** TI ships Matter over Wi-Fi on the CC3551E with one example, the light; Matter's own thermostat examples have ten vendor folders and none for TI. This is the first Matter thermostat on a CC35xx known to this repo. TI's lighting example became a thermostat by changing the data model and one application file, and Apple Home took it on the first scan inside the commissioning window.

What to watch for:

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Every image is silent after TI's CSI image, TI's light included | **Tool or docs**: the CSI bundle lays the flash out differently, and programming another bundle over it does not fix that | `full_flash_erase` before programming |
| A pairing scan hangs on "Connecting" | **Setup or handling**: TI's commissioning window is 300 s | Erase and program right before pairing |
| Only one tool can hold the debug probe | **Setup or handling**: a second programmer on the same probe gives -615 debug errors and lost images | One tool per probe at a time |
| The log UART turns to 0x00 and 0x80 bytes after Bluetooth starts | **Unknown** | Open; debug visibility only |

Build time was about 5 minutes on a warm container.

**Left open.** The radar's presence line into the occupancy endpoint (the 4-wire visit), then Google Home, Alexa and Home Assistant from COMPATIBILITY.md, and the setpoint latency.

**Ask.** Has anyone seen Alexa or Google Home take a Matter device with the test vendor ID 0xFFF1 without a developer project?

# Can Zephyr run LVGL with a touch screen on the TI LP-MSPM0G3519?

**Short answer.** It builds, it does not reach the screen. Zephyr 4.4.2 with its LVGL module (9.5.0) links for the board at 253.5 kB of flash and 49.5 kB of RAM using a dummy display. The panel's SPI and the touch chip's I2C have no driver for the MSPM0 family in this Zephyr tree, so it cannot draw on the Waveshare panel. The blinky NMI on this board is also still open.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). 1 kB = 1,024 bytes.

**Question.** Does the Zephyr route work for a touch UI on the G3519, and what does it cost against this repo's bare-metal LVGL build?

**Vendor position.** Zephyr's LVGL page lists the module, a display API and a `st7796s` driver; the board page for `lp_mspm0g3519` lists UART, GPIO and a console. The tree read was a Zephyr 4.4.2 checkout (dated 2026-08-06): `drivers/display/display_st7796s.c` and `drivers/input/input_ft5336.c` exist; `drivers/spi` and `drivers/i2c` contain no file for MSPM0.

**What was tried.**

- `west update lvgl` fetched LVGL 9.5.0 (this repo's bare-metal build uses 9.6.0).
- An app in `thermostat-system/g3519-zephyr/`: a thermostat-shaped screen (title, badge text, setpoint, plus and minus buttons), a devicetree overlay with a `zephyr,dummy-dc` display of 320x480, LVGL pool 12 kB, Montserrat 14 and 20, `CONFIG_SIZE_OPTIMIZATIONS`.
- Built with `west build -b lp_mspm0g3519` and the cross-compile toolchain used by the board's other Zephyr builds. Not flashed, because it draws nothing and the board holds the thermostat screen for other tests.

**How far it got.** Configure, compile, link. Not flashed.

| Measure | Zephyr 4.4.2 + LVGL 9.5.0, dummy display | This repo's bare-metal LVGL 9.6 thermostat |
|---|---|---|
| Flash | 253.5 kB (99 percent of the 256 kB the board file allows; the chip has 512 kB) | 242.4 kB (includes a 48 px font and the radar parser) |
| RAM | 49.5 kB (77 percent of the 64 kB the board file allows; the chip has 128 kB) | 27.3 kB plus 6 kB stack |
| Frames per second | not run | 8 refreshes a second under the radar replay |

The two columns are not the same feature set: Zephyr's LVGL turns on its default widget set and a kernel; this repo's is the trimmed config. The reading is "same order, Zephyr costs roughly 10 kB more flash and 20 kB more RAM for fewer features", not a precise price.

**The line.** The missing piece is a driver, not memory: no `spi_mspm0` and no `i2c_mspm0` in Zephyr's `drivers` folder. This repo's bare-metal port drives SPI1 by DMA and bit-bangs the touch I2C (the touch chip answers only software I2C on this board), and a Zephyr port would need an SPI driver at minimum, plus a GPIO-bit-banged I2C node (`i2c-gpio` exists in Zephyr).

**Ask.** Is an MSPM0 SPI controller driver on Zephyr's roadmap, and is there a branch?

<!-- experiment
