# Can an MSPM0 host TI's CC1407P radio, the BP-CC1407P-9-FE, and send sensor readings to another board?

**Short answer.** Yes. TI ships no MSPM0 code for the BP-CC1407P-9-FE radio BoosterPack plug-in module, but TI's host driver from its Zephyr fork runs on an LP-MSPM0G5187 with its driver files unchanged; only its two Zephyr-only files are replaced by this repo's bare-metal layer. The G5187 reads temperature, humidity and light from a Sensors BoosterPack and sends them every 1.04 s at 915 MHz. An LP-CC1354P10-1 running TI's own receive example, moved to 915 MHz, received 21,658 of 21,658 packets over about 6 h 15 min, ending 2026-10-11 06:00, with no checksum errors, at -14 dBm on the same desk. A bridge on the Mac posts the readings to Home Assistant. Range and a comparison with TI's supported host are not done.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md) (SPI, CRC, RSSI, BoosterPack, HAL). 1 kB = 1,024 bytes. Code and wiring: [mspm0g5187/radio](../../mspm0g5187/radio/README.md); receiver: [cc1354p10/radio-rx](../../cc1354p10/radio-rx/README.md). Checked on an Intel Mac, macOS 15.7.9, CCStudio 21.0.1, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS, UniFlash 9.6.0, MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07 with SysConfig 1.26.3 (sender), F2 SDK 8.33.00.16 with SysConfig 1.28.0 (receiver), TI's driver from `simplelink-zephyr` tag `v3.7.0-ti-1.00.01_ga`.

**Question.** The CC1407P is a radio that a host drives over SPI. Can a plain MSPM0, the part a sensor-node designer might pick, be the host, and can it talk to the radio inside a TI CC13xx?

**Vendor position.** TI's BoosterPack page, read 2026-10-07, says the plug-in's host driver "can be ported to other MCUs". TI's examples cover seven CC13xx and CC26xx LaunchPad variants under its TRX plug-in 1.00.00.52. They also cover the LP-EM-CC2745R10-Q1 under its Zephyr fork. No MSPM0 host is listed. **Tag: Tool or docs.** A board has to supply eight functions to the driver: start an SPI transfer, set chip select, read the radio's data-out line, set reset, turn the interrupt on or off, wait some microseconds, and start and stop a one-shot timer.

**What was tried.**

- **Host layer.** TI's driver has two files that call Zephyr's kernel, SPI and GPIO. `portability/cc1407p-host/hal_bare.c` (written 2026-10-09) replaces them with the same logic and the eight functions above. `mspm0g5187/radio/hooks_mspm0g5187.c` supplies those eight in DriverLib, with SysTick as the timer and polled SPI at 1 MHz.
- **Wiring.** The LP-MSPM0G5187 has header pins on J1 and J3 only, and the Sensors BoosterPack uses them, so the radio sits beside the stack. Six signals go to J20, the 2x4 header by the microSD slot: SPI port UC3 on PB9, PB8 and PB7, chip select PB6, reset PB10, interrupt PB11. Power and ground come from pins that pass up through the sensor pack.
- **Sender.** TI's `ti_cc140xp_genfsk_tx` sample's sequence and its 50 kbps 2-GFSK settings, 915 MHz, the high-power amplifier at its top level. The payload is text, `FRL n=12 t=24.80C rh=36.9% lux=207.20`, 37 to 39 bytes.
- **Receiver.** TI's `rfPacketRx` for the LP-CC1354P10-1 (prop_rf examples for F2 SDK 8.33), changed to 915 MHz, keeping packets that fail the checksum, appending RSSI and printing each packet. Its default settings match the CC1407P's in symbol rate, deviation, preamble, sync word 0x930B51DE, length field and whitening.

**How far it got.** Verified on the boards:

| Step | Result |
|---|---|
| Driver open and version read | Firmware 3.0.0.25, hash 0x8352f9e3, 5 of 5 reads, after two wiring fixes (below) |
| Sender | Every packet reported finished by the radio (`status=16`) |
| Receiver, 30 s with both ends logged | 28 of the 29 live packets printed; the missing one is covered by the six-hour count below; the counter rose 14 in the 14 s between its two count lines |
| Receiver, unattended | 21,658 good packets by 06:00:48 against sender sequence 291 to 21,948 (21,658 sent), about 6 h 15 min at 1.04 s each; 0 checksum errors; 0 lost, plus or minus one at the start |
| One hour, both ends logged | 3,508 of 3,508 from 05:58:56 to 06:59:37, 0 checksum errors |
| Signal | -14 dBm median, range -15 to -14; distance on the desk not measured |
| Home Assistant | Four sensors posted every 10 s, 253 posts logged from 06:03 |
| Image sizes | Sender 20.4 kB of flash and 5.4 kB of RAM with TI's default 24 SPI buffers; receiver 29.2 kB of flash |

**The line.** None reached. The closest call was the wiring, not the software. **Tag: Setup or handling.** If the radio answers with a valid checksum on everything it sends and a checksum error (`04 02 f0 00`) on everything it receives, its data-in wire is open: holding the reset and interrupt pins low in turn did not stop it answering, and forcing the data-in pin high or low did not change its reply. Here the two inner-row wires were missing and the data wire sat in pin 16 instead of 15. Check all six signals on J20 before debugging the driver.

**Ask.**

- **Open question:** Has anyone used an MSPM0 as the host for the CC140xP radios? The port needed only the eight board functions above and the two replaced Zephyr files.
- **For readers:** if you run this link outdoors, report the distance at which packets start to drop.

FILE: docs/experiments/2026-10-10-mspm0g5187-npu-live-light.md | Can the LP-MSPM0G5187's NPU count people from a live light reading on the BP-BASSENSORSMKII?
==============================================================================

<!-- experiment
id: E177
board: LP-MSPM0G5187
date: 2026-10-10
status: parked
reached: run
line: The room-occupancy model runs on the NPU once a second. Its input is a live light reading from the BP-BASSENSORSMKII's OPT3001, taken over I2C. Each call takes 1.30 to 1.32 ms, within 1 percent of the time on stored test vectors. The bench was lit at 316 to 319 lux, source not recorded. -->
# Can the LP-MSPM0G5187's NPU count people from a live light reading on the BP-BASSENSORSMKII?

**Short answer.** It runs. The 636-parameter room-occupancy model reads the Sensors BoosterPack's OPT3001 light sensor over I2C once a second, runs on the TinyEngine NPU in 1.30 to 1.32 ms (within 1 percent of its time on stored test vectors), and prints the count on the serial port. With the bench lit as it was (316 to 319 lux, the light source not recorded) it reads 0 people for 15 samples while the window fills, then 1 person from sample 18 on. Whether the count follows the light is untested: no run varied it. **Unknown (suspected: setup or handling, or the model's training range).** Two things could be behind the "1 person", and neither is tested: this repo's program holds the three inputs this BoosterPack lacks (sound, CO2, motion) at empty-room values, and 317 lux is twice the brightest window the model was trained on. This shows a real sensor driving the NPU. It does not measure occupancy.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md) (NPU, TinyEngine, OPT3001, lux, logits, SysTick, soft float, the BoosterPack's sensors). Board page: [LP-MSPM0G5187 README](../../mspm0g5187/README.md), [FAQ](../../mspm0g5187/FAQ.md). Its time on the NPU with stored data: [NPU against CPU on the LP-MSPM0G5187](2026-10-09-mspm0g5187-npu-vs-cpu.md). Run 2026-10-10 on an Intel Mac, macOS 15.7, MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1, SysConfig 1.26.3, pyserial 3.5.

**Question.** Every NPU number came from test vectors baked into the image. The Sensors BoosterPack (BP-BASSENSORSMKII, six sensors) arrived, and the question was whether one of its readings could feed the model on the chip, in the window layout the model was trained on, without changing the model.

**Vendor position.** TI's NPU examples for this board take sensor data from a different BoosterPack, the TIDA-010997 with a BMI270 motion sensor over SPI. That example is `fall_detection_ai_npu/README.md` in MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07, under `examples/nortos/LP_MSPM0G5187/edgeAI/`. The other source is TI's Edge AI Studio tool over serial at 115200, described in `timeseries_data_capture/README.md` in the same folder. None uses the BP-BASSENSORSMKII. TI's user guide for the BoosterPack (SLAU829, May 2020) lists the OPT3001 at I2C address 0x44, powered when header pin 27 is high.

**Setup.** The BoosterPack sits on the LaunchPad with its pin 1 (marked 3V3) in pin 1 of J1 on the LaunchPad development kit. No wires, no jumpers. The program drives pin 27 (PA15) high to power the light sensor; the I2C bus is on header pins 9 (PA9, clock) and 10 (PA8, data). Flash the program with UniFlash's DSLite and read the LaunchPad kit's backchannel serial port at 115200 baud, 8N1; 48 seconds of output cover the window fill and the steady state. The model has 636 parameters.

**What was tried.** The model takes 4 channels of 32 samples: light in lux, sound in volts, CO2 in ppm, and a motion flag. The program keeps a 128-value window. Every second it reads the OPT3001's result register, converts it to lux (exponent and mantissa, as the OPT3001 data sheet gives it), shifts the light channel by one and puts the new reading last. Sound, CO2 and motion stay at 0.08 V, 355 ppm and 0, the medians of the empty-room windows in the model's 20 test vectors. The light channel starts at 0, so the first 31 calls see a window that is part dark, part lit. Then it calls the NPU, waits for the NPU's done interrupt, counts the cycles with SysTick, picks the largest of the four logits, lights LED1 when the count is not 0, and prints one line: sample number, lux, the four logits, the count, the cycles. The window moves one sample a second instead of one every 30 s as in the dataset.

**How far it got.** Run, on the bench in the room light of the afternoon (316 to 319 lux, the source not recorded), no one touching the board. 48 lines were saved from the first sample; an earlier 45-line run from sample 31 on agrees.

| What | Reading |
|---|---|
| Light at the sensor | 316 to 319 lux, steady |
| NPU time per call | 1.30 to 1.32 ms at 80 MHz (104k to 106k cycles); the stored-vector run measured 1.292 ms on its fastest vector and 1.323 ms on its slowest |
| Count, samples 1 to 15 | 0 |
| Count, sample 16 | 1, then 0 again at 17 |
| Count, samples 18 to 48 | 1 |
| Logits from sample 32 on (window full) | 21, 25, -45, -128 for 0, 1, 2 and 3 people |

The logits are the model's int8 outputs, so -128 is the floor. The win for "1 person" over "0" is 3 to 4 units (24 or 25 against 21) on a scale where the top logit sits 152 to 153 above the floor: a narrow call that small input changes could flip. Program size from the linker map: 11.7 kB of flash; in RAM 1.1 kB of data plus a 2 kB stack.

The dataset's lit, occupied windows sit at 115 to 157 lux and its empty ones at 0 to 10 (the same 20 test vectors), so 317 lux is above anything the model saw in training. It still lands on the lit side.

The cycle count climbs by about 1.6 percent from the first call to the 32nd, then stays at exactly the same count from sample 32 on, although the lux still wanders by 1 to 2. **Unknown.** Sample 32 is when the last zero leaves the window, so the time depends on the values in the window somehow; where the NNC build converts the float inputs was not looked at.

**The line.** None reached. The loop is a one-second busy wait plus the read, the NPU call and the print; the chip never sleeps, and the loop's own time was not measured.

**What limits the answer.** **Unknown (suspected: setup or handling, or the model's training range).** Only one of the four inputs is a real sensor. In the model's 20 test windows CO2 and light are both high when people are in, so a lit room with CO2 pinned at the empty-room value (the program's choice) is a mix the training data never had; and 317 lux is twice the brightest window it saw (the model's range). Expect it to say occupied whenever the light is on. Not tested. A covered sensor (0 lux, inside the training range) checks the first cause only; a dimmed or shaded light at 115 to 157 lux is the check that separates the two.

**Ask.** Anyone at the bench: cover the light sensor for a minute and read the count on the serial line (expected: 0 within 32 samples). Then dim or shade the light until the sensor reads 115 to 157 lux and read it again: a 1 there means the fixed channels alone give the answer, a 0 means the out-of-range light did.

**What a reader should take.** Feeding the NPU from a live sensor is a 100-line program: read, shift, call, print. The model's time does not change with real data. What changes is what the number means, and that is set by which sensors the training data had, not by the chip.

==============================================================================

<!-- experiment
id: E178
board: IWRL6432BOOST
date: 2026-10-10
status: parked
reached: run
line: 2x2 and 2x3 ran. The presence demo refuses 1x1 with error -40107. In an empty room neither gave a false alarm in 240 frames. # What do you get from all the antennas of the TI IWRL6432BOOST radar, against using one transmitter and one receiver?

**Short answer.** 2x2 and 2x3 are measured; 1x1 is refused by TI's demo. With 2 transmit by 2 receive and with 2 by 3, an empty room for 60 s gave 0 flags in 240 frames, and a person sitting still at 2 m and at 4 m was held in 100 percent of frames. The person was first flagged 4 to 6 s after sitting down and the flag cleared 11 to 15 s after leaving, which is the demo's hold time. Walking in from behind the door was detected at about 6.5 m on 2x3. These are single passes with no spread, so a one- or two-second difference between 2x2 and 2x3 is inside the person's own timing. The tool applies an antenna setting over the radar's command line, runs voice-cued passes (walking in, sitting still, an empty room), and writes a customer-facing comparison page. TI's prebuilt demo does not read its command line while it runs with the shipped `lowPowerCfg 1`, so the first change after a boot needs one press of the board's reset button, and every setting is run with `lowPowerCfg 0`. Overnight in the empty test room, the 2x3 setting at a 12-frame hold gave 0 false alarms in 87,602 frames (6.08 h; 95 percent upper bound 0.49 an hour). TI's Wi-Fi presence model on the LP-EM-CC35X1, logging on the same clock for the first 1.19 h of that window, classed 0 of 2,065 results as present.

How to read the data and pick a presence radar with it: [the evaluation guide](../guides/evaluate-a-presence-radar.md).

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). The antenna setting is `channelCfg <receive mask> <transmit mask> 0`: 7 3 0 is three receivers and two transmitters (2x3), 3 3 0 is 2x2, 1 1 0 is 1x1. Board: [IWRL6432BOOST](../../iwrl6432boost/README.md). Page: [radar evaluation](../../site/radar-eval.html). Files: `iwrl6432boost/eval/`. Read and run 2026-10-10 on macOS 15.7 with Radar Toolbox 4.00.00.05.

**Question.** TI sells one 60 GHz presence radar family with 2 transmit and 3 receive channels. A product that only needs "is someone there" could use fewer antennas. What does the full set buy in distance, delay and false alarms?

**Vendor position.** The demo's source (`Motion_and_Presence_Detection/src/source/mmw_cli.c`) reads `channelCfg` as receive mask, transmit mask, miscellaneous control, counts the set bits as antennas, and errors if more than the maximum receivers are selected. In `motion_detect.c`: "Sensor Stop command is honoured only when Low Power Cfg is disabled". The data sheets for the IWRL6432 (SWRS298B), IWRL6432 WCSP (SWRS311), IWRL6432AOP (SWRS323B) and IWRL1432 (SWRS313A, 76 to 81 GHz) all list 3 receivers and 2 transmitters; the AOP part can use one transmitter at a time. Read 2026-10-10. No part in the family has a single antenna pair, so 1x1 is a setting of the same chip, not a cheaper part.

**What was tried.**

1. Read the demo source for what `channelCfg` and the rest of the presence configuration require. `compRangeBiasAndRxChanPhase` takes all 13 values whatever the setting, so it is left as shipped.
2. Wrote `radar_eval.py`: `accept` (apply each setting, read every CLI answer, check the stream), `empty` (empty-room false-alarm window), `run` (voice-cued walking and seated passes, each started on a timer or with Enter), `restore` (shipped configuration back). Presence is any zone flag in TLV 315; range comes from which box fired and the minor-motion range profile (TLV 303, 128 bins, 0.121 m a bin by arithmetic from the chirp settings: 256 real samples at 12.5 Msps with a 60.5 MHz/us slope, not calibrated against a measured distance).
3. Checked the analysis on synthetic frames: a seated pass with a known 2.5 s entry and 3.2 s exit gave 2.5 s and 3.25 s; a walk with known presence from 10 s gave 5.5 m at the 4 s a metre pace; an empty-room set with two known flags gave 2.
4. Tried the command line on the running demo: `sensorStop` at 125 attempts in 6 s, with and without carriage returns, got no answer and the stream carried on (consistent with the source comment above).
5. Read the stream at the shipped setting for 60 s: 231 frames, no missing frame numbers, 3.85 frames a second, 608 bytes a frame, TLVs 303, 306 and 315, four zones.

**How far it got.** Run, for 2x2 and 2x3. 1x1: configure and start refused. After one reset the demo took the 1x1 lines (`channelCfg 1 1 0`, everything else as shipped except `lowPowerCfg 0`) but `sensorStart` failed with `Error in setting up range profile:-40107`, and the command line then went silent (a second reset is needed). After a second reset 2x2 was accepted (25 of 25 lines Done, 32 frames in 8 s at 3.999 a second, 768 bytes a frame, TLVs 301, 303, 306, 315). The 2x3 setting started next in the same boot got every line Done but no frames, and the demo went silent again, so the demo seems to take one start per boot (suspected). The 2x2 and 2x3 passes are in the results below and in the findings log.

**2x2 results (2026-10-10, one boot, 60 s empty room, one pass each).** Empty room: 0 flags in 240 frames (95 percent upper bound 181 flags an hour, because the window is 60 s). Seated at 2 m: held in 100 percent of the 40 s, first flagged 5.6 s after the cue, cleared 10.7 s after the person left; range-profile peak at bin 22, which is 2.66 m by the arithmetic bin size, so the profile reads about 0.6 m long. Seated at 4 m: held 100 percent, first flagged 3.9 s after the cue, cleared 11.5 s after leaving, peak at 4.6 m, far zone flagged in every frame. Walking in: the person was already flagged at the 8 m start, so the arrival distance is at least 8 m and no more is known. The clear time of about 11 s is the demo's own hold time, not the person's walk. An earlier set on the same boot (listed in the results folder as early and backlog) is not used: the macOS serial driver delivered buffered frames late, and the person was still in view. If you see a 60 s window with far more frames than 4 a second times 60, drain the serial port to live frames before each pass; the tool now does.

**The line.** One receiver with the shipped range and angle lines is refused (-40107, range profile setup). Suspected, not tested: `sigProcChainCfg` (its azimuth FFT size of 64 assumes more than one receiver), `rangeSelCfg`, `cfarCfg` or `aoaFovCfg`, which a single antenna cannot satisfy; the fix is probably a 1-receiver variant of those lines, not run. The demo takes no command while it runs with `lowPowerCfg 1`, so the setting cannot change without a reset. What 1x1 would do to the stream is not known because the demo does not accept it with these lines. The 2x2 and 2x3 numbers are one pass per cell. Not run: whether the demo accepts one receiver with the shipped `aoaFovCfg` and `sigProcChainCfg` lines (angle estimation needs more than one virtual antenna; an error from the demo is itself the result).

- Use a point-cloud demo (TI's Out of Box or mmWave Demo images, in the toolbox) to get a distance for each detected object instead of box membership. That needs a flash, which costs two switch moves on this board.
- TI's toolbox ships a people-tracking configuration (`IWRL6432BOOST_Tracking_3Persons_7m_wall_mount.cfg`); the tracking image would give a track for each person, and needs a flash cycle.
- A corner-reflector pass for a fixed-range target.
- Measure power per setting with an external meter; the presence demo does not report it on this board.
- Repeat each pass three or more times and report the median and the spread.

**Ask.** If you have run a 1 transmit, 1 receive presence configuration on an IWRL6432 or IWRL1432, which settings did the demo need changed to accept it?

## Findings log

- The demo ignored the command line while it streamed. The cause is in the source: with `lowPowerCfg 1` the stop command is not honoured. So every eval configuration is sent with `lowPowerCfg 0`, and the first change after a boot needs one press of S2 (NRST).
- The 1x1 setting (`channelCfg 1 1 0`) was refused. `sensorStart` answered `Error in setting up range profile:-40107`, and the demo then stopped answering until the next reset. Suspected lines (not tested): `sigProcChainCfg`, `rangeSelCfg`, `cfarCfg`, `aoaFovCfg`.
- After the next reset, 2x2 started and streamed (4.0 frames a second, 768 bytes a frame). 2x3 started second in the same boot sent every line as Done but gave no frames and the demo went silent. Rule: one configuration start per boot; each further setting costs one S2 press. It is unknown whether 2x3 itself or the second start caused it; a later boot ran 2x3 first and it worked, which points at the second start.
- Spoken cues for the walking and seated passes have to make sense with the screen off: a cue that said only "enter" and "leave" left the person without a place to stand. Every cue is now a full sentence spoken twice (where to be, what to do, for how long, what happens next), and passes start on a 10 s timer.
- The first empty-room window read 1,746 frames in 60 s: the macOS serial driver had kept 12 minutes of stream while an answer was awaited, and clearing the port buffer did not clear it. That window and the first walk and seated passes (person still in view) are set aside (`-backlog`, `-early` in the results folder). The tool now reads and discards until frames arrive one at a time before each pass.
- Forwarding frames to the G3519 from the reading loop made a slow screen delay the radar reads (frames arrived in bursts of 14 with one timestamp). It now runs in its own thread and drops frames when full.
- In the 2x2 round the walking person stood at the 8 m mark in the room, in view of the radar. Presence was on at the first frame, so no arrival distance could be read (at least 8 m). For 2x3 the instruction became: start outside the room behind the door, open it on "go" and walk in.
- Second 2x2 set, with the Wi-Fi sensor running at the same time. Empty room 60 s: 0 flags in 240 frames. Seated at 2 m: first flagged 5.6 s after the cue, held 100 percent, cleared 10.7 s after leaving, range-profile peak 2.66 m. Seated at 4 m: first flagged 3.9 s, held 100 percent, cleared 11.5 s, peak 4.6 m, far zone on in every frame. The profile reads about 0.6 m long at both distances.
- 2x3 set (first start in its boot). Empty room 60 s: 0 flags after the first 14.2 s, which is the person leaving plus the demo's hold time (counted as carry-over, not a false alarm). Walk-in from behind the door: first flagged 6.7 s after the cue at about 6.5 m by the 4 s a metre pacing. Seated at 2 m: first flagged 6.2 s, held 100 percent, cleared 12.3 s, peak 2.78 m, far zone on in 20 percent of frames. Seated at 4 m: first flagged 4.3 s, held 100 percent, cleared 14.1 s, peak 4.6 m, far zone every frame. One pass per cell, so a difference of a second or two between 2x2 and 2x3 is inside the person's own timing.
- The two are not comparable. 2x2 has no usable walk-in (see the walking start position above), so the walk-in distance is measured for 2x3 only. 1x1 has nothing. One pass per cell; no spread.
- TI's CSI presence model on the LP-EM-CC35X1 ran alongside (2,075 results). Every result in the passes is class 1 (present), including the empty-room windows: 34 results in the 2x2 window (probability 0.91 to 0.99) and 34 in the 2x3 window (0.90 to 0.99). In this room the Wi-Fi presence model never reports clear in these passes, so it gives no clear time. The radar did: 0 flags in the empty windows. Same behavior as the earlier Wi-Fi presence experiment.
- After the 2x3 round the radar was left running the 2x3 configuration with `lowPowerCfg 0` (identical to the shipped configuration apart from that line) rather than sending the shipped file again, because a second start in the same boot is what hung it before. The stock `lowPowerCfg 1` file goes back at the next boot.
- A fast-clear configuration (`minor2emptyThre` cut from 20 to 6, `PresenceDetect-fastclear.cfg`) was tried to make the screen's presence badge clear sooner than the demo's hold of about 5 s. With a person seated at the bench the demo reported empty for 11 minutes 19 s and showed presence again only when the person walked in. The state machine re-detects a still person only on a larger motion once the window is short. Test a fast-clear setting on a seated person before trusting it. TI's page states the rule (a motion status is kept if at least one detection was recorded in the last `minor2emptyThre` frames) and does not say a short window stops holding a still person. Detail: [the thermostat page](2026-10-10-thermostat-mcu-only.md).
- The feeder that forwards radar frames and Wi-Fi results to the thermostat screen has to run detached from the shell; started as a background process of a command, it exits when the command's pipes close.
- The 12-frame hold: after one more S2 press, `PresenceDetect-hold12.cfg` (`minor2emptyThre` 12, about 3 s, `lowPowerCfg 0`, 2x3 antennas) was sent, with all lines Done in 7 s. It is the configuration of the overnight run.
- The overnight baseline ran in the empty test room (the rest of the house was occupied but quiet). The feeder logs every radar frame to a per-day frames file on the Mac and the Wi-Fi logger writes its results to a CSV. The window starts where the hold change took effect and the frame log resumed.
- The overnight result was computed by `iwrl6432boost/eval/overnight.py`: 87,602 frames at 4.00 a second (one gap of 20 frames) up to the first presence flag of the next morning, 0 presence frames, 0 frames with point-cloud points. **False alarms: 0 in 6.08 h**, 95 percent upper bound 0.49 an hour by the rule of three (row `radar_false_alarm presence-2x3-hold12-overnight`). Whether the morning flag was a person is not verified; the flags that followed (4.7 s, 9.5 s, then 121 s) look like someone passing through and settling. The walk-out clear time cannot be read from this log, because the person's exit at the start of the window was not timed. The Wi-Fi logger's loop stopped after 1.19 h (cause not found in its log); over those 1.19 hours it classed 0 of 2,065 results as present, median probability 0.013 (row `cc35x1 ai_presence_accuracy wifi-csi-empty-overnight`), against every empty-room window present in the evening passes with one person moving in the house.

**Cross-reference, Wi-Fi sensor at the same time (2026-10-10).** The 2x2 and 2x3 in-and-out passes were run with the CC35X1 Wi-Fi CSI presence demo logging on the same Mac clock. The Wi-Fi model said "present" in every window of every pass, empty room included, so "radar or Wi-Fi" equals Wi-Fi alone and "radar and Wi-Fi" equals the radar alone; "radar confirms Wi-Fi" kept the radar's near-zero misses but had about a third false alarms (113 of 337 moments in the 2x2 round, 112 of 338 in the 2x3 round) against the radar alone's 22 to 24%, mostly in the 11 to 15 s after the person left. Method, tables and limits: [the Wi-Fi presence page](2026-10-09-cc35x1-wifi-csi-presence.md), section "Side by side with the radar, 2026-10-10".

FILE: docs/experiments/2026-10-10-tda4-c7x-vs-a72.md | How much faster is the SK-TDA4VM's C7x and MMA than its two Cortex-A72 cores when a TI model-zoo network runs on the CPU instead?
==============================================================================

<!-- experiment

# How much faster is the SK-TDA4VM's C7x and MMA than its two Cortex-A72 cores when a TI model-zoo network runs on the CPU instead?

Terms used here are in [docs/vocab.md](../vocab.md) (Cortex-A72, C7x, MMA, TIDL, execution provider, fp32 and int8, the model zoo and its name prefixes) and the board's [FAQ](../../tda4/FAQ.md). Board page: [tda4/README.md](../../tda4/README.md). Numbers: `dl_inference_ms` rows in `data/results/tda4.csv`.

**Short answer.** On the SK-TDA4VM, eight TI model-zoo networks ran 13 to 135 times faster on the C7x DSP with its MMA accelerator than on the two Cortex-A72 cores: 2.9 ms against 37 ms for the smallest, 13.8 ms against 1,767 ms for the pose model. The CPU ran the zoo's fp32 graphs and the accelerator its int8 artifacts, so the ratio is what a developer pays when a model falls back to the CPU on this image, not a like-for-like comparison of the two cores; timing only, outputs not compared.

**Question.** TI's SK-TDA4VM has two general-purpose Cortex-A72 cores and a C7x DSP with a matrix accelerator (MMA) that TI rates at 8 TOPS. If a model runs on the accelerator, how much time does it save against running the same model on the Arm cores, and does the saving depend on the model's size?

**Vendor position.** TI, SK-TDA4VM product page and the TDA4VM data sheet (read 2026-10-09): "C7x floating point, vector DSP, up to 1.0 GHz, 80 GFLOPS, 256 GOPS" with a "Deep-learning matrix multiply accelerator (MMA), up to 8 TOPS (8b) at 1.0 GHz". TI's Edge AI model-zoo page lists inference times on the C7x for four models (2.03 ms MobileNetV1 mlperf, 3.04 ms regNetx-200mf, 5.03 ms yolox-nano-lite 416, 5.9 ms ssdLite mobDet 320, read 2026-10-09). TI publishes no CPU-only figures for these models, and the zoo ships them compiled for the accelerator only.

This repo's expectation before the run: "10 to 100 times on convolutional models; less on tiny ones where the call overhead dominates".

**What was tried.** Board: SK-TDA4VM (J721EXSKG01EVM, PROC112A1), TI Edge AI SDK 11.00.00.08, Linux 6.12.17-ti, onnxruntime 1.15.0, no display, no Ethernet, everything over the serial console, 2026-10-09 to 10.

1. Accelerator: each ONNX and TFLite model in `/opt/model_zoo` through ONNX Runtime or TFLite with TI's TIDL delegate, using the zoo's precompiled int8 artifacts. Random input, one warm-up, 30 timed runs, median wall time in Python. The runtime's log confirmed every node went to the C7x (274 of 274 for the pose model).
2. CPU: the same ONNX files through ONNX Runtime's CPU execution provider with two threads, one per A72, as the zoo ships them: fp32 graphs, not quantized for a CPU. Random input, one warm-up, three timed runs, median.
3. The three TVM models in the zoo through the DLR runtime (2026-10-10) on the accelerator only; the zoo holds no CPU build of them.

**How far it got.** Measured, timing only. All 14 zoo models ran on the accelerator; the 8 that have an ONNX file also ran on the Arm cores. The CPU runs on the detection models print ONNX Runtime's warning `execution_frame.cc:857 VerifyOutputSizes] Expected shape from model of {51} does not match actual shape of {200} for output labels`; whether the two sides return identical outputs, only how long each took.

| Model (TI zoo name) | Task | C7x and MMA, ms | Two A72 cores, ms | Ratio |
|---|---|--:|--:|--:|
| ONR-CL-6360-regNetx-200mf, 224 | classification | 2.89 | 37.4 | 13x |
| ONR-OD-8200-yolox-nano-lite, 416 | detection | 4.66 | 193.0 | 41x |
| ONR-OD-8020-ssd-lite-mobv2, 512 | detection | 6.10 | 438.5 | 72x |
| ONR-SS-7618-deeplabv3lite-mobv2 robokit, 768x432 | segmentation | 11.75 | 900.5 | 77x |
| ONR-SS-8610-deeplabv3lite-mobv2 ade20k, 512 | segmentation | 7.30 | 714.1 | 98x |
| ONR-KD-7060-human-pose-yolox-s, 640 | keypoints | 13.76 | 1,767.0 | 128x |
| ONR-OD-8220-yolox-s-lite, 640 | detection | 11.68 | 1,523.1 | 130x |
| ONR-OD-8420-yolox-s-lite widerface, 640 | detection | 11.16 | 1,504.0 | 135x |

Accelerator only (no CPU build in the zoo): TFL-CL-0000 MobileNetV1 2.17 ms, TFL-OD-2020 ssdLite mobDet 320 6.40 ms, TFL-SS-2580 deeplabv3 mobv2 12.11 ms, TVM-CL-3090 MobileNetV2 2.93 ms, TVM-OD-5120 ssdLite mobDet 320 12.97 ms, TVM-SS-5710 deeplabv3lite cocoseg21 8.85 ms. TI's four published figures are within 10 percent of the values measured here. The TVM build of ssdLite mobDet 320 (DLR 1.13.0 runtime, fp32 NHWC input) is 12.97 ms against 6.40 ms for the TFLite build of the same network (TFLite runtime, uint8 input; the TFLite runtime's version was not recorded). Two things differ, the runtime and the input format, and they were not tested apart: **Unknown (suspected: the input conversion inside the graph).**

**The line.** No line was reached: everything ran. The result is the shape of the ratio.

The ratio grows with the model. The smallest network (regNetx-200mf; the name says about 200M floating-point operations per image) gains 13x; the three 640x640 YOLOX-s networks gain 128x to 135x. On the accelerator the big models take only 4 to 5 times longer than the small one (13.8 ms against 2.9 ms), while on the CPU they take 40 to 50 times longer (1,767 ms against 37 ms). Suspected, not profiled: the accelerator's time has a floor of a few milliseconds that does not shrink with the model (loading the input, running the graph through the runtime, reading the output back), while the CPU's time grows with the arithmetic. No operations were counted, so this is the shape of the table, not a measurement of either.

What the ratio is not. The CPU ran fp32 graphs through a generic runtime; the accelerator ran int8 artifacts TI compiled for it. An int8 CPU build with Arm's optimized kernels would probably cut the CPU time, by how much was not measured (an estimate, nothing built), and the zoo ships none. So these numbers measure what a developer sees on this image when a model falls back to the CPU (for example because an operator is not supported by TIDL), not the two cores' arithmetic against each other.

**Ask.** If you have run one of TI's zoo models on the A72 cores in int8, what did you get, and with which runtime?

# Does the SK-TDA4VM reach a first inference in under an hour from the sealed box, with only public documents?

Terms used here are in [docs/vocab.md](../vocab.md) (U-Boot, UART boot, boot ROM, xmodem and ymodem, the model zoo) and the board's [FAQ](../../tda4/FAQ.md). Board page: [tda4/README.md](../../tda4/README.md). The card-writing times were taken with a stopwatch; the other two figures below were observed and not saved.

**Short answer.** No, not at this bench: about 2 h 30 min of work from the sealed SK-TDA4VM box to a Linux prompt and about 40 minutes more to the first model inference. The hour went on two things TI's documents do not mention, a card that did not boot and a macOS console driver; the 62 timed minutes of card writing alone pass the hour, so the verdict does not rest on the two estimates. With a written card the board itself is fast.

**Question.** TI sells the SK-TDA4VM as a kit a developer can start prototyping a vision application on in under an hour. From a sealed box, with a Mac, the public documents and no network cable, how long does it take to see the first model run?

**Vendor position.** TI, SK-TDA4VM product page (read 2026-10-09): the kit "enables prototyping a vision-based application in less than an hour". TI, Edge AI SDK getting-started guide 11.00 (read 2026-10-09): "the board will take less than 20sec to boot and display a wallpaper". The guide's first steps: download the image, write it to a micro-SD card with a card writer, insert the card, connect a display, Ethernet and the USB-C supply, power on. The SK-TDA4VM user guide (SPRUJ21, read 2026-10-09) lists a micro-SD card among the kit contents (wording not saved) and names the board's serial bridge chip and a Windows driver for it; it names no macOS driver.

This repo's expectation before the run: "Yes, if power and card are right; the supply is the likely stop".

**What was tried.** Board: SK-TDA4VM (J721EXSKG01EVM, PROC112A1) with the micro-SD card from its box, an Intel Mac on macOS 15.7.9, a 20 V class USB-C supply, the micro-B console cable. No display, no Ethernet and no micro-SD card reader at the bench. The second sitting (2026-10-09, 21:20 to 22:50) is in the stopwatch and timeline files and the 62-minute figure comes from them; the earlier driver work is in neither, so its 90 minutes is an estimate.

1. Console. Plugged the micro-B cable in; the Mac showed no serial port. Installing the CP210x driver, approving it in System Settings and replugging gave four ports; working out which of the four is the Linux console took more time (the user guide's order did not match the Mac's naming). About 90 minutes in the first sitting, observed 2026-10-09 and not saved; part of it was this repo's own search for the right port.
2. First power-on. Every port silent, a reset changed nothing. Inferred: the card from the box was blank. It was not read before writing, and the chip's boot ROM prints nothing when it finds no image. One kit; whether every kit ships this way is unknown.
3. Writing the card with no reader. Downloaded the image to a second Mac (4 min), pulled the four bootloader files out of it and cut the image into 256 MiB compressed pieces (12 min together), loaded U-Boot (the bootloader that runs before Linux) into the chip over the serial port (UART boot, set by the SW1 switches), tried U-Boot's mode that shows the card to the Mac as a USB disk (it crashed), then put the pieces on a USB stick and wrote the card from U-Boot (5.4 min of writing). 62 minutes of work from the first console check to the Linux login, 11 of them hands-on and 51 waiting, over 81 minutes on the wall clock with the idle gaps (the stopwatch counts a 3-minute question to the person at the bench as waiting; the timeline marks it idle, which would make it 59).
4. First boot: 27.7 s from the first bootloader byte to the login prompt, including the root file system growing to the card.
5. First inference: TI's pose model through ONNX Runtime with the TIDL delegate, from the zoo on the card, about 40 minutes after the login prompt (observed, not saved), most of it reading the zoo's layout and the runtime's Python interface over the serial cable.

**How far it got.** Measured. The first inference ran; the question is the clock.

| Stage | Clock | What took the time |
|---|---|---|
| Box to a working console | about 90 min (not saved) | the macOS driver and finding the right port among four |
| Console check to Linux login | 62 min of work (11 hands-on, 51 waiting; 81 min on the wall) | the card from the box did not boot; no card reader; the serial write path |
| First bootloader byte to login prompt, written card | 27.7 s first boot, 24.2 s after (3.8 s more from a typed `reboot`) | the board itself |
| Login to first model inference | about 40 min (not saved) | learning the zoo and the runtime over a 115,200 baud console |
| Sealed box to first inference | about 3 h 10 min of working time (two of the three parts are estimates) | |

With a card reader, the same path would be the download (4 min), the write (roughly 10 minutes at this image size, an estimate, not measured) and the 24 s boot; the first inference would then be the time it takes to type the runtime example, which is minutes. TI's hour may be reachable on a Linux PC with a reader and a display; that path was not timed. At this bench it was not reached.

**The line.** The stop was tools, not the board. Two gaps in the public path cost the hour:

1. The micro-SD card in the box did not boot, and no document read says the included card needs the image written to it. **Tool or docs.** The user guide says a card is included; the getting-started guide says to write the image but not that the included card needs it. The boot ROM's silence looks exactly like a dead board.
2. The serial console needs a driver on macOS that TI's documents do not mention (CP2108, four ports), and the port order in the user guide does not match what the Mac shows. **Tool or docs.** Some of those 90 minutes were this repo's own search for the right port among the four, which a logger on all four ports would have cut short. **Setup or handling.**

Neither is a hardware fault. Once past them the board was fast: a 24 s boot (to a login prompt with no display; TI's under 20 s is to a wallpaper on a display, a different end point that was not timed), every zoo model running on the accelerator in one evening, hardware video decode at about 450 frames a second on a 263-frame clip with start-up inside the time (about 500 steady, see the zero-copy experiment).

**Ask.** Did your SK-TDA4VM ship with a written card? How long did your first boot take from a sealed box, and on which computer?

# Can the SK-TDA4VM be a Holoscan Sensor Bridge: camera in, Hololink frames out over 1000BASE-T?

Terms used here are in [docs/vocab.md](../vocab.md). Code: [tda4/hsb/](../../tda4/hsb/), upstream source in [third-party/holoscan-sensor-bridge/](../../third-party/holoscan-sensor-bridge/).

**Question.** A builder wants a camera into a TI processor and the frames sent to an NVIDIA Holoscan host over 1 Gbit Ethernet in the form Holoscan already receives, the Holoscan Sensor Bridge protocol ("Hololink"). Can the TDA4VM do the device side, on the Arm cores or on an R5F, and what does it cost?

**Vendor position.** NVIDIA, Holoscan Sensor Bridge documentation (read 2026-10-10): the device enumerates with BOOTP broadcasts once a second (device UDP port 12267, reply port 12268) carrying an "NVDA" vendor field; the host configures it through the Ethernet Control Bus, 14-byte register read and write requests on UDP 8192; frames go out as RoCE v2 RDMA WRITE packets (opcode 0x2A) ending in a WRITE WITH IMMEDIATE (0x2B) that carries 128 bytes of frame metadata. For hosts without a ConnectX NIC, "standard Linux sockets can be used to transmit and receive Ethernet frames that follow the RoCE packet structure ... enabling ... integration with custom FPGA or sensor platforms that generate RoCE-formatted packets." The repository ships an "HSB Emulator", "a minimally featured emulation of the HSB framework's IP for use in testing and development within a hosted or embedded environment", with Linux and STM32F767 (Cortex-M7) targets.

TI: no position. Nothing in TI's documentation mentions Holoscan or Hololink.

**What was tried.** Board: SK-TDA4VM, TI Edge AI SDK 11.00.00.08 (Linux 6.12, gcc 13.3, CMake 3.28, zlib, Python 3.12), no display, everything over the serial console; Ethernet to the home switch came later the same day.

1. Read NVIDIA's protocol documents and host source (`data_channel.cpp`, `enumerator.cpp`, `hololink.cpp`) and the emulator source (`src/hololink/emulation`).
2. Took the emulator's Linux target as is (`third-party/holoscan-sensor-bridge/`, commit 4b192ae). Its CMake enables CUDA unconditionally, but the only CUDA call is a device-to-host copy for GPU-resident buffers, so it was built with a plain Makefile and a 9-line stub header for that call (`tda4/hsb/Makefile`, `stub/cuda_runtime.h`). One build fix: NVIDIA's include order puts the platform headers first; this repo's headers had to match.
3. Wrote `serve_frames.cpp` (70 lines, after NVIDIA's `serve_linux_file.cpp`): one `HSBEmulator`, one RoCE v2 data plane, frames from a raw file at a set rate.
4. Wrote `hsb_host_check.py`, a host-side verifier that does what NVIDIA's host library does: listen for the BOOTP broadcast and decode the vendor field, configure the data plane over ECB with the same register writes as `DataChannel::configure_roce` (packet size in 128-byte pages, frame length, host MAC, IP and port, QP, R_Key, buffer address, page increment, buffer count, sensor enable mask), then receive on the configured port, reassemble by RETH virtual address, and check PSN order, bytes written, frame numbers and each frame's CRC-32 against the source file.
5. Ran both on the board over a dummy network interface (192.0.2.2 device, 192.0.2.1 host, broadcast address set), since the bench had no cable.
6. With a cable in, ran the same sender on `eth0` and the checker on a Mac on the same switch, at 720p 10 and 30 fps and 1080p 30 fps, with `perf stat` on the sender.

**How far it got.** Measured. Build 27 s. Enumeration, control plane and data plane all worked at the first try once the interface had a broadcast address.

| Step | Result |
|---|---|
| Enumeration | BOOTP request seen 0.55 to 0.91 s after the checker started: 300 bytes, vendor tag 0xE0, "NVDA", Ethernet port 0, enumeration version 2, UUID and serial present, HSB IP version 0x2602 |
| Control plane | 18 ECB transactions (one read of the version register, 15 writes, two read-modify-writes of the enable mask), every reply status 0 |
| Data plane, 1280x720 RAW8 (921.6 kB) at 10 fps | 200 of 200 frames intact against the source CRCs, 655 packets per frame (921.6 kB in 1.4 kB payloads), 0 PSN gaps, 75.5 Mbit/s |
| Data plane, 1920x1080 RAW8 (2.07 MB) | 3 of 3 frames intact, 1,473 packets per frame |
| Metadata packet | opcode 0x2B, immediate = page and PSN, bytes written 921.6 kB, frame number counting up, QP and R_Key as configured. Fields arrive in network byte order (the FPGA document says little-endian; the emulator uses `htonl`) |
| MTU 9000 | 3 of 3 frames intact at 235 packets per frame; the sender held 60 fps and its cost per frame fell 3.8 times |
| Receiver limit | At 30 fps the Python checker (78 percent of a core) overran the default socket buffer and dropped 11 percent of packets, so frames assembled corrupt; raising `net.core.rmem_max` and running at 10 fps fixed it. The kernel's receive-buffer-error counter stopped climbing. This is the checker's limit, not the device's; NVIDIA's receiver is C++ |

Device-side cost, `serve_frames` process alone, `perf stat` task-clock over 10 s after a host configured it (the first pass used `/proc` tick accounting, which undercounts this sender 1.9 times because it wakes on the timer tick; those rows stay in the CSV marked as such):

| Stream | Nominal rate | MTU | A72 cost | Per packet | RSS |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1920x1080 RAW8, 60 fps asked, about 42 fps reached | 995 Mbit/s asked | 1500 (1,473 packets per frame) | 98 percent of one core, saturated | 15.8 µs, 31.7 thousand cycles, 24.6 thousand instructions per packet; 23.3 ms of A72 per frame | 11 MB |
| 1920x1080 RAW8, 60 fps held | 995 Mbit/s | 9000 (235 packets per frame) | 37 percent of one core | 26.4 µs per packet; 6.2 ms of A72 per frame, 3.8 times cheaper per frame | 11 MB |
| other rates (tick-accounted, scaled by 1.9) | | 1500 | about 31 percent at 720p30, 62 at 720p60, 70 at 1080p30 | | |

How the rates were read: the sender prints a line every 300 frames. In the first perf run its lines 17.2 s and 24.3 s after start, inside the perf window, are 300 frames apart, about 42 fps at MTU 1500; in a rerun at MTU 9000 the lines at 8.0 s and 13.0 s are 300 frames apart, 60 fps; a repeat run reproduced both readings within 1 percent. An earlier version of this page divided by the 60 fps asked for and gave 11.1 µs per packet and 2.65 times; the sender never reached 60 at MTU 1500. The cost is per packet, flat across rates: the payload copy, the RoCE headers, a software CRC-32 over the packet and one `sendto`. Jumbo frames are the first lever; the Holoscan host guide already sets MTU 4200 for RoCE.

Caveat: on loopback the kernel also receives every packet, so system-wide load was higher (about half of both cores at 1080p60, most of it softirq).

**On the wire (2026-10-10, later).** With the board on the home network at 1000 Mb/s and the checker on a Mac on the same switch (macOS caps its socket buffer at 8 MB, so the checker ran with 7 MB), MTU 1500 on the whole path:

| Stream | Frames intact | Rate the receiver saw | Sender cost, perf over 8 s | Per packet |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1280x720 RAW8, 10 fps | 100 of 100 | 10.1 fps, 76.0 Mbit/s | not measured | |
| 1280x720 RAW8, 30 fps | 300 of 300 | 30.1 fps, 226.7 Mbit/s | 21.9 percent of one A72 | 11.1 µs, 22.2 thousand cycles |
| 1920x1080 RAW8, 30 fps | 5 (the checker lost packets: 68,404 sequence gaps) | about 21.5 frames a second of data, 357 Mbit/s | 37.4 percent of one A72 | about 11.8 µs at that rate |

So on a real link the sender costs about 11 µs per packet, and the 15.8 µs loopback figure above carries extra work (suspected: loopback delivers each packet to the receiver inside the sender's send call). Why the 1080p stream ran below 30 fps over the wire without saturating a core is unknown (suspected: the checker's lost packets, the switch or the send buffer). Jumbo frames could not be tried on this path: the home switch and the Mac run MTU 1500.

**The line.** No line reached on the device side: the protocol works over a real 1 GbE link at 720p30 with the repo's checker. The stop is this: NVIDIA's `LinuxReceiverOperator` on a Linux host taking the stream. That needs a Linux PC with the `hololink` Python package (no GPU is needed for the receive path); the cable is now on the bench.

R5F: not run. NVIDIA's emulator has a Cortex-M7 target with lwIP, so the code is MCU-shaped; a TDA4VM R5F port means TI's RTOS SDK with lwIP on the CPSW and a camera-to-R5F buffer path. Written up as phase two in the study.

- Jumbo frames (the host guide uses MTU 4200 for RoCE): about 4 percent less overhead and a third as many packets.
- `SEPARATE_FRAMEMETADATA_PACKET=1` and the CoE (IEEE 1722) data plane, which NVIDIA added for hosts without RDMA.
- A C++ receiver on the board for a higher-rate loopback check.
- PTP: the metadata carries timestamps; the emulator fills them from the system clock.

**Ask.** A reader with a Holoscan host: run NVIDIA's `linux_imx274_player.py`-style receiver against this board's stream and report fps and drops. And report the camera format, since 1 GbE caps at about 1080p RAW10 at 30 fps.

<!-- experiment
id: E171
board: SK-TDA4VM
date: 2026-10-10
status: line found
reached: verified
line: The TDA4VM's SA2UL crypto block is in the Edge AI kernel and the kernel prefers it (cbc-aes-sa2ul at priority 30,000), but no shipped tool reaches its AES from user space: openssl's afalg engine fails because CONFIG_CRYPTO_USER_API_SKCIPHER is off, and the cryptodev module the image carries has no openssl engine built for it. Driven through /dev/crypto by a 48-line program of this repo, the block does AES-128-CBC at 185 MB/s on 16 kB blocks for 16 percent of one core and 886 MB/s on 64 kB blocks with the core fully busy; the A72's own crypto instructions do 1,490 MB/s. # Does the SK-TDA4VM's SA2UL crypto block beat the Cortex-A72's crypto instructions for bulk AES and SHA on TI's Edge AI Linux?

Terms used here are in [docs/vocab.md](../vocab.md) (SA2UL, AF_ALG and /dev/crypto, ioctl, crypto driver priority, IPsec and dm-crypt) and the board's [FAQ](../../tda4/FAQ.md). Board page: [tda4/README.md](../../tda4/README.md). Numbers: `openssl_speed_mbps` rows in `data/results/tda4.csv`. kB = 1,024 bytes; MB/s = 1,000,000 bytes a second.

**Short answer.** No. On the SK-TDA4VM `openssl speed -engine afalg` fails with `socket bind failed` because the kernel has no user-space cipher interface, and driven through `/dev/crypto` by this repo's own program the SA2UL does AES-128-CBC at 185 MB/s on 16 kB blocks against 1,490 MB/s for the A72's own instructions. It loses on speed at every block size that could be compared (the CPU rate is measured only up to 16 kB) and, through that path, saves no A72 time per byte for AES either (0.86 against 0.67 ms per MB at 16 kB).

**Question.** The TDA4VM has a hardware crypto engine (the SA2UL: AES, SHA, a random number generator) and two Cortex-A72 cores with Arm's crypto instructions. For bulk encryption and hashing from a Linux program, which one is faster, and does the hardware block at least free the CPU?

**Vendor position.** TI, TDA4VM data sheet (read 2026-10-10): the security accelerator "SA2UL" supports AES, 3DES, SHA-1, SHA-2 and HMAC. TI, Processor SDK Linux documentation for J721E, "Hardware crypto accelerator" (read 2026-10-10, written for the non-Edge-AI SDK): the SA2UL driver registers with the kernel's crypto API, and the page shows `openssl speed` numbers obtained through the `cryptodev` module. TI, Edge AI SDK 11.00.00.08 documentation: no mention of the crypto block. TI's documentation for its AM62x chips (a smaller Linux family with the same kind of crypto block), as read for this repo's notes on 2026-10-09 and not re-read today, shows the CPU ahead of the hardware block for bulk AES on that chip (figures not re-read here), which is where the expectation came from: "no for bulk, yes in CPU load".

**What was tried.** Board: SK-TDA4VM (J721EXSKG01EVM), TI Edge AI SDK 11.00.00.08, Linux 6.12.17-ti, openssl 3.2.4, no network, everything over the serial console, 2026-10-10.

1. `openssl speed -engine afalg -evp aes-128-cbc` (2026-10-09): the engine loads and then prints `ALG_PERR: /usr/src/debug/openssl/3.2.4/engines/e_afalg.c(463): Failed to bind socket : No such file or directory`.
2. Why. `/proc/crypto` lists `cbc-aes-sa2ul`, `ecb-aes-sa2ul`, `sha256-sa2ul`, `hmac(sha256-sa2ul)` and two `authenc` combinations, all self-tests passed, AES at priority 30,000 (the CPU's `cbc-aes-ce` is 300). `/proc/config.gz`: `CONFIG_CRYPTO_USER_API_HASH=m`, `CRYPTO_USER_API_SKCIPHER` and `_AEAD` not set, `DM_CRYPT` not set, `CRYPTO_DEV_SA2UL=m`. So user space can open an AF_ALG socket for a hash or the RNG, not for a cipher. The image also loads the out-of-tree `cryptodev` module (`/dev/crypto`, driver 1.14) with its header in `/usr/include/crypto/cryptodev.h`, but this openssl has no `devcrypto` engine (`openssl engine -t` lists only the dynamic loader) and no `cryptsetup` or `kcapi` tools are installed.
3. This repo's own path. `sa2ul_bench.c`: AES-128-CBC through `/dev/crypto` (`CIOCGSESSION`, then one `CIOCCRYPT` per block; `CIOCGSESSINFO` confirmed the kernel chose `cbc-aes-sa2ul`) and SHA-256 through an AF_ALG hash socket; 8 MiB of data at 16 B and 1 kB blocks, 256 MiB at 16 kB and above; pinned to one A72; the process's own CPU time from `getrusage`. `openssl speed` on the same core, in the same run, for the CPU columns (969 MB/s for SHA-256 here; the night before it read 967).

**How far it got.** Measured, on the hardware block and on the CPU.

| Block size | SA2UL AES-128-CBC via /dev/crypto | CPU share while doing it | CPU AES-128-CBC (openssl) | SA2UL SHA-256 via AF_ALG | CPU share | CPU SHA-256 (openssl) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 16 B | 0.8 MB/s | 47% | 314 MB/s | 0.8 MB/s | 48% | 31 MB/s |
| 1 kB | 42 MB/s | 38% | 1,394 MB/s | 41 MB/s | 39% | 673 MB/s |
| 16 kB | 185 MB/s | 16% | 1,490 MB/s | 165 MB/s | 14% | 969 MB/s |
| 64 kB | 886 MB/s | 100% | (16 kB is openssl's largest) | 837 MB/s | 100% | |
| 1 MB | 820 MB/s | 99% | | 808 MB/s | 99% | |

CPU share is the calling process's user plus system time over the run's wall time, on one core. The CPU columns are by definition one core fully busy.

**The line.** Two lines, one in software and one in the hardware's reach.

Software: the stop for a normal user is `CONFIG_CRYPTO_USER_API_SKCIPHER` being off in the Edge AI kernel, with no openssl engine for the `cryptodev` module the image loads anyway. **Tool or docs.** Nothing shipped on the image lets an application use the hardware AES; a program has to talk to `/dev/crypto` itself.

Hardware: the block loses to the A72's crypto instructions on throughput at every block size, by 8 times at 16 kB and still by 1.7 to 1.8 times at 64 kB and 1 MB against the CPU's 16 kB rate (openssl reports no larger block). The CPU-load argument does not hold either through this path: at 16 kB the block delivers 185 MB/s for 16 percent of a core, which is 0.86 ms of A72 time per megabyte, while the CPU encrypting the data itself spends 0.67 ms per megabyte at 1,490 MB/s. At 64 kB and above the calling core is fully busy. **Unknown (suspected: the `ioctl` copying each block into the kernel and back, plus waiting for the result; the two were not separated).** SHA-256 tells the same story on speed: 165 against 969 MB/s at 16 kB. On CPU time per byte SHA-256 is mixed: at 16 kB the block costs 0.85 ms of A72 time per MB against 1.03 for the CPU, its one cell where it saves CPU, at a sixth of the speed; at 1 kB it costs 9.4 against 1.5.

Untested, so only a guess: the block may win for kernel-side users (IPsec, dm-crypt, the kernel's own TLS) that hand it pages without a copy, for keys the CPU should never see, or when the A72 cores are busy with something else and can wait on an interrupt. None of those is on this image.

**Ask.** If you have the SA2UL running under IPsec or dm-crypt on a J721E, what throughput and CPU load did you see, and on which SDK?

FILE: docs/experiments/2026-10-10-tda4-zero-copy-decode.md | Can the SK-TDA4VM's hardware video decoder feed the C7x with no Cortex-A72 copy of the pixels, and what does the zero-copy path save?
==============================================================================

<!-- experiment
id: E172

reached: verified
line: Yes. # Can the SK-TDA4VM's hardware video decoder feed the C7x with no Cortex-A72 copy of the pixels, and what does the zero-copy path save?

Terms used here are in [docs/vocab.md](../vocab.md) (GStreamer, NV12, zero copy, DMABUF, TIOVX, VPAC, C7x, fakesink and fpsdisplaysink, maxrss) and the board's [FAQ](../../tda4/FAQ.md). Board page: [tda4/README.md](../../tda4/README.md). Numbers: `gst_pipeline_fps` rows in `data/results/tda4.csv`. MB = 1,000,000 bytes; MiB = 1,048,576 bytes.

**Short answer.** Yes. On the SK-TDA4VM, TI's two zero-copy settings (`capture-io-mode=5` on the decoder, `tiovxmemalloc` after it) took a decode-to-detection pipeline from 56.2 to 110.8 frames a second and cut the Cortex-A72's share from 65 to 33 percent of one core. If your pipeline into TIDL runs well below the model's rate with one core nearly full, check for those two settings first.

**Question.** In a vision pipeline the decoded frames are the big data: a 1280x768 frame in NV12 is 1.47 MB, and at 100 frames a second that is 147 MB/s. If the Cortex-A72 has to copy each frame from the decoder's buffer into the accelerator's, that copy costs CPU time and caps the rate. TI's pipelines set two things that are meant to avoid the copy. Do they, and by how much?

**Vendor position.** TI, Edge AI SDK 11.00.00.08 documentation, "Data flows" and the GStreamer plugin pages (read 2026-10-09): the decode-to-inference pipelines use `v4l2h264dec capture-io-mode=5 ! tiovxmemalloc`, where mode 5 is DMABUF import and `tiovxmemalloc` allocates the shared buffers the TIOVX plugins (`tiovxmultiscaler`, `tiovxdlpreproc`, `tidlinferer`) pass between the hardware blocks. TI's `edgeai-gst-apps` prints exactly this chain when run with `-v`; the pipeline below is that print with a measuring sink in place of the display.

Expectation before the run: "Yes with `v4l2h264dec capture-io-mode=5 ! tiovxmemalloc`; TI's dataflows use exactly this", with the A72 load as the result.

**What was tried.** Board: SK-TDA4VM (J721EXSKG01EVM), TI Edge AI SDK 11.00.00.08, Linux 6.12.17-ti, no display, no network, 2026-10-10. Input: 20 copies of TI's `video0_1280_768.h264` (300 frames each) concatenated, so the pipeline runs past one clip. Model: `ONR-OD-8200-yolox-nano-lite-mmdet-coco-416x416` from the zoo on the C7x (4.66 ms per inference measured alone).

Three pipelines through `gst-launch-1.0`, 20 s each, `fpsdisplaysink` over `fakesink sync=false` so nothing paces the frames:

1. Zero copy: `filesrc ! h264parse ! v4l2h264dec capture-io-mode=5 ! tiovxmemalloc pool-size=12 ! video/x-raw,format=NV12 ! tiovxmultiscaler ! video/x-raw,width=416,height=416 ! tiovxdlpreproc model=M out-pool-size=4 ! application/x-tensor-tiovx ! tidlinferer target=1 model=M ! fpsdisplaysink ...`
2. Plain: the same with `v4l2h264dec ! video/x-raw,format=NV12` (no `capture-io-mode`, no `tiovxmemalloc`).
3. Decode only: pipeline 1 without the scaler, preprocessor and model.

CPU time from `/usr/bin/time` on the process and from `/proc/stat` for the whole system. A thermal guard waited until the hottest zone read 80 C or less before each run (the log line printed a moment later reads up to 80.5 C) and would have stopped a run at 90 C (the board reset at 92.6 C during an earlier heavy run; see the FAQ entry on heat); it never fired.

**How far it got.** Measured; every pipeline ran. Two runs of each gave the same CPU time to 1 percent.

| Pipeline | Frames a second | Process CPU, one core | Whole system, two cores | Peak memory (`maxrss`) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Zero copy (mode 5, tiovxmemalloc) | 110.8 | 33% (6.6 s in 20 s; 3.4 user, 3.2 system) | 19% | 364 MiB |
| Plain (no shared buffers; by TI's description the A72 copies each frame, not profiled here) | 56.2 | 65% (13.1 s in 20 s; 11.8 user, 1.4 system) | 35% | 355 MiB |
| Decode only, zero copy | about 490 by wall clock (6,000 frames in 12.3 s including start-up; `fpsdisplaysink` averaged 499.6) | 50% (1.2 user, 5.0 system) | | 109 MiB |

**The line.** No line: the zero-copy path works as TI's data flows say. The numbers say what it is worth: half the A72 time per second at twice the frames, so about a quarter of the A72 time per frame (3.0 ms against 11.7 ms). Per frame the plain path spends 11.7 ms of A72 time and the zero-copy path 3.0 ms; the 8.7 ms difference is the most the copy can cost; copying a 1.47 MB frame in 8.7 ms would be a rate of about 170 MB/s, so this is a ceiling on the copy's cost and not a measured copy speed, because the two pipelines also differ in other plugin work. That copy was the largest extra cost measured; why it caps the rate at 56 fps when the core was only 65 percent busy is **Unknown (suspected: one thread doing the copy out of buffer memory the CPU cannot cache; not profiled).** The decoder alone does about 490 frames a second and the model about 215.

The zero-copy pipeline itself is not at either hardware limit (110.8 fps against 215 for the model). Its remaining 33 percent of a core split as 3.2 s of system time and 3.4 s of user time in 20 s; suspected, not profiled: buffer handoffs between the decoder, the scaler and the DSP, and the plugins' own work. TI's data-flow documentation says the scaler and preprocessor run on the VPAC hardware, not the A72; that was not checked here.

**Ask.** If you run a camera or a file into TIDL on a TDA4 and your frame rate is lower than the model's, check for a missing `capture-io-mode=5` or `tiovxmemalloc` first; report what you found.

FILE: docs/experiments/2026-10-10-thermostat-mcu-only.md | Can an MCU-only thermostat work: a LaunchPad with an LVGL touch screen, a radar sending presence, and a Wi-Fi radio feeding Home Assistant?

<!-- experiment

# Can an MCU-only thermostat work: a LaunchPad with an LVGL touch screen, a radar sending presence, and a Wi-Fi radio feeding Home Assistant?

**Short answer.** The screen half works on the LP-MSPM0G3519 with live radar data: a radar frame reaches the panel 111 ms later (median, 2,310 frames in 10 minutes, none dropped), in 248 kB of flash and 28 kB of RAM. The path is radar, then a Mac script that sends the radar its configuration and forwards frames, then the G3519 over USB. The wired radar, the radio leg and the Home Assistant leg from the real radio have not run: the radio firmware needs the home network name put in at build time and replaces the Matter image on the CC35X1.

**Two-page screen and an overnight run.** The screen now has two pages. The thermostat page shows the held presence badge, a "Motion now" chip from the radar's point-cloud TLV 301, the temperature and the setpoint. A Sensors page shows the radar's held presence, motion, nearest distance, point count, SNR, zone, frames per second and the Wi-Fi model's class, probability and age, with 30 s history strips. The LVGL heap is 28 kB; 12 kB crashed with two screens. At 81 percent CPU on the Sensors page the screen's serial ring buffer began dropping bytes (ring drops rising), a limit to fix in the firmware. A feeder (`thermostat-system/tools/feeder.py`) forwards radar frames and the Wi-Fi logger's `W,` lines to the board. It has to run detached from the shell (`nohup ... & disown`): a feeder started as a background process of a command exits when that command's pipes close. A 12-frame hold (`PresenceDetect-hold12.cfg`, about 3 s) ran overnight with the test room empty, logging every frame to a per-day file; its false-alarm result is on the [radar antenna page](2026-10-10-radar-antenna-eval.md).

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). 1 kB = 1,024 bytes. Wire format: [PROTOCOL.md](../../thermostat-system/PROTOCOL.md).

**Question.** Can three TI boards, each doing one job, make a thermostat: radar presence in, a touch screen with a setpoint, Wi-Fi out to Home Assistant, with no Linux board?

**Vendor position.** TI's radar data sheet calls this "Topology 1": the radar does the signal processing and sends only the result to a host. This is from the IWRL6432 data sheet, read 2026-10-09. For the host link, TI's E2E answer on the IWRL6432BOOST says "You can directly access the UART rx and tx from J8.5 and J8.7 ... S1.4 must be in ON position for UART to be routed to the LP/BP connector". That is E2E thread 1497790, read 2026-10-10. TI publishes no thermostat reference with a radar, Matter or video; the newest is from 2020.

**What was tried.**

- Radar to G3519: the radar's shipped demo sends 384-byte frames at 115,200 baud, about 4 a second. The G3519 parses them with the same C parser as the AM13E230 page ([radar parser page](2026-10-09-am13e230-radar-host-parser.md); code in `am13e230/radar-parser/`). Presence is any set zone bit in TLV 315.
- Screen: LVGL 9.6 on the G3519, Waveshare 3.5 inch panel as wired for the earlier display tests. A thermostat screen: presence badge, temperature (a fixed 20.8 C, no sensor read), setpoint 15.0 to 30.0 C in 0.5 steps with plus and minus buttons, radar frame counter, live stats. Source `thermostat-system/g3519/`, build `thermostat-system/g3519/build.sh` (TI Arm Clang 5.1.1, -Oz, 80 MHz, 40 MHz SPI), flashed with DSLite on probe <probe serial>; TI's demo is restored at the end.
- Test source, because the radar was busy: `thermostat-system/tools/replay.py` sends frames of the 60 second shipped-demo capture (a UART capture of TI's shipped demo) into the G3519's USB serial port at 4 frames a second. Frame numbers are renumbered from 1 and the zone-bit byte of TLV 315 is rewritten to flip presence every 8 frames, because nobody stood in front of the radar when the capture was made. Everything else in each frame is the radar's.
- Radio: TI's `mqtt_client` with a UART0 line reader and the thermostat topics (`thermostat-system/cc35x1/`), built for the CC35X1. Broker and Home Assistant bridge: `thermostat-system/tools/hub.py` (a small MQTT broker that posts each update to Home Assistant by REST; Home Assistant has no MQTT integration).
- Wiring (4 wires, pictures `docs/arrivals/img/thermostat-*-wires.png`): radar J8 pin 5 to G3519 J1 pin 3 (PA9); radar J8 pin 2 (GND) to G3519 J3 pin 22 (GND); G3519 J1 pin 4 (PA8) to CC35X1 P1 pin 3 (P28); CC35X1 P1 pin 22 (GND) to radar J8 pin 4 (GND). Pins read from the radar schematic SWRR180 sheet 15 (DCA_LP_RS232_TX on J8 pin 5, RX on pin 7) and checked against the E2E answer above. Radar S1.4 ON, then a reset.

**How far it got.**

| Step | Result |
|---|---|
| Configure, compile, link | Yes. 242.4 kB of flash and 27.3 kB of RAM (bss; the 6 kB stack is extra) |
| Flash, boot, run | Yes, DSLite "Program verification successful", the board prints one STAT line a second |
| Replay, 240 frames | 239 of 240 SHOWN lines matched (frame 1 is the sync frame); no ring-buffer drops |
| Frame write to frame on the panel | median 89.7 ms, max 98.9 ms (33 ms of that is the 384 bytes on a 115,200 baud wire); on the board, last byte to end of redraw: median 51.3 ms, max 60.4 ms |
| Screen refreshes | 8 a second (7 to 10), 25 percent CPU, two refreshes per radar frame |
| Radar bytes in | 1.5 kB a second (4 frames of 384 B), 12.3 kbit/s of the 115.2 kbit/s wire |
| Checked by eye | Yes: the + and - taps change the setpoint |
| Broker to Home Assistant (a fake publisher standing in for the CC35X1) | Home Assistant took the three states in 33 to 106 ms per update, median 37 ms (10 updates). Entities `binary_sensor.fxl_therm_presence`, `sensor.fxl_therm_setpoint`, `sensor.fxl_therm_temp` exist now |
| CC35X1 firmware | builds (1.2 MB flash, 471.2 kB RAM, from `tiarmsize`); never flashed |
| Live radar through the Mac bridge, 600 s (Motion and Presence 2D, PresenceDetect.cfg) | 2310 frames at 3.85 a second, no gaps in the radar's frame numbers, 2310 shown, 0 ring drops. Frame arriving at the Mac to frame on the panel: median 110.8 ms, p95 153.2, max 255.1; on the board, last byte to end of redraw: median 51.6, max 122.1. Presence changed 7 times; each change reached the panel in 111 to 120 ms. Seen by a person: frame counter climbing, "Someone is here" held while a person sat in the zone |
| Two-page screen, firmware 97c3a0a2 | Thermostat page plus Sensors page (radar and Wi-Fi columns, 30 s strips) running on the G3519; LVGL heap 28 kB; ring drops rise at 81 percent CPU on the Sensors page |
| Fast-clear configuration (`minor2emptyThre` 6), seated person | Failed the expectation: the demo reported empty for 11 minutes 19 seconds while a person sat still at the bench, and re-armed only when they walked in. See the finding below |
| 12-frame hold (`minor2emptyThre` 12), room empty overnight | Ran overnight; result on the [radar antenna page](2026-10-10-radar-antenna-eval.md); the walk-out clear time is not computed |
| Wired radar, radar to Home Assistant latency | not run |

**Fast-clear finding.** To make the badge clear faster than the shipped hold of about 5 s, the shipped configuration was changed to `minorStateCfg ... minor2emptyThre 6` (`PresenceDetect-fastclear.cfg`). With a person seated at the bench the demo then reported empty for 11 minutes and 19 seconds and showed presence again only when the person walked in. TI's page for the demo says a motion status is kept if at least one motion detection was recorded in the last `minor2emptyThre` frames. With a small count, a still person's small motions fall outside the window and the state machine does not re-detect until a larger motion, so the setting stops holding a seated person. **Tool or docs.** If you shorten the hold, test it with a seated person before putting it on a live screen. A value of 12 was used for the overnight run. A hold of 6 should not be used for a seated person.

**The line.** Not reached: the wire from the radar and the radio leg. Two things gate them. The first is four jumper wires and a switch change, which need the radar running TI's demo. The second is the CC35X1 image: the build needs the home network name and password put into the firmware, and the image replaces the Matter light that is paired in Apple Home; the pairing probably has to be redone.

**Why the wired path waits.** TI's prebuilt Motion and Presence 2D demo sends nothing after boot until its configuration (`PresenceDetect.cfg`, 27 lines, about 7 s) is sent over the CLI, and the CLI is the same UART. The flash pass measured this on 2026-10-10; the radar has no command to save the configuration. With S1.4 ON the Mac cannot send it, so the radar's own wire needs a host that sends the cfg after each boot. The earlier shipped image streamed without it, but it was overwritten by the first flash and cannot be read back. The live numbers above therefore come from the Mac bridge (`thermostat-system/tools/bridge.py`: the Mac sends the cfg, reads the radar's USB port and forwards each frame to the G3519).

**One-wire fix, not built.** Wire a spare G3519 UART TX to J8 pin 7 (the radar's RX), bake the 27 cfg lines into the screen firmware, and send them after the radar's banner at every start. Then the radar's J8 pin 5 to the G3519 carries the frames as in the wiring picture, and the Mac is not needed.

**Open points about this page's own numbers.**

- The 89.7 ms replay figure includes the Mac's write time, so it is a bench figure for "radar frame to panel", not the radar's own latency. The real radar adds its frame time (about 250 ms between frames, unmeasured here).
- One STAT line in 71 had a SHOWN line spliced into it: a line printed from inside a refresh event. Unexplained; no frame was lost.
- A single replay run and a single live run, not three.
- The live run cannot give the radar's detect or clear delay: the entry and exit were not timed, so those rows are not measured.
- The radar capture has no person in it; presence in the replay is rewritten, so this page says nothing about detection.

**Ask.** Whether the demo as shipped streams on J8 pin 5 with S1.4 ON and a reset alone, or needs rebuilt radar firmware. The measured behavior above (silent until the configuration is sent) says the configuration step is needed.

**Restyle (2026-10-11).** The screen is redrawn in the Fox Red Labs palette (Paper background, Ink text, Fox Red only for the presence badge and logo, Ink-outline buttons), with the horizontal logo in the header (A8 image, 120x59, `g3519/src/frl_logo.c`) and Barlow 14/20/48/64 fonts generated by `tools/make_assets.py`. Same pages, buttons, SHOWN and STAT lines. Size: flash 249.4 kB before, 191.8 kB after (Montserrat 48 was 634 kB of source; text+data from `tiarmsize`), RAM (bss) 27.7 kB before and after, 33.7 kB with the stack raised to 12 kB. It needs `LV_DRAW_SW_SLIM 0` and `LV_USE_IMAGE 1` (the slim patch removes the image decoder; drawing an image with it crashes). A host render of both pages checked the layout, and the board then ran with the radar live at 6 to 8 screen refreshes a second with no drops. If the board prints its start-up banner and then no STAT lines, the LVGL heap is too small: the two-page screen peaks at 14.9 kB, and a 12 kB heap hard-faults in `lv_draw_fill_dsc_init`. Build with `MEM_KB=28` (now the default in `build.sh`; flash 191.7 kB, bss 43.7 kB).

FILE: docs/experiments/2026-10-11-am263p-four-cores-mixed-os.md | Can the LP-AM263P run four cores at once, with different operating systems, including Zephyr?
==============================================================================

<!-- experiment
id: E179
board: LP-AM263P
date: 2026-10-11
status: works
reached: verified
line: All four Cortex-R5F cores of the LP-AM263P ran CoreMark at once at 1,462 to 1,464 per second each (5,854 together), within 0.1% of each core alone.
