# Can the LP-AM263P run four cores at once, with different operating systems, including Zephyr?

**Short answer.** Yes, from a Mac, loaded over the USB cable. On the LP-AM263P (AM263P4 chip, four Cortex-R5F cores at 400 MHz):

| What | Result |
|---|---|
| CoreMark on all four cores at once | 1,462.1, 1,464.1, 1,463.7 and 1,464.1 per second, 5,854 together; each within 0.1% of its score alone |
| Message round trip between cores (TI's IPC) | 3.49 µs FreeRTOS to one bare-metal core, 3.81 µs each to three at once; ThreadX 3.36 and 3.87 µs |
| Zephyr | Zephyr 4.4.2 boots and prints on core 0 with out-of-tree board files from this repo; upstream Zephyr has no AM263P support |
| Two operating systems at once | TI's FreeRTOS on core 0 printed a line and a counter that Zephyr on core 1 kept writing into shared memory (the counter is bumped after a fixed busy loop, about 36 times a second: proof Zephyr is running, not a timer and not Zephyr's IPC) |

The Zephyr port is a first step: it has no system timer (so no `k_sleep`), no pin-control driver and runs only on cores 0 and 1. The rest of the page says what each test is and what it took.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md) (DSLite, development boot, GEL, IPC, ThreadX, out-of-tree, lockstep). Bare metal means no operating system: one loop and interrupt handlers. VIM is the R5F's interrupt controller and RTI is the AM263P's timer block. The four cores are named by cluster and position: core 0 = R5FSS0-0, core 1 = R5FSS0-1, core 2 = R5FSS1-0, core 3 = R5FSS1-1. Code, logs and the Zephyr files: `am263p/bench/multicore/`, `am263p/zephyr/`, `am263p/data/logs/multicore/`, `am263p/data/logs/zephyr/`. Problems and fixes: [LP-AM263P FAQ](../../am263p/FAQ.md). Rows: `data/results/am263p.csv`, tests `coremark` (variants `ti-port-o3-ocsram-*`), `ipc_roundtrip_us` and `zephyr_support`.

**Question.** The AM263P is sold on having four real-time cores that can run separately or in pairs. Do four cores really give four times the work, how fast can they talk, and can each one run a different operating system, including Zephyr?

**Vendor position.** TI's MCU+ SDK 26.01 (read 2026-10-11):

- The IPC Notify page: "low latency IPC between different core's ... extremely fast transfer of message values". It gives no number.
- The SDK ships multicore examples with FreeRTOS or ThreadX on R5FSS0-0 and no RTOS on the other three cores (`examples/drivers/ipc/ipc_notify_echo`, `system_freertos_nortos`, `system_threadx_nortos`).
- The Zephyr 4.4.2 tree on the Mac used here has board support for the R5F cores of TI's AM64x and AM243x parts (`boards/ti/am243x_evm`, contributed by TI) and no AM263P board or SoC.

**What was tried.** LP-AM263P Rev A, MCU+ SDK 26.01.00.08, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1, SysConfig 1.28, Zephyr 4.4.2 with Zephyr's own GCC 12.2 toolchain, Intel Mac. Every image is loaded into RAM over the debug probe with DSLite, one core at a time with a small Python script that loads each core's image and reads its serial output. No switch was moved.

1. **Message round trips.** TI's `ipc_notify_echo`, unchanged except a timer on core 0: core 0 sends a number to each remote core, each sends it back, 1,000,000 times per core. Core 0's FreeRTOS clock could not be used: the echo interrupts starve its timer tick, and in a first run it read 664 µs for an exchange the remote cores' own clocks timed at about 3.9 s (that first log was overwritten by a rerun). In the saved logs the last-started remote core's own clock reads 3.81 to 3.89 s for the exchange; the cores loaded earlier read longer because their clocks were already running while the others loaded. The timer is the CPU's cycle counter, which needs no interrupt.
2. **CoreMark on every core.** TI's CoreMark example inside the same four-core project. All chosen cores wait at a common start line (`IpcNotify_syncAll`), then run. Each core's code and data sit in its own 256 kB of on-chip RAM. Each core writes its score into a shared table, and core 0 prints the table. This repo's copy of TI's `core_main.c` has three changes, each marked with a comment: 1) its driver open calls are removed, because the wrapper opens the drivers once; 2) its driver close calls are removed, because core 0's console must stay open; 3) it calls `frl_cm_export()` to hand its result to the table.
3. **Zephyr.** An out-of-tree SoC (`am263p/zephyr/soc/ti/am26x`) and board (`lp_am263p`) for upstream Zephyr 4.4.2. They reuse Zephyr's existing drivers for TI's interrupt controller (VIM) and for the UART, with the AM263P's addresses from TI's SDK headers. A small start-up hook sets UART0's clock and pins to the values TI's SDK uses.
4. **Two operating systems at once.** TI's FreeRTOS on core 0 and Zephyr on core 1, sharing only memory.

**How far it got.** Everything ran and was checked. TI's IPC example reported "All tests have passed" in every run. Every CoreMark run had CoreMark's correct checksums. Each CoreMark and IPC configuration was loaded three times. The Zephyr results with the current build are one load each: its boot banner in the standalone load, its banner after a TI program with the start-up script, and Zephyr's line and counter printed by core 0 in the mixed load. An earlier start-up-script load printed nothing from Zephyr; that build did not set the UART clock (the clock setting in `soc.c` came later).

**CoreMark per core** (per second, median of 3 loads; core 0 runs FreeRTOS, the others bare metal):

| Core | Alone | All four at once | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| R5FSS0-0 | 1,463.4 | 1,462.1 | -0.09% |
| R5FSS0-1 | 1,464.1 | 1,464.1 | 0.00% |
| R5FSS1-0 | 1,463.7 | 1,463.7 | 0.00% |
| R5FSS1-1 | 1,463.5 | 1,464.1 | +0.04% (inside run-to-run spread) |
| Sum | | 5,854.0 | 4.00 times one core, on CoreMark |

**Message round trip** (1,000,000 per remote core, median of 3):

| Core 0 runs | One remote core | Three remote cores at once |
|---|---|---|
| FreeRTOS | 3.49 µs | 3.81 µs each |
| ThreadX | 3.36 µs | 3.87 µs each |

**The line.** Nothing stopped, but two results have limits to state.

- CoreMark is the easy case for four cores: its code and data are small (suspected: they stay in each core's own caches, so the cores barely touch shared memory; not measured). A program that streams data through the shared on-chip RAM or the flash would contend more; none was tested.
- The Zephyr port boots and runs code, but without a timer driver nothing that sleeps or times out works. The AM263P's timers (RTI) have no Zephyr driver.

Three things cost time and are worth knowing:

- **Tool or docs:** after a reset of the board, loads to the third core (R5FSS1-0; the fourth was not checked) failed with "Does not match the target endianness". The image was fine. Each core needs its start-up script (GEL) run once; then the loads work.
- **Unknown:** loaded with their start-up scripts, core 2's (R5FSS1-0) console lines never reached core 0's console in these runs, even though it ran (its echoes and results arrived); core 3's lines did. Results pass through shared memory, not the console.
- **Unknown:** Zephyr loaded straight after a TI program, with the connection file that skips the start-up script, printed nothing, and markers it writes at each start-up stage stayed at zero (read over the probe; those reads were not saved): suspected: some state TI's program left behind stops Zephyr's start-up assembly. Which state it is was not found. Loaded on its own, or after a TI program with the start-up script, it boots and prints its banner.

- A control loop on one core while the other three run CoreMark: done since, on the same page (no change to the cycle); a neighbour that streams memory is still open.
- Lockstep, where two cores run the same code as a safety check: done since, on [lockstep and a loaded neighbour](2026-10-11-am263p-lockstep-and-loaded-loop.md) (reached from the debugger; TI's lockstep connection file did not get there in these tries).
- A Zephyr timer driver for the AM263P's RTI timers, then Zephyr's IPC with TI's mailbox hardware instead of raw shared memory.
- Zephyr on cores 2 and 3, and Zephyr on all four.

**To repeat this.** You need CCStudio 21 (DSLite), MCU+ SDK 26.01, Python with pyserial, and your probe's serial. Load the images one core at a time over the probe, core 0 last or first as noted, and read the serial output.

1. CoreMark on all four cores: build TI's CoreMark example for each core with the SDK makefile. Expect four lines like `FRL_CMR core 2 score 1463.7 errors 0`, then `FRL_CM_ALL mask 0xf got 0xf`.
2. TI's `ipc_notify_echo` example with FreeRTOS (or ThreadX) on core 0 and no RTOS on cores 1 to 3: build the system project with the SDK makefile and load all four cores. Expect `FRL_IPC ... remote_cores 3 ns_per_round_trip_per_core 3809`, then `All tests have passed!!`.
3. Zephyr on core 1 beside FreeRTOS on core 0: build a Zephyr app for the R5FSS0-1 core with a board, SoC and devicetree root of your own (the steps are in the [LP-AM263P FAQ](../../am263p/FAQ.md), "Does Zephyr run on the LP-AM263P?"), and a FreeRTOS image for core 0 that releases core 1. Expect core 1 to print "Zephyr 4.4.2 on R5FSS0-1" with a rising counter.

The loader needs a connection file for your probe, `AM263Px_ZCZ_C_<serial>.ccxml`, and a copy without the GEL script, `AM263Px_nogel_<serial>.ccxml`.

**Ask.** If you have Zephyr's timer or IPC running on an AM26x part, compare notes in an issue.

==============================================================================
FILE: docs/experiments/2026-10-11-am263p-lockstep-and-loaded-loop.md | Does lockstep, or a busy neighbour core, slow the LP-AM263P's control loop?
==============================================================================

<!-- experiment
id: E140
board: LP-AM263P
date: 2026-10-11
status: works
reached: verified
line: The LP-AM263P's R5F cores ran in lockstep from the debugger (the lockstep status bit set on both clusters, both checker cores refused a debug connection), at the same speed as split mode except 3 cycles on one build: TI's CoreMark 1,464.52 per second against 1,464.53, the repo's current loop 1.236 µs with the TMU in both. A current loop on core 0 kept the same timing to the cycle (mean 493.5 cycles, worst 844) while the other three cores ran CoreMark or copied memory in their own on-chip RAM. When they copied in the RAM right next to core 0's, its mean stayed the same but its worst pass, the first one with cold caches, rose from 2.11 µs to 2.51 to 2.70 µs. With the loop's handler, data and stacks in the core's own TCM, its worst pass was 1.26 µs alone and beside the same copies.
stop: none
-->
# Does lockstep, or a busy neighbour core, slow the LP-AM263P's control loop?

**Short answer.** Lockstep: no. A busy neighbour: not on average, but it can raise the worst case, and putting the loop in TCM, the core's own tightly coupled memory, removed that in this test. On the LP-AM263P (AM263P4 chip, four Cortex-R5F cores at 400 MHz), lockstep pairs two cores to run one program in step, so a hardware fault in either shows up as a mismatch. Split mode is the usual setup, where each core runs its own program. The TMU is the chip's built-in sine and cosine hardware.

| What | Split mode or alone | Changed setup | Difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| TI's CoreMark example, per second | 1,464.53 | 1,464.52 in lockstep | none |
| Current loop with the TMU, trigger to new PWM value (1,000 interrupts) | 1.235 µs | 1.236 µs in lockstep | none |
| Same, TI's software math library | 1.454 µs | 1.455 µs in lockstep | none |
| Same, C library sine and cosine | 2.060 µs | 2.068 µs in lockstep | 3 cycles (0.4%) |
| Current loop with the TMU on core 0 (200,000 interrupts) | 1.234 µs, worst 2.11 µs | 1.234 µs, worst 2.11 µs, with CoreMark on cores 1 to 3 | none, to the cycle |
| Current loop with the TMU on core 0, cores 1 to 3 copying memory in their own RAM | 1.234 µs, worst 2.11 µs | 1.234 µs, worst 2.11 µs, with the copies at 179 MB/s (library memcpy) or 779 MB/s (the repo's word loop) together | none, to the cycle |
| Current loop with the TMU on core 0, cores 1 to 3 copying in the RAM next to core 0's (899 MB/s together) | 1.234 µs, worst 2.11 µs | 1.234 µs, worst 2.51 to 2.70 µs | mean none; worst pass up to 28% longer |
| Current loop with the TMU on core 0, hot path in TCM, the same copies beside it | 1.194 µs, worst 1.26 µs | 1.194 µs, worst 1.26 µs | no change from the copies; 3.2% faster than the on-chip RAM build |

Lockstep costs half the cores, not speed. Busy neighbours left the loop's average alone in every test; only copies into the RAM beside core 0's block moved anything, and only the first pass, which runs with cold caches. In TCM the first pass is no longer slower than the rest: the worst case was 1.26 µs against 2.11 µs for the on-chip RAM build alone, and the spread (worst minus best) 0.09 to 0.10 µs against 0.905 µs, with or without the neighbours.

Core names, as TI writes them:

- Cluster 0: core 0 = R5FSS0-0, core 1 = R5FSS0-1. Cluster 1: core 2 = R5FSS1-0, core 3 = R5FSS1-1.
- In lockstep, core 1 checks core 0 and core 3 checks core 2.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md) (lockstep, split mode, TMU, TCM, GEL, DSLite, development boot). 1 kB = 1,024 bytes. Problems and fixes: [LP-AM263P FAQ](../../am263p/FAQ.md) ("Lockstep", "Using all four cores"). Code: `am263p/tools/lockstep.js`, `am263p/tools/lockstep_run.py`, `am263p/bench/ctrl/ctrl.c`. Logs: `am263p/data/logs/lockstep/` and `am263p/data/logs/e139/`. Every number is also a row in `data/results/am263p.csv`.

**Question.** The AM263P can pair its R5F cores in lockstep for functional safety. What does that cost a control loop? And in split mode, does a loop on one core slow down when the other three are busy?

**Vendor position.** TI's MCU+ SDK 26.01 documentation (read 2026-10-11):

- Bootloader page: "The SBL runs on R5 core in Lock Step Mode." and "The SBL will switch to Dual core or continue in lock step mode depending on whether App Image loaded by SBL contains the R5 Core 1 image or not."
- CCM page: "The R5F sub-system, when bootstrapped to lockstep mode, has a logic that compares the outputs of the two cores and asserts an interrupt whenever an error is detected."
- Smart placement page: "TCM-A 0x0 32KB (in split) or 64KB (in lockstep)", the same for TCM-B.

None of these gives a speed for lockstep, or says how to reach it from a debugger.

**What was tried.** LP-AM263P Rev A, MCU+ SDK 26.01.00.08, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1, CCStudio 21 (DSLite and its scripting), Intel Mac. Every program is loaded into RAM over the debug probe; no switch was moved and no flash was written.

1. **Lockstep.** TI's lockstep connection file printed "Lockstep Reset" but left both clusters in split mode (its own check said "Dual-Core"). Reading TI's GEL scripts showed why. The chip comes out of reset in lockstep: the lockstep field in MSS_CTRL `R5SS0_CONTROL` resets to 0x7. TI's usual connection file switches both clusters to split mode on every connect, and the lockstep file never writes that field back. So `am263p/tools/lockstep.js` connects without a GEL script, issues the debugger's System Reset, and runs TI's own GEL steps for unlocking, clocks and memory, leaving out the split-mode switch. Then it loads the program on core 0 and runs it. Each run reads the lockstep status bit (0x100 in `R5SS0_STATUS_REG` and `R5SS1_STATUS_REG`) before and after, and tries a debug connection to core 1.
2. **The same programs in lockstep and split mode.** TI's CoreMark example, and this repo's current loop from the [three-chip comparison](2026-10-11-current-loop-three-mcus.md): EPWM0 at 50 kHz starts an ADC conversion, the ADC interrupt runs one field-oriented-control step from the C2000's `foc.c` and writes the new PWM value. Three runs each, 1,000 interrupts per run, in the TMU, SDK and C-library variants.
3. **A busy neighbour.** The TMU loop for 200,000 interrupts (4 s) on core 0. Cores 1 to 3 ran one of four loads through the whole window: TI's CoreMark (60k iterations, about 41 s), each in its own 256 kB of on-chip RAM; a 64 kB block copied back and forth between two buffers in its own RAM for 40 s with the C library's `memcpy`; the same with the repo's own 8-byte word loop, about 4 times faster; and the word loop with one buffer moved into the 256 kB just below core 0's block (0x70000000 plus 64 kB per core, `-DFRL_MEMNEAR`; SysConfig's generated linker file names 0x70000000 to 0x7003FFFF `SBL`, the bootloader's area, and nothing in this repo's programs is placed there). 64 kB is meant to be larger than the R5F's data cache, so the copies keep going out to the on-chip RAM (the cache size was not checked; the SDK pages read here do not give it). Each copy run checks that the two buffers match at the end (`-DFRL_MEMSTRESS` in `am263p/bench/multicore/coremark4/cm4.c`). Core 0 is loaded first, because its connect clears on-chip RAM and would stop the others. Its program waits 20 s before starting, and the other three are loaded during the wait. Three runs loaded and three runs with core 0 alone, same image.

**How far it got.** Everything ran and was checked.

- Lockstep: bit 8 (0x100, lockstep) was set in both clusters' status registers after the reset, after setup and after every run: R5SS0 read 0x100, then 0x101 after setup (bit 0 is not explained in the pages read, and which setup step sets it was not found); R5SS1 read 0x100 throughout. Core 1 refused a debug connection in every run (DSLite error -1170, "Unable to access the DAP"). That was expected of a checker core; TI's pages do not say it. Cluster 1's checker, core 3, refused the same way in a later check. CoreMark printed its correct checksum for TI's 15k-iteration build (crcfinal 0x65c5) in all three runs: 1,464.508, 1,464.524 and 1,464.531 per second.
- Neighbour: cores 1 to 3 were loaded 4, 8 and 12 s after core 0, during its 20 s wait, so CoreMark had started before the loop began. When the loop finished, each CoreMark core's progress marker in shared memory read 3, "CoreMark running" (read over the probe). All three then finished with the correct checksum for the 60k-iteration build, crcfinal 0xbd59.

**Current loop, lockstep against split** (µs, median of 3 runs of 1,000 interrupts; split figures are the [three-chip comparison's](2026-10-11-current-loop-three-mcus.md)):

| Sine and cosine from | Trigger to handler, split | Lockstep | Trigger to new PWM value, split | Lockstep | Worst of the three runs, split | Lockstep |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| TMU | 0.632 | 0.632 | 1.235 | 1.236 | 2.14 | 2.14 |
| TI's software math library | 0.636 | 0.637 | 1.454 | 1.455 | 2.35 | 2.35 |
| C library | 0.654 | 0.662 | 2.060 | 2.068 | 2.74 to 2.80 | 2.69 to 2.81 |

With the TMU and the software math library, the worst pass in every run is the first interrupt after the load, with cold caches (the same cycle count every run). With the C library it is a later pass (the first takes 2.51 µs, the worst 2.69 to 2.81 µs), in both modes. The C-library variant is about 3 cycles slower in lockstep (median of the run means 827.3 cycles against 824.0, and every lockstep run above every split run); the other two match to within a cycle. The cause was not found.

**Current loop beside three CoreMark cores** (TMU, 200,000 interrupts, cycles at 400 MHz, every run):

| | Trigger to handler, mean | Trigger to new PWM value: best | mean | worst |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Core 0 alone (cores 1 to 3 run nothing from this repo) | 255.0 to 255.2 | 482 | 493.5 | 844 |
| Cores 1 to 3 running CoreMark | 255.1 to 255.2 | 482 | 493.5 | 844 |

With either copy in the cores' own RAM the loop read exactly the same, in all three runs each: mean 493.5, best 482, worst 844 cycles.

**Copies next to core 0's RAM.** Three runs against the three alone:

| | Trigger to handler, mean | worst | Trigger to new PWM value: best | mean | worst (the first pass) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Core 0 alone | 255.0 to 255.2 | 318 | 482 | 493.5 | 844 |
| Cores 1 to 3 copying next to core 0's RAM | 255.0 to 255.2 | 344 to 376 | 482 | 493.4 to 493.5 | 1,004 to 1,080 |

The mean did not change, so the other passes did not either on average; the program records only the worst pass, which was the first one each time. The first pass after the load fetches its code and data from the on-chip RAM, with cold caches; it was slower here, with three cores writing beside it. Suspected cause: the neighbours' traffic shares a path to the RAM with core 0's block; no TI description of how the on-chip RAM is split into banks was found. With it, the loop's spread from best to worst (jitter) went from 0.905 µs to 1.405 to 1.495 µs, and its worst pass from 10.5% of the 20 µs period to 13.1 to 13.5%.

**The loop in TCM.** TCM is memory wired to one core. Suspected: other cores' traffic does not reach it; whether other cores or DMA can address it was not checked. The loop was rebuilt with `-DFRL_TCM`: the ADC handler and `foc_step` in TCM-A beside TI's interrupt dispatcher, and the variables, the main stack and the interrupt stacks in TCM-B. The linker file is SysConfig's own with those groups moved; the rest of the program and its heap stay in on-chip RAM. The only on-chip RAM call left in the handler, a 64-bit divide for the timing, runs after both timestamps are taken. Three runs each, cycles:

| | Trigger to handler, mean | worst | Trigger to new PWM value: best | mean | worst |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| TCM, core 0 alone | 236.6 to 236.7 | 246 | 466 | 477.7 to 477.8 | 502 to 504 |
| TCM, cores 1 to 3 copying next to core 0's RAM | 236.6 to 237.0 | 246 | 466 | 477.8 | 502 to 506 |

The first pass now takes 494 cycles, no longer the worst. The loop is also 3.2% faster on average (477.7 against 493.5 cycles), and the copies beside it ran at −0.08% to +0.72% of their rates beside the on-chip RAM build, a little faster in two of three runs.

**Memory copy on cores 1 to 3** (MB/s per core = bytes copied, not read plus written, per second, with 1 MB = 1,000,000 bytes; median of 3 runs, which differ by under 0.3%):

| Copy | Core 1 | Core 2 | Core 3 | Together |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| C library `memcpy` (in this build `TI_memcpy_small`, a byte loop) | 59.2 | 58.6 | 61.4 | 179 |
| The repo's 8-byte word loop | 247.5 | 235.3 | 296.5 | 779 |
| The repo's 8-byte word loop, one buffer next to core 0's RAM | 327.2 | 262.2 | 309.1 | 899 |

The copy rates were the same with and without the loop on core 0, to within 0.3%. Why the cores copy at different rates, and why the copy next to core 0's RAM is faster than within their own, was not found. The reworked build that moves the buffer was checked against the old one: built for the cores' own RAM it copied at 247.7, 235.4 and 296.5 MB/s, within 0.1% of the old build.

Back to the CoreMark neighbour: CoreMark on cores 1 to 3 did not slow down either: 1,463.0, 1,460.2 and 1,461.4 per second beside the loop. The control for that is CoreMark only, no loop: the same images with core 0 running a silent loop gave the same scores to 0.01 (3 runs each). Both CoreMark sets are a little under the four-core page's figures for one core alone (1,463.4 to 1,464.1) because this build runs 60k iterations with no common start; compare only within one build.

**The line.** Nothing stopped. The limits:

- The worst case moved only for the first pass after a load. A loop that misses its cache often (more code than the cache, or data in shared memory) would feel the neighbours on every pass; not tested. TCM-A holds 31.9 kB in split mode, and the program's `.text` section alone is 31.9 kB (0x7FA0 bytes in the on-chip RAM build's map) before the start-up and interrupt code, so only the hot path moved. Streaming from the flash or by DMA was not run. A faster copy than the word loop would load the memory harder; not run.
- Lockstep was reached from the debugger in development boot, not through TI's bootloader. Only TI's CoreMark example (code in on-chip RAM) was run in lockstep; the CoreMark build with its code in TCM was not. The bootloader route (lockstep when the image has no core 1 program) was not run.
- TI's doubled TCM in lockstep, checked for TCM-A only: in lockstep a word written at 0xC000 (past 32 kB) read back separately from one at 0x4000; in split mode the debugger could not access 0xC000 at all. The same test on TCM-B (0x8C000) read back separately in both modes, so it does not show the TCM-B size; what sits at that address in split mode was not found.

Three things cost time and are worth knowing:

- **Tool or docs:** TI's lockstep connection file did not reach lockstep after split-mode connects had run. Suspected, from reading TI's GEL scripts: it never writes the lockstep field back. It also left both clusters' FORCE_WFI register at 0x7, and after that every load with TI's usual connection file reran the previous program instead of the new one, until a System Reset from the debugger. A probe reset did not clear it. The register reads are in `board-state-2026-10-11.md` (copied from the terminal). Check after any reset change: load two programs with different banners in turn.
- **Tool or docs:** each connect to core 0 with TI's usual connection file clears on-chip RAM, so programs already running on cores 1 to 3 stop. Load core 0 first.
- **Our mistake:** the first neighbour runs loaded core 0 last, so the loop ran alone; reading the other cores' progress markers during the run caught it before anything was written.

- A loop whose code or data does not fit the cache, beside neighbours copying next to its RAM; neighbours running from flash or a DMA stream.
- Two loops on two clusters at once (core 0 and core 2), each with its own PWM and ADC.
- Lockstep through TI's bootloader from flash, and a fault injected to see the compare logic fire.

**To repeat this.** You need CCStudio 21, MCU+ SDK 26.01, Python with pyserial and your probe's serial. The steps:

1. Lockstep: build TI's CoreMark example with the SDK makefile. Connect to core 0 without a GEL script, issue the debugger's System Reset, run TI's GEL steps for unlocking, clocks and memory, and leave out the split-mode switch. Load the program and read both clusters' status registers. Expect SS0 0x100 and SS1 0x100 after the reset, core 1 refusing a debug connection, and CoreMark 1,464.5 per second.
2. Loop alone: build TI's `adc_soc_epwm` example with `-DUSE_TMU` and 1,000 interrupts. Expect a minimum of 484 cycles.
3. Busy neighbour: load core 0 first with `-DUSE_TMU -DN_IRQ=200000 -DSTART_DELAY_S=20`, then CoreMark with 60k iterations on cores 1 to 3. Expect a minimum of 482, a mean of 493.5 and a maximum of 844 cycles.
4. Copy neighbour: the same with a copy loop (`-DFRL_MEMSTRESS=40`, with `-DFRL_WORDCOPY` for the word loop). Next to core 0's RAM, add `-DFRL_MEMNEAR`; expect a maximum of 1,004 to 1,080 instead of 844.
5. Loop in TCM: build with `-DFRL_TCM` and a linker file that moves the handler to TCM-A and the data and stacks to TCM-B. Expect a minimum of 466, a mean of 477.7 and a maximum of 502 to 506, alone or beside the copies.

Loading one core at a time over the probe: load core 0 first, because each connect to core 0 clears on-chip RAM.

**Ask.** If you have run the AM263P's lockstep compare logic with an injected fault, or measured a control loop beside a memory-heavy neighbour, compare results in an issue.

FILE: docs/experiments/2026-10-11-am263p-pru-rgb-scanout.md | Can the TI LP-AM263P's PRU generate a parallel RGB display bus from on-chip RAM, and how does that compare with SPI and the AM263x's GPMC bus?
==============================================================================

<!-- experiment
id: E184
board: LP-AM263P
date: 2026-10-11
status: works
reached: verified
line: The LP-AM263P's PRU generates a parallel RGB565 bus from a frame buffer in on-chip RAM with no CPU time: 800x480 at 45.6 frames a second and 480x480 at 76.3 at a 22.2 MHz pixel clock, each frame's pixel sum matched at the output register and two data bits counted at the pads. 28.6 MHz fails: the PRU's read widget delivers 48.9 MB/s. CPU copying in the frame buffer's RAM bank breaks 800x480. No panel was attached.
stop: none

# Can the TI LP-AM263P's PRU generate a parallel RGB display bus from on-chip RAM, and how does that compare with SPI and the AM263x's GPMC bus?

**Short answer.** Yes for the bus, not shown on a panel. The PRU-ICSS beside the four Cortex-R5F cores produced the full pixel stream and timing from RAM, checked by a pixel sum for every frame at its output register and by edge counts on two data pins; no panel was attached, and the clock, sync and enable pins were not routed to pads:

| Frame | Pixel clock | Frames a second | Frame sums matched (register level) | R5F time spent |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 800x480 RGB565 | 22.2 MHz | 45.6 | every frame after the first (the first frame after loading was wrong until a start-up drain was added) | none measurable (under 0.01 percent of an H.264 decode) |
| 480x480 RGB565 | 22.2 MHz | 76.3 | every frame after the first, as above | none measurable |
| 800x480 RGB565 | 28.6 MHz (TI's example clock), one run | 58.3 | wrong in every frame | not applicable |

The PRU reads on-chip RAM at 48.9 MB/s through its read widget (56.9 MB/s with blocking reads), which on that path needs 9 PRU cycles a pixel: 7 was run and failed, 8 is arithmetic (256 cycles a block against 262) and was not run. The frame buffer must sit in RAM banks the CPUs leave alone (480x480 fits one 512 kB bank; 800x480 spans two): an R5F copying at 209 MB/s in the same 512 kB bank corrupted every 800x480 frame. The same bus over the AM263P's SPI would manage 10.7 full 540x540 frames a second at the chip's 50 MHz limit (arithmetic). The GPMC parallel memory bus that could also drive a display exists on the AM263x; it is absent from the AM263P's SDK and data sheet (removal from the silicon is suspected, not confirmed), so it is compared from the AM263x data sheet only.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). The **PRU-ICSS** is TI's programmable real-time unit subsystem: two 200 MHz cores with single-cycle control of their own pins. **RGB565** is 16 bits a pixel. A **parallel RGB** panel takes a pixel clock, a data-enable line, horizontal and vertical sync and the pixel bits, and has no frame memory of its own, so it must be refreshed continuously. The **xfr2vbus read widget** is the PRU's DMA helper that fetches 64 bytes into its registers. **OCSRAM** is the AM263P's on-chip RAM, six banks of 512 kB (3 MB on the data sheet; 2 MB start in this repo's layout, see the board's FAQ). **eGPO** is a PRU's direct output pins. **ICSS_M** and **ICSS_G** are the two PRU subsystem versions (AM261, AM263, AM263P; AM243x, AM64x). **EDMA** is the SoC's DMA engine. An **8080 bus** is the parallel write-strobe interface of panels that keep their own frame memory, such as the ST7796S controller on the 3.5 inch touch panel used elsewhere in this project. The **scratchpad** is a set of shared register banks two PRUs can pass data through in one cycle. **GPMC** is TI's general-purpose memory controller, a 16-bit external bus. 1 kB = 1,024 bytes. Code: `am263p/bench/pru-display/`. Logs: `am263p/data/logs/pru-display/`. Rows: `data/results/am263p.csv`, tests `display_scanout_fps`, `pru_read_bw` and `display_scanout_cpu_cost`.

**Question.** If the SPI link to a screen is the limit on the AM263P, can the PRU act as a display controller, how much screen does it drive, what does it cost the CPU, and how does that compare with the GPMC bus on the AM263x?

**Vendor position.**

- TI's open-pru repository ships `examples/LCD_interface` (read 2026-10-11, commit e6cf59b): "PRU direct GPOs to output data from frame buffer memory to parallel RGB24 interface ... 800x480 pixel with 24 bit color and 60 Hz frame rate. PRU resources used are limited to 200 MHz clock and functions available across ICSS_M (AM261/AM263) and ICSS_G (AM243/AM64) devices. The demo is built with AM243x LP." It uses both PRU cores and a PWM block of the AM243x's ICSS_G for VSYNC; there is no AM263x or AM263P build.
- The AM263Px data sheet (SPRSP81D) lists "20-channel enhanced output (eGPO) per PRU". SysConfig's AM263Px device data (version 1.28.1) gives PRU1 pads for all 20 outputs and PRU0 pads for 16 (outputs 0 to 6 and 8 to 16).
- The AM263x data sheet (SPRSP74E) lists a "General-Purpose Memory Controller (GPMC) – 16-bit parallel data bus with 22-bit address bus", with a functional clock of up to 133 MHz in asynchronous mode. The AM263x SDK's GPMC driver "Currently enabled for Memory Type: PSRAM". In the AM263Px SDK 26.01 the GPMC clock code is commented out under `//FIXME REMOVE GPMC FOR AM263PX`, and there is no GPMC base address, pin or driver.

**What was tried.** LP-AM263P Rev A, MCU+ SDK 26.01.00.08, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1, TI's PRU compiler 2.3.3 (macOS installer, installed unattended in about a minute, 126 MB), TI open-pru e6cf59b for the AM263Px PRU linker file, Intel Mac. Everything was loaded into RAM over the debug probe; no flash was written and no switch was moved.

1. **A cycle-exact scan-out firmware for one PRU.** `gen_scan.py` writes PRU assembly in which every pixel clock is a fixed number of PRU cycles: clock low, pixel on the bus, a running sum of the pixel, clock high, and free slots for control work. Bits 0 to 15 carry the pixel, 16 the clock, 17 data-enable, 18 and 19 the syncs, so one PRU drives the whole bus (on the AM263P only PRU1 has pads for all 20). Pixels come from OCSRAM through the read widget, 64 bytes (32 pixels) at a time. Blanking clocks run in hardware loops. A Python check confirms every pixel and loop body is exactly one pixel clock long.
2. **Self-checks with no scope.** The firmware sums every pixel value it puts on the bus and compares each frame's sum with the sum the R5F computed from the buffer; it counts 64-byte blocks that are not ready two pixels before use; it counts frames. The R5F times frames against its own cycle counter. Two pixel bits are patterned (bit 15 set on even lines, bit 14 on line 0), their pads (PR0_PRU0_GPIO15 and GPIO14, the Ethernet PHY 2 transmit lines, which are inputs on the PHY) are switched to the PRU, and the R5F counts their rising edges through the GPIO input register.
3. **What the read path delivers.** `bw.asm` brings 4,096 blocks of 64 bytes into the PRU by each path and times them with the PRU's cycle counter.
4. **What it costs the CPU.** The same H.264 decode (320x240 baseline, 30 frames, two passes) before the PRU starts and while it scans out. Then the R5F copies memory for 5 s, first in other RAM banks, then in the frame buffer's own bank.
5. **Two widget behaviors that had to be found first**, with a small probe program: the widget's status byte reads 0x0B and 0x08 while a block arrives and 0x05 when it is complete, whatever the configuration; and a read before the block is complete returns a partly filled copy of the same block without moving on.

**How far it got.** Verified at the output register and two pads: frames, pixel sums and pad edges match the prediction to the frame, three runs each at 22.2 MHz (28.6 MHz: one run).

| Read path into the PRU, 64-byte blocks | PRU cycles a block | MB/s at 200 MHz |
|---|---|---|
| Read widget from OCSRAM (wait for ready, then read) | 262 | 48.9 |
| Blocking burst read (`lbbo`) from OCSRAM | 225 | 56.9 |
| Two 32-byte reads from OCSRAM | 237 | 54.0 |
| Read from the PRU's own data RAM or the shared RAM | 20 | 640 |

| Scan-out | Frames a second (predicted) | Sum matched | Late blocks | Pad edges a second, even-line bit and line-0 bit (predicted) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 800x480, 9 cycles, 22.2 MHz | 45.612 (45.612) | 276 of 276 | 0 | 10,950 and 45.5 (10,947 and 45.6) |
| 480x480, 9 cycles, 22.2 MHz | 76.312 (76.313) | 459 of 459 | 0 | 18,311 and 76.5 (18,315 and 76.3) |
| 800x480, 7 cycles, 28.6 MHz | 58.348 | 0 of 351 | 48 percent | not used |

| Load beside the scan-out | 800x480 | 480x480 |
|---|---|---|
| H.264 decode on core 0 (decoder in banks 0 and 1) | decode cycles changed by under 0.01 percent; 0 bad frames | the same |
| R5F copying at 275 MB/s in banks 0 and 1 | 0 late, 0 bad | 0 late, 0 bad |
| R5F copying at 209 MB/s in the frame buffer's bank | every frame bad, 51 percent of blocks late | every frame right, 30 percent of blocks flagged at the early check |

**The line.** 28.6 MHz is the line for one PRU on the read widget: at 7 cycles a pixel a 32-pixel block is used every 224 PRU cycles and arrives every 262. **Chip limit** on the read-widget path, as measured: one read in flight, about 1.3 µs (262 cycles) from request to the last byte. Blocking reads take 225 cycles but stall the PRU, so this firmware did not use them. The other line is RAM-bank sharing: the frame buffer needs RAM banks of its own (one 512 kB bank for 480x480, two for 800x480), or the CPU's traffic in that bank has to stay light. What this test does not show: a picture. No panel was attached, the clock, sync and data-enable pins were not on pads (bits 16 to 19 on PRU0 have one pad, the clock's, and it was not switched over), and the timing was not looked at with a scope. The frame sums prove the right pixels went to the output register on time; the pad counts prove two of the bits reach the pins.

**No TI example for this chip: how it was done, what went wrong, and how hard it was.** TI ships a PRU display example for the AM243x only, so this is the first PRU display scan-out on an AM263P known to this repo. What existed: TI's AM243x example (both PRUs, an AM243x-only PWM block for vertical sync, a different pin map), TI's AM261 PRU FFT (the only ICSS-M code found that uses the read widget), the AM263Px PRU linker file in open-pru, and the SDK's PRU register headers. What was done instead of porting the AM243x code: a Python script that writes cycle-exact firmware for one PRU, so any panel timing is one command, plus self-checks (frame sums, late-block counts, pad edge counts) so the result could be proven without a scope or a panel.

| What went wrong | Cause | Cost | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| Every 64-byte block counted as late | **Tool or docs**: the widget's status byte is read through register r18 and reads 0x05 when ready, whatever the configuration; no document says either | one wrong run | a ten-line probe program recorded the status as a block arrived |
| The picture came out shifted by 32 pixels | **Our mistake**: a drain after configuring the widget swallowed block 0 | one wrong run | stop and drain at the end of each frame, configure at the start |
| The first frame after loading was wrong | **Setup or handling**: the widget kept state from the previous program | one bad frame | drain once at start-up |
| 28.6 MHz could not work | **Chip limit**: one read in flight, 262 PRU cycles a block from OCSRAM | the clock dropped to 22.2 MHz | two PRUs or EDMA into PRU RAM would lift it (not run) |
| PRU0 has pads for 16 outputs, not 20 | **Tool or docs**: the data sheet says 20 per PRU; the device data in SysConfig shows 16 for PRU0 and 20 for PRU1 | design moved to PRU1 for a product, PRU0 for this test | put a 20-signal bus on PRU1 |
| A load test reported 12 GB/s | **Our mistake**: the compiler removed copies nothing read | one run | volatile copies with a printed result |
| The AM263P has no GPMC | **Tool or docs**: only an SDK code comment says it was removed (whether it is gone from the silicon is not confirmed) | the GPMC comparison is from the AM263x data sheet | none on this part |

| Effort | |
|---|---|
| Elapsed, compiler download to the first checked frame | about 35 minutes, with no hands needed |
| Board runs | 8 scan-out runs, 1 probe, 1 bandwidth run; RAM loads only, nothing written to flash |
| Hands needed at the bench | none |
| Tools added | TI's PRU compiler 2.3.3 (one unattended install, 126 MB) |

Verdict: the PRU did exactly what the arithmetic said, to the frame, once its read path was understood. The documentation side took the effort: the read widget is the only fast way for the PRU to read on-chip RAM, and its ready signal, its partial reads and its speed on this part had to be found by experiment. A builder new to PRU assembly was not timed; this run, with a probe-first approach and a generated firmware, took one sitting.

**Against SPI and GPMC.**

| Display path on these chips | What it is | Full-frame rate | CPU cost | Measured here |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SPI to a panel with frame memory (ST7796S class), AM263P | One data line at 50 MHz at most; the panel keeps the image | 540x540: 10.7 a second at 50 MHz, 3.2 at the 15 MHz the ST7796S panel used here is rated for | the CPU or DMA feeds every changed pixel | arithmetic from the data sheet clock; an LP-MSPM0G3519 measured 67.2 ms for 320x480 at 40 MHz |
| PRU parallel RGB, AM263P | 16 bits a pixel clock, continuous refresh from a frame buffer | 800x480 at 45.6, 480x480 at 76.3 | none measurable | yes, this page |
| PRU 8080 bus to a panel with frame memory, AM263P | The PRU strobes 16-bit writes; only changed areas are sent | set by the panel's write cycle | none | not built |
| GPMC 16-bit bus, AM263x only | A memory bus that can strobe an 8080-style panel, fed by DMA | set by the panel's write cycle; the bus allows a write every few cycles of a clock of up to 133 MHz | DMA, little CPU | not on the AM263P; AM263x not on this bench |

The PRU path is the fastest of the four reachable on the AM263P, and the only one that refreshes a panel without frame memory. Its price is RAM: 450 kB for 480x480 or 750 kB for 800x480 of the 2 MB that starts in this repo's layout, in banks of its own (one for 480x480, two for 800x480).

- A real panel on PRU1's pads. On the LaunchPad those pads go to Ethernet PHY 1 (receive lines are outputs on the PHY), so it needs a board that routes them; on a product board it is the plan.
- 28.6 MHz or more with both PRUs: one fetches with blocking reads into the scratchpad or shared RAM while the other drives the bus (TI's AM243x example splits the work across both cores).
- The SoC's EDMA copying lines into the PRU's shared RAM, so the PRU reads at 640 MB/s and the pixel clock is set by the panel.
- 540x540 (a common square 4 inch panel): the line is not a whole number of 32-pixel blocks, so it needs a 544-pixel stride; 540x540 at 60 Hz needs about 20.8 MHz, under the 22.2 measured.
- An 8080 bus from the PRU to the ST7796S panel used here, with the touch screen.

**To repeat this.** You need TI Arm Clang 5.1.1, the MCU+ SDK, the PRU compiler (`ti-cgt-pru` 2.3.3), pyserial and your probe's serial. Build the PRU scan-out program for the panel timing, link it into an R5F image with the SDK makefile, load it over the probe and read the serial output:

- 800x480 at 9 PRU cycles per pixel: the default timing.
- 480x480 at 9 cycles: horizontal total 560, vertical total 520, horizontal sync 20, horizontal back porch 40.

Expect `FRL_PRU idle ... fps_x1000=45612`, a sum equal to the expected sum, `badsum=0` and `late=0`.

Common problems and fixes are also in the [LP-AM263P FAQ](../../am263p/FAQ.md), section "PRU display".

**Ask.** Has anyone run TI's open-pru LCD example on an AM261x or AM263x, and what read bandwidth did the widget give there? Is the AM263P's GPMC gone from the silicon or only from the SDK?

FILE: docs/experiments/2026-10-11-cc1407p-cc1354p10-interop.md | Can TI's CC1407P and CC1354P10 talk to each other on every protocol they share?
==============================================================================

<!-- experiment

# Can TI's CC1407P and CC1354P10 talk to each other on every protocol they share?

**Short answer.** Packets went both ways on nine of the eleven protocol pairs tried, and seven of them were clean. The CC1407P, hosted by an LP-MSPM0G5187, and an LP-CC1354P10-1 exchanged packets on 2-GFSK 50 kbps and all eight Wi-SUN FSK modes; the CC1354P10 received 20 of 20 from the CC1407P in every one. The CC1407P received 20 of 20 in seven of them, and lost packets in modes 4a and 5 in both runs. Pings were answered 20 of 20 both ways in five protocols and partly in four, with round trips of 7 to 19 ms, timed on the MSPM0 host from handing over the ping to the answer arriving, so SPI time and the other radio's turnaround are included. TI's two long-range modes, the CC1407P's XLR and the CC1354P10's SimpleLink Long Range, did not exchange a packet. The same connection showed the CC1407P receiving for the first time, carrier sense answering correctly at low thresholds although the driver header calls it not functional, and a live range test in Home Assistant.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md#sub-1-ghz-radio-protocols-cc1407p). Code, tables and evidence: [mspm0g5187/radio](../../mspm0g5187/radio/README.md#two-radios-the-cc1407p-against-a-cc1354p10) and [cc1354p10/radio-rx](../../cc1354p10/radio-rx/README.md#as-a-test-partner-for-the-cc1407p). Checked on an Intel Mac, macOS 15.7.9, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS, MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07, F2 SDK 8.33.00.16 with SysConfig 1.28.0, radio firmware 3.0.0.25.

**Question.** The CC1407P is a stand-alone sub-1 GHz transceiver; the CC1354P10 is a wireless MCU with its own sub-1 GHz radio. Anyone mixing them needs to know which protocols carry across.

**Vendor position.** TI lists Wi-SUN FSK modes 1a to 5 for both. **Tag: Tool or docs.** TI does not say whether the two chips interoperate, and does not relate XLR to SimpleLink Long Range.

**What was tried.**

- Both boards run lab firmware. `radio_lab.c` on the G5187 and `partner.c` on the CC1354P10 take the same text commands: send, receive, ping, echo. `lab.py` on the Mac drives both and logs both serial ports.
- Eleven pairs, two runs. Nine protocols, plus XLR against two SimpleLink Long Range rates. Each pair gets 20 packets of 40 bytes each way, then 20 pings of 30 bytes each way. The ping is this repo's own `FRL PING` packet. The CC1354P10 used SysConfig's own setting for each protocol. Both radios reported every send as done.
- Ping turnaround changed between runs. In the first, a host command started the CC1407P's receive after each ping, and only the 50 kbps modes got answers. Suspected: the answer came first. In the second, the CC1407P's transmit chains to its receive on the radio itself.

**How far it got.** Verified on the boards, run 2. Run 1 agreed except where the ping method changed.

| Pair | CC1407P receives | CC1354P10 receives | Pings from CC1407P | Pings from CC1354P10 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2-GFSK 50 kbps | 20 of 20 | 20 of 20 | 20 of 20, 17.9 ms | 20 of 20 |
| Wi-SUN 1a, 1b, 3, 4b | 20 of 20 each | 20 of 20 each | 20 of 20 each, 8.1 to 19.2 ms | 20 of 20 each |
| Wi-SUN 2a, 2b | 20 of 20 each | 20 of 20 each | 9 and 17 of 20 | 20 of 20 each |
| Wi-SUN 4a | 16 of 20 | 20 of 20 | 4 of 20 | 14 of 20 |
| Wi-SUN 5 | 6 of 20 | 20 of 20 | 11 of 20 | 3 of 20 |
| XLR against SimpleLink Long Range 5 and 2.5 kbps (two pairs) | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |

Evidence: the DONE lines from both radios in both runs, and for run 2 each radio's send count and the packets the CC1354P10 printed. In run 2 the signal was about 5 dB lower from mode 2a on than in run 1.

**The line.** None for packets in the first three rows of the table. Three limits.

- **Modes 4a and 5, CC1354P10 to CC1407P.** **Tag: Unknown.** The CC1407P's sync counter (packets whose start it found) equals its CRC counter (packets that passed the checksum), so the missed packets are never detected. The CC1354P10's setting names give 200 kbps with 50 kHz deviation (4a) and 300 kbps with 75 kHz (5); they were not compared with the CC1407P's register values.
- **Pings at 2a, 2b, 4a and 5.** **Tag: Unknown.** Packets went 20 of 20 at 2a and 2b while pings from the CC1407P came back 9 and 17 of 20; pings from the CC1354P10 at mode 5 were 9 of 20 in run 1 and 3 in run 2.
- **XLR and SimpleLink Long Range.** **Tag: Unknown (suspected: settings mismatch).** The CC1407P decoded the header 7 and 16 times and passed no checksum; the CC1354P10 decoded nothing. They run at different rates (XLR 20 ksps with spreading 2; SimpleLink Long Range 5 and 2.5 kbps), and no TI document found pairs them.

**Ask.**

- **Open question:** which CC13xx settings interoperate with which CC1407P profiles?
- **For readers:** if you run modes 4a or 5 between these chips, report what you see.

==============================================================================

<!-- experiment

date: 2026-10-11

line: The same motor-control step (one current-loop pass, F28-style C code, sine and cosine on each chip's TMU) runs trigger-to-new-PWM in a mean 1.24 µs on the LP-AM263P (400 MHz Cortex-R5F), 1.33 µs on the LP-AM13E230 (200 MHz Cortex-M33) and 2.58 µs on the LAUNCHXL-F2800137 (120 MHz C28x). # How fast is the same current loop on the LP-AM263P (AM263P4), LP-AM13E230 and LAUNCHXL-F2800137?

**Short answer.** One pass of a field-oriented current loop, from the PWM event that starts the ADC to the new PWM compare value, with the same C code on each chip and the chip's trig unit (TMU) doing sine and cosine. Mean of 1,000 passes:

| LaunchPad | CPU | Trigger to handler (ADC conversion + interrupt entry) | Handler (FOC step + PWM write) | Trigger to new PWM value |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| LP-AM263P | Cortex-R5F, 400 MHz | 0.63 µs | 0.61 µs | **1.24 µs** |
| LP-AM13E230 | Cortex-M33, 200 MHz | 0.37 µs | 0.97 µs | **1.33 µs** |
| LAUNCHXL-F2800137 | C28x, 120 MHz | 0.56 µs | 2.03 µs | **2.58 µs** |

The AM263P runs the control code itself about 1.6 times faster than the AM13E230, and gets to the handler 0.27 µs later, so the totals are close. At 50 kHz the AM263P's loop takes about 6% of the 20 µs period on average and at most 10.7%.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). TMU = trigonometric math unit, hardware that computes sine and cosine. FOC = field-oriented control, the usual way to drive a brushless motor; one step reads currents, transforms them, runs two regulators and computes three PWM duty values. Problems and fixes: [LP-AM263P FAQ](../../am263p/FAQ.md). Rows: `data/results/<board>.csv`, tests `control_loop`, `isr_entry`, `control_loop_worst_pct`, `control_loop_jitter`. Code: TI's `adc_soc_epwm` example with the repo's control loop added, on each board.

**Question.** If a product spins a motor, how much of the control period does the current loop take on each of these chips, measured the same way?

**Vendor position.** TI's AM263Px MCU+ SDK 26.01 page for its TMU example (read 2026-10-11): "This example calls the mathlib operations for 500 different input values. Calls the math library operations with TMU mathlib APIs, SDK mathlib APIs and CLANG mathlib APIs. Compares the performance between these three versions". TI publishes per-function cycle counts like these; no published trigger-to-PWM time was found for a whole loop on these LaunchPad development kits.

**What was tried.** The same `foc.c` and `foc.h` on every chip, unchanged (one file, `foc.c` sha1 c69a210d, included by all three builds) (single-precision float; sine and cosine through each chip's TMU). On each LaunchPad: a PWM time base at 50 kHz whose period start triggers one ADC conversion of a pin with nothing driven; the ADC's end-of-conversion interrupt runs one FOC step and writes the PWM compare value. The PWM counter is read at the handler's first line and after the compare write, so both times are measured from the trigger. 1,000 passes per run. Intel Mac, macOS 15.7.9.

- LP-AM263P (2026-10-11): MCU+ SDK 26.01.00.08, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1, -Os (TI's example makefile), code in on-chip RAM; TI's `adc_soc_epwm` example with two SysConfig lines changed (EPWM0 period 3999, ADC trigger at counter zero); interrupt through TI's interrupt dispatcher; 3 runs per variant.
- LP-AM13E230 (2026-10-09): AM13E230x SDK 26.01.00.03, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1, -O2, code in flash with cache; 1 run.
- LAUNCHXL-F2800137 (earlier runs): TI's C2000 compiler and C2000Ware, code in flash; 1 run per row.

**How far it got.** Ran and checked on all three. On the AM263P: no PWM period missed in 3,000 passes per variant, and the PWM clock checked against the CPU clock (200 MHz, half a count per CPU cycle).

**AM263P with three ways to compute sine and cosine** (means; best and worst in cycles at 400 MHz; median of 3 runs):

| Sine and cosine from | Trigger to new PWM value | Best | Worst | Trigger to handler |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TMU | 1.24 µs | 484 | 856 | 0.63 µs |
| TI's software mathlib | 1.45 µs | 576 | 940 | 0.64 µs |
| C library | 2.06 µs | 738 | 1,094 | 0.65 µs |

With the TMU and the mathlib, the worst pass is the first one after the program loads (cold caches). With the C library the first pass takes 2.51 µs and the worst is a later pass (2.74 to 2.80 µs); which pass was not found.

**The line.** Nothing stopped. The comparison has limits:

- **Setup or handling:** code location differs: on-chip RAM on the AM263P (it has no internal flash), flash with cache on the AM13E230, flash on the F2800137 (2.32 µs with the step copied to RAM).
- **Setup or handling:** compiler settings differ (-Os on the AM263P, -O2 on the AM13E230), and so do the cores and how each TMU is reached. Clock speed is not the only variable.
- **Chip limit:** each chip's ADC converts at its own speed, and the conversion is inside the trigger-to-handler time; the conversion alone was not measured.
- **Setup or handling:** the AM263P's interrupt goes through TI's interrupt dispatcher. A handler wired to the core's fast interrupt (FIQ) would enter sooner: an earlier software-pended test measured 195 cycles through the dispatcher and 144 as FIQ (best of 200; worst 227 and 205).
- The AM263P figures are medians of 3 runs; the AM13E230 and F2800137 figures are single runs.

- The AM263P handler on FIQ, and the step in the core's tightly coupled memory.
- The AM263P's ADC early-interrupt option, as on the F2800137's `early` rows (0.39 µs to the handler there).
- The same loop on core 1 while the other three cores run CoreMark, to see whether shared memory traffic moves it.
- A real motor and power stage.

**Ask.** If you run current loops on any of these parts, post your trigger-to-PWM numbers and how you measured them.

FILE: docs/experiments/2026-10-11-esp32c6-ble-proxy-and-zigbee.md | Can one ESP32-C6 be a Bluetooth proxy and a Zigbee end device at once?
==============================================================================

<!-- experiment

# Can one ESP32-C6 be a Bluetooth proxy and a Zigbee end device at once?

**Short answer.** Not in ESPHome 2026.9.1 on this board. The combined image builds and boots, and the proxy half works, but the Zigbee end device never joined ZHA. Removing Bluetooth and keeping Wi-Fi did not help either. A version with the Bluetooth scan cut to a tenth of the time was tried only with an invalid permit, so its join is untested. The same Zigbee component with no Wi-Fi and no Bluetooth joined in 6 s. While the Zigbee half is only searching, the proxy hears about 10 percent fewer advertisements.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). 1 kB = 1,024 bytes. The ESP32-C6 has one 2.4 GHz radio front end that Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and 802.15.4 (Zigbee, Thread) share by taking turns.

**Question.** Does a Bluetooth proxy board also work as a Zigbee end device, and what does each cost the other?

**Vendor position.** ESP-IDF's coexistence table marks Bluetooth scanning with an 802.15.4 end device as supported with conditions, and with a router as not supported. ESPHome's Zigbee page says Wi-Fi in station mode with an end device works fine.

**What was tried.** ESPHome 2026.9.1, ESP-IDF 5.5.5, one board. All images use the house proxy's name and keys. The advertisement counter is `on_ble_advertise`, printed every 10 s with a phase label that alternates every 60 s. Zigbee "fast" reports a counter each second, and "idle" reports nothing.

| Image | Flash | Static RAM | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Proxy plus counter, no Zigbee (baseline) | 1.40 MB | 179 kB | 804 advertisements per 10 s over 16 windows, standard deviation 17 |
| Proxy plus Zigbee end device, scanning all the time | 1.59 MB | 194 kB | never joined; 727 per 10 s over 18 windows, sd 38, idle 726 and fast 727 |
| The same with a 30 ms scan window in 320 ms | 1.59 MB | 194 kB | join not tested, permit call refused, see below; 120 per 10 s; board reset about every 55 s |
| Wi-Fi plus Zigbee end device, no Bluetooth | 1.01 MB | 154 kB | never joined; board reset about every 12 s |
| Zigbee end device alone, the first Zigbee experiment | 492 kB | 83 kB | joined 5.8 s after boot |

Joining: ZHA was opened with `zha.permit` (250 s) at the start of each try. The combined image was flashed, without erasing, onto a board that had joined with the Zigbee-only image. It kept its network data and printed `The BDB Device Reboot failed with status(0x03), please retry` every 1.6 s for 60 s. The 30 ms window try and the first Wi-Fi-only try used a 300 s permit. Home Assistant rejects that, because the limit is 254 s, so they did not count. The Wi-Fi-only image was repeated with 250 s. The 30 ms image was not repeated, and the board is no longer reachable to repeat it. The device was removed from ZHA afterwards by IEEE address; the device list matched the list from before, and its entities were gone.

**How far it got.** Boot, Wi-Fi, API connection to Home Assistant and the proxy ran in the first image. Zigbee reached the network search and stopped there. No traffic could be compared with the Zigbee side joined. So "with and without Zigbee traffic" became "without the Zigbee stack, and with it searching". That gave 804 against 727 advertisements per 10 s, a drop of 9.6 percent. The fast and idle phases did not differ because nothing was joined to report.

**The line.** The end device's search for a network returns status 0x03, no network found, at every try with the proxy scanning all the time. The Bluetooth scan was ESPHome's default for a proxy: the window is raised to the interval, so the receiver is on all the time. With a 30 ms window, 9 percent, the join was not tested. In the full-scan case the only evidence of what the 802.15.4 receiver heard is the status code. The two images that reset, the 30 ms window and the Wi-Fi-only one, restart through a software reset a moment after a Wi-Fi disconnect. There is no panic text in the log, and the cause was not isolated. The Zigbee-only image had neither problem.

**Ask.** Has anyone run ESPHome's Zigbee end device together with Wi-Fi on an ESP32-C6 that joined? What did you change?

FILE: docs/experiments/2026-10-11-esp32c6-bthome-beacon.md | Does a vendor-free BTHome header work on the ESP32-C6 with less glue than on the TI CC2340R5?
==============================================================================

<!-- experiment
id: E40
board: ESP32-C6-DevKitC-1
date: 2026-10-11
status: works
reached: verified
line: The vendor-free BTHome header drops onto Espressif's NimBLE_Beacon example with 40 lines of glue against TI's 58. That is 35 in one new file and 5 changed elsewhere. The Mac decodes the packets as version 2, with temperature and counting packet ids.

# Does a vendor-free BTHome header work on the ESP32-C6 with less glue than on the TI CC2340R5?

**Short answer.** Yes. `ports/bthome/common/bthome.h` built into Espressif's `NimBLE_Beacon` example with no change to the header. The port is one new file of 35 code lines plus 5 changed lines in the example, 40 in all, against 58 for the TI port. The Mac's Bluetooth scanner decoded the packets as BTHome version 2, unencrypted, with a packet id that counts up and the chip temperature. Home Assistant was not used: the board is the house Bluetooth proxy, so the Mac scanner is the proof.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). 1 kB = 1,024 bytes. BTHome is the open advertising format that Home Assistant reads with no pairing (bthome.io).

**Question.** Espressif's NimBLE beacon already builds raw advertising data. Does the same header that went onto the TI board drop on with fewer lines of glue?

**Vendor position.** Espressif ships the example as `examples/bluetooth/ble_get_started/nimble/NimBLE_Beacon` in ESP-IDF v6.1: a non-connectable advertiser with a fixed name, appearance and URI. It has no sensor and no BTHome. Read on 2026-10-11.

**What was tried.** ESP-IDF v6.1 with newlib and GCC 15.2.0, one ESP32-C6-DevKitC-1-N8, the example copied to `ports/bthome/esp32c6/NimBLE_Beacon/`.

- New `main/src/app_bthome.c` has 47 lines, 35 of them code. It installs the chip temperature sensor and builds the payload through `bthome.h`: packet id, then temperature in hundredths of a degree. It hands the payload to `ble_gap_adv_set_fields` as 16-bit service data for UUID 0xFCD2 and repeats every 10 s from a timer. Advertising is non-connectable at a 1 s interval, name "FRL C6".
- `main/src/gap.c`: one declaration and one call to `bthome_start` in place of the stock `start_advertising()`. It adds 3 lines and removes 1.
- `main/CMakeLists.txt`: two components added to the requirements and one include directory for `common/`.

Lines are counted the way the TI port counts them: non-blank lines that are not comment-only (`grep -vcE '^\s*$|^\s*(//|/\*|\*)'`). Run it: build with `idf.py` (newlib) and flash with `idf.py flash`, then run `ports/bthome/host/bthome_scan.py 75 "FRL C6"` on the Mac.

**How far it got.** Verified, first build. Build 604 kB of application image and 89.8 kB of the 441.5 kB of static RAM. Flash took 4.2 s. The serial line printed `BTHome: 36.4 C, packet 0, set_fields 0` at boot and a new packet every 10 s. The Mac scanner, using bleak and CoreBluetooth, printed, for example:

```text
'FRL C6' rssi=-33 raw=40000302a80c {'version': 2, 'encrypted': False, 'trigger': False, 'packet_id': 3, 'temperature_c': 32.4}
'FRL C6' rssi=-34 raw=40000502440c {'version': 2, 'encrypted': False, 'trigger': False, 'packet_id': 5, 'temperature_c': 31.4}
```

The scanner showed ids 3, 4 and 5 and did not print ids 0 to 2, which the serial line says went out in the first 30 s. The scanner was started two seconds before the flash and printed nothing until id 3; the cause, in the Mac's scan start-up, was not isolated.

**The line.** No limit reached. Changing the advertising fields while the set is advertising is allowed in NimBLE, and `set_fields` returned 0 each time. The port needs no stop and restart. The TI port does, in `GapAdv_prepareLoadByHandle`. The die temperature reads 31 to 36 C against a room near 21 C: it is the chip's own sensor right after boot and was not checked against a thermometer, the same caveat as the TI board. Not in Home Assistant, and not encrypted.

**Ask.** None.

# What does a minimal ESPHome device cost on the ESP32-C6-DevKitC-1?

**Short answer.** The numbers are small: the image with Wi-Fi, the Home Assistant API, over-the-air (OTA) updates and the logger is 816 kB of flash and 138 kB of static RAM, and it boots with 305 kB of heap free. The two things that should have worked did not here. That image never found the home Wi-Fi network in four boots, and the version that did (with an idle Bluetooth scanner added) stalled in an OTA update after 0.1 percent, twice.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). 1 kB = 1,024 bytes. ESPHome is the tool that turns a YAML file into firmware for a Home Assistant sensor. The numbers below are the yardstick for an ESPHome port to a TI chip.

**Question.** How much flash, RAM and heap does the smallest useful ESPHome device take on the chip ESPHome was built for, and how long does a YAML edit take to reach the board?

**Vendor position.** ESPHome 2026.9.1 builds on ESP-IDF 5.5.5 for the ESP32-C6 and lists Wi-Fi, the API, OTA and logger as the base of every device. Source: esphome.io, read 2026-10-11. The estimate written before the run was about 1 MB of flash and over 200 kB of free heap.

**What was tried.** `esp32c6/proxy/frl-esphome-minimal.yaml` has Wi-Fi, API with encryption, OTA, logger and the debug heap sensor. It ran on ESPHome 2026.9.1 and ESP-IDF 5.5.5, on one ESP32-C6-DevKitC-1-N8 with 8 MB flash, erased and flashed over USB with esptool.

1. First compile took 287 s, including the one-off download of ESP-IDF at 2.6 GB on disk. A recompile after a one-line edit took 137 s and 147 s on the two images below, while other builds ran on the Mac.
2. Flash and boot: the write took 6 s. The boot log prints `Free Heap Size: 311944 bytes`.
3. Wi-Fi: the log said `No networks found` after every scan for 100 s, in four boots, two of them after a full erase. The same board and place joined the home network in under 10 s, at -52 dB, with the Bluetooth proxy image.
4. A second image, the same YAML plus an `esp32_ble_tracker:` line, an idle Bluetooth scanner, joined at once. Its file is `esp32c6/proxy/frl-esphome-minimal-tracker.yaml`. Its sizes: 1.34 MB of flash, 178 kB of static RAM, 210 kB of free heap at boot.
5. OTA: from that image `esphome upload` connected, finished the encrypted handshake, started the transfer, and the board logged `Progress: 0.1%` after 2.6 s and nothing after. Three attempts each time, 234 s and 299 s, ended in `Operation timed out` or `Connection reset by peer`. The board kept answering ping, with 0 to 33 percent loss and 5 to 500 ms round trips, but printed nothing until reset. The same happened with the Bluetooth proxy image.

**How far it got.** Compile, link, flash, boot and run for both images. Wi-Fi joined only on the image with the Bluetooth scanner. OTA never completed, so the OTA update time and the "YAML edit to updated device" time were not measured; the edit-to-compiled time of 137 s and the USB write of 6 s were.

**The line.** Sizes come from the `idf.py size` totals. The minimal image is 816 kB of flash, 21 percent of the 3.75 MB app partition, with static RAM at 138 of 441.5 kB and 305 kB of heap free at boot. The two failures are not explained. For the Wi-Fi failure, one configuration difference separates the image that failed from the images that joined: the Wi-Fi and Bluetooth coexistence code, which the minimal image leaves out. Switching it on through the YAML had no effect on the build. For the OTA stall, ESPHome logs `Stopping scan for OTA` and the board then goes quiet.

**Ask.** Has anyone seen an ESPHome Wi-Fi-only image on an ESP32-C6 that finds no networks until a Bluetooth or 802.15.4 component is added? What does your OTA stall look like?

# Can an ESPHome device on Thread reach Home Assistant through the Apple TV?

**Short answer.** The Thread half works; the Home Assistant half needs one command that was not run. An ESPHome image for the ESP32-C6 with the `openthread:` component attached to the house Thread network 1.2 s after reset and the MacBook pinged it 20 times out of 20. The Mac that runs Home Assistant finds its name through the border router but sends nothing to it, because macOS does not install the route to the Thread network by itself. Adding the route needs `sudo` (administrator rights) on that Mac.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). 1 kB = 1,024 bytes. Thread is the low-power mesh network used by Matter devices; a border router (here an Apple TV) joins it to the home network.

**Question.** Does ESPHome's Thread support give an ESP32-C6 a path to Home Assistant on a Mac in Docker?

**Vendor position.** ESPHome's `openthread` component takes a dataset, which is a Thread network's keys and channel, and attaches the device as a full Thread device. It cannot run with Wi-Fi on the same device, and its source lists a conflict with `wifi`.

**What was tried.** `esp32c6/proxy/frl-esphome-thread.yaml`: `openthread:` with the dataset read from Home Assistant and kept in the git-ignored secrets file, `network: enable_ipv6`, API with encryption, OTA, logger, a heap and a temperature sensor. ESPHome 2026.9.1, ESP-IDF 5.5.5, one ESP32-C6-DevKitC-1-N8, flashed over USB after a full erase. The house network is on channel 25 with an Apple border router as leader.

**How far it got.** Ran. From the reset to `SRP client has started`, which needs an attached device, took 1.2 s, the same on the first boot after the erase and on a later reset. The device registers itself with the border router, which publishes its name `frl-esphome-thread.local` on the home network. From the MacBook `ping6 frl-esphome-thread.local` returned 20 of 20, round trip 21.7 ms at best, 35.2 ms on average, 126.5 ms worst, through a route that was already on the Mac. It was `fd00:db8::/64` via the Apple TV's link-local address on Wi-Fi, added by hand earlier. From the Home Assistant Mac the name resolved to the right Thread address but 3 of 3 pings were lost; that Mac has no route to that prefix. Adoption in the Home Assistant ESPHome integration was not attempted for that reason.

**The line.** Tools, not the chip: `sudo route add -inet6 fd00:db8::/64 <Apple TV link-local address>%en0` (`fd00:db8::/64` is an example prefix; use the Thread prefix your network advertises) on the Home Assistant Mac, which needs a password, and which the Docker container would need as well (not tested). The numbers for the yardstick: 748 kB of flash image, 106.5 kB of static RAM, 368 kB of heap free at boot, against 305 kB for the Wi-Fi image of the first experiment. Only one device was joined; Home Assistant never saw this one.

**Ask.** What is the cleanest way to give a Dockerized Home Assistant a route to a Thread network that an Apple border router advertises?

# Does ESPHome's Zigbee end device work on the ESP32-C6 and what does it cost?

**Short answer.** Yes for sensors, no for switches. A YAML file with a `zigbee:` block built a 492 kB image that joined the house Zigbee network through Home Assistant's ZHA 5.8 s after boot and sent a counter every 2 s; all 31 values reached Home Assistant in order. The plan's 20 toggles could not be run, because ESPHome's Zigbee component supports only sensors and binary sensors on the ESP32 (switch and number are nRF52 only, its documentation says).

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). 1 kB = 1,024 bytes. ZHA is Home Assistant's Zigbee integration. This is the nearest yardstick for the same plan on a TI chip with a 36 kB RAM budget.

**Question.** Does ESPHome's Zigbee component work as an end device on the ESP32-C6 into ZHA, and how big is it?

**Vendor position.** ESPHome's Zigbee page, read 2026-10-11, lists the ESP32-C5, C6 and H2, says the H2 is more reliable than the C6, warns that some C6 boards work only next to the coordinator, and says Wi-Fi in station mode with an end device works fine.

**What was tried.** `esp32c6/proxy/frl-esphome-zigbee.yaml`: Zigbee end device, one template sensor that counts up every 2 s with `report: force`, the chip temperature, the logger. No Wi-Fi, no API, no OTA, as a CC2340R5 build would be. ESPHome 2026.9.1, esp-zigbee-lib 2.0.4, ESP-IDF 5.5.5. The board was erased, flashed, ZHA opened with `zha.permit` (250 s), and the script `esp32c6/zigbee/report_bench.py` read the counter entity every 20 ms for 60 s while the serial log ran beside it.

**How far it got.** Verified. The device log said `Joined network successfully ... Channel(20)` 5.8 s after boot; the entities were in Home Assistant 6.4 s after boot: counter, temperature, signal strength, link quality and an identify button. The counter reached Home Assistant 31 times out of 31 printed, none missing, none out of order. The latency was not measured to better than about 0.2 s, because the serial log is read in chunks. The gaps between values in Home Assistant matched the 2 s send period. The chip temperature showed 95.7 in Home Assistant while the same chip reads about 31 to 36 C in ESP-IDF; the unit was not checked.

The board was removed from ZHA afterwards with `zha.remove` and its IEEE address; the device list was identical to the list before the test and its entities were gone.

**The line.** No limit reached on the join. The cost: 492 kB of flash image, 82.7 of 441.5 kB of static RAM (18.7%), 385 kB of heap free at boot. The CC2340R5 has 36 kB of RAM in total. This image needs 83 kB of static RAM with ESP-IDF, FreeRTOS and ESPHome's runtime included, so a like-for-like port needs a larger part such as the CC2755. The switch limit is in ESPHome's component, not the chip: its ESP32 code builds the Analog Input and Binary Input clusters only.

**Ask.** Has anyone driven a light or switch from ESPHome's Zigbee component on an ESP32 by declaring the On/Off cluster?

FILE: docs/experiments/2026-10-11-esp32c6-lp-core-occupancy.md | Can the ESP32-C6's low-power core run the 8.5k-weight room-occupancy model?
==============================================================================

<!-- experiment
id: E42
board: ESP32-C6-DevKitC-1
date: 2026-10-11
status: works
reached: verified
line: The 8k room-occupancy network runs on the ESP32-C6's low-power core and passes 20 of 20 test windows with every logit equal to the reference, in 214 ms (3.36 million LP cycles); the float input step does not fit, so the main core quantizes the input.

# Can the ESP32-C6's low-power core run the 8.5k-weight room-occupancy model?

**Short answer.** Yes, the network part. The low-power (LP) core classified all 20 test windows correctly with every logit equal to onnxruntime's, in 213.8 ms each, with the main core only handing over a 128-byte input and reading the answer back through shared memory. The whole model, including the float input step, does not link: it needs about 0.6 kB more than the 16 kB of LP SRAM before the stack. The stack-free fit of the network alone leaves 2.3 kB free.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). 1 kB = 1,024 bytes. The LP core is a second RISC-V core (RV32IMAC, no float unit) that runs while the main core sleeps; its code, data and stack all live in the 16 kB LP SRAM.

**Question.** How small a core runs the 8k model, and does the C6's LP core, which can run on its own while the main core sleeps, hold it?

**Vendor position.** ESP-IDF v6.1 ships an LP core build system (`examples/system/ulp/lp_core`) and says the LP core runs "up to 20 MHz" with 16 kB of LP SRAM shared between its code, data and the variables it shares with the main core (read 2026-10-11). The expectation written before the run was about 130 ms, the L1306's 84 ms times 1.6 for the clock.

**What was tried.** ESP-IDF v6.1, GCC 15.2.0, the example `build_system` as base, the model file `occ_cnn_8k.c` unchanged (the same file every other board runs), `-Os`, newlib, the reserve for the LP program set to 16.0 kB (`CONFIG_ULP_COPROC_RESERVE_MEM`).

1. Whole model on the LP core (input window as 128 floats, quantize and run): link error. At the default 15.5 kB reserve with `-O3` the LP region overflows by 3.7 kB; at 16.0 kB and `-Os`, the data ends 0x24c (588) bytes past where the stack must start, before any stack. The sections: 9.4 kB of weights (`.rodata`), 4.1 kB of code (the float step pulls in the C compiler's software-float routines), 2.7 kB of buffers (two 1 kB working buffers inside the model, a 512 B float input, a 128 B int8 copy).
2. Split the model the way its two functions already split: the main core runs `occ_cnn_8k_quantize_input` (float to int8, 128 values) and writes 128 bytes into LP SRAM; the LP core runs `occ_cnn_8k_run_q` (the int8 network) and writes four logits and a class back. Code drops to 1.9 kB, buffers to 2.2 kB; the data ends 2.3 kB before the stack top.
3. Flash the image; the main core posts each of the 20 windows, waits for the LP core, compares class and logits, and times the round trip with the main core's timer. The LP core also reads its own cycle counter around the network call.

**How far it got.** Verified, twice from a reset. 20 of 20 classes and logits right. Round trip 213.80 to 213.86 ms in the first run and 213.83 to 213.91 ms in the second; the LP core's own counter reads 3.36 million cycles. Cycles over time give an effective clock of 15.7 MHz, not the 20 MHz the documentation gives as the top; the cause (the LP core's clock source is not set in this project) was not isolated.

**The line.** RAM. The whole model is over the LP SRAM by 588 B plus its stack. The network alone fits with 2.3 kB left for the stack. For comparison, the main core at 160 MHz runs the whole model in 7.1 ms at `-O3` (1.14 million cycles) and 15.1 ms at `-Os` (2.42 million cycles); the LP core takes 3.36 million cycles for the network alone, about 1.4 times the main core's `-Os` cycles for the whole model, and 30 times as long in wall time. The measured 214 ms is 1.6 times the 130 ms expected.

**Ask.** What clock does the C6's LP core run at by default in ESP-IDF v6.1? Measured: 15.7 MHz against the 20 MHz in the documentation.

FILE: docs/experiments/2026-10-11-esp32c6-zigbee-and-thread.md | Can one ESP32-C6-DevKitC-1 run Zigbee and Thread at the same time?
==============================================================================

<!-- experiment
