# Can ESPHome's own commands build and flash the LP-EM-CC35X1 as a Wi-Fi device?

**Short answer.** Yes, up to the last step. An ESPHome platform `cc35xx` (in `ports/esphome-ti/components/cc35xx/`) builds ESPHome's generated code with TI's compiler on top of TI's Wi-Fi SDK, signs it with TI's Toolbox, and flashes it with `esphome upload`. The board boots in 1.9 s, joins Wi-Fi 5.3 s after a reset, writes ESPHome's log to the board's serial port, announces `frl-cc35x1.local` with the `_esphomelib._tcp` service, and serves ESPHome's native API. A native-API client running on the board itself, over the loopback interface, got the hello, the device info, three entities and 20 of 20 switch commands confirmed, with the LED's output latch matching every one. What is not proven: Home Assistant adopting it over Wi-Fi. The test network isolates its clients from the home LAN, so the Home Assistant leg needs a network that does not.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). The native API is the protocol every ESPHome device speaks with Home Assistant (TCP port 6053). mDNS is how Home Assistant finds ESPHome devices without an address. Loopback is the network interface inside a device that talks to itself (127.0.0.1). The Toolbox is TI's SimpleLink Wi-Fi Toolbox, which signs images and programs this chip. Related: the [ESPHome CC27xx platform page](2026-10-13-esphome-cc27xx-platform.md) (the same platform idea for TI's Zigbee chips). Code and maker path: [ports/esphome-ti/README.md](../../ports/esphome-ti/README.md).

Contents: question, vendor position, expectation, what was tried, how far it got, the line, ideas, ask, build and soak findings.

**Question.** ESPHome's own documentation lists the chips it builds for, and no TI chip is among them. Most of the 151,326 Home Assistant installations that use ESPHome run Wi-Fi devices (Home Assistant's public analytics, read 2026-10-13). The CC3551E is TI's Wi-Fi 6 and Bluetooth LE microcontroller. Can it be one of those devices, built and flashed with ESPHome's own commands?

**Vendor position.** TI ships no ESPHome support for any chip. TI's Wi-Fi SDK 10.20.00.39 ships FreeRTOS, lwIP with sockets, select, a loopback interface and the mDNS responder, set by `LWIP_SOCKET`, `LWIP_HAVE_LOOPIF 1` and `LWIP_MDNS_RESPONDER LWIP_UDP` in `lwipopts.h`, and an `mqtt_client` example that joins a network from a compiled-in name and password. ESPHome's documentation for adding a platform is its source: external components may be target platforms with their own compile and upload steps (`IS_TARGET_PLATFORM`, `run_compile`, `upload_program`, used by the CC27xx platform).

**Expectation.** RAM is the risk: the Matter thermostat image on this chip used 579 kB static of about 669 kB. ESPHome's core plus Wi-Fi, sockets and the API on TI's Wi-Fi stack was expected to fit with room, because TI's mqtt_client example is smaller than the Matter image.

**What was tried.**

- A platform `cc35xx` modeled on the `cc27xx` platform: ESPHome's code generation as usual (the platform answers to ESPHome's Zephyr code paths for pins and preferences), then `ti35_build.py` copies TI's `mqtt_client` example as the board support, runs SysConfig, compiles TI's C and ESPHome's C++ with TI Arm Clang 5.1.1, links with TI's libraries and linker file, and signs with the Toolbox's makefile. `esphome upload` erases the whole flash and programs the signed bundle.
- A Wi-Fi backend for ESPHome (`shim/wifi_component_cc35xx.cpp`, 261 lines, the same functions as ESPHome's Pico W backend) on TI's driver: start, station role, connect, disconnect, scan, RSSI, addresses from lwIP's interface. TI's `wifi_if.c` is reused unchanged except for two lines added to its event handler (the channel at connect and the end of a scan) and a block of entry points appended to it.
- ESPHome's logger, mDNS and the socket wake hooks for this platform (`shim/logger_cc35xx.cpp`, `shim/mdns_cc35xx.cpp`, `shim/esphome/core/wake/wake_zephyr.h`), and ESPHome's compiler flags passed through to TI's compiler.
- Four ESPHome files take their lwIP branch instead of their Zephyr one in the build copy (the socket and IP-address headers, `socket.cpp`, the logger). ESPHome's installed files are not edited.
- An on-board API client (`shim/api_selftest.cpp`, built with `api_self_test: true`) because no client on the house network can reach the board on the guest network.

**How far it got.** Run, on an isolated test network (guest network). It took fourteen build rounds in all, the first five of them failures listed in the findings below.

| Step | Result |
|---|---|
| Code generation | Yes, for `wifi`, `api`, `socket`, `mdns`, `logger`, a GPIO switch and two sensors; three keys (`power_save_mode`, `max_connections`, `max_send_queue`) need values in the YAML, because ESPHome's defaults are per platform |
| Compile and link | Yes: 64 files, 1,274 kB of flash used of 2,687 kB, 74 kB of main RAM and 86.7 kB of TCM free (rows below) |
| Sign and flash | Yes: `esphome upload` erased and programmed in 60 s |
| Boot and ESPHome setup | Yes: 1.9 s from a reset to ESPHome's setup; ESPHome logs "setup() finished successfully" |
| Join Wi-Fi | Yes: 5.3 and 5.7 s from a reset to an address on two clean joins; on a third the access point dropped the first association, ESPHome scanned (3 networks) and joined another access point, address at 16.9 s |
| mDNS | Announces `frl-cc35x1.local` with 1 service (the board's log); not seen from another device (isolated network) |
| Native API, on the board | Yes over loopback, every 5 minutes: hello in 30 ms, device info (103 bytes), 3 entities, 20 of 20 switch commands confirmed, LED latch matched 20 of 20, median 120 ms (114 to 120) |
| Native API from Home Assistant | Not run: port 6053 unreachable from the Mac and the Home Assistant host on the house network |

| Measure | Value | Row |
|---|---|---|
| Flash used | 1,274 kB | `radio_flash_used wifi-esphome-api` |
| Main RAM free after link, TCM free | 74.0 kB, 86.7 kB | `radio_ram_left wifi-esphome-api` |
| Free heap, running, minimum seen | 139.7 kB | the board's alive lines |
| `esphome compile`, cold and warm | 55.7 s, 23.3 s | `blink_build esphome-cc35xx-compile-cold`, `-warm` |
| Reset to address | 5.3 s median of two clean joins | `radio_join wifi-esphome-guest` |
| Switch command to confirmed state, on the board | 120 ms median | `radio_cmd_latency esphome-api-loopback` |

**The line.** The network, not the chip. Everything up to a Home Assistant client works on the board; the test network isolates its clients, so port 6053 is unreachable from other devices. The next run is Home Assistant's ESPHome integration on the home network: add the device (or let mDNS offer it), switch the LED 20 times, read both sensors, leave it a day.

What remains to make it a stranger's ten-minute path, each a known piece of work: encryption for the API (needs a real random source, TI's TRNG driver), preferences that survive a reset (TI's NV storage), Wi-Fi setup without the password in the YAML (Improv over serial or a setup access point), platform defaults for the three keys, and over-the-air updates.

**Ask.** If you have built an out-of-tree ESPHome platform: is there a supported way to give it platform defaults for `wifi: power_save_mode`, `api: max_connections` and `max_send_queue` (ESPHome's `SplitDefault` lists only its own platforms), and to declare its UARTs to the logger without patching `uart_selection`?

## Build and soak findings (what to expect if you rebuild)

- **Five build rounds, each failure naming one thing.** ESPHome's logger has no UART list for an unknown platform (logger left out first). TI's `lwipopts.h` sets `LWIP_COMPAT_SOCKETS 1`, which turns `connect()` and `close()` into macros and breaks ESPHome's socket class (a one-line override for ESPHome's files). Renaming every Zephyr branch in the socket files also hid a helper ESPHome needs (narrowed to the files that pull Zephyr's headers). TI's `osi_kernel.h` declares `Report()` without C linkage guards, so C++ files cannot call it (a C wrapper). The station's channel query is answered only for the access-point role (`AP role is not up!`; the channel now comes from the connect event).
- **First image on the board.** Boot, ESPHome setup, join, an address from the access point, then silence after the channel query. Not explained; the next image without that call ran.
- **Logger.** The loop ran but the Wi-Fi component's loop printed nothing, so the logger was made to work: the logger's Zephyr branch takes its generic path in the build copy, a 20-line backend writes to TI's console, and ESPHome's compiler flags (log level among them) reach TI's compiler. ESPHome's own log then showed a normal ESP32-like start: fast connect, connected, API waiting for a client.
- **Isolated network.** Port 6053 was unreachable from the Mac and the Home Assistant host: the test network isolates its clients. If you see this, test from a network that lets clients reach each other.
- **On-board API client.** mDNS runs on lwIP's responder. The first run gave 20 of 20, median 296 ms, LED matched 10 of 20. Both were artifacts of the test client: it wrote each frame header and body in two writes (Nagle's algorithm with a delayed ACK) and read the pin's pad value, which reads 0 while it drives. With one write per frame and the output latch read back: 120 ms, 20 of 20.
- **Reset without a reflash.** This showed a real gap: when the access point dropped the first association, ESPHome fell back to scanning, and the backend had no scan, so the board stayed without an address. Scanning was added (TI's `Wlan_Scan`, results from the scan event); on the next three resets it joined in 5.7 s and 5.3 s, and on the third it scanned and joined another access point.
- **Soak, first rounds.** On-board API test every 5 minutes, console captured. Rounds 1 to 4: each 20 of 20 confirmed, LED latch 20 of 20, median 120 ms (minimum 111 to 114, maximum 121 to 122), free heap 140.8 kB every round, minimum 136.0 kB.
- **Random source.** The placeholder random source (a linear congruential generator) is weak. It now reports failure, so anything that needs real randomness stops instead of using it, and the platform refuses `api: encryption` at config time with a plain message until TI's TRNG driver is wired in. The same change went into the Zigbee platforms' shim. The image still compiles; the soak image is plain-text API, unaffected.
- **24-hour soak.** 281 rounds, 5,616 of 5,620 switch commands confirmed (99.9%), all four misses in rounds 19 and 20 on the first day; every round's median was 120 ms. The access point dropped the board 22 times and it reconnected on its own each time; the board never restarted. Free heap stayed at 140.7 kB with a lowest point of 135.7 kB.

==============================================================================

# Can TI's Motion and Presence demo on the IWRL6432BOOST board's IWRL6432 radar report room zones with no reflash, and can each zone become a Home Assistant sensor?

**Short answer.** Zones come from a configuration change alone. The shipped demo's command line takes up to 12 `mpdBoundaryBox` lines and puts one 2-bit state per box in every frame (type 315). Built here: a four-zone configuration, and `zones.py`, which reads frames, logs each zone's on and off, counts zone changes and writes a live page once a second. The Home Assistant posting code is switched off. The radar did not answer, so nothing was measured on it. What was measured is a replay of 2026-10-10 recordings made with the demo's own four boxes: a still person lit more than one box most of the time. The live measurements (20 minutes empty, a timed walk-through) are not taken.

How to run it and what each part does: [iwrl6432boost/zones/README.md](../../iwrl6432boost/zones/README.md). Evaluation background: [the antenna evaluation](2026-10-10-radar-antenna-eval.md), [how to evaluate a presence radar](../guides/evaluate-a-presence-radar.md).

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). A zone is a floor-plan rectangle (x sideways, y out from the radar); the 2D demo reads only x and y of a cluster's center. Board: [IWRL6432BOOST](../../iwrl6432boost/README.md). Files: `iwrl6432boost/zones/`. Read and run 2026-10-13 on macOS 15.7, MMWAVE-L-SDK 05.05.04.02 source, Radar Toolbox 4.00.00.05.

**Question.** A room radar for a home needs to say which area is occupied (the desk, the door), beyond whether anyone is there. The shipped demo already has boxes. How far do they get with no firmware change, and is the result good enough to post each area to Home Assistant?

**Vendor position.** The demo's CLI help (captured 2026-10-10) reads `mpdBoundaryBox: <zone_number> <xMin> <xMax> <yMin> <yMax> <zMin> <zMax>`. In the SDK source (`mmw_cli.c`): each line adds a box (`numBoundaryBoxes++`), the zone number is not used, and nothing clears the boxes until the next boot. `mpdproc.c` assigns a cluster to a box when its center's x and y are inside (z is not tested in the 2D build), keeps a state per box (`STATE_EMPTY` 0, `STATE_MINOR` 1, `STATE_MAJOR` 2) and allows 12 boxes. `motion_detect.c` sizes the type 315 payload as `ceil(boxes / 4) + 1` bytes. TI's user guide does not list the state values or the byte layout. Read 2026-10-13.

**Empty room, replay.** The 2x2 empty pass had 0 frames lit; the 2x3 empty pass had all four boxes lit for its first 14 s (the antenna evaluation counts that as the person leaving plus the 12-frame hold, not a false alarm) and none after.

**Expectation, written before any run.** Four boxes accepted, all lines Done; 4.0 frames a second; empty room for 20 minutes: 0 zone events (the shipped four boxes gave 0 presence frames in 87,602 empty-room frames); a person walking in lights the door end first and the desk last, with a neighbouring box sometimes lit; the desk stays lit while the person sits; every box clears about 3 s plus the walk out after the person leaves (the hold is 12 frames).

**What was tried.**

1. Chose depth bands, not left and right. The recorded seated passes on the center line lit the left box 87 to 92 percent and the right box 0 to 38 percent, so an x split near x = 0 is unreliable. Edges: desk 0.25 to 3.5 m, middle 3.5 to 5.5, far room 5.5 to 6.5, door end 6.5 to 7.5, each from x = -3.5 to 3.5. The 3.5 m edge sits between the range profile's reading of the 2 m chair (2.78 m) and the 4 m chair (4.6 m). Layout from the antenna evaluation's setup, not re-surveyed.
2. Wrote `zones.json`, and `zones.py cfg` generates `cfg/PresenceDetect-zones.cfg`: the 12-frame-hold configuration with the four box lines replaced, `lowPowerCfg 0`, 2 by 3 antennas.
3. Wrote `zones.py` (`apply`, `run`, `walk`, `check`, `replay`, `selftest`) and `draw_map.py`. The self test checks the generated lines, the decoder on a hand-made 315 payload (zones 2, 0, 0, 1), the tracker's episodes and hold arithmetic, the live page's colors and the Home Assistant request shape against a local mock server. It passes.
4. Rendered the live page from a made-up two-zone state in headless Chrome to check the layout (`iwrl6432boost/zones/img/live-page-layout-check.png`). A picture of the layout, not a measurement.
5. Replayed the 2x3 and 2x2 passes from the antenna evaluation's recordings through the same tracker (`zones.py replay`): per box, when it lit and cleared against the cue, and, for the seated passes, how often a box on the wrong side of the 3.5 m line lit.
6. Tried to start the radar. `lsof` showed nothing holding its port and no feeder or logger was running. The port `/dev/cu.usbmodemRI32RI321` ended every read at once (`device reports readiness to read but returned no data`). `xds110reset -s RI32RI32` and `xds110reset -a toggle -d 100 -s RI32RI32` changed nothing. A 5 s power cycle of the probe's hub port (`uhubctl -l 20-1 -p 3 -a cycle -d 5`, only that port) brought the probe back, and macOS then named the application port `/dev/cu.usbmodem3` (the old name stayed as a dead node). On it `version`, `help` and plain newlines got no answer at 115,200 baud, and nothing came at 1,250,000, 921,600 or 460,800 baud, with the line read for 3 to 16 s each and a reset toggle in the middle of one read.

**How far it got.** Compile: the configuration and the program build and pass their own checks. Run on the radar: not reached. The board has answered in neither run nor flash mode since a rewiring on 2026-10-12, through a reset, a replug and a power cycle with the barrel jack.

**Replay results (2026-10-10 recordings, the demo's four shipped boxes: left and right of x = 0, near 0 to 3.5 m, far 3.51 to 7 m; one pass per cell).** Seated window = the 45 s between the enter and leave cues. The four rows below are the full table.

| Pass | Either near box lit | Either far box lit | Near and far both lit | Any box lit | Lit on the wrong side of the 3.5 m line (against the range profile peak) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2x3 seated 2 m | 87% | 32% | 32% | 87% | 37% of lit frames |
| 2x3 seated 4 m | 73% | 88% | 70% | 91% | 76% |
| 2x2 seated 2 m | 88% | 20% | 20% | 88% | 23% |
| 2x2 seated 4 m | 92% | 92% | 92% | 92% | 100% |

Reading: at 4 m the near box was lit most of the time with the person's profile peak at 4.6 m. In the 2x3 walk-in the near and far left boxes lit together at 6.7 s, the moment the person appeared at about 6.5 m by the evaluation's cue timing; a box covering 0 to 3.5 m lit for a person 6.5 m away, which is the misassignment this page is about. One box per person did not hold. **Unknown (suspected: Chip limit).** The body's clusters may straddle the line (the profile read the chairs 0.78 m and 0.6 m long), multipath may add points, and the 2 by 3 angle estimate is coarse. Not tested: the cluster radius, the minimum points per cluster, a higher mount.

**Serial load and frame rate (recorded 2026-10-10, not re-measured).** 4.003 frames a second, 704 bytes a frame on the 2 by 3 setting: 2,818 B/s, 24.5 percent of the 11,520 B/s a 115,200 baud link carries (computed).

**What the shipped demo cannot do.**

- Count people or track them. A zone is occupied or not. TI's People Tracking material for the same Motion and Presence Detection demo (the file `IWRL6432BOOST_Tracking_3Persons_7m_wall_mount.cfg` is named in the antenna evaluation and is not in the toolbox copy on this Mac, so unverified) gives a track per person. The prebuilt 2D and 3D images are in the toolbox. Loading one needs flash mode (S1 position 1 OFF, S2, flash, back, S2), done by hand at the board. The shipped demo's help text lists `trackingCfg`, `boundaryBox`, `gatingParam`, `stateParam`, `allocationParam` and `profileSwitchCfg`, so the shipped image may run the tracker if sent those lines.
- Height. The 2D build ignores z. The 3D image uses it for sit against stand.
- Clean attribution: see the replay.

For scale, public sources only: Aqara's FP2 page says up to 30 zones, up to 5 people at once, wall mounting needed for zones. Hi-Link's HLK-LD2450 manual: 24 GHz, up to 3 targets with x and y in millimeters at 10 frames a second, 6 m, one region filter. Neither was tested here.

**The line.** The radar does not answer on USB in any state reachable without changing switches, cause unknown. Everything that depends on it is unmeasured: empty-room false zone events in 20 minutes, per-zone detect and clear times, the page against a live person, the frame rate with the four boxes (the recording also had four boxes, so no change is expected).

- Derive zones in software from the minor-motion range profile (type 303) instead of the demo's boxes. The profile peak is unreliable with nobody in the room (it sits on a fixed reflector near 6.5 m), so it would need a background subtraction first.
- Send TI's tracking lines to the shipped image and count tracks.
- A cluster radius and minimum points sweep to see whether the two-boxes-lit result moves.
- Debounce in the host: ignore a zone that lights for fewer than N frames.
- Home Assistant over MQTT discovery once a token or broker exists.

**Ask.** If you have used `mpdBoundaryBox` zones on an IWRL6432 and a person on a zone line lit one box only, which cluster and state settings did you use?

## Findings log

- No feeder or radar process was running and no port lock was held when the port was tried.
- The port gave a read error at once. Three probe resets and a 5 s power cycle of the probe's USB port did not wake the radar (the 2026-10-12 record says a power cycle of USB and the barrel jack together also failed). After the cycle macOS listed the application port as `/dev/cu.usbmodem3`; the old node stays as a dead entry. If you see a dead port name after a probe power cycle, look for the new name. No answer came at any baud rate in either mode.
- The replay and the page checks were built without the radar.

==============================================================================

<!-- experiment

reached: run

# Can the LP-MSPM0G5187's NPU learn your smoke or CO alarm by ear and ignore every other sound?

**Short answer.** Partly. Through its own microphone, the board reported a smoke alarm pattern played from a laptop speaker 9.4 s after it started, kept 14 of 16 look-alike sounds silent with nothing learned, and gave 0 alarms in 3.4 hours of a quiet room. Learning your alarm (S2, then its test button) has run only on audio streamed over USB, where the board then ignored 18 of 18 look-alikes, a 31 dB quieter copy and another pitch. A real smoke alarm's horn has not been tried.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md) (NPU, I2S, PCM1809, dBFS, false trip). Code, build and file list: [mspm0g5187/alarm](../../mspm0g5187/alarm/README.md). Errors and fixes: [LP-MSPM0G5187 FAQ, alarm listener](../../mspm0g5187/FAQ.md). Checked 2026-10-12 and 2026-10-13 on an Intel Mac, macOS 15.7, MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS, SysConfig 1.26.3, UniFlash 9.6.0 (DSLite), TI's neural network compiler (NNC) for MSPM0, on one LP-MSPM0G5187 Rev. A (probe firmware 3.0.0.38). 1 kB = 1,024 bytes.

**Question.** The board checks a sound against the alarm it learned: the same tone (within 4 %) and nearly the same loudness (no more than 10 dB quieter). You do not want to replace a working smoke or CO alarm with a connected one. Can a small board sit beside it, learn it with one press of the alarm's test button, and tell you when it goes off, without tripping on a whistle, a kettle, a ringtone or the same alarm on TV?

**Vendor position.** TI ships no alarm-sound example. The SDK's nearest example is `glass_break_detection_ai_npu`: "both feature extraction (using filterbanks) and classification are performed using AI models. The inference runs on the TinyEngine hardware accelerator". It does not listen. Its README says "The pre-loaded test vector containing vibration data is fed to the AI model" (MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07, read 2026-10-13). The only SDK example that reads the board's microphone is `device_uac_microphone_i2s`, which sends the audio to a computer over USB. So the microphone path, the features, the model and the learn step were written by us, built from those two examples and TI's NNC.

The patterns come from NFPA 72, the US fire alarm code: smoke is temporal-3 (three 0.5 s beeps 0.5 s apart, then 1.5 s quiet) and CO is temporal-4 (four 0.1 s pulses 0.1 s apart, then 5 s quiet). Each timing is allowed plus or minus 10 %.

**What was tried.** Expectations were written first. Two of them: under 3 ms per inference, and detection 8 to 12 s after an alarm starts.

- **Microphone.** The onboard ICS-40720 into the PCM1809 converter, I2S on PB10, PB11 and PB12 at 47.6 kHz, using TI's USB-microphone settings. The DMA interrupt filters the audio and keeps every third sample (15,873 a second).
- **Features.** Every 64.5 ms, two 512-point FFTs give 13 numbers: nine band levels, the total level, the loudest tone's frequency, how tonal it is and its level. The C code on the board and a Python twin on the Mac agree to 0.0 dB median on the same audio.
- **Model.** A five-layer 1-D CNN, 13.8k parameters, 8-bit, compiled for the NPU with TI's NNC. Every 1.03 s it looks at the last 8.3 s and answers other, smoke or CO. It was trained on 2,000 synthetic scenes: real ringtones, alert sounds, speech and music from a Mac, plus look-alike beeping (oven timers, backup beepers, microwaves, alarm clocks, alarm patterns with the timing 35 % off, chirps, whistles).
- **Decision.** An alarm needs the same answer in 6 of the last 8 inferences and a timing check against the NFPA 72 pattern. Once an alarm is learned, it also needs the learned tone and level. The learned record is 16 bytes in data flash, so it survives a power cut.
- **Three test rigs,** each closer to real life: audio streamed over USB into the same code (no sound played), a laptop speaker beside the board, and a quiet room overnight.

**How far it got.**

| Step | Result | Recorded |
|---|---|---|
| Build | `alarm_detect` links: 78.7 kB of flash (of 128 kB), 29.7 kB of RAM (of 32 kB) | Linker size, 2026-10-13 |
| NPU against the Mac | Same class as onnxruntime on 6 of 6 test windows | Self-test, 2026-10-12 |
| Microphone | Works: a 995 Hz tone came through clean; a quiet room reads -79.6 dBFS | Mic check, 2026-10-13 |
| Held-out synthetic scenes, on the Mac | 0 false trips in 2 hours; 162 of 167 alarms beside the board caught | Mac replay, 2026-10-13 |
| Audio over USB, on the board | Learned a smoke alarm and saved it; alarmed on it; 0 of 18 decoys; ignored it 31 dB quieter, at 3,600 Hz, and a CO pattern; with CO added, the learned horn reports smoke or CO and names which | USB inject runs, 2026-10-13 |
| Laptop speaker, real microphone | Smoke pattern: ALARM 9.4 s after it started. 14 of 16 look-alikes silent with nothing learned. With the alarm learned, applied afterwards to the logged answers (a replay, not a live decision), 0 of 16, and the quiet copy (about 22 dB down) and the other tone ignored | Live run, 2026-10-13 |
| Overnight, quiet room, nothing learned | 12.1k inferences in 3.4 hours, 0 alarms | Live run, 2026-10-13 |
| A real smoke alarm's horn | Not run | needs a real alarm beside the board |

The two look-alikes that alarmed with nothing learned were CO-like patterns (three pulses, and four pulses with a 1.5 s gap). **Our mistake.** The CO timing check accepted any pulse group. It now needs two groups 5.8 s apart, and both look-alikes stay silent on the board with nothing learned.

**The line.** Nothing is blocked, but learning has not run on the real microphone, and a real horn has not been tried. That is the open question. A smoke alarm is 85 dB or more at 3 m and has harmonics and sometimes a warble. The test tones were synthetic and came from a laptop speaker. If the model never calls the real horn smoke, the fix is to record it with the capture image and add it to training. That has not been needed, and it will not be known until the test runs.

**This is a first on this part.** TI has no alarm-sound example for the MSPM0G5187, so the whole path is a port of two of its examples, as the vendor position explains.

| What went wrong | Tag | Cost | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| The microphone read zeros | **Setup or handling** | One evening | Two radio wires on PB10 and PB11 (header J20) were holding the microphone's clock lines; taken off |
| The learned record did not save, then stopped the board at boot | **Our mistake** | About an hour, three flashes | One 64-bit write to the data flash instead of two; the sector erased back with OpenOCD |
| CO look-alikes alarmed | **Our mistake** | Half a morning, no retraining | The CO timing check now needs two groups 5.8 s apart |
| The learn press over USB landed during an alarm, which clears it | **Our mistake** | One live slot | A separate learn command |
| 20.2 ms per inference in the self-test and 32.4 ms median live, against 1 to 3 ms expected | **Unknown (suspected: Our mistake)** | None: one inference a second keeps up | Suspected: most of the time is the CPU scaling 2,048 inputs to 8 bits before the NPU, not the NPU; not profiled. Feeding 8-bit input directly is the next idea |

Effort: an evening, a night and a morning (2026-10-12 to 13); flashes were not counted; one hands-on step (two wires off J20). Verdict: good. The NPU part was the easy part. The work was in the features, the decision rule and the false-trip testing.

- Record a real smoke alarm and a real CO alarm with the capture image and add them to training.
- Doorbells: the same learn step would work for a two-tone chime, but it needs a third pattern (no standard cadence) and was not built.
- Feed the NPU 8-bit input directly, as TI's glass-break model does, to cut the 20 to 32 ms.
- Battery: the listener ran from USB. Current was not measured.
- One chip: run the model in software on the radio chip and drop the MSPM0G5187. Estimated, not built.

**Telling a phone.** The board prints `ALARM smoke` or `ALARM co` on its USB serial port. A Mac script (`host/listen.py`) turns that into a Mac notification and a Home Assistant sensor (`sensor.alarm_listener`). For a house without a Mac, the same lines go to a radio board as `SMOKE 1`, `SMOKE 0`, `CO 1` and `CO 0`:

- **Zigbee:** an LP-EM-CC2340R5 shows up in Home Assistant as a smoke sensor and a CO sensor, with no custom code on the Home Assistant side. Serial line to Home Assistant took 38 ms median for smoke and 56 ms for CO, 20 of 20 each ([run](../../mspm0g5187/alarm/radio/zigbee.md)).
- **Matter over Thread:** an LP-EM-CC2755P10 builds and boots as a Matter smoke and CO alarm. It has not been paired to a phone ([run](../../mspm0g5187/alarm/radio/matter-thread.md)).
- **Matter over Wi-Fi:** not built.

None of the three radio chips has an NPU, so the listener stays on the MSPM0G5187 and talks to the radio over two wires.

**Ask.** Do you have a smoke or CO alarm whose horn sounds unlike the standard? Report which one it is. The next test is a real horn beside the board, and more kinds of alarm make it a better test.

FILE: docs/experiments/2026-10-13-mspm0g5187-wakeword-onboard-mic.md | Can TI's "OK Kilby" wake-word model listen to the LP-MSPM0G5187's own microphone and light an LED?
==============================================================================

<!-- experiment
id: E22
board: LP-MSPM0G5187
date: 2026-10-13
status: waiting
reached: run
line: TI's wake-word model runs on the board's NPU from a rebuilt I2S microphone input and detected a synthetic "OK Kilby" 120 of 120 times across six macOS voices (replay through the serial port); the board's own microphone has not been heard because two CC1407P wires still sit on the microphone's clock pins.
stop: this repo
-->
# Can TI's "OK Kilby" wake-word model listen to the LP-MSPM0G5187's own microphone and light an LED?

**Short answer.** The model and the rebuilt input path work; the microphone itself is not proven. With the Mac sending synthetic "OK Kilby" to the same code over the serial port, six macOS voices were detected 20 of 20 times each (peak -20 dBFS), Samantha 10 of 10 at each of -40, -30, -10 and -3 dBFS, and the median `WAKE` line came 0.03 to 0.49 s after the end of the phrase. Ten minutes of silence gave 0 false triggers; ten minutes of other sentences gave 0 on 131 sentences without "okay" or "Kilby" and 18 in a set where three of nine contain one of them. TI's example as shipped, with nothing on its microphone pin, gave 0 detections in 11.4k inferences. The live run (the Mac's speaker, the board's microphone) is built as `run_live.sh` and waits for two wires to come off header J20.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md#wake-words-and-the-onboard-microphone-lp-mspm0g5187) (wake word, I2S, PCM1809, decimation, LPC, dBFS, false trigger, replay). Build errors, the microphone and the UART: the [board README's FAQ](../../mspm0g5187/wakeword/README.md#faq). Code and patch: [mspm0g5187/wakeword](../../mspm0g5187/wakeword/README.md). Checked on an Intel Mac, macOS 15.7, MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS, SysConfig 1.26.3, DSLite from UniFlash 9.6.0, one LP-MSPM0G5187 Rev. A (probe <probe serial>, firmware 3.0.0.38).

**Question.** A builder wants "say the wake word, an LED lights" on the LP-MSPM0G5187, using the model TI ships for its NPU. TI's example reads a microphone this board does not carry. Can it read the one the board has?

**Vendor position.** TI's `wakeword_detection_ai_npu` README: "continuously listens for the wakeword 'OK Kilby' using audio data captured via the ADC peripheral", "Analog microphone connected to PB22 (AIN24)", "Captures audio at 8 kHz from an analog microphone connected to the ADC12 peripheral", and a detection is "6 consecutive positive predictions". Its hardware table lists the LaunchPad and an analog microphone, not a BoosterPack. PB22 is BoosterPack header pin 6, where the BOOSTXL-EDUMKII puts its microphone. The board's own microphone (an ICS-40720) feeds a PCM1809 audio converter that reaches the chip on PB10, PB11 and PB12 over I2S; TI's `device_uac_microphone_i2s` is the only example that reads it, and its README says only "send an I2S signal to the Launchpad via a I2S controller or external peripheral".

**What was tried.** Expectation first: the plan written before the board arrived said, "possible but real work: the model wants 8 kHz samples and LPC features from 20 ms frames; the PCM1809 gives 32-bit I2S at a higher rate, so the input stage needs decimation and scaling". Numeric expectations were not written before the control and replay runs (they ran in one sitting); the live-run expectations in the README table were written after replay and before any live run.

- **Control.** TI's example, three build fixes only, as the pin floats: a serial report added, otherwise as shipped (no optimization), 180 s; then with `-O2`, 118 s.
- **Port.** I2S capture by DMA from TI's `device_uac_microphone_i2s` setup, a multiplier-free decimator (CIC order 4 by 3, half-band FIR by 2, 47.6 kHz to 7,936.5 Hz), TI's model, LPC, window and detection rule unchanged, the loop pipelined, `-O2`. Everything changed is in [`changes.patch`](../../mspm0g5187/wakeword/changes.patch) and the files beside it.
- **Replay.** The same image path with the audio from the Mac over the serial port: `say -v <voice> "OK Kilby"` rendered to 8 kHz, peak scaled, sent at 8 kHz, 20 per voice, six voices, then four levels, then silence and sentences for 10 minutes each. The bytes arrive by DMA into a ring.
- **Live.** `run_live.sh`: the same image, the Mac speaking through its speaker beside the board, serial lines stamped on the Mac clock. Written, not run.

**How far it got.**

| Step | Result | Recorded |
|---|---|---|
| Build TI's example as shipped | Failed three ways, fixed in a copy | `mspm0g5187/wakeword/build.sh` |
| Control, 180 s and 118 s | 0 detections in 11.4k inferences; ADC rate 6.63 kHz; loop 27.5 ms (no optimization) and 24.1 ms (`-O2`) per 20 ms frame | Serial report, 2026-10-13 |
| Build the I2S port | Links: 68.4 kB flash, 25.6 kB RAM | Linker map |
| Run the I2S image | Runs: 7,749 Hz of audio decimated, steady for two minutes; the microphone itself read zeros with the radio wires on | Serial report, 120 s |
| Replay, six voices | 120 of 120 | Replay run |
| Replay, levels | 40 of 40 | Replay run |
| False triggers, replay | 0 in silence; 0 in 131 plain sentences; 18 in 125 sentences that include three near-miss ones | Replay runs, 10 minutes each |
| Live microphone | Not run | needs two wires off J20 |

**The line.** The model's end is clean; the microphone's end is open. What stopped the live run:

- **The wires.** PB10 and PB11 are the audio converter's clocks and, on header J20, the CC1407P radio's reset and interrupt wires. With them on, the capture read all zeros and an earlier one words with the value in the low 16 bits. **Tag: Unknown (suspected: the wires; not checked with them off).**
- **TI's example input, as shipped.** Even with a microphone it would not keep up: the ADC interrupt ran at 6.63 kHz, not 8 kHz, and LPC (685k cycles, 8.5 ms) then the NPU (899k cycles, 11.2 ms) take 24.1 ms a frame at `-O2` (part of it unaccounted for) against 20 ms between frames. **Tag: TI example default.** The cause of the 6.63 kHz is not found.
- **A divider comment off by one.** TI's I2S dividers (7 and 48) give about 41.7 kHz on this chip, not the 47.6 kHz its source says; with 6 the count was 7,749 Hz after the by-six decimation, 2.4 percent under the 7,936.5 Hz target. **Tag: Tool or docs.**
- **Interrupts and the NPU.** The first replay used a receive interrupt and lost bytes (245 overrun errors in 1,400 frames) while the NPU ran; one lost byte garbles everything after it, and the first set of results was thrown away. DMA into a ring fixed it. **Tag: Our mistake.** The first build used an interrupt. Why the interrupts were late is **Unknown**. The counts were observed 2026-10-13 and not saved.
- **The 60-tap filter.** The first decimator, a 60-tap FIR in the I2S interrupt, took 44k cycles of every 1 ms because a multiply takes about 30 cycles on this core. The CIC and half-band version takes about 8.4k (the 60-tap figure was observed, not saved). **Tag: Our mistake.**

**No vendor example for this input path.** TI ships the model, the example for the analog microphone, and the I2S capture for a USB microphone, nothing that joins them. What existed: the three examples. Method: kept TI's `lpc_float`, `feature_extraction.c`, `buffer_manager.c`, `post_inference.c` and `model.a` unchanged, wrote the input stage and the loop, and checked the result with replayed speech first. What went wrong:

| Problem | Cause tag | Cost | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| Example did not build with the installed compiler | Tool or docs | three failed builds | `build.sh` |
| Decimation filter used half the CPU | Our mistake | one measured run | CIC plus half-band |
| Receive interrupt lost bytes, first results invalid | Our mistake | the first replay set | DMA ring |
| I2S rate wrong by one divider | Tool or docs | one measurement | divider 6 |
| Microphone silent with radio wires on | Unknown (suspected: the wires) | the live run | two wires off J20 |

Effort: one sitting at the bench with no hands needed until the wires. Verdict: the model side took one rebuilt input stage and gave 120 of 120 on synthetic speech, which is worth a real-speaker test; TI's example as shipped is not usable from a terminal and not real time at `-O2`; the microphone side is untested, and whether the wires are the whole story is not known.

**Ask.**

- **For readers:** if you run the rebuilt image with a real speaker, send the hit rate and the room.

FILE: docs/experiments/2026-10-15-am13e230-bldc-drv8376evm.md | Can the LP-AM13E230 spin a Hall-sensor brushless motor through TI's DRV8376EVM, with no motor BoosterPack and no C2000?
==============================================================================

<!-- experiment

# Can the LP-AM13E230 spin a Hall-sensor brushless motor through TI's DRV8376EVM, with no motor BoosterPack and no C2000?

**Short answer.** Yes. A six-step program on the LP-AM13E230 spun the motor through the DRV8376EVM with no motor BoosterPack and no C2000. Numbers and the method are on the [program page](../../am13e230/bldc-drv8376/README.md); rows `bldc_rpm` in `data/results/am13e230.csv`.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md), [LP-AM13E230 FAQ](../../am13e230/FAQ.md). Six-step is the simplest brushless drive, two phases on at a time, switched by the three Hall sensors; FOC is the smooth version TI's SDK solutions use. Board page: [LP-AM13E230 README](../../am13e230/README.md). Program page: [bldc-drv8376 README](../../am13e230/bldc-drv8376/README.md).

![The DRV8376EVM with the Hall block, motor and supply terminals marked](../../site/media/wiring/drv8376evm-wiring.png)

![The LP-AM13E230 with the switches, the EVM sockets and the pins it uses marked](../../site/media/wiring/am13e230-bldc-drv8376.png)

**Question.** The EVM was made for the LAUNCHXL-F280049C with TI's GUI firmware. The AM13 SDK's four motor solutions all want a BOOSTXL-DRV8323RH or DRV8329A. Can the EVM run from the LP-AM13E230 at all, and how much code does a first run take?

**Vendor position.** The DRV8376 "implements a 6x or 3x PWM control scheme for sensored or sensorless field-oriented, sinusoidal, or trapezoidal control using an external microcontroller" (product page, read 2026-10-15). The EVM guide lists the F280049C as the controller and gives no other LaunchPad. The mode, slew, gain and overcurrent settings are resistors on the EVM (guide section 2.6); the design files are Altium only, so which resistors are fitted is read from the board, or by the program at start.

**What was tried.** Board LP-AM13E230 Rev E2, AM13 SDK 26.01.00.03, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1. The DRV8376EVM is a BoosterPack: TI's pin table for it (user's guide SLVUD20, tables 2-1 and 2-2) maps onto the headers of the LaunchPad development kit so the six gate inputs land on the six MCPWM4 outputs, checked against the F280049C LaunchPad pin map SPRUII7 and the LP-AM13E230 silkscreen. The motor is an Anaheim Automation BLY171S-24V-4000 (label: 24 V, 4,000 rpm, 1.8 A, 1.5 ohm and 2.1 mH line to line, 2.45 V per krpm, delta, eight poles, Halls at 120 electrical degrees). The EVM's mode, slew, gain and overcurrent settings are resistors on the board (guide section 2.6) and the design files are Altium only, so the program reads the PWM mode at start. The code is `am13e230/bldc-drv8376/` (six-step from the Halls, serial commands, a learn routine for the Hall table), about 350 lines, built to 32 kB. Power was a 12 V 0.5 A adapter.

**How far it got.** Verified. Configured, compiled, linked, flashed, booted, ran and measured. The program learned the Hall table hands free in about 25 s and spun the motor from standstill.

**The line.** It spins, open loop in duty, unloaded. Measured (medians of three runs, `data/results/am13e230.csv`): 924, 2,312, 3,632 rpm forward at 20, 40, 60 percent duty; 891, 2,091, 3,442 reverse at 20, 40, 60; bus 12.4 to 12.5 V; no driver fault. Three wrong turns, each with its cause, are written up on the program page under "What went wrong first": a missing Hall-power jumper made every Hall line read high; holding a line vector parked the rotor on a Hall boundary so the state flickered; and the EVM's phase-voltage read-back could not tell the PWM mode, so the program forces 6x. The EVM's shipped settings were found to be 6x PWM by behavior, not by its voltage sense. No TI example targets this board and driver pairing, so the method was worked out here.

**Ask.** Which LaunchPad development kits besides the F280049C are supported for the DRV8376EVM? Which config resistors ship fitted (the design files are Altium only)? Is there a current-sense reference path that works without hand-fitting the VREF jumper?

# Can a CC2340R5 Bluetooth tag carry a machine's telemetry to a CC35X1 hub, and a phone, with no internet?

**Short answer.** Yes. Over 10 minutes the hub logged 283 of 283 events from the equipment, a median 1.4 s after the equipment sent each one, with totals identical to the equipment's. 269 of 274 per-run summaries arrived, and the tag's own model classified the run events 95.9% right. The project page: [tool-telemetry/README.md](../../tool-telemetry/README.md).

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md), [CC2340R5 FAQ](../../cc2340r5/FAQ.md), [CC35X1 FAQ](../../cc35x1/FAQ.md). Wire formats: [PROTOCOL.md](../../tool-telemetry/PROTOCOL.md).

![The hub's dashboard on a phone, replaying recorded bench runs: each asset tag with its run count, overcurrent trips, run lengths and a runs-per-10-s chart](../../site/media/tool-telemetry-dashboard-phone.png)

**Question.** Can a machine's motor MCU hand its counters to a cheap Bluetooth tag over a UART, can the tag advertise them for any phone (legacy) and in full for a Bluetooth 5 hub (extended) at once, and can a Wi-Fi hub collect every machine nearby and serve a phone with no internet?

**Vendor position.** TI's `basic_ble` example for the LP-EM-CC2340R5 ships one legacy advertising set; its SysConfig offers extended advertising as an option (`extAdv`, which adds `-DUSE_AE`). TI's network_terminal for the CC35X1 has extended scanning built in: "Set Ble Scan Configuration. Default Parameters: extended 1M PHY, scan interval of 100ms and scan window of 50ms." (`str.c`, SDK 10.20.00.39, read 2026-10-17), and brings up an access point with its own DHCP server. Neither SDK has an example that joins the two.

**What was tried.** LP-EM-CC2340R5 (probe <probe serial>), F3 SDK 9.21.00.36, `basic_ble` patched by `tool-telemetry/tag/apply.py`: a UART task parsing the equipment's lines, the peripheral's legacy set reloaded with the 25-byte frame, a second set created in code as extended, non-connectable, every 1 s, and a 35-node decision tree classifying each run event. LP-EM-CC35X1 (probe <probe serial>), Wi-Fi SDK 10.20.00.39, `network_terminal` patched by `tool-telemetry/gateway/apply.py`: at boot it runs the example's own commands (`wlan_start`, `ble_start`, `wlan_ap_role_up`, `wlan_sta_role_up`, `wlan_connect`), then scans passively with NimBLE's `ble_gap_ext_disc` (100 ms interval, 70 ms window), keeps a 2,048-record log and serves the app and a JSON API on port 80 from two worker tasks. The equipment was `sim/toolsim.py` writing into the tag's USB serial port at 3 times real speed; `sim/e2e.py` timed every event from the equipment's line to the hub's log, both through the hub's UART and through its HTTP API, with the phone app open in a browser.

**How far it got.** Verified, on the bench. The codecs agree byte for byte in C and Python (9,014 checks). Seven 5 and 10 minute runs; the last:

| What | Result |
|---|---|
| Equipment lines | 1,264 sent, 1,264 good, 0 bad |
| Events at the hub | 283 of 283; median 1.4 s, 95% within 5.0 s, max 9.2 s (hub UART) |
| Totals | identical: 275 run events, 9 trips, 661 s run |
| Run summaries | 269 of 274; the hub counted the 5 it missed |
| On-tag classifier | 95.9% right on 269 live run events; 9 of 9 jams |
| Hub web server | 17 of about 2,400 requests timed out with the app and a 4-per-second poller at once; one client alone 60 of 60, mean 0.11 s |

**The line.** Nothing stopped the chain. What it took, with the cause of each wrong turn:

| Problem | Cause tag | Cost | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ble_start` refused, then the access point refused a 12-character name as "max 32 characters" | Tool or docs | 20 min | Wi-Fi first, quoted SSID |
| Hub records lost behind `Received VLAN packet - drop it` with no line end | Tool or docs | 15 min | parse the marker anywhere in a line |
| Hub froze the Bluetooth side when a client stalled | Our mistake: lock held across `send()` | one run | build under the lock, send after |
| Two 44 kB response buffers took the hub off the network | Our mistake: FreeRTOS heap has 48 kB to spare | one flash | two 24 kB buffers, 100-record pages |
| Tag died 10 to 20 s after boot | Our mistake: `snprintf` on TI's 1 kB BLE thread | 40 min | format on a task of its own |

No TI example joins a CC23xx advertiser with a CC35xx scanner and access point, so the method was worked out here. Effort: about five hours, no hands at the bench (both boards were already plugged in). Verdict: good. TI's examples did the hard parts (the stack, the scanner, the access point, DHCP). The code is about 900 lines of C and the sharp edges came from it or were small.

**Ask.** Anyone who has run a CC35xx access point and a NimBLE scan side by side for days: did the scan duty or the heap hold up?

FILE: docs/experiments/2026-10-18-am62l-renode-presilicon.md | Can the AM62L's DDR-less Zephyr image be run before the board arrives, and what does the simulator settle?

<!-- experiment
id: E208

# Can the AM62L's DDR-less Zephyr image be run before the board arrives, and what does the simulator settle?

**Short answer.** Yes, for the questions a functional simulator can answer. Antmicro's `dts2repl` turned the Zephyr build's device tree into a Renode platform (Cortex-A53, GICv3 at the AM62L's addresses, the 16550 UART0 at 0x02800000 with the K3 register stride, the 144 kB SRAM span at 0x707F0000), and the bare-EL3 image booted on it and printed `Hello World! am62l_evm/am62l3/a53`. The run found one real defect before any hardware: with 6 translation tables the kernel panics when the pin-control driver maps its registers; 8 tables fix it and cost 8 kB. The chip-specific blocks (clock tree, the two-phase boot ROM, the TIFS firmware) have no model in Renode, QEMU or gem5, and timing and power are outside a functional simulator, so those are what the board run measures. Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). 1 kB = 1,024 bytes.

**Question.** Before a TMDS62LEVM arrives, can the Zephyr image meant to run from its on-chip SRAM with the DDR never initialized be booted in a simulator, and which of the board's open questions does that settle?

**Vendor position.** The AM62L's Linux SDK documents the boot flow and the SRAM map (software-dl.ti.com, AM62LX 12.01.00.05.03, read 2026-10-18); no simulator is listed among its tools. QEMU's Arm machine list (qemu.org, "Arm System emulator") has no TI K3 entry. Renode's supported platforms (renode.readthedocs.io, "Supported boards", read 2026-10-18) include generic Cortex-A53 platforms "with GICv3 and GICv2". Renode's `dts2repl` README: "a tool for converting device tree sources into Renode's .repl files", used for the Zephyr dashboard's roughly 300 boards. Renode 1.17.0 runs natively on Apple-silicon Macs (`brew install renode/tap/renode`).

**What was tried.** 2026-10-18 on an M4 Mac (macOS 26.3). Zephyr upstream at commit a915b2f, image `build-sram-all` (`am62l-evm/zephyr/sram-all.overlay` plus `bare-el3.conf`: one core, EL3 entry, no SCMI, no PSCI, UART0 only, 144 kB SRAM at 0x707F0000). `dts2repl build-sram-all/zephyr/zephyr.dts -o am62l-sram.repl` (the tool prints nothing without `-o`). One edit to the generated file: the generic timer frequency from the tool's 62.5 MHz default to the chip's 200 MHz. Renode 1.17.0 from the Homebrew tap (the tap must be trusted first: `brew trust renode/tap`), `renode --console --disable-xwt` with `am62l-evm/zephyr/renode/run.resc`: load the platform, `sysbus LoadELF`, UART0 to a file, run three simulated seconds. Debugging with `cpu0 LogFunctionNames true` to see the function trace. Files: `am62l-evm/zephyr/renode/` (platform, script, runner).

**How far it got.** Configure, compile, link, load and run. First run: the trace went `__reset`, `z_arm64_el3_init`, `z_arm64_el2_init`, `z_arm64_el1_init`, `z_arm64_mm_init`, `arm_gic_init`, `pinctrl_ti_k3_init`, `arch_mem_map`, then `printk`, a synchronous exception, `z_fatal_error`, `arch_system_halt`: the pin-control driver maps its 0x4084000 register page, the MMU needs a new table, none is left (6 configured), the kernel logs and panics; nothing reaches the UART because the console driver initializes after pin control. Second run with `CONFIG_MAX_XLAT_TABLES=8`: boots and prints the banner and the hello line on UART0.

**The line.** No stop. The numbers: 6 translation tables fail at the pin-control mapping; 8 work; the image grows from 116 kB to 124 kB (defaults) and 120 kB (tight settings) in the 144 kB map; the 80 kB map is 44 kB over at defaults, 40 kB tight, 24 kB with no C-library heap, so the real floor for this image is 104 kB. What the simulation cannot say: whether UART0 has a clock when Zephyr starts without TIFS (Renode has no clock tree; every TI control register is a tag that reads 0), whether the boot ROM will load the image as its phase-1 payload (no ROM model), what the secure ROM does when BL-1 never reports done, and every speed, boot-time and power number (Renode is functional, not cycle-accurate). The board run measures these.

**Ask.** If you have run Zephyr on a TI K3 A53 in Renode or QEMU with a platform closer to the chip (clock and control-module models), say which files; and if you know the AM62L ROM's maximum phase-1 image size from the TRM (SPRUJB4), say the section.

# Can a reader flash every TI family on the bench with an open tool instead of CCStudio, UniFlash or the Toolbox?

For four of six families on USB today, yes or nearly: upstream OpenOCD built from git programmed TI's blink on the LP-MSPM0G3519 in 0.95 s, and TI's own OpenOCD fork programmed it on the LP-EM-CC2340R5. The LP-AM13E230 and LP-MSPM33C321A have open drivers that read the chip exactly; their write was not run here. The LP-EM-CC35X1 cannot be opened without TI's Toolbox, and the C2000 UART flasher does not build on a Mac as shipped.

Terms: [docs/vocab.md](../vocab.md). **SACI** is the CC23xx device management interface on its security access port. **NONMAIN** is the MSPM0 and MSPM33 configuration flash. **nRST** is the chip's reset pin, which the XDS110 can drive. 1 kB = 1,024 bytes.

| Board | Open tool | Result | Gate reached | Time |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| LP-MSPM0G3519 | OpenOCD master, `mspm0` driver (TI's, upstream) | Works | Backup, identity, dump equal to DSLite, blink, restore, read back equal | 0.95 s blink (6 runs, 0.86 to 1.09 s) |
| LP-EM-CC2340R5 | TI's fork `ti-openocd`, `cc23xx` driver | Works, with a broken verify step | Backup, blink written and read back right, restore, read back equal | 6.2 s, command exits 1 at verify |
| LP-AM13E230 | OpenOCD master, `am13e230x` driver (TI's, upstream) | Not run (write) | Identity and dump equal to the motor demo's build | 6.7 s for the 520 kB read |
| LP-MSPM33C321A | TI's fork, `mspm33` driver; master has none | Not run (write) | Identity and dump equal to DSLite, both tools | 5.3 s (fork), 7.8 s (master, generic) |
| LP-MSPM0C1104 | OpenOCD master, `mspm0` driver | Can't today | Identity through the configuration port only | 0.5 s |
| LP-EM-CC35X1 | TI's fork, `ti_cc35x1e_launchpad.cfg` | Can't | Debug port identity only; core port closed | n/a |
| LAUNCHXL-F2800137 | C2000Ware `serial_flash_programmer` | Can't on a Mac as shipped | Source read; host not built | n/a |
| LP-AM263P (returned) | MCU+ SDK `uart_uniflash.py`; OpenOCD `am263p-launchpad.cfg` | Not run | Docs read | n/a |

**Question.** For every TI family on the bench, can a reader flash it with an open tool (OpenOCD from git, or an open UART flasher TI ships in source) instead of CCStudio, UniFlash or the Toolbox?

**Vendor position.** OpenOCD master (`bb5a52da`, 2026-10-16) carries TI's own contributions: `tcl/target/ti/mspm0.cfg` with `src/flash/nor/mspm0.c`, `tcl/target/ti/am13e230x.cfg` with `src/flash/nor/am13e230x.c` (both "Copyright (C) 2026 Texas Instruments"), and `am263p-launchpad.cfg` on the `k3` target. Zephyr's `lp_mspm33c321a` board page says: "OpenOCD support for MSPM33 is not upstream in the OpenOCD project. A custom TI OpenOCD fork must be built before using `west flash`" and gives `git clone -b ti-release https://github.com/TexasInstruments/ti-openocd` (read 2026-10-18). TI hosts Mac builds of that fork for its VS Code debug extension at <https://software-dl.ti.com/ccs/esd/vscode/ti-embedded-debug/ti-openocd.html> (1.3.1.50, 2026-03-31; the page says later builds move to ti.com). C2000Ware's `serial_flash_programmer/README.txt`: "Before running serial_flash_programmer.exe, the microcontroller must be attached to a COM port, must be running the SCI boot loader."

**What was tried.** Intel Mac, macOS 15.7.9, 2026-10-18 14:50 to 15:30. Two OpenOCD builds:

| Build | Source | Build time on this Mac |
|---|---|---|
| Upstream | `openocd-org/openocd` master `bb5a52da`, built earlier today for the CC23xx port (`ports/openocd-cc23xx/README.md`) | 37 s make |
| TI's fork | `TexasInstruments/ti-openocd` branch `ti-release`, head `cb22a31e` (2026-07-02), GPL-2.0-or-later per its source headers (GitHub shows no license tag), `./configure --enable-cmsis-dap --enable-cmsis-dap-v2 --enable-xds110 --disable-werror` | clone 13 s, bootstrap and configure 45 s, make 54 s; reports itself as "0.12.0+dev" |

The fork adds, over master: flash drivers `mspm33.c`, `cc23xx.c`, `cc27xx.c` with a shared `cc_lpf3_base.c` and `cc_lpf3_flash.c`, its own `mspm0.c` and `am13e230x.c`; target files `ti_mspm33.cfg`, `ti_cc23xx.cfg`, `ti_cc27xx.cfg`, `ti_cc2341.cfg`, `ti_cc35x1e.cfg`; board files for the LP-MSPM33C321A, eleven CC23xx and CC27xx LaunchPad development kits and the CC35x1E LaunchPad. For the MSPM33 it adds `mspm33_board_reset`, `mspm33_factory_reset`, `mspm33_mass_erase` and `mspm33_start_bootloader`.

Every board command ran with one tool at a time on the probe, after `lsof` showed no process on its serial ports. Each board was backed up before any write, and the backups are not in the repo.

**How far it got.**

*LP-MSPM0G3519 (<probe serial>).* The board was found with main flash blank (all 0xFF; data flash and NONMAIN equal to the 2026-10-08 backup). Neither DSLite ("Connection to MSPM0 core failed") nor OpenOCD ("Could not find MEM-AP to control the core") could reach the core; the debug port answered and the configuration port read DEVICEID 0x0BBA902F. OpenOCD's `mspm0_board_reset` (nRST from the XDS110) brought the core port back. Then: DSLite backup twice, identical; OpenOCD read of main (512 kB), data (16 kB) and NONMAIN identical to DSLite; master named the part, "Chip is MSPM0G3519SPZR rev 0", where xPack 0.12.0-7 says "Unidentified PART". TI's `gpio_toggle_output` (480 bytes, built in 6 s) programmed with `program blink.hex verify reset exit` in 1.04, 0.97 and 1.09 s, and with `program blink.hex verify` plus `mspm0_board_reset` in 0.93, 0.86 and 0.89 s, each "Verified OK". PB22, PB26 and PB27 toggled about every 500 ms, read through the debugger by a second tool. Restore: TI's demo (the first 13.0 kB of the backup) written with OpenOCD, main erase 0.94 s, write 4.5 s; DSLite read main, data and NONMAIN back identical to the 2026-10-08 backup; the core runs the demo's delay loop. The board is on TI's demo, not blank: that is the state its bench row records.

*LP-EM-CC2340R5 (<probe serial>).* DSLite backup twice, identical, equal to this morning's restored tag image. TI's fork, `program blink-cc2340r5.hex verify reset exit` with TI's SDK `drivers/empty` hex: SACI chip erase, main (3 sectors) and the CCFG written over SACI, "MAIN and CCFG Programmed", then "Verify Failed: Target not examined", exit 1, no reset, 6.2 s. Read back with this repo's `cc23xx` build: main flash equal to the hex, the rest erased, CCFG equal to the board's (the user record kept); after a reset DIO14 toggled about once a second. Two more tries at 15:20 failed to connect at the same moment five probes dropped off USB (below); they are not counted. Restore with this repo's `cc23xx` driver: 512 kB written in 10.2 s, verified in 0.9 s, read back with the CPU held in the boot ROM identical to the 15:16 backup, main and CCFG; left running the tag image.

*LP-AM13E230 (<probe serial>).* Read-only by choice: the board runs the guarded FOC image with a Hall calibration. OpenOCD master with TI's `am13e230x-launchpad.cfg` (JTAG): CPUID 0x411FD210, DID 0x2F, "MAIN flash: 512 KB (256 sectors), 2 bank(s)", NONMAIN 8 kB. Main flash and NONMAIN dumped in 6.7 s; two dumps identical; main flash equal to the motor demo's `foc.out` of 2026-10-17 23:18 (71.1 kB of load image, the rest 0xFF). DHCSR read 0x01000001 before and after: the core never halted. DSLite was not used, because it connects with a halt and the FOC README says a halt leaves the PWM at its last duty. The same driver wrote this board on 2026-10-10 (12.6 kB in 0.106 s, [AM13E230 Zephyr page](2026-10-09-am13e230-zephyr-upstream.md)).

*LP-MSPM33C321A (<probe serial>).* DSLite read of main (1 MB at 0x10000000), data (32 kB) and NONMAIN (2 kB), equal to the 2026-10-17 backup. Master has no MSPM33 file, so a generic Cortex-M33 over SWD was declared: DPIDR 0x6BA02477, AP0 an AHB5 memory port, DEVICEID 0x0BBB702F from the configuration port, CPUID 0x411FD210, all three dumps identical to DSLite in 7.8 s. TI's fork with `ti_mspm33_launchpad.cfg`: three flash banks found, the same three dumps identical in 5.3 s. No write, by decision: the demo's backup is the only way back to it.

*LP-MSPM0C1104 (MC110001).* DEVICEID 0x3BBA102F from the configuration port; no core port, before or after `mspm0_board_reset` ("DebugSS failed to come up within timeout"). This board had not shown its core port since 2026-10-15. Found 2026-10-19: its program faulted before `main` and reset the chip in a loop; recovered without an unplug ([mspm0c1104-lockout-root-cause](2026-10-19-mspm0c1104-lockout-root-cause.md)), and upstream `board/ti/mspm0-launchpad.cfg` now connects to it normally.

*LP-EM-CC35X1 (<probe serial>).* The fork's `ti_cc35x1e.cfg` declares no flash bank: it is debug only. Its `init_board` runs `simplelink-wifi-toolbox programmer -i XDS110 -param1 <serial> debug --debug_action_req_path <file>` on every connect, so TI's Toolbox opens the debug port first. With `init_board` stubbed out: DPIDR 0x4BA02477, access ports 0x102E0001, 0x002E0002 and 0x002E0000, and no memory port for the core. Nothing was halted or reset.

*LAUNCHXL-F2800137.* Read only, board untouched. The host source (`serial_flash_programmer.cpp` and four files in `source/`, 5,640 lines) includes `windows.h` and `conio.h` and talks to the port with `CreateFile`, `DCB`, `ReadFile` and `WriteFile`; it ships as a Visual Studio 2019 solution and a Windows `.exe`. It lists `f280013x`. It was not built: a Mac needs that serial layer rewritten. The flash kernel for this chip is not prebuilt in the programmer folder; it is `driverlib/f280013x/examples/flash/CCS/flash_ex3_sci_flash_kernel.projectspec`, whose post-build step runs `hex2000 -boot -sci8 --boot_align_sect -a`. On the board (user guide SPRUJ32, tables 3-3 and 3-4): boot switch S3 to GPIO24 = 0 (left), GPIO32 = 1 (right) for "Boot from SCI / Wait boot", and S2 SEL1 = 0 (the default) so GPIO28 and GPIO29 reach the XDS110's serial port.

*LP-AM263P (returned to its owner).* From the MCU+ SDK 26.01.00.08 docs: `tools/boot/uart_uniflash.py` is Python (pyserial, tqdm, xmodem, pyelftools), named for COM ports and `/dev/ttyACM0`, so it should run on a Mac. It needs the board in UART boot mode (the SDK's EVM setup page shows the LaunchPad kit's switch positions as a picture), the prebuilt flash writer `sbl_prebuilt/am263px-lp/sbl_uart_uniflash.release.tiimage` and a config such as `mcelf_sbl_ospi.cfg` that lists the bootloader and the application; it writes the external OSPI flash. OpenOCD's `am263p-launchpad.cfg` sets the XDS110, JTAG at 250 kHz and the `k3` target, with no flash bank: debug and RAM load only.

**The line.**

| Family | Where it stops | Cause tag |
|---|---|---|
| MSPM0 | Nowhere for a reader. A chip with blank flash hides its core until an nRST | Tool or docs |
| CC23xx | TI's fork writes correctly but its `program` command fails at verify: its examine-start hook reads `$DEVICE_BLANK`, which is never set (`tcl/target/ti_lpf3.cfg` line 415), so the target is never examined and the reset never runs | Tool or docs |
| AM13 | Not reached: write not run here | None |
| MSPM33 | Not reached: write not run here; upstream has no driver | Tool or docs |
| CC35xx | The debug port opens only after TI's closed Toolbox sends its signed request; no flash bank for the external flash in any OpenOCD | Tool or docs |
| C2000 | No C28x core in OpenOCD; TI's UART flasher host is Windows code | Tool or docs |

How TI's fork and this repo's driver differ on the CC23xx (source read and the run above):

| | TI's fork `cc23xx` | This repo's `cc23xx` |
|---|---|---|
| Erase | SACI chip erase, once per run; later erase requests are "discarded" | The boot ROM's sector erase, only the sectors an image covers |
| Main flash write | SACI pipelined program, sectors padded with 0xFF, then a SACI check | The boot ROM's program call on the halted CPU, 2 kB at a time |
| CCFG | Written over SACI, user record skipped | Never written; refused unless equal |
| Blank chip | Its examine-start hook rewrites the CCFG permission fields from the image to allow debug and flash, then programs (code read, not run) | Not handled |
| Blink on the CC2340R5 | 6.2 s, exit 1 at verify, no reset | 0.37 s with verify and reset |

The two times are not like for like: the fork erases the whole chip and writes the CCFG; the driver here erases three sectors.

What happened along the way: at about 15:20 five probes dropped off USB together (<probe serial>, <probe serial>, <probe serial>, <probe serial>, <probe serial>) and came back by 15:25. The cause is not known; the two failed fork tries on the CC2340R5 fell in that window.

**Ask.** Would TI take the fork's `mspm33`, `cc23xx` and `cc27xx` drivers upstream, and fix the `DEVICE_BLANK` line in `ti_lpf3.cfg`? Would TI publish the CC35xx debug-unlock request so OpenOCD can open the port without the Toolbox? Would C2000Ware ship the serial flash programmer's host with a POSIX serial layer?

FILE: docs/experiments/2026-10-18-openocd-cc23xx-driver.md | Can upstream OpenOCD flash a TI LP-EM-CC2340R5 or LP-EM-CC2755P10 through the XDS110, the way it flashes an MSPM0?
==============================================================================

<!-- experiment
id: E206
board: LP-EM-CC2340R5, LP-EM-CC2755P10
date: 2026-10-18
status: waiting
reached: verified
line: On the LP-EM-CC2340R5, upstream OpenOCD with the new cc23xx driver programmed and verified TI's blink in 0.37 s and the LED pin toggled; a 511 kB image took 10.5 s to write and read back identical. An SDK hex fails verify on the 128-byte CCFG user record, and the CC2755P10 path has not run.
stop: tools; the LP-EM-CC2755P10 was away from the bench, and an SDK hex's CCFG user record differs from a programmed chip's

# Can upstream OpenOCD flash a TI LP-EM-CC2340R5 or LP-EM-CC2755P10 through the XDS110, the way it flashes an MSPM0?

Yes on the LP-EM-CC2340R5: `openocd -f board/ti_lp_em_cc2340r5.cfg -c "program blink.hex verify reset exit"` programmed TI's blink in 0.37 s with a new `cc23xx` flash driver. The CC2755P10 path builds and has not run. Code, cfg files and build steps: [ports/openocd-cc23xx/](../../ports/openocd-cc23xx/README.md).

Terms: [docs/vocab.md](../vocab.md), [LP-EM-CC2340R5 FAQ](../../cc2340r5/FAQ.md), [LP-EM-CC2755P10 FAQ](../../cc2755p10/FAQ.md). SACI is the chip's device management interface on its security access port. 1 kB = 1,024 bytes.

| Step | LP-EM-CC2340R5 | LP-EM-CC2755P10 |
|---|---|---|
| Identity and a 512 kB dump identical to DSLite's | Works | Not run |
| Reset through SACI, halt in the boot ROM | Works, 17 ms | Not run |
| Erase and write one 2 kB sector | Works, 10 ms and 34 ms | Not run |
| `program ... verify reset` of TI's blink | Works, 0.37 s, LED pin toggles | Not run |
| Put a 511 kB image back and read it identical | Works, 10.5 s plus 0.9 s verify | Not run |

**Question.** Can OpenOCD built from git program a CC23xx or CC27xx LaunchPad development kit over the XDS110's CMSIS-DAP interface, with no CCStudio or UniFlash?

**Vendor position.** OpenOCD master (2026-10-16) has target files for CC13x0, CC13x2, CC26x0, CC26x2 and CC32xx and none for CC23xx or CC27xx. TI's CC27xx TRM (SWCU195A, section 9.2.3) lists two SACI erase commands, `SACI_CMD_FLASH_ERASE_CHIP` and `SACI_CMD_FLASH_ERASE_MAIN_APP` ("Erases all (non-retained) MAIN sectors"), and `SACI_CMD_FLASH_PROG_MAIN_SECTOR`, which programs "all or a part of one MAIN sector". The SDK's `driverlib/hapi.h` gives the CPU a ROM call that erases one sector, `HapiFlashSectorErase(key, addr)`.

**What was tried.** OpenOCD master `bb5a52da` with Homebrew's autoconf, automake, libtool, pkgconf, libusb, hidapi and jimtcl, on macOS 15.7.9 (Intel). The driver (`ports/openocd-cc23xx/src/cc23xx.c`, about 930 lines) does the following:

- It identifies the chip by DEVICEID and PARTID from the configuration access port and refuses unknown parts.
- It resets through SACI (RSTCTL 0x5C, the debug-open check, EXIT_SACI_HALT, a halt in the boot ROM's wait loop), as TI's CCStudio scripts do.
- It erases and writes with the boot ROM's `HapiFlashSectorErase` and `HapiFlashProgram` on the halted CPU.
- It never sends a chip erase, refuses the HSM area (0xE8000 and up on the CC27xx), and lets a CCFG or SCFG section through only when it equals the chip's.
- It leaves the debug port dormant when OpenOCD exits.

The LP-EM-CC2340R5 was backed up twice with DSLite first, then run through the steps in the table, then put back.

**How far it got.** Verified on the LP-EM-CC2340R5. The blink's red LED pin (DIO14) read on, off, on at about 1 s steps through the debugger. The board's own image went back and read identical with the CPU held before it started. After it booted, DSLite read 139 bytes changed in the last sector: records the image writes to its settings sector at start.

**The line.**

- SACI cannot erase one 2 kB sector, so erase and write go through the CPU and the boot ROM. A chip whose CCFG closes debugging cannot be flashed this way.
- PROG_MAIN_SECTOR does not erase first, measured: 16 bytes of 0xF0 programmed over 0x0F read back 0x00, and the rest of the sector kept its 0x0F.
- A TI SDK hex fails `verify` in 128 bytes: SDK builds fill the CCFG user record with 0x00, a programmed chip has it blank, and the driver does not write it. Main flash is correct. A hex with main flash only verifies.
- OpenOCD's exit puts the SWD port in JTAG state. TI's DSLite then failed with `Error -615 ... The target failed to see a correctly formatted SWD header`. The driver's `cc23xx dormant`, run before shutdown, fixed it.

There is no TI example to start from. The nearest sources were TI's CCStudio GEL scripts (`cc23xx_dap_saci_util.gel`, `cc23xx_xds.gel`, `cc23xx_util.gel`), the two TRMs, the SDK's `hapi.h` and `flash.h`, and this repo's SACI scripts (`cc2755p10/recovery/saci_program.js`, `site/flash/cc-saci.js`).

| What went wrong | Cause | Cost | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| The plan assumed a SACI sector erase | **Tool or docs**: the TRM lists no such command and does not say PROG_MAIN_SECTOR leaves the sector unerased | About 30 min of reading | Erase and write through the boot ROM; SACI for reset and CRC |
| `program` of TI's blink hex failed `verify` | **Tool or docs**: the SDK hex's CCFG user record is 0x00, the chip's is 0xFF | One extra run | Program main flash only, or the chip's own CCFG |
| DSLite could not connect after OpenOCD (`Error -615`) | **Third-party behavior**: OpenOCD leaves an SWD port in JTAG state; TI's tools expect it dormant | One failed restore attempt | `cc23xx dormant` before shutdown, in the target files |

Effort: about 3 hours, about 15 OpenOCD and 16 DSLite sessions on one board, no hands needed, two Homebrew packages added.

Verdict: good on the CC2340R5. The whole program-verify-reset cycle for a blink is under half a second, and a full 511 kB image takes about 11 s. The CC27xx needs its first run.

1. The same gates on the LP-EM-CC2755P10 (probe LB07021W): its debug check is REQ_KEY_ID, and it adds the SCFG and HSM banks.
2. Write the CCFG user record when the chip's is blank and the image's is not, so an SDK hex verifies as is (a one-time write: the record cannot be changed afterwards without a chip erase).
3. A SACI-only path for a chip whose CPU port is closed: ERASE_MAIN_APP, then PROG_MAIN_PIPELINED, with the CCFG left in place.
4. Send the driver upstream to OpenOCD after the CC27xx run.

**Ask.** Has anyone driven EXIT_SACI_HALT on a CC27xx from a debugger other than CCStudio, and did the CPU stop at boot status 0xC1?

Sources: TI SWCU195A (CC27xx TRM) sections 9.1.3, 9.2.3, 9.2.4, 9.3.2; TI SWCU193A (CC23xx TRM) section 8.3.2.2; CCStudio 21.0.1 `ccs_base/emulation/gel/cc23xx_*.gel`; SimpleLink Low Power F3 SDK 9.21.00.36 `driverlib/hapi.h`, `flash.h`; OpenOCD `src/target/adi_v5_swd.c`, `src/flash/nor/rp2xxx.c`. Logs: `ports/openocd-cc23xx/README.md`, test log.

# Does a popular ESP32 Bluetooth gamepad library carry over to TI, ST and C2000 boards, and on which boards does it give the same bytes?

Same bytes on five boards. On the LP-EM-CC2340R5 the Bluetooth gamepad runs as far as advertising and Device Information; a Mac received the live build's button presses as HID reports, 15 of 15. The port is in [`ports/esp32-ble-gamepad/`](../../ports/esp32-ble-gamepad/README.md).

Terms: [docs/vocab.md](../vocab.md). 1 kB = 1,024 bytes. Measured 2026-10-19 and 2026-10-20 on an Intel Mac, macOS 15.7.9.

**Question.** [ESP32-BLE-Gamepad](https://github.com/lemmingDev/ESP32-BLE-Gamepad) (lemmingDev, MIT, 1,602 stars, 25 open issues, last push 2026-09-21) is a Bluetooth LE gamepad library for Arduino-ESP32. Its README lists CI builds for four Espressif chips including the ESP32-C6. Which of its parts run on other boards, and does a fresh AI assistant, started from this repo's `llms.txt` and `PORTING.md`, get there?

**Vendor position.** Espressif's Arduino core and NimBLE-Arduino carry the project; the library states that it "depends only on NimBLE-Arduino and has no chip-specific code". TI ships no HID-over-GATT example for the CC2340R5 (`ports/ble-hid-remote/README.md`). TI's CCStudio 21.0.1 ships a migration skill, `ti-ccstudio-migrate-to-ti`, for non-TI sources.

**What was tried.**

- Expectation, written before any build: the C6 builds the library as shipped; the report is 20 bytes (the job text said start and select are on by default); the ST and TI cores match the C6 bytes; the C28x differs because it has no 8-bit type; the CC2340R5 run exceeds its time budget on the HID service.
- Original: the unmodified library, NimBLE-Arduino 2.5.1, Arduino-ESP32 3.3.12 (arduino-cli), plus a check sketch that prints the descriptor and four reports. The ESP32-C6 was board A; its backup was read first and written back at the end.
- Targets: one fresh Sonnet 5.5 run per board from a script with a job text: the repository and commit, the board and probe, "start from llms.txt and PORTING.md". Three runs on the LP-EM-CC2340R5: two with this repo's docs, one told to use TI's migration skill. The three CC2340R5 runs were build-only, because the debug link was down at that point; run 1's image was flashed afterwards, once a probe reseat restored the link.
- The check after each run: `check/gp_serial.py` reads the console and compares MAP and RPT1 to RPT4 with the C6 golden file.

**How far it got.**

| Board | Reached | Result | Run time |
|---|---|---|---|
| ESP32-C6 | verified | library: 5 of 5 lines are the reference; Mac scan and 12 connects (3 windows of 4) pass | n/a |
| ESP32-C6, G3519's core | verified | 5 of 5 lines same: the code a fresh run wrote for another chip agrees with the library on the original chip | n/a |
| LP-MSPM0G3519 | verified | 5 of 5 lines same; 9.9 kB flash, 2.0 kB RAM | 15.3 min, 48 turns |
| NUCLEO-U083RC | verified | 5 of 5 lines same; 3.6 kB flash, 880 B RAM | 5.3 min, 28 turns |
| LAUNCHXL-F2800137 | verified | 5 of 5 lines same; 8.1 kB of code, run from RAM | 9.9 min, 41 turns |
| LP-EM-CC2340R5, docs, run 1 | verified | host proof same; image 189.4 kB flash, 33.8 kB RAM; flashed: 5 of 5 lines same on the UART, advertises, Device Information equal to the C6's | 7.7 min, 31 turns |
| LP-EM-CC2340R5, docs, run 2 | link | host proof same; image 188.5 kB flash, 33.9 kB RAM | 6.9 min, 29 turns |
| LP-EM-CC2340R5, TI migration skill | link | host proof same; image 189.4 kB flash, 33.4 kB RAM | 8.3 min, 45 turns |
| Restore, CC2340R5 | done | the tag image written back from the two equal reads; CCFG identical; 140 bytes differ in the last flash sector (0x7F000 to 0x7FFFF, settings the firmware rewrites after boot) | |
