# Can an LP-MSPM0C1104 with 1 kB of RAM drive a 128 x 128 Sharp screen?

**Short answer.** Yes. Drawing one row band at a time, the chip showed a title, shapes and a live counter on the BOOSTXL-SHARP128 with 4.9 kB of its 16 kB of flash and 609 B of its 1 kB of RAM. A 2 kB frame buffer cannot exist on this chip, and none is needed. The cost is time: 154 ms for the whole picture with 1-row bands, 41 ms with 16-row bands.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md) (RAM, stack, SPI, linker). FAQ: [LP-MSPM0C1104](../../mspm0c1104/FAQ.md). Code and tests: [Sharp128 README](../../portability/boosterpacks/sharp128/README.md). 1 kB = 1,024 bytes.

**Question.** The panel needs 2 kB for a full picture and the chip has 1 kB. Does it fit at all, and what does it cost?

**Vendor position.** SLAU786 describes the panel and the pins and says nothing about RAM; TI ships no example for this BoosterPack on any MSPM0 kit (MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07, searched 2026-10-07 and 2026-10-20). The panel takes a picture one row at a time, each row addressed on its own (Sharp LS013B7DH03 specification), so a frame buffer is a choice and not a need.

**What was tried.** LP-MSPM0C1104 on probe MC110001 with the BOOSTXL-SHARP128 stacked, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS at -Os, SPI at 1.000 MHz read back from the chip. Expectation written before the run: flash under 8 kB, RAM under 700 B, the picture complete, and a full picture in 40 to 80 ms (wire time 21 to 24 ms plus drawing). The code is `portability/boosterpacks/sharp128/` (`sg_render_bands` draws the scene once per band; `examples/hello/hello.c`). The chip's SysTick does nothing, so the clock is TIMG14. Five band heights were built and run.

**How far it got.**

- Built: 4.9 kB of flash, 609 B of RAM with a 512 B stack.
- Ran: the program reached its counter loop (23 counts after 6 s at four a second) and stayed there; a camera frame shows the panel lit with shapes, too small to read the text; a look at the panel confirms the picture.
- Stack: the painted stack showed 352 of 512 B used; the generated linker file's 64 B default would overflow.
- Measured, one run each (whole picture drawn and sent): 1 row 153.7 ms and 609 B of RAM; 2 rows 92.7 ms and 625 B; 4 rows 63.3 ms and 657 B; 8 rows 49.3 ms and 721 B; 16 rows 41.1 ms and 849 B. One 1-row update takes 260 us. The bus carried a thousand bytes in 9.5 ms against 8 ms of clock.
- Stretch (video from a microSD card with Petit FatFs, no frame buffer): the player is built (7.2 kB of flash, 779 B of RAM) and runs on a Mac against a simulated card, 30 of 30 frames equal; on the board it stops at the card check because no card is on the bench.

**The line.** Not reached for the screen. The expectation held: the picture fits in 609 B and the time is inside 40 to 80 ms from 4-row bands up. The 1-row case is slower (154 ms) because the scene is drawn 128 times. The video path stops at **no microSD card on the bench** (error -2, card not ready); its frame rate is unknown. The simulated 30 frames a second counts bus time only.

- A card in the slot: copy `VIDEO.BIN` from `player/video_to_frames.py`, run `boards/c1104_run.py` on `player.out`, read `player_res` (frames, late, fps, card rate).
- Drawing faster: the scene redraw per band is most of the 154 ms; a scene built from rows or sprites would cost little per band.
- A faster byte loop: the bus runs at 84 percent of the clock rate because of CPU gaps between bytes.
- 256-byte reads with Petit FatFs (16 rows) to cut card reads from 16 to 8 a frame.

**Ask.** Has anyone driven this panel from a 1 kB part with a different method, or measured the microSD video path with a card? Reports are welcome.

==============================================================================

<!-- experiment

-->
# Can the LP-MSPM0G5187's TinyEngine NPU run fixed DSP filters faster than the CPU?

**Short answer.** Yes. On 256-sample blocks at 80 MHz the NPU of the LP-MSPM0G5187 runs a 64-tap FIR (four channels) in 0.566 ms and an 8-band filter bank in 0.967 ms. TI's compiler for the CPU takes 16.824 ms and 36.713 ms, so 29.7 and 38.0 times slower. Against hand-written C loops the gain is 21.6 times for four FIR channels and 5.8 times for one. Every image returned the integer reference byte for byte.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). FAQ: [LP-MSPM0G5187](../../mspm0g5187/FAQ.md). Folder with code, models and every run: [mspm0g5187/npu-dsp](../../mspm0g5187/npu-dsp/README.md). NPU is the chip's neural processing unit. NNC is TI's neural network compiler. 1 kB = 1,024 bytes.

**Question.** Many DSP steps are the same math as network layers. Can a hand-built graph with fixed weights run them on the NPU, faster than the CPU?

**Vendor position.** TI's NNC guide (v2.1.2) lists the layers the NPU accepts and says "Support for layer configs that can run on the hardware NPU accelerator will improve as we implement more microcode." A first convolution with one input channel (FCONV) takes any kernel height with width 1 and output channels in multiples of 4, which fits a FIR. Max pooling and 1x1 convolutions are listed. A fully connected layer needs at least 16 inputs with 8-bit weights.

**Expectation, written before the runs.** FIR and bank on the NPU. NPU 0.7 to 1.5 ms and 1.4 to 3 ms; NNC CPU 10 to 20 ms and 20 to 40 ms; ratios 8x to 20x. Weight error near minus 45 to minus 50 dB; end to end 35 to 40 dB. NPU output within 1 count of the reference. A hand-written C FIR near 1.8 ms for one channel, so the gain against it only 1x to 3x.

**What was tried.** Eight graphs, built as ONNX in the integer form of TI's NPU quantization flow, no training: FIR (4 filters, 64 taps), the same with stride 4, an 8-band bank, the bank with a max pool over the block and a 1x1 comparator (four variants), and a 64-point DFT as a fully connected layer. Each was compiled by NNC 2.1.2 for the NPU and as CPU code, linked bare metal with int8 input and output, run on the board with a checked first call and 20 timed calls, and compared with hand-written C for the FIR and the bank.

**How far it got.** Verified. Compiler reports list FCONV, MAXPOOL, PWCONV and FC as offloaded. All 16 images returned 0 differing output bytes.

| Graph | NPU | NNC CPU | NPU against NNC CPU | Hand-written C |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| FIR, 4 channels | 0.566 ms | 16.824 ms | 29.7x | 12.224 ms; one channel 3.286 ms |
| FIR, 4 channels, stride 4 | 0.185 ms | 4.304 ms | 23.3x | |
| Filter bank, 8 bands | 0.967 ms | 36.713 ms | 38.0x | 22.742 ms |
| Bank, max pool 256, comparator | 0.677 ms | 33.273 ms | 49.1x | |
| DFT, 64 points | 0.195 ms | 0.830 ms | 4.3x | |

**What differed from the expectation.**
- The NPU was faster than predicted (0.566 ms against 0.7 to 1.5): 1.45 multiply-adds per cycle on the FIR, 1.69 on the bank. The ratio to the NNC CPU build (29.7x and 38x) is above the predicted 8x to 20x because that build takes about 20 cycles per multiply-add.
- The hand-written C FIR was slower than predicted: 16 cycles per tap, 3.286 ms, not 1.8 ms. The fair single-filter gain is therefore 5.8x, not 1x to 3x. The NPU cannot run fewer than four output channels.
- End-to-end accuracy was 34.6 to 35.4 dB, just under the 35 to 40 dB predicted; the taps alone gave 42.7 to 53.5 dB. A signal of about 35 counts rms cannot beat about 36 dB through an 8-bit output that floors.
- The 64-point DFT reached only 0.26 multiply-adds per cycle (4.3x).

**What stopped or surprised.** The first compile of the comparator left the 1x1 layer on the CPU. The cause found: a re-scaling shift of exactly 2^0 let the compiler drop a multiply, so the layer pattern no longer matched. A shift of 2^-1 offloaded it (PWCONV listed). A comparator on a signed band output sees positive peaks only.

**Not measured.** Energy, a streaming loop with the 63-sample overlap, CPU work beside the NPU, a second flash of each image, the LP-AM13E230.

Method, accuracy tables, limits and reproduce commands: [README](../../mspm0g5187/npu-dsp/README.md). Results rows for the store: `mspm0g5187/npu-dsp/RESULTS-ROWS.csv`.

**The line.** No limit reached on the chip. Output channels come in multiples of 4, the weights are 8-bit (about 35 dB end to end), and the DFT reaches only 0.26 multiply-adds per cycle.

**Ask.** Has anyone run a fixed-weight filter on this NPU with more than 8-bit accuracy needs, or on the LP-AM13E230? Reports are welcome.

<!-- experiment

line: A Zephyr hello world linked into the AM62L's 144 KB of on-chip SRAM, loaded over JTAG into the Cortex-A53 with the DDR never initialized, no TF-A and no TIFS, boots at EL3 and prints its banner and the hello line on UART0 at 115200. # Can Zephyr run on the AM62L's Cortex-A53 from on-chip SRAM with the DDR never initialized?

**Short answer.** Yes, for hello world. A JTAG load of the 124 KB `build-sram-all` image into the 144 KB of SRAM at 0x707F0000 starts one A53 core at EL3, and UART0 prints `*** Booting Zephyr OS build a915b2f12675 ***` and `Hello World! am62l_evm/am62l3/a53`. UART0 is clocked and on rate with no TIFS firmware, no TF-A and no DDR running. The pin-control write that Zephyr makes at start-up landed, so the pad partition is unlocked once the boot ROM has run. The earlier Renode run (the same image booting in a simulator) held on the chip. Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). FAQ: [AM62L](../../am62l-evm/FAQ.md). 1 KB = 1,024 bytes.

**Question.** Can Zephyr run on one A53 core of the AM62L from the chip's on-chip SRAM, with the LPDDR4 never initialized and no firmware under it, and does the console UART work in that state?

**Vendor position.** The AM62L evaluation module user guide (SPRUJG8B, tables 2-5 to 2-9) gives the boot-mode switch settings; the shipped settings are full pincount, BOOTMODE 0x0243, primary boot from the SD card (MMCSD port 1), no backup, 25 MHz clock. Zephyr's `am62l_evm` board in upstream (commit a915b2f) is written for a start from U-Boot with the DDR up and TF-A and TIFS running; its documentation loads the image from U-Boot or debugs it with OpenOCD newer than 0.12.0. No document read for this run describes a start with the DDR off.

**What was tried.** 2026-10-21 on an M4 Mac with CCStudio 21.0.1 (DSLite 21.0.0.4166) and the board's on-board XDS110 (firmware 3.0.0.32; DSLite warns it wants 3.0.0.43 and proceeds). Boot switches as shipped, with no SD card in the slot, so the boot ROM waits in its SD loop. Image: `build-sram-all` (`am62l-evm/zephyr/sram-all.overlay` plus `bare-el3.conf`: one core, EL3 entry, no SCMI, no PSCI, UART0 only, 8 translation tables), one load segment at 0x707F0000, entry 0x707F08BC, built on a second Mac against Zephyr a915b2f. Connection: `am62l-evm/tools/load_sram.sh --list-cores` shows CortexA53_0, CortexA53_1 and SMS_CM4_0_TIFS. The stock CCStudio board file's A53 startup script (GEL) sets the PLL and runs the DDR initialization on connect, so the run uses a copy of the board file with the GEL removed (`am62l-evm/tools/AM62L_TMDS62LEVM_nogel_board.xml`) and a connection file that lists all the drivers the A53 needs (`cortexA53`, `cortexM`, `etbcs`, `csstm`, `ctset2` beside the DAP driver; with only the DAP driver DSLite answers "An invalid processor ID has been found"). `load_sram.sh --listen --core 0` halts A53_0 in the ROM's wait loop, writes the ELF, sets the program counter to the entry point and leaves the core running. UART A (the FT4232 port A, the SoC's UART0) is read by `am62l-evm/tools/capture.py`, which opens the port and sets 115200 itself. Files: `am62l-evm/tools/`, `am62l-evm/zephyr/`.

**How far it got.** Configure, compile, link, load, run and verified. The capture log has the banner and the hello line 9.836 s after the capture started; the 9 s is DSLite's connect and load, not the chip. Reads after the run (`load_sram.sh --peek`): the kernel's current thread is the idle thread (main returned), the UART0 line-status register reads 0x60 (transmitter empty), the mode register MDR1 reads 0, and the pad registers for UART0 RXD and TXD (0x040841B4 and 0x040841B8) hold 0x00050000 and 0x00010000, the values Zephyr's pin-control driver writes. Separately, a 'U' stream image (`am62l-evm/zephyr/apps/uart-stream`, a polled `uart_poll_out` loop) produced 11.6 kB/s of clean 0x55 bytes, which is 115200 baud at 10 bits per byte, so the line rate is exact.

**The line.** No stop. The numbers: 124 KB image in a 144 KB map (20 KB spare); one core at EL3; DDR never initialized; no firmware under it. What the run does not show: any speed (no CoreMark, no memory timing), any boot time (the 9 s is the debugger, and the ROM was not involved), any power figure, whether the boot ROM accepts the image as its phase-1 payload (not run; it needs a signed image and the UART boot setting), the second A53 core, or any peripheral beyond UART0. The load went through the debugger, so this says the chip can run the image, not that a product could start it that way. A serial lesson from the run: on macOS a baud set with `stty -f` in one command reverts when that command closes the port, so a following `cat` reads at 9600 and a 115200 line looks silent; set the rate in the same program that reads.

**Ask.** If you know the AM62L boot ROM's maximum phase-1 image size or the format it expects for a UART-boot payload, say the TRM (SPRUJB4) section. If you have run a K3 A53 from SRAM with the DDR off and a different UART setup, say what you saw.

<!-- experiment
id: E27
board: LP-MSPM33C321A
date: 2026-10-21
status: parked
reached: run
line: The board's QSPI flash was read twice with the SDK read path (identical, 16 MB part), the Doom data file was written into a blank run of it without touching the out-of-box video, and the rp2040-doom engine ran all three demos from it on the chip with the same frame checksums as the emulator. Frame time is 45.7 ms with a 16 kB cache and 50.3 ms with 8 kB (21.9 and 19.9 frames a second) with the display and sound stubbed; the QSPI wait is 8.6 and 13.1 ms of it.
stop: speed
-->
# Can the LP-MSPM33C321A's QSPI flash be dumped safely and hold the Doom data file?

**Short answer.** Yes. The 16 MB QSPI flash was read twice (identical, SHA-256 `7928a618...acd1a5`), the video that came with the board occupies only its first 197 kB, and the 1,758 kB Doom data file went into a blank run at offset 0x640000. A third dump showed every byte outside that run unchanged. The engine then played all three demos from the chip with the emulator's frame checksums.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). 1 kB = 1,024 bytes; 1 MB = 1,048,576 bytes. **WHX** is the converted game-data file; **QE** is the flash's quad-enable bit.

**Expectation (written before the first board run).** The file reads back with CRC-32 `e9018e36` in about 175 ms; the three frame-checksum chain values equal the emulator's (`fe183649`, `c6686ada`, `fc7b6c2d`) and so do the cache counters; a frame takes about 41 ms with an 8 kB cache (3.6 million instructions at 1.3 cycles plus 549 misses at 22 microseconds) and about 37 ms with 16 kB; QSPI share about 12 ms.

**Question.** Can the LP-MSPM33C321A's on-board QSPI flash be read in full without losing the video that shipped in it, and can it hold the 1,758 kB Doom data file so the engine runs on the chip?

**Vendor position.** The board guide lists an 8 MB NOR flash. The chip's own identification and SFDP density say 16 MB (JEDEC C2 20 18); the guide's figure is wrong for this board.

**What was tried.** A read-only identify and dump (twice), a guarded write of the data file into a blank run, a third dump to prove nothing else moved, then the engine on the chip with a software page cache over the QSPI. The steps, guards and results are in the next section.

**How far it got.** Run: all three demos play to the end on the chip with the emulator's frame checksums, 19.9 frames a second with an 8 kB cache and 21.9 with 16 kB.

**The line.** Speed with the display and sound stubbed: 50.3 ms a frame at 8 kB and 45.7 ms at 16 kB, of which the QSPI wait is 13.1 and 8.6 ms. A 16 kB cache leaves 2.7 kB of RAM free. The panel, keys and sound are not on.

**Ask.** Has anyone read the same flash part with a different tool and found a different density than the board guide's 8 MB? The display and keys work needs the Educational BoosterPack stacked on this board.

## What was done

Plan: dump twice and compare, write only into a blank run behind guards, dump a third time and compare. Code: `ports/doom/m33-whx/board/` (`qspi_dump.c`, `qspi_write.c`, `doom_board.syscfg`, build scripts) and `ports/doom/m33-whx/tools/` (`qspi_host.py`, `run_board.py`). Dumps and logs stay outside the repository (the dump is TI's video).

| Step | Result |
|---|---|
| Identify (read-only) | ID C2 20 18; SFDP density 0x07FFFFFF bits, so 16 MB, not the 8 MB the board guide says; status 0x40 (QE already set, no block-protect bit); config register 0x07; normal read and fast read agree on the first 64 bytes |
| Dump A and B | 128 blocks of 128 kB each, every block checked against a CRC-32 computed on the chip; the two files are identical; 12 to 13 minutes each over the probe |
| Where the data is | Blocks 0 to 3 of 64 kB hold the video; the last non-0xFF byte is at 0x302FD; everything above is 0xFF. Highest blank run of 28 blocks: 0xE40000 to the end of the 16 MB. Offset 0x640000 (the plan's figure for an 8 MB part) is blank too and was used |
| Write | 14 chunks, 7,033 pages of 256 bytes, 0.2 to 0.4 s of chip time per 128 kB. Guards on the chip: ID, no protect bit, window, staged-data CRC, target all 0xFF, read-back compare. Each chunk: blank_ok 1, verify_bad 0 |
| Dump C | Outside 0x640000..0x7F7877 equal to dump A; the run equals `DOOM1.whx` byte for byte |
| Run on the chip | Section below |

Changes from the plan, each forced by what the chip or the board showed:
1. The size is 16 MB, not 8 MB. A larger part only adds room; the dump covers all of it.
2. Command 0x35 is not sent. On this Macronix part it enters QPI mode; the config register is read with 0x15.
3. The data does not leave over the application UART. The Education BoosterPack covers those pins, so each 128 kB block goes to chip RAM and the host reads it with DSLite. A DSLite `load` of 4 bytes is the request; it restarts the program, so the mailbox sits outside every linked section. DSLite counts the length of a memory range in 32-bit words.
4. The QE bit was already set, so the quad read (0xEB, 1-4-4, 6 dummy clocks, 40 MHz) needed no write to the flash status register.

## Run on the chip (Doom, all three demos)

Image: rp2040-doom with the page cache, 30 kB zone, `PXINIT=1`, 160 MHz, clock stepped 35 ms a read as in the emulator so the demos play the same tics per frame. Frame time is DWT cycles in the frame loop with the checksum time left out; the display and sound are stubs. The file in flash is checked against its CRC-32 before the demos start.

| | Chip | Emulator |
|---|---|---|
| File in flash | CRC-32 `e9018e36`, read in 339 ms (7,033 reads) | n/a |
| Frame-checksum chain after demo 1, 2, 3 | `fe183649`, `c6686ada`, `fc7b6c2d` | same |
| Frames, game tics at the end | 1,736 / 3,092 / 3,881; 5,197 / 9,235 / 11,571 | same |
| Cache reads, all three demos (8 kB) | 2,131,318 misses in 125.7 million accesses (98.33, 98.36, 98.17 % per demo) | same, count for count |

| Cache | Frame time, mean (longest) | Frames a second | QSPI wait a frame | Misses a frame | RAM free |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8 kB | 50.3 ms (104.8) | 19.9 | 13.1 ms (worst 27.6) | 549 | 10.7 kB |
| 16 kB | 45.7 ms (97.8) | 21.9 | 8.6 ms (worst 20.3) | 360 | 2.7 kB |
| 8 kB with hit counters | 61.6 ms | 16.2 | 13.1 ms | 549 | |

Per demo at 8 kB: 51.0, 47.4 and 53.6 ms a frame; demo 3 is the busiest, as in the emulator.

What the numbers say:
- A miss costs 23.8 microseconds, 3.8k cycles. The bus time is 526 clocks at 40 MHz (2.1k CPU cycles); the SDK's polled read adds about 1.7k. The model assumed 400 cycles of software, so the model's QSPI wait (8.6 ms at 8 kB) was 1.5 times too low; the model's preference for 128-byte pages may not hold, since the software cost per read is higher than it assumed (not run).
- The CPU part of a frame is 37.1 ms at either cache size, which is about 5.9 million cycles for the 3.6 million instructions the emulator counts: 1.65 cycles an instruction (flash wait states, branches, byte accesses).
- The expectation said 41 ms (8 kB) and 37 ms (16 kB); the chip took 50.3 and 45.7 ms. The QSPI term was right (12 ms expected, 13.1 measured); the CPU term was low (29 ms expected, 37.1 measured, 1.3 against 1.65 cycles an instruction).
- Each displayed frame here holds three game tics. The three demos advance at 59.7 tics a second at 8 kB and 65.7 at 16 kB, against the 35 the game needs, so the engine runs the demo logic 1.7 to 1.9 times faster than real time. At real-time pacing a frame holds about one tic and costs less than these figures; that case was not measured.
- Counting cache hits costs 11 ms a frame (61.6 against 50.3): the counters are in the hottest path, so the timing builds leave them out.

## What this does not cover

The screen, the keys and the sound are stubs. The six levels the demos do not play, save and load and the automap were not run. One chip, one flash. The video was not played after the write (nobody at the board); the dump comparison shows its 197 kB unchanged.

## Reproduce

```bash
# read-only dump (flash the firmware, then the host script, both under the probe lock)
ports/doom/m33-whx/board/build_qspi_dump.sh
python3 tools/frl/lock.py exec --serial <probe> -- python3 -I ports/doom/m33-whx/tools/qspi_host.py dump <out.bin>
python3 -I ports/doom/m33-whx/tools/qspi_host.py analyze <out.bin> 28
# write the data file (guarded), then run the engine
ports/doom/m33-whx/board/build_qspi_write.sh
python3 tools/frl/lock.py exec --serial <probe> -- python3 -I ports/doom/m33-whx/tools/qspi_host.py write ports/doom/wad-cache/DOOM1.whx 0x640000 <dumpA.bin>
WHXCACHE=8 PXINIT=1 BOARD=1 WHX_CRC32=0xe9018e36 ports/doom/m33-whx/build.sh 30
python3 tools/frl/lock.py exec --serial <probe> -- python3 -I ports/doom/m33-whx/tools/run_board.py <doom.out> c8
```
The figures are in the tables above.

# Does TI's Jailhouse hypervisor run on the AM62L EVM, and how fast do its demo cells start?

**Short answer.** Yes, as TI documents it. With the Jailhouse kernel and device tree from the SDK image on a USB stick, `jailhouse enable` took 0.27 s, the bare-metal `uart-demo` and `gic-demo` printed on UART1 at once, and the Linux inmate booted to a login on UART1 about 20 s after `cell start`. Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). FAQ: [AM62L](../../am62l-evm/FAQ.md). 1 KB = 1,024 bytes.

**Question.** TI ships a Jailhouse image for the TMDS62LEVM. Does its documented demo sequence run, what does each stage cost in time, and does the second core run an inmate while Linux stays up on the first?

**Vendor position.** TI documents the flow in the Linux SDK 12.01.00.05.03 Hypervisor page, Jailhouse: https://software-dl.ti.com/processor-sdk-linux/esd/AM62LX/12_01_00_05_03/exports/docs/linux/Foundational_Components/Hypervisor/Jailhouse.html . This run follows its commands. TI's page boots from an SD card; this run booted from a USB stick (below). The page names no Zephyr or FreeRTOS inmate.

**What was tried.** 2026-10-22 from 14:32 to 14:46 on one board, console on UART A, inmate output on UART1 (FT4232 port B), both at 115200.

- Files: from `tisdk-jailhouse-image-am62lxx-evm-12.01.00.05.03.rootfs.wic.xz` (sha256 26f62e139ac72b644be93ef3fe9d42173cfa4152f861dba81547483d370ce5e0) the Jailhouse kernel (`Image-jailhouse`, version 6.18.38-ti-g7bb6651c0bbf-dirty), its device tree (`dtb-jailhouse/k3-am62l3-evm.dtb`, with a 1 GB no-map reservation `jailhouse@c0000000` at 0xC0000000), the inmate cpio (142 MB), `/usr/sbin/jailhouse`, `/usr/share/jailhouse`, the kernel module directory and `/usr/lib/firmware/jailhouse.bin` were copied under new names onto the USB stick that already held the default image. The image's root partition does not fit the stick, so only these were copied. The image's own `tiboot3.bin`, `tispl.bin` and `u-boot.img` differ from the default image's (TI's page says its U-Boot carries a fix for the reserved memory) and were sent over UART.
- Boot: `reboot` from Linux returned the ROM to UART boot with SW3 as set for UART boot; `am62l-evm/tools/uart_boot.py` sent the three files (U-Boot reached 415.6 s after the ROM ping), then at `=>`:

```
usb start
load usb 0:2 ${loadaddr} /boot/Image-jailhouse
load usb 0:2 ${fdtaddr} /boot/dtb-jailhouse/k3-am62l3-evm.dtb
setenv bootargs console=ttyS0,115200n8 earlycon=ns16550a,mmio32,0x02800000 root=/dev/sda2 rootwait rw cma=64M
booti ${loadaddr} - ${fdtaddr}
```

  TI's page gives no kernel arguments and lists no overlay; `cma=64M` is the value in the image's `uEnv.txt`. No `fdt apply` was used. Kernel start to login prompt: 22.7 s. The kernel reserved `jailhouse@c0000000` (1,048,576 KiB) and reported 2 GB RAM.
- Demo sequence, commands from TI's page, run as root on UART A:

```
modprobe jailhouse
jailhouse enable /usr/share/jailhouse/cells/k3-am62l3-evm.cell
jailhouse cell create /usr/share/jailhouse/cells/k3-am62l3-evm-inmate-demo.cell
jailhouse cell load inmate-demo /usr/share/jailhouse/inmates/uart-demo.bin
jailhouse cell start inmate-demo
jailhouse cell shutdown inmate-demo
jailhouse cell destroy inmate-demo
(create, load gic-demo.bin and start the same way)
jailhouse cell create /usr/share/jailhouse/cells/k3-am62l3-evm-linux-demo.cell
jailhouse cell load k3-am62l3-evm-linux-demo /usr/libexec/jailhouse/linux-loader.bin -a 0x0 -s "kernel=0xc0800000 dtb=0xc0600000" -a 0x1000 /boot/Image-jailhouse -a 0xc0800000 /boot/tisdk-jailhouse-inmate-am62lxx-evm.cpio -a 0xc314a000 /usr/share/jailhouse/inmate-k3-am62l3-evm.dtb -a 0xc0600000
jailhouse cell start k3-am62l3-evm-linux-demo
jailhouse cell shutdown k3-am62l3-evm-linux-demo
jailhouse cell destroy k3-am62l3-evm-linux-demo
jailhouse disable
```

  The Linux load line differs from TI's only in the kernel file name (`/boot/Image-jailhouse` for TI's `/boot/Image`).

**How far it got.** Configure, load, run and verified for each stage.

| Stage | Result | Time |
|---|---|---|
| `modprobe jailhouse` | rc 0 | not timed |
| `jailhouse enable` | hypervisor v0.12 on CPU 1 and CPU 0, SMMU, PVU and PCI units, root cell `k3-am62l3-evm` running on CPUs 0 and 1, UART A kept working | 0.27 s |
| `uart-demo` | `Hello N from cell!` on UART1 with no pad or clock setup beyond TI's cell and device tree; 7,852 lines in the first 15 s (the line rate of 115200 baud) | first line within 1 s of `cell start` |
| `gic-demo` | `Initializing the GIC...`, `Initializing the timer...`, then one `Timer fired` line about every 105 ms; 359 samples: jitter 764 ns minimum, 16,919 ns maximum, 1,499 ns mean | first line within 1 s of `cell start` |
| Linux inmate | kernel 6.18.38 boots from the 142 MB cpio on UART1 (ttyS3), login banner, `root` logs in, `nproc` 1; the root cell sees CPU 0 only while it runs | `cell load` 5.07 s; kernel first line within 1 s of `cell start`; login banner about 20 s after |
| shutdown, destroy, `jailhouse disable` | rc 0; CPU 1 returned to the root cell (`online` 0-1) | disable 0.09 s |

While a cell was created or destroyed the root cell logged `scmi_protocol scmi_dev.1: Timeout waiting for a free TX channel !` once each time, and `disable` logged an `OF: ERROR: memory leak, expected refcount 1 instead of 5` for the virtual PCI node. Nothing stopped and no later command failed; no cause was investigated. The timings are the host clock at the moment the command was sent against the host-stamped UART1 capture, good to about one second except `enable`, `load` and `disable`, which are `time` figures from the board.

**After the run.** A `reboot` from the Jailhouse kernel (hypervisor disabled and the module removed first) put the ROM back in UART boot and the ROM pinged, but three sends of `tiboot3.bin` (the image's own once, the default image's twice) were each followed by 330 s without the ping from SPL for `tispl.bin`; the same sender had passed twice that day, including once from a warm `reboot`. The board was left in that state and needs a full power cycle (J17), after which the default kernel boots with its usual U-Boot commands. **Tag: Unknown.** Cause not found.

**The line.** No stop on TI's documented flow. What the run does not show: inmate-to-root traffic (`ivshmem-demo`, the shared-memory network, the crash test), a Zephyr or FreeRTOS cell, interrupt latency under load, power, a cell started after Linux has run for hours, or the micro-SD boot TI's page assumes (the card on hand failed earlier the same day). The expectations written before the run were mostly cautious: UART1 was expected to stay silent until its pads and clock were set; it printed with the SDK's configuration unchanged.

**Zephyr as an inmate (research only, no build).** Upstream Zephyr has Jailhouse pieces: a `jailhouse_debug_console` driver (`drivers/console/jailhouse_debug_console.c`), Jailhouse mentions in the board docs of the NXP i.MX93 EVK, NXP LS1046A RDB and MediaTek Genio 510 and 700 EVKs, and an ivshmem service (`doc/services/virtualization/ivshmem.rst`). The Jailhouse tree and NXP's fork carry Zephyr cell files for other boards (`configs/arm64/imx8mp-zephyr.c`, `imx8mm-zephyr.c`, `qemu-arm64-zephyr-demo.c`). None is for the AM62L. The earlier Zephyr image (45.1 kB, linked at 0xE0000000, ring console at 0xEFFFF000, EL1) lies inside TI's 1 GB reserved window (0xC0000000 to 0xFFFFFFFF); a cell would need the AM62L cell file's memory region for it, a CPU 1 assignment, and either UART1 (the inmate-demo cell already grants it) or the ring. That is port work and was not run.

**Ask.** If you know why the root cell logs the SCMI `Timeout waiting for a free TX channel` on each cell create and destroy (the inmate's CPU is stopped and restarted through PSCI), say where it is documented.

# Can Linux run on one A53 core of the AM62L and Zephyr on the other, with no hypervisor?

**Short answer.** Yes, for a Zephyr hello world with a timer tick beside a booted Linux. U-Boot started Zephyr on core 1 with a PSCI `CPU_ON` call; Linux then booted on core 0 with `maxcpus=1 mem=1536M cpuidle.off=1`. Three minutes after Linux came up, `/sys/devices/system/cpu/online` read 0 and Linux read Zephyr's console ring at 0xEFFFF000 through `/dev/mem`: the head counter moved from 5,888 to 5,954 (bytes written) in 3 s and the last lines were `tick 269` and `tick 270`. The first version, with Zephyr in the on-chip SRAM, did not run, because Linux and TF-A use that SRAM. Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). FAQ: [AM62L](../../am62l-evm/FAQ.md). 1 KB = 1,024 bytes.

**Question.** With Linux on A53 core 0, can a Zephyr image run on core 1 with no hypervisor, no remoteproc and no kernel module, and keep running while Linux is up?

**Vendor position.** TI ships a Jailhouse image for this board as its documented way to run an RTOS beside Linux. SDK download page: https://www.ti.com/tool/download/AM62L-LINUX-SDK/12.01.00.05.03. This run does not use it.

**What was tried.** 2026-10-22 between 10:55 and 11:30, on the AM62L evaluation module with an M4 Mac on UART0 (115200). Boot path: the micro-SD slot failed with the card on hand (U-Boot printed `Transfer data timeout`, and after a reseat `Card did not respond to voltage select! : -110`; the board's eMMC answered normally, so the card is the suspect). The board was booted over UART instead: SW3.4 ON, SW3.3 ON, SW3.2 ON, SW3.1 OFF (SW3.4 is the first row of the user guide's table; a full power cycle is needed, because the SW7 warm reset does not re-read the switches). The boot ROM sends `C` on UART0; `am62l-evm/tools/uart_boot.py` sent `tiboot3.bin` (XMODEM), `tispl.bin` and `u-boot.img` (YMODEM) from TI's Linux SDK 12.01.00.05.03 SD image, about 7 minutes to the U-Boot prompt. The SDK `.wic.xz` was written with `dd` to a 32 GB USB thumb drive on the Mac; U-Boot's `usb start` finds it, `load usb 0:2` reads the kernel (`Image-6.18.38-ti-00934-g8933766be737-dirty`) and `ti/k3-am62l3-evm.dtb`, and `booti` runs with `root=/dev/sda2`. Kernel to login prompt: about 30 s. A `usb start` after hot-plugging the stick into the running board hung U-Boot; a cold start with the stick already in works.

SRAM beside Linux was ruled out first. From Linux, `/dev/mem` shows WKUP SRAM at 0x707F0000 holding 34 KB of live code (TF-A's stub), and reads of MAIN SRAM above 0x70810000 raise a bus error (firewalled from the normal world); Linux's device tree claims 0x70800000 to 0x7080FFFF (`oc_sram`, with the SCMI mailbox at its start). So the SRAM images from the earlier plan were not used.

The DDR image (`build-ddr-core1`, `am62l-evm/zephyr/core1-ddr.overlay` plus `core1-ddr.conf`): Zephyr a915b2f, `apps/core1-hello`, linked at 0xE0000000 in a 256 MB DDR region, entry 0xE00008BC, `zephyr.bin` 44.0 kB (sha256 6543a9a3fa6233850a789302c08976b47ac75688649a8705d74d8a9073dc0778). It contains no PSCI, SCMI or SMC code, leaves the GIC distributor untouched (`am62l-evm/zephyr/patches/gic-skip-distributor.patch`) and writes its console to a 4 KB ring at 0xEFFFF000. The start, in U-Boot: `load usb 0:2 0xE0000000 /boot/zephyr-core1.bin`, then `am62l-evm/tools/psci_stub.py` writes a 7- or 8-instruction AArch64 stub with `mw.l` and runs it with `go`.

**How far it got.** Configure, build, load, run and verified. The stub got PSCI_VERSION 0x10001 (PSCI 1.1), AFFINITY_INFO for core 1 returned 1 (off), CPU_ON(MPIDR 0x1, 0xE00008BC) returned 0, and AFFINITY_INFO then returned 0 (on). The ring, read with `md` in U-Boot, held `*** Booting Zephyr OS build a915b2f12675 ***`, `core1-hello: MPIDR_EL1=0x80000001 (Aff0=1) CurrentEL=EL1`, then `tick 0`, `tick 1`, `tick 2`. So TF-A starts a secondary core at non-secure EL1 on this build, which answers the open question left by the earlier SRAM image. Linux then booted on core 0 with `maxcpus=1 mem=1536M cpuidle.off=1` (`Memory: 1450680K/1572864K available`). The ring lies outside Linux's memory, so `/dev/mem` allowed the read: magic 0x52524C46, head 5,888 then 5,954 (bytes written) 3 s later, last lines `tick 269` and `tick 270`. `dmesg` shows no SError, Oops or stall.

**The line.** No stop. The numbers: Zephyr 44.0 kB in DDR, one core, EL1 non-secure, started by PSCI; Linux on the other core with 1,536 MB, no hypervisor, no remoteproc, no kernel module. What the run does not show: any interrupt beyond Zephyr's own timer, any shared peripheral, Zephyr surviving Linux's cpuidle (it was turned off), a Linux reboot while Zephyr runs, Zephyr in SRAM beside Linux (the SRAM is not available), and any timing or power figure. Zephyr was started from U-Boot, not by Linux, so this does not show Linux starting or stopping the RTOS.

**Ask.** If you know whether TF-A on the AM62L reserves or relocates the WKUP SRAM stub, or which firewall setting opens MAIN SRAM above 0x70810000 to the normal world, say where it is documented.

# How much H.264 video can the AM62L decode in software, from 320x240 to 1080p?

**Short answer.** One Cortex-A53 core of the AM62L (TMDS62LEVM, 1.25 GHz) decodes a 1080p30 baseline stream at 600 kbit/s in software at 34 fps, so a 1080p30 camera stream fits on one core with about 12 percent to spare. A 540x540 stream takes about 17 percent of one core at 30 fps. Main profile (CABAC, B-frames) at 1080p runs at 23.5 fps on one core and 35.5 fps on two. Every decoded frame matches the Mac's decode bit for bit.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). FAQ: [AM62L](../../am62l-evm/FAQ.md). Streams and harness: `portability/h264/`. Rows: `data/results/am62l-evm.csv`, tests `video_sw_decode_fps` and `video_sw_decode_ram`.

**Question.** The AM62L has no video decoder block. Can its two A53 cores decode a 1080p, 30 fps, 600 kbit/s camera stream and a 540x540 stream in software, and how many cores does each need?

**Setup.**

- Board: TMDS62LEVM, TI Linux SDK 12.01.00.05.03, kernel 6.18.38, root file system on a USB stick, booted over UART. Both A53 cores at 1.25 GHz, performance governor. The LVGL demo service was stopped.
- Decoders: ffmpeg 8.0.1 from the SDK image (its native `h264` decoder, built with GCC 15.3.0), and the repo's h264bsd harness built on the board with GCC 15.3.0 `-O3`, single thread, timed with `CLOCK_MONOTONIC` around the decoder calls.
- Streams: `portability/h264/streams`, 30 frames each. The 540x540 stream (baseline, one reference frame, 15 fps); the Big Buck Bunny 640x360 clip; and the 30 fps streams capped at 600 kbit/s in baseline and in main (CABAC, two reference frames, two B-frames) at 320x240 to 1920x1080. For ffmpeg each stream was concatenated 10 times, 300 frames a run.
- Check: ffmpeg's MD5 of all decoded frames equals the Mac's ffmpeg 9.0.2 on all 9 streams. h264bsd's YUV CRCs equal the Mac build on all 4 baseline streams (the 640x360 clip gives `3f93a620`).
- Runs: 3 per point, median reported. Spread under 3 percent except one 2-thread 640x360 run.

Reproduce, from the repo on a Mac with the board on the network:

```
cd portability/h264/streams
for s in prof-baseline-1920x1080; do for i in $(seq 10); do cat $s.h264; done > x10-$s.h264; done
scp x10-*.h264 root@BOARD:/root/
ssh root@BOARD 'ffmpeg -hide_banner -benchmark -threads 1 -i x10-prof-baseline-1920x1080.h264 -f null -'
```

`-stream_loop` does not work on a raw `.h264` file (ffmpeg cannot seek it and stops with `Operation not permitted`); concatenate the file instead. Each copy starts with its own parameter sets and IDR frame, so it decodes as one stream.

**Result.**

| Stream | 1 thread | 2 threads | Frame time, 1 thread |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 540x540, baseline | 172.1 fps | 246.5 fps | 5.8 ms |
| 640x360 Big Buck Bunny, baseline | 174.7 | 245.1 | 5.7 ms |
| 320x240, 600 kbit/s, baseline | 451.1 | 538.6 | 2.2 ms |
| 640x360, 600 kbit/s, baseline | 231.7 | 310.2 | 4.3 ms |
| 1280x720, 600 kbit/s, baseline | 75.7 | 110.3 | 13.2 ms |
| 1920x1080, 600 kbit/s, baseline | 34.0 | 50.2 | 29.4 ms |
| 640x360, 600 kbit/s, main | 146.5 | 210.4 | 6.8 ms |
| 1280x720, 600 kbit/s, main | 52.6 | 77.0 | 19.0 ms |
| 1920x1080, 600 kbit/s, main | 23.5 | 35.5 | 42.6 ms |

ffmpeg on the AM62L, measured. User plus system time with one decoder thread is 99 to 122 percent of one core, because ffmpeg's reader and writer threads add to it. A second decoder thread gives 1.19 to 1.51 times, not 2: ffmpeg's frame threads share the two cores with its own reader and writer.

The repo's h264bsd decoder on the same board:

| Stream | fps | Cycles per pixel at 1.25 GHz | Decoder RAM (heap peak plus input buffer) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 540x540 | 97.5 | 44.0 | 1.15 MB |
| 640x360 Big Buck Bunny | 102.8 | 52.8 | 1.61 MB |
| 1280x720, 600 kbit/s | 40.8 | 33.3 | 3.55 MB |
| 1920x1080, 600 kbit/s | 17.0 | 35.4 | 8.02 MB |

ffmpeg is 1.7 to 2.0 times faster than h264bsd on the same core.

**Against the expectation** (written before the run):

| Point | Expected | Measured | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| 540x540, 1 thread | 80 to 140 fps | 172.1 | faster |
| 640x360 clip, 1 thread | 70 to 130 fps | 174.7 | faster |
| 1280x720, 1 thread | 30 to 55 fps | 75.7 baseline, 52.6 main | baseline faster, main within |
| 1920x1080, 1 thread | 12 to 25 fps | 34.0 baseline, 23.5 main | baseline faster, main within |
| 1920x1080, 2 threads | 22 to 40 fps | 50.2 baseline, 35.5 main | baseline faster, main within |
| 2-thread gain | 1.6 to 1.9 times | 1.19 to 1.51 | lower |
| h264bsd, 640x360 clip | 50 to 110 fps | 102.8 | within |

The earlier estimate "1080p30 no" holds for main profile on one core and is wrong for baseline: 34.0 fps on one core.

**Limits.**

- Decode only. Scaling, color conversion and display are not timed; the HDMI test in the battery shows that a CPU copy path to the display is slow on this chip (`data/results/am62l-evm.csv`, `gst_pipeline_fps`).
- The streams are a test pattern with a moving box. Camera footage at the same 600 kbit/s cap carries more detail per frame and costs more to decode; the 640x360 film clip cost 1.3 times the test pattern of the same size with h264bsd.
- Nothing else ran beside the decoder: no LVGL, no Matter link, no radar.
- Power during decode was not measured.
- One board, one SDK image.

**What this means.** On this evidence an AM62L decodes a 1080p baseline stream at 30 fps with one core, and a 540x540 stream with most of a core free. A main-profile 1080p stream needs both cores and leaves little for a user interface. At 1280x720 or smaller (both profiles under 20 ms a frame on one core) there is room for LVGL.

# Does Chocolate Doom run on the AM62L with no GPU, and does a wired PS4 controller reach it?

**Question.** Does Chocolate Doom run on the AM62L with no GPU, and does a wired PS4 controller reach it?

**How far it got.** It runs, slowly. `-timedemo demo1`: 5,026 game tics in 26,903 real tics, 6.54 fps, one run of 12.8 minutes (three would take 38 minutes). Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). FAQ: [AM62L](../../am62l-evm/FAQ.md).

**Setup.** Chocolate Doom 3.1.0 and SDL 2.32 from Debian trixie arm64 in a container (the SDK image has Docker, no apt), shareware `doom1.wad` v1.9 (MD5 `f0cefca49926d00903cf57551d901abe`, not committed), no sound, `force_software_renderer 1`, aspect ratio correction on, 1920x1080 on HDMI.

| Video path | fps | Note |
|---|---|---|
| SDL wayland on Weston 15, pixman renderer | 6.54 | one full timedemo |
| SDL `kmsdrm` direct | about 6 | page flips counted over 17 s |
| SDL `dummy` or `kmsdrm` with the software renderer | did not start | `CreateUpscaledTexture ... max texture size 0x0`; `kmsdrm` exits with code 255 and no message |

**The line.** The limit is about 6 fps. `top -H` shows two `llvmpipe` threads at 50 to 80 percent and the Doom thread mostly waiting: SDL's KMS/DRM window needs OpenGL, and with no GPU Mesa's software renderer does the 320x200 to 1080p scaling. The Doom engine itself was not the limit. A direct frame-buffer port (doomgeneric style) would avoid it; LVGL's fbdev backend draws a full 1080p scene at 54 fps on the same cores ([HMI shootout](2026-10-24-am62l-hmi-shootout.md)).

**Expectation (before the run).** 35 fps (the engine's cap) or close, from a Doom-class game on two A53 cores at 1.25 GHz. Missed by a factor of five for the reason above.

**Controller.** The wired DualShock 4 enumerates as `Sony Computer Entertainment Wireless Controller` on `hid-generic`, `/dev/input/event1`. `evtest` during the first play window logged 15 button presses (`BTN_EAST` 11, `BTN_C` 2, `BTN_SOUTH` 1, `BTN_MODE` 1) and left-stick `ABS_X` and `ABS_Y` from 3 to 127, centered near 120. Stick up is the low end of `ABS_Y`, which is the direction Doom's joystick code reads as forward. That proves the pad reaches Linux with the right polarity; it does not prove the game acted on it.

**Not seen by a person.** The two play windows ran out before anyone watched the screen (the first ended at its timeout and showed the Weston desktop; the second saw no input). So these remain unchecked: Doom walking forward on stick up, and the 4:3 shape (`aspect_ratio_correct 1` should draw 320x200 as 1440x1080 centered; the EDID reports a 370 by 140 mm panel, so the monitor's own shape is also unknown). The bench camera returned no frame, so no picture exists. Demo recording (`-record`) did not write a file when the game was ended by a signal, so no lump was available as proof either. Check both by hand before calling a game port done.

**Not run.** The RetroArch core with the pad mapped: the timedemo used up the time. Controller-to-game proof: needs a person at the board, as above. Second and third timedemo runs: 13 minutes each, not started.

Rows: `gui_fps`, variants `chocolate-doom-3.1.0-timedemo-demo1-weston-pixman-1080p`, `chocolate-doom-3.1.0-timedemo-demo1-kmsdrm-1080p`, `retroarch-core-controller` (not_run).

# What can the AM62L's two A53 cores do for edge AI with no accelerator?

**Question.** What can the AM62L's two A53 cores do for edge AI with no accelerator?

**How far it got.** Small classifiers are cheap, speech recognition is slower than real time, and a 0.5B language model talks at about 3 tokens per second. All numbers are medians of 3 on one board, both cores at 1.25 GHz, 1 kB = 1,024 bytes. Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). FAQ: [AM62L](../../am62l-evm/FAQ.md).

**Expectation (written before the runs).** whisper.cpp tiny.en 0.4 to 0.9 x real time, base.en 1 to 2.5; Qwen2.5-0.5B 1 to 3 tokens/s generation (memory-bandwidth ceiling 4 to 6 at the lab's 1.6 to 2.4 GB/s); YAMNet 40 to 150 ms; Silero 1 to 4 s per window. Source: the AM62L CoreMark and STREAM rows.

| Test | Threads | Result | Expected | Hit? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| whisper.cpp tiny.en, 11.0 s clip, total time | 2 / 1 | 24.5 s (2.23x) / 44.0 s (4.00x) | 0.4 to 0.9x | No, 3x slower |
| whisper.cpp base.en | 2 / 1 | 52.2 s (4.75x) / 96.4 s (8.76x) | 1 to 2.5x | No |
| Qwen2.5-0.5B Q4_0 generation | 2 / 1 | 2.89 / 1.68 tokens/s | 1 to 3 | Yes |
| Qwen2.5-0.5B Q4_0 prompt | 2 / 1 | 5.23 / 2.84 tokens/s | 5 to 20 | Low end |
| YAMNet (LiteRT, XNNPACK) per 0.975 s window | 2 / 1 | 20.2 / 30.4 ms | 40 to 150 | Faster |
| Silero en_v5 (ONNX Runtime) per 3 s window | 2 / 1 | 868 / 1,440 ms | 1,000 to 4,000 | Faster |

**The line.** Speech recognition is slower than real time on these cores. Why whisper missed: the encoder always processes a 30 s window, and it is most of the time: 15.7 s of the 24.5 s tiny.en run (29.2 s of 44.0 s on one thread). The encode time falls 1.86x from one thread to two, so both cores are used. The expectation took the 11 s clip as the cost; the cost is set by the 30 s window, so a clip longer than 30 s costs proportionally more and a shorter one costs the same. No second method was run to check the absolute rate.

**What was tried.** whisper.cpp and llama.cpp built on the board (GGML_NATIVE, NEON, no dot-product instructions on A53; builds took about 1 h and 2.5 h with two cores). Models: ggml-tiny.en and base.en, qwen2.5-0.5b-instruct-q4_0.gguf. TI's `yamnet_audio_classification.tflite` and `en_v5_static.onnx` come with the SDK image (`/usr/share/oob-demo-assets/models`). Inference through pip packages (see Added to the board). Other processes stopped during every run.

**Added to the board** (all on the USB-stick root file system; none on eMMC): pip `cmake`, `ninja`, `onnxruntime` 1.31.0, `ai-edge-litert` 2.3.0 (with flatbuffers, protobuf, ml_dtypes, tqdm, typing-extensions, backports.strenum); git clones of whisper.cpp and llama.cpp and the model files in `/root/bw` (about 1 GB). The PS5 driver build is on the [SD card and PS5 driver page](2026-10-24-am62l-sd-card-and-ps5-driver.md).

**Not run.** The webserver demo's NNStreamer pipeline (the two models were run directly instead). Power during inference (no rail reading taken).

Rows: `data/results/am62l-evm.csv`, tests `linux_asr_rtf`, `linux_llm_tok_s`, `linux_infer_ms`.

# How fast can the AM62L draw a 1080p HMI with no GPU?

**Question.** How fast can the AM62L draw a 1080p HMI with no GPU?

**How far it got.** Median of three 30 s runs per row, 1920x1080 at 60 Hz on the HDMI monitor, both A53 cores at 1.25 GHz. Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). FAQ: [AM62L](../../am62l-evm/FAQ.md).

| Toolkit and backend | fps | CPU, percent of both cores | RAM (resident set) |
|---|---|---|---|
| LVGL 9.3.0, fbdev (`/dev/fb0`) | 54.1 | 29.8 | 2.0 MB |
| LVGL 9.3.0, DRM (`/dev/dri/card0`, dumb buffers) | 18.0 | 45.8 | 1.6 MB |
| Slint 1.17.1, `linuxkms-software` | 41.9 | 46.7 | 24.6 MB |

One core would read twice the CPU figure: the DRM and Slint rows keep one core about 92 percent busy, so they are limited by one rendering thread. The fbdev row has no vsync and is paced by the 16 ms refresh timer, so it is not CPU bound.

**Expectation (before the run).** 30 to 60 fps for LVGL fbdev, from the 60 Hz refresh and the 1.25 GHz A53 filling about 2 million pixels a frame; no number existed for the other two. fbdev landed inside it. The DRM backend came in at a third of fbdev, which was not expected.

**The scene.** Same in both toolkits (`am62l-evm/hmi/main.c`, `am62l-evm/hmi/scene.slint`): 12 bars animated left to right (1.5 to 3.5 s ease-in-out), 12 counters and one large counter updated every 16 ms, dark background. The two are written separately, so they are the same scene, not the same draw calls.

**What was tried.** `am62l-evm/hmi/run_hmi.sh`: `ti-lvgl-demo` stopped, no containers, wait for a 1-minute load under 0.3 (readings 0.26 to 0.33), 5 s warm-up, 30 s window. CPU is the process's utime plus stime over the window; RAM is VmRSS (the frame buffer mapping is not in it). LVGL fps is counted at its refresh-ready event. Slint prints no rate on this build, so page flips were counted with `strace --seccomp-bpf -e trace=ioctl`; the same method on the LVGL DRM backend read 17.1 against 18 counted inside LVGL, so the Slint figure is probably 5 percent low.

**The line.** LVGL's DRM backend renders at a third of fbdev's rate and the cause is not isolated. Unexplained: LVGL fbdev renders three times as fast as LVGL DRM on the same CPU. Both use the same software draw; the DRM path commits atomically to a dumb buffer. Not isolated (one guess, a slow uncached mapping, is untested).

**Not run.**
- Qt Quick software renderer: Slint covered the software-toolkit test, and Qt is not on the image or in the Debian container used here.
- A picture of each screen was not taken. The scene source is in the repo.
- Slint with the Skia (GL) renderer: the board has no GPU, so only the software renderer was measured.

Rows: `gui_fps` and `host_cpu_load`, variants `lvgl-9.3-fbdev-1080p`, `lvgl-9.3-drm-1080p`, `slint-1.17.1-linuxkms-software-1080p`.

# Can the AM62L run the Raspberry Pi software people run most, and what does each cost?

**Question.** Can the AM62L run the Raspberry Pi software people run most, and what does each cost?

**How far it got.** Yes, with no new operating system. TI's SDK 12.01 image (Arago 2026.04, kernel 6.18.38) already runs Docker 29.3.0 with overlayfs and cgroup v2; the four containers pulled from Docker Hub and ghcr.io and ran as published for arm64. Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). FAQ: [AM62L](../../am62l-evm/FAQ.md). Commands, versions and every number: [am62l-evm/linux-apps/README.md](../../am62l-evm/linux-apps/README.md), rows in `data/results/am62l-evm.csv` (tests `linux_app_*`).

**Expectation (before the runs).** None was written down before these runs. The board's measured idle (561 mW, 4,256 CoreMark per core) was known, and the plan assumed Debian or Armbian would be needed for apt and containers. That assumption was wrong: the image's package manifest lists `docker-moby` and `containerd`, and the running system had them.

**What we tried.** Four containers (Mosquitto, Node-RED, Pi-hole, Home Assistant) were pulled and run on TI's SDK image, and each was given one real action. gpiozero and Blinka were run against the user LED.

| App | Real action | Result | Costs |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mosquitto 2 | publish and subscribe, in the container and from a Mac | received both ways | 2.6 MiB, 2.4 s to the port |
| Node-RED 5.0.9 | deploy an http-in flow over the admin API, call it | JSON back 2.5 s after the deploy | 110 MiB, 17.7 s to the editor |
| Pi-hole 2026.10.0 | `dig` four names | `doubleclick.net`, `googleadservices.com`, `ads.google.com` answered 0.0.0.0; `example.com` resolved | 24.8 MiB, 4.6 s to the first answer |
| Home Assistant 2026.10.4 | onboarding, MQTT integration, one discovery sensor | `sensor.frl_bench_frl_test_sensor` = 21.5 | 557 MiB, 67.7 s to the onboarding API |

Idle power across all of them stayed within 5 mW of 567.6 mW (8 INA228 rails, 30 s means). CPU idle fell from 93.0% to 88.9% at worst (Node-RED), apart from Home Assistant's first minute after the MQTT integration (82.5%, not steady).

**Python GPIO.** `gpioinfo` showed LD8 (GPIO0_123) and SW5 (GPIO0_90) claimed by the kernel's heartbeat LED and `gpio-keys` drivers; unbinding them frees the lines. gpiozero 2.0.1 on the lgpio factory and Adafruit Blinka 9.2.0 (with a new `AM62L_EVM` board file, starting from the BeaglePlay one) both toggled GPIO0 bank 3 OUT_DATA bit 27, read from `/dev/mem`. Reading the LED pin back gives 0 whatever was written, so a library's `toggle()` does nothing; the demos keep their own state.

**Three workarounds.** (1) `lgpio` has no wheel for Python 3.14 and needs swig below 4.4 (`PyInt_*` errors with 4.5.1), `--no-build-isolation`, and the C library built from source. (2) gpiozero 2.0 raises `PinUnknownPi` on a board that is not a Raspberry Pi until it is given a board description. (3) Blinka does not know the board until its import tables and Adafruit-PlatformDetect get an AM62L entry. All three are in the README.

**The line.** Nothing blocked the four apps. What did not work: `opkg` cannot fetch: its feed host does not resolve outside TI's network, and there is no apt. A first Home Assistant MQTT call returned 400 until the form's `other_settings` keys were sent. The Pi-hole blocklist loads minutes after the first DNS answer.

**Not run.** SW5 press and release: it needs a person at the board and nobody pressed it. LED seen by a person or camera: not checked, the camera link was down. Three runs per app: Home Assistant's pull alone took 655 s. Zigbee2MQTT and Frigate: they need a radio and a detector.

Rows: `data/results/am62l-evm.csv`, tests `linux_app_ram_mb`, `linux_app_idle_pct`, `linux_app_ready_s`, `linux_app_pull_s`, `linux_app_image_mb`, `rail_power_mw` variants `app-*`.

<!-- experiment
id: E250
board: TMDS62LEVM (AM62L evaluation module)
date: 2026-10-24
status: works
reached: verified
line: A shared-memory message link between Linux on A53 core 0 and Zephyr on core 1 ran on the AM62L EVM, with Linux starting Zephyr itself (PSCI CPU_ON from a kernel module, no U-Boot step). Two virtio-style rings with RPMsg framing sit in DDR outside Linux's memory; Linux rings Zephyr with SGI 7, Zephyr rings Linux by setting SPI 868 pending. Echo round trip, median of three medians, 56-byte payload: 5.7 us by interrupt both ways, 4.0 us polling both ways; 496-byte payload 18.4 and 17.2 us; 18.1 us from a userspace write and read. Streaming 20,000 messages: Linux to Zephyr 667,000 messages/s (331 MB/s at 496 bytes), Zephyr to Linux 295,000 messages/s by interrupt (146 MB/s) and 520,000 by polling (258 MB/s). -->
# How fast can Linux on one AM62L core talk to Zephyr on the other?

**Short answer.** A message round trip takes 5.7 us with a doorbell interrupt in both directions and 4.0 us with both sides polling (56-byte payload, median of three runs of 2,000). A full 496-byte message takes 18.4 us, almost all of it Zephyr copying 496 bytes through non-cacheable DDR. Streaming 496-byte messages runs at 331 MB/s from Linux to Zephyr and 146 MB/s back (258 MB/s back when Linux polls). Rates here use 1 kB = 1,000 bytes. Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). FAQ: [AM62L](../../am62l-evm/FAQ.md).

**Question.** With Linux on core 0 and Zephyr on core 1 and no hypervisor ([Linux and Zephyr on separate cores](2026-10-22-am62l-linux-zephyr-amp.md)), can the two exchange RPMsg-style messages through shared DDR with a hardware doorbell each way, and what do latency and throughput look like?

**What was tried.** `am62l-evm/rpmsg/zrpmsg_shm.h` (layout), `zrpmsg.c` (Linux kernel module), `am62l-evm/zephyr/apps/core1-rpmsg` (Zephyr), `rebuild_rpmsg.sh`, `bench.sh`, `rows.py`.
- Window: 0xEFF00000 to 0xEFFFEFFF, outside Linux's memory (`mem=1536M`), mapped Normal non-cacheable on both sides (Linux `memremap` write-combine, Zephyr a `zephyr,memory-region` node, attr 0).
- Two virtio split rings of 128 buffers of 512 bytes; each message is a 16-byte RPMsg header plus up to 496 bytes. Linux is the driver side, Zephyr the device side. Notification suppression follows the virtio flags.
- Linux to Zephyr doorbell: SGI 7 written to `ICC_SGI1R_EL1` from the module. Zephyr to Linux: a write of `GICD_ISPENDR` for SPI 868 (INTID 900), which the module maps with `irq_create_fwspec_mapping` and `request_irq`. Either side can poll instead.
- Linux loads `zephyr.bin` (44.0 kB, sha256 45e426f1838d89f9d51aa5ac2006e5eb3152b9d03c76d40f24e2edc92d77f004, entry 0xE00008BC) to 0xE0000000 and calls PSCI CPU_ON for core 1. READY came back in under 5 ms. Zephyr stops itself with PSCI CPU_OFF on a STOP message, so images can be reloaded without a reboot (about 10 reloads in the run).
- The module was built on the board with its own gcc 15.3 against the SDK kernel source (`modules_prepare` with the board's `/proc/config.gz`; no MODVERSIONS, so only `vermagic` has to match). Steps are in the board FAQ.

**How far it got.** Results (2026-10-24, kernel 6.18.38, both cores 1.25 GHz performance governor, one core online; shared system counter at 200 MHz, so 5 ns steps; every row is in `data/results/am62l-evm.csv`).

| Echo round trip, payload | Both by interrupt | Zephyr interrupt, Linux poll | Zephyr poll, Linux interrupt | Both poll |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 56 bytes | 5.66 us | 4.40 us | 5.09 us | 4.03 us |
| 496 bytes | 18.38 us | 17.58 us | 17.95 us | 17.19 us |

Breakdown, both by interrupt, 56 bytes: doorbell to Zephyr 1.48 us, Zephyr work 2.39 us, answer to the Linux handler 1.75 us. Polling cuts the two hops to 1.06 and 0.56 us. At 496 bytes Zephyr's work is 15.0 us: 62 reads and 62 writes of non-cacheable DDR (the 271 ns load latency in the README). A sleeping kernel thread that waits for the reply adds the scheduler wake: 12.7 us (56 bytes) and 25.2 us (496 bytes) in total. From a userspace `write` then `read` on `/dev/zrpmsg`: 18.1 us (56 bytes) and 35.1 us (496 bytes). p99 values run 2 to 5 times the median (a few microseconds of Zephyr timer ticks and Linux interrupts).

| Streaming, 20,000 messages | Payload | Messages/s | kB/s |
|---|---|---|---|
| Linux to Zephyr (same with Zephyr polling) | 64 bytes | 673,000 | 43,100 |
| Linux to Zephyr | 496 bytes | 668,000 | 331,000 |
| Zephyr to Linux, Linux by interrupt | 64 / 496 bytes | 299,000 / 295,000 | 19,100 / 146,500 |
| Zephyr to Linux, Linux polling | 64 / 496 bytes | 533,000 / 520,000 | 34,100 / 257,700 |

Linux to Zephyr costs about 1.5 us a message whatever the size, because neither side copies the payload. Zephyr to Linux by interrupt is slower because Zephyr rings the doorbell for every message (a device-memory write plus the Linux handler); polling removes that. Pooled medians of 6 runs per row; every payload's first and last byte and sequence number checked, 0 bad.

**Findings that cost time (each is a line in the board FAQ).**
1. Only SGIs 0 to 7 can be enabled from the non-secure world. A write to `GICR_ISENABLER0` of core 1's redistributor from Linux set bits 0 to 7 and ignored bit 8 to 15. The first build used SGI 8 and never got an interrupt.
2. Ending Zephyr with PSCI CPU_OFF inside the SGI handler left SGI 7 active and pending in core 1's redistributor (read through `/dev/mem`: `ISACTIVER0` 0x80, `ISPENDR0` 0x80). The next start then never received a doorbell. Fix: stop from the main loop, and clear the active and pending bits at start. A cache clean and invalidate of the image window (`dc civac`) before each reload was added in the same step as a precaution; its separate effect was not isolated.
3. `wake_up_interruptible` does not wake `wait_event_timeout` (uninterruptible): every wait ran the full 200 ms. Use `wake_up`.
4. Queued messages from an earlier command made every later reply one off; the module now drains stale replies before each command.

**The line.** What this does not show: OpenAMP or rpmsg-lite compatibility (the framing matches RPMsg, the name service and endpoints are not implemented); remoteproc; a cacheable shared window (needs core 1's cluster coherency checked, not run); cpuidle on (it was off); both cores' interrupts under load; Zephyr surviving a Linux reboot.

**Side check 1: CoreMark recheck.** The 4,256 on one core was not a clock problem: governor `performance`, `scaling_cur_freq` 1,250,000 kHz, and a dependent-add loop measured 1,246.1 to 1,246.5 MHz. The same binary gave 4,254.4. So 3.40 CoreMark per MHz is what GCC 15.3 -O2 produces on this A53, and the expectation of 6,000 to 7,000 was wrong.

**Side check 2: Zephyr as the ROM's phase-1 payload.** Expectation, written before: about 25 percent chance of a banner. Result: no. With the board in UART boot, the ROM accepted the full 54-block XMODEM transfer of `mkphase1.sh` output (certificate plus the 53,392-byte `build-sram-all` image) and returned to its `C` ping about 3 s later, for four variants: default (extended boot info, random 4096-bit key, load 0x707F0000), `--legacy`, `--degenerate`, and both. No Zephyr output on UART A. The SoC is AM62LX SR1.1 HS-FS (U-Boot banner). TI's own `tiboot3.bin` carries four components (SBL at 0x70800000, TIFS, board configuration, TIFS inner certificate); the self-made one had one. A fifth attempt that re-signed TI's own `tiboot3.bin` with the self-made key stopped being acknowledged part-way and was not pursued further; the ROM then needed about 4 minutes to start pinging again. The follow-on runs (the same image from SD card and OSPI NOR) were not run because they need this to work.

**Ask.** Whether the AM62L boot ROM on an HS-FS part accepts any image not signed with the customer key, and what the minimum component list is.

# How late can a 200 us timer wake up on the AM62L's stock Linux?

**Question.** How late can a 200 us timer wake up on the AM62L's stock Linux?

**How far it got.** Idle, the worst wake-up in 60 s was 389, 645 and 442 us (median 442). With `stress-ng --cpu 2 --vm 1 --vm-bytes 128M` it was 726, 1,835, 93,699, 1,074 and 375 us (median 1,074). Average stays 8 us idle and 13 to 14 us loaded. A soft real-time loop at 1 ms is safe on average and not guaranteed. Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). FAQ: [AM62L](../../am62l-evm/FAQ.md).

**Expectation.** The earlier single runs gave 474 us idle and 546 us loaded; a repeat should land in the same range. It did idle. Loaded it did not: four of five runs were higher than 546 us and one was 93.7 ms.

**The line.** The worst case under load is the limit, not the average. The 93,699 us happened in one of five loaded runs and did not come back in two repeats. Whether it was the first sample after cyclictest started (stress-ng had begun 3 s earlier) or a mid-run spike was not separated; the run had no histogram or trace. Treat it as an unexplained outlier, not a typical value.

**What was tried.** `cyclictest -m -p 90 -i 200 -l 300000 -q`, one thread per run (60 s), kernel 6.18.38 PREEMPT, performance governor, 1.25 GHz. Every run's worst case is listed in the short answer.

**Not run.** PREEMPT_RT: no RT kernel is on the boot media and booting one means writing another image. OpenPLC v4 runtime: the arm64 container image pulled (1.45 GB), then removed unstarted.

Rows: `sched_jitter_us`, variants `idle-60s-x3`, `load-2cpu-60s-x5`, `preempt-rt-idle`, `openplc-v4-cycle`.

# Do the TI Drivers examples built from the CC35X1 (Wi-Fi SDK) source run on the LP-EM-CC2340R5?

**Short answer.** Yes. All 11 examples built from the Wi-Fi SDK `.c` files inside the F3 SDK project for the LP-EM-CC2340R5, flashed and ran with no fault. The image is byte-identical to the one built from TI's own F3 example for each of the 11, so TI's own behavior and the twin's are the same code. 7 showed the behavior the source defines, 3 (gpiointerrupt, spicontroller, spiperipheral) only started up, and the pwmled1 fade was not observed.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). FAQ: [LP-EM-CC2340R5](../../cc2340r5/FAQ.md). The build side: 22 of 22 builds ok. Checked 2026-10-24 on one LP-EM-CC2340R5 with an LP-XDS110 probe, F3 SDK 9.21.00.36, Wi-Fi SDK 10.20.00.39, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS, SysConfig 1.28.0.

**Question.** An earlier check built the 11 shared examples and stopped there. Do they behave like TI's own on this chip?

**Setup.** The board held the house Zigbee light. Main flash (512 kB) and CCFG (2 kB) were read twice and compared equal before any write. Each hex was flashed with DSLite (no verify, 11 to 17 s), the chip was reset through the probe, and the back-channel serial port was held open at 115200 baud. Text was typed where the example asks for it. For LED-only examples the GPIO output register was read through the debugger. Afterwards the backup was flashed back and main flash and CCFG read back equal to the backup (0 differing bytes).

**Expectation.** Because baseline and swapped images are identical, any difference from TI's own example would point at the chip or the board, not the code. TI's source defines: ADC values printed, LED toggling, SHA-256 digest of typed text, echo, a wait for a missing I2C target, wiring notices for SPI.

**Result.**

| Example | Seen |
|---|---|
| adcsinglechannel | banner and raw and microvolt values for two ADC configs |
| empty | LED pin read high and low across 6 reads |
| exception | LED pin high; no serial, as in the source |
| gpiointerrupt | LED0 high at start; buttons not pressed |
| i2ccontroller | "Sending GET_STATUS until target responds"; no target fitted |
| pwmled1 | runs, no serial; fade not watched |
| sha2hash | "abc" gives BA7816BF...15AD, equal to sha256 on the Mac |
| spicontroller, spiperipheral | wiring notice and init line; no partner wired |
| uart2echo | echoes the 5 typed bytes |
| watchdog | LED pin both states across 6 reads over about a minute, no reset |

**The line.** The pin-read checks show an output changing, not its rate. Button, SPI, I2C and PWM behavior needs a hand, a partner board or a camera.

**Gotcha found.** `portability/everywhere/crossbuild_f3_wifi.sh` names SysConfig 1.26.3, which is no longer installed; with 1.28.0 the F3 9.21 projects build (22 builds, 11 to 40 s each).

**Ask.** A second LP-EM-CC2340R5 or a logic analyzer would close the SPI and PWM lines.

# Does the CC1407P host driver run on the LP-EM-CC2755P10, as plain C and as TI's Zephyr samples?

**Short answer.** The host side runs; the radio side was not tested. A no-RTOS build with this repo's HAL runs on the chip and exercises every hook, then waits in `TRX_Host_open`, which has no timeout, for a reply from a radio that is not connected. TI's four Zephyr samples (rf_diagnostics, genfsk_tx, genfsk_rx, carrier_wave) built, flashed and started; only rf_diagnostics prints a line.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). FAQ: [LP-EM-CC2755P10](../../cc2755p10/FAQ.md). Code: `cc2755p10/host-cc1407p/` and `portability/cc1407p-host/`. Checked 2026-10-24, one LP-EM-CC2755P10 on an LP-XDS110, TI's Zephyr fork v3.7.0-ti-1.00.01_ga, F3 SDK 9.21.00.36.

**Question.** The earlier plain-C and Zephyr builds only compiled. What happens when they run on the chip?

**Setup.**

- Plain C: TI's driver files unmodified, `hal_bare.c`, `app_tx.c` without its stub start-up code, and `hb_p10.c` (SPI, GPIO, a one-shot timer and an interrupt on TI Drivers). Pins from `ports/cc1407p-zephyr/boards/lp_em_cc2755p10.overlay`: SCLK DIO3, POCI DIO4, PICO DIO5, CS DIO7, RESET DIO16, SPI_INT DIO28. No radio connected.
- Zephyr: the four samples built with that overlay and no shield, flashed as hex files carrying the board's own CCFG and SCFG.
- The plain-C image counts every hook call; the counters were read from RAM with the debugger.

**Expectation.** With no radio the driver cannot get a reply. A reset pulse, a chip-select transfer and a timeout would be a good sign for the hooks.

**Result.**

| Counter (read from RAM) | Value |
|---|---|
| RESET asserted | 1 |
| SPI transfers started, completed, failed | 1, 1, 0 |
| CS asserted, released | 1, 2 |
| SPI_INT interrupt enabled, fired | 1, 0 |
| One-shot timer started, fired | 2, 2 |
| POCI reads, read high | 1, 0 |
| Where it stands | stage 1: inside `TRX_Host_open`, which loops until the radio answers; no fault (CFSR and HFSR 0) |

The Zephyr samples: rf_diagnostics printed `RF Diagnostics Example` and nothing more; genfsk_tx, genfsk_rx and carrier_wave printed nothing, not even the Zephyr boot line. That fits the same wait in the driver with the log thread starved, but it was not confirmed by a debugger.

**The line.** No radio. `TRX_Host_open` (`third-party/ti-cc140xp-host/host/trx_host.c`) ends with `while(TRX_HOST_IS_PENDING(handle));`, so a host with no radio, or one that never answers, hangs there. A host that must survive a missing radio needs its own timeout around the open call.

**Ask.** The BP-CC1407P on the LP-EM-CC2755P10: red LED jumper off and one wire from BoosterPack pin 23 to pin 10 (`cc2755p10/FAQ.md`). Then the transmit sample can be paired with the CC1354P10 receiver that already hears the radio.

# Does a compile shim get TI's CC1407P host driver running on the LAUNCHXL-F2800137?

**Short answer.** The shim fixes the build and nothing else. The driver then builds a different first message than an Arm core does. With `portability/cc1407p-host/c28x/c28x_compat.h` the 7 driver files, the bare HAL and a bench program compile and link with 0 errors and run on the LAUNCHXL-F2800137. So the driver still needs a field-by-field message packer for 16-bit-char chips. No radio was attached; the radio was a fake that answers every transfer with zeros.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). Follows [E73](2026-10-08-f2800137-cc1407p-host-driver.md), which only compiled. Code, results table and causes: `portability/cc1407p-host/c28x/README.md`. Checked 2026-10-24 on macOS 15.7 (Intel), C2000 compiler 25.11.1.LTS, C2000Ware 26.02.00.00 LTS, probe <probe serial>.

**Question.** E73 found 524 errors as shipped and said all 7 files compile with C2000Ware's `uint8_t` and the packed attribute defined away. Is that the whole fix, and what does the driver do when it runs?

**Setup.**

- Shim: `--preinclude=c28x_compat.h` (16-bit `unsigned char` as `uint8_t`, empty `__packed__`). TI's files are untouched.
- Image: TI's driver, `hal_bare.c`, a fake-radio glue file and a bench program, RAM load, `-O2`.
- Reference: the same files built with clang on a Mac, where a byte is 8 bits.
- Run: load over the onboard XDS110, run to the breakpoint at `bench_done`, read the result variables. Twice, identical.

**Expectation.** From E73: struct sizes differ, so the first message differs; the CRC routine, which takes a byte array, matches.

**Result.**

| Check | PC reference | F2800137 |
|---|---|---|
| Files that compile without the shim | | 1 of 12 (the startup assembly); 750 errors |
| Files that compile with the shim | | 12 of 12, 0 errors, 51 warnings |
| Flash, RAM | | 8.4 kB, 8.7 kB (stack used 86 of 1k words) |
| CRC-16 of `123456789` | 0x29B1 | 0x29B1 |
| First SPI message | `00 04 11 00 02 32 00 00 E9 71` (10 bytes) | `00 11 00 00 01 00 00 00 C8` (9 units) |

The message differs in length, in the length byte, in the request number (0x32, CONFIG_LIST, is missing) and in the CRC. `TRX_Host_open` waits for the radio's answer and never returns, so the bench stops after the first transfer.

**The line.** TI's code lays structs and a 32-bit bit-field union over the SPI buffer, and a C28x struct member takes a whole 16-bit word. A header file cannot change that. Also, 29 shifts of `1 << 16` and up overflow a 16-bit `int`.

**Next.** Write a packer (`pack_TRX_Request_*` and the header) that fills a byte-per-word buffer field by field, run it against the same PC reference bytes, then try a real BP-CC1407P.

**Board state.** RAM load only. Flash read before and after: SHA-256 identical to the as-received image; the board was reset into TI's demo.

# Do the G3519 DriverLib examples retargeted to the LP-MSPM0G5187 run, and do they do what TI's example does?

**Short answer.** Mostly yes. The three DMA examples do not: the data moves but the example never sees the done flag. An earlier build pass reported 117 failed builds; 41 of them were names such as `UART0` and `SPI1` not declared; those errors come from stale generated files copied with each example, and with them deleted 79 of 122 `driverlib` examples build instead of 64.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). Rows are in `data/results/mspm0g5187.csv` (variant `g3519-port-<example>`). Checked 2026-10-24 on one LP-MSPM0G5187, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS, MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07, SysConfig 1.28.0 (1.26.3 was no longer installed, so the run is unvalidated).

**Question.** An earlier pass built 141 retargeted G3519 examples for the G5187 and never ran one. Do they run, and does each show what TI's example shows?

**Setup.** `port_mspm0.py` retargets the SysConfig device lines and unlocks pin and channel assignments; `run_sweep.py` flashes and runs with its safety gates; result variables were read through the debugger; pin toggles were timed with a millisecond clock. The board was backed up (main 128 kB and data 8 kB, read twice equal) and restored equal at the end. No external wiring.

**Expectation.** Set before the run: togglers toggle, breakpoint examples stop with the result variables TI names, input examples run idle, `sysctl_hfxt_run` hangs as the AGENTS file already says.

**Result.**

| Finding | Evidence |
|---|---|
| 15 examples match TI's description | systick half-period 497 ms (TI 500), a 2 s timer at 2,000 and 2,064 ms, CRC 0x2C81, flash controller `gErrorType` 0 in four examples, SPI loopback received equals sent, UART transmit `MSP!` on the backchannel |
| 3 DMA examples fail | destination words correct; `gChannel0InterruptTaken` 0 because SysConfig assigned channel 1 and the handler tests channel 0; the native G5187 build passes |
| Stale generated files | the SDK ships `ti_msp_dl_config.c` and `.h` beside each example; the source includes them before SysConfig's output, so a port compiles G3519 names (`UART0`, `SPI1`, `GPIOC`). 64 build with them, 79 of 122 without |
| TI Drivers examples keep the G3519 linker map | `drivers/uart_echo` builds, then locks the debugger out; recovered with the wait-for-debug hold, backup read back equal |
| 37 ran, cannot be judged | need a button, signal or second device; no fault |

**The line.** A build is not a port. After SysConfig, check that `DMA_CHx_CHAN_ID` and the linker file match the chip, and delete the stale `ti_msp_dl_config.*` beside the source. UART receive, I2C, comparators and PWM shape are not confirmed here.

**Gotcha found.** The sweep scripts name SysConfig 1.26.3; with 1.28.0 installed they stop at the first call until the path is changed. The safety gates read load addresses only, so the stack top of a TI Drivers image is not checked.

**Limits.** The 22 low-power and key examples were skipped. `sram_parity` was not retried on the corrected build.

# Does the bare-metal CC1407P host build run on the LP-MSPM0L1306 and the LP-MSPM0G5187 after it links?

**Short answer.** It runs on both, up to the point a radio is needed. Each board printed its banner, pulsed the radio's reset, asserted chip select and clocked out the driver's first frame, `00 04 11 00 02 32 00 00 e9 71`, the same ten bytes the LP-MSPM0G5187 sent in its recorded link of 2026-10-10. No radio was wired, so no reply was judged. The L1306 image is 14.1 kB of flash and 2.2 kB of RAM with a 4-buffer pool.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). Files: `mspm0l1306/radio-host/` (new build for the L1306) and `mspm0g5187/radio/`. Checked 2026-10-24 with TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS, SDK 2.11.00.07, SysConfig 1.28.0 (unvalidated).

**Question.** An earlier pass linked the host driver for nine boards and measured size only. Does the linked image start and behave on two of them?

**What we tried.** The linked host image was flashed to each board with no radio wired, and the serial output was read.

**Expectation.** From the G5187 trace of 2026-10-10: `Cr R t c p S0a>` then the ten-byte frame. With nothing on the bus the reply is not meaningful.

**Result.**

| Board | Seen |
|---|---|
| LP-MSPM0G5187 | banner, `CrRtcpS0a>0004110002320000e971<00...`, reply all `00` (POCI low) |
| LP-MSPM0L1306 | same banner and frame, reply all `ff` (POCI high); then the driver waits inside the SPI-complete handler (halted in `hb_delay_us`, 3 s after reset) |

**The line.** The radio, wired to SPI0 PA6, PA5, PA4, PA3, PA7 and PA2 on the L1306, closes it. The 4-buffer pool is TI's driver with one constant changed; whether it works with so few buffers is unknown until a radio answers.

**Gotcha found.** `mspm0g5187/radio/radio_host.c` prints "LP-MSPM0G5187" in its banner whichever board runs it.

**Next.** Wire a BP-CC1407P-9-FE to the LP-MSPM0L1306 (six signals plus 3V3 and GND, pins in `mspm0l1306/radio-host/README.md`).
