# Do TI's MSPM0 DriverLib examples run on the MSPM33, and the MSPM33's on the MSPM0G3519, with the app files unchanged?

**Short answer.** Yes for GPIO, UART, timers, SPI and CRC, in both directions. The example's own SysConfig file goes with it, the target's SysConfig rejects the lines that do not apply, and the app builds and runs. Each result below was read over the probe from pins, registers and RAM variables the app defines. I2C and ADC stopped at build: the MSPM33's I2C is the UNICOMM block with new function names and its ADC is the HSADC block.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). Method, tools and the migration notes: [PORTING.md section 7](../../portability/everywhere/PORTING.md). Checked 2026-10-24 on macOS 15.7 (Intel), MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07, MSPM33 SDK 1.04.00.00, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS, SysConfig 1.28.0 (the validated 1.26.3 is not installed), probes <probe serial> and <probe serial>. Both boards were backed up first (main flash twice, equal) and restored and read back equal after.

**Question.** An earlier pass carried 83 G3519 examples to the MSPM33 and ran 40 with clean fault registers, but no run read what an example does. Do the examples do what they say, and does the reverse direction work?

**Setup.**

- Tool: `portability/everywhere/crossport_pair.py` (either direction). Swap the device header, unlock pins, drop the source chip's clock-tree lines, comment out each line SysConfig rejects, build with the target SDK's makefile. App `.c` files are copied as they are.
- Where the target SDK has no example by that name, the base project is the target's `empty` example.
- G3519 pins: PA8 to PA13 (console and CAN header), PA15 and PA25 (DAC to ADC wire), PA18, the 3.5 inch display pins and the LEDs are reserved as inputs in the configuration, so SysConfig cannot give them to a peripheral. No wire was moved.
- Check: `portability/everywhere/bench_pair_run.py` flashes, lets the app run 1 to 1.5 s, then reads CFSR and HFSR, the GPIO output registers 8 times 0.23 s apart, and the RAM variables or timer registers the test names. SPI and UART tests use the chips' internal loopback, so no wires.

**Expectation.** From the earlier passes: GPIO, UART and timers should run, SPI should run where the block exists on both sides, I2C and ADC should fail at build.

**Result.**

| Example | MSPM0G3519 to MSPM33 | MSPM33 to MSPM0G3519 |
|---|---|---|
| gpio_toggle_output | Works: 4 pins toggle | Works with 5 app lines edited (see below) |
| systick_periodic_timer | Works: pins toggle in the handler | Works |
| timx_timer_mode_periodic_sleep | Works | Works |
| timx_timer_mode_pwm_edge_sleep | Works: LOAD 1999, compare 500 and 1000 as configured | Works: same values |
| spi_controller_internal_loopback_poll | Works: gRxData 1 equals gTxData | Works |
| UART loopback (G3519: uart_rw_multibyte_fifo_poll, MSPM33: uart_tx_rw_multibyte_fifo_poll) | Works: rxPacket reads MSP! | Works: same |
| uart_internal_loopback_spgss0_uc1 and the interrupt version | no G3519 twin | Works: rxData 5 equals txData 5, pass LED pin high |
| crcp_calculate_checksum | Works: CRCOUT 0x2C81 | Works: 0x2C81 |
| UART standby, UART DMA console, UART RX | build stops (group alias, DMA instance, pull-up on open drain) | build stops |
| I2C controller | build stops: DL_I2C_ClockConfig unknown | build stops: 12 DL_I2CC_ names differ |
| ADC12 and HSADC | build stops: no ADC12 block | build stops: no HSADC block |

Builds with the app untouched: 8 of 12 in each direction. Silicon runs: 8 forward (7 checked, 1 needs a wire), 9 reverse (all checked).

**What needed more than the SysConfig move.**

- The UART examples expect a wire from TX to RX. Adding `UART1.enableInternalLoopback = true;` to the configuration (the app is untouched) lets them run without one. Cause tag: Setup or handling, the source example is written for a wire.
- The MSPM33 `gpio_toggle_output` names a port per LED (`GPIO_LEDS_USER_LED_2_PORT`) because its three LEDs sit on three ports. The G3519 LEDs share port B, so SysConfig writes one `GPIO_LEDS_PORT` and the unedited app does not build. Five lines changed. Cause tag: tool or docs, the generated names depend on the pin choice.
- The `BKPT` an example ends with sets HFSR bit 31 on the Cortex-M33 and nothing on the Cortex-M0+, which has no HFSR. A clean run reads zero in CFSR on both.

**The line.** I2C and ADC do not move: the MSPM33's I2C is the UNICOMM block with new function names and its ADC is the HSADC block, so they need a rewrite, not a port.

**Not checked.** The LEDs and the PWM pins were not watched and the PWM frequency was not measured; the checks are register reads. I2C and ADC need a rewrite, not a port. No example here touched flash, NONMAIN or the display wires.

**Second attempt, the CC1407P host driver.** TI's host driver (7 files, unmodified) plus this repo's bare HAL and a fake radio, built as a normal SDK image for both boards (`portability/cc1407p-host/build_board.sh`). On both, the first SPI message the driver builds is `00 04 11 00 02 32 00 00 E9 71`, the same 10 bytes as the PC reference, and the CRC-16 check value is 0x29B1. The 9 structs that go on the wire have the PC sizes; two API structs are smaller on both Arm cores (1-byte enums) and are not sent. 10.8 kB of flash on the MSPM33 and 10.6 kB on the G3519, 5.8 kB of RAM. No radio was attached, so no packet was sent from either board.

**Board state.** Main and data flash read back equal to the saved copies on both boards after the runs.

# What can the AM62L show on its HDMI screen besides Doom?

**Short answer.** Five things, one after another, from one loop script (`am62l-evm/showcase/run.sh`): Doom drawn straight into the framebuffer, TI's LVGL demo, Android 12 in a Redroid container mirrored by scrcpy, SuperTuxKart 1.5 (native arm64) and RetroArch with a homebrew Game Boy game on the PS4 pad. The chip has no GPU, so the split is clear: software 2D runs at full speed, software 3D does not.

![SuperTuxKart on the HDMI panel at 640x480, STK's counter reads 2/2/2 fps](../../am62l-evm/bench/logs/showcase/stk-640x480-race.jpg)

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). **Redroid** is Android in a Docker container; it needs the binder driver from the [E285 kernel](2026-10-25-am62l-kvm-binder-kernel.md). **scrcpy** mirrors an Android screen over adb as an H.264 stream. **llvmpipe** is Mesa's software OpenGL. **modesetting** is the generic Xorg driver for a KMS display. Scripts: `am62l-evm/showcase/`; rows in `data/results/am62l-evm.csv`.

**Question.** What can the AM62L show on its HDMI screen besides Doom?

**What we tried.** Five things were run in turn from one loop script on the HDMI output, each timed once.

**Expectation (before the runs).** From the Doom framebuffer test (E275) and the open-games test (E286): LVGL and Doom smooth; SuperTuxKart about 4.5 fps at 640x480 (offscreen number); Android a few frames a second because every frame is rendered in software, encoded to H.264 and decoded again; a Game Boy core at full speed.

**How far it got.**

| Item | How it reaches the screen | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Doom (shareware, `doom_fb`) | writes `/dev/fb0` directly | 186 to 193 fps timedemo (E275); smooth |
| TI LVGL demo (`ti-lvgl-demo`, `lvglsim`) | fbdev | Runs; 118 MB resident, about 15 percent of one core on the home screen; frame rate not measured |
| Android 12 (Redroid, software GLES) | Xorg, scrcpy 5.0.1 full screen | 1.1 frames a second shown while Settings scrolls (0 to 2; 1 to 5 more decoded and dropped); the app renders a frame in 450 ms (median); boot to `sys.boot_completed` 70 s |
| SuperTuxKart 1.5 arm64 | Xorg, HDMI mode 640x480, full screen | 2 fps (STK counter min/avg/max 2/2/2); the race starts about 7 min after launch |
| RetroArch 1.20 + Gambatte, Tobu Tobu Girl | Xorg, HDMI mode 640x480, gl driver | 48 fps on RetroArch's counter (full speed is 59.7); PS4 pad configured automatically |
| Same, HDMI mode left at 1920x1080 | Xorg | 10.4 fps |

Every new number is one run.

## Games you can play on this board

Measured on this board with no GPU, best first. "Playable" means 25 fps or more.

| Game | Path | fps | Playable |
|---|---|--:|---|
| Doom, shareware (`doom_fb`) | straight to the framebuffer, 1280x1000 | 186 to 193 (timedemo, E275) | Yes |
| Tobu Tobu Girl, homebrew Game Boy (RetroArch, Gambatte) | Xorg, 640x480 HDMI mode, PS4 pad | 48 | Yes |
| Doom, shareware (dsda-doom 0.29) | Xorg, OpenGL on llvmpipe, 640x480 | 27.2 (timedemo, E286, offscreen) | Yes |
| Doom, shareware (dsda-doom 0.29) | same, 1280x720 | 10.5 (E286, offscreen) | No |
| Chocolate Doom 3.1 | Weston, llvmpipe scaler | 6.5 (E276) | No |
| SuperTuxKart 1.5 arm64 | Xorg, 640x480 HDMI mode | 2 on the panel, 4.5 offscreen (E286) | No |

The loop in `run.sh` plays the games first: SuperTuxKart, dsda-doom, RetroArch, then Android, Doom on the framebuffer and the LVGL demo.

**The line.**

It shows the display paths that work without a GPU: direct framebuffer writes and a CPU-drawn X screen at a low HDMI mode, where the monitor does the scaling for free. Switching the HDMI mode to 640x480 took RetroArch from 10.4 to 48 fps, because llvmpipe no longer scales every frame to 1080p. It does not show sound, input latency, or why SuperTuxKart draws 2 fps on the panel against 4.5 fps offscreen in E286 (Xorg's shadow framebuffer copy is one suspect, not tested). Android's rate is set by its software renderer (450 ms a frame) before scrcpy's encode and decode add their share.

## Run it

```sh
# board, kernel 6.18.38-ti-kvm (binder for Redroid)
sh /root/frl/showcase/setup.sh                             # frl-show container: Xorg, RetroArch, adb, build tools
docker exec frl-show sh /root/frl/showcase/build_scrcpy.sh # scrcpy client against the v5.0.1 server
nohup sh /root/frl/showcase/run.sh 120 > /root/frl/showcase/out/loop.log 2>&1 &
sh /root/frl/showcase/run.sh stop                          # back to Doom alone
```

## If you try it

If the Android picture sits in the top-left corner instead of filling the screen, start a window manager (`openbox`) before scrcpy, and set Redroid to landscape with `wm size 1280x720`. If scrcpy prints `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR is invalid`, set it to any private directory; the warning is harmless. If a game draws below 15 fps on llvmpipe at 1080p, switch the HDMI mode with `xrandr --output HDMI-1 --mode 640x480` and let the monitor scale. If scrcpy has no package for arm64 Debian trixie, build the client from source with meson against the prebuilt server (`build_scrcpy.sh`).

**Restore.** `run.sh stop` stops the loop, X, scrcpy, the games and the LVGL service, pauses Redroid and starts the framebuffer Doom demo again. The `frl-show` container stays on the board (about 900 MB of packages).

# Will the AM62L boot a 6.18.38 kernel with KVM and binder?

**Question.** Will the AM62L boot a 6.18.38 kernel with KVM and binder?

**Short answer.** Yes. The custom kernel `6.18.38-ti-kvm` boots from the SD card to login, `dmesg` shows `kvm [1]: Hyp nVHE mode initialized successfully`, `/dev/kvm` exists, binderfs mounts with `binder`, `hwbinder` and `vndbinder`, `binfmt_misc` mounts, and `hid-playstation` loads. A KVM guest runs CoreMark at 3.9k to 4.0k iterations per second against 4.1k to 4.2k on the host with the same binary. Redroid 12 (Android in a container, on binder) reaches `sys.boot_completed=1` in 86 s and shows its launcher.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). **KVM** is Linux's hypervisor; **nVHE** is its mode for cores without the ARMv8.1 Virtualization Host Extensions (the A53 is ARMv8.0). **binder** is Android's IPC driver; **binderfs** creates its devices. **Redroid** runs Android's user space in a container. Build and install: `am62l-evm/kernel-kvm/README.md`; rows in `data/results/am62l-evm.csv`.

**What was tried.** The SDK 12.01 kernel (6.18.38, tag `cicd.wrynose.202607100005`, commit `8933766be`) keeps the board's running config, plus `am62l-evm/kernel-kvm/kvm-binder.config`: KVM, binder and binderfs, binfmt_misc, the PlayStation, Sony and uinput drivers. Built with Debian gcc 14.2 in a native arm64 container: `Image` 22.5 MB, 732 modules. The device tree in the bundle is byte-identical to the card's.

**Expectation (before the run).** Boots to login in about the stock time; `Hyp mode initialized` because every CPU already starts at EL2; a guest within a few percent of the host on CoreMark (KVM runs guest code natively).

**How far it got.**

| Step | Result |
|---|---|
| Recovery path first: reboot on the stock kernel, stop U-Boot's autoboot on the console, boot stock by hand | Works: at `=>`, `load mmc 1:2 ${loadaddr} /boot/Image-6.18.38-ti-00934-g8933766be737-dirty`, `load mmc 1:2 ${fdtaddr} /boot/dtb/ti/k3-am62l3-evm.dtb`, `setenv bootargs ...`, `booti ${loadaddr} - ${fdtaddr}`; login 19.4 s after `booti` |
| `kernel-swap.sh backup` | 50 MB: both Image files, the dtb, the stock modules; copied off the board and checked against SHA256SUMS |
| `kernel-swap.sh install`, reboot (normal autoboot) | Login 32.8 s after the reboot command; last kernel line before login at 17.7 s (stock: 18.2 s) |
| KVM | `CPU: All CPU(s) started at EL2`, `kvm [1]: Hyp nVHE mode initialized successfully`, vgic-v2, IPA limit 40 bits; `/dev/kvm` present |
| binder | `mount -t binder binder /dev/binderfs` gives `binder`, `binder-control`, `hwbinder`, `vndbinder` |
| binfmt_misc, PlayStation driver | mounts; `modprobe hid-playstation` loads, and the pad then reports the standard button names |
| VM: Alpine 3.22 `virt` kernel, QEMU 10.0.13, `-accel kvm -cpu host -smp 2 -m 512`, initramfs that runs CoreMark | Guest init at 0.50 s guest uptime; QEMU start to power-off 19.9 to 20.2 s, of which CoreMark is about 15 s |
| CoreMark, same static binary (GCC 14.2 -O2), host vs guest, 3 runs each | host 4.08k, 4.08k, 4.15k; guest 4.02k, 3.93k, 3.93k iterations/s |
| Redroid `12.0.0_64only-latest` (1.97 GB image, 305 s to pull), `--privileged`, adb on loopback | `sys.boot_completed=1` at 86 s; focus `com.android.launcher3/...QuickstepLauncher`; screen 720x1280; whole-board RAM peak 989 MB during boot, 1,166 MB used after |

**Fixes made on the way.** `kernel-swap.sh` assumed `/boot/dtb/k3-am62l3-evm.dtb`; on the card it is `/boot/dtb/ti/k3-am62l3-evm.dtb` (U-Boot's `fdtfile=ti/k3-am62l3-evm.dtb`), so the script now uses that path. U-Boot loads `/boot/Image` and the dtb from the ext4 root (`bootpart=1:2`, `name_kern=Image`); the `Image` on the FAT partition is not used. QEMU needs `-nic none` when the `ipxe-qemu` ROMs are not installed (`failed to find romfile "efi-virtio.rom"`).

**The line.** What it does not show: real-time latency or power with the new kernel; a guest with a disk or network; an Android app running, its frame rate, or input; KVM with more than one guest; whether a cold power cycle (rather than `reboot`) boots the same way.

**Restore.** From the booted new kernel: `kernel-swap.sh restore`, then reboot. If it does not boot: stop U-Boot at `=>` and use the four commands in the first table row (proven on this card). The backup is in `/root/kernel-backup-20261025-174552` on the board and copied off it.

**If you try it.** If `kernel-swap.sh backup` stops on a missing dtb, read `fdtfile` with `printenv fdtfile` at the U-Boot prompt and point `DTB` at it. If QEMU stops on `efi-virtio.rom`, add `-nic none` or install `ipxe-qemu`. Pass `-machine virt,gic-version=2` to QEMU: the kernel reports a GICv2-style virtual interface (`vgic-v2`).

# Do open 3D games run on the AM62L, and does Steam's download path work without an account?

**Short answer.** 3D games run but are not playable: the chip has no GPU, so Mesa's llvmpipe draws every frame on the two A53 cores. SuperTuxKart 1.5, native arm64 build, AI race with 4 karts: 4.5 fps at 640x480 and 2.4 fps at 1280x720. Doom drawn in software is the other end: 186 to 193 fps straight to the framebuffer (E275), 27.2 fps at 640x480 and 10.5 fps at 1280x720 through dsda-doom on X. Steam's own download path works with an anonymous login, natively on arm64: Valheim's dedicated server, 2,088 MB on disk, in 371 s (5.6 MB/s).

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). **llvmpipe** is Mesa's software OpenGL. **Box64** runs x86-64 Linux programs on 64-bit Arm. **steamcmd** is Valve's command-line Steam client, 32-bit x86 only. **DepotDownloader** is an open-source Steam download client (SteamKit2) with an arm64 Linux build. Scripts: `am62l-evm/steam/games/`; rows in `data/results/am62l-evm.csv`.

**Question.** Without a Steam account, how close does the AM62L get to "Steam games": can it fetch Steam content, and what frame rate does a real open 3D game reach, natively and as an x86 binary?

**Expectation.** Single-digit fps for any 3D game (the HMI tests drew a fixed LVGL scene at 54 fps and Chocolate Doom through llvmpipe at 6.5 fps); an x86 build under Box64 slower again.

**Setup.** TI SDK 12.01 Linux (kernel 6.18.38), both A53 cores at 1.25 GHz, 2 GB RAM; Debian trixie arm64 container; Xvfb, Mesa 25.0.7 llvmpipe (LLVM 19.1.7). The framebuffer Doom demo kept running on HDMI during every run, so these numbers share the CPU with it (it uses about a third of one core).

**Result.**

| Workload | Resolution | Result | Notes |
|---|---|--:|---|
| SuperTuxKart 1.5 arm64, `--profile-time` race, lighthouse, 4 karts | 640x480 | 4.48 fps | 3,005 frames in 671 s; renderer OpenGL ES 3.2 on llvmpipe |
| Same | 1280x720 | 2.42 fps | 3,005 frames in 1,242 s |
| SuperTuxKart 1.5 x86_64 under Box64 0.3.4 (Debian) | 640x480 and 1280x720 | crash | segmentation fault after the OpenGL 4.5 feature checks, 15 to 18 s after start |
| dsda-doom 0.29.0 (installed by Debian's prboom-plus package), `-timedemo` DEMO1, shareware WAD | 640x480 | 27.2 fps | 5,026 game tics in 6,460 real tics; default settings |
| Same | 1280x720 | 10.5 fps | 16,823 real tics |
| Steam download, anonymous, DepotDownloader 3.4.0 arm64 | app 1007 (Steamworks SDK Redist) | 107 MB in 28.9 s | 36.7 MB transferred |
| Same | app 896660 (Valheim dedicated server) | 2,088 MB in 371 s | 1,912 MB transferred, 5.2 MB/s on the wire; the server is an x86_64 program and was not started |
| steamcmd (x86) under Box64 0.3.4 BOX32, `+login anonymous` | app 1007 | stops | updates itself, then `PltResolver32: Symbol __sched_cpualloc ... not found` and hangs |

Box64 git (420eda6, 2026-10-23) wraps `__sched_cpualloc`; its build on the board was paused for the timed runs and then stopped at about 1 percent (a full build on two A53 cores is over an hour). So steamcmd and the x86_64 game were not retried with it.

**What it does not show.** Any frame rate on the HDMI screen (the Doom demo owned it; all runs drew to Xvfb), sound, input latency, a Steam game (needs an account), OpenArena or Quake (no timedemo data shipped with the Debian packages), RetroArch cores, three runs per row (one each), and the cause of the Box64 crash (desktop GL path; the arm64 build uses GLES).

**The line.** A 3D game is a slide show at 2 to 5 fps on this chip, natively; x86 translation would cut that further. 2D and software-rendered games are the class that fits: Doom written straight to the framebuffer runs at 186 to 193 fps, and through X at 10 to 27 fps.

**If you try it.** If SuperTuxKart's x86_64 build segfaults under Box64 0.3.4 after the GL feature list, run the arm64 build instead (the release ships one). If dsda-doom says `Unable to find required file "demo1"`, extract the DEMO1 lump to a `.lmp` file and pass its path. If steamcmd under Box64 stops on `__sched_cpualloc`, use DepotDownloader's arm64 build for anonymous downloads, or a Box64 built after 2026-09-13.

# Does the Steam client run on the AM62L?

**Short answer.** The native arm64 client reaches its sign-in window with two small fixes (Second push, below). The x86 client under Box64 0.3.4 does not: it installs and stops before its login window. Inside a Debian trixie arm64 container, Box64 0.3.4 runs Valve's 32-bit bootstrap, which downloads and installs the client (504,927 kB in 436 s) and then the 64-bit client (424,455 kB in 357 s). Neither client draws a window. The 32-bit client stops on a missing C library call, and the 64-bit client restarts itself as the 32-bit one.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). **Box64** runs x86-64 Linux programs on 64-bit Arm by translating their code; its **BOX32** mode runs 32-bit x86 programs. **binfmt_misc** is the kernel feature that lets Linux start a foreign binary through a translator automatically. **llvmpipe** is Mesa's software OpenGL. Scripts: `am62l-evm/steam/`; rows in `data/results/am62l-evm.csv` (variants `steam-*`). Checked 2026-10-25 on TI SDK 12.01 Linux (kernel 6.18.38), both A53 cores at 1.25 GHz, 2 GB RAM, no swap.

**Contents.** First try: the x86 client under Box64. Second push: the native arm64 client. Third push: a safer setup and what it costs. Fourth push: signed in, and Windows games through Proton on an ARMv8.0 core.

**Question.** How far does the x86 Steam client get on two A53 cores with no GPU: install, login window, store page, a light 2D game?

**What we tried.** The x86 Steam client was run under Box64 in a Debian arm64 container, then Valve's native arm64 client with a series of fixes (the pushes below).

**Expectation.** Very slow or a stop before the store page: Steam's interface is a Chromium browser, and every instruction is translated on a 1.25 GHz in-order core.

**Result.**

| Step | What happened | Time | Whole-system RAM used |
|---|---|--:|--:|
| 32-bit bootstrap under BOX32 | runs; asks for its data link (`~/.steam/steam`) | 4 s | 637 MB |
| `steam.sh` with native `sh` | every x86 helper fails with `Exec format error` | 1 s | 623 MB |
| Bootstrap with the links made by hand | downloads, extracts and installs the client | 436 s | 952 MB |
| Its relaunch | goes through `/bin/sh`, `Exec format error` (no binfmt_misc) | | |
| 32-bit client started under BOX32 | `PltResolver32: Symbol __sched_cpualloc ... not found`, stops | | 629 MB |
| 64-bit client (`steamrt64/steam`) under Box64 | updates itself, verifies, then `Running steamrt64 client but not opted in. Re-starting the scout environment` | 357 s | 1,090 MB |
| `steam.sh` under an emulated x86-64 bash | the runtime checks abort in GLib (`g_module_open` not found), then the same 32-bit stop | 62 s | 586 MB |

The virtual screen stayed black in every screenshot. Installed size: 2,467 MB.

**What it does not show.** No login window, store page or game, so no frame rate.

**If you try it.** If you see `Exec format error` from `steam.sh`, the kernel cannot start x86 binaries by itself: `zcat /proc/config.gz | grep BINFMT_MISC`. Run the 32-bit bootstrap directly with `box64` and make `~/.steam/steam` point at its folder. If you see `__sched_cpualloc ... not found`, the Box64 build is too old for this Steam client.


## Second push: the native arm64 client

**Result.** Valve publishes an arm64 Linux client in its public beta channel (`steam_client_publicbeta_linuxarm64`, the same layout the UbuntuAsahi `steam-arm64` script uses). On the A53 it needs four changes, after which it updates itself and draws **Sign in to Steam** (account field, password field and QR code) between 20 and 43 s after start. No account was entered; that window is the stop point.

| Try | What happened | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| Client as downloaded (110 MB zip, 324 MB) | `Illegal instruction` at once | Built for ARMv8.1 LSE atomics (`ldaddal`, `swpa`, `cas`): 344 sites in `steam`, 1,711 in `steamwebhelper`, 5,882 in `steamclient.so`; the A53 is ARMv8.0 | `lse_trap.so` (below) |
| With `lse_trap.so` | `Failed to load steamui.so` | Valve's FFmpeg adds `av_malloc_tracked`, `av_mallocz_tracked`, `av_register_malloc`; stock FFmpeg 8 lacks them (Debian trixie has FFmpeg 7, testing has 9, Ubuntu 26.04 has 8) | `avshim.so`: the three calls on top of stock FFmpeg 8 |
| With both | Downloads a 670,648 kB update, installs it in about 6 minutes, restarts | expected | none |
| Restarted | `steamwebhelper` restarts every 10 s ("not responding", 64 restarts) | `steamwebhelper.sh` pins the browser to CPUs 2 to 6 (`taskset 0x7c`); the AM62L has CPUs 0 and 1 | drop the `taskset` |
| Browser starts | Client and browser die with `SIGBUS` in `memset` | CEF filled Docker's default 64 MB `/dev/shm` (158 MB in use once fixed) | `docker run --shm-size=512m` |
| Browser ready | "Unexpected Transport Error (0x3008)" dialog | The client checks its UI socket with `lsof`, absent from the container | install `lsof` |
| All fixes | **Sign in to Steam** drawn, 20 to 43 s after start | | |

Whole-system RAM in use with the sign-in window open: 1,180 to 1,330 MB of 1,960 MB (this includes the Doom framebuffer demo that kept running, about 500 MB of system baseline). The FFmpeg 8 container is Ubuntu 26.04; Mesa llvmpipe (LLVM 21.1.8); flags `-noverifyfiles -no-cef-sandbox -cef-disable-gpu -cef-disable-gpu-compositing`.

**The trap library.** `am62l-evm/steam/lse_trap/lse_trap.c` is an `LD_PRELOAD` library: a `SIGILL` handler decodes each LSE instruction (LD<op>, SWP, CAS, CASP, and LDAPR) and does the same operation with load-exclusive and store-exclusive, then steps past it. Atomics on unaligned addresses (legal with ARMv8.4 LSE2) run under one lock, and a `SIGBUS` handler covers unaligned LDAR and STLR. Its self-test (`test_lse.c`, built with `-march=armv8.1-a`) dies with `SIGILL` alone and prints PASS with the library: 2 threads, 1,000,000 increments each, 14.3 s, about 7 microseconds per trapped atomic. Any ARMv8.1 arm64 binary can run on an A53 this way, slowly.

**Other paths.** Box64 git has wrapped `__sched_cpualloc` for BOX32 since 2026-09-13 (after release 0.4.4), so a git build would pass the first stop of the x86 client; not built (the build host had no network, and the native client went first). The board runs 32-bit Arm programs (`CONFIG_COMPAT=y`; an `armhf` container reports `armhf`), so the Pi-Apps recipe (box86 for the 32-bit client plus box64) can run here. FEX-Emu still lists ARMv8.0 as supported but plans ARMv8.4 as its floor (FEX issue 4120).

**What it does not show.** No store page, library or game: those need a signed-in account. No frame rate. Speed of the trap path beyond startup.

**If you try it.** If you see `Illegal instruction` from `steamrtarm64/steam`, preload `lse_trap.so`. If you see `undefined symbol: av_malloc_tracked`, preload `avshim.so` on FFmpeg 8. If `steamwebhelper` restarts every 10 s, remove `taskset 0x7c` from `steamwebhelper.sh`. If the client dies with `SIGBUS` in `memset`, give the container `--shm-size=512m`. If you see "Unexpected Transport Error (0x3008)", install `lsof`. Scripts: `am62l-evm/steam/fetch_arm64.sh`, `setup_arm64.sh`, `run_arm64.sh` (`LSE_TRAP=1 AVSHIM=1`).

**Board state after the second push.** All Steam containers, images and files were removed (7.5 GB freed).


## Third push: a safer setup, and what it costs

**Result.** The client reaches a drawn **Sign in to Steam** page as an unprivileged user with Chromium's sandbox on, on Docker's default bridge network, with the scripts mounted read-only. Rewriting each LSE instruction after its first trap cuts trapped atomics at the idle sign-in page from about 2,280 per second to under 10, and time to the drawn page from 56 to 57 s to 46 to 49 s. What remains is the price of drawing a Chromium page in software: about half of one core while the page sits idle. Swap does not change it. Stop point: the sign-in page; no account is entered.

**Setup** (`am62l-evm/steam/setup_arm64_user.sh`, `run_user.sh`). Ubuntu 26.04 arm64 container, user `ubuntu` (uid 1000), `--init --shm-size=512m`, scripts at `/s` read-only, Steam's home at `/data`. Chromium's sandbox needs user namespaces: the kernel has `CONFIG_USER_NS=y` and `user.max_user_namespaces = 7770`, and Docker's default seccomp profile blocks `unshare(CLONE_NEWUSER)`, so this one container runs with `--security-opt seccomp=unconfined`. With that, `unshare -Ur` works as uid 1000, the renderer processes show `Seccomp: 2` (filter on) and the zygote runs in its own PID namespace; `-no-cef-sandbox` is no longer used. `--network host` is not needed.

**Hot-patching the atomics** (`lse_trap/lse_patch.h`, `LSE_PATCH=1`). At the first trap of each LSE instruction in a file-backed code page (never JIT code), the handler writes a stub for that exact instruction (its registers, size and operation) with `ldaxr`/`stlxr` (`ldaxp`/`stlxp` for CASP) into a code page within branch range, and turns the instruction into a branch to it. LDAPR becomes LDAR in place. MIN and MAX atomics, and sites first met on an unaligned address, stay on the trap path; a stub that later meets an unaligned address faults, and the SIGBUS handler undoes its pushes and emulates the instruction. Static patching of the files was not used: every client update replaces the binaries, and patching in memory leaves the files untouched. Check (`test_patch.c`: every patched form at 1 to 8 bytes, SP-relative base, flags across CAS, CASP, an aligned-then-unaligned site, a two-thread race): PASS 5 of 5 runs; one atomic add costs 6.7 to 6.9 microseconds trapped and 18 to 19 ns patched.

**Expectation.** Startup a few seconds faster (the earlier trap count was in the millions); idle CPU dominated by rendering, so little change there.

**Each mode to the drawn sign-in page** (one run each, two where shown; Doom kept running on HDMI outside the container through every run; "painted" is the first screenshot with over 1,000 colors; CPU is the container's cgroup time; board RAM is the highest `free` used during the run, 540 to 560 MB before it):

| Mode | Window, s | Painted, s | CPU to painted, core-s | Idle CPU at the page, % of one core | Traps per s at idle | Board RAM peak, MB |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Trap only (every LSE a signal) | 37, 37 | 56, 57 | 75, 76 | 57, 57 | 2,275, 2,283 | 1,280, 1,278 |
| Hot-patched, sandbox on | 33, 30 | 49, 46 | 63, 61 | 54, 53 | 4, 0 | 1,409, 1,302 |
| Hot-patched, `-no-cef-sandbox` | 34 | 47 | 61 | 58 | 6 | 1,271 |
| `-cef-disable-gpu -cef-disable-gpu-compositing` | 28 | 44 | 57 | 33 | 0 | 1,370 |
| `-cef-single-process` | 31 | 52 | 67 | 56 | 67 | 1,335 |
| `-nofriendsui -nochatui` | 33 | 48 | 63 | 54 | 0 | 1,456 |
| `-silent` | 33 | 48 | 61 | 55 | 10 | 1,264 |
| `-no-browser` | 35 | 56 | 69 | 55 | 8 | 1,538 |
| Big Picture (`-gamepadui`) | 32 | 137 | 195 | 141 | 6 | 1,421 |
| Lean: no GPU flags plus no friends or chat | 33, 33 | 47, 47 | 59, 59 | 38, 39 | 4, 10 | 1,224, 1,341 |
| Lean with a 1 GB swap file on the SD card | 33 | 46 | 58 | 38 | 5 | 1,220 |
| Hot-patched with the swap file | 33 | 49 | 64 | 55 | 0 | 1,391 |

`-silent`, `-no-browser` and `-cef-single-process` change nothing measurable here (the client prints no error for `-no-browser` and still opens its browser). The two GPU flags cut idle CPU by about 40 percent. Big Picture draws its full-screen interface in software and needs 2.8 times as long. Over both swap runs 12 MB went to swap (3,107 pages out, 1,247 in): Steam to the sign-in page fits in the 2 GB.

**Limits.**

| Limit | Cause | Fixable here? |
|---|---|---|
| Every page is drawn in software; half a core at an idle sign-in page, 1.4 cores for Big Picture | no GPU driver for Chromium (Mesa llvmpipe or SwiftShader) | No. The GPU flags trim it by about 40 percent |
| Two in-order A53 cores at 1.25 GHz | the chip | No |
| About 0.6 to 1.0 GB of RAM for the client at the sign-in page, 0.4 to 0.7 GB left of 1.96 GB | Chromium plus the client | Partly: the lean flags; swap only helps cold pages |
| ARMv8.0: no LSE atomics | Valve builds for ARMv8.1 and newer | Yes: trap plus hot-patch; each site traps once (about 7 microseconds) |
| x86 games | need Box64 or FEX; FEX plans to drop ARMv8.0 | Partly; Box64 only |
| Sandbox needs `seccomp=unconfined` for the container | Docker's default profile blocks user namespaces | A custom profile that allows `unshare` would narrow it |
| Crash dumps go to Valve | the client's breakpad reporter uploads without asking | No switch found; keep `/dev/shm` empty between starts so it does not crash |
| A killed browser leaves its shared memory in `/dev/shm`; the next start dies with `SIGBUS` | Chromium cleanup | Yes: empty `/dev/shm` before a start (`modes_host.sh`) |

**What it does not show.** Anything past the sign-in page: store, library, a game, frame rate. One run per mode (two for trap, hot-patched and lean). Board RAM includes Xvfb and the Doom demo.

**If you try it.** If you see `undefined symbol: __atomic_compare_exchange_16` from a preload library, the library calls libatomic: write 16-byte atomics with `ldaxp`/`stlxp`. If every start after the first crashes with a minidump, empty `/dev/shm` in the container. If `unshare -Ur` fails as a normal user in the container, give that container `--security-opt seccomp=unconfined`.

## Fourth push (2026-10-27): signed in, and Valve's Windows path on an ARMv8.0 core

**Result so far.** Signed in, the arm64 client draws the store, downloads games and registers Valve's own arm64 tools for Windows games: FEX (Valve's x86 translator build), Steam Linux Runtime 4 and Proton Experimental. Valve's FEX does not run on the A53 as shipped. Rebuilt from the same commit for ARMv8.0, it runs x86-64 programs at once, and Proton's Wine processes start under it. Backyard Baseball '97 (the 1997 32-bit Windows program) starts, its `SteamAPI_Init` succeeds, and the arm64 client lists the game as Running and records play time. It quits about 10 s later without drawing a window: Wine's desktop process (explorer) is not ready within Wine's wait, so the game has no display driver. That is the stop point on 2026-10-27.

**Each stop and its fix.**

| Stop | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Game exits at once, no message | Valve's `fex-compat-tool` is a Python script; the container had no `python3` | Install `python3` in the container |
| `RootFS path doesn't exist. This is required on AArch64 hosts` | Valve's arm64 SteamOS ships an x86-64 root file system at `/usr/share/guestos/fex-mesa`; a plain Linux has none | FEX's published Arch Linux image (1.36 GB download, 4.4 GB unpacked, 120 s plus 452 s on the board), linked at that path |
| FEX exits with code 4 (SIGILL) after about 110 s, no message | Valve's `FEX` binary holds 257 ARMv8.1 atomic instructions; the trap library catches them until FEX installs its own signal handler, then the first one kills the guest | Build FEX from Valve's commit (`37265b1`) with `-DTUNE_CPU=none -DTUNE_ARCH=armv8-a -DBUILD_FEXCONFIG=OFF -DBUILD_STEAM_SUPPORT=ON`, about 5 minutes on an Apple-silicon Mac mini in a Debian arm64 container; the 15 atomic sites left sit behind run-time CPU checks. `uname -m` under FEX: `x86_64` in under 1 s |
| `Failed to remap /proc/pid/cmdline data (prctl failed)` | Needs `CAP_SYS_RESOURCE` | Harmless; FEX goes on |
| First launch stays at Steam's "Launching" for over 25 minutes | Steam's `legacycompat/iscriptevaluator.exe` (an old game's install script) waits with almost no CPU (22 s in 26 min) | Skip it: start the game's exe through the same chain by hand (`am62l-evm/steam/run_proton.sh`) |
| `steamclient_init unable to load native steamclient library`, then an assertion in `lsteamclient` | This arm64 client ships only the arm64 `steamclient.so`; Proton's bridge needs the x86 one, and for a 32-bit game the 32-bit one, whose libraries `libopenal.so.1`, `libnm.so.0` and `libudev.so.1` are not in Steam Linux Runtime 4 | Link `~/.steam/sdk32` and `sdk64` to the x86 client's `ubuntu12_32` and `linux64` (left by the first try) and copy the three libraries from Valve's `steamrt3c` runtime into `ubuntu12_32`; the glibc loader log (`LDDBG=1` in `run_proton.sh`) names each missing one |
| `nodrv_CreateWindow: The explorer process failed to start` | Under FEX, Wine's explorer loads `winex11.drv` and is still starting when Wine stops waiting for it (about 30 s) | Second reading of the log: this line comes from Proton's wrapper process, not the game. The game process starts, loads `steam.dll`, prints one `lsteamclient` fixme and then logs nothing for ten minutes: it hangs in Steam API setup. The 32-bit `steamclient.so` in use is from the *stable* x86 client (2026-10-26) while the running client is the *public beta* arm64 build (version 1793056502); the bridge between them is version-matched. Next: fetch `steam_client_publicbeta_ubuntu12` at that version and use its `ubuntu12_32` instead |

**ScummVM, for comparison.** The same purchased Backyard Baseball '97 files load in ScummVM 2.9.0 (Debian) and in ScummVM built from source on 2026-10-27: the title screen and clubhouse draw full screen at 4:3, and both stop with an assertion in the SCUMM script stack (`_scummStackPos`) at Play Ball. The Steam files' `BASEBALL.HE0` (MD5 `b855daca2b7c40fc45592cdf5ce54f86`) is not in ScummVM's table, which lists a different Steam fingerprint for this game.

**The line.** The x86 client under Box64 0.3.4 draws no window. Valve's native arm64 client reaches its sign-in page once atomics the A53 lacks are supplied, then signs in and downloads games, but Valve's FEX does not run on the A53 as shipped, and the Windows game it launched quit without drawing a window.

# Can a packer give the LAUNCHXL-F2800137 the same CC1407P wire bytes as an Arm chip?

**Short answer.** Yes for the transmit path. `portability/cc1407p-host/wire/` packs and unpacks 14 message types field by field. On the LAUNCHXL-F2800137 and on a Mac the stream is the same 315 octets (digest DC1DF5B1), and every message equals what TI's structs produce on a byte-addressed host. The driver itself is not changed to call it, and no radio was attached.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). Follows [E244](2026-10-24-f2800137-cc1407p-host-shim.md). Code and results: `portability/cc1407p-host/wire/README.md`. Checked 2026-10-25, C2000 compiler 25.11.1.LTS, C2000Ware 26.02.00.00 LTS, probe <probe serial>.

**Question.** E244 ended with a different first message on the C28x. Does a packer that never lays a struct over a buffer fix the wire format?

**What we tried.** A field-by-field packer for 14 message types was built for the C28x and for a Mac, and the bytes it produces were compared with what TI's structs produce.

**Expectation.** Same bytes, because every offset is explicit and the only C28x differences are 16-bit `int` shifts and 16-bit `char`. The risk was a layout misread from the TRX.h comments.

**Result.** 17 of 17 cases equal on both targets (messages, the first transaction of TI's unmodified driver, a two-request transaction with padding and CRC, and radio-to-host parsing). A hand-moved offset fails the Mac test. The RAM image reads back identical bytes over the debugger. Cost: 677 words of code.

**The line.** What it does not show: RX, test and extended command layouts are not written. The reference is TI's structs plus one real driver transaction, not a capture of the full driver flow (it waits in `TRX_Host_open` for a radio). `LRF_*_byteCount` is half the octet count on the C28x, a trap for any port.

**Board state.** RAM load only. Flash read before and after: SHA-256 identical to the as-received image; TI's demo prints again.

<!-- experiment

On 2026-10-31, standard ONNX Runtime int8 compiled for the NPU put 0 layers on it (CPU speed), TI's post-training option put every layer there with no retraining at a 0 to 9.7 point accuracy cost, and ResNet-8 through TI's QAT ran in 198.2 ms on the NPU build against 201.6 ms with CMSIS-NN, because the residual layers stay on the CPU.

# Does a model run on the LP-AM13E230 straight from the file the training tool wrote, in float, with no vendor quantization step?

**Short answer.** Yes, for all nine tried. A float32 1-D CNN trained by torch and exported to ONNX as is, a scikit-learn decision tree and random forest through skl2onnx, and an XGBoost model from its own JSON file each went to portable C with `tools/byom` (plain Python 3.10 or newer, no package installed) and gave the training tool's class on 20 of 20 held-out windows on the board, with outputs within 3e-6 of torch and 1.2e-7 of XGBoost. On the Cortex-M33's FPU at 200 MHz the float models take 0.392, 1.194, 5.581 and 22.48 ms (692 to 33.2k parameters), which is 0.80, 0.96, 1.10 and 1.20 times the int8 plain-C build of the same architectures. TI's NPU build of the int8 models stays 3.7, 5.8, 8.9 and 2.4 times faster than float. The trees take 1.4 us, 24 us and 80 us, and the XGBoost model has the best test-set accuracy of the seven (93.2 percent).

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). 1 kB = 1,024 bytes. NPU is the chip's neural-network accelerator; NNC is TI's neural network compiler; ONNX is the exchange file format most training tools export; a multiply-add is one weight times one input.

**Question.** An engineer has a trained model in the form the training tool gives (an ONNX file, a scikit-learn or XGBoost model). Does it run on this chip as it is, how fast, and does it still give the same answers?

**Vendor position.** TI's NNC 2.1.2 user's guide takes an ONNX model quantized with TI's model optimizer (`tinyml_torchmodelopt`, 8-bit quantization-aware training) and compiles it for the NPU or the CPU (<https://software-dl.ti.com/mctools/nnc/mcu/users_guide/compiling.html>, read 2026-10-09). Its setup page asks for Python 3.10 and a Linux or Windows machine (read 2026-10-30); there is no macOS or Arm build, which is why this repo's NNC compiles ran on a GitHub Linux machine (E33). The guide's model types are neural networks; decision trees and gradient-boosted trees are not covered. The AM13E230 data sheet gives the Cortex-M33 a single-precision FPU.

**What was tried.** The seven models were trained on the Mac mini with the training tools' own exporters (`tools/byom/examples/train_occupancy.py`: torch 2.15 opset 17, scikit-learn 1.9 through skl2onnx 1.20, XGBoost 3.4 `save_model` JSON and onnxmltools 1.16), on the same UCI room-occupancy windows as the int8 models (`mspm0g3507/mcu-bench/edgeai/`): the four CNNs with the exact layer specs of `occ_cnn_500` to `occ_cnn_30k`, trained in float for 60 epochs and never quantized; the trees on 16 window features (last, mean, min and max of each channel). `tools/byom/byom.py check` read each file (its own protobuf reader, no `onnx` package), wrote portable C99 (float32 loops, two static buffers, no runtime), compiled it with the Mac's `cc` and compared it with the training tool's outputs on 20 held-out windows (5 per class), then wrote the vectors as a header. Then `am13e230/bench/byom/build.sh` built one image per model with TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS at `-O3`, hard float, the AM13E2x SDK 26.01.00.03.STS start-up and the 200 MHz clock of TI's CoreMark example; `run.sh` erased, flashed and ran each image three times from reset and read the result block over the probe: the class of every vector against the training tool's class and the true label, the largest output difference, and the fastest of 5 calls per vector on the DWT cycle counter. Rows: `data/results/am13e230.csv` (`byom_latency`, `byom_agreement`).

**How far it got.** Verified: 24 of 24 runs gave 20 of 20 classes matching the training tool, and every run of an image gave the same cycle count on the fastest vector (the 30k model differed by 3 cycles on one run). Expectation, written before the runs (`_agent/runs/2026-10-30-byom/EXPECTATION.md`): float at 6 to 12 cycles per multiply-add, so 0.35 to 0.7, 1.0 to 2.0, 4.7 to 9.5 and 18 to 37 ms; all four landed inside (6.8, 7.0, 7.1 and 7.4 cycles per multiply-add). The tree guesses were low: under 1 us, 2 to 5 us and 10 to 30 us against 1.4, 24 and 80 us measured; a node costs about 35 to 40 cycles here (a 12-byte node read from flash with three wait states, a compare, a data-dependent branch and, at each leaf, one add per class), not the few cycles assumed.

| Model | Parameters | Multiply-adds | Test accuracy (float, this run) | float32 C from the ONNX file | int8 plain C `-O3` (E33 rows) | TI NNC CPU, int8 | TI NNC NPU, int8 | NPU gain over float |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| occ_cnn_500 | 692 | 11,456 | 88.8 % | 0.392 ms | 0.489 ms | 0.499 ms | 0.107 ms | 3.7x |
| occ_cnn_2k | 1,852 | 33,984 | 88.8 % | 1.194 ms | 1.25 ms | 1.376 ms | 0.205 ms | 5.8x |
| occ_cnn_8k | 8,684 | 157,952 | 92.9 % | 5.581 ms | 5.055 ms | 5.544 ms | 0.630 ms | 8.9x |
| occ_cnn_30k | 33.2k | 610,688 | 81.8 % | 22.48 ms | 18.71 ms | 22.91 ms | 9.535 ms | 2.4x |

The int8 columns are the 2026-10-08 and 2026-10-09 rows on the same board, clock and compiler; their models were trained from the same specs with TI's quantization-aware step, test accuracy 88.4, 88.5, 90.9 and 85.4 percent (`mspm0g3507/mcu-bench/edgeai/uci-room-occupancy/*/result.json`). The float and int8 models are separate training runs, so the accuracy columns compare recipes, not one model two ways. Parameters count the float model's as trained (including the input normalization); the int8 models carry 636 to 32,836 after folding.

| Model | Nodes | Weights in flash | Test accuracy | Fastest vector | Slowest vector | Image flash / RAM |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| scikit-learn decision tree, depth 8 | 65 | 1.8 kB | 87.8 % | 1.4 us | 2.2 us | 11.4 kB / 9.2 kB |
| scikit-learn random forest, 20 trees, depth 6 | 876 | 24.3 kB | 83.4 % | 24.3 us | 34.9 us | 32.3 kB / 9.2 kB |
| XGBoost, 120 trees, depth 4, from its JSON file | 1,290 | 22.4 kB | 93.2 % | 80.1 us | 113.3 us | 36.0 kB / 9.2 kB |
| the same XGBoost model through onnxmltools | 1,290 | 22.4 kB | 93.2 % | 80.2 us | 112.7 us | 36.0 kB / 9.2 kB |

Image sizes are the whole program (harness, 20 vectors, SDK start-up, two 1 kB to 4 kB work buffers on the CNNs); the model's own flash and working RAM are in each row's conditions. Test accuracy is on the 1,001-window test split of the block protocol; the 20 vectors are 5 per class, so "x of 20 match the true label" in the rows is a check of the vectors, not an accuracy figure (the 30k float model, the least accurate, matched 5 of 20).

## Second run, same day: TFLite, the tool's own int8, and tuned loops

Three more questions, run the same way (three runs each, expectation first in `_agent/runs/2026-10-30-byom/EXPECTATION-2.md`).

**A TFLite file.** The same CNN family built in Keras and exported with `tf.lite.TFLiteConverter`, float32 (6.1 kB) and int8 with a representative dataset (5.8 kB), read by the tool's own flatbuffer reader (`tools/byom/tflite.py`, no TensorFlow on the host). The float file gives the interpreter's class on 20 of 20 vectors within 1.9e-6 on the host and the board, and runs in 0.304 ms with the tuned loops. The int8 file is read on the float path (weights dequantized, the interpreter's activation requantization dropped): it agrees with the interpreter on 15 of 20 vectors. That file is also the first-person evidence for the quantization pain in the survey: TFLite's default int8 conversion took this model from 92.1 to 83.4 percent test accuracy, and its interpreter matches only 10 of 20 true labels on the vectors, because the per-tensor int8 constant that scales the four input channels (0.023 to 5.98) cannot hold the small values. The float file matches 18 of 20.

**The tool's own int8.** `byom.py quantize`: symmetric int8, one scale per output channel for weights, one per tensor for activations from the 20 vectors as the calibration set, int32 accumulation, exact integer requantization (the C and the Python reference give the same integers). Expectation: 6 to 9 cycles per multiply-add, so 0.34 to 0.52, 1.0 to 1.5, 4.7 to 7.1 and 18 to 27 ms; all four landed inside.

| Model | Int8 by the tool | Classes vs the float model | Largest output difference | Weights | TI's int8 path, CPU (NNC) | TI's NPU |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| occ_cnn_500 | 0.447 ms | 20 of 20 | 0.30 of 9.35 | 892 B | 0.499 ms | 0.107 ms |
| occ_cnn_2k | 1.227 ms | 19 of 20 | 0.26 of 6.06 | 2.3 kB | 1.376 ms | 0.205 ms |
| occ_cnn_8k | 5.386 ms | 20 of 20 | 0.44 of 8.8 | 10.1 kB | 5.544 ms | 0.630 ms |
| occ_cnn_30k | 19.95 ms | 20 of 20 | 0.17 of 8.31 | 35.5 kB | 22.91 ms | 9.535 ms |

So an int8 scheme any engineer can read (and any accelerator tool can be compared against) keeps the float model's answers on 79 of 80 vectors and runs within 1.2 times of the vendor's int8 CPU code. The NPU column is the vendor's and stays the only way under 1 ms on the 8k model.

**Tuned float loops (`--fast`).** A zero-padded copy of the input, no bounds checks in the inner loop, the output tile accumulated per weight. Expectation: 2 to 4 cycles per multiply-add. Measured 5.3, 5.0, 4.7 and 4.4 cycles per multiply-add: 0.302, 0.846, 3.703 and 13.57 ms, 1.3, 1.4, 1.5 and 1.7 times faster than the plain loop, short of the expectation. A second form that accumulates in a register instead of memory was measured slower on all four (0.344, 0.938, 3.928, 14.69 ms; rows `-fastreg`), so the first form is what `--fast` writes. The remaining gap to the NPU is 2.8, 4.1, 5.9 and 1.4 times. A real kernel library (CMSIS-NN, or the vendor's) is the next rung; these loops are what plain C gets to.

**A real kernel behind the same front end (`quantize --kernels cmsis-nn`).** The same int8 models, with the convolutions and the fully connected layer written as CMSIS-NN calls (`arm_convolve_s8`, `arm_fully_connected_s8`, Apache-2.0, built from `third-party/cmsis-nn` with the M33's DSP extension) and the pools kept as plain loops in CMSIS-NN's NHWC order. Expectation: 1.5 to 3 cycles per multiply-add. Measured 8.6, 3.7 and 2.8 cycles per multiply-add on the 500, 8k and 30k models: 0.491, 2.894 and 8.540 ms. The smallest model lost (0.447 ms plain): CMSIS-NN's per-call setup and im2col copy cost more than its 11k multiply-adds save. The 8k model gained 1.9 times over the plain int8 loop and the 30k model 2.3 times, and on the 30k model CMSIS-NN on the CPU (8.540 ms) is faster than the vendor's NPU build (9.535 ms), because the NPU build keeps one convolution on the CPU in plain code. Classes 20 of 20 against the float model on all three; the outputs matched the plain int8 reference to the count on every vector (CMSIS-NN's rounding did not differ here).

| Model | Plain int8 (ours) | CMSIS-NN int8 (ours) | Vendor int8, CPU | Vendor NPU |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| occ_cnn_500 | 0.447 ms | 0.491 ms | 0.499 ms | 0.107 ms |
| occ_cnn_8k | 5.386 ms | 2.894 ms | 5.544 ms | 0.630 ms |
| occ_cnn_30k | 19.95 ms | 8.540 ms | 22.91 ms | 9.535 ms |

**The vendor's compiler on an Arm host.** TI's index offers NNC 2.1.2 as a CPython 3.10 wheel for Linux x86-64 (and Windows); asked on 2026-10-30, it had nothing for Python 3.12 on any host and nothing for Linux aarch64 (`pip download` from an Apple Silicon Mac with Python 3.12, and from arm64 and amd64 Linux containers with Python 3.10 and 3.12). `tools/byom/nnc-container/` is a Docker image of that exact pair (python:3.10-slim, linux/amd64) with the wheel and TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS inside, both checked against the sha256 values on record. On the Apple Silicon Mac mini, under Docker's x86 emulation, the image built in 2 min 2 s and compiled `occ_cnn_500` for the NPU in 10.0 s; its generated C differs from the GitHub-built copy (E33) only in two variable names and the input path. Linked and run here: 20 of 20 vectors, 0.1065 ms, against 0.1067 ms for the GitHub build (row `occ_cnn_500-nnc-npu-container`). So the wheel's host limits are a packaging fact, not a compiler one.

The tool also gained a page over the same commands (`tools/byom/web.py`: model and vectors in, table, check and a zip of the C out, on this computer only; with a target board chosen it builds, flashes and shows the measured time, checked on the AM13E230), a LICENSE (BSD-3 on the tool, nothing on the generated C) and a run on an Arm Mac mini with a stock Python 3.12 and no packages (both checks in 0.7 s).

**A second board, 2026-10-31: the LP-MSPM0G5187 (Cortex-M0+, no FPU, 80 MHz).** The same C for `occ_float_500` (tuned loops) and `xgb`, the same 20 vectors and the same three-run method, through `mspm0g5187/bench/byom/` (SysTick cycle counter, DSLite flash, OpenOCD read-back). Expectation written first: 11 to 23 ms for the CNN (80 to 160 cycles per multiply-add in software float) and 0.3 to 0.6 ms for XGBoost. Measured: 29.09 ms (2.33 million cycles, about 203 cycles per multiply-add) and 1.01 ms (80.8k cycles, about 170 cycles per node visited), 20 of 20 classes on both, every run within 4 cycles of the others. Both are above the expectation: the soft-float library costs more per operation than assumed. Against the AM13E230 (0.302 and 0.080 ms) the M0+ is 96 and 13 times slower; the clock explains 2.5 times of that, software float the rest, and trees suffer less because a tree is compares and branches. Rows: `byom_latency` and `byom_agreement` in `data/results/mspm0g5187.csv`.

**A third board, 2026-11-08: the NUCLEO-U083RC (Cortex-M0+, no FPU, 48 MHz).** The same C and vectors through `nucleo-u083rc/bench/byom/` (ST's HAL clock setup, SysTick cycle counter, GCC 14.3.1 `-O3` from STM32CubeCLT, STM32CubeProgrammer flash and verify, result block read under hardware reset). Expectation first: 29 to 68 ms for the CNN and 1.0 to 2.4 ms for XGBoost, scaled from the G5187's cycles. Measured: 57.90 ms (2.78 million cycles, about 243 per multiply-add) and 1.47 ms (70.7k cycles, about 147 per node visited), 20 of 20 classes on both, three identical runs, largest output differences 2.86e-06 and 1.19e-07 as on the other boards. Both inside the band. The same core costs 20 percent more cycles per multiply-add under GCC's soft-float library than under TI's, and 12 percent fewer per tree node. ST's demo was backed up before (identical to the stored copy) and restored after, read back identical. Rows: `byom_latency` and `byom_agreement` in `data/results/nucleo-u083rc.csv`. The FRDM-MCXA153 half did not run: its MCU-Link did not enumerate on USB.

**An image model, 2026-10-31: MLPerf Tiny ResNet-8 on CIFAR-10.** The benchmark's own float file (`pretrainedResnet.tflite` from mlcommons/tiny: 78k parameters, 12.5 million multiply-adds per 32x32 colour image), read by `tools/byom` after it gained skip connections (a tensor read twice is kept in a slot; a two-tensor ADD adds the slot back; the int8 add is exact integer arithmetic). Expectation first (`_agent/runs/2026-10-31-resnet/EXPECTATION.md`): float does not fit, int8 at 0.38 to 0.56 s plain and 0.18 to 0.23 s with CMSIS-NN.

| ResNet-8 on the LP-AM13E230, 200 MHz | Weights | Working RAM | Time per image | Matches float (20 images) | CIFAR-10 accuracy (1,000 images, host) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| float32 as trained | 304 kB | 224 kB | does not fit: the link needs 297 kB of RAM, the chip has 96 kB | 20 of 20 on the host | 88.1 % |
| int8 by the tool, plain C | 79 kB | 56 kB | 444.6 ms (7.1 cycles per multiply-add) | 20 of 20 | 88.4 % |
| int8 by the tool, CMSIS-NN | 79 kB | 56 kB | 201.6 ms (3.2 cycles per multiply-add) | 20 of 20 | same integers to within one count |

Both times landed inside the expectation; three runs each, cycle-identical to within 3 cycles. The TFLite interpreter scores 88.1 percent on the same 1,000 images and MLPerf's own int8 file 87.8, so the tool's int8, calibrated on 20 images, loses nothing. The 20 float test images take 245 kB of flash, so the board build lets constants span both flash banks (the linker's split operator on `.rodata`). The NPU build follows in the third-day section below. Rows: `byom_latency` and `byom_agreement`, variants `resnet8-*`, in `data/results/am13e230.csv`.

## Third day, 2026-10-31: does the NPU take a standard int8 model?

TI's NNC guide says the NPU needs a model "quantized with the TI-NPU quantization scheme" and that float or CPU-quantized models run their layers on the CPU (<https://software-dl.ti.com/mctools/nnc/mcu/users_guide/ti-npu-qat.html>, read 2026-10-31). This run measures that. The same four float CNNs from the first run (retrained with the same recipe, logits within 4e-6 of the shipped ONNX files) were quantized three ways and each compiled by NNC 2.1.2 with `--target="c, ti-npu"` in `tools/byom/nnc-container` on the Mac mini, then flashed and run three times each with `am13e230/bench/occupancy-nnc/` (expected class: the float model's). Expectation first (`_agent/runs/2026-10-31-npu-std-int8/EXPECTATION.md`).

- **ONNX Runtime int8** (`quantize_static`, QDQ format, per-channel weights, MinMax on 256 training windows), the way most engineers quantize an ONNX file. Two forms: everything quantized, and the input normalization left in float (the sensor channels span 0 to 1 for PIR and 365 to 1,075 ppm for CO2, so one int8 scale on the raw input crushes the small channels).
- **TI's post-training quantization** (`TINPUTinyMLPTQFxModule` in `tinyml_torchmodelopt` 1.5.0, the PTQ path of TI's own examples: calibration passes with no backpropagation, then convert and export). It installed with `--no-deps` on torch 2.15 on the Arm mini.

| Model | ORT int8, all quantized | ORT int8, input in float | TI PTQ | Float model, CPU (first run) | TI QAT, NPU (E33) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| NPU layers (NNC report) | 0 | 0 | all | n/a | all |
| occ_cnn_500 | 0.655 ms, 6 of 20 | 0.646 ms, 20 of 20 | 0.107 ms, 7 of 20 | 0.392 ms | 0.107 ms |
| occ_cnn_2k | 1.608 ms, 10 of 20 | 1.558 ms, 19 of 20 | 0.205 ms, 10 of 20 | 1.194 ms | 0.205 ms |
| occ_cnn_8k | 6.447 ms, 9 of 20 | 6.439 ms, 19 of 20 | 0.630 ms, 10 of 20 | 5.581 ms | 0.630 ms |
| occ_cnn_30k | 21.38 ms, 6 of 20 | 21.31 ms, 20 of 20 | 9.458 ms, 12 of 20 | 22.48 ms | 9.535 ms |
| Test accuracy (1,001 windows, host), float 88.8 / 88.8 / 92.9 / 81.8 % | 81.4 / 85.8 / 84.7 / 78.9 % | 89.0 / 88.7 / 92.9 / 81.7 % | 87.0 / 84.3 / 83.2 / 81.8 % | | |

"x of 20" is the board's class against the float model's on the 20 vectors; the host gives the same count on every build (onnxruntime on the same file). The TI QAT column is a separate training run (E33), shown for its time.

What it shows:

- **A standard int8 model compiles for the NPU target and runs entirely on the CPU.** NNC's offload report lists every operator of every ONNX Runtime build as not offloaded; it considered only the max-pool (refused: NCHW layout and input padding) and never matched a convolution. The builds run in NNC's generic C at 0.95 to 1.65 times the time of the float model on the M33's FPU (the smallest model loses most), so quantizing this way buys nothing in time on this chip.
- **TI's own post-training option reaches the NPU with no retraining.** Every layer offloads on three models (the 30k keeps one convolution on the CPU: NNC warns its weights and bias could overflow the 18-bit accumulator), and the NPU times land within 1 percent of the QAT builds' (0.1067, 0.2051, 0.6299 and 9.458 ms against 0.1067, 0.2051, 0.6297 and 9.535 ms). The price is accuracy: 0 to 9.7 points of test accuracy on these models, and 7 to 12 of 20 vectors agreeing with float, against 19 or 20 for ONNX Runtime with the input left in float. QAT exists to win that back.
- **The answer to "does TI need its own scheme?" is yes, measured**: the NPU's pattern matcher takes TI's quantized graph form (the Mul, Floor and Clip requantization TI's exporter writes) and nothing else. TI's PTQ is the cheapest way in.

Rows: `ai_occ_latency`, variants `occ_float_*-ort-int8-nnc`, `-ort-int8-infloat-nnc` and `-ti-ptq-nnc-npu`, in `data/results/am13e230.csv`; each row's note holds the NPU layer count and the agreement.

**ResNet-8 on the NPU, same day.** TI's NPU path needs a torch model through TI's quantization-aware training, so ResNet-8 was rebuilt in torch from the MLPerf weights (88.1 % on the first 1,000 test images, the same as the TFLite float file) and put through `TINPUTinyMLQATFxModule` (8-bit, 8 epochs on CIFAR-10 with crop and flip, about 75 s an epoch on the Mac mini's CPU). Two things broke on the way. Torch's FX lowering refused the graph where a fused add and ReLU also fed the explicit pad that copies TF's bottom-and-right "same" padding on the stride-2 convs; moving the ReLU after the pad got past that, but TI's convert step then produced a model that gave class 5 for every image (10 percent) although the fake-quantized model scored 88.6. The standard PyTorch block (padding 1 on every 3x3 conv, no pad modules) converts correctly; it shifts the stride-2 convs by one pixel against MLPerf's weights (float falls to 60.2 percent), so the float model was fine-tuned 6 epochs from those weights (87.2 percent on 10,000 images) before QAT. Result: the int8 ONNX file scores 86.3 percent on 10,000 test images and 87.1 on the first 1,000. Expectation first (`_agent/runs/2026-10-31-resnet-npu/EXPECTATION.md`, revised before any board run): 120 to 250 ms, about the CMSIS-NN time.

| ResNet-8 on the LP-AM13E230, 200 MHz | On the NPU (NNC report) | RAM | Time per image | Board vs host, 20 images |
|---|---|--:|--:|--:|
| int8 by tools/byom, CMSIS-NN, CPU (above) | nothing | 56 kB | 201.6 ms | 20 of 20 |
| TI QAT, NNC `ti-npu` | 4 of 9 convs, the average pool and the FC | 85.7 kB workspace | 198.2 ms | 20 of 20 (18 of 20 true labels) |
| TI QAT, NNC CPU only (`type=soft`) | nothing | 106.1 kB workspace | does not fit: 96 kB of data RAM | |

The NPU build is 1.02 times faster than our CMSIS-NN build: NNC leaves the five convs that feed a residual add (the second 3x3 conv of each block and the two 1x1 shortcuts, 7.3 of 12.5 million multiply-adds) and the three adds on the CPU, where they run as NNC's generic C. TI's NPU layer table has no standalone add and a 1x1 convolution with a residual input (PWCONVRES) that this graph did not match (<https://software-dl.ti.com/mctools/nnc/mcu/users_guide/layer_configs_npu.html>). The NPU build also only fits because its workspace is smaller than the CPU build's: the harness's 12 kB input buffer and result block had to move to the 32 kB code RAM (`am13e230/bench/resnet-nnc/linker.sh`). Three runs, 39.64 million cycles on all three. Rows: `ai_ic_latency` and `ai_ic_agreement`, variant `resnet8-ti-qat-nnc-*`.

**Published ResNet-8 results from other vendors, beside ours.** The image model above is MLPerf Tiny's image-classification task, so published results exist for the same model file and data set (<https://github.com/mlcommons/tiny/tree/master/benchmark/training/image_classification>). MLPerf Tiny v1.4 (closed division, July 2026, <https://github.com/mlcommons/tiny_results_v1.4>) has STMicroelectronics results on seven systems; time per image below is 1 / the median throughput in each system's `ic/performance/results.txt`, and the core, clock and stack come from its `systems/*.json`. Every ST entry used "TensorFlow Int8 Quantization" and STEdgeAI-Core. No NXP part appears in any MLPerf Tiny round, v0.5 to v1.4, closed or open (the submitter folders of all seven results repositories, read 2026-10-31), so there is no published NXP number on this task to put here.

| ResNet-8, one 32x32 image | Core, clock | Engine | Time | Million cycles | Top-1 | Source |
|---|---|---|--:|--:|--:|---|
| STM32H7P5 (system status: Preview) | Cortex-M7, 550 MHz | Neural-ART NPU, 550 MHz | 0.96 ms | 0.5 | 88 % | v1.4 `NUCLEO_H7P5II_NPU` |
| STM32H7P5 (Preview) | Cortex-M7, 550 MHz | CPU | 21.1 ms | 11.6 | 87 % | v1.4 `NUCLEO_H7P5II_CM7` |
| STM32H7A3 | Cortex-M7, 280 MHz | CPU | 41.7 ms | 11.7 | 87 % | v1.4 `NUCLEO_H7A3ZI_Q` |
| STM32U3C5 | Cortex-M33, 96 MHz | HSP accelerator | 50.0 ms | 4.8 | 87 % | v1.4 `NUCLEO_U3C5ZIT6_Q_HSP` |
| STM32L4R5 | Cortex-M4, 120 MHz | CPU | 165.6 ms | 19.9 | 87 % | v1.4 `NUCLEO_L4R5ZI-P` |
| STM32U3C5 | Cortex-M33, 96 MHz | CPU | 182.7 ms | 17.5 | 87 % | v1.4 `NUCLEO_U3C5ZIT6_Q_CM33` |
| AM13E230 (ours) | Cortex-M33, 200 MHz | CPU, tools/byom int8 + CMSIS-NN | 201.6 ms | 40.3 | 88.4 % (1,000 images) | rows `resnet8-*` |
| AM13E230 (ours) | Cortex-M33, 200 MHz | TI NPU build (TI QAT + NNC) | 198.2 ms | 39.6 | 87.1 % (1,000 images) | row `resnet8-ti-qat-nnc-npu` |

How to read it. MLPerf's top-1 is on the benchmark's own accuracy subset, ours on the first 1,000 test images, so the accuracy column is a sanity check, not a ranking. On the same core type, ST's CPU build of the Cortex-M33 takes 17.5 million cycles per image and ours 40.3 million: STEdgeAI's generated code does the image in 2.3 times fewer cycles than tools/byom's int8 plus CMSIS-NN, so our CPU column is not the M33's best. Clock and memory differ too: the AM13E230's code runs from flash with 3 wait states at 200 MHz. ST's NPU entry ran a model quantized with TensorFlow's standard int8 tool; whether the Neural-ART compiler needs anything beyond that for other models was not checked here.

**The line.** Nothing stopped. Three limits on what the numbers say:

- The C is a reference implementation (one plain loop nest per layer, bounds checks in the inner loop), so 7 cycles per multiply-add is a floor for "any C compiler, any core", not what a tuned kernel or CMSIS-NN would reach on this core. Int8 plain C from the same kind of loops sits at 6 to 9 cycles per multiply-add here, which is why float as trained lands within 20 percent of it on a core with an FPU.
- The NPU gain is real and needs TI's quantization scheme: the NPU build is the only column that moves the 8k model under 1 ms, and that build only exists through TI's model optimizer (QAT, or its post-training option) and NNC. A float model and a standard int8 model have no NPU path (third-day section). On a residual image model the NPU takes under half the work and gains 2 percent.
- The AM263P (Cortex-R5F, FPU, no NPU) is off the bench, so its float figure is not measured here; its existing rows run TI's own float TVM models at 1.7 to 2.9 ms (`data/results/am263p.csv`, `ai_vendor_example`).

**Next moves.** CMSIS-NN or the vendor's kernels behind the same `byom` front end, to see how far the M33 can close on the NPU past plain C. The int8 TFLite arithmetic itself (the interpreter's requantization) so int8 TFLite files match their interpreter. The same harness on the LP-MSPM0G5187 (no FPU: float in software) and on an R5F board, to put one table across M0+, M33 and R5F. Train the float and int8 models from one checkpoint so the accuracy columns compare one model two ways.

**Limits.** One room, one dataset, 20 vectors per model on the board. Time is the fastest of 20 vectors, best of 5 calls, a best case with no sensor read or feature extraction (the tree models' 16 features were computed on the Mac). Energy was not measured. No peak-performance claim: none of the C is a tuned kernel.

# Can the AM62L run SNES and PlayStation emulation at full speed on HDMI?

**Short answer.** Yes, for the free content that could be tested. Snes9x 2005 (a libretro core) holds 60 fps at 640x480, 800x600, 1280x720 and 1920x1080, with the core using 2.5 to 3.6 ms of each 16.7 ms frame. PCSX-ReARMed holds 60 fps on a PlayStation GPU test program at 3.6 ms a frame. Audio through ALSA, a second video thread and the largest HDMI mode each cost under 1.5 ms more. What made the difference from the showcase's 48 fps is the display path: the same Gambatte Game Boy core runs at 60 fps here at 640x480 and at 1920x1080, where RetroArch under Xorg in a container gave 48 fps and 10.4 fps.

Terms: [vocab](../vocab.md). **libretro** is the plug-in interface emulator cores share; a core is one `.so` file. **DRM/KMS** is the Linux display interface that writes to the screen without X. A **dumb buffer** is plain memory the display controller scans out. **HLE BIOS** is PCSX-ReARMed's built-in replacement for Sony's boot code, so no BIOS file is needed. **Vblank** is the display's 60 Hz refresh tick. Code and logs: `am62l-evm/lean/`; rows in `data/results/am62l-evm.csv`.

**Question.** The earlier HDMI showcase ran a Game Boy core at 48 fps. A Game Boy is far lighter than an SNES, so was that the CPU, or the way the picture reached the screen? And does the chip (two Cortex-A53 at 1.25 GHz, no GPU) hold SNES and PlayStation at full speed when nothing sits between the emulator and the display?

**Expectation.** Written before the runs: Gambatte at 60 fps in any mode once X and the container are gone; SNES homebrew at 60 fps with a core time under 8 ms; PlayStation uncertain, because its GPU is emulated in software too.

**Setup.** TI SDK 12.01 Linux (kernel 6.18.38-ti-kvm), both cores at 1.25 GHz, `performance` governor, 2 GB RAM, HDMI-A-1 connected, nothing else running (the showcase loop and containers stopped). Everything runs on the board, as root, from a text console.

- Frontend: `am62l-evm/lean/lean_fe.c`. It loads a core with `dlopen`, calls `retro_run` once per frame, copies the frame to a dumb buffer, and flips on vblank. Integer nearest-neighbor scaling in software (2x at 640x480, 3x at 1280x720, 4x at 1080p for a 256x224 SNES picture), 16-bit RGB565 throughout. Options: `-t` video thread, `-a` audio through ALSA `plughw:0,0`, `-n` no vblank wait (free run).
- Cores built on the board with GCC 15.3: Snes9x 2005 (libretro, commit a79dfe9, about 3 minutes), PCSX-ReARMed r26 (commit 7b0e8f8, ARM64 dynarec and NEON GPU, about 19 minutes). Gambatte is the Debian core copied out of the showcase container.
- Measurement: 2 s warm-up, then 10 s, three runs per row, median. Frame time is the core's `retro_run` alone, timed with the monotonic clock. A vblank is missed when two flips are more than 1.5 frames apart. CPU use is the share of each core's time that was not idle, from `/proc/stat`.
- Content (all free to redistribute; no commercial title, no Sony BIOS):

| File | What it is | Source and license |
|---|---|---|
| `Mode7LZ77.sfc`, `Transparency.sfc`, `effectsandmusic.sfc` (plus `Mode1ContinuousScroll`, `DynamicEngineMetaSprite`, `breakout`, `music` for the free-run table) | PVSnesLib example programs: a rotating Mode 7 plane, full-screen transparency, sprites with sound effects and music | PVSnesLib 4.6.0 release (`github.com/alekmaul/pvsneslib`), MIT license as stated by the repository; per-asset credits not audited. sha256 (first 12 hex) of the three main files: `04ccdd4d7043`, `9e641a051f40`, `e10465545dff` |
| `benchmark.exe`, `animated-triangle.exe` | PlayStation test programs: flat triangles drawn by the GPU, and one rotating triangle | `github.com/JaCzekanski/ps1-tests`, release build-158, MIT. sha256 (first 12 hex) `372255c4d617` and `9b30c615dfd1` |
| `tobu.gb` | Tobu Tobu Girl, a Game Boy game (control run) | gbdev database; code MIT, assets CC BY 4.0, Tangram Games. sha256 (first 12 hex) `5d3871cae77d` |

**Result.** Medians of three 10 s runs, `scale` is the software scaling and copy per frame. Raw lines: `am62l-evm/lean/matrix-2026-11-01.txt`.

| Core and content | HDMI mode (scale) | Options | fps | Core ms per frame (p95) | Scale ms | Vblanks missed | CPU, core 0 / core 1 |
|---|---|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--|
| Snes9x 2005, Mode 7 | 640x480 (2x) | | 60.00 | 2.48 (2.66) | 0.46 | 0 of 600 | 12 / 20 percent |

| Gambatte, Tobu Tobu Girl (control) | 640x480 (3x) | | 60.00 | 0.87 (0.98) | 0.35 | 0 of 600 | 14 / 11 |
| Same | 1920x1080 (7x) | | 60.00 | 0.87 (0.99) | 1.30 | 0 of 600 | 16 / 18 |

Audio ran clean: 0 underruns and 0 dropped samples in every run, and ALSA took 384,670 frames in 12 s at 32,040 Hz (SNES) and 531,250 at 44,100 Hz (PlayStation), so the stream was real-time. Largest single core frame in any vblank-locked run: 14.1 ms (Mode 7, 1080p), still inside the 16.7 ms budget.

Headroom, from free-run (`-n`, no vblank wait): the heaviest SNES program here (transparency) runs 272 fps at 640x480 and 194 fps at 1080p including scaling. The other free-run readings, one 6 s run each at 640x480: Mode 7 354 fps, Mode 1 scrolling 540, sprites 1,117, breakout 633, music 846, effects and music 1,053. The PlayStation benchmark free-runs at 250 fps (three runs); the rotating-triangle program takes 1.0 ms a frame.

**What made the difference from the 48 fps showcase.** The control: Gambatte core, same board, same monitor, same 640x480 mode. Showcase (RetroArch under Xorg `modesetting` with `AccelMethod none`, Mesa llvmpipe doing the scaling, in a container): 48 fps at 640x480 and 10.4 fps at 1080p. Lean frontend: 0.87 ms of core time and 60 fps at both modes. The core never was the cost. The cost was a software OpenGL scaler on two A53 cores plus X, and it grows with the screen: 1080p is 6.75 times the pixels of 640x480, and the showcase frame rate fell 4.6 times between the two. Writing integer-scaled lines straight into the scan-out buffer costs 0.35 ms at 640x480 and 1.3 to 1.9 ms at 1080p.

**Does the display controller scale?** No. The AM62L's tidss driver exposes one plane (id 35, primary, RGB565, XRGB8888 and YUV formats, no scaling property). `drmModeSetPlane` with a 256x224 source on a 1:1 destination works (60 fps, 0.2 ms of copying per frame); every destination larger than the source (2x, 3x, 4x) returns `EINVAL`. So hardware scaling is not an option on this chip, and the CPU does the scaling. It is cheap at integer ratios, using one `memcpy` of a prepared line per output line. Writing into a dumb buffer is write-combined memory, so the frontend never reads back from it.

**Things that went wrong, so they do not cost the next person time.**

- Snes9x 2010 did not build in a reasonable time: GCC 15.3 spent over 14 minutes and 800 MB on `src/tile.c` at `-O2` and the build was stopped. Snes9x 2005 builds in about 3 minutes and was enough.
- The first matrix run of the 1080p free-run row printed no result line (cause not found); three reruns gave 192 to 194 fps and are the ones quoted.
- Controller input to the PlayStation core did not register in three tries (port device set, bitmask polling added, button pulses), so the GPU benchmark stayed at its default of 100 flat triangles instead of being pushed up. The result is a light PlayStation load.
- The lab camera feed was down, so the HDMI panel was not photographed. What backs "on HDMI": the connector reports connected, every flip returned a vblank event at 60.00 Hz, and a frame dumped from the core shows the Mode 7 scene drawn correctly (a rotating Mode 7 plane). Nobody has looked at the monitor.

**What it does not show.**

- Commercial games. Only free homebrew and test programs were run, and they may be lighter than a typical cartridge or disc. The heaviest SNES program used 3.6 ms of 16.7 ms, so a commercial title would need to cost about 4.6 times more per frame before it drops below 60 fps. That is arithmetic on the measured number, not a run. A title with sprites, HDMA effects, a coprocessor and music all at once can cost more than any program here.
- PlayStation games. The 100-triangle test does not stress the software GPU (fill rate and texture mapping dominate it in a real game). Whether 3D PlayStation games hold 60 fps on two A53 cores is open; the core's built-in HLE BIOS runs test programs but was not tried on a disc image (no free disc image was on hand).
- Sound out of the speaker. The audio stream was accepted by ALSA but nobody listened at the codec. (Input was added the same day: see "Play on the TV" below. The benchmark rows above still used scripted button pulses.)
- Three runs per row from one board; no second builder.

**The line.** SNES: full speed on this chip, at every HDMI mode the monitor offers, with audio and with a video thread; 4.6 times headroom on the heaviest free program. PlayStation: full speed on the free test programs; the chip's capability for commercial titles is not measured. Both need a frontend that writes to DRM directly: RetroArch on X or a container is the wrong stack for this chip.

**If you try it.** Build the three pieces on the board, then run:

```
gcc -O3 -march=native -o lean_fe lean_fe.c -I<folder with libretro.h> -I/usr/include/libdrm -ldl -ldrm -lasound -lpthread -lm
./lean_fe -c snes9x2005_libretro.so -g Mode7LZ77.sfc -m 1920x1080 -d 30 -p
./lean_fe -c pcsx_rearmed_libretro.so -g benchmark.exe -m 640x480 -d 30 -a
```

If `lean_fe` prints `no 640x480 mode`, the connector has no such mode: `modetest -M tidss` lists the EDID modes. If it prints `card0: Permission denied` or the picture does not change, stop the showcase loop and `ti-lvgl-demo` first (`sh am62l-evm/showcase/run.sh stop`, `systemctl stop ti-lvgl-demo`); one program owns the display at a time. If `SetPlane ... failed: Invalid argument` appears with `-s hw`, that is the missing plane scaler, use the default `-s sw`. If a build of Snes9x 2010 sits on `tile.c` for many minutes, use Snes9x 2005.

## Play on the TV: gamepad, game picker, boot service (added 2026-11-01)

`lean_fe` now reads gamepads from `/dev/input/event*` and has a picker (`-M /root/games`) that lists the games in big text and starts the chosen one with the right core. Usage, mapping, pads and how to add games: [AM62L EVM README, "Play on the TV"](../../am62l-evm/README.md). `am62l-evm/lean/frl-lean.service` starts the picker at boot and replaces the `ti-lvgl-demo` screen.

- **Pad on the bench:** Sony DualShock 4 over USB (`054c:05c4`, `/dev/input/event1`; its motion sensors and touchpad are separate event devices and are skipped). Other pads are mapped by the standard Linux gamepad button codes (Xbox, PlayStation, 8BitDo) and by the usual generic USB SNES-pad layout; none of those were plugged in.
- **Mapping:** libretro positions, so the bottom face button is B and the right one A on every pad. D-pad hat, d-pad buttons and the left stick all work; the stick's dead zone is 30 percent of its travel. Select and Start held together for 2 seconds end the game and return to the picker.
- **Input latency** (`emu_input_ms`, `data/results/am62l-evm.csv`): kernel timestamp of a button event to the vblank that shows the frame drawn after it. Snes9x 2005 running breakout at 1080p with audio: mean 31.9 ms over 121 presses, fastest 16.6 ms, slowest 155.9 ms (a rare stall, cause not found). The presses came from a virtual pad made with uinput, not from a hand on the DualShock, so a real pad adds its USB poll (4 ms at its default 250 Hz). The TV's own delay is not included. The input is read once at the start of each frame, which puts the floor at one frame (16.7 ms) and the average near one and a half; reading it later in the frame, just before the core runs, would cut about 10 ms and was not tried.
- **Games that ship in the picker** (all free to redistribute, sources and sha256 in `am62l-evm/lean/games-sources.tsv`): the seven PVSnesLib examples and two ps1-tests programs used above, and fifteen Game Boy homebrew games from the gbdev database that list an open-source license (MIT or GPL-3.0-or-later): Tobu Tobu Girl and its Deluxe version, Max Pirate and Max Pirate Extra Boom, PlantBoy, Rex Runner, JP, Carazu, Geometrix, Big2Small, Rebound, Renegade Rush, uCity, PostBot, CrossConnect, Tuff. No commercial game and no BIOS is in the repo or on the board. The SNES list is demos plus one breakout clone: no free SNES homebrew game with a clear license was added (the search was cut short).
- **Not checked:** nobody has yet looked at the TV or played on it (the picker started without errors and the connector reported connected); PlayStation input (the earlier scripted presses did not register either); save files are not written (`retro_get_memory_data` is not used), so games that save lose progress when the picker restarts them.
