## From a terminal, no AI step, on the LP-MSPM0C1104

Copy TI's example, build it with make, flash it with OpenOCD. No window to click.

Status: Works. Boards: c1104.

Folders this version uses (in a sparse clone, fetch them first, then read `mspm0c1104/AGENTS.md`):

```bash
git sparse-checkout add mspm0c1104 mspm0g3507/mcu-bench/sdk-common tools/frl
```

### Parts

| Part | Quantity | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| LP-MSPM0C1104 LaunchPad development kit | 1 | the board |
| Micro-USB data cable | 1 | power and programming |

### Before you start

- A Mac with the free tools from step 1: CCStudio 21.0.1 (1.9 GB download, 8.1 GB installed, free myTI login; it brings TI Arm Clang 5.1.1), the MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07 (0.4 GB, 2.2 GB installed), SysConfig 1.26.3 (0.96 GB installed) and xPack OpenOCD 0.12.0-7 (2 MB). Checked on an Intel MacBook on macOS 15.7.9 only.
- The code is in this repository. Clone it with `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git` and fetch the folders listed for this version. This page calls the folder you clone it into `<repository folder>`. It holds the helper scripts `sdkmake.sh` and `tools/ocd.sh`.

### Two ways to do this

**Build it yourself.** Install the tools, build the image from source and flash it, step by step. The steps follow.

**Or ask an AI assistant.** Paste this prompt:

```text
Run git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git, then read fox-red-labs/START.md and follow it to build docs/builds/blink.md on my {kit}. Ask me before installing anything or writing to the board.
```

### Steps

1. **Mac, terminal.** Install the tools once, all free: CCStudio 21.0.1 from [TI's CCStudio download page](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/CCSTUDIO) (1.9 GB download, 8.1 GB installed, free myTI login) (it brings TI Arm Clang 5.1.1), the MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07 from [TI's MSPM0 SDK download page](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/MSPM0-SDK) (0.4 GB download, 2.2 GB installed), and xPack OpenOCD 0.12.0-7 from [its GitHub release page](https://github.com/xpack-dev-tools/openocd-xpack/releases/tag/v0.12.0-7) (2 MB; the file `xpack-openocd-0.12.0-7-darwin-x64.tar.gz` on an Intel Mac, `xpack-openocd-0.12.0-7-darwin-arm64.tar.gz` on Apple Silicon). The helper script `sdkmake.sh` in this repository expects the SDK at `/Applications/ti/mspm0_sdk_2_11_00_07`, SysConfig 1.26.3 at `/Applications/ti/sysconfig_1.26.3` and the compiler under `/Applications/ti/ccs2101`. SysConfig 1.26.3, the version this repo's scripts point at, came with the SimpleLink Wi-Fi SDK installer (10.20.00.39, which you do not need otherwise; you can get SysConfig alone from [TI's SysConfig page](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/SYSCONFIG), 0.96 GB installed) on the test Mac (it put it in `/Applications/ti/sysconfig_1.26.3`); CCStudio 21.0.1 carries its own 1.28.1, which this repo's scripts do not point at.

   You should see: `/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/tools/compiler/ti-cgt-armllvm_5.1.1.LTS/bin/tiarmclang --version` prints 5.1.1, and `openocd --version` prints 0.12.0.

   If your tools live elsewhere, set `FRL_MSPM0_SDK`, `FRL_SYSCONFIG` and `FRL_TICLANG` to where they are; `sdkmake.sh` reads them through `tools/frl/toolenv.py`.

2. **Bench.** Plug the board into the Mac with a micro-USB data cable. The board shows up as an XDS110 probe with two serial ports; there is no driver to install. Read your probe's serial number with `ls /dev/cu.usbmodem*` (the text after `usbmodem`, minus the last digit), or with `/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/ccs_base/common/uscif/xds110/xdsdfu -e` from CCStudio.

   You should see: The Mac lists the probe and two serial ports. The LP-MSPM0C1104 shows its red LED on or blinking before you flash anything.

   If nothing appears, try another cable; a charge-only cable looks the same.

3. **Terminal.** Copy TI's example out of the SDK and build it, from the `mspm0c1104` folder of this repository. The build took 3.5 s.

   ```text
   cd <repository folder>/mspm0c1104
   cp -R /Applications/ti/mspm0_sdk_2_11_00_07/examples/nortos/LP_MSPM0C1104/driverlib/gpio_toggle_output .
   ../mspm0g3507/mcu-bench/sdk-common/sdkmake.sh gpio_toggle_output/ticlang
   ```

   You should see: A build with no errors that leaves `gpio_toggle_output/ticlang/gpio_toggle_output.out`.

   On an LP-MSPM0C1104 board older than version E3 the LED does not blink: the red LED moved from PA4 to PA22, and TI's example toggles PA22. Check the version printed on the board (and that jumper J7 is on).

4. **Terminal.** Flash it with OpenOCD. Replace `<serial>` with your probe's (0.64 s at a 2.5 MHz adapter speed).

   ```text
   openocd -f interface/xds110.cfg -c "adapter serial <serial>" -f target/ti_mspm0.cfg -c init -c "reset halt" -c "program gpio_toggle_output/ticlang/gpio_toggle_output.out verify" -c "reset run" -c shutdown
   ```

   You should see: OpenOCD ends with `** Verified OK **`, and the red LED blinks.

   OpenOCD prints `Error: checksum mismatch - attempting binary compare` first; that is normal, and the next line is the real result.

5. **Terminal.** Change the delay in `gpio_toggle_output.c`, then rebuild and flash again with the two commands above. The run changed the delay constant from 12,000,000 to 3,000,000.

   You should see: The blink rate changes. On the C1104 the proof was reading the LED pin: the toggle period went from 496 ms to 124 ms. A person did not watch it.

   If the rate does not change, check the build finished with no errors before flashing; the old image keeps running.

### Expected result

The board's red LED blinks the shipped pattern after a flash that takes under a second, then blinks at the rate you set after you change the delay and flash again. Build under 5 s, flash under 2 s.

### What this shows

- TI's gpio_toggle_output example builds with one make wrapper and flashes with OpenOCD on the LP-MSPM0C1104, with no CCStudio window and no AI step.
- On the C1104 a changed delay changed the pin's toggle period from 496 ms to 124 ms, read from the pin.

### Limits

- That an AI assistant can drive this route: no AI step was timed on either board.
- A person's first-hour time: the C1104 number is a scripted run's, with tools installed and hands-on time zero.
- That the C1104's change was seen by a person; it was read from the pin.
- The helper scripts look for the tools in the TI install folders; another place is named with the FRL_ variables the start page lists. Checked on one Mac.
- Nothing here ran through CCStudio on these two boards.

### Numbers and sources

| | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| C1104 build and flash | builds 3.1, 3.5 and 4.3 s; OpenOCD flash 0.58 to 0.67 s at a 2.5 MHz adapter speed, 1.3 s at the default 100 kHz; first command to proof 77 s |  |
| Tools | MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS, SysConfig 1.26.3, xPack OpenOCD 0.12.0-7, Intel Mac on macOS 15.7.9 | `mspm0l1306/README.md` |

## CCStudio and Claude Code, on the LP-MSPM0G3507

One board, one USB cable, and Claude Code in CCStudio to build and flash TI's example.

Status: Works. Boards: g3507.

Folders this version uses (in a sparse clone, fetch them first, then read `mspm0g3507/AGENTS.md`):

```bash
git sparse-checkout add mspm0g3507 portability/toolchains
```

### Parts

| Part | Quantity | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| LP-MSPM0G3507 LaunchPad development kit | 1 | the board |
| Micro-USB data cable, plus a USB-C adapter if your Mac has only USB-C ports | 1 | power and programming |

### Before you start

- A Mac with at least 12 GB free. Checked on an Intel MacBook on macOS 15.7.9.
- Free TI downloads with a free myTI login: CCStudio 21.0.1 (1.9 GB download, 8.1 GB installed) and the MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07 (0.4 GB download, 2.2 GB installed), both the current versions on ti.com on 2026-10-08. The links are in steps 2 and 3.
- Claude Code with a Claude subscription, for steps 6, 8 and 9. The blink itself needs no AI; TI's example blinks as shipped.

### Two ways to do this

**Build it yourself.** Install the tools, build the image from source and flash it, step by step. The steps follow.

**Compiler.** Where a TI MSPM0 SDK example ships a gcc makefile, GCC builds it as well as TI Arm Clang does. All 224 no-RTOS DriverLib examples that ship one built unchanged for the LP-MSPM0G3507 and LP-MSPM0L1306, and 87 of 87 ran on the L1306 with no fault. GCC 12.2 from the Zephyr SDK ran through three small wrapper scripts named `arm-none-eabi-*`; TI names Arm GNU 9-2019-q4. GCC code was a median 15 percent larger. Copy the SDK's example folder somewhere first, go into its `gcc` folder, and put the folder of a GCC install (the one that holds `bin/arm-none-eabi-gcc`) in place of `<GCC folder>`. Details: `portability/toolchains/gcc-mspm0/README.md`.

```text
make MSPM0_SDK_INSTALL_DIR=/Applications/ti/mspm0_sdk_2_11_00_07 SYSCONFIG_TOOL=/Applications/ti/sysconfig_1.26.3/sysconfig_cli.sh GCC_ARMCOMPILER=<GCC folder>
```

**Or ask an AI assistant.** Paste this prompt:

```text
Run git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git, then read fox-red-labs/START.md and follow it to build docs/builds/blink.md on my {kit}. Ask me before installing anything or writing to the board.
```

### Steps

1. **Mac.** Check you have at least 12 GB free (Apple menu, System Settings, General, Storage). Make a free myTI account on ti.com if you do not have one. Delete each installer file once it has finished installing.

   You should see: At least 12 GB free. CCStudio and the SDK take 10.3 GB once installed.

   If the Mac runs short during the CCStudio install, the installer file is probably still on disk; delete it.

2. **Browser, then installer.** Download CCStudio 21.0.1 for macOS from [TI's CCStudio download page](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/CCSTUDIO) (1.9 GB) and install it. It goes to `/Applications/ti/ccs2101`. Open it once when the installer finishes, then delete the installer file.

   You should see: CCStudio opens to its start page. About 19 minutes in all on the test Mac, 7 of them your time.

   If TI shows a short export approval form before the download, fill it in (about a minute). If CCStudio quits without a window on first launch, open it yourself from Applications.

3. **Browser.** Open [TI's MSPM0 SDK download page](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/MSPM0-SDK) (0.4 GB download, 2.2 GB installed) and download the macOS file, `mspm0_sdk_2_11_00_07.app.zip` (0.4 GB). On that page it is the macOS `.app.zip` entry for version 2.11.00.07.

   You should see: The zip lands in your downloads folder after about 3 minutes.

   If nothing seems to download, look in your browser's downloads. The SDK downloads in the browser, not inside CCStudio.

4. **Installer.** Unzip the file, open the installer and click through it. It installs to `/Applications/ti/mspm0_sdk_2_11_00_07` (2.2 GB). Then delete the zip and the installer.

   You should see: The folder `/Applications/ti/mspm0_sdk_2_11_00_07` exists. 1 minute of clicks and 2 min 48 s of waiting on the test Mac.

   If CCStudio lists no SDK afterwards, quit CCStudio and open it again.

5. **CCStudio.** Choose Help, Get Started with AI. Set Agent to Claude Code and tick Enable. Provider: Anthropic. Scope: pick Workspace. Leave Auth Token and Base URL blank, tick "Enable CCStudio IDE ecosystem MCP servers for Claude Code", click Apply, and log in to Claude in the chat panel if it asks. Keep CCStudio open from here on: its build and flash servers only run while it is open.

   You should see: The chat panel answers, and all four of CCStudio's tool servers (project, debug, SysConfig, serial) respond.

   If several chat panels open, close the extras; one is enough. Scope starts on Global; Workspace keeps the change out of every other Claude Code session on your Mac.

6. **Terminal.** Install Claude Code if you do not have it (`curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash`, then `claude` once to log in). Save the file below as `ccs-mcp.json` in the folder you will work in, and start Claude Code with `claude --mcp-config ccs-mcp.json`. In VS Code, open that folder and start Claude Code from its panel the same way.

   ```text
   {"mcpServers": {
     "ccs-project":   {"command": "/usr/bin/env", "args": ["-u", "ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE", "/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/tools/node/node", "/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/Code Composer Studio.app/Contents/Resources/app/plugins/ccs-ai/extension/dist/mcp-server-proxy.js", "project"]},
     "ccs-debug":     {"command": "/usr/bin/env", "args": ["-u", "ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE", "/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/tools/node/node", "/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/Code Composer Studio.app/Contents/Resources/app/plugins/ccs-ai/extension/dist/mcp-server-proxy.js", "debug"]},
     "ccs-sysconfig": {"command": "/usr/bin/env", "args": ["-u", "ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE", "/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/tools/node/node", "/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/Code Composer Studio.app/Contents/Resources/app/plugins/ccs-ai/extension/dist/mcp-server-proxy.js", "sysconfig"]},
     "ccs-serial":    {"command": "/usr/bin/env", "args": ["-u", "ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE", "/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/tools/node/node", "/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/Code Composer Studio.app/Contents/Resources/app/plugins/ccs-ai/extension/dist/mcp-server-proxy.js", "serial"]}
   }}
   ```

   You should see: Claude Code starts with the four servers ccs-project, ccs-debug, ccs-sysconfig and ccs-serial registered. Saving this file and starting Claude Code by hand, as written here, has not been timed on a fresh Mac.

   If Claude Code says a server timed out, check CCStudio is open with a workspace and that step 5's Apply was pressed. If CCStudio is not in `/Applications/ti/ccs2101`, change that path in all four lines.

7. **Bench.** Plug the board into the Mac with the USB cable, at the micro-USB port on the debugger end of the board. There is no driver to install.

   You should see: The Mac sees a debug probe and two serial ports; `/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/ccs_base/common/uscif/xds110/xdsdfu -e` lists the probe. A board that was used before may already be blinking its old program.

   If the Mac sees nothing, try another micro-USB cable: a charge-only cable looks the same. A USB-C-only Mac needs an adapter.

8. **Terminal or VS Code, Claude Code.** Type the line below. Claude Code imports TI's example through CCStudio, cuts the delay, builds it, flashes it and starts it. Look at the RGB LED. If Claude Code asks permission to use a `ccs-project` or `ccs-debug` tool, say yes; it asks once per tool.

   ```text
   I plugged in an LP-MSPM0G3507 and CCStudio is open. Import TI's gpio_toggle_output example for LP_MSPM0G3507, make the blink 5 times faster, then build it, flash it and run it.
   ```

   You should see: The RGB LED blinks about five times a second. The delay went from 0.5 s to 0.1 s (the constant 16000000 to 3200000).

   If the board blinked before you typed anything, that was a program already on it; this step replaces it, so a faster blink is your proof.

9. **Terminal or VS Code, Claude Code.** Now make it yours. Type the line below. Claude Code edits the loop, rebuilds and flashes again.

   ```text
   Change the program so the RGB LED shows blue for 2 seconds, then red for 2 seconds, then green for 2 seconds.
   ```

   You should see: The LED shows blue, then red, then green, two seconds each. You check the LED; the AI cannot.

   If the colors are wrong, say what you see in plain words and ask again. The AI edits the same file and flashes again.

### Expected result

The RGB LED blinks about five times a second within about 3 minutes of plugging in, once the tools are installed, then shows blue, red and green two seconds each when you ask for that.

### What this shows

- TI's gpio_toggle_output example imports, builds, flashes and runs on the LP-MSPM0G3507 from one typed sentence to Claude Code, through CCStudio's tool servers.
- A change you ask for in plain English reaches the board: the delay went from 0.5 s to 0.1 s and a person saw the LED change.

### Limits

- A clean-machine setup time: the Mac already had git, Claude Code and Node, and was logged in to Claude and myTI. About 30 minutes of clearing disk space was not counted.
- That CCStudio's own chat panel does the same: it answers, but no blink has been run through it.
- That step 6 works as written on a fresh Mac: saving the file by hand was not timed.
- Any result on Apple Silicon, Windows or Linux, or with an assistant other than Claude Code.
- The board was already programmed, so this is not a first-flash-from-new run.
- CCStudio must stay open: its build and flash servers only run while it is.

### Numbers and sources

| | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Time, plug-in to a changed blink | 2 min 29 s on the wall clock, 09:13:32 to 09:16:01 on 2026-10-05, with the tools already installed: import 2 s, build 6 s, flash and start 38 s, about a minute before any prompt was typed |  |
| Time, first-time setup | about 29 min on 2026-10-04 (11 of your time, 18 waiting); the Mac already had git, Claude Code and Node and was logged in to Claude and myTI, so this is not a clean-machine number |  |
| Software | CCStudio 21.0.1 (/Applications/ti/ccs2101), MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07, Intel MacBook, macOS 15.7.9 |  |
| Disk | CCStudio and the SDK take 10.3 GB once installed (CCStudio 1.9 GB download, SDK 0.4 GB download becoming 2.2 GB) |  |

## From a terminal, no AI step, on the LP-MSPM0G3519, LP-MSPM0C1104, LP-MSPM0L2228 and LP-MSPM0G3507

One command backs the board up, copies TI's blink example, builds it, flashes it and checks the LED.

Status: Works. Boards: g3519, c1104, l2228, g3507.

Folders this version uses (in a sparse clone, fetch them first, then read `mspm0g3519/AGENTS.md`):

```bash
git sparse-checkout add mspm0g3519 mspm0c1104 tools/frl
```

### Parts

| Part | Quantity | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| LP-MSPM0G3519 LaunchPad development kit | 1 | the board (LP-MSPM0G3519) |
| LP-MSPM0C1104 LaunchPad development kit | 1 | the board (LP-MSPM0C1104) |
| USB data cable | 1 | power and programming |

### Before you start

- The code is in this repository. Clone it with `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git` and fetch the folders listed for this version. This page calls the folder you clone it into `<repository folder>`; `start.sh` and `tools/frl` are in it. Checked on an Intel Mac on macOS 15.7 only.

### Steps

1. **Mac, terminal.** Install the tools once, all free: [MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/MSPM0-SDK), [TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/ARM-CGT-CLANG), [SysConfig 1.26.3](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/SYSCONFIG), [xPack OpenOCD 0.12.0-7](https://github.com/xpack-dev-tools/openocd-xpack/releases/tag/v0.12.0-7). The tools come to about 0.9 GB to download and 5 GB on disk; only the MSPM0 SDK asks for a myTI login. No CCStudio window is needed. `python3 tools/frl/frl.py doctor --board <board id>` lists anything missing, with links. If your tools live elsewhere, `tools/frl/toolenv.py` reads the `FRL_` variables from the start page.

   You should see: `python3 tools/frl/frl.py doctor --board <board id>` ends with every tool found.

   If a tool is missing, the doctor command names it and prints its download link.

2. **Bench.** Plug the board into the Mac with a data cable. The board shows up as an XDS110 probe with two serial ports; there is no driver to install. Read your probe's serial number with `ls /dev/cu.usbmodem*` (the text after `usbmodem`, minus the last digit), or with `/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/ccs_base/common/uscif/xds110/xdsdfu -e` from CCStudio.

   You should see: The Mac lists the probe and two serial ports.

   If nothing appears, try another cable; a charge-only cable looks the same.

3. **Terminal.** From the root of this repository, run the line for your board with your probe's serial number. It backs the board up, copies TI's example (examples/nortos/<board>/driverlib/gpio_toggle_output), builds it, flashes it and checks the LED. Leave off `--probe` only if one probe is plugged in; with several, it stops with FRL-E002.

   ```text
   ./start.sh mspm0g3519 blink --probe <serial>
   ./start.sh mspm0c1104 blink --probe <serial>
   ```

   You should see: The run ends with a line that starts `OK:` and the LED on the board blinks. LED checked: LP-MSPM0G3519: LED2 red (PB26); LP-MSPM0C1104: LED1 red (PA22).

   If it stops with FRL-E002, several probes are plugged in: name yours with `--probe`. On the LP-MSPM0C1104, jumper J7 must be on or the red LED stays dark, and the route never mass-erases that chip.

4. **Terminal.** Ask for a different pattern: run the same command with `--pattern` and four or more times in milliseconds (on, off, on, pause).

   ```text
   ./start.sh mspm0g3519 blink --probe <serial> --pattern 150,150,150,900
   ./start.sh mspm0c1104 blink --probe <serial> --pattern 150,150,150,900
   ```

   You should see: The run ends with `OK:` and says the LED repeats the pattern you asked for.

   If the check fails, read the line it prints; the check decides the result, not the LED you see.

### Expected result

The board's LED blinks after the flash, and the one-command run ends with an OK line.

### What this shows

- TI's blink example builds and flashes on the LP-MSPM0G3519 and LP-MSPM0C1104 from one command, with no AI step.
- The run checks the LED through the debugger and passes the pattern you asked for.

### Limits

- That an AI assistant can drive this route: no AI step was timed for it.
- A person's first-hour time: the run times are scripted runs with the tools already installed.
- The helper scripts look for the tools in the TI install folders; another place is named with the `FRL_` variables. Checked on one Mac.
- Checked on an Intel Mac on macOS 15.7 only.
- The route lists SysConfig 1.26.3 as validated. The recorded runs used SysConfig 1.28.0, named with `FRL_SYSCONFIG`, so treat 1.26.3 as the documented version and 1.28.0 as the one that ran.
- The LP-MSPM0C1104 whole run was not timed as one command; its build, write and check are timed separately.

### Numbers and sources

| | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| LP-MSPM0G3519 | 9.5 s from the command to a checked pattern on two warm runs, 30.0 s on the first run; build 10.0 s and write 0.9 s in the 2026-10-24 run | `mspm0g3519/FAQ.md` |
| LP-MSPM0C1104 | build 8.9 s, write and read-back 1.0 s, then 0.6 s on three repeat writes, LED check passed each time | `docs/frl.md` |

# A Bluetooth sensor your phone can find

Build and flash TI's data_stream example on the LP-EM-CC2340R5, see it advertise from a Mac, then connect and time a 20-byte echo. No sensor value is sent.

The page: [site/project-bluetooth-sensor.html](../../site/project-bluetooth-sensor.html). This file is its text. Terms: [vocabulary](../vocab.md).

<!-- generated from site/data/projects.json by tools/render_build_md.py; edit the data, not this file -->

## TI's data_stream example seen and echoed by a Mac, on the LP-EM-CC2340R5

The board advertises as Data Stream. A Python script on the Mac connects to it and times an echo. It carries no sensor reading.

Status: Works. Boards: cc2340r5.

Folders this version uses (in a sparse clone, fetch them first, then read `cc2340r5/AGENTS.md`):

```bash
git sparse-checkout add cc2340r5 cc2755p10/ble tools/ai_runs
```

### Parts

| Part | Quantity | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| LP-EM-CC2340R5 LaunchPad development kit | 1 | the board |
| LP-XDS110ET debugger | 1 | debug probe |
| A Mac with Bluetooth | 1 | the phone stand-in that scans and connects |

### Before you start

- TI's SimpleLink Low Power F3 SDK 9.21.00.36, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS, SysConfig 1.26.3 and UniFlash 9.6.0 (DSLite), all free from TI with a myTI login. Checked on an Intel MacBook, macOS 15.7.9.
- Python 3 with the `bleak` Bluetooth library: `python3 -m pip install bleak`.
- The code is in this repository. Clone it with `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git`, then `git sparse-checkout add cc2340r5 cc2755p10 tools`. Below, `<repository folder>` is that clone.

### Steps

1. **Bench.** Clip the LP-EM-CC2340R5 onto the LP-XDS110ET probe and plug the probe into the Mac with a USB data cable.

   You should see: The Mac lists the probe, and two serial ports appear.

   If nothing appears, try another cable; a charge-only cable looks the same.

2. **Terminal (Mac).** Copy TI's data_stream example out of the SDK into a working folder and build it with TI Arm Clang. Run it in the example's `freertos/ticlang` folder.

   ```text
   cp -R /Applications/ti/simplelink_lowpower_f3_sdk_9_21_00_36_LTS/examples/rtos/LP_EM_CC2340R5/ble/data_stream ~/data_stream
   cd ~/data_stream/freertos/ticlang
   make -j4 SIMPLELINK_LOWPOWER_F3_SDK_INSTALL_DIR=/Applications/ti/simplelink_lowpower_f3_sdk_9_21_00_36_LTS \
        SYSCONFIG_TOOL=/Applications/ti/sysconfig_1.26.3/sysconfig_cli.sh \
        TICLANG_ARMCOMPILER=/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/tools/compiler/ti-cgt-armllvm_5.1.1.LTS
   ```

   You should see: The build ends without an error and leaves `data_stream.hex` in that folder.

   If make cannot find the SDK, SysConfig or the compiler, change the three paths to where yours are installed.

3. **Terminal (Mac).** Flash the image with DSLite, using the board's CC2340R5.ccxml from the `cc2340r5` folder of the repository. Replace `<home>` with your home folder. The write erases the whole chip first.

   ```text
   cd <repository folder>/cc2340r5
   /Applications/ti/uniflash_9.6.0/dslite.sh --mode flash -c CC2340R5.ccxml -e -f -u <home>/data_stream/freertos/ticlang/data_stream.hex
   ```

   You should see: DSLite prints that the flash finished. In the recorded run it connected and wrote on the first try.

   If it cannot connect, check that the probe is seated on the board and unplug and replug it. Do not use a mass erase to fix a connection error.

4. **Terminal (Mac).** Scan for ten seconds from the Mac.

   ```text
   python3 tools/ai_runs/blescan.py 10
   ```

   You should see: A line `Data Stream` with a signal strength in dBm. At 1 to 2 m the recorded runs read about -42 dBm.

   If the name is missing, press the board's reset button, run the scan again and keep the Mac close. The Mac shows only some of the advertisements, so a short scan can miss it.

5. **Terminal (Mac).** Connect to it and time the echo. The script writes 20, 64 and 128 bytes, 50 times each, and waits for the board to send the text back with its letter case flipped.

   ```text
   python3 cc2755p10/ble/ds_echo.py
   ```

   You should see: `connected + services` in about 0.55 s, then a line per size. The recorded run on this board: 45 ms median for 20 bytes, 105 ms for 64, 135 ms for 128.

   If it prints `found None`, the scan did not see the board: repeat step 4 first. If bytes come back wrong, the script says so on the size's line.

### Expected result

The Mac sees a device called Data Stream, connects to it in about half a second, and gets 20 bytes echoed back in about 45 ms. The board sends back what the Mac wrote; it does not read a sensor.

### What this shows

- TI's own Bluetooth example builds from a terminal, flashes, and is found and connected to by a Mac with no pairing.
- A round trip over Bluetooth takes 45 ms for 20 bytes on this board (one run of 50).

### Limits

- A sensor reading in the advertisement or the connection. No sensor was read over Bluetooth on any board in this repository for this project.
- A phone app: only a Mac script was timed.
- That the advertisement reaches a phone. No phone run is recorded for this example.
- One board, one Mac and one run each, so the timings are single figures.
- The 45 ms echo is probably paced by the connection interval macOS picks, not by the radio. The interval was not read.
- The 1.40 s from flash to first sight was measured with TI's basic_ble example, not data_stream.

### Numbers and sources

| | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Software | SimpleLink Low Power F3 SDK 9.21.00.36, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS, SysConfig 1.26.3, DSLite 9.6.0.5764 |  |
| Connect | 0.55 s to connect and list services, ATT MTU 65 |  |
| Echo | 45.0 / 105.0 / 135.1 ms median round trip at 20 / 64 / 128 bytes, goodput 3.5 / 4.8 / 7.4 kbit/s |  |
| First seen after flash | 1.40 s at 100 ms interval, 0.56 s at 20 ms (basic_ble) |  |

## MSPM0 LaunchPad: make and OpenOCD

The simplest route: the board's own USB cable, one build line, one flash line.

Status: Works. Boards: l1306.

Folders this version uses (in a sparse clone, fetch them first, then read `mspm0l1306/AGENTS.md`):

```bash
git sparse-checkout add mspm0l1306 mspm0g3507/mcu-bench/sdk-common tools/frl
```

### Parts

| Part | Quantity | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| LP-MSPM0L1306 LaunchPad development kit | 1 | the board |
| Micro-USB data cable | 1 | power and programming |

### Before you start

- A Mac with CCStudio 21.0.1 (1.9 GB download, 8.1 GB installed), the MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07 (0.4 GB, 2.2 GB installed), SysConfig 1.26.3 (0.96 GB installed) and xPack OpenOCD 0.12.0-7 (2 MB). Links are in step 1. Checked on an Intel MacBook on macOS 15.7.9 only.
- The code is in this repository. Clone it with `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git` and fetch the folders listed for this version. This page calls the folder you clone it into `<repository folder>`. It holds the two helper scripts. About 12 GB free for the tools.

### Steps

1. **Mac, terminal.** Install the tools once, all free: CCStudio 21.0.1 from [TI's CCStudio download page](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/CCSTUDIO) (1.9 GB download, 8.1 GB installed, free myTI login) (it brings TI Arm Clang 5.1.1), the MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07 from [TI's MSPM0 SDK download page](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/MSPM0-SDK) (0.4 GB download, 2.2 GB installed), SysConfig 1.26.3 ([TI's SysConfig page](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/SYSCONFIG), 0.96 GB installed), and xPack OpenOCD 0.12.0-7 from [its GitHub release page](https://github.com/xpack-dev-tools/openocd-xpack/releases/tag/v0.12.0-7) (2 MB; the file `xpack-openocd-0.12.0-7-darwin-x64.tar.gz` on an Intel Mac, `xpack-openocd-0.12.0-7-darwin-arm64.tar.gz` on Apple Silicon). Then clone this repository into `<repository folder>` for the helper scripts `sdkmake.sh` and `tools/ocd.sh`. SysConfig 1.26.3, the version this repo's scripts point at, came with the SimpleLink Wi-Fi SDK installer on the test Mac (it put it in `/Applications/ti/sysconfig_1.26.3`); CCStudio 21.0.1 carries its own 1.28.1, which this repo's scripts do not point at.

   You should see: `/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/tools/compiler/ti-cgt-armllvm_5.1.1.LTS/bin/tiarmclang --version` prints 5.1.1.

   If your tools live somewhere other than `/Applications/ti`, edit the paths at the top of `mspm0g3507/mcu-bench/sdk-common/sdkmake.sh`.

2. **Bench.** Plug the board into the Mac with a micro-USB data cable. It shows up as an XDS110 probe with two serial ports; there is no driver to install. Read your probe's serial number from the port names.

   ```text
   ls /dev/cu.usbmodem*
   ```

   You should see: Two ports named `/dev/cu.usbmodem<serial>1` and `...4`. The part between `usbmodem` and the last digit is your probe's serial number.

   If nothing appears, try another cable; a charge-only cable looks the same.

3. **Terminal.** From the `mspm0l1306` folder of this repository, copy one of TI's examples out of the SDK and build it with one make line. Any example folder works the same way; the blink is the one that was timed.

   ```text
   cd <repository folder>/mspm0l1306
   cp -R /Applications/ti/mspm0_sdk_2_11_00_07/examples/nortos/LP_MSPM0L1306/driverlib/gpio_toggle_output .
   ../mspm0g3507/mcu-bench/sdk-common/sdkmake.sh gpio_toggle_output/ticlang
   ```

   You should see: A build with no errors that leaves `gpio_toggle_output/ticlang/gpio_toggle_output.out`. It took 3.3 s for the blink. 167 of the board's 170 SDK examples build this way.

   If the build cannot find SysConfig or the compiler, the paths in `sdkmake.sh` do not match your install (step 1).

4. **Terminal.** Flash it with OpenOCD. `tools/ocd.sh` picks the probe by serial number and refuses to run if it is missing; set `PROBE` to your serial first (`<probe serial>` below stands for it). To find yours, run `/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/ccs_base/common/uscif/xds110/xdsdfu -e` if you have CCStudio (it prints `Serial Num:`), else `system_profiler SPUSBDataType | grep -A3 XDS110`. Run it from the same folder as the build step.

   ```text
   export PROBE=<probe serial>
   tools/ocd.sh "reset halt" "program gpio_toggle_output/ticlang/gpio_toggle_output.out verify" "reset run"
   ```

   You should see: OpenOCD ends with `** Verified OK **` in about 0.6 s, and the RGB LED cycles.

   OpenOCD prints `Error: checksum mismatch - attempting binary compare` first; that is normal, and the next line is the real result.

### Expected result

One build line and one flash line take TI's example from the SDK to a running program on the board in under 5 seconds of machine time. No window, nothing to click.

### What this shows

- TI's example builds with one make line and flashes with one OpenOCD line on the LP-MSPM0L1306: 3.3 s and 0.6 s for the blink, and the RGB LED cycled.
- 167 of 170 of the board's SDK examples build from the terminal, and all 148 that do not write the boot configuration were flashed and run by script without losing the debugger.

### Limits

- That an AI assistant can type these lines. The route was timed with a script and by hand, not with an assistant.
- That the 3 examples that do not build are the chip's fault: their causes were not all traced.
- That every example does something you can see: many need extra wiring to show they work.
- The helper scripts look for the tools in the TI install folders; another place is named with the FRL_ variables the start page lists. Checked on one Mac.
- `tools/ocd.sh` refuses to run until `PROBE` is set to your probe's serial number.

### Numbers and sources

| | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Blink build and flash | build 3.3 s, OpenOCD program and verify 0.6 s (UniFlash's command line takes 15.0 s for the same image) | `mspm0l1306/README.md` |
| Examples that build | 167 of 170 SDK examples build from the terminal |  |
| Tools | MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS, SysConfig 1.26.3, xPack OpenOCD 0.12.0-7, Intel Mac on macOS 15.7.9 | `mspm0l1306/README.md` |

## SimpleLink LaunchPad: make and UniFlash

The LP-EM-CC2340R5 route: a clip-on probe, a connection file, one make line, one flash line.

Status: Works. Boards: cc2340r5.

Folders this version uses (in a sparse clone, fetch them first, then read `cc2340r5/AGENTS.md`):

```bash
git sparse-checkout add cc2340r5
```

### Parts

| Part | Quantity | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| LP-EM-CC2340R5 LaunchPad development kit | 1 | the board |
| LP-XDS110ET debugger | 1 | the debug probe |

### Before you start

- A Mac with the SimpleLink Low Power F3 SDK 9.21.00.36 LTS, CCStudio 21.0.1 (TI Arm Clang 5.1.1), SysConfig 1.26.3 and UniFlash 9.6.0. Checked on an Intel MacBook on macOS 15.7.9 only.
- The code is in this repository. Clone it with `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git` and fetch the folders listed for this version. This page calls the folder you clone it into `<repository folder>`. It holds the example copy and the connection file. The probe's serial number from step 2.

### Steps

1. **Mac, terminal.** Install the tools once, all free: the SimpleLink Low Power F3 SDK 9.21.00.36 LTS from [TI's SDK page](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/SIMPLELINK-LOWPOWER-F3-SDK) (the macOS installer, 536 MB), CCStudio 21.0.1 from [TI's CCStudio download page](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/CCSTUDIO) (1.9 GB download, 8.1 GB installed, free myTI login) (it brings TI Arm Clang 5.1.1), SysConfig 1.26.3 and UniFlash 9.6.0 from [TI's UniFlash page](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/UNIFLASH) (0.3 GB download, 1.9 GB installed). Clone this repository into `<repository folder>` for the example copy in `cc2340r5/src`. SysConfig 1.26.3, the version this repo's scripts point at, came with the SimpleLink Wi-Fi SDK installer (10.20.00.39, which you do not need otherwise; you can get SysConfig alone from [TI's SysConfig page](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/SYSCONFIG), 0.96 GB installed) on the test Mac (it put it in `/Applications/ti/sysconfig_1.26.3`); CCStudio 21.0.1 carries its own 1.28.1, which this repo's scripts do not point at.

   You should see: `/Applications/ti/uniflash_9.6.0/dslite.sh --help` prints its options, and the folder `/Applications/ti/simplelink_lowpower_f3_sdk_9_21_00_36_LTS` exists.

   If your tools live elsewhere, pass your own three paths on the make line in step 4.

2. **Bench.** Clip the LP-XDS110ET probe onto the LP-EM-CC2340R5 and plug the probe's USB-C cable into the Mac. The board has no USB port and no debugger of its own. Read the probe's serial number.

   ```text
   /Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/ccs_base/common/uscif/xds110/xdsdfu -e
   ```

   You should see: `xdsdfu` lists the probe with its serial number.

   If a flash later fails with `The target failed to see a correctly formatted SWD header` (error -615), unplug the cable, pull the probe off the board, press it back on and plug in again.

3. **Terminal.** Make the connection file with CCStudio's command line rather than by hand: a hand-written file left SWD off and gave misleading errors. Replace `<any empty folder>` with a new empty folder. It takes about four seconds. The file lands in `targetConfigs/CC2340R5.ccxml` inside the imported project; put your probe's serial number in it. The repository's `cc2340r5/CC2340R5.ccxml` is the file used here.

   ```text
   /Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/ccs-server.app/Contents/MacOS/ccs-server-cli.sh -noSplash -workspace <any empty folder> -application com.ti.ccs.apps.importProject -ccs.location /Applications/ti/simplelink_lowpower_f3_sdk_9_21_00_36_LTS/examples/rtos/LP_EM_CC2340R5/drivers/empty/freertos/ticlang/empty_LP_EM_CC2340R5_freertos_ticlang.projectspec
   ```

   You should see: A `targetConfigs/CC2340R5.ccxml` file in the imported project.

   Do not trust `dslite.sh -p` as a connection test: it printed the flash operations without talking to the chip while every real connection failed.

4. **Terminal.** Build TI's `drivers/empty` blink. A copy is in `cc2340r5/src`. The three paths are where TI's installers put the tools; the SDK's own build settings point at folders that do not exist.

   ```text
   cd cc2340r5/src/freertos/ticlang
   make SIMPLELINK_LOWPOWER_F3_SDK_INSTALL_DIR=/Applications/ti/simplelink_lowpower_f3_sdk_9_21_00_36_LTS \
        SYSCONFIG_TOOL=/Applications/ti/sysconfig_1.26.3/sysconfig_cli.sh \
        TICLANG_ARMCOMPILER=/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/tools/compiler/ti-cgt-armllvm_5.1.1.LTS
   ```

   You should see: `empty.out` and `empty.hex` appear. The build took 22 s.

   If make stops on a folder that does not exist or a placeholder user name, the SDK's `imports.mak` is being read; pass all three paths on the make line as above.

5. **Terminal.** Flash it with UniFlash's command line, from the `cc2340r5` folder. `-u` runs the program afterwards and `-e` prints progress (it is not erase). Do not add `-v`: verify reports one mismatch in the boot configuration area and ends with `a data verification error occurred, file load failed`, although the program was written and ran.

   ```text
   /Applications/ti/uniflash_9.6.0/dslite.sh --mode flash -c CC2340R5.ccxml -e -f -u src/freertos/ticlang/empty.hex
   ```

   You should see: The flash took 7 s and the red LED (DIO14) is on for one second and off for one second. The host confirmed it by eye.

   If you see error -615 or `Unable to access the DAP`, check the connection file has SWD on (step 3) and the probe is seated (step 2).

### Expected result

A build of about 22 seconds and a flash of about 7 seconds put TI's blink on the board, and the red LED toggles once a second, from a terminal and with no window.

### What this shows

- TI's blink for the LP-EM-CC2340R5 builds with one make line and flashes with one UniFlash line from a Mac terminal, and the host saw the red LED blink.
- The gotchas are known and written down: probe seating, the connection file, the SDK's build paths and the verify mismatch.

### Limits

- A typical first-time duration: the 9 minutes included 8 of probe trouble, and the board was used, not sealed.
- That verify works: with `-v` UniFlash reports a mismatch in the boot configuration area on every image flashed, cause unknown.
- That an AI assistant can type these lines unaided; one in VS Code did them in a recorded run.
- The probe is a second board to buy; the LP-EM-CC2340R5 cannot be powered or flashed without one.
- UniFlash's command line needs a connection file that no TI command-line tool writes; step 3 uses CCStudio to make it.

### Numbers and sources

| | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Build | 22 s, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS, SimpleLink Low Power F3 SDK 9.21.00.36 LTS, SysConfig 1.26.3 | `cc2340r5/README.md` |
| Flash | 7 s with UniFlash 9.6.0 and the XDS110 probe; verify (-v) reports one mismatch at 0x4E020750 in the CCFG user record | `cc2340r5/README.md` |
| Whole run | about 3 min hands-on and 9 min machine time, board in hand to blinking LED, 8 of them a probe connection problem |  |

## C2000 LaunchPad: scripted build and load

The LAUNCHXL-F2800137 route: C2000Ware, a build script and CCStudio's scripting runner, no window.

Status: Works. Boards: f2800137.

Folders this version uses (in a sparse clone, fetch them first, then read `c2000-launchpad/AGENTS.md`):

```bash
git sparse-checkout add c2000-launchpad
```

### Parts

| Part | Quantity | What it is for |

| LAUNCHXL-F2800137 LaunchPad development kit | 1 | the board |

### Before you start

- A Mac with CCStudio 21.0.1 (C2000 compiler 25.11.1.LTS, SysConfig 1.28.1, scripting) and C2000Ware 26.02.00.00 LTS core. Checked on an Intel MacBook on macOS 15.7.9 only.
- The code is in this repository. Clone it with `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git` and fetch the folders listed for this version. This page calls the folder you clone it into `<repository folder>`. It holds the scripts in `c2000-launchpad/tools`.

### Steps

1. **Mac, terminal.** Install CCStudio 21.0.1 with every device family (about 10 GB; it brings the C2000 compiler and SysConfig). Then get only the parts of C2000Ware this chip needs from TI's public GitHub repository (no myTI login). The two commands below give the same files as a full checkout. The scripts in this repository's `c2000-launchpad/tools` expect CCStudio in `/Applications/ti/ccs2101` and C2000Ware in `/Applications/ti/c2000ware_core_26_02_00_00`.

   ```text
   git clone --filter=blob:none --depth 1 --sparse --branch REL_C2000Ware_v26.02.00.00.LTS https://github.com/TexasInstruments/c2000ware-core-sdk.git /Applications/ti/c2000ware_core_26_02_00_00
   git -C /Applications/ti/c2000ware_core_26_02_00_00 sparse-checkout set .metadata boards device_support/f280013x driverlib/.meta driverlib/f280013x libraries utilities/clb_tool/clb_syscfg utilities/cmd_tool utilities/dcsm_tool/dcsm_syscfg utilities/transfer
   ```

   You should see: `ls /Applications/ti/c2000ware_core_26_02_00_00/driverlib/f280013x/examples/led` lists the blink example. C2000Ware takes 427 MB on disk including its git folder.

   If your tools live elsewhere, edit the paths at the top of each script in `c2000-launchpad/tools`.

2. **Bench.** Plug the board into the Mac and check the onboard probe's firmware. If it is older than 3.0.0.43, update it first with the two `xdsdfu` commands in the board's FAQ. Then put your probe's serial number in place of the serial in the `.ccxml` copy named with <probe serial>; that file sets the 2-pin cJTAG mode this board needs.

   ```text
   cd /Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/ccs_base/common/uscif/xds110
   ./xdsdfu -e
   ```

   You should see: `xdsdfu` lists the probe with its firmware version and serial number. The test probe arrived on 3.0.0.19 and TI's tools would not connect until it was on 3.0.0.43.

   If UniFlash or CCStudio prints `A firmware update is required for the XDS110 probe` and times out after 45 seconds, update the probe firmware. If the connection fails with error -2131, `Unable to access device register`, the connection file lacks the cJTAG setting (SWD Mode Settings = 4).

3. **Terminal.** From the `c2000-launchpad` folder, copy TI's blink example and build it for RAM. `c2kbuild.sh` runs SysConfig, compiles with TI's projectspec flags and links.

   ```text
   cp -R /Applications/ti/c2000ware_core_26_02_00_00/driverlib/f280013x/examples/led /tmp/led_ex1_blinky
   tools/c2kbuild.sh /tmp/led_ex1_blinky RAM
   ```

   You should see: A build that leaves `/tmp/led_ex1_blinky/build-RAM-Ooff/led_ex1_blinky.out`. It took 4.6 s.

   If the build cannot find C2000Ware or the compiler, the paths at the top of `tools/c2kbuild.sh` do not match your install.

4. **Terminal.** Load it and watch the LED pin (GPIO20, sampled 8 times 250 ms apart) with CCStudio's scripting runner. Separate UniFlash command-line calls each reconnect, so they cannot watch a running program.

   ```text
   /Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/scripting/run.sh tools/c2krun.js /tmp/led_ex1_blinky/build-RAM-Ooff/led_ex1_blinky.out blink
   ```

   You should see: The load took 3.9 s and the pin was seen toggling (observed 2026-10-06; the output was not saved). This is a RAM load: the program is gone at power-off.

   The first connection can print `Configuring Debugger (may take a few minutes on first launch)`; it took 1.8 s on the board tried, but give the first connection a long timeout. To keep the program, build with `FLASH` in place of `RAM` and run the same command on `build-FLASH-Ooff/led_ex1_blinky.out`; the blink example was not timed from flash.

### Expected result

A build of under 5 seconds and a RAM load of under 5 seconds, then the LED pin toggling, all from a terminal. A flash image needs the `FLASH` build and was not timed for the blink.

### What this shows

- TI's blink example for the LAUNCHXL-F2800137 builds from a Mac terminal in 4.6 s and runs from RAM in 3.9 s, with the LED pin seen toggling.
- 138 of 139 C2000Ware examples for the chip build by script with TI's own flags plus three additions the projects do not list.

### Limits

- A flash write of the blink: the timed load was to RAM. The flash route is described but the blink was not timed from flash.
- That a person watched the LED: the pin was sampled by the script.
- Anything about Apple Silicon or CCStudio's window.
- The probe may need a firmware update before TI's tools connect.
- 4-pin JTAG does not work on the board as shipped; the connection file must use 2-pin cJTAG.
- The route needs CCStudio's scripting runner because UniFlash's command-line calls each reconnect.

### Numbers and sources

| | Value | Source |

## With the frl script from a terminal on the LP-MSPM0G3519

One command copies TI's example, builds it with make, flashes it and checks the LED. No window to click.

Status: Works. Boards: g3519.

Folders this version uses (in a sparse clone, fetch them first, then read `mspm0g3519/AGENTS.md`):


### Parts

| Part | Quantity | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| LP-MSPM0G3519 LaunchPad development kit | 1 | the board (LP-MSPM0G3519) |
| USB data cable | 1 | power and programming |

### Before you start

- The code is in this repository. Clone it with `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git` and fetch the folders listed for this version. This page calls the folder you clone it into `<repository folder>`; `start.sh` and `tools/frl` are in it. Checked on an Intel Mac on macOS 15.7 only.

### Steps

1. **Mac, terminal.** Install the tools once, all free: [MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/MSPM0-SDK), [TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/ARM-CGT-CLANG), [SysConfig 1.26.3](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/SYSCONFIG), [xPack OpenOCD 0.12.0-7](https://github.com/xpack-dev-tools/openocd-xpack/releases/tag/v0.12.0-7). The tools come to about 0.9 GB to download and 5 GB on disk. `python3 tools/frl/frl.py doctor --board <board id>` lists anything missing, with links. If your tools live elsewhere, `tools/frl/toolenv.py` reads the `FRL_` variables from the start page.

   You should see: `python3 tools/frl/frl.py doctor --board mspm0g3519` ends with every tool found.

   If a tool is missing, the doctor command names it and prints its download link.

2. **Bench.** Plug the board into the Mac with a data cable. The board shows up as an XDS110 probe with two serial ports; there is no driver to install. Read your probe's serial number with `ls /dev/cu.usbmodem*` (the text after `usbmodem`, minus the last digit), or with `/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/ccs_base/common/uscif/xds110/xdsdfu -e` from CCStudio.

   You should see: The Mac lists the probe and two serial ports.

   If nothing appears, try another cable; a charge-only cable looks the same.

3. **Terminal.** From the root of this repository, run the route. It copies TI's blink example out of the SDK, builds it with make, flashes it and checks the LED. The build and the flash are separate lines in the run's output.

   ```text
   ./start.sh mspm0g3519 blink --probe <serial>
   ```

   You should see: The run ends with a line that starts `OK:` and the LED blinks.

   If it stops with FRL-E002, several probes are plugged in: name yours with `--probe`.

### Expected result

TI's example builds from a terminal with no IDE, the board's LED blinks, and the run ends with an OK line.

### What this shows

- TI's blink example for the LP-MSPM0G3519 builds with make and flashes from a terminal, with no IDE window and no AI step.

### Limits

- That an AI assistant can drive this route: no AI step was timed for it.
- A person's first-hour time: the run times are scripted runs with the tools already installed.
- Checked on an Intel Mac on macOS 15.7 only.
- The route lists SysConfig 1.26.3 as validated; the recorded runs used 1.28.0.

# Audio and video codecs on a LaunchPad

Pick a codec, build it for the board, flash it and compare every frame with a Mac build. LC3, Opus, MP3 and Plaits run on the LP-MSPM33C321A, and H.264 on it and the LP-AM13E230.

## LC3 (LE Audio) on the LP-MSPM33C321A

Build the Mac reference and the board image, then flash and compare every frame.

Status: Works. Boards: mspm33c321a.

Folders this version uses (in a sparse clone, fetch them first, then read `ports/lc3/AGENTS.md`):

```bash
git sparse-checkout add ports/lc3 ports/llama2c mspm33c321a tools mac-setup
```

### Parts

| Part | Quantity | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| LP-MSPM33C321A LaunchPad development kit | 1 | runs the codec and times it with its cycle counter |

### Before you start

- A Mac with the MSPM33 SDK 1.04.00.00, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS, SysConfig 1.28.0 and CCStudio 21.0.1 in the default `/Applications/ti` folders (`mac-setup/README.md`), and a C compiler for the Mac reference.
- The code: `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git`, then `git sparse-checkout add ports portability mspm33c321a tools mac-setup`. Every command on this page runs from the repository folder.
- Run `cd ports/llama2c && PYTHON=python3 ./build.sh O2` once from the repository folder; the codec builds reuse its `gen160` SysConfig output (point `G` at it if a build cannot find it).
- The runner flashes the board and leaves the benchmark image on it. To keep what is on the board, back it up first with the command in `mspm33c321a/AGENTS.md`.

### Steps

1. **Mac, terminal.** Build the strict and fast-math references with a per-frame CRC for each frame.

   ```text
   cd ports/lc3
   host/build.sh
   ```

   You should see: The Mac references are built under `ports/lc3/results/host`.

   If the compiler is missing, install the Xcode command line tools and run it again.

2. **Mac, terminal.** Build at -O2 with the float unit on and strict arithmetic. Nothing is flashed.

   ```text
   target-m33/build.sh O2 hard strict
   ```

   You should see: The script ends with `built .../lc3.out` and a size line.

   If it cannot find the SysConfig output, set `G` to the `gen160` folder from the prerequisites.

3. **Mac, terminal.** Flash the image, wait for the finished flag, read the results back over the probe and compare every checksum with the Mac reference. It prints cycles, the share of real time and the stack use. It plays no sound and drives no pin.

   ```text
   cd ../..
   PROBE=<probe serial> python3 ports/lc3/run_board.py <path of lc3.out>
   ```

   You should see: The CRCs match and the printed shares are about 12, 16 and 24 percent for encoding at 16, 24 and 48 kHz.

   If the probe is not found, pass the serial of your probe that `xdsdfu -e` lists.

### Expected result

The board encodes and decodes LC3 frames with every checksum equal to the Mac's.

### What this shows

- LE Audio's codec runs in real time on a Cortex-M33 at 160 MHz with room left: the heaviest encode is 24.2 percent of a 10 ms frame.
- The output is bit-exact against the Mac build in all three configurations, and the 7.5, 5 and 2.5 ms frames, packet-loss concealment and two channels also match in 9 of 9 runs.

### Limits

- Codec only: a generated test signal, no Bluetooth link and no sound output.
- A Cortex-M0+ at 80 MHz is modelled in an emulator, not run: it needs about 329 percent of real time for the 16 kHz encode.
- Build size is 157.8 kB of flash with every feature and 83.2 kB with LC3 only at -Os.
- A fast-math build makes different encoder bytes from the strict build; both are valid LC3 but not byte-identical.

### Numbers and sources

| | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Encode, 16 / 24 / 48 kHz | 198k / 249k / 388k cycles a frame |  |
| Decode, 16 / 24 / 48 kHz | 73k / 114k / 168k cycles a frame |  |

- The code: `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git`, then `git sparse-checkout add ports portability mspm33c321a tools mac-setup`. Every command on this page runs from the repository folder.

### Steps

1. **Mac, terminal.** Build the stock and the 32-bit-macro references with a CRC for each frame.

   ```text
   cd ports/opus
   INT64=0 host/build.sh
   ```

   You should see: The references are built under `ports/opus/results/host`.

   If the compiler is missing, install the Xcode command line tools and run it again.

2. **Mac, terminal.** Build at -Os. Nothing is flashed.

   ```text
   target-m33/build.sh fixed Os
   ```

   You should see: The script ends with `built .../opus.out` and a size line.

   If it cannot find the SysConfig output, set `G` to the `gen160` folder from the prerequisites.

   ```text
   cd ../..
   PROBE=<probe serial> python3 ports/opus/run_board.py <path of opus.out> fixed --ref fixed32
   ```

   You should see: Every packet and decoded block CRC matches the 32-bit-macro reference.

   If the probe is not found, pass the serial of your probe that `xdsdfu -e` lists.

### Expected result

The board encodes and decodes Opus voice and music frames with every checksum equal to the Mac's.

### What this shows

- CELT at 48 kHz encodes in 29 to 54 percent and decodes in 17 to 22 percent of real time at 160 MHz; SILK decodes in 5 percent.
- The fixed-point build is bit-exact against the Mac in 12 of 12 runs.

### Limits

- Mono, constant bit rate, a generated signal; no radio and no sound output.
- The SILK encoder keeps up only at complexity 0 (56 percent); at complexity 5 it needs 2.5 times the core.
- Flash is 331.4 kB at -O2 and 164.7 kB at -Os.
- A Mac build with its default 64-bit multiply macros differs from CELT complexity 5 and up.

### Numbers and sources

| | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| CELT 48 kHz 10 ms, complexity 5 | 858k cycles to encode, 358,367 to decode | `ports/opus/README.md` |
| SILK 16 kHz 20 ms, complexity 0 | 1.79M cycles to encode, 155,615 to decode | `ports/opus/README.md` |

## MP3 decoding (minimp3) on two LaunchPad kits

Decode a 5-second MP3 on the Cortex-M33 and on the Cortex-M0+ and compare every frame with the Mac.

Status: Works. Boards: mspm33c321a, g3519.

Folders this version uses (in a sparse clone, fetch them first, then read `ports/minimp3/AGENTS.md`):

```bash
git sparse-checkout add ports/minimp3 ports/llama2c mspm33c321a mspm0g3519 tools mac-setup
```

### Parts

| Part | Quantity | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| LP-MSPM33C321A LaunchPad development kit | 1 | runs the codec and times it with its cycle counter |
| LP-MSPM0G3519 LaunchPad development kit | 1 | the Cortex-M0+ run, with no float unit |

### Before you start

- A Mac with the MSPM33 SDK 1.04.00.00, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS, SysConfig 1.28.0 and CCStudio 21.0.1 in the default `/Applications/ti` folders (`mac-setup/README.md`), and a C compiler for the Mac reference.
- The code: `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git`, then `git sparse-checkout add ports portability mspm33c321a tools mac-setup`. Every command on this page runs from the repository folder.
- Run `cd ports/llama2c && PYTHON=python3 ./build.sh O2` once from the repository folder; the codec builds reuse its `gen160` SysConfig output (point `G` at it if a build cannot find it).
- The runner flashes the board and leaves the benchmark image on it. To keep what is on the board, back it up first with the command in `mspm33c321a/AGENTS.md`.
- The Cortex-M0+ build uses `arm-none-eabi-gcc` and reads the board through DSLite while the core runs; an OpenOCD connect resets this board through the XDS110 and clears the results.

### Steps

1. **Mac, terminal.** Build the references, decode both clips and compare them with the SSE build and ffmpeg.

   ```text
   cd ports/minimp3
   tests/check_host.sh
   ```

   You should see: The check ends with the clips matching.

   If `ffmpeg` is missing, install it; it is needed only to remake the clips.

2. **Mac, terminal.** Build at -O2 with the hardware float unit. Nothing is flashed.

   ```text
   target-m33/build.sh O2 hard
   ```

   You should see: The script ends with `built .../mp3.out`; flash is 153.4 kB.

   If it cannot find the SysConfig output, set `G` to the `gen160` folder from the prerequisites.

3. **Mac, terminal.** Flash the image, wait for the finished flag, read the results back over the probe and compare every checksum with the Mac reference. The stereo clip reads 0.151 and the mono clip 0.109 times real time. It plays no sound and drives no pin.

   ```text
   cd ../..
   PROBE=<probe serial> python3 ports/minimp3/run_board.py <path of mp3.out>
   ```

   You should see: Every frame checksum matches, 194 of 194 per clip.

   If the probe is not found, pass the serial of your probe that `xdsdfu -e` lists.

4. **Mac, terminal.** Build the soft-float image with `arm-none-eabi-gcc`, then flash the LP-MSPM0G3519, wait and compare. It takes about 2 minutes.

   ```text
   PATH=<gnu arm bin>:$PATH OUT=<dir> ports/minimp3/target-g3519/build.sh -O2
   PROBE=<probe serial> python3 ports/minimp3/run_board_g3519.py <dir>/mp3.elf
   ```

   You should see: The stereo clip reads 9.84 and the mono clip 7.38 times real time, with every frame checksum equal.

   If the results read zero, an OpenOCD connect reset the board; read it with DSLite instead.

### Expected result

Both boards decode the clip with every frame checksum equal to the Mac's; the M33 keeps up in real time and the M0+ does not.

### What this shows

- A Cortex-M33 at 160 MHz decodes stereo MP3 in 15 percent of real time with the hardware float unit.
- The Cortex-M0+ at 80 MHz, with no float unit, needs about 787 MHz to keep up with stereo.

### Limits

- Decode only: no audio is played.
- minimp3 has no fixed-point path, so there is no fixed-point row.
- The M0+ image is 150.3 kB of flash and 34.1 kB of static RAM plus a 32 kB stack.
- The M0+ timer is SysTick plus an overflow count; a bare SysTick read would understate each frame.

### Numbers and sources

| | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| LP-MSPM33C321A | 0.151 (stereo) and 0.109 (mono) times real time |  |
| LP-MSPM0G3519 | 9.84 (stereo) and 7.38 (mono) times real time |  |

   ```text
   cd ../..
   PROBE=<probe serial> python3 ports/plaits/run_board.py <path of plaits.out> --ref /tmp/plaits-host/ref.txt
   ```

   You should see: 24 of 24 engines match the Mac, 23 of them under 37 percent of real time in every block.

   If the probe is not found, pass the serial of your probe that `xdsdfu -e` lists.

### Expected result

All 24 engines render with every block checksum equal to the Mac's.

### What this shows

- A full synthesizer voice costs about a quarter of the core: 23 of 24 engines stay under 37 percent of real time in every block.
- The output is bit-exact against the Mac in all 24 engines.

### Limits

- Synthesis only: the sound goes to a RAM buffer, with no DAC, MIDI or listening test. The Audio BoosterPack page plays a tone and a tune through a DAC.
- The speech engine has three blocks over real time, where the harmonics jump.
- One voice and one fixed note sequence.
- Flash is 202.2 kB at -O2. Switching to six of the engines costs one slow block, so switch while the output is muted.

### Numbers and sources

| | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Block cost | 4.3k cycles (chiptune) to 13.8k (modal) of a 40k-cycle block | `ports/plaits/README.md` |

## H.264 video decoding on two LaunchPad kits

Decode small H.264 streams on the LP-MSPM33C321A and the LP-AM13E230 and compare the frames with the Mac.

Status: Works. Boards: mspm33c321a, am13e230.

Folders this version uses (in a sparse clone, fetch them first, then read `portability/h264/AGENTS.md`):

```bash
git sparse-checkout add portability/h264 mspm33c321a am13e230 tools mac-setup
```

### Parts

| Part | Quantity | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| LP-MSPM33C321A LaunchPad development kit | 1 | runs the codec and times it with its cycle counter |
| LP-AM13E230 LaunchPad development kit | 1 | the second board |

### Before you start

- A Mac with TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS, CCStudio 21.0.1 for `DSLite`, the MSPM33 SDK 1.04.00.00 and the AM13E2x SDK 26.01.00.03 in the default `/Applications/ti` folders (`mac-setup/README.md`).
- The code: `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git`, then `git sparse-checkout add portability mspm33c321a am13e230 tools mac-setup`. Every command on this page runs from the repository folder.
- The decoder is h264bsd at a pinned commit (Apache-2.0); `fetch_src.sh` clones it into a work folder and lowers two parameter-set tables. Use baseline streams: main profile is refused.
- Back up the board before the first flash with the command in its `AGENTS.md`.

### Steps

1. **Mac, terminal.** Build the decoder and the harness for the Mac and decode every test stream. It prints one `H264R` line per stream and pass.

   ```text
   portability/h264/build_host.sh
   ```

   You should see: One `H264R` line per stream, each with its frame checksums.

   If `fetch_src.sh` cannot clone the decoder, check the network and run it again.

2. **Mac, terminal.** Build the 176 by 144 set at -Os for the LP-MSPM33C321A; `s240` adds a 240 by 240 stream. The LP-AM13E230 has `am13e230/tools/build_h264.sh`.

   ```text
   mspm33c321a/tools/build_h264.sh s176 Os
   ```

   You should see: The script ends with `built .../h264.out` and a size listing.

   If the SDK is not found, install it as `mac-setup/README.md` says and run it again.

3. **Mac, terminal.** Flash the `.out` with DSLite as the board's `AGENTS.md` shows. The program leaves one record per stream in RAM (`h264_rec`). The results were read back over the probe, and `portability/h264/parse_rec.py` turns the dump into the same `H264R` lines as step 1.

   You should see: The board's lines carry the same frame checksums as the Mac's and a cycle count per frame.

   If a line shows a nonzero status or concealed frames, the stream is not baseline or did not fit; use a stream from `portability/h264/streams`.

### Expected result

Each board decodes the streams with every frame checksum equal to the Mac's.

### What this shows

- Small H.264 baseline video decodes in software on both boards: 176 by 144 at 57.4 frames a second on the LP-MSPM33C321A and at 86.1 on the LP-AM13E230.
- The decoded frames equal the Mac's.

### Limits

- Decode only: no display, and the numbers are test-pattern streams.
- Streams of 240 by 240 and up do not fit the LP-AM13E230's RAM, and 320 by 240 and up do not fit the LP-MSPM33C321A's.
- Baseline profile only. The decoder is a software decoder with no video block.

### Numbers and sources

| | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| LP-MSPM33C321A | 176 by 144 at 57.4 frames a second (-Os), 240 by 240 at 33.3; 110.9 kB of RAM for the first | `data/results/mspm33c321a.csv` |
| LP-AM13E230 | 176 by 144 at 86.1, 160 by 112 at 109.9, 128 by 96 at 149.8 frames a second | `data/results/am13e230.csv` |

# A DNS ad blocker on a Wi-Fi board

The LP-EM-CC35X1 answers DNS on your network. Names on a 71,492-name blocklist get 0.0.0.0; everything else is forwarded to your router. Nothing changes until you point one device at it.

The page: [site/project-dns-ad-blocker.html](../../site/project-dns-ad-blocker.html). This file is its text. Terms: [vocabulary](../vocab.md).

<!-- generated from site/data/projects.json by tools/render_build_md.py; edit the data, not this file -->

## The blocker on the LP-EM-CC35X1

Make the blocklist table, build the firmware with your Wi-Fi name inside, program the board and ask it with dig.

Status: Works. Boards: cc35x1.

Folders this version uses (in a sparse clone, fetch them first, then read `ports/dns-sinkhole/AGENTS.md`):

```bash
git sparse-checkout add ports/dns-sinkhole cc35x1 tools mac-setup
```

### Parts

| Part | Quantity | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| LP-EM-CC35X1 LaunchPad development kit | 1 | the Wi-Fi board that answers DNS |
| LP-XDS110ET debugger | 1 | programs the board |

### Before you start

- A Mac with TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS, the SimpleLink Wi-Fi SDK 10.20.00.39 and the Wi-Fi Toolbox (`mac-setup/README.md`), and a 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi network the board can join.
- The code: `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git`, then `git sparse-checkout add ports/dns-sinkhole cc35x1 tools mac-setup`. Every command on this page runs from the repository folder.
- The blocklist is StevenBlack/hosts (MIT). It merges third-party lists: read its README for their terms before redistributing the file. Do not commit it.
- The Wi-Fi name and password are compiled into the image. Keep the built image out of git. Back up the board first with the command in `cc35x1/AGENTS.md`.

### Steps

1. **Mac, terminal.** Download the hosts file.

   ```text
   cd ports/dns-sinkhole
   curl -fsS -o hosts.txt https://raw.githubusercontent.com/StevenBlack/hosts/master/hosts
   ```

   You should see: `hosts.txt` exists and lists tens of thousands of names.

   If curl fails, check the network and run it again.

2. **Mac, terminal.** Hash and sort the names: 5 bytes per domain.

   ```text
   python3 gen_blocklist.py hosts.txt -o blocklist.bin
   ```

   You should see: `blocklist.bin` is about 349 kB.

   If Python reports a syntax error, use Python 3.12 or newer (`.python-version`).

3. **Mac, terminal.** Build the full blocker. The Wi-Fi name comes from the Mac's saved networks and the password from a file you name. It takes about two minutes. `APP=min ./build.sh` builds stage 1, which answers 192.0.2.1 to every name.

   ```text
   APP=full BLOCKLIST=$PWD/blocklist.bin WIFI_ENV=<file with WIFI_PASSWORD=...> ./build.sh
   ```

   You should see: The script prints the build folder with `ex/freertos/ticlang/toolbox/tool_settings.json`.

   If it cannot read the network name, macOS hides it from command-line tools: set it in the file you pass as `WIFI_ENV`.

4. **Mac, terminal.** Program the signed build with the Wi-Fi Toolbox, then reset the board. Add `-param1 <probe serial>` when more than one probe is connected.

   ```text
   /Applications/ti/simplelink_wifi_toolbox_macos_4_3_23/simplelink-wifi-toolbox programmer -i XDS110 programming --tool_settings <build folder>/ex/freertos/ticlang/toolbox/tool_settings.json
   ```

   You should see: The programmer reports success; the console at 115200 baud shows the board's address.

   If the programmer fails with error -260 on every call, remove any BoosterPack and replug the probe cable.

5. **Mac, terminal.** Ask for a listed name and an unlisted one. Your Mac's settings do not change.

   ```text
   dig @<board ip> doubleclick.net
   dig @<board ip> www.python.org
   ```

   You should see: The first answer is 0.0.0.0. The second is the real address.

   If dig times out, check the board joined your network: the console prints its address, and a router may hand it a new one, so reserve it.

6. **Mac, browser.** Set one device's DNS server to the board's address in its network settings. To go back, set it to automatic. The board is not inline, so unplugging it only affects devices pointed at it.

   ```text
   curl http://<board ip>/
   ```

   You should see: The counters page shows blocked and forwarded names rising as that device browses.

   If the device loses the network, set its DNS back to automatic.

### Expected result

The board answers 0.0.0.0 for blocklisted names and the real address for the rest.

### What this shows

- A 71,492-name blocklist fits the board as a sorted table of 5-byte hashes searched in place in flash: 349 kB of flash and 0.7 kB of RAM.
- A blocked name is answered in a median 6 ms.

### Limits

- No DNSSEC: answers are relayed as the upstream gave them, not validated.
- Nobody ran it as a household's only resolver for days.
- Exact name match only: a listed name does not block its subdomains.
- IPv4 and UDP only, no caching, 16 queries in flight, a 2.5 s forward timeout.
- A 40-bit hash means an unlisted name matches with a probability of about 7e-8. The largest list the application slot takes is about 304,000 names (link arithmetic, not booted).

### Numbers and sources

| | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Blocked name | median 6 ms, 95th percentile 20 ms | `ports/dns-sinkhole/README.md` |
| Forwarded name | median 70 ms, 95th percentile 172 ms (router directly: 52 and 99) | `ports/dns-sinkhole/README.md` |
| Forwarding defences | random 16-bit ID from the hardware generator, a fresh random UDP port per query, random upper and lower case in the name | `ports/dns-sinkhole/README.md` |
