# Doom on a TI board

The Doom engine runs on a microcontroller kit, and on the AM62L Linux board it draws straight to the HDMI screen. Shareware data only; you supply the game file.

The page: [site/project-doom.html](../../site/project-doom.html). This file is its text. Terms: [vocabulary](../vocab.md).

<!-- generated from site/data/projects.json by tools/render_build_md.py; edit the data, not this file -->

## A. On a microcontroller kit (LP-EM-CC35X1, LP-MSPM33C321A)

A Cortex-M33 with 256 to 512 kB of RAM plays the three shareware demos. Build and flash from a Mac.

Status: Works. Boards: mspm33c321a, cc35x1.

Folders this version uses (in a sparse clone, fetch them first, then read `ports/doom/AGENTS.md`):

```bash
git sparse-checkout add ports/doom third-party tools mac-setup cc35x1
```

### Parts

| Part | Quantity | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| LP-EM-CC35X1 LaunchPad development kit | 1 | plays the demos with no screen; the console prints frame checksums and the rate |
| LP-XDS110ET debugger | 1 | programs the LP-EM-CC35X1 |
| LP-MSPM33C321A LaunchPad development kit | 1 | plays the demos on a screen; its 16 MB QSPI flash holds the game data |
| BOOSTXL-EDUMKII Educational BoosterPack MKII | 1 | the 128 by 128 screen the M33 draws on |

### Before you start

- A Mac with TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS, the SimpleLink Wi-Fi SDK 10.20.00.39 and the Wi-Fi Toolbox (CC35X1 path), or the MSPM33 SDK 1.04.00.00 with SysConfig 1.28.0 (M33 path). Versions are in `mac-setup/README.md`.
- The game data. The shareware DOOM1.WAD is downloaded by `fetch.sh` and checked by SHA-1; this repository never holds it. The engine is GPL-2.0 (`ports/doom/LICENSING.md`).
- The code: `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git`, then `git sparse-checkout add ports/doom third-party tools mac-setup cc35x1`.
- The CC35X1 flash holds the board's demo or another image. Back it up first with the command in `cc35x1/AGENTS.md`; the restore is a full flash erase.

### Steps

1. **Mac, terminal.** Fetch the engine at its pinned commit, patch it, download the shareware data file and convert it to the compact WHX format (1.7 MB).

   ```text
   cd ports/doom
   ./fetch.sh
   m33-whx/convert.sh
   ```

   You should see: `wad-cache/DOOM1.whx` exists. `fetch.sh` checked the data file against its SHA-1.

   If `fetch.sh` stops on a hash mismatch, delete `wad-cache/` and run it again; do not use a file it refused.

2. **Mac, terminal.** Build and sign the image. The converted data file is linked into it and read in place from the board's flash.

   ```text
   target-cc35x1-whx/build.sh
   ```

   You should see: The script prints a build folder and the signed Toolbox files under `ex/freertos/ticlang/toolbox/`.

   If the link fails on region size, the build used the dual-image layout; the script switches OTA off, so rerun it from a clean checkout.

3. **Mac, terminal.** Connect the XDS110 probe and program the signed build with the Wi-Fi Toolbox, then reset the board.

   ```text
   /Applications/ti/simplelink_wifi_toolbox_macos_4_3_23/simplelink-wifi-toolbox programmer -i XDS110 programming --tool_settings <build folder>/ex/freertos/ticlang/toolbox/tool_settings.json
   ```

   You should see: The programmer reports success for every region and the board resets.

   If the programmer fails with error -260 on every call, remove any BoosterPack and replug the probe cable.

4. **Mac, serial terminal.** Open the probe's serial port at 921,600 baud. The console prints a checksum line every 100 frames and a line at each demo end.

   You should see: `CRC n xxxxxxxx` lines, then `DEMOEND k frames=` three times (1,736, 3,092 and 3,881 frames), `EXIT`, `FPS after400` near 39 and `DONE`.

   If the port prints nothing, check the baud rate: the console is 921,600 here, not 115,200.

5. **Mac, terminal.** The M33 has 1 MB of flash, so the data file goes in the board's QSPI flash first (`ports/doom/m33-whx/E27-qspi-dump-and-load.md`). Then build the real-time screen image with the page cache and flash it with DSLite as in the other M33 pages.

   ```text
   EDU=1 BOARD=1 WHXCACHE=8 RT=1 NOCRC=1 WHX_CRC32=0xe9018e36 m33-whx/build.sh 30
   ```

   You should see: With the Educational BoosterPack on the LaunchPad the 128 by 128 screen shows the Doom title, then the first demo at about 22 frames a second.

   If the screen stays blank, the QSPI write did not finish: read the flash back (the dump firmware in `m33-whx/board/`) and compare it with `wad-cache/DOOM1.whx`.

### Expected result

The LP-EM-CC35X1 plays the three shareware demos to the end and prints the rate and frame checksums on its console. The LP-MSPM33C321A draws the game on the BoosterPack screen.

### What this shows

- The rp2040-doom design fits a 256 kB chip: 228 kB of static data and zone, against 164 kB static plus 800 kB zone for the plain engine.
- The CC35X1 plays three demos at 39.2 frames a second, with frame checksums equal to a Cortex-M33 emulator running the same image.
- The MSPM33C321A reads 1.7 MB of game data from its QSPI flash through a software page cache (98 to 99 percent hits) and draws in real time at 22.7 frames a second.

### Limits

- It has been played by hand with the BoosterPack's stick and buttons; the frame rate during hand play was not timed.
- The 3.5 inch touch panel image for the CC35X1 builds and links; it has not been run on a panel.
- Sound, and the other six levels of the shareware episode: only the three demo levels were played.
- The CC35X1 rate is on a stepped game clock, about three game tics per frame, so the demo runs faster than real time. It is not the same test as the M33's real-time 22.7.
- A 16 kB page cache on the M33 leaves 151 bytes of RAM free.
- The LP-MSPM0G3519 (128 kB of RAM) and LP-MSPM0G3507 (32 kB of RAM, 128 kB of flash) stop at static data alone.

### Numbers and sources

| | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Design | rp2040-doom: data kept compressed (WHX, 1.7 MB) and read in place; 16-bit pointers into a 256 kB window; a new renderer | `ports/doom/WRITEUP.md` |
| CC35X1 frame rate | 39.2 frames a second at 160 MHz, render files at -O2, statics in the 128 kB fast RAM | `data/results/cc35x1.csv` |
| M33 frame rate | 22.7 (8 kB cache) and 24.5 (16 kB cache), real time, on the screen | `data/results/mspm33c321a.csv` |
| QSPI read | 256 bytes in 23.8 microseconds | `data/results/mspm33c321a.csv` |

## B. On the AM62L Linux board, straight to the screen

The TMDS62LEVM draws Doom to the HDMI framebuffer with no GPU, 186 to 193 frames a second on the timing run, played with a game pad.

Status: Works. Boards: am62l.

Folders this version uses (in a sparse clone, fetch them first, then read `ports/doom/AGENTS.md`):

```bash
git sparse-checkout add ports/doom am62l-evm tools
```

### Parts

| Part | Quantity | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| TMDS62LEVM (AM62L evaluation module) | 1 | runs Linux and the game |
| PS4 DualShock 4 game pad on a USB cable | 1 | plays the game |

### Before you start

- The AM62L booted from TI's SDK 12.01 Linux image with a network connection (`am62l-evm/README.md`). The image has no compiler, so the build runs in a Debian trixie arm64 container on the board.
- The code: `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git`, then `git sparse-checkout add ports/doom am62l-evm tools`.
- The shareware DOOM1.WAD comes from `fetch.sh` on the Mac; the repository never holds it.

### Steps

1. **Mac, terminal.** Fetch the engine at its pinned commit, patch it and download the shareware data file.

   ```text
   cd ports/doom
   ./fetch.sh
   ```

   You should see: `src-upstream/doomgeneric/` and `wad-cache/DOOM1.WAD` exist, and the data file's SHA-1 was checked.

   If it stops on a hash mismatch, delete `wad-cache/` and run it again.

2. **Mac, terminal.** Copy `srclist.sh`, `linux-fb/`, `src-upstream/doomgeneric/` and `wad-cache/DOOM1.WAD` into `/root/doom` on the board, keeping their folder names.

   You should see: `/root/doom` on the board holds the four items.

   If the board does not answer on the network, check its address on the serial console first.

3. **Board, serial or ssh.** Build in the container on the board. It takes about 75 seconds on the two cores.

   ```text
   sh linux-fb/build.sh /root/doom
   ```

   You should see: `build/fb/doom_fb` exists.

   If the container cannot pull its image, the board has no route to the registry: fix the network, then rerun.

4. **Board, HDMI monitor.** Stop the display demo that owns the screen, then run the timing demo.

   ```text
   systemctl stop ti-lvgl-demo
   ./build/fb/doom_fb -iwad wad-cache/DOOM1.WAD -timedemo demo1 -nosound
   ```

   You should see: The monitor shows the game at 4:3 and the last line reports 186 to 193 frames a second.

   If the screen stays on the display demo, `ti-lvgl-demo` did not stop: run `systemctl stop ti-lvgl-demo` again.

5. **Board, HDMI monitor.** Plug the pad into the board and start the game. Stick up walks forward; Cross fires, Square uses, Circle runs, Options is the menu.

   ```text
   DOOM_FPS_EVERY=5 ./build/fb/doom_fb -iwad wad-cache/DOOM1.WAD -nosound
   ```

   You should see: The game takes the pad and prints its frame rate every five seconds.

   If the buttons do the wrong thing on a DualShock 4, the kernel has `hid-generic` on the pad; the game prints `hid-generic DualShock 4 button table` at start and uses it. Any other pad uses the standard names.

6. **Board, serial or ssh.** Stop the game and start the display demo again.

   ```text
   pkill doom_fb
   systemctl start ti-lvgl-demo
   ```

   You should see: The monitor shows the board's display demo again.

   If the screen stays black, start the display demo again.

### Expected result

The AM62L draws Doom on its HDMI output with no GPU, and a game pad plays it.

### What this shows

- A frame-buffer port reaches 186 to 193 frames a second at 1280 by 1000; the same engine through Weston and a software GL renderer reaches 6.5.
- The picture is 320 by 200 scaled by whole numbers to 1280 by 1000 and reads as 4:3 on the monitor.

### Limits

- The timing figure is the engine's own timing run, not the monitor's refresh rate: there is no vsync, so a fast turn can tear.
- Sound: the game runs with `-nosound`.
- The board reaches 413 frames a second unscaled and 241 at 960 by 800; the scale you pick sets the rate.
- 320 by 200 shown 4 by 5 times is 1280 by 1000, aspect 1.28 against the 1.33 of a 4:3 screen; it is the nearest whole-number pair that fits 1080 lines.

### Numbers and sources

| | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Timing demo | demo1: 185.8 to 192.7 frames a second at 1280 by 1000, 240.6 at 960 by 800, 412.9 at 320 by 200 | `data/results/am62l-evm.csv` |
| Build | GCC 14.2.0 -O2 static in a Debian trixie arm64 container, about 75 s on the board | `ports/doom/linux-fb/README.md` |

# Configure a TI radio chip with an ESPHome YAML

Add a TI platform to an ESPHome YAML, run esphome compile and esphome upload, and a development kit joins Home Assistant: Zigbee on the LP-EM-CC2755P10 and LP-EM-CC2340R5. The LP-EM-CC35X1 builds and joins Wi-Fi; Home Assistant adoption has no recorded run on it.

The page: [site/project-esphome.html](../../site/project-esphome.html). This file is its text. Terms: [vocabulary](../vocab.md).

<!-- generated from site/data/projects.json by tools/render_build_md.py; edit the data, not this file -->

## ESPHome Zigbee router on the LP-EM-CC2755P10

ESPHome's own compile and upload put a Zigbee router on the board; it joins Home Assistant in about 6 s.

Status: Works. Boards: cc2755p10.

Folders this version uses (in a sparse clone, fetch them first, then read `ports/esphome-ti/AGENTS.md`):

```bash
git sparse-checkout add ports/esphome-ti
```

### Parts

| Part | Quantity | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| LP-EM-CC2755P10 LaunchPad development kit | 1 | the board |
| LP-XDS110ET debugger | 1 | the debugger that programs the board |
| Home Assistant with the Zigbee Home Automation (ZHA) integration | 1 | the hub the board joins |
| A Mac to build and flash from | 1 | runs ESPHome and the flasher |

### Before you start

- A Mac. Only macOS was tried, on an Intel Mac. ESPHome 2026.9.1 and the TI tools of steps 1 and 2 at exactly these versions: other versions were not run.
- Home Assistant with the Zigbee Home Automation (ZHA) integration and a working Zigbee coordinator.
- Close any CCStudio debug connection before step 6; it holds the debug probe.
- The code is in this repository. Clone it with `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git` and fetch the folders listed for this version. This page calls the folder you clone it into `<repository folder>`.

### Steps

1. **Mac, terminal.** Make a Python 3.12 virtual environment and install ESPHome 2026.9.1 into it. The `cbor2<6` pin is needed on an Intel Mac, where cbor2 6 has no wheel and wants a Rust compiler.

   ```text
   python3.12 -m venv venv && ./venv/bin/pip install "cbor2<6" esphome==2026.9.1
   ```

   You should see: pip finishes in about 26 s and the environment holds 222 MB.

   If pip stops asking for a Rust compiler, the `cbor2<6` pin is missing.

2. **Mac, installers.** Install TI's tools once, about 8 GB in all: the SimpleLink Low Power F3 SDK 9.21.00.36, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS (it comes with CCStudio 21.0.1), SysConfig 1.26.3 and UniFlash 9.6.0. The downloads need a free myTI login. The platform looks under `/Applications/ti`, `~/ti` and `/opt/ti`.

   You should see: The four folders sit under `/Applications/ti`.

   If a build later stops with `TI F3 SDK not found` (or Arm Clang, SysConfig, DSLite), install that tool, or point to it with `ESPHOME_TI_F3_SDK`, `ESPHOME_TI_CGT`, `ESPHOME_TI_SYSCONFIG` or `ESPHOME_TI_DSLITE`.

3. **Mac, terminal.** Copy the `components/` folder and `frl-cc27xx.yaml` from `ports/esphome-ti` into one empty folder, and run the remaining steps there. Set `probe_serial:` in the YAML to your debug probe's serial number, or leave it out and pass `--device <your-probe-serial>` to `upload`. `/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/ccs_base/common/uscif/xds110/xdsdfu -e` prints the serial.

   ```text
   cp -R <repository folder>/ports/esphome-ti/components <repository folder>/ports/esphome-ti/frl-cc27xx.yaml .
   ```

   You should see: The folder holds `components/` and `frl-cc27xx.yaml`.

   If ESPHome later says `Cannot upload Over the Air as the ota configuration is not present`, run `upload` from the folder that holds `components/`, with ESPHome 2026.9.1.

4. **Mac, terminal.** Build the firmware. The YAML adds the `cc27xx` platform with `external_components`.

   ```text
   ./venv/bin/esphome compile frl-cc27xx.yaml
   ```

   You should see: The build ends without errors in 35 s cold, 27 s warm. The image is 262.7 kB of flash and 37.6 kB of RAM (124.4 kB free).

## ESPHome Zigbee end device on the LP-EM-CC2340R5

The same compile and upload on the 36 kB Bluetooth chip, as a Zigbee end device; it joins Home Assistant in 7 to 19 s.

- A Mac. Only macOS was tried, on an Intel Mac. ESPHome 2026.9.1 and the TI tools of steps 1 and 2 at exactly these versions: other versions were not run.

- Close any CCStudio debug connection before step 6; it holds the debug probe.
- The code is in this repository. Clone it with `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git` and fetch the folders listed for this version. This page calls the folder you clone it into `<repository folder>`.

   ```

### Steps

   ```

   You should see: The folder holds `components/`, `frl-cc35xx.yaml` and `secrets.yaml`.

   If compile stops with `KeyError: 'power_save_mode'` (or `max_connections`, `max_send_queue`), keep those three keys in the YAML; they have no platform default on `cc35xx`.

2. **Mac, terminal.** Build the firmware.

   ```text
   ./venv/bin/esphome compile frl-cc35xx.yaml
   ```

   You should see: The build ends without errors in 56 s cold, 23 s when repeated.

   If a tool is missing the build stops with its name and version; install it or set its override variable.

3. **Mac, terminal.** Flash the board. This erases the whole flash and writes the signed image.

   ```text
   ./venv/bin/esphome upload frl-cc35xx.yaml --device <your-probe-serial>
   ```

   You should see: The upload takes about 60 s.

   If nothing appears on the serial port afterwards, read the port at 115200 baud; programs from the Toolbox start by themselves after a full erase. An image programmed over TI's Wi-Fi CSI image without the erase stays silent (see the CC35X1 FAQ).

4. **Mac, terminal.** Read the board's application serial port at 115200 baud, and reset the board.

   You should see: ESPHome's log appears and shows `[I][wifi]: Connected` about 5 s after the reset, then the API waiting for a client.

   If the log stops after `Starting scan`, use ESPHome 2026.9.1 with this platform's current Wi-Fi backend.

### Expected result

The board prints ESPHome's log on its serial port, joins your Wi-Fi about 5 s after a reset and serves ESPHome's native API on port 6053. Adding it to Home Assistant's ESPHome integration has not been run.

### What this shows

- ESPHome 2026.9.1's own `compile` and `upload` commands build and flash a CC3551E through the `cc35xx` platform in this repository.
- The board joined Wi-Fi in 5.3 to 5.7 s after a reset and an API client on the board confirmed 20 of 20 switch commands.
- Over a 24-hour soak 5,616 of 5,620 commands were confirmed and the board never restarted.

### Limits

- That Home Assistant adopts the device: the test network isolates its clients, so port 6053 was not reachable from Home Assistant.
- That the API is secure: it runs without encryption until TI's random-number driver is wired in.
- That it survives a power cycle with its settings: preferences do not persist.
- The API runs without encryption, settings do not survive a reset, the network name and password are built into the image, and there are no over-the-air updates.

# Draw a digit. Watch the microcontroller recognize it

Draw one digit on the touch screen and see the board's prediction after you lift your finger. The model runs locally on the microcontroller.

## Draw on a touch screen

The demonstrated build: screen, 11 wires, one board.

Status: Works. Boards: g3507.

Folders this version uses (in a sparse clone, fetch them first, then read `mspm0g3507/AGENTS.md`):

```bash
git sparse-checkout add mspm0g3507 third-party/bitnetmcu ports/bitnetmcu
```

### Parts

| Part | Quantity | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| LP-MSPM0G3507 LaunchPad development kit | 1 | the board |
| Waveshare 3.5 inch capacitive touch LCD (ST7796S screen, FT6336U touch) | 1 | the screen and touch panel |
| ELEGOO jumper wires (120-piece pack) | 12 female-to-female as tested (11 are required); 13 with the optional MISO wire | the wires from the screen to the LaunchPad header |
| Micro-USB data cable | 1 | power and programming |

### Before you start

- A Mac with CCStudio 21.0.1, the MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07 and xPack OpenOCD 0.12.0, installed in step 1. CCStudio brings TI Arm Clang 5.1.1. Checked on an Intel Mac on macOS 15.7 only.
- A micro-USB data cable, and your LaunchPad kit's XDS110 serial number. Step 5 shows where to read it. The flash script refuses to run without it, on purpose.
- About 12 GB free for the tools. No Python and no AI tool are needed for this version; the scripts use bash, sed and grep, which macOS has. The code is in this repository. Clone it with `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git` and fetch the folders listed for this version. This page calls the folder you clone it into `<repository folder>`.

### Wiring

The 40-pin edge is four 10-pin headers. Hold the board with the USB connector at the top: J1 (pins 1 to 10) and J3 (21 to 30) are the two left rows, J4 (31 to 40) and J2 (11 to 20) the two right rows. Pin 1 of J1 and pin 21 of J3 are the top pins of the left rows, nearest the USB connector; J4 and J2 count the other way, so pin 40 and pin 20 are at the top. A diagram drawn on TI's board drawing, checked against the SysConfig pin output the demo is built with (`mspm0g3507/display-test/gen80/ti_msp_dl_config.h`). Signal and supply are both 3.3 V: the module's level translator takes the LaunchPad kit's 3V3, and nothing is driven at 5 V. No jumper on the LaunchPad moves.

| Module pin | Board pin | What it is | Needed |
|---|---|---|---|
| VCC pin (not the 3V3 pin) | J1 pin 1 (3V3) | power, 3.3 V only | required |
| GND | J2 pin 20 (GND) | ground | required |
| SCLK | J1 pin 7 (PB9) | screen clock, SPI1 | required |
| MOSI | J2 pin 15 (PB8) | screen data in, SPI1 | required |
| LCD_CS | J2 pin 13 (PB6) | screen chip select | required |
| LCD_DC | J4 pin 39 (PB1) | command or data | required |
| LCD_RST | J4 pin 40 (PB4) | screen reset | required |
| LCD_BL | J4 pin 38 (PA28) | backlight on | required |
| TP_SDA | J1 pin 10 (PB3) | touch data, software I2C | required |
| TP_SCL | J1 pin 9 (PB2) | touch clock, software I2C | required |
| TP_INT | J2 pin 11 (PB16) | touch interrupt. The program reads it once at start for a diagnostic value and finds touches by polling the touch chip, so the demo does not need it. Wired in the tested setup. | optional |
| TP_RST | J2 pin 12 (PB0) | touch reset | required |
| MISO | J2 pin 14 (PB7) | screen read-back; only to diagnose a dark screen | optional |
| 3V3 pin and SD_CS | not connected | the module's own 3V3 pin, which stays empty, and its SD card select | leave off |

### Steps

1. **Mac, terminal.** Install the tools once, all free. CCStudio 21.0.1 comes from [TI's CCStudio download page](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/CCSTUDIO) (1.9 GB download, 8.1 GB installed, free myTI login); it brings TI Arm Clang 5.1.1. The MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07 comes from [TI's MSPM0 SDK download page](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/MSPM0-SDK) (0.4 GB download, 2.2 GB installed). xPack OpenOCD 0.12.0 comes from [its GitHub release page](https://github.com/xpack-dev-tools/openocd-xpack/releases/tag/v0.12.0-7) (2 MB; the file `xpack-openocd-0.12.0-7-darwin-x64.tar.gz` on an Intel Mac, `xpack-openocd-0.12.0-7-darwin-arm64.tar.gz` on Apple Silicon); get the macOS x64 archive and unpack it in your home folder. The OpenOCD connection file is in this repository, so nothing else is needed. Checked on an Intel Mac; on Apple Silicon CCStudio runs under Rosetta 2 by TI's own notes. Then clone this repository into `<repository folder>`. To fetch only the board folder, use the sparse-checkout line in its README. The model and upstream code are already in the tree under `third-party/bitnetmcu`: GPL-3.0, commit 0715bfc, unchanged.

   You should see: `/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/tools/compiler/ti-cgt-armllvm_5.1.1.LTS/bin/tiarmclang --version` prints 5.1.1, and `ls ports/bitnetmcu/touch` shows `digit_touch.c`, `build.sh`, `flash.sh`, `lcd_touch.h`, `prepare.h` and `font5x7.h`.

   If `third-party/bitnetmcu` is empty, the clone did not bring the third-party folder; it is part of this repository and is not a submodule, so re-clone. If your tools live somewhere else, step 4 and step 6 show how to point the scripts at them.

2. **Bench.** With the LaunchPad unplugged, run the wires in the table above from the display to the header, power from the 3V3 pin only. Leave the display's own 3V3 and SD_CS pins empty. The 13th wire, MISO, is only for diagnosing a dark screen.

   You should see: Every wire sits on the header row the picture shows; nothing is plugged into the display's 3V3 or SD_CS.

   If you are not sure a wire is on the right pin, count from the header's pin 1 and check it against the table before plugging in. Pin 1 is the corner nearest the USB connector, J1.

3. **Mac, terminal.** Tell the build where your SDK and compiler are, check them, and build. The two paths below are the installer defaults on this Mac; change them to where yours are. Keep the quotes: they let a path with spaces work. The build uses the tracked SysConfig output for an 80 MHz CPU and 20 MHz SPI.

   ```text
   # replace <repository folder> with the folder you cloned this repository into
   export SDK="/Applications/ti/mspm0_sdk_2_11_00_07"
   export CC="/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/tools/compiler/ti-cgt-armllvm_5.1.1.LTS"
   cd <repository folder>/ports/bitnetmcu/touch
   ./build.sh --check
   ./build.sh
   ```

   You should see: `check OK: every tool and setting this script needs was found`, then two lines, FLASH and SRAM, then `built .../out/digit_touch.out`. On 2026-10-10 the image was 42.3 kB of flash and 5.0 kB of RAM. The linker map says 42.3 kB and 5 kB, and 4 kB of that RAM is the stack setting.

   If the check prints `Not ready` it names each missing item and how to fix it; set `SDK` or `CC` to the folder it says and run it again. Downloads: [MSPM0 SDK](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/MSPM0-SDK), [CCStudio](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/CCSTUDIO).

4. **Bench, then terminal.** Plug the LaunchPad in with a micro-USB data cable and list its serial ports. Your probe id is the text after `usbmodem` without the last digit: `usbmodemAB1234561` and `usbmodemAB1234564` are the two ports of probe `AB123456`. Flashing needs this id and will not guess it, so it can never flash a board that is not yours.

   ```text
   ls /dev/cu.usbmodem*
   ```

   You should see: Two `cu.usbmodem` lines per board, with the same text and last digits 1 and 4. The backlight may come on but the screen stays dark until step 5.

   If nothing appears, the cable is charge-only; swap it for a data cable. If several boards are plugged in, unplug the others, or run `system_profiler SPUSBDataType | grep -A6 XDS110` and read the `Serial Number` line of the board you mean.

5. **Mac, terminal.** Flash and start it. Set `OCD` to the folder you unpacked OpenOCD into, the one that holds `bin/openocd`, and `PROBE` to your id from step 4; `<probe serial>` stands for your id, so replace it, brackets included. The check runs first and never opens the probe. To find yours, run `/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/ccs_base/common/uscif/xds110/xdsdfu -e` if you have CCStudio (it prints `Serial Num:`), else `system_profiler SPUSBDataType | grep -A3 XDS110`.

   ```text
   export OCD="$HOME/xpack-openocd-0.12.0-7"
   export PROBE=<probe serial>
   cd <repository folder>/ports/bitnetmcu/touch
   ./flash.sh --check
   ./flash.sh
   ```

   You should see: `check OK`, then `Verified OK` and `running: the screen should say DRAW A DIGIT`. The script retries up to three times, because on this board OpenOCD's verify fails on about every other load and passes on the next. **Unknown (suspected: Tool or docs).** The retry handles it.

   If `PROBE: not set` appears, step 4 shows how to read it. If all three tries fail with `Verify Failed`, see [the OpenOCD CRC mismatch entry](../../site/board-mspm0g3507.html#openocd-reports-a-crc-mismatch-after-program-file-verify-but); if it says no device, replug and check the probe id against `ls /dev/cu.usbmodem*`.

6. **Bench.** Look at the screen.

   You should see: "DRAW A DIGIT", a black box and a red CLEAR button, in portrait.

   If the screen is dark or shows static with every wire right, see [the screen stays dark entry](../../site/board-mspm0g3507.html#the-screen-stays-dark-or-shows-static-even-though-every-wire): the chip-select gap or a wire is the usual cause. If the backlight is off, LCD_BL on J4 pin 38 is the first wire to check.

7. **Bench.** Draw one digit, 0 to 9, inside the box with a finger, then lift the finger.

   You should see: About half a second after you lift, the answer and the time it took appear under the box. The inference takes 33 or 34 ms at 80 MHz.

   If nothing follows the finger, touch is not answering: [the touch chip at address 0x38 entry](../../site/board-mspm0g3507.html#the-touch-chip-does-not-answer-on-i2c1-at-address-0x38-is-it) has the two checks: the software I2C pins and TP_RST.

8. **Bench.** Touch the box again or tap CLEAR to try another digit.

   You should see: The box clears and the next digit is read the same way. It reads one digit at a time: "10" came out as 6 and "12" as 4 in the video, because the model knows single digits only.

   If a digit is read wrong, draw it larger and centered; the drawing is scaled and centered like the MNIST training digits before it is read.

### Expected result

A digit drawn with a finger is answered on screen about half a second after you lift the finger. The inference time, 34 ms at 80 MHz, appears beside it. The demo waits half a second on purpose before it reads the drawing. The 560 ms from lift to answer is computed from the wait, the 25 ms of preparation and the inference. It was not measured end to end.

### What this shows

- The 64-wide BitNetMCU model runs on the LP-MSPM0G3507 and reads the ten digits that ship with it, 10 of 10, through the same drawing path a finger uses. The self-test does this at power-up. The author reports 99.55% on MNIST for this model.
- Finger-drawn digits were read on camera: counted from the video, seven of the nine drawings were single digits and all seven were read right. No larger count exists.
- One inference takes 2.71M cycles on the demo's path, 34 ms at 80 MHz; turning the drawing into the model's 16 x 16 input takes another 25 ms.

### Limits

- How often it reads a stranger's handwriting right. The 10 stored digits are a port check and not an accuracy measurement. The only count of finger drawings is the seven in the video.
- The 99.55% is the author's figure on the MNIST test set. It is not measured here, and it is not on finger input.
- Pen-to-answer time. The demo waits half a second after the finger lifts, then spends 25 ms preparing and 34 ms inferring, so the answer appears about 560 ms after the lift. That figure is computed and was not measured end to end. The 34 ms is the model alone.
- Letters or two-digit numbers: the model was trained on single digits.
- That 20 MHz SPI is safe everywhere. The data sheet rates SPI1's standard-drive pins to 16 Mbit/s. The panel's allows about 15 MHz. The display test read back only 64 pixels of one row at 20 and 40 MHz. It worked here on 10 to 20 cm wires.
- Touch runs over software I2C on PB3 and PB2 because the chip's I2C block did not get an answer from the touch controller through the module. The translator is suspected and was not checked.
- Chip select needs a 10 microsecond gap between commands or the screen drops the second one; the driver has it, a rewritten driver must keep it.
- SPI runs at 20 MHz, over the 16 Mbit/s the data sheet gives these pins and the 15 MHz the panel allows. If you see wrong colors or noise, change the divider in `digit_touch.c` (`DL_SPI_setBitRateSerialClockDivider(LCD_SPI_INST, 1)`) from 1 to 2 for 13.3 MHz.

### Numbers and sources

| | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Model | BitNetMCU 64-wide CNN, 11.0 kB of weights, commit 0715bfc, unchanged | `ports/bitnetmcu/README.md` |
| Inference | 2.71M cycles on the demo's drawing path (34 ms at 80 MHz); the separate benchmark image measures 2,750,868 at 80 MHz with two flash wait states | `ports/bitnetmcu/README.md` |
| Preprocessing | 1.97M cycles, 25 ms at 80 MHz, in software floating point: the digit's larger side scaled to 20 of 28 pixels, center of mass centered, shrunk to 16 x 16, normalized like the training data | `ports/bitnetmcu/touch/prepare.h` |
| Clock and SPI | 80 MHz CPU from the SysPLL (display80.syscfg), SPI1 at 20 MHz, 16-bit frames | `mspm0g3507/display-test/README.md` |
| Compiler and SDK | TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS at -O3, MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07, SysConfig 1.26.3, xPack OpenOCD 0.12.0 | `docs/experiments/2026-10-07-mspm0-bitnetmcu.md` |
| Screen driver | ST7796S over SPI and FT6336U over bit-banged I2C, copied from the display test with the I2C delay scaled to the clock | `mspm0g3507/display-test/README.md` |
| Image | 43,304 bytes of flash (42.3 kB) and 5,128 bytes of RAM (5.0 kB, of which 4,096 is the stack setting), from the linker map of the 2026-10-10 build |  |

## Run stored test digits without a screen

The port check: the ten digits that ship with the model, read on the board and compared with the Mac. No wiring, no touch input.

Status: Works. Boards: g3507, l1306, cc1354p10, f2800137, c1104.

Folders this version uses (in a sparse clone, fetch them first, then read `mspm0g3507/AGENTS.md`):

```bash
git sparse-checkout add mspm0g3507 ports/bitnetmcu mspm0c1104
```

### Parts

| Part | Quantity | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| LP-MSPM0G3507 LaunchPad development kit | 1 | the board these steps use |
| Micro-USB data cable | 1 | power and programming |

### Before you start

- A Mac with CCStudio 21.0.1, the MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07 and xPack OpenOCD 0.12.0, installed in step 1. CCStudio brings TI Arm Clang 5.1.1, and its `tiarmnm` is the symbol tool the run script uses. Intel Mac, macOS 15.7 only. Python 3 reads the answers back. macOS offers it with the command line tools.
- A LaunchPad, either the LP-MSPM0G3507 or, for steps 5 and 6, the LP-MSPM0L1306. You also need a micro-USB data cable and that board's XDS110 serial number. Step 3 shows where to read it. The run script refuses to start without it, on purpose.
- The other boards use their own folders and tools: `ports/bitnetmcu/c2000/` with TI C2000 compiler 25.11.1, and `mspm0c1104/`. Each README has its commands. The CC1354P10 row is a stored result. The code is in this repository. Clone it with `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git` and fetch the folders listed for this version. This page calls the folder you clone it into `<repository folder>`.

### Steps

1. **Mac, terminal.** Install the tools once, all free. CCStudio 21.0.1 comes from [TI's CCStudio download page](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/CCSTUDIO) (1.9 GB download, 8.1 GB installed, free myTI login); it brings TI Arm Clang 5.1.1. The MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07 comes from [TI's MSPM0 SDK download page](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/MSPM0-SDK) (0.4 GB download, 2.2 GB installed). xPack OpenOCD 0.12.0 comes from [its GitHub release page](https://github.com/xpack-dev-tools/openocd-xpack/releases/tag/v0.12.0-7) (2 MB; the file `xpack-openocd-0.12.0-7-darwin-x64.tar.gz` on an Intel Mac, `xpack-openocd-0.12.0-7-darwin-arm64.tar.gz` on Apple Silicon); get the macOS x64 archive and unpack it in your home folder. The OpenOCD connection file is in this repository, so nothing else is needed. Checked on an Intel Mac; on Apple Silicon CCStudio runs under Rosetta 2 by TI's own notes. Then clone this repository into `<repository folder>`. To fetch only the board folder, use the sparse-checkout line in its README.

   You should see: `/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/tools/compiler/ti-cgt-armllvm_5.1.1.LTS/bin/tiarmclang --version` prints 5.1.1, and `ls ports/bitnetmcu/mspm0` shows `build.sh`, `run.sh` and `main.c`.

   If your copies live elsewhere, steps 2 to 6 set `SDK`, `CC` and `OCD` to your paths; each script prints what it could not find.

2. **Mac, terminal.** Build the 64-wide model for the LP-MSPM0G3507 at 80 MHz. The two paths are the installer defaults on this Mac; change them to where yours are. Keep the quotes: they let a path with spaces work. The check runs first and builds nothing.

   ```text
   # replace <repository folder> with the folder you cloned this repository into
   export SDK="/Applications/ti/mspm0_sdk_2_11_00_07"
   export CC="/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/tools/compiler/ti-cgt-armllvm_5.1.1.LTS"
   cd <repository folder>/ports/bitnetmcu/mspm0
   ./build.sh --check g3507 80
   ./build.sh g3507 cnn_64 O3 80
   ```

   You should see: `check OK`, then the FLASH and SRAM lines of the linker map and a new `build-g3507-cnn_64-O3-80` folder. The lines read 23.0 kB of flash and 3.3 kB of RAM.

   If the check prints `Not ready` it names each missing item and how to fix it. Downloads: [MSPM0 SDK](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/MSPM0-SDK), [CCStudio](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/CCSTUDIO). Clock 80 exists for the G3507 only; the L1306 uses 32.

3. **Bench, then terminal.** Plug the LaunchPad in with a micro-USB data cable and list its serial ports. Your probe id is the text after `usbmodem` without the last digit: `usbmodemAB1234561` and `usbmodemAB1234564` are the two ports of probe `AB123456`. Flashing needs this id and will not guess it, so it can never flash a board that is not yours. No wiring is needed: the test digits are in the image.

   ```text
   ls /dev/cu.usbmodem*
   ```

   You should see: Two `cu.usbmodem` lines per board, with the same text and last digits 1 and 4.

   If nothing appears, the cable is charge-only; swap it for a data cable. If several boards are plugged in, unplug the others, or run `system_profiler SPUSBDataType | grep -A6 XDS110` and read the `Serial Number` line of the board you mean.

4. **Mac, terminal.** Run it on the LP-MSPM0G3507. Set `OCD` to the folder you unpacked OpenOCD into, the one that holds `bin/openocd`, and `PROBE` to your id from step 3; `<probe serial>` stands for your id, so replace it, brackets included. The script flashes, fills RAM with a pattern, lets the board classify the ten digits for 20 seconds, then reads the answers, cycles and stack depth back over the debugger. To find yours, run `/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/ccs_base/common/uscif/xds110/xdsdfu -e` if you have CCStudio (it prints `Serial Num:`), else `system_profiler SPUSBDataType | grep -A3 XDS110`.

   ```text
   export CC="/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/tools/compiler/ti-cgt-armllvm_5.1.1.LTS"   # run.sh finds its symbol tool, tiarmnm, inside this folder
   export OCD="$HOME/xpack-openocd-0.12.0-7"
   export PROBE=<probe serial>
   cd <repository folder>/ports/bitnetmcu/mspm0
   ./run.sh --check build-g3507-cnn_64-O3-80
   ./run.sh build-g3507-cnn_64-O3-80
   ```

   You should see: `check OK`, `magic 0xb17e0001 (done), clock 80000000 Hz, right 10 of 10`, `answers 3209069277`, `cycles 2748503 to 2754797 (mean 2,750,868; 34.39 ms)` and `stack: 3072 bytes reserved, deepest use 2288 bytes`.

   If `right` is under 10 or the magic says NOT DONE, the image did not run to the end: reflash, and check you built clock 80 for this board. `run.sh` already retries OpenOCD's verify three times; for the known verify failure see [the OpenOCD CRC mismatch entry](../../site/board-mspm0g3507.html#openocd-reports-a-crc-mismatch-after-program-file-verify-but). If it prints `PROBE: not set`, step 3 shows how to read it.

5. **Mac, terminal.** Only with an LP-MSPM0L1306: build the same model for it at 32 MHz. `STACK=3600` reserves 3.5 kB of the board's 4 kB of RAM for the stack, as the saved result did. The model's deepest use is 2.2 kB. The default 3,072 also links, so the number only sets the headroom shown in step 6.

   ```text
   # replace <repository folder> with the folder you cloned this repository into
   export SDK="/Applications/ti/mspm0_sdk_2_11_00_07"
   export CC="/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/tools/compiler/ti-cgt-armllvm_5.1.1.LTS"
   cd <repository folder>/ports/bitnetmcu/mspm0
   ./build.sh --check l1306 32
   STACK=3600 ./build.sh l1306 cnn_64 O3 32
   ```

   You should see: `check OK`, then the FLASH and SRAM lines and a new `build-l1306-cnn_64-O3-32` folder. The lines read 21.4 kB of flash and 3.6 kB of the board's 4 kB of RAM, which leaves 396 bytes.

   If the link fails with a stack or RAM error, the model is too big for 4 kB: use `cnn_64`, or a smaller model (`cnn_16small`, `12k`, `1k`). `STACK` is the stack size in bytes.

6. **Mac, terminal.** Run it on the LP-MSPM0L1306. Use the id of this board, read as in step 3; `<probe serial>` stands for your id, so replace it, brackets included. Before OpenOCD starts the script asks TI's `xdsdfu` tool, which is inside CCStudio, whether that probe is plugged in; set `XDSDFU` to its path if yours is elsewhere. To find yours, run `/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/ccs_base/common/uscif/xds110/xdsdfu -e` if you have CCStudio (it prints `Serial Num:`), else `system_profiler SPUSBDataType | grep -A3 XDS110`.

   ```text
   export CC="/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/tools/compiler/ti-cgt-armllvm_5.1.1.LTS"   # run.sh finds its symbol tool, tiarmnm, inside this folder
   export OCD="$HOME/xpack-openocd-0.12.0-7"
   export PROBE=<probe serial>
   cd <repository folder>/ports/bitnetmcu/mspm0
   ./run.sh --check build-l1306-cnn_64-O3-32
   ./run.sh build-l1306-cnn_64-O3-32
   ```

   You should see: `check OK`, `magic 0xb17e0001 (done), clock 32000000 Hz, right 10 of 10`, `answers 3209069277`, `cycles 2646151 to 2653623 (mean 2,649,196; 82.79 ms)` and `stack: 3600 bytes reserved, deepest use 2288 bytes`.

   If it prints `Probe ... missing`, that id is not on the USB bus: replug, and compare with `ls /dev/cu.usbmodem*`. If `right` is under 10 or the magic says NOT DONE, reflash and check you built clock 32 with `STACK=3600`. Otherwise the stack line reads 3 kB reserved.

### Expected result

`right 10 of 10` and the answers `3209069277`, the same ten the Mac gives from `host/host_main.c`.

### What this shows

- Every board that ran it gave the same ten answers as the Mac for the model it ran, and the board table says which model. So the port is correct.
- Cycle counts per digit are comparable with the author's CH32V002 figure: fewer at 32 MHz on the MSPM0 boards, 0.5% more at 80 MHz with two flash wait states.

### Limits

- Nothing about handwriting: no touch input, no finger. Passing ten stored vectors is a functional check of the port and is no accuracy estimate.
- A passing stored run on a board does not mean the touch build works there; that needs the screen driver on that board.
- On the LP-MSPM0L1306 only the 64-wide model was run, with a 3.5 kB stack leaving 396 bytes of RAM; the SRAM-loop variant does not fit.
- The author's cycle counts were not rerun on his chip; the comparison is chip plus compiler.

### Numbers and sources

| | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Cycles per digit, 64-wide model | G3507 2,640,383 at 32 MHz and 2,750,868 at 80 MHz; L1306 2,649,196 at 32 MHz; CC1354P10 about 1.13M at 48 MHz; F2800137 2,551,750 from RAM and 2,897,585 from flash at 120 MHz; author's CH32V002 2,736,250 | `ports/bitnetmcu/README.md` |
| Stack | 2.2 kB deepest use on the MSPM0 boards (RAM painted before the run) |  |
| Models | 64-wide CNN 11.0 kB (99.55%), 16-wide 3.2 kB (98.92%), 12k fully connected 12.3 kB (99.02%), 1k 1.1 kB (94.22%); accuracies are the author's on MNIST | `ports/bitnetmcu/README.md` |
| C28x patches | `1L << shift` in ReLUNorm, signed test-data bytes, a 2-word alignment on one shared buffer; the arithmetic is unchanged |  |

# Button, knob and dimmer on a breadboard

The board's S2 button toggles an LED, then a knob sets how bright it is.

The page: [site/project-hobby-button-knob-dim.html](../../site/project-hobby-button-knob-dim.html). This file is its text. Terms: [vocabulary](../vocab.md).

<!-- generated from site/data/projects.json by tools/render_build_md.py; edit the data, not this file -->

## Button, knob and dimmer

The board's S2 button, one knob, one LED, on a breadboard.

Boards: g3519.

Folders this version uses (in a sparse clone, fetch them first, then read `portability/hobby/button-knob-dim//AGENTS.md`):

```bash
git sparse-checkout add portability/hobby/button-knob-dim/
```

### Parts

| Part | Quantity | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| LP-MSPM0G3519 LaunchPad development kit | 1 | the board, with the S2 button the build reads |
| Freenove Ultimate Starter Kit for Raspberry Pi Pico, board not included (FNK0058) | 1 | a red LED, a 220 to 330 Ohm resistor and a 10 kOhm knob (potentiometer) |

### Before you start

- The code is in this repository. Clone it first: `git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git`. This page calls the folder you clone it into `<repository folder>`; every command below runs from inside it.
- Three free TI tools from ti.com: the MSPM0 SDK, SysConfig and TI Arm Clang. The build stops and names the missing tool and its download page when one is absent.

### Wiring

The button is S2 on the board and needs no wire. The knob's outer pins go to 3.3 V and ground, and its middle pin to the analog pin. The LED goes from its pin through the resistor to ground. Serial output needs no wiring: it goes through the board's USB debugger at 115200 baud.

| Module pin | Board pin | What it is | Needed |
|---|---|---|---|
| Button S2 | onboard (PB3) | the board's S2 button; no wire needed | required |
| LED, long leg, through the resistor | J3 pin 28 (PB27) | PWM output | required |
| LED, short leg | J2 pin 20 (GND) | ground | required |
| Knob, middle pin (wiper) | J1 pin 2 (PA14) | analog input | required |
| Knob, outer pin 1 | J1 pin 1 (3V3) | power, 3.3 V only | required |
| Knob, outer pin 2 | J2 pin 20 (GND) | ground | required |

### Steps

1. **Bench.** With the USB cable unplugged, put the LED with its resistor and the knob on the breadboard and wire them as in the pin table. The button is S2 on the board, so it needs no wire.

   You should see: Two small circuits on the breadboard, each ending at the LaunchPad. Nothing is lit.

   If the LED never lights later, turn it around: the long leg goes to the resistor side.

2. **Terminal.** Build and flash the program. Plug the board into your computer with the USB cable first.

   ```text
   cd portability/hobby/button-knob-dim && ./build.sh --board mspm0g3519 --flash
   ```

   You should see: The build finishes and the flash reports done. Build time: measured at the first run.

   If the build stops and names a missing tool, install that tool from the page it names and run the command again. If the flash cannot find the board, try another USB cable: a charge-only cable looks the same.

3. **Bench.** Press S2, the button on the board.

   You should see: The LED toggles on each press.

   If nothing happens, check that the LED's resistor leg is on J3 pin 28 and its other leg on ground. The pins are listed in `portability/hobby/button-knob-dim/PINS.md`.

4. **Bench.** Turn the knob slowly from one end to the other.

   You should see: The LED gets brighter as you turn one way and dimmer the other way. The serial port (115200 baud) prints a line like `adc=914 led=on duty=22` twice a second.

   If it only jumps between off and full, the middle pin is on a digital pin or the outer pins are swapped; check the pin table.

5. **Bench.** Open `portability/hobby/button-knob-dim/app.c` in a text editor. Change `PWM_PERIOD_US`, stop the knob at half brightness, or make S2 hold the LED on for two seconds. Run the command from step 2 after each change.

   You should see: The change shows within seconds of the flash.

   If the old behavior is still there, the flash did not finish: run the command from the build step again and wait for done.

### Expected result

S2 toggles the LED and the knob sets its brightness from off to full. The PWM rate is 1 kHz by design; the measured brightness range and build time: measured at the first run.

### What this shows

- A knob, an LED and one resistor connect to a LaunchPad with five wires; the button is already on the board.
- Digital input, analog input and PWM output are three separate peripherals; this build uses each once.

### Limits

- That the program runs: nobody has run this build yet.
- Any timing or brightness figure: those are measured at the first run.
- The LED is driven straight from a pin through 220 Ohm.
- The pins are listed in the build folder's PINS.md, one table per board.

### Numbers and sources

| | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Size on the LP-MSPM0G3507 | 3.2 kB flash of 128 kB, 712 B RAM of 32 kB (the linker reserves 512 B of the RAM for the stack) | `portability/hobby/README.md` |
| Size on the LP-MSPM0G3519 | 3.2 kB flash of 512 kB, 456 B RAM of 128 kB | `portability/hobby/README.md` |
| Size on the LP-MSPM0L1306 | 3.1 kB flash of 64 kB, 268 B RAM of 4 kB | `portability/hobby/README.md` |
| Build | MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS at -Os, SysConfig 1.28.0, built 2026-11-08 | `portability/hobby/README.md` |

# Parking sensor that beeps faster as you get close

An RCWL-1601 ultrasonic sensor and a buzzer; the closer you get, the faster it beeps and the serial port prints the distance.

The page: [site/project-hobby-parking-sensor.html](../../site/project-hobby-parking-sensor.html). This file is its text. Terms: [vocabulary](../vocab.md).

<!-- generated from site/data/projects.json by tools/render_build_md.py; edit the data, not this file -->

## RCWL-1601 parking sensor

An ultrasonic sensor and a passive buzzer.

Boards: g3519.

Folders this version uses (in a sparse clone, fetch them first, then read `portability/hobby/parking-sensor//AGENTS.md`):

```bash
git sparse-checkout add portability/hobby/parking-sensor/
```

### Parts

| Part | Quantity | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| LP-MSPM0G3519 LaunchPad development kit | 1 | the board |
| Adafruit RCWL-1601 ultrasonic distance sensor (Adafruit 4007) | 1 | distance sensor; it runs at 3.3 V so its echo pin is safe for the LaunchPad |
| Freenove Ultimate Starter Kit for Raspberry Pi Pico, board not included (FNK0058) | 1 | passive buzzer with a 330 Ohm resistor in series, jumper wires and a breadboard |

### Before you start

- The code is in this repository. Clone it first: `git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git`. This page calls the folder you clone it into `<repository folder>`; every command below runs from inside it.
- Three free TI tools from ti.com: the MSPM0 SDK, SysConfig and TI Arm Clang. The build stops and names the missing tool and its download page when one is absent.

### Wiring

Power the sensor from 3.3 V. The kit's own HC-SR04 is a 5 V part whose echo pin would put 5 V on the LaunchPad, so leave it in the box. The kit's passive buzzer is a magnetic one: wire a 330 Ohm resistor in series with its plus leg, because straight on a pin it draws more current than the chip's pin may give.

| Module pin | Board pin | What it is | Needed |
|---|---|---|---|
| RCWL-1601 VCC | J1 pin 1 (3V3) | power, 3.3 V | required |
| RCWL-1601 GND | J2 pin 20 (GND) | ground | required |
| RCWL-1601 Trig | J4 pin 35 (PB5) | trigger pulse out | required |
| RCWL-1601 Echo | J4 pin 36 (PB4) | echo pulse in, timed on a free-running counter | required |
| Passive buzzer, plus leg, through a 330 Ohm resistor | J2 pin 14 (PB7) | tone output (a PWM pin) | required |
| Passive buzzer, other leg | J2 pin 20 (GND) | ground | required |

### Steps

1. **Bench.** With the USB cable unplugged, wire the sensor and the buzzer as in the pin table. Put the sensor where you can wave a hand in front of it.

   You should see: Four wires to the sensor and two to the buzzer. Nothing is lit.

   If the sensor has a header with SCL and SDA printed beside Trig and Echo, use the Trig and Echo pins: the other pair is for its serial modes.

2. **Terminal.** Build and flash the program. Plug the board into your computer with the USB cable first.

   ```text
   cd portability/hobby/parking-sensor && ./build.sh --board mspm0g3519 --flash
   ```

   You should see: The build finishes and the flash reports done. Build time: measured at the first run.

   If the build stops and names a missing tool, install that tool from the page it names and run the command again. If the flash cannot find the board, try another USB cable: a charge-only cable looks the same.

3. **Bench.** Hold your hand about 30 cm in front of the sensor, then move it slowly toward the sensor.

   You should see: The buzzer beeps slowly at first and faster as your hand gets closer, and the serial port (115200 baud) prints a line like `dist=34 cm` ten times a second. Beyond 100 cm it stays silent.

   If the serial port prints `dist=none`, check the echo wire first: a loose echo wire reads as no object in range.

4. **Bench.** Hold a ruler beside the sensor and hold a flat object at 10, 30 and 100 cm.

   You should see: The distance the program prints at each mark matches the ruler. The error at each distance: measured at the first run.

   If the readings are far too large, soft or angled surfaces reflect little sound; use a flat, hard object.

5. **Bench.** Open `portability/hobby/parking-sensor/app.c` in a text editor. Change the distance where the beeping stops, the gap between beeps, or the pitch. Run the command from step 2 after each change.

   You should see: The change shows within seconds of the flash.

   If the old behavior is still there, the flash did not finish: run the command from the build step again and wait for done.

### Expected result

The beep rate rises as the object gets closer. Distance error at three ranges, the measuring rate and image size: measured at the first run.

### What this shows

- Distance is the time an echo takes to return, halved and multiplied by the speed of sound.
- A timer capture times the echo without the program waiting on it.

### Limits

- That the program runs: nobody has run this build yet.
- How accurate it is: the error at three ranges is measured at the first run.
- The sensor reads a cone, not a line, and soft surfaces return little echo.
- The kit's HC-SR04 is a 5 V part and is not used here.

### Numbers and sources

| | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Size on the LP-MSPM0G3507 | 3.1 kB flash of 128 kB, 524 B RAM of 32 kB (the linker reserves 512 B of the RAM for the stack) | `portability/hobby/README.md` |
| Size on the LP-MSPM0G3519 | 3.1 kB flash of 512 kB, 268 B RAM of 128 kB | `portability/hobby/README.md` |
| Size on the LP-MSPM0L1306 | 3.1 kB flash of 64 kB, 268 B RAM of 4 kB | `portability/hobby/README.md` |
| Build | MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS at -Os, SysConfig 1.28.0, built 2026-11-08 | `portability/hobby/README.md` |

# Send a message to a satellite

Goal: a message from an LP-EM-CC2755P10 received by a satellite about 550 km up. Not achieved.

The page: [site/project-hubble-satellite.html](../../site/project-hubble-satellite.html). This file is its text. Terms: [vocabulary](../vocab.md).

<!-- generated from site/data/projects.json by tools/render_build_md.py; edit the data, not this file -->

## Where it stands

- **g3507**: Not for this chip. No radio.
- **cc2340r5**: Not for this chip. The chip's 8 dBm output is below the 20 dBm the satellite link needs; it works for Hubble's ground network only.
- **l1306**: Not for this chip. No radio.
- **f2800137**: Not for this chip. No radio on this chip.
- **cc2755p10**: Could work. Hubble's satellite sample builds, flashes and transmits every 10 s with a 256-bit key; the matching Bluetooth beacon image was heard and decoded on a Mac, 4 of 4 packets in 40 s at -54 to -57 dBm. The board went outside for one pass on 2026-10-18; nothing has reached the dashboard.

# Jack-o'-Lantern Jukebox

Halloween music and color-changing light from an LP-MSPM33C321A LaunchPad, the BOOSTXL-AUDIO and a power bank. No wiring.

The page: [site/project-jack-o-lantern-jukebox.html](../../site/project-jack-o-lantern-jukebox.html). This file is its text. Terms: [vocabulary](../vocab.md).

<!-- generated from site/data/projects.json by tools/render_build_md.py; edit the data, not this file -->

## The show on the LP-MSPM33C321A with the BOOSTXL-AUDIO

One LaunchPad, one BoosterPack and a USB power bank. Build and flash once from a Mac.

Status: Works. Boards: mspm33c321a.

Folders this version uses (in a sparse clone, fetch them first, then read `portability/boosterpacks/audio/AGENTS.md`):

```bash
git sparse-checkout add portability/boosterpacks/audio mspm33c321a tools mac-setup
```

### Parts

| Part | Quantity | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| LP-MSPM33C321A LaunchPad development kit | 1 | plays the show: 1 MB of flash holds the recordings, and its RGB LED is the light |
| BOOSTXL-AUDIO audio BoosterPack plug-in module | 1 | the sound: a DAC8311 converter, a TPA301 amplifier and a small speaker |
| USB power bank with a USB-C cable | 1 | powers the show with no computer attached; pick one with an always-on or low-current mode |

### Before you start

- A Mac with the MSPM33 SDK 1.04.00.00, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS and SysConfig 1.28.0 in the default `/Applications/ti` folders, and CCStudio 21.0.1 for its `DSLite` flasher (`mac-setup/README.md`). Only an Intel Mac with macOS 15.7 was tried.
- Your board's probe serial in the target file: copy `mspm33c321a/MSPM33C321A_<probe serial>.ccxml` and put your serial in place of `<probe serial>` (`xdsdfu -e` lists it).
- The code is in this repository: `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git`, then `cd fox-red-labs` and `git sparse-checkout add portability/boosterpacks/audio mspm33c321a tools mac-setup`. Every command on this page runs from that folder.
- The board ships with a demo in its flash. To keep it, back it up first with the command in `mspm33c321a/AGENTS.md`.

### Steps

1. **Mac, terminal.** Build the 16 kHz show image with the five recordings from `portability/boosterpacks/audio/tracks/`. The script uses TI's SDK makefile and only builds; it never flashes.

   ```text
   OUT=build/halloween bash portability/boosterpacks/audio/boards/mspm33c321a/build.sh halloween
   ```

   You should see: The last lines are `built build/halloween/gpio_toggle_output/ticlang/gpio_toggle_output.out` and the flash use from the map, about 913 kB of 1 MB.

   If it stops at once with exit code 2, the script did not find the MSPM33 SDK or TI Arm Clang: install them in the default `/Applications/ti` folders.

2. **Mac, terminal.** Plug the LaunchPad into the Mac by USB-C with no BoosterPack on it. Check the image never puts the chip to sleep, then flash it with DSLite. Copy `mspm33c321a/MSPM33C321A_<probe serial>.ccxml` to `mspm33c321a/MSPM33C321A_<serial>.ccxml` and put your probe serial in place of `<probe serial>`. The flash line is assembled from the board's flash command and this build's output path.

   ```text
   python3 tools/preflight_image.py mspm33c321a build/halloween/gpio_toggle_output/ticlang/gpio_toggle_output.out
   /Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/ccs_base/DebugServer/bin/DSLite flash -c mspm33c321a/MSPM33C321A_<serial>.ccxml -e -f -v build/halloween/gpio_toggle_output/ticlang/gpio_toggle_output.out
   ```

   You should see: The check prints `SAFE`, DSLite finishes with the verify passing, and a serial terminal at 115200 shows `HALLOWEEN SHOW, BOOSTXL-AUDIO app, ... sample rate 16000 Hz, recorded tracks 5`.

   If DSLite reports `Device Connection Error ... low power mode`, reset the probe with `xds110reset -s <serial> -a toggle -d 200` (it sits beside `xdsdfu`) and flash again.

3. **Bench.** Unplug the USB cable first: the swap happens with the board unpowered. Pull off any other BoosterPack. Plug the BOOSTXL-AUDIO onto the same rows, its pin 1 on J1 pin 1 (3V3). Check jumper J5 on the pack sits on SPI DAC, as shipped, and push the pack's volume slider to the top.

   You should see: The pack sits flat on J1 to J4 with its speaker facing up.

   If the pack does not seat, check both header rows line up; it goes on one way only, pin 1 to 3V3.

4. **Bench.** Plug the power bank into the LaunchPad kit's USB-C socket. Nothing else is connected.

   You should see: The Mountain King recording opens the show and the RGB LED swaps orange and purple on the beat. Songs shuffle and loop, with a scare sound between them.

   If you hear nothing, check J5 sits on SPI DAC and the slider is up. If nothing happens at all, the bank switched off at low load: use one with an always-on or low-current mode.

5. **Bench.** S2 short: next song. S1 short: next light theme (pumpkin, fire, lightning, ghost, heartbeat, witch, music). S2 held 0.7 s: next sound mode (clean, haunted, graveyard, mad lab). S1 held 0.7 s: volume step. Both together, released within 2 s: shuffle on or off. Both held 2 to 5 s: speaker EQ on or off, to compare.

   You should see: Every action beeps, blinks the LED and prints a line on the serial console at 115200. Settings start fresh at each power-up.

   If the board does not start after you held S1 while plugging in, that button starts the chip's bootloader: unplug and plug in again without touching it.

6. **Mac, terminal.** Install `ffmpeg` first (`brew install ffmpeg`). The tool cuts, filters and encodes any audio file into the show; then run steps 1 and 2 again. The five shipped recordings use 174 s and leave room for about 22 s more: to add a longer song, delete one of them from `portability/boosterpacks/audio/tracks/` first.

   ```text
   python3 portability/boosterpacks/audio/tools/add_track.py "<any audio file>" --start 30 --length 35 --title "My spooky song" --no-build
   ```

   You should see: The tool prints the track it wrote; after steps 1 and 2, your song joins the shuffle.

   If the build reports the flash is full, shorten the new track with `--length` or drop another one from the folder.

### Expected result

After flashing and stacking the pack, the LaunchPad plays the show from a power bank with no computer: recordings and synth songs on shuffle, scare sounds between them, and the RGB LED following the music.

### What this shows

- One LaunchPad with 1 MB of flash plays recorded orchestra and organ music: five 30 to 40 s cuts at 10 kHz in IMA ADPCM, 849.6 kB together, played back at 16 kHz.
- The sample interrupt keeps time with room to spare: 15,999 frames a second, 0 late, with the worst interrupt at 5.8k of its 10k-cycle budget.
- A speaker EQ fitted from a measured tone sweep: 300 Hz high-pass, five peaking filters and a bass enhancer for a speaker whose response spreads 15.5 dB from 500 Hz to 4 kHz.

### Limits

- The power bank's current draw and run time were not measured.
- The pack's microphone gets no power on this LaunchPad (BoosterPack pin 5 is not wired to the chip), so the clap and knock listener is off here.
- Loudness stops rising above about volume step 10 of 16: a 1 kHz tone through a laptop microphone rose 8.6 dB from step 4 to 10 and 0.7 dB from 10 to 16. Whether the amplifier, the speaker or the microphone limits it was not separated.
- Some power banks switch off under about 50 to 100 mA; the show has no low-power mode, so pick a bank that stays on.
- The speaker EQ was fitted from a laptop's built-in microphone, taken as flat.

### Numbers and sources

| | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| DAC frames a second | 15,999, 0 late ticks over 480 s |  |
| Worst sample interrupt | 5.8k of 10k cycles at 160 MHz |  |
| Speaker EQ | 300 Hz high-pass, five peaking filters and a bass enhancer, fitted to a stepped tone sweep heard by a laptop microphone; the measured spread from 500 Hz to 4 kHz is 15.5 dB, the fit predicts 6.4 dB with the EQ |  |
| Image size | 913.0 kB of 1 MB flash; 19.3 kB RAM |  |
| Software | MSPM33 SDK 1.04.00.00, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS -O2, SysConfig 1.28.0, Intel Mac, macOS 15.7 | `portability/boosterpacks/audio/halloween/README.md` |

# Camera AI on a TI Linux board, timed

Boot TI's Edge AI Linux on a starter kit and run TI's ready-made models on its C7x accelerator. Read each model's time per picture over a serial cable.

The page: [site/project-linux-vision.html](../../site/project-linux-vision.html). This file is its text. Terms: [vocabulary](../vocab.md).

<!-- generated from site/data/projects.json by tools/render_build_md.py; edit the data, not this file -->

## TI's model zoo on the C7x, over the serial console

The demonstrated build: the SK-TDA4VM, its serial cable, and no network or display.

Status: Works. Boards: tda4.

Folders this version uses (in a sparse clone, fetch them first, then read `tda4/AGENTS.md`):

```bash
git sparse-checkout add tda4
```

### Parts

| Part | Quantity | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| SK-TDA4VM starter kit (TDA4VM Jacinto 7 vision processor, J721EXSKG01EVM) | 1 | the board |
| USB-C power supply that gives 20 V at 3 A or more (60 W class), for the SK-TDA4VM | 1 | power for the board |
| USB stick, FAT32, 4 GB or more | 1 | carries the image to the board when you have no card reader |

### Before you start

- A Mac, checked on an Intel Mac, macOS 15.7.9. It needs Homebrew (from brew.sh, which needs the Xcode command line tools: 1.8 GB installed here) and Python 3 with pip (the command line tools bring both). Step 1 installs lrzsz 0.13.1 (0.3 MB installed), xz 5.8.4 (2.6 MB installed) and pyserial 3.5 (under 1 MB). The code is in this repository. Clone it with `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git` and fetch the folders listed for this version. This page calls the folder you clone it into `<repository folder>`.
- A second computer with 15 GB free for the unpacked image. The 1.1 GB download unpacks to 13.8 GB; a second Mac was used. Not needed if you have a micro-SD card reader and use TI's route.
- About an hour: 62 counted minutes from the first console check to the Linux login, 11 of them hands-on and 51 waiting. The serial driver install the evening before is not included.

### Steps

1. **Mac, browser and terminal.** One-time setup before the board: install the CP210x VCP driver on the Mac, a free download from the bridge chip's maker. Then in System Settings, Privacy and Security, click Allow. Then install the helpers the card-writing scripts use with Homebrew and pip. Checked with lrzsz 0.13.1, pyserial 3.5 and xz 5.8.4 on an Intel Mac, macOS 15.7.9.

   ```text
   brew install lrzsz xz
   pip install pyserial
   ```

   You should see: After step 2 plugs the board in, four serial ports appear: `/dev/cu.SLAB_USBtoUART`, `...UART1`, `...UART2` and `...UART4`.

   If System Settings never shows the Allow prompt, scroll to the bottom of Privacy and Security, where a "System software ... was blocked" notice names the driver. **Third-party behavior.**

2. **Bench.** Check SW1 (BOOT CTL) is all four sliders OFF, the micro-SD card is seated under the board, and plug a micro-B cable from J4 to the Mac. Leave the board unpowered for now. The 20 V USB-C supply goes to J14, the power port at the board's edge. Never plug it into J12, the data port.

   You should see: The four serial ports from step 1 appear on the Mac. The Linux console is `/dev/cu.SLAB_USBtoUART1` on the test Mac; the chip's UART-boot port is `...UART2`.

   If the console later goes silent after you move the cable to another USB port, probe all four ports again: the console can come back under another name. A 5 V charger can reset the board during boot.

3. **Terminal (Mac).** Open the console first, then power the board: log all four ports with timestamps, one per port, using `python3 tda4/tools/conlog.py <port> <log>`, at 115200 baud, 8N1. Power on the board from the 20 V supply.

   You should see: On a kit whose card carries no image, silence on all four ports before and after a press of SW2 (reset). That was the case on the test kit, so the card in the box was probably blank.

   If you connect after the board has booted you may see nothing even after Enter: press SW2 with the console open. Silence also looks like a wrong SW1 setting or the wrong port, so check both before writing the card.

4. **Browser, second computer.** On a second computer with 15 GB free, download `tisdk-edgeai-image-j721e-evm.wic.xz` from TI's SK-TDA4VM software page. The file is 1.1 GB, from Processor SDK Linux Edge AI 11.00.00.08, and no login is needed. Check it and record your own hash, because the page shows no checksum.

   ```text
   xz -t tisdk-edgeai-image-j721e-evm.wic.xz
   ```

   You should see: `xz -t` prints nothing and exits cleanly. The test file was 1 GB.

   With a micro-SD card reader, TI's route is shorter: write the file to the card with balenaEtcher, or from a terminal with `tda4/tools/write-card.sh diskN path/to/image.wic.xz`, then skip to step 8. That route was not run on this kit.

5. **Terminal (second computer).** No card reader, so the card is written from the board itself. On the second computer, unpack the image and mount the boot partition, using the disk number `hdiutil` prints in place of `diskN`. Then split the image into compressed pieces. Then copy `tiboot3.bin`, `sysfw.itb`, `tispl.bin` and `u-boot.img` from `/tmp/boot` to the folder with `tda4/tools/uart_boot.py`. Keep the pieces that are not all zeros. For this image they are 000 to 030, 032, 040, 041 and 048, 1.95 GB in all. Copy them into a `tda4/` folder on a FAT32 USB stick of 4 GB or more.

   ```text
   xz -dk tisdk-edgeai-image-j721e-evm.wic.xz
   hdiutil attach -imagekey diskimage-class=CRawDiskImage -nomount tisdk-edgeai-image-j721e-evm.wic
   diskutil mount -mountPoint /tmp/boot /dev/diskNs1
   split -b 268435456 -a 3 -d tisdk-edgeai-image-j721e-evm.wic wic.
   gzip -1 wic.*
   ```

   You should see: A 13.8 GB raw image after `xz -dk`; `hdiutil` prints a disk number to use for `diskN`.

   Edit the console port in the scripts in `tda4/tools/` and the piece list in `write_from_stick.py` for your Mac and image. Skip all-zero pieces: `gzcat f | tr -d '\0' | wc -c` is not 0 for the ones to keep.

6. **Bench, then terminal (Mac).** Power off. Set SW1: 1 ON, 2 OFF, 3 ON, 4 OFF (UART boot). Put the stick in a USB-A port. Run the script, then power on or press SW2.

   ```text
   python tda4/tools/uart_boot.py
   ```

   You should see: A stream of `C` on the UART-boot port, then the four boot files go in: xmodem, then ymodem, about 3.5 minutes at 9.7 kB/s. Then `U-Boot 2025.01` and a `=>` prompt on the console port.

   If it stops at the third file (`spl: ymodem err - Timed out`), press SW2 and run it again. Use the current version of the Python script, and no shell loop. Do not try U-Boot's `ums` command: it crashes U-Boot on this kit and you are back at this step.

7. **Terminal (Mac).** Write the card from the stick, piece by piece.

   ```text
   python tda4/tools/write_from_stick.py unzip
   ```

   You should see: For each piece, `load usb 0:1`, `unzip` and `mmc write` ending in `blocks written: OK`; 323 seconds for the whole image; at the end `mmc part` lists TI's two partitions.

   A piece that takes more than a minute is stuck: reset with SW2 and begin again from step 6. If the write was interrupted, run `write_from_stick.py unzip` again from U-Boot: every piece goes to a fixed block address, so a rerun overwrites the same places.

8. **Bench, then terminal (Mac).** Power off. Set all four sliders of SW1 to OFF (SD boot). Make sure the console is being logged, then power on.

   You should see: `U-Boot SPL`, `Starting kernel`, `Welcome to Arago`, then `tda4vm-sk login:` at 27.7 seconds on the first boot. The root file system grows to the card during it. Log in as `root`, no password.

   The red `Direct firmware load for j7-mcu-r5f0_1-fw failed with error -2` lines and `Failed to start Start psplash boot splash screen` are harmless: three R5F cores have no firmware on the image and there is no display.

9. **Terminal (Mac).** Push TI's model-timing script to the board over the console after making its folders. The board has no network in this route.

   ```text
   python3 tda4/tools/lcmd.py "mkdir -p /root/push /root/night"
   python3 tda4/tools/push_serial.py tda4/bench/zoo/zoo_bench.py /root/push/zoo_bench.py
   ```

   You should see: The push prints a matching sha256 for the file when it arrives.

   Push files as 76-column base64 only, which `push_serial.py` does; a single long line hangs the console at a `>` prompt.

10. **Terminal (Mac).** Run it in the background so the console's Ctrl-C cannot kill it. The script times every precompiled model in `/opt/model_zoo` through its runtime with TI's TIDL delegate on the C7x and its matrix accelerator, 30 timed runs each. Then read the log. These command lines are assembled from the script, its log and the FAQ rule; the recorded run typed them in pieces.

   ```text
   python3 tda4/tools/lcmd.py "setsid nohup python3 /root/push/zoo_bench.py 30 > /root/night/zoo_tidl.log 2>&1 < /dev/null &"
   python3 tda4/tools/lcmd.py "cat /root/night/zoo_tidl.log"
   ```

   You should see: One line per model, such as `ONR-KD-7060-human-pose-yolox-s-640x640 | keypoint_detection | onnxrt | tidl-c7x | [1, 3, 640, 640] | median 13.76 ms | min 13.72 | max 13.86 | n 30 | rss 284 MB`. The 14 zoo models came out between 2.17 ms (MobileNetV1) and 13.76 ms (YOLOX-s pose 640). The TVM models need `tda4/bench/zoo/tvm_bench.py` the same way.

   If a model takes hundreds of milliseconds, it ran on the CPU. Load the model's precompiled `artifacts` folder instead of the bare ONNX file. Then check the runtime log lists every node on the C7x, 274 of 274 for the pose model. Start long jobs with `setsid nohup`; a plain `nohup ... &` died at the next connect.

### Expected result

A Linux login prompt 27.7 seconds after power-on, and one timing line per zoo model, each between 2.17 and 13.76 ms on the C7x. The pose model, the biggest, reads 13.76 ms.

### What this shows

- TI's Edge AI Linux boots on the SK-TDA4VM from a card written with no card reader, Ethernet or display. That was one kit and one Mac.
- All 14 of TI's zoo models run on the C7x and its matrix accelerator in 2.17 to 13.76 ms each. TI's four published figures are within 10 percent of the measured values.
- The same eight ONNX models take 13 to 135 times longer on the two Arm cores with the CPU provider. A model that falls back to the CPU costs that much on this image.

### Limits

- No picture was shown to the models: the input is random numbers, and outputs were not compared. These are times only; accuracy was not measured.
- The CPU comparison is fp32 on the CPU against int8 on the accelerator. It shows the cost of falling back to the CPU and is no like-for-like comparison of the two cores.
- These timings come from one run. No independent builder has repeated them.
- Sustained load was not shown to be safe. The board reset about 60 seconds into a two-thread CoreMark plus TIDL loop. A five-minute pose graph took the hottest zone to 91.5 C.
- A card reader, an Ethernet link, a display or a camera were never used, so the camera and display paths are untested.
- The board had no card reader, Ethernet or display; the whole route is the serial cable at 9.7 kB/s for the boot files. TI's own route, which needs a reader and a display, was not run.
- TI's getting-started page assumes a display and Ethernet; the model-zoo layout was learned by listing folders.
- The board resets under heavy sustained load; it runs on a 20 V supply of unknown wattage with a passive heatsink and no fan.
- The TVM build of ssdLite mobDet 320 is 12.97 ms against 6.40 ms for the TFLite build. **Unknown (suspected: the input conversion inside the graph).**

### Numbers and sources

| | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Board and image | SK-TDA4VM (J721EXSKG01EVM) revision PROC112A1, TI Edge AI SDK 11.00.00.08, Linux 6.12.17-ti, gcc 13.3, Python 3.12 | `tda4/README.md` |
| Runtimes | ONNX Runtime 1.15.0 with the TIDLExecutionProvider, TFLite through libtidl_tfl_delegate, DLR 1.13.0 for the three TVM models | `tda4/RESULTS-tda4.md` |
| Method | Precompiled int8 artifacts from /opt/model_zoo, random input, one warm-up, 30 timed runs, median wall time in Python; timing only, outputs not compared |  |
| C7x time per picture | 2.17 ms (MobileNetV1 mlperf 224) to 13.76 ms (YOLOX-s pose 640); regNetx-200mf 2.89 ms, YOLOX-nano-lite 416 4.66 ms, ssd-lite-mobv2 512 6.10 ms |  |
| Two A72 cores, same ONNX models | fp32 graphs on the CPU provider, 3 timed runs: 37.4 ms to 1,767 ms, 13 to 135 times slower; the zoo ships no int8 CPU build | `docs/experiments/2026-10-10-tda4-c7x-vs-a72.md` |
| Against TI's published figures | TI's four published C7x figures (2.03, 3.04, 5.03 and 5.9 ms) are within 10 percent of the measured values | `docs/experiments/2026-10-10-tda4-c7x-vs-a72.md` |
