# A Matter light in Apple Home

Build the lighting example, flash the CC35X1, add it to Apple Home. Phone tile and board buttons switch the red LED.

The page: [site/project-matter-device.html](../../site/project-matter-device.html). This file is its text. Terms: [vocabulary](../vocab.md).

<!-- generated from site/data/projects.json by tools/render_build_md.py; edit the data, not this file -->

## TI's Matter light in Apple Home

TI's lighting example, unmodified. The red LED becomes a light tile in Home.

Status: Works. Boards: cc35x1.

Folders this version uses (in a sparse clone, fetch them first, then read `cc35x1/AGENTS.md`):

```bash
git sparse-checkout add cc35x1
```

### Parts

| Part | Quantity | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| LP-EM-CC35X1 LaunchPad development kit | 1 | the board |
| LP-XDS110ET debugger | 1 | the debugger that programs the board |
| iPhone with the Home app | 1 | the Matter controller you pair with |
| Apple TV (the Home hub) | 1 | the hub the phone controls the accessory through |
| A Mac to program from | 1 | runs the Toolbox and programs the board |
| Linux or Docker host | 1 | builds the image |

### Before you start

- A Mac with SimpleLink Wi-Fi Toolbox 4.3.23 (free from TI), tested on an Intel Mac, macOS 15.7.9. The Matter build needs Ubuntu 22.04, so add a Linux or Docker host (a Mac with OrbStack and 6 GB free worked). Clone with `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git` and fetch this version's folders. Below, `<repository folder>` is that clone.
- Your probe serial number: the eight characters `/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/ccs_base/common/uscif/xds110/xdsdfu -e` prints (needs CCStudio 21.0.1).
- One step cannot be undone. Activation burns TI's example key into the chip's fuses, and every image is signed with it from then on. Step 2 checks first.
- A Home hub and an iPhone with the Home app. Bluetooth on, phone on the hub's Wi-Fi.

### Steps

1. **Bench.** Set the debugger's TGT VDD jumper to EXT and push the board's 20-pin edge into the debugger. Plug both USB-C cables into the Mac. Leave J4 and J6 on the lower two pins.

   You should see: The Mac lists the probe and `xdsdfu -e` prints its serial number.

   Use both cables. TI says the debugger can brown out during Matter transmissions otherwise.

2. **Terminal (Mac).** In `/Applications/ti/simplelink_wifi_toolbox_macos_4_3_23`, run the read-only activation check. If it prints the fuse table, go on. Only if it stops with `Process is stopped. Life cycle OPERATIONAL is not valid.`, activate by hand as under “If something goes wrong.”

   ```text
   ./simplelink-wifi-toolbox programmer -i XDS110 -param1 <probe serial> get_fuse_data --flash_type IS25WJ064F --activation_type sdk_example_key --verbose
   ```

   You should see: The check prints the fuse table instead of the error. Activation took about 5 seconds.

   Activation cannot be undone. If the fuse table prints, the chip is already activated: do nothing. Only for the exact lifecycle error, type this by hand, never paste it: `./simplelink-wifi-toolbox programmer -i XDS110 -param1 <probe serial> custom_activation --flash_type IS25WJ064F --activation_type sdk_example_key --authentication_enabled yes`. The Copy button copies only the check, on purpose.

3. **Terminal, Linux or Docker host.** Build from the repository's `cc35x1/matter` folder. The script downloads four tools, checks each against a published SHA-256, fetches TI's repository at the pinned commit and leaves images in `/path/to/work/out/debug`. Copy `toolbox` to the Mac.

   ```text
   ./build.sh /path/to/work
   ```

   You should see: A signed 1,758.3 kB image (`toolbox/primary_vendor_image.sign.bin`, 1.7 MB). The clean build took 673 seconds (11 minutes 13 seconds) under emulation on an Apple silicon Mac.

   Needs 6 GB free. Afterward run `docker volume rm frl-matter-build`. If the SysConfig 1.28.0 installer is gone, the script uses 1.28.1 build 4785, which built this image.

4. **Terminal (Mac).** From the repository root, set TB to the copied toolbox folder and run `cc35x1/matter/mac_paths.sh` to swap Linux paths for local ones. Then change to the Toolbox folder and program the image.

   ```text
   TB="/absolute/path/to/copied/toolbox"
   cc35x1/matter/mac_paths.sh "$TB"
   cd /Applications/ti/simplelink_wifi_toolbox_macos_4_3_23
   ./simplelink-wifi-toolbox programmer -i XDS110 -param1 <probe serial> programming --tool_settings "$TB/tool_settings.mac.json"
   ```

   You should see: The Toolbox reports success after about a minute.

   If another TI image was on the board (above all Wi-Fi CSI presence) and the serial port stays silent, save what you need, erase, and program again: `./simplelink-wifi-toolbox programmer -i XDS110 -param1 <probe serial> full_flash_erase --flash_type AUTO_DETECT --activation_type sdk_example_key`. This wipes the old image and settings. Skip it on a clean board. `mac_paths.sh` has run only on saved thermostat build folders and synthetic paths, not a fresh light build. If it reports a missing file, recopy `toolbox` and rerun.

5. **Bench.** Press S1 (reset) to open a pairing window. The Toolbox does not reset the board. If it was paired before, hold SW1 for 1 second first to wipe the pairing.

   You should see: The board advertises over Bluetooth. At 115200 baud the log shows the start. One Wi-Fi disconnect line per boot is TI's known issue MATTER-456.

   Scan within 5 minutes. The thermostat image, same TI code, closed at 300 seconds. Matter's default is 15 minutes, untimed on the light. The blinking green LED only means Identify.

6. **Phone (Home app).** In the Home app tap +, then Add Accessory, and scan `cc35x1/matter/setup-qr.png`. If the scan fails, tap More options, My Accessory Isn't Shown Here, Enter Code, and type the code `cc35x1/matter/payload.py` prints.

   You should see: The phone finds the accessory and warns Uncertified Accessory.

   Stay within a few meters, Bluetooth on. Not sure it is advertising? Press S1 again.

7. **Phone (Home app).** Tap Add Anyway, wait about a minute, pick a room and name, tap Done.

   You should see: A progress screen, then room and name. In the board's log from the Bluetooth connect: secure channel at 3 s, Wi-Fi at 16 s, commissioning done at 63 s.

   If pairing stalls, press S1 and restart from step 6.

8. **Phone and bench.** Tap the light tile. Then press SW1 (on) and SW2 (off) on the board.

   You should see: The tile shows On with a yellow bulb and the red LED follows. Buttons change the tile within about a second.

   It is called "Matter Accessory" until you rename it.

### Expected result

After about a minute Apple Home adds a light. The tile toggles the red LED and the buttons change the tile. Commissioning took 63 seconds from the Bluetooth connect, per the device log.

### What this shows

- TI's lighting example builds from source in a Linux container and runs on the CC3551E, 1,758.3 kB signed.
- An iPhone commissions it over Bluetooth and Wi-Fi. The tile toggles the LED and the buttons update the tile. One run, 2026-10-09.

### Limits

- Google Home, Alexa and Home Assistant have no recorded run.
- 63 seconds is one run. Toggle latency is untimed.
- Setup after a reflash is unmeasured. A new image loses the pairing.
- The Matter test vendor ID `0xFFF1` makes Apple Home show Uncertified Accessory.
- TI supports Ubuntu 22.04 only. This build ran in a linux/amd64 container under emulation, hence 11 minutes.
- Commissioning from a Mac with the matter.js shell stopped at the Bluetooth link: macOS refused a UUID. Phones are fine.
- Matter over Thread is not for this chip: the CC3551E has no 802.15.4 radio.

### Numbers and sources

| | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Software | TI Matter release `matter-v1.5-ti-1.2-ea.2`, commit `33a45a1ba707418ee9f764723a5b98f2718e8abd`, example `examples/lighting-app/ti/cc35xx` | `cc35x1/matter/README.md` |
| Toolchain | SimpleLink Wi-Fi SDK 10.20.00.39, Toolbox 4.3.23, SysConfig 1.28.1, Arm GNU 12.3.rel1, CMake 3.21.3 | `cc35x1/matter/README.md` |
| Flash and RAM | 1,752.1 kB of code and constants plus initialized data; 578.9 kB of initialized plus zero-initialized data (heap and stacks not counted) | `cc35x1/matter/README.md` |
| Build record | 673 s clean: packages 74, tools 20, source 9, submodules 118, bootstrap 175, Wi-Fi SDK libraries 69, lighting app 208 | `cc35x1/matter/README.md` |
| Commissioning | 63 s from the Bluetooth connect to commissioning completed (secure channel 3 s, Wi-Fi joined 16 s) |  |
| Core and clock | Arm Cortex-M33 at 160 MHz on the CC3551E | `cc35x1/README.md` |

## A Matter thermostat in Apple Home

A thermostat built from TI's lighting example on the CC35X1, paired into Apple Home.

Status: Could work. Boards: cc35x1.

Folders this version uses (in a sparse clone, fetch them first, then read `cc35x1/AGENTS.md`):

```bash
git sparse-checkout add cc35x1
```

### Parts

| Part | Quantity | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| LP-EM-CC35X1 LaunchPad development kit | 1 | the board |
| LP-XDS110ET debugger | 1 | the debugger that programs the board |
| iPhone with the Home app | 1 | the Matter controller you pair with |
| Apple TV (the Home hub) | 1 | the hub the phone controls the accessory through |
| A Mac to program from | 1 | runs the Toolbox and programs the board |
| Linux or Docker host | 1 | builds the image |

### Before you start

- A Mac with SimpleLink Wi-Fi Toolbox 4.3.23 (free from TI), tested on an Intel Mac, macOS 15.7.9. The Matter build needs Ubuntu 22.04, so add a Linux or Docker host (a Mac with OrbStack and 6 GB free worked). Clone with `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git` and fetch this version's folders. Below, `<repository folder>` is that clone.
- Your probe serial number: the eight characters `/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/ccs_base/common/uscif/xds110/xdsdfu -e` prints (needs CCStudio 21.0.1).
- One step cannot be undone. Activation burns TI's example key into the chip's fuses, and every image is signed with it from then on. Step 2 checks first.
- A Home hub and an iPhone with the Home app. Bluetooth on, phone on the hub's Wi-Fi.

### Steps

1. **Bench.** Set the debugger's TGT VDD jumper to EXT and push the board's 20-pin edge into the debugger. Plug both USB-C cables into the Mac. Leave J4 and J6 on the lower two pins.

   You should see: The Mac lists the probe and `xdsdfu -e` prints its serial number.

   Use both cables. TI says the debugger can brown out during Matter transmissions otherwise.

2. **Terminal (Mac).** In `/Applications/ti/simplelink_wifi_toolbox_macos_4_3_23`, run the read-only check. Only if it stops with `Process is stopped. Life cycle OPERATIONAL is not valid.`, run the second command once. One at a time.

   ```text
   ./simplelink-wifi-toolbox programmer -i XDS110 -param1 <probe serial> get_fuse_data --flash_type IS25WJ064F --activation_type sdk_example_key --verbose
   ```

   You should see: The check prints the fuse table instead of the error. Activation took about 5 seconds.

   Activation cannot be undone. If the fuse table prints, stop. Only for the exact lifecycle error, type this, do not paste: `./simplelink-wifi-toolbox programmer -i XDS110 -param1 <probe serial> custom_activation --flash_type IS25WJ064F --activation_type sdk_example_key --authentication_enabled yes`. Copy copies the check only, on purpose.

3. **Terminal, Linux or Docker host.** Build from the repository's `cc35x1/matter` folder. It is TI's `matter-v1.5-ti-1.2-ea.2` tag, commit `33a45a1ba707418ee9f764723a5b98f2718e8abd`, with a thermostat data model and application swapped into the lighting example. Copy the `toolbox` folder from `/path/to/work/out/debug` to the Mac.

   ```text
   ./build-thermostat.sh /path/to/work
   ```

   You should see: A signed 1,747.9 kB image (`toolbox/primary_vendor_image.sign.bin`). A warm container took 5 minutes 1 second. Cold was never timed in one piece; about 12 minutes is an estimate.

   Needs 6 GB free in a Docker volume (`frl-matter-build`). Afterward run `docker volume rm frl-matter-build`. TI builds Matter on Ubuntu 22.04 only.

4. **Terminal (Mac).** From the Toolbox folder, erase the flash, then program the image. First run `cc35x1/matter/mac_paths.sh` from the repository: the build leaves Linux paths in `tool_settings.json` and the Toolbox needs absolute Mac ones. One command at a time.

   ```text
   TB=<absolute path of the copied toolbox folder>
   cc35x1/matter/mac_paths.sh "$TB"
   cd /Applications/ti/simplelink_wifi_toolbox_macos_4_3_23
   ./simplelink-wifi-toolbox programmer -i XDS110 -param1 <probe serial> full_flash_erase --flash_type AUTO_DETECT --activation_type sdk_example_key
   ./simplelink-wifi-toolbox programmer -i XDS110 -param1 <probe serial> programming --tool_settings "$TB/tool_settings.mac.json"
   ```

   You should see: Erase takes about 16 seconds, programming about 60. On an erased flash the image starts by itself.

   Always erase first if another image was on the board, above all Wi-Fi CSI presence. Without it, every later image stayed silent, TI's light included. `mac_paths.sh` has run only on a sample file. If the Toolbox reports a path error, make every path in `tool_settings.json` absolute by hand.

5. **Terminal (Mac).** Optional. Read the board's serial port, `/dev/cu.usbmodem<probe serial>1`, at 115200 baud (8N1). The command below, from the repository, sets the baud and prints the log. Ctrl+C stops it.

   ```text
   python3 cc35x1/matter/logread.py /dev/cu.usbmodem<probe serial>1
   ```

   You should see: Within 2 seconds: a boot line, Wi-Fi start, the Matter server and `THERMO ready: UART2_1 115200, endpoint 1 thermostat, endpoint 2 occupancy`. Bluetooth advertising starts about 5 seconds after the boot line.

   After Bluetooth starts the log fills with 0x00 and 0x80 bytes. Cause unknown. Pairing and control still work. A silent port usually means wrong baud. `logread.py` has run only against a virtual port; any serial program set to 115200 8N1 works.

6. **Phone (Home app).** The window is 300 seconds. In the Home app tap +, then Add Accessory, and scan `cc35x1/matter/setup-qr.png`. If you cannot scan, choose More options and type the code `cc35x1/matter/payload.py` prints. At Uncertified Accessory tap Add Anyway, then pick a room and name.

   You should see: The accessory appears as a thermostat named "Matter Accessory".

   If the scan finds it and hangs on "Connecting", the 300-second window has closed. Erase and program again (step 4), then scan within 5 minutes.

7. **Phone (Home app).** Open the thermostat tile, set Heat and move the heating setpoint to 67 F.

   You should see: Heat at 67 F. Current temperature reads 69 F: the board's fixed 20.8 C fallback, since no sensor is wired.

   With no sensor line, SW1 and SW2 step the board's setpoint by 0.5 C.

### Expected result

Within the window Apple Home adds a thermostat and the heating setpoint changes from the phone. The idle board reports about 150 kB of heap free. Pairing time is unmeasured here; the light took 63 s.

### What this shows

- TI ships no thermostat for the CC3551E. This one runs, Apple Home adds it and it takes a heating setpoint change. One iPhone, 2026-10-11.
- Swapping the data model and one application file in the lighting example was enough. It paired on the first scan.
- The image is 10.4 kB smaller than TI's light: 1,747.9 kB against 1,758.3 kB signed.

### Limits

- Google Home, Alexa and Home Assistant have no recorded run. Their result rows are waiting.
- The occupancy endpoint is not driven: no presence line is wired.
- Temperature is a fixed 20.8 C fallback, not a sensor. No driver path to the chip's own temperature turned up.
- Setpoint latency, local control offline, four controllers at once and setup after a reflash are unmeasured.
- The board's log of the write was not recorded. The evidence is the phone screen.
- Programming over the Wi-Fi CSI presence image left the board silent until a full erase. The Toolbox guide does not mention it.
- The Matter test vendor ID `0xFFF1` makes Apple Home show Uncertified Accessory. The device is not certified.
- The 300-second window means erase, program and pair in one sitting.
- Unknown. After Bluetooth starts the log UART turns to 0x00 and 0x80 bytes at every rate tried, 1,200 to 115,200 baud.
- Matter over Thread is not for this chip: the CC3551E has no 802.15.4 radio.

### Numbers and sources

| | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Software | TI Matter release `matter-v1.5-ti-1.2-ea.2`, commit `33a45a1ba707418ee9f764723a5b98f2718e8abd`, plus the thermostat example from this repository (Thermostat on endpoint 1, Occupancy Sensing on endpoint 2) | `cc35x1/matter/README.md` |
| Toolchain | SimpleLink Wi-Fi SDK 10.20.00.39, Toolbox 4.3.23, SysConfig 1.28.1 (TI pins 1.28.0; the Linux installer for it was no longer served), Arm GNU 12.3.rel1, CMake 3.21.3, in a linux/amd64 container | `cc35x1/matter/README.md` |

# Type Python at a prompt on a TI chip

MicroPython's own Zephyr port builds with one config file and runs on the LP-EM-CC2340R5 and the LP-MSPM33C321A: a prompt on the probe's serial port and Pin from Python.

The page: [site/project-micropython.html](../../site/project-micropython.html). This file is its text. Terms: [vocabulary](../vocab.md).

## MicroPython on the LP-EM-CC2340R5

MicroPython's own Zephyr port gives a prompt on the 36 kB Bluetooth chip; Pin, ADC, interrupts, PWM, SPI and I2C run from Python.

Status: Works. Boards: cc2340r5.

Folders this version uses (in a sparse clone, fetch them first, then read `ports/micropython/zephyr-cc2340r5/AGENTS.md`):

```bash
git sparse-checkout add ports/micropython/zephyr-cc2340r5
```

### Parts

| Part | Quantity | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| LP-EM-CC2340R5 LaunchPad development kit | 1 | the board |
| LP-XDS110ET debugger | 1 | the debugger that programs the board |
| A Mac to build and flash from | 1 | builds and flashes |

### Before you start

- A Mac. Only an Intel Mac, macOS 15.7, was tried. Python 3.12 or newer, `ninja`, `cmake`, UniFlash 9.6.0 and `pyserial` (`python3 -m pip install pyserial`) for the REPL helper.
- About 5 GB for the Zephyr 4.4.2 workspace, the Zephyr SDK 0.17.4 GCC 12.2.0 cross compiler and a Python 3.12 environment with `west`, plus 62 MB for MicroPython.
- Close any CCStudio debug connection before step 5; it holds the debug probe.
- The code is in this repository. Clone it with `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git` and fetch the folders listed for this version. This page calls the folder you clone it into `<repository folder>`.

### Steps

1. **Mac, terminal.** Install the Zephyr 4.4.2 workspace, the compiler and the `west` environment; `NO_FLASH=1` stops the script after its build so it does not touch a board. Then clone MicroPython v1.29.0 (commit `0fd6c573e`); nothing in it is edited.

   ```text
   NO_FLASH=1 <repository folder>/cc2340r5/zephyr/setup-intel-mac.sh
   git clone --depth 1 --branch v1.29.0 https://github.com/micropython/micropython.git <MP>
   ```

   You should see: The script ends with `NO_FLASH set. Built, not flashed.` and `<MP>` holds MicroPython.

   If a download fails, rerun the script; it keeps what it already fetched.

2. **Mac, terminal.** Copy `prj_cc2340r5.conf` and `lp_em_cc2340r5.overlay` from `ports/micropython/zephyr-cc2340r5` into a folder `<proj>`, then build. The conf replaces MicroPython's own `prj.conf`, which overflows the chip's RAM by 46.8 kB; the overlay adds the ADC channels.

   ```text
   . <zephyr workspace>/.venv/bin/activate
   export ZEPHYR_TOOLCHAIN_VARIANT=cross-compile CROSS_COMPILE=<toolchain>/arm-zephyr-eabi/bin/arm-zephyr-eabi-
   cd <zephyr workspace>/zephyr
   west build -p always -b lp_em_cc2340r5 <MP>/ports/zephyr -d <build> -- -DCONF_FILE=<proj>/prj_cc2340r5.conf -DEXTRA_DTC_OVERLAY_FILE=<proj>/lp_em_cc2340r5.overlay
   ```

   You should see: About 3 minutes later the build ends with zero errors: 174.9 kB of flash (34.15 %) and 29.9 kB of RAM (82.99 %). The image is `<build>/zephyr/zephyr_crc32.hex`.

   If the link stops with ``region `RAM' overflowed by 47888 bytes``, the build used MicroPython's own `prj.conf`: pass `-DCONF_FILE` as shown. If it stops with `relocation truncated to fit: R_ARM_THM_JUMP11 ... nlr_push_tail`, keep `CONFIG_MICROPY_CONFIGFILE="mpconfigport.h"` and do not use the minimal conf.

3. **Bench.** Clip the LP-XDS110ET onto the board and plug it into the Mac with its USB-C cable; the board has no USB port of its own. Read the probe serial with `/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/ccs_base/common/uscif/xds110/xdsdfu -e`.

   You should see: The probe shows up as an XDS110 and `xdsdfu -e` prints its serial number.

   If `xdsdfu -e` lists nothing, check the clip-on connection and use a data cable.

4. **Mac, terminal.** Back up the main flash and the CCFG before the first write, then flash the `_crc32` image, which carries the boot checksums. Restore later with the same `flash` command on `restore.hex`.

   ```text
   DSLITE=<UniFlash folder>/deskdb/content/TICloudAgent/osx/ccs_base/DebugServer/bin/DSLite; CCXML=cc2340r5/CC2340R5.ccxml; BK=<backup folder outside the repo>
   $DSLITE memory -c $CCXML -r 0x0,0x20000 -o $BK/main_flash.bin
   $DSLITE memory -c $CCXML -r 0x4E020000,0x200 -o $BK/ccfg.bin
   python3 cc2340r5/oad/images.py merge $BK/restore.hex $BK/main_flash.bin@0x0 $BK/ccfg.bin@0x4E020000
   $DSLITE flash -c $CCXML -e -f -u <build>/zephyr/zephyr_crc32.hex
   ```

   You should see: DSLite writes the image and reports success; the restore hex reads back byte for byte against the backup.

   If the flash fails, close CCStudio or any other program that holds the probe, and rerun it.

5. **Mac, terminal.** Open the REPL with the helper that holds the serial port open and sends lines (115200 baud, `/dev/cu.usbmodem<your-probe-serial>1`).

   ```text
   python3 ports/micropython/zephyr-cc2340r5/repl.py /dev/cu.usbmodem<your-probe-serial>1 out.log --reset -- 'print(1+1)'
   ```

   You should see: `out.log` holds the banner `MicroPython v1.29.0 on 2026-10-24; zephyr-lp_em_cc2340r5 with cc2340r5`, then the line `2`.

   If nothing appears, check that the port is the probe's second serial port and that no other program holds it.

6. **Mac, terminal.** Drive DIO15, the green LED pin, and read an ADC pin from Python. Pins are named by Zephyr devicetree label and number; the ADC number is the channel from the overlay, not the DIO number.

   ```text
   python3 ports/micropython/zephyr-cc2340r5/repl.py /dev/cu.usbmodem<your-probe-serial>1 out.log -- 'import machine' 'led = machine.Pin(("gpio0", 15), machine.Pin.OUT)' 'led.on(); print(led.value())' 'led.off(); print(led.value())' 'print(machine.ADC(("adc0", 2)).read_u16())'
   ```

   You should see: `out.log` shows `1` after led.on(), `0` after led.off(), then an ADC number (about 42,000 to 48,000 on a floating pin). The LED itself was not watched; the state is known from the read-back.

   If `AttributeError: 'Pin' object has no attribute 'toggle'`, use `led.value(1 - led.value())`. After a Ctrl-D soft reboot a pad you made an output stays one: use `machine.reset()`.

### Expected result

MicroPython 1.29.0 runs on the LP-EM-CC2340R5: a prompt at 115200 baud, DIO15 driven from Python, and the ADC read.

### What this shows

- MicroPython's own Zephyr port runs unmodified on a chip with 36 kB of RAM, once its `prj.conf` is replaced by one file that drops networking, sensors and file systems.
- The image is 174.8 kB of flash and 29.9 kB of RAM with a 20 kB Python heap (19.1 kB free after boot).
- Pin.irq (10 of 10 edges), PWM with duty_ns, SPI and I2C calls ran from the REPL.

### Limits

- That the LED blinked to the eye: the pin read-back changed and the LED was not watched.
- That SPI data is right: the loopback wire was not fitted; the HDC2080 read and I2C.scan() did not work.
- That the `duty_u16` form of PWM is right in MicroPython 1.29.0: it overflows at 1 kHz; use `duty_ns` or apply the one-cast patch in the folder.
- That it works on Windows or Linux: only an Intel Mac was used.
- There is no file system, so scripts are typed or pasted at the prompt and re-sent after each reset.
- Pin.irq loses its edge when Pin.init() is called on the same pin; call irq() again after init().
- An empty Python loop takes 0.63 microseconds a pass at 48 MHz.

### Numbers and sources

| | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| MicroPython | v1.29.0, commit 0fd6c573e, unmodified | `ports/micropython/zephyr-cc2340r5/README.md` |
| Zephyr | 4.4.2, Zephyr SDK 0.17.4 GCC 12.2.0 as a cross compiler | `ports/micropython/zephyr-cc2340r5/README.md` |
| Image | 174.8 kB of flash (34.2 % of 512 kB), 29.9 kB of RAM (83.0 % of 36 kB), 20 kB heap |  |
| Free heap after boot | 19.1 kB of the 20 kB heap |  |
| Python speed | 10,000 empty loop passes in 6,323 microseconds; ADC.read_u16() about 7.2 microseconds |  |

## MicroPython on the LP-MSPM33C321A

MicroPython's own Zephyr port runs unmodified on the 160 MHz Cortex-M33 with its stock config, on Zephyr main plus TI's open pull requests.

Status: Could work. Boards: mspm33c321a.

Folders this version uses (in a sparse clone, fetch them first, then read `ports/micropython/zephyr-mspm33c321a/AGENTS.md`):

```bash
git sparse-checkout add ports/micropython/zephyr-mspm33c321a
```

### Parts

| Part | Quantity | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| LP-MSPM33C321A LaunchPad development kit | 1 | the board |
| A Mac to build and flash from | 1 | builds and flashes |

### Before you start

- A Mac or Linux machine; only an Intel Mac, macOS 15.7, was tried. git, `cmake` and `ninja` on the path, a Python 3.12 environment with `west`, the Zephyr SDK 0.17.4 GCC 12.2.0 `arm-zephyr-eabi` (`cc2340r5/zephyr/setup-intel-mac.sh` installs both), UniFlash 9.6.0 (DSLite). About 1.5 GB for the Zephyr tree and 0.3 GB for the build.
- Zephyr main at `1405adc9a604` plus TI's open pull requests for the UART, clock and GPIO drivers: Zephyr's released board has no serial port, GPIO, I2C or SPI driver. `zephyr-tree.sh` pins each pull request to a commit, and pull requests move.
- Close any CCStudio debug connection before step 4; it holds the debug probe.
- The code is in this repository. Clone it with `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git` and fetch the folders listed for this version. This page calls the folder you clone it into `<repository folder>`.

### Steps

1. **Mac, terminal.** Clone MicroPython v1.29.0 (commit `0fd6c573e`) from a fresh folder outside this repository; nothing in it is edited.

   ```text
   git clone --depth 1 --branch v1.29.0 https://github.com/micropython/micropython.git mp
   ```

   You should see: The `mp` folder holds MicroPython.

   If the clone fails, check the network; the tag is v1.29.0.

2. **Mac, terminal.** Build the Zephyr tree this port needs: Zephyr main plus the pinned pull requests, with `picolibc` and `cmsis_6`. Run it from `ports/micropython/zephyr-mspm33c321a`. The kinds are `uart`, `i2c` and `spi`; this version uses `uart`.

   ```text
   ./zephyr-tree.sh "$PWD/zw" uart
   ```

   You should see: About 10 minutes later the `zw` folder holds the merged Zephyr tree.

   If a later build stops with ``fatal error: alloca.h: No such file or directory``, the picolibc module is missing: `west update picolibc` (the script does it) and pass the folder as `PICO`.

3. **Mac, terminal.** Build MicroPython's `ports/zephyr` for `lp_mspm33c321a` with MicroPython's own `prj.conf` plus `mspm33c321a.conf` (watchdog off, GPIO, I2C, SPI).

   ```text
   MP="$PWD/mp" ZW="$PWD/zw" OUT="$PWD/out" KIND=uart ./build.sh
   ```

   You should see: About 4 minutes later `out/zephyr/zephyr.hex` exists: 292.3 kB of flash (28.5 % of 1 MB) and 83.6 kB of RAM (32.7 % of 256 kB) with the GPIO driver.

   If the build stops naming a variable, set it. If `machine_wdt.c` stops the build, `CONFIG_WATCHDOG=n` is missing; use `mspm33c321a.conf`.

4. **Mac, terminal.** Back up the board, pad the image to a multiple of 16 bytes (DSLite writes 128-bit words), convert it to hex at 0x10000000 and flash it. Restore later with the same `flash` command on a hex made from the saved `main-flash.bin`.

   ```text
   python3 tools/benchmark/backup.py save mspm33c321a --probe <your-probe-serial>
   python3 -c "b=open('out/zephyr/zephyr.bin','rb').read(); open('p.bin','wb').write(b+b'\xff'*(-len(b)%16))"
   arm-zephyr-eabi-objcopy -I binary -O ihex --change-addresses 0x10000000 p.bin p.hex
   DSLite flash -c mspm33c321a/MSPM33C321A_<your-probe-serial>.ccxml -e -f -v p.hex
   ```

   You should see: DSLite writes and verifies the 1 MB image in about 20 s.

   If DSLite says `Error in image size ... should be divisible by 16`, the padding step was skipped. If the next call says `Error initializing emulator (Error -261)`, run `xds110reset -s <your-probe-serial> -a toggle -d 200` and flash again.

5. **Mac, terminal.** Open the REPL on the probe's serial port (115200 baud) and read two pins with their pull resistors on: PA12 pulled up, then pulled down.

   ```text
   python3 ports/micropython/zephyr-mspm33c321a/repl.py /dev/cu.usbmodem<your-probe-serial>1 out.log --reset -- 'print(1+1)' 'import machine' 'print(machine.Pin(("gpioa", 12), machine.Pin.IN, machine.Pin.PULL_UP).value())' 'print(machine.Pin(("gpioa", 12), machine.Pin.IN, machine.Pin.PULL_DOWN).value())'
   ```

   You should see: `out.log` holds the banner `MicroPython v1.29.0 on 2026-10-25; zephyr-lp_mspm33c321a with mspm33c321a`, then `2`, then `1` for the pull-up and `0` for the pull-down.

   If `ValueError: device gpioc not found` appears, `CONFIG_GPIO` is off: build with `mspm33c321a.conf`. Send one-line statements; a multi-line `def` typed line by line is indented wrongly. If a read of `machine.I2C` hangs the console, press the reset button; use writes only.

### Expected result

MicroPython 1.29.0 prints its banner and a >>> prompt at 115200 baud on the LP-MSPM33C321A, pulled-up and pulled-down inputs read 1 and 0, and float math works.

### What this shows

- MicroPython's own Zephyr port runs unmodified, with its own `prj.conf` as shipped, on the Cortex-M33 chip.
- The image is 292.3 kB of flash and 83.6 kB of RAM with a 48 kB Python heap (47.1 kB free after boot).
- machine.Pin and float math run from the REPL on the `KIND=uart` image; machine.SPI calls ran from the `KIND=spi` image.

### Limits

- That machine.I2C works: it opens and writes return, but every read hangs until a hardware reset.
- That machine.ADC or machine.PWM work: Zephyr has no driver for this chip's ADC or PWM.
- That the LED blinked to the eye: the pin state is known from the output register and the LED was not watched.
- That the image from the fresh-folder build ran: it produced an image that was not flashed.
- Zephyr's released `lp_mspm33c321a` board has no serial port, GPIO, I2C or SPI driver; this port needs Zephyr main plus TI's open pull requests, and pull requests move.
- I2C and SPI cannot be in one image: pull requests 110526 and 119347 carry different copies of the UNICOMM driver, so each gets its own build (`KIND=i2c`, `KIND=spi`).
- `Pin.value()` reads 0 right after `led.on()`; read the output register instead.
- An empty Python loop costs 803 CPU cycles a pass at 160 MHz (5.0 microseconds); the cause is not found.

### Numbers and sources

| | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| MicroPython | v1.29.0, commit 0fd6c573e, unmodified | `ports/micropython/zephyr-mspm33c321a/README.md` |
| Zephyr | main 1405adc9a604 plus open pull requests 116768 and 118511 (UART console and GPIO; 110526 for I2C and 119347 for SPI, each with 118511), GCC 12.2.0 from Zephyr SDK 0.17.4 | `ports/micropython/zephyr-mspm33c321a/README.md` |
| Image | 292.3 kB of flash (28.5 % of 1 MB), 83.6 kB of RAM (32.7 % of 256 kB), 48 kB heap |  |
| Free heap after boot | 47.1 of 48 kB after gc.collect() |  |
| Python speed | 10,000 empty loop passes in 50,182 microseconds |  |

# Update a board's firmware by radio

A CC2340R5 took a signed update over Bluetooth from a Mac in 43 s; a CC35X1 installed one over Wi-Fi in 8 s. The Zigbee update from Home Assistant has not finished.

The page: [site/project-ota-update.html](../../site/project-ota-update.html). This file is its text. Terms: [vocabulary](../vocab.md).

<!-- generated from site/data/projects.json by tools/render_build_md.py; edit the data, not this file -->

## Update a CC2340R5 over Bluetooth from a Mac terminal

TI's dual-image OAD example with TI's MCUboot; a Python script sends the signed image. 43 s from scan to the version read back, one run.

Status: Works. Boards: cc2340r5.

Folders this version uses (in a sparse clone, fetch them first, then read `cc2340r5/AGENTS.md`):

```bash
git sparse-checkout add cc2340r5 tools mac-setup
```

### Parts

| Part | Quantity | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| LP-EM-CC2340R5 LaunchPad development kit | 1 | the board that gets updated |
| LP-XDS110ET debugger | 1 | flashes the first image and reads the backup |

### Before you start

- A Mac with Bluetooth, and Bluetooth permission for your terminal app (System Settings, Privacy and Security, Bluetooth). Checked on macOS 15.7.9.
- SimpleLink Low Power F3 SDK 9.21.00.36 LTS, SysConfig 1.26.3, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1 LTS and UniFlash 9.6.0; install steps in mac-setup/README.md.
- Python 3 with bleak (steps below). The code is in this repository: `cc2340r5/oad/` and `tools/oad/`.
- Your probe's serial number goes in `cc2340r5/CC2340R5.ccxml`.

### Steps

1. **Terminal (Mac).** Make a Python environment with bleak, then set the path of the public key compiled into TI's MCUboot (change the SDK path if yours differs). The client uses the key to check the signature.

   ```text
   python3 -m venv ~/ble && ~/ble/bin/pip install bleak
   export KEYS=/Applications/ti/simplelink_lowpower_f3_sdk_9_21_00_36_LTS/source/third_party/mcuboot/boot/ti/source/mcuboot_app/keys.c
   ```

   You should see: bleak installs without errors.

   If the build script cannot find Python, it looks for `$HOME/.venvs/ble/bin/python`; set `PY` to your environment's python when you run it.

2. **Terminal (Mac).** From the repository root. The script builds two copies of TI's `basic_ble_oad_dual_image` example and signs them: v1 is named `FRL OAD 1` and toggles the green LED every second, v2 is `FRL OAD 2` and toggles the red LED four times a second.

   ```text
   cc2340r5/oad/build.sh
   ```

   You should see: About two minutes: 'v1 built in 65 s', 'v2 built in 49 s'. `cc2340r5/oad/images/` holds `mcuboot_dual_image.hex`, `frl_oad_v1.bin` and `frl_oad_v2.bin` (236 kB each).

   If it stops on a missing path, the SDK, SysConfig and compiler paths are at the top of `build.sh`; change them to your install.

3. **Terminal (Mac).** A dry run parses the image header, recomputes the SHA-256 and checks the signature against TI's key.

   ```text
   ~/ble/bin/python tools/oad/oad_client.py --dry-run --keys-c $KEYS cc2340r5/oad/images/frl_oad_v2.bin
   ```

   You should see: `sha256_ok True`, `signature_ok True`, `version 2.0.0+0`, a transfer plan of 1024 blocks of 236 data bytes, then `dry run OK`.

   If a line says False, rebuild; the check was tested on five deliberately broken copies and refused all of them.

4. **Terminal (Mac).** Before writing, read the whole flash and the boot configuration to a folder outside the repo (the board may hold a Zigbee network key). DSLite's `memory -r` takes the length as a count of 32-bit words, not bytes. Then merge them into a restore file.

   ```text
   export DSLITE=/Applications/ti/uniflash_9.6.0/deskdb/content/TICloudAgent/osx/ccs_base/DebugServer/bin/DSLite CCXML=cc2340r5/CC2340R5.ccxml BK=$HOME/cc2340r5-oad-backup && mkdir -p $BK
   $DSLITE memory -c $CCXML -r 0x0,0x20000 -o $BK/main_flash.bin
   $DSLITE memory -c $CCXML -r 0x4E020000,0x200 -o $BK/ccfg.bin
   python3 cc2340r5/oad/images.py merge $BK/restore.hex $BK/main_flash.bin@0x0 $BK/ccfg.bin@0x4E020000
   ```

   You should see: `main_flash.bin` is 512 kB and `ccfg.bin` is 2 kB.

   If `main_flash.bin` is not 512 kB, you gave the length in bytes; use 0x20000 words.

5. **Terminal (Mac).** One command writes both files, because UniFlash erases the whole chip at the start of every program load.

   ```text
   $DSLITE flash -c $CCXML -e -f -u cc2340r5/oad/images/mcuboot_dual_image.hex cc2340r5/oad/images/frl_oad_v1.bin,0x6000
   ```

   You should see: About 13 s. The green LED toggles once a second and `FRL OAD 1` is advertising.

   If the probe reports error -615 when it runs the app, MCUboot was not flashed with it; run the same command again with both files.

6. **Terminal (Mac).** The client finds the board by name, sends the 1,024 blocks, sends the enable command and waits for the new name.

   ```text
   ~/ble/bin/python tools/oad/oad_client.py --name "FRL OAD 1" --expect-name "FRL OAD 2" --keys-c $KEYS --json oad-run.json cc2340r5/oad/images/frl_oad_v2.bin
   ```

   You should see: The running version, progress every 5% with kbit/s, then the download time, the time from enable to the new name and the new version. Recorded run: 31.4 s, 7.8 s, version 2.0.0, packet size 251.

   If it stops before sending with 'ATT MTU ... would corrupt the image', the Mac agreed a packet size under 243; try again, or see the protocol section of `cc2340r5/oad/README.md`.

7. **Terminal (Mac).** Read the image header at 0x6000; the version is byte 20.

   ```text
   $DSLITE memory -c $CCXML -r 0x6000,0x8 -o $BK/hdr.bin && xxd $BK/hdr.bin
   ```

   You should see: Byte 20 reads 02 after the update and 01 before. The red LED should now toggle four times a second (not watched on the recorded run).

   If it still reads 01, MCUboot did not install the image; it refuses an image that is not newer than the running one.

8. **Terminal (Mac).** The same chip erase clears the flash first, then the backup is written.

   ```text
   $DSLITE flash -c $CCXML -e -f -u $BK/restore.hex
   ```

   You should see: The board is as it was before step 5.

   If it does not start, read `cc2340r5/FAQ.md` before writing again.

### Expected result

The client prints a clean transfer of 1,024 blocks with no retries, then the board resets and advertises `FRL OAD 2`, and the version read back is 2.0.0.

### What this shows

- A CC2340R5 can take a signed firmware update over Bluetooth from a Mac terminal: 31.4 s transfer, 7.8 s to the new name, one run.
- TI's dual-image example keeps your app running during the download; each slot is 236 kB and the app uses 192 kB.
- The image check (SHA-256 and signature) runs on the Mac before any radio is used.

### Limits

- A repeat: one run, one Mac.
- That the red LED toggles: the name, version and header say v2 runs, but the LED was not watched.
- A Zigbee update from Home Assistant: that did not finish (see the Zigbee version below).
- Wi-Fi: the CC2340R5 has none.
- TI documents OAD with a phone app or a Windows tool; the Mac terminal client is this repository's own, written from the SDK source.
- The dual-image layout halves the room for the app (236 kB per slot).
- Checked on one Intel Mac, macOS 15.7.9.

### Numbers and sources

| | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Speed | 61.5 kbit/s of image data: 236 kB in 31.4 s, ATT MTU 251 | `cc2340r5/oad/README.md` |
| Image | 236 kB sent, 18.5% of it 0xFF padding | `cc2340r5/oad/README.md` |

## Update a CC35X1 over Wi-Fi from a Mac

TI's ota_example downloads a signed image from an HTTPS server on the Mac. 8 s to install on the first run, one attempt.

Status: Works. Boards: cc35x1.

Folders this version uses (in a sparse clone, fetch them first, then read `cc35x1/AGENTS.md`):

```bash
git sparse-checkout add cc35x1 site tools
```

### Parts

| Part | Quantity | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| LP-EM-CC35X1 LaunchPad development kit | 1 | the board that gets updated |

### Before you start

- A Mac and the board on the same Wi-Fi network. SimpleLink Wi-Fi SDK 10.20.00.39, Wi-Fi Toolbox 4.3.23, SysConfig 1.28.0, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS, and Node.js for the driver.
- The chip must already be activated (a one-time step that burns a key into its fuses) and the Toolbox must work; see cc35x1/AGENTS.md before programming anything.
- The code is in this repository: `cc35x1/ota/` and `site/flash/cc35-ota.js`.

### Steps

1. **Terminal (Mac).** The script copies TI's `ota_example`, puts the version in its banner, builds it and signs it with the Toolbox. The default output folder is `out/cc35x1-ota`.

   ```text
   cc35x1/ota/build.sh 0.0.1.0
   ```

   You should see: It prints the build folder and lists `primary_vendor_image.sign.bin` and `tool_settings.json`.

   If it prints 'build failed' or 'signing failed', read the log it names. The SDK, Toolbox and compiler paths are at the top of `build.sh`.

2. **Terminal (Mac).** This puts the example on the two-slot flash layout the update needs. Use absolute paths inside `tool_settings.json`. The Toolbox does not reset the board afterward.

   ```text
   cd /Applications/ti/simplelink_wifi_toolbox_macos_4_3_23 && ./simplelink-wifi-toolbox programmer -i XDS110 -param1 <probe serial> programming --tool_settings <absolute path to out/cc35x1-ota/v0.0.1.0/freertos/ticlang/toolbox/tool_settings.json>
   xds110reset -s <probe serial>
   ```

   You should see: After the reset, the serial port (115200) shows `CC35xx OTA Example Application FRL 0.0.1.0`.

   If the Toolbox refuses, the chip may not be activated; stop and follow cc35x1/AGENTS.md. This chip cannot be read back, so keep the signed bundle of the image it ran before.

3. **Terminal (Mac).** The server lists a file as new only when its header version is higher than the running one. Copy the signed file into a folder under the name the server expects, with TI's server script beside it.

   ```text
   cc35x1/ota/build.sh 0.0.2.0
   ```

   You should see: The same listing, this time under `v0.0.2.0`. Copy its `primary_vendor_image.sign.bin` to `vendor_image_0.0.2.0.bin` in a new folder.

   If the server later shows nothing as NEW, check the version is higher and the file is named `vendor_image_<version>.bin`.

4. **Terminal (Mac).** Use TI's own server and playground certificates from the Wi-Fi SDK's `tools/ota_https_server/` folder (copy the folder, or run it in place). With Python 3, run its `ota_server.py` with `--dir <your folder>` from step 3. Find your Mac's Wi-Fi address.

   You should see: The server listens on port 8443 of your Mac's Wi-Fi address.

   If the board cannot reach it later (`Server query failed (HTTPS: -11 ...)`), check the address and that the Mac and board are on the same network.

5. **Terminal (Mac).** The bridge relays the probe's serial port to a local TCP port. Run it under the lab's port lock.

   ```text
   python3 tools/frl/lock.py exec --serial <probe serial> -- python3 cc35x1/ota/bridge.py /dev/cu.usbmodem<probe serial>1 7701 &
   ```

   You should see: The command returns to the prompt with the bridge running in the background.

   If the port is busy, close any serial monitor that has it open.

6. **Terminal (Mac).** The driver walks the example's menu: scan, join your network, query the server, download, install, reboot into the trial image, then keep or go back. Your Wi-Fi name and password come from the environment only. Use `--end keep` to accept the new image or `--end revert` to go back.

   ```text
   FRL_WIFI_SSID=<network name> FRL_WIFI_PASSWORD=<password> node cc35x1/ota/drive.mjs --server https://<Mac Wi-Fi address>:8443 --end keep
   ```

   You should see: Lines for each phase ending '== download', '== install', '== reboot into trial' and 'after: 0.0.2.0'. In the 2026-10-22 runs: join 2.2 to 2.7 s, download 3.6 s, install under 0.1 s, restart 3.1 s.

   If the menu says 'Invalid input', the driver sent a line feed; answers end with a carriage return only. If a slot shows FAILED the board erases it first (download took 20.5 s).

### Expected result

The driver prints each phase with its time, the board reboots into version 0.0.2.0, and the slot table after shows the new version active.

### What this shows

- A CC35X1 downloads, verifies, installs and boots a new signed image over Wi-Fi from a Mac server: install and reboot in 8 s on the 2026-10-09 attempt.
- A reset without accepting rolls the board back to the OTA app, as TI documents.
- Four rounds on 2026-10-22 (update, go back, update and keep, update into the other slot) all ended as expected.

### Limits

- A repeat of the 8 s figure: it is one attempt with a 27.7 kB image.
- Updates from Home Assistant or the internet: the server was a Mac on the home network.
- Safety against power loss mid-update: not tested.
- The chip must be activated first, which burns fuses and cannot be undone.
- The chip cannot be read back, so a restore needs a saved signed bundle.
- Checked on one Intel Mac and one board.

### Numbers and sources

| | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Install | download about 1 s, install and reboot 8 s, 27.7 kB image, one attempt | `data/results/cc35x1.csv` |
| Phases (1.29 MB image) | scan 1.9 s, join 2.2 to 2.7 s, download 3.6 s, restart 3.1 s | `cc35x1/AGENTS.md` |

# Post-quantum key exchange on a LaunchPad

A TI board and a Mac agree on a secret key with ML-KEM-768, a method meant to stay safe against quantum computers, then swap one encrypted line. The same code also runs on four more boards.

The page: [site/project-post-quantum.html](../../site/project-post-quantum.html). This file is its text. Terms: [vocabulary](../vocab.md).

<!-- generated from site/data/projects.json by tools/render_build_md.py; edit the data, not this file -->

## The key exchange with a Mac on the LP-CC1354P10-1

Host test, build, then load the board and watch the exchange over USB serial.

Status: Works. Boards: cc1354p10.

Folders this version uses (in a sparse clone, fetch them first, then read `cc1354p10/AGENTS.md`):

```bash
git sparse-checkout add cc1354p10 portability/pqc-join third-party tools mac-setup
```

### Parts

| Part | Quantity | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| LP-CC1354P10-1 LaunchPad development kit | 1 | makes the key pair and finishes the key |

### Before you start

- A Mac with CCStudio 21.0.1, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS, the SimpleLink CC13xx/CC26xx SDK 8.33.00.16 and OpenSSL 3.5 or later (`mac-setup/README.md`). The host test also needs Python with the `cryptography` package.
- The code: `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git`, then `git sparse-checkout add cc1354p10 portability/pqc-join third-party tools mac-setup`.
- This board's debugger connects only just after power-on, so loading needs a USB hub port the Mac can switch with `uhubctl` (`cc1354p10/FAQ.md`).
- The run script backs up the board's 1 MB of flash first and writes it back at the end; it prints `READBACK MATCHES BACKUP` when the board is as it was.

### Steps

1. **Mac, terminal.** Build the board code for the Mac, run both sets of known-answer tests and the whole exchange against the Mac side. No board is needed.

   ```text
   portability/pqc-join/test/run.sh
   ```

   You should see: The last line is `pqc-join host test: OK`.

   If it stops on the OpenSSL version, install OpenSSL 3.5 or later and put it first on your path.

2. **Mac, terminal.** Build at -O3, the timed build. It touches no hardware and takes about 20 seconds once SysConfig has run.

   ```text
   cc1354p10/pqc-join/build.sh -O3
   ```

   You should see: The script ends with the path of the `.out` image.

   If SysConfig is not found, install it as `mac-setup/README.md` says and run the line again.

3. **Mac, terminal.** Set `UHUB` to your hub and port, and `RESTORE_IMG` to the `.out` you want left on the board afterwards. The run takes about two and a half minutes: 22 s to back up the flash, 18 s on the board, then restore and read-back.

   ```text
   UHUB=<your hub>:<port> RESTORE_IMG=<path to the .out to leave running> cc1354p10/pqc-join/run.sh -O3
   ```

   You should see: The console shows `board> KAT PASS`, then `key check  Mac d01a2f61  board d01a2f61  MATCH`, then `board> DECRYPTED (76 bytes, tag ok)` and the Mac's line. The script ends with `READBACK MATCHES BACKUP`.

   If the exchange stops at `join: making an ML-KEM-768 key pair`, the image did not start the random generator; build from this repository's `pqc_board.c`, which calls `TRNG_init()` before `TRNG_open()`.

### Expected result

The board and the Mac end with the same 4-byte key check and the board prints the decrypted line.

### What this shows

- ML-KEM-768 takes 20.8, 24.0 and 29.1 ms on a 48 MHz Cortex-M33; ML-DSA-44 verifies in 50.5 ms and signs in 154 ms on average.
- The board's own work in the exchange is about 73 ms; the wire at 115,200 baud takes about 420 ms.
- The same portable C, unmodified mlkem-native 2.0.0 and mldsa-native 2.0.0, runs on four more boards (the other rows below).

### Limits

- The exchange with a Mac ran on this board only. On the other four boards the algorithms ran and passed their vectors; no exchange was run.
- No protection against power or fault attacks is claimed. This is a demonstration of the math and its cost. Do not use it for real keys.
- Signing needs 50 kB of stack, so a board needs about 64 kB of RAM for ML-DSA-44; the LP-MSPM0G5187 (32 kB) runs ML-KEM-768 only.
- Signing time varies from 77 to 361 ms with the message, because a candidate signature is sometimes thrown away and retried.

### Numbers and sources

| | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| ML-KEM-768 at 48 MHz | 997k / 1.15M / 1.4M cycles for key pair, encapsulate, decapsulate | `data/results/cc1354p10.csv` |
| ML-DSA-44 at 48 MHz | 2.37M cycles key pair, 2,421,949 verify, 7,406,767 mean sign over 16 messages | `data/results/cc1354p10.csv` |
| Flash | ML-KEM 82.4 kB and ML-DSA 109 kB at -O3; 9.7 kB and 13.6 kB at -Os | `data/results/cc1354p10.csv` |

# Print a message from the chip to your Mac

Flash TI's console example and read its text in a terminal on your computer, over the board's own USB cable. No extra wire.

The page: [site/project-print-a-message.html](../../site/project-print-a-message.html). This file is its text. Terms: [vocabulary](../vocab.md).

## TI's console example on the LP-MSPM0L1306

Copy TI's UART console example, build it, flash it, and read its text in a terminal on the Mac.

Status: Works. Boards: l1306.

Folders this version uses (in a sparse clone, fetch them first, then read `mspm0l1306/AGENTS.md`):

```bash
git sparse-checkout add mspm0l1306 mspm0g3507/mcu-bench/sdk-common tools/frl
```

### Parts

| Part | Quantity | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| LP-MSPM0L1306 LaunchPad development kit | 1 | the board |
| Micro-USB data cable | 1 | power, programming and the serial text |

### Before you start

- A Mac with CCStudio 21.0.1 (1.9 GB download, 8.1 GB installed), the MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07 (0.4 GB, 2.2 GB installed), SysConfig 1.26.3 (0.96 GB installed) and xPack OpenOCD 0.12.0-7 (2 MB). Links are in step 1. Checked on an Intel MacBook on macOS 15.7.9 only.
- The code is in this repository. Clone it with `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git` and fetch the folders listed for this version. This page calls the folder you clone it into `<repository folder>`. It holds the helper scripts. About 12 GB free for the tools.

### Steps

1. **Mac, terminal.** Install the tools once, all free. Get CCStudio 21.0.1 from [TI's CCStudio download page](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/CCSTUDIO) (1.9 GB download, 8.1 GB installed, free myTI login). It brings TI Arm Clang 5.1.1. Get the MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07 from [TI's MSPM0 SDK download page](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/MSPM0-SDK) (0.4 GB download, 2.2 GB installed). Get SysConfig 1.26.3 ([TI's SysConfig page](https://www.ti.com/tool/download/SYSCONFIG), 0.96 GB installed). Get xPack OpenOCD 0.12.0-7 from [its GitHub release page](https://github.com/xpack-dev-tools/openocd-xpack/releases/tag/v0.12.0-7) (2 MB; the file `xpack-openocd-0.12.0-7-darwin-x64.tar.gz` on an Intel Mac, `xpack-openocd-0.12.0-7-darwin-arm64.tar.gz` on Apple Silicon). Then clone this repository into `<repository folder>`. The helper scripts `sdkmake.sh` and `tools/ocd.sh` are in it. This repo's scripts point at SysConfig 1.26.3. It came with the SimpleLink Wi-Fi SDK installer on the test Mac and sits in `/Applications/ti/sysconfig_1.26.3`. CCStudio 21.0.1 carries its own 1.28.1. This repo's scripts do not point at it.

   You should see: `/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/tools/compiler/ti-cgt-armllvm_5.1.1.LTS/bin/tiarmclang --version` prints 5.1.1.

   If your tools live somewhere other than `/Applications/ti`, edit the paths at the top of `mspm0g3507/mcu-bench/sdk-common/sdkmake.sh`.

2. **Bench.** Leave the jumpers as the board shipped: J16 and J17 on the XDS side, the right-hand position, which carries the chip's UART to the USB cable. Plug the board into the Mac with a micro-USB data cable. Find the probe's serial number: the port names are `/dev/cu.usbmodem<serial>1` and `...4`.

   ```text
   ls /dev/cu.usbmodem*
   ```

   You should see: Two ports. The one ending in 1 is the chip's UART0 at 115200 8N1; the one ending in 4 is not used here. With probe serial <probe serial>, the port is `/dev/cu.usbmodem<probe serial>1`. Or read the serial with `/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/ccs_base/common/uscif/xds110/xdsdfu -e`.

   If no ports appear, try another cable; a charge-only cable looks the same. If you moved J16 and J17 to BP for a loop-back test, move them back to XDS or the serial window stays silent.

3. **Terminal.** Copy TI's console example out of the SDK, from the `mspm0l1306` folder of this repository, and build it.

   ```text
   cd <repository folder>/mspm0l1306
   cp -R /Applications/ti/mspm0_sdk_2_11_00_07/examples/nortos/LP_MSPM0L1306/driverlib/uart_tx_console_multibyte_repeated_fifo_dma .
   ../mspm0g3507/mcu-bench/sdk-common/sdkmake.sh uart_tx_console_multibyte_repeated_fifo_dma/ticlang
   ```

   You should see: A build with no errors that leaves `uart_tx_console_multibyte_repeated_fifo_dma/ticlang/uart_tx_console_multibyte_repeated_fifo_dma.out`.

   If the make line cannot find SysConfig or the compiler, the paths in step 1's `sdkmake.sh` do not match your install.

4. **Terminal.** Flash it with OpenOCD. `tools/ocd.sh` picks the probe by serial number and refuses to run if it is missing; set `PROBE` to your serial first (`<probe serial>` below stands for it). To find yours, run `/Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/ccs_base/common/uscif/xds110/xdsdfu -e` if you have CCStudio (it prints `Serial Num:`), else `system_profiler SPUSBDataType | grep -A3 XDS110`. Run it from the same folder as the build step.

   ```text
   export PROBE=<probe serial>
   tools/ocd.sh "reset halt" "program uart_tx_console_multibyte_repeated_fifo_dma/ticlang/uart_tx_console_multibyte_repeated_fifo_dma.out verify" "reset run"
   ```

   You should see: OpenOCD ends with `** Verified OK **` after about 2 s. In the sweep this example flashed in 2.3 s.

   OpenOCD prints `Error: checksum mismatch - attempting binary compare` first; that is normal, and the line after it is the real result.

5. **Terminal.** Open the chip's serial port. To leave `screen`, press Ctrl-A then K. This step is assembled, not recorded: the sweep read the port with a script, and this example's port was read by a script, not opened in `screen`.

   ```text
   screen /dev/cu.usbmodem<probe serial>1 115200
   ```

   You should see: The line `==== MSPM0 Console Test ====` appears on your Mac, sent by the chip. TI's README says the example writes to the console once a second.

   If the window stays empty, check the port ends in 1 and the baud is 115200.

### Expected result

A line of text from the chip appears in a terminal window on your Mac every time the example sends it, at 115200 baud, with no extra wires.

### What this shows

- The LP-MSPM0L1306 sends text to a terminal on the Mac over the board's own USB cable, using TI's unmodified example.
- The same example printed readable text on the LP-MSPM0G3507 in the example sweep.

### Limits

- That text typed on the Mac reaches the chip: this example only transmits. The one-wire loop-back tests check both directions and are separate demos. They use J4 pin 34 to pin 33 on the G3507 and J1 pin 4 to pin 3 on the L1306.
- That `screen` shows the text as the sweep script did: the sweep read the port with a script, and `screen` is the method this repository's LVGL demo uses. The two were not compared with this example.
- A speed or reliability figure: the loop-back demos give those: every byte right from 9.6 kbaud to 4.5 Mbaud.
- The route is written for the LP-MSPM0L1306. The G3507 has its own flash command and probe file, and was not run by hand in this form.
- TI's example needs the board's shipped jumper settings; the loop-back tests move J16 and J17 and the serial window goes silent until they are put back.

### Numbers and sources

| | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Example | TI's uart_tx_console_multibyte_repeated_fifo_dma for LP_MSPM0L1306: UART0 on PA8 (TX) and PA9 (RX) through the DMA, timer-driven; verdict running, 195 bytes read, flash 2.3 s, in the sweep |  |
| Serial settings | UART0, 115200 8N1, on the probe port whose name ends in 1 | `mspm0l1306/FAQ.md` |
| Tools | MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS, xPack OpenOCD 0.12.0-7, Intel Mac on macOS 15.7.9 | `mspm0l1306/README.md` |


# Room presence with a 60 GHz radar

TI's IWRL6432BOOST streams presence and range frames over USB with no setup. A short script reads them and a timed test scores detection, delay and false alarms.

The page: [site/project-radar-presence.html](../../site/project-radar-presence.html). This file is its text. Terms: [vocabulary](../vocab.md).

<!-- generated from site/data/projects.json by tools/render_build_md.py; edit the data, not this file -->

## TI's Motion and Presence demo, read and timed

The IWRL6432BOOST as shipped, a USB cable, a Mac, and a person to walk and sit.

Status: Works. Boards: iwrl6432boost.

Folders this version uses (in a sparse clone, fetch them first, then read `iwrl6432boost/AGENTS.md`):

```bash
git sparse-checkout add iwrl6432boost tools
```

### Parts

| Part | Quantity | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| IWRL6432BOOST 60 GHz mmWave radar evaluation module | 1 | the radar board |
| Micro-USB B cable, a stand and a tape measure | 1 | power and data; the stand and tape for the timed test |

### Before you start

- A Mac with Python 3 and pyserial. No TI tools are needed to read the shipped stream. The timed test speaks its cues with macOS `say`.
- The code is in this repository. Clone it with `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git` and fetch the folders listed for this version.
- Keep 20 cm between the board and a person while it transmits.

### Steps

1. **Bench.** Plug the board's micro-USB port (J5) into the computer. Leave the switches as shipped. Keep 20 cm between the board and a person while it transmits (TI's board guide).

   You should see: Lights D6 (5 V) and D3 (power good) come on; the antenna side faces the room.

   No lights: try another cable; the port is micro-USB B.

2. **Terminal (Mac).** The board adds two serial ports; the one ending in 1 carries the data.

   ```text
   ls /dev/cu.usbmodem*
   ```

   You should see: Two ports, one ending in `1` and one in `4`.

   No ports listed: check the cable is a data cable and the board is powered.

3. **Terminal (Mac).** Make a venv with pyserial, then capture 15 s at 115,200 baud from the port ending in 1 into a file with any serial tool.

   ```text
   python3 -m venv ~/radar-venv && ~/radar-venv/bin/pip install pyserial
   ```

   You should see: A capture file of about 6 kB (4 frames a second, 384 bytes each).

   An empty file: check that you read the port ending in 1, then press the board's reset button (S2) and capture again.

4. **Terminal (Mac).** The parser prints one line per frame. Test it without a board first with `--selftest`.

   ```text
   python3 iwrl6432boost/tools/tlv_parse.py capture.bin
   ```

   You should see: Frame number, bytes, detected objects and the block types; presence blocks are type 315 and range profiles 303.

   The self test fails: you are not at the top of the repository.

5. **Terminal (Mac).** Open `iwrl6432boost/eval/radar_link.py` and set `PORT` and `CFG` (written for this bench's folders) to your port and configuration folder. Then apply each setting and check the stream.

   ```text
   python3 iwrl6432boost/eval/radar_eval.py accept
   ```

   You should see: The board's answer to every configuration line, then a stream check for 1x1 (refused with error -40107), 2x2 and 2x3.

   The demo ignores its command line until one press of the board's reset button (S2) after power-up.

6. **Terminal (Mac) and the room.** Put the board on a stand at about 1.5 m, antenna toward the room, a tape line out from it, and two chairs at 2 m and 4 m. Leave the room for the empty run, then run the cued walk-in and seated passes; Enter in the terminal confirms that the person is in place, and the tool speaks the cues.

   ```text
   python3 iwrl6432boost/eval/radar_eval.py empty --seconds 60
   python3 iwrl6432boost/eval/radar_eval.py run --passes walk,sit2,sit4
   ```

   You should see: A results file per setting in `iwrl6432boost/eval/results/`: flags in the empty room, detect delay after the cue, hold while seated, and the distance at first flag on the walk-in.

   Put the shipped configuration back afterwards with `restore`.

7. **Terminal (Mac).** Restore the shipped configuration.

   ```text
   python3 iwrl6432boost/eval/radar_eval.py restore
   ```

   You should see: The board prints the shipped lines again and streams at about 4 frames a second.

   Press reset (S2) if it does not answer.

### Expected result

The board streams presence and range frames about four times a second. In the timed test a seated person at 2 m and 4 m is held as present on 2x2 and 2x3 (100 percent of frames, one pass each).

### What this shows

- A person sitting still at 2 m and 4 m was held in 100 percent of frames on 2x2 and 2x3. An arrival was flagged 4.7 to 6.2 s after the cue, which includes the person's reaction and walk. With a modified configuration (PresenceDetect-hold12.cfg) the empty room gave 0 flags in 6.08 h, until a flag whose cause was not checked.
- A short Python parser reads the frames, and the timed test needs no change to the board's firmware.

### Limits

- How many people are in the room: the demo reports four floor zones on or off.
- Anything past 4 m seated or about 7 m walking: not tested.
- Your room: glass, metal shelving and fans change the result. One room, one afternoon, one pass per cell, so no spread.
- Power use: the demo does not report it and no measurement was made.
- The steps are from the 2026-10-09 and 2026-10-10 runs.
- The tool's serial port and configuration paths are written for this bench (`PORT`, `CFG` in `radar_link.py`).
- Checked on one Intel Mac only.

### Numbers and sources

| | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Frame rate | 4.00 a second as shipped; 3.85 a second with the evaluation setting | `iwrl6432boost/README.md` |
| Range bin | 0.121 m (derived from the settings, not checked against a measured distance) | `docs/guides/evaluate-a-presence-radar.md` |
| Chip | IWRL6432, 2 transmit and 3 receive channels, 57 to 64 GHz; Cortex-M4F core | `iwrl6432boost/README.md` |

# How fast a microcontroller reacts to an interrupt

Count the CPU cycles from an interrupt to the first line of its handler, on the LP-MSPM0L1306 with no wiring, or on the LP-EM-CC2340R5.

The page: [site/project-reaction-time.html](../../site/project-reaction-time.html). This file is its text. Terms: [vocabulary](../vocab.md).

<!-- generated from site/data/projects.json by tools/render_build_md.py; edit the data, not this file -->

## Measure it on the LP-MSPM0L1306

Build and run the timing program; read the answer from the chip's RAM. No wires.

Status: Works. Boards: l1306.

Folders this version uses (in a sparse clone, fetch them first, then read `mspm0l1306/AGENTS.md`):

```bash
git sparse-checkout add mspm0l1306 mspm0g3507/zephyr
```

### Parts

| Part | Quantity | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| LP-MSPM0L1306 LaunchPad development kit | 1 | the board |
| Micro-USB data cable | 1 | power and programming |

### Before you start

- An Intel Mac, macOS 15.7.9.
- CCStudio 21.0.1, which brings TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS, and MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07. They sit at the paths set on the first lines of `bench/timing/build.sh`; change them there if yours differ.
- xPack OpenOCD 0.12.0-7 and the Arm `nm` tool from the Zephyr SDK 0.17.4 compiler, in `~/zephyr-toolchain`. Running `NO_FLASH=1 ./setup-intel-mac.sh` in `mspm0g3507/zephyr` installs both without flashing anything. It also sets up a Zephyr checkout and virtual environment that this project does not use, so it takes a few minutes and some disk.
- The code is in this repository. Clone it with `git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/Fox-Red-Labs/fox-red-labs.git` and fetch the folders listed for this version. This page calls the folder you clone it into `<repository folder>`. Take the board folder alone with the sparse-checkout line in its README, or clone the whole repository.
- The board ships with TI's out-of-box demo. Save it first with `python3 tools/frl/frl.py backup --board mspm0l1306 --probe <serial>`, and put it back afterwards with `python3 tools/frl/frl.py restore "<backup folder>" --probe <serial>`.

### Steps

1. **Mac, terminal.** Find your board's debug probe serial number with TI's `xdsdfu` tool from CCStudio. The scripts talk to one probe only.

   ```text
   /Applications/ti/ccs2101/ccs/ccs_base/common/uscif/xds110/xdsdfu -e
   ```

   You should see: A line `Serial Num: <your serial>` for the LaunchPad.

   If nothing is listed, replug the board with a data cable and close any serial window open on it.

2. **Bench.** Plug the LP-MSPM0L1306 into the Mac with the micro-USB cable. No wires and no jumpers move.

   You should see: The board powers up and shows its out-of-box demo.

   If a script later says `Probe ... missing`, the serial number in step 1 does not match a connected board.

3. **Mac, terminal.** Build the timing program at -O3. It sets the CPU to 32 MHz, times loops and a GPIO toggle, then pends a spare interrupt, I2C1 on line 25, and reads SysTick on the handler's first line.

   ```text
   cd mspm0l1306/bench/timing
   ./build.sh O3
   ```

   You should see: `build-O3/timing.out` and `timing.map` exist.

   If the compiler is not found, change the `SDK` and `CC` lines at the top of `build.sh`.

4. **Mac, terminal.** Flash it, let it run 1.5 seconds, halt it and read the 11-word result struct from RAM. Replace <serial> with your probe.

   ```text
   PROBE=<serial> ./run.sh O3
   ```

   You should see: `** Verified OK **`, then two lines of RAM words. The first word is 7141e001, which means the program finished. The second word, 01e84800, is the CPU clock: 32,000,000 Hz. On the second line the first word is the best interrupt time in cycles and the second is the worst: `00000019 00000019`, which is 25 and 25. The third is the sample count, `000000c8`, which is 200.

   If `Verified OK` does not appear, the flash failed: check the serial from step 1. If the first word is not 7141e001, the program did not finish; run it again.

5. **Mac, terminal.** Optional: repeat at -O2 and -Os to see that the compiler setting changes the answer.

   ```text
   ./build.sh O2
   PROBE=<serial> ./run.sh O2
   ./build.sh Os
   PROBE=<serial> ./run.sh Os
   ```

   You should see: -O2 reads `0000001c 0000001c`, which is 28 cycles. -Os reads `00000019 00000019`, which is 25 cycles.

   A number that differs by a few cycles is worth rerunning twice. Every saved run gave the same count on all 200 tries.

### Expected result

The chip answers an interrupt in 25 cycles at -O3, the same on all 200 tries: about 0.8 microseconds at 32 MHz. At -O2 it is 28 cycles.

### What this shows

- On an LP-MSPM0L1306 with no operating system, the time from raising an interrupt to the first line of its handler is 25 cycles at -Os and -O3 and 28 at -O2. It was the same on every one of 200 tries, so there is no jitter at this resolution.
- The same program shows what the operating system adds. Through Zephyr the same measurement reads 119 to 137 cycles, and under FreeRTOS 38 to 39. See the Zephyr and FreeRTOS projects.
- A GPIO toggle is one register write at 1.00 cycles at -O2 and -O3. It was not checked with a scope.

### Limits

- Reaction time to an outside signal. The interrupt is raised in software by writing the pending bit, so the pin, input filter and any peripheral that would raise the interrupt are not in the number.
- A like-for-like number across chips. Each count includes one SysTick read, and a read pair costs 2 cycles. The timers, clocks and flash wait states differ per board.
- How long it takes a handler to do useful work: the number stops at the handler's first line.
- Pin speed. The one-cycle toggle is the CPU side only; no scope was on the bench.
- Interrupt line 25 (I2C1) is used because this chip's interrupt controller has only the 13 lines that have a peripheral; the program does not use I2C1 otherwise.
- The count includes one SysTick read of 2 cycles and the store that pends the interrupt.
- -O2 is 3 cycles slower than -Os and -O3 on interrupt entry. Why was not investigated.

### Numbers and sources

| | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Clock | 32 MHz SYSOSC; cycle counter is SysTick on the CPU clock (the Cortex-M0+ has no DWT counter) | `mspm0l1306/bench/timing/main.c` |
| Interrupt entry, pend to handler | 25 / 25 (-Os), 28 / 28 (-O2), 25 / 25 (-O3) cycles best / worst of 200 |  |
| GPIO toggle | 1.12 (-Os), 1.00 (-O2, -O3) cycles for one register write; 1.05 cycles per pass of a driver-call loop at -O2 and -O3 (13.00 at -Os) |  |
| Other chips, same method | LP-MSPM0G3507 at 80 MHz: 29 to 36 cycles; LP-EM-CC2340R5 at 48 MHz: 28 to 29; LAUNCHXL-F2800137 at 120 MHz: 30 (code in RAM) to 32 (from flash) | `data/results/mspm0g3507.csv` |
| Tools | TI Arm Clang 5.1.1.LTS, MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07, xPack OpenOCD 0.12.0-7, checked 2026-10-06 |  |

- Your probe's serial number (`xdsdfu -e`). Put yours in `cc2340r5/CC2340R5.ccxml` and in the `SERIAL_DEV` name, `/dev/cu.usbmodem<serial>1`. Then set the `CCXML` line near the top of `run.sh` to where your copy of the repository is.

### Steps

1. **Bench.** Clip the LP-XDS110ET onto the LP-EM-CC2340R5's 20-pin edge, set the TGT VDD jumper to XDS, and plug the probe into the Mac with its USB-C cable.

   You should see: The Mac sees the probe and two serial ports. The second one is `/dev/cu.usbmodem<serial>1`.

   If a flash later fails with `The target failed to see a correctly formatted SWD header` (error -615), unplug the USB cable, pull the probe off the board, press it back on and plug in again. That cleared it here. The likely cause is the seating.

2. **Mac, terminal.** Build and check without touching the hardware. The script also refuses to flash unless the generated boot configuration keeps the debug port, chip erase, flash program and return to factory all allowed.

   ```text
   cd cc2340r5/baremetal
   ./run.sh O3 --build-only
   ```

   You should see: A memory summary and `CCFG OK: debug port, chip erase, flash program and return to factory all allowed.` The -O3 image is 36.8 kB of flash.

   If the build fails, the last 30 lines of the build log print; a tool path in `run.sh` is the usual cause.

3. **Mac, terminal.** Build, flash with UniFlash and capture the serial report. The script opens the serial port first, then flashes with `dslite.sh --mode flash ... -e -f -u build-O3/bench.hex`, and stops capturing at `BENCH DONE` or after 300 seconds. The run includes CoreMark, so it takes a while.

   ```text
   ./run.sh O3
   ```

   You should see: The report scrolls by, ending in `BENCH DONE`. It is saved to `results/run-O3.txt`. It contains `R,irq_latency_best,29.00,1,...` and `R,irq_latency_worst_of_200,29.00,1,...` and `I,irq_samples,200`.

   If it says the serial port is not present, the board is not plugged in or `SERIAL_DEV` has the wrong serial. Do not add `-v` (verify) to the flash command: it reports a mismatch in the boot configuration area although the program ran.

4. **Mac, terminal.** Optional: run the -Oz build too.

   ```text
   ./run.sh Oz
   ```

   You should see: `R,irq_latency_best,28.00,1,...`, the same 28 for the worst of 200.

   The old program on the board repeats its report every 10 seconds, so make sure the capture holds this build's own `I,optimization` line before you trust a file.

### Expected result

The chip answers an interrupt in 29 cycles at -O3 and 28 at -Oz, about 0.6 microseconds at 48 MHz. It is the same on all 200 tries.

### What this shows

- On an LP-EM-CC2340R5 with no operating system, the time from raising an interrupt to the first line of its handler is 29 cycles at -O3 and 28 at -Oz. It is the same on all 200 tries.
- Through Zephyr on the same chip the same measurement reads 48 to 60 cycles.

### Limits

- Reaction time to an outside signal. The interrupt is pended through the NVIC by software, so no pin or peripheral is in the number.
- A like-for-like number across chips: each count includes one SysTick read, 5 cycles here. The timers, clocks and flash wait states differ per board.
- Run-to-run spread over many boards or sessions: each build was run once on one board.
- The interrupt is the radio block's line, LRFD IRQ0 on line 6. It matches the one the Zephyr run used. The handler is a direct vector installed with `HwiP_plug`, with no wrapper.
- The clock was read back as 48 MHz and a 0.3-second host-timed check gave 48.02 and 48.07 MHz.
- Verify (`-v`) reports a mismatch at 0x4E020750 on every image flashed on this board; the program area verified and the program ran each time.

### Numbers and sources

| | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Interrupt entry, pend to handler | 29 cycles at -O3 and 28 at -Oz, best and worst of 200 identical; includes one 5-cycle SysTick read | `cc2340r5/baremetal/README.md` |
| Through Zephyr | 48 best, 60 worst of 200; includes a 9-cycle timer read quantized to 12 cycles | `data/results/cc2340r5.csv` |
| Under FreeRTOS | 39 cycles, with one run at 202 when an interrupt met the 1 ms tick; includes one counter read | `data/results/cc2340r5.csv` |
| Clock and flash | 48 MHz; flash wait states read live as 2 (1T) and 2 (2T); cache, prefetch and micropredictor on | `cc2340r5/baremetal/README.md` |
| Tools | F3 SDK 9.21.00.36, SysConfig 1.26.3, UniFlash 9.6.0, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1; macOS 15.7.9 | `cc2340r5/baremetal/README.md` |
